topic: HMAC verification of a Connect message
stem: A listener framework parses each incoming Connect JSON body into an object, and the code then re-serializes that object and computes HMAC-SHA256 with the shared secret, but the comparison against X-DocuSign-Signature-1 fails for many genuine messages. What should the developer change?

options.text: Compute the HMAC-SHA256 hash over the raw request body exactly as received, before any parsing
Compare the computed hash against the Authorization header instead of X-DocuSign-Signature-1
Verify the signature with Docusign's public X.509 certificate instead of the shared secret
Compute the hash only over the envelopeId value so formatting differences no longer matter

answerText: Compute the HMAC-SHA256 hash over the raw request body exactly as received, before any parsing
explanation: Docusign hashes the message body (including line ends) with each HMAC key; re-serializing changes whitespace and key order, so the hash must be recomputed over the raw body bytes as received.
whyNotOthers: A is right because the HMAC is computed over the exact message body, so any re-serialization breaks the match. The trap is C: Connect can also sign with an X.509 certificate, but HMAC is a symmetric scheme verified with the shared secret, not a public certificate. B fails because the Authorization header carries an OAuth for Connect bearer token, not the HMAC; D fails because the signature covers the whole body, not one field.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. The X-DocuSign-Signature-N value is the HMAC-SHA256 of the whole message body as sent, so the listener must hash the raw, unparsed body with the same secret and compare.
optionExplanations.B: The Authorization header holds a Bearer token when OAuth for Connect is enabled; the HMAC values are only in the X-DocuSign-Signature-N headers.
optionExplanations.C: HMAC is symmetric: only Docusign and your app hold the secret key. Public-certificate verification belongs to a different mechanism, not to HMAC.
optionExplanations.D: The HMAC covers the entire message body, so hashing a single field can never reproduce the header value.

concept.title: Connect HMAC: hash the raw body
concept.line: Compute HMAC-SHA256 with the shared secret over the raw body as received; re-serializing parsed JSON changes whitespace and key order.

stem: Marisol builds a claims workflow for Pinecrest Insurance: Collect Data with Web Forms, then Verify Someone's Identity, then Send Documents for Signature. After the claimant signs, the completed claim packet must be stored automatically in the company's Box folder, and the adjuster must also receive an email. The IT team has already set up a Connect listener for envelope events and suggests reusing it. When Marisol opens the step library, she cannot find any Box step. What must happen so she can add the storage step?

options.text: Add a Use eSignature API step that includes an eventNotification object pointing at a Box webhook
An admin installs and authorizes a Box extension app from the App Center, which then appears as a Store Files apps step
Install a Connected Fields extension for Box so the packet is pushed during the signing ceremony
Add a Send an Email step addressed to the Box folder's upload address after the signing step

answerText: An admin installs and authorizes a Box extension app from the App Center, which then appears as a Store Files apps step
explanation: Apps steps (Read, Store Files, Writeback) come from extension apps that an admin has installed and authorized for the account from the App Center; until a Box app is installed, no Box step appears.
whyNotOthers: B is right because the missing Box step is the clue: apps steps only appear for extension apps an admin has authorized. The trap is A: eventNotification sends envelope status webhooks, not documents to Box, and Connect is outbound notification, not storage. C fails because Connected Fields targets the eSignature Add Fields and signing extension points and is not supported in Maestro workflows; D is a notification step, not a file storage integration.

optionExplanations.A: Wrong. eventNotification configures envelope-level webhooks for status events; it does not archive files to cloud storage.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. Store Files apps steps (Box, Google Drive, Dropbox, OneDrive, SharePoint) come from extension apps an admin installs from the App Center.
optionExplanations.C: Wrong. Connected Fields verifies field data in eSignature; it is not supported in Maestro workflows and does not store files.
optionExplanations.D: Wrong. Send an Email is a utility notification step; it does not perform an authorized file store to Box.

concept.title: Apps steps need installed extension apps
concept.line: Maestro apps steps (Read, Store Files, Writeback) appear only after an admin installs and authorizes the extension app from the App Center.

decode.prompt: What is actually blocking Marisol?

options.text: Receive envelope status events in an external listener after signing
Notify the adjuster by email once the claim packet is complete
Make a third-party storage destination available as a workflow step, which depends on an account-level app install
Push documents to an external system while the signer is still in the signing ceremony

decode.explanation: The question is why no Box step exists in the step library; the Connect listener and the adjuster email are side details. Steps that store files only appear once an extension app is installed and authorized.
clues: 'cannot find any Box step' -> the step library lacks an apps step, so an extension app is missing
'stored automatically in the company's Box folder' -> a Store Files apps step in Maestro
'IT team has already set up a Connect listener' -> red herring, Connect only notifies
decode.needs: An admin-installed Box extension app so a Store Files apps step appears in Workflow Builder.

topic: Embedded web form instances: identify and prefill
stem: Meridian Health's HR portal will create 100 embedded web form instances, one for each new hire, from a single template-based web form configuration. The portal must map every instance one-to-one to the employee record in the HR database so it can later pull the submitted values back, and fields such as legal name and department must already be filled in when the employee opens the form. During design review the HR lead also asks whether the form could simply be shared as a public link to save effort. Which two choices meet the requirements? (Select two)

options.text: Create a separate web form configuration per employee so each configuration ID maps to one HR record.
Set clientUserId on each Instances:createInstance call to the employee's ID from the HR database.
Send a recipients array with a roleName in each createInstance call so each employee is identified by role.
Pass formValues keyed by the field names that Configurations:getForm returns for the configuration.
Share the public web form URL with query parameters appended for each employee's known values.

answerText: Set clientUserId on each Instances:createInstance call to the employee's ID from the HR database.; Pass formValues keyed by the field names that Configurations:getForm returns for the configuration.
explanation: Embedded instances require a clientUserId (up to 100 characters) that comes from your own system and ties the instance to one user, and prefill uses formValues whose keys are the field names from Configurations:getForm.
whyNotOthers: B and D are right because clientUserId is the per-user correlation key for embedded instances and formValues is the prefill mechanism. The trap is C: roleName in recipients differentiates users of remote instances, not embedded ones. A fails because one configuration serves all instances and configurations cannot be created through the API, and E drops the per-employee instance tracking the portal needs.

optionExplanations.A: The configuration ID is shared by all 100 instances, and web form configurations cannot be created through the API.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. clientUserId is required for embedded instances and should be an identifier from your own system.
optionExplanations.C: recipients with roleName identify users of remote (email) instances; embedded instances are identified by clientUserId.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. formValues prefills fields; its keys are the field (API reference) names returned by Configurations:getForm.
optionExplanations.E: A public link creates no tracked instance per employee, so values cannot be mapped back one-to-one.

concept.title: Embedded web form: clientUserId and prefill
concept.line: Embedded instances need clientUserId (up to 100 chars, from your system); prefill with formValues keyed by field names from Configurations:getForm.

decode.prompt: Which requirements decide the design here?

options.text: Make the form reachable by anyone with a link to minimize setup
Tie each embedded instance to one person using an identifier from the HR system, and pre-populate known fields when it opens
Create one reusable form definition per employee so each has its own configuration
Identify each employee by a signing role, as with envelope recipients

decode.explanation: 'map every instance one-to-one to the employee record' means a per-instance user identifier from your own system, and 'already be filled in' means prefill values keyed by the form's field names.
clues: 'embedded web form instances' -> each instance needs a clientUserId
'map one-to-one to the employee record' -> clientUserId set to the HR employee ID
'already be filled in' -> formValues keyed by field names from getForm
'public link' -> red herring, public forms cannot identify or prefill per employee
decode.needs: Embedded createInstance calls with clientUserId = employee ID and formValues for prefill.

stem: Brightwell Insurance's claims portal uses Confidential Authorization Code Grant. After an agent clicks Allow Access, Docusign redirects to the registered callback, and the handler logs the code and a state value that matches the one the portal generated. To smooth load, the handler puts the code on a message queue; a worker picks it up about four minutes later and POSTs to /oauth/token with grant_type=authorization_code and an Authorization: Basic header holding base64(integrationKey:secretKey). Every exchange fails under production traffic, yet the same worker succeeds in a test where the queue is empty. What is the most likely cause?

options.text: The authorization code is valid for only 120 seconds, so it expires while it waits in the queue
The state value must also be sent to /oauth/token, and the worker drops it from the queue message
The Basic header must encode secretKey:integrationKey, with the secret key placed first
The redirect URI is not registered, so Docusign issued a code that cannot be exchanged

answerText: The authorization code is valid for only 120 seconds, so it expires while it waits in the queue
explanation: An authorization code is valid for only 120 seconds (2 minutes); a code exchanged 'about four minutes later' has expired, while the empty-queue test exchanges it in time.
whyNotOthers: A is right because the deciding clue is the four-minute queue delay versus success when the queue is empty. The trap is B: state protects the redirect against CSRF and is checked at the callback, not sent to the token endpoint. C reverses the correct integrationKey:secretKey order, and D contradicts the stem, since the redirect reached the registered callback.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. The code expires after 120 seconds and must be exchanged right away.
optionExplanations.B: state is checked at the callback to prevent CSRF; it is not a token-request parameter.
optionExplanations.C: The Basic value is base64(integrationKey:secretKey); the stem's header is already correct.
optionExplanations.D: The redirect reached the registered callback and the empty-queue test works, so the URI is fine.

concept.title: Authorization code lives 120 seconds
concept.line: An authorization code is valid only 120 seconds (2 minutes); exchange it at /oauth/token immediately, not after queueing.

decode.prompt: What does the failure pattern point to?

options.text: Register the callback address before any code can be issued
Format the client credentials differently in the token request header
Exchange the authorization code within its short validity window, because the delay before exchange is the variable that changes
Carry the anti-forgery state value through to the token exchange

decode.explanation: The same worker succeeds when the queue is empty and fails only when the code waits about four minutes, so the time between issue and exchange is the cause.
clues: 'about four minutes later' -> code is exchanged after its 120-second lifetime
'succeeds in a test where the queue is empty' -> header and grant type are correct
'state value that matches' -> CSRF check already fine, irrelevant to the token call
decode.needs: Exchange the authorization code within 120 seconds of receiving it.

topic: Changes not allowed after an app is live
stem: Once an extension app has been published and is live, which change can the developer NOT make by updating the app registration?

options.text: Change the params.uri endpoint of an existing action
Replace the screenshots and long description of the App Center listing
Rotate the client secret stored in the connection's settings
Switch the distribution from PRIVATE to PUBLIC

answerText: Switch the distribution from PRIVATE to PUBLIC
explanation: After an extension app has been published to make it live, its distribution type (public or private) cannot be changed, and regions where it is currently available cannot be removed.
whyNotOthers: D is right because distribution type is locked once the app is live. The trap is A: changing an endpoint sounds risky, but updating registration details to follow changes in the API service is explicitly supported. B (listing content) and C (connection credentials) are also normal registration updates.

optionExplanations.A: Updating action endpoints is a supported registration update, for example when the API service changes.
optionExplanations.B: Listing text and images can be updated through the App Center Listing settings or the manifest.
optionExplanations.C: Connection settings such as client ID and client secret can be updated in the registration.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. After publishing, the distribution type cannot be changed (nor can regions where the app is available be removed).

concept.title: Locked after an app goes live
concept.line: Once an extension app is published live, its distribution type (public/private) cannot change and current regions cannot be removed.

topic: Message format required for Maestro workflow events
stem: Lumen Health built a Maestro workflow that collects patient intake data and ends in signing. Developer Marco Ruiz reused the clinic's existing account-level Connect configuration, which a contractor set up years ago in XML SIM format because a SOAP-based billing system parses it. Envelope events still reach the listener, HMAC validation passes, and retries are enabled, but no workflow-completed events ever arrive. Marco wants workflow events without breaking the billing parser. What is the correct fix?

options.text: Switch the existing configuration to XML aggregate mode so workflow events are bundled with envelope events
Create a separate configuration that uses the JSON SIM format and subscribes to the workflow events
Add an eventNotification object to the envelopes the workflow sends so the workflow events follow them
Enable HMAC on a second XML SIM configuration dedicated to the Maestro listener

answerText: Create a separate configuration that uses the JSON SIM format and subscribes to the workflow events
explanation: Maestro workflow events are delivered only in the JSON SIM message format. Because the billing system needs the XML feed, the clean fix is a separate JSON SIM configuration for the workflow events.
whyNotOthers: B is right because workflow events require JSON SIM, and a second configuration keeps the legacy XML feed intact for billing. The trap is D: HMAC and retries are already fine, and any XML configuration, secured or not, will never carry workflow events. A fails because aggregate is still XML; C fails because eventNotification only adds envelope-level events for a single envelope and does not produce workflow lifecycle events.

optionExplanations.A: Aggregate mode is an XML-only legacy option that combines envelope events; it does not make workflow events available.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. Workflow events are delivered only in JSON SIM format, so a dedicated JSON SIM configuration receives them while the XML feed keeps serving billing.
optionExplanations.C: eventNotification creates an envelope-level webhook for envelope and recipient events on that envelope; it does not deliver Maestro workflow events.
optionExplanations.D: Security is not the problem: HMAC was already passing. The format is XML, and workflow events require JSON SIM regardless of security settings.

concept.title: Maestro events need JSON SIM
concept.line: Maestro workflow events are delivered only in JSON SIM; keep an XML feed and add a separate JSON SIM configuration for workflow events.

decode.prompt: What does Marco really need?

options.text: Receive workflow events in the only message format that carries them, while leaving the legacy XML feed untouched
Attach workflow notifications to each envelope the workflow sends
Bundle workflow events together with envelope events in the existing feed
Secure the workflow feed with message signatures so it is delivered

decode.explanation: HMAC, retries and envelope delivery all work, so only the message format matters; Maestro events require JSON SIM and the billing parser still needs XML, so two configurations are needed.
clues: 'XML SIM format because a SOAP-based billing system parses it' -> existing config must stay XML
'no workflow-completed events ever arrive' -> workflow events are JSON SIM only
'HMAC validation passes, retries enabled' -> security and reliability are not the issue
decode.needs: A separate JSON SIM Connect configuration subscribed to Maestro workflow events.

topic: Composite templates: sequence and role mapping
stem: Tomas at Northwind HR sends one envelope per new hire containing a generated offer letter plus two server templates, Benefits and Tax Forms. Each server template defines a role named "employee" with its tabs. In each composite template object he adds the server template and an inline template that maps the new hire to roleName "employee". Envelopes are created, but the new hire receives the documents with none of the template tabs, and the inline recipient appears as an extra recipient with no fields. In his JSON every inline template has sequence 1 and every server template has sequence 2. What should Tomas change?

options.text: Move the inline recipients into a separate composite template object placed after the server template objects
Switch to the template reference model and list both template IDs with templateRoles for "employee"
Supply the offer letter with the inline template's documents property instead of the document property
Give each server template a lower sequence than the inline template in the same composite template object

answerText: Give each server template a lower sequence than the inline template in the same composite template object
explanation: Templates in a composite template object are applied in sequence order and, for attributes, later sequences overwrite earlier ones. The server template must have the lower sequence so the "employee" role exists before the inline template maps a recipient to it; the clue is inline = 1, server = 2.
whyNotOthers: D is right because the role must be established first. The trap is B: template reference is simpler, but it cannot combine multiple templates in one envelope. A fails because role mapping happens inside one composite template object, so a separate object would not bind to these roles. C is unrelated to tab mapping and goes against the best practice of using the composite document property.

optionExplanations.A: Role mapping happens within the same composite template object; a separate object would not attach the recipient to these roles.
optionExplanations.B: The template reference model cannot combine multiple templates (plus a generated document) in one envelope.
optionExplanations.C: Best practice is the composite object's document property; moving the document does not fix role mapping.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. Attributes apply in sequence order (last in wins), so the server template must come first to create the role.

concept.title: Composite templates: sequence order
concept.line: Templates apply in sequence order, later overwriting earlier; give the server template a lower sequence so its role exists before the inline template maps it.

decode.prompt: Which requirement decides the fix?

options.text: Change how the generated offer letter document is attached
Abandon composite templates in favor of simple template references
Separate recipients and server templates into different composite objects
Ensure the role defined by the server template exists before the inline template maps a person to it within the same composite object

decode.explanation: Templates in one composite object apply in sequence order, and the inline sequence 1 runs before server sequence 2, so the recipient is mapped to a role that does not exist yet and becomes an extra recipient.
clues: 'every inline template has sequence 1 and every server template has sequence 2' -> wrong application order
'none of the template tabs' -> roleName match failed
'inline recipient appears as an extra recipient' -> role not yet defined when mapped
decode.needs: Server template with a lower sequence than the inline template in each composite template object.

stem: Halvorsen Bank owns the integration key for an internal JWT Grant service that impersonates 300 relationship managers, all with addresses in halvorsenbank.com. The bank's Docusign organization has Access Management, and that domain is claimed. One colleague proposes emailing each manager a consent link; another found an ISV guide that builds an /oauth/auth URL with scope=openid and admin_consent_scope. The bank wants a single administrator action that covers every manager. What is the documented way to do this?

options.text: Send each manager the individual consent URL with scope=signature%20impersonation, as JWT accepts only individual consent
Open /oauth/auth with scope=openid and admin_consent_scope=signature%20impersonation, as described for external apps
Add impersonation to the JWT payload scope, which grants consent automatically for users in a claimed domain
In Docusign Admin, open Connected Apps and authorize the application with the signature and impersonation scopes

answerText: In Docusign Admin, open Connected Apps and authorize the application with the signature and impersonation scopes
explanation: Because the bank owns the integration key, this is admin consent for an internal app: an administrator authorizes it in Docusign Admin > Connected Apps, which needs Access Management and a claimed domain and covers users in that domain.
whyNotOthers: D is right because the clue is that the bank 'owns the integration key', which makes it an internal app. The trap is B: the openid plus admin_consent_scope URL is the method for external (ISV) apps whose key belongs to another organization. A is not one admin action (and JWT also accepts admin consent), and C fails because a JWT payload cannot grant consent.

optionExplanations.A: Individual consent works per user, but it is 300 actions, and JWT also accepts admin consent.
optionExplanations.B: This URL pattern is admin consent for external apps owned by another organization.
optionExplanations.C: Consent is never granted by the JWT payload itself.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. Internal app: Docusign Admin > Connected Apps, needs Access Management and a claimed domain.

concept.title: Admin consent for internal apps
concept.line: Internal app admin consent is granted in Docusign Admin > Connected Apps; needs Access Management and a claimed domain (not the external-app consent URL).

decode.prompt: Which requirement decides the consent approach?

options.text: Grant impersonation consent once for every user in the organization's own claimed domain, for an app the organization owns
Have the token request itself confer consent for domain users
Collect consent individually from each impersonated user
Use the consent flow designed for apps owned by another company

decode.explanation: Owning the integration key makes it an internal app, and 'a single administrator action that covers every manager' with a claimed domain and Access Management means admin consent in Docusign Admin.
clues: 'owns the integration key' -> internal app, not the ISV/external path
'domain is claimed' and 'Access Management' -> prerequisites for admin consent
'single administrator action' -> not per-user consent links
decode.needs: Admin consent for an internal app via Docusign Admin > Connected Apps with signature and impersonation.

topic: Connect message format for Maestro events
stem: Dev lead Hannah at Corvid Health has a Connect configuration that has delivered envelope events to her listener for years using the XML Aggregated message format, with HMAC signatures and retries enabled. Her team now triggers Maestro workflows from the patient portal and wants workflow-started, workflow-failed and workflow-completed events in the same listener. She adds the workflow events to a copy of the configuration, keeps every other setting, and runs a test instance, but no workflow events arrive although envelope events still do. What change is required?

options.text: Turn on Include HMAC for the copy, because workflow events are only sent to authenticated listeners
Add an eventNotification object to each envelope the workflow creates, overriding the account configuration
Enable Require Acknowledgement so failed workflow messages are retried
Set the configuration's message format to JSON SIM, the only format that carries Maestro events

answerText: Set the configuration's message format to JSON SIM, the only format that carries Maestro events
explanation: Maestro workflow events are only available with the JSON SIM event message format; the copied configuration still uses XML Aggregated.
whyNotOthers: D is right because the clue is that every other setting, including the XML Aggregated format, was kept. The trap is A: HMAC is a recommended security option but it is already on and is not the requirement for workflow events. B configures envelope-level webhooks, not Maestro events, and C improves delivery reliability but cannot make an unsupported format carry workflow events.

optionExplanations.A: Wrong. HMAC is already enabled and is optional message authentication, not the requirement for workflow events.
optionExplanations.B: Wrong. eventNotification gives envelope-level Connect for one envelope; it does not subscribe to workflow-started or workflow-completed.
optionExplanations.C: Wrong. Acknowledgement and retries help reliability; they do not change the message model that workflow events require.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. Maestro events (workflow-started, workflow-failed, workflow-completed) are only delivered in JSON SIM.

concept.title: Maestro events: JSON SIM only
concept.line: Maestro workflow events are only available with the JSON SIM message format, not XML Aggregated; HMAC is unrelated.

decode.prompt: What actually differs between envelope and workflow events here?

options.text: Override account-level notifications on each envelope
Make delivery reliable by forcing retries of failed messages
Deliver workflow events in the specific message format they require, since every other setting already works
Authenticate the listener so workflow events are permitted

decode.explanation: Envelope events still arrive with the copied settings, so delivery, HMAC and retries are fine; the copy kept XML Aggregated, which cannot carry Maestro events.
clues: 'XML Aggregated message format' -> the setting that blocks Maestro events
'keeps every other setting' -> copied format is still XML
'envelope events still do' arrive -> listener and security are fine
decode.needs: Set the configuration's message format to JSON SIM for Maestro workflow events.

stem: At 10:00 a user revokes an app's individual consent under Manage Profile > Connected Apps. The app uses Confidential Authorization Code Grant and holds an access token issued at 08:30 and a refresh token. What happens?

options.text: Both tokens stop working at 10:00, and the app's next API call is rejected
The refresh token is invalidated, but the access token keeps working until it expires at 16:30
The access token stops working, but the refresh token can still get new tokens for 30 days
Nothing changes until an administrator also revokes the consent in Docusign Admin

answerText: The refresh token is invalidated, but the access token keeps working until it expires at 16:30
explanation: Revoking consent invalidates refresh tokens and blocks new tokens, but an access token already issued keeps working until it expires; an Auth Code access token issued at 08:30 lasts 8 hours, to 16:30.
whyNotOthers: B is right because live access tokens survive revocation until they expire. The trap is A: it assumes revocation kills the access token at once. C reverses which token is affected, and D fails because individual consent is revoked by the user; admin revocation is only needed for admin-granted consent.

optionExplanations.A: Live access tokens keep working until expiry; revocation does not end them immediately.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. Refresh token invalidated; access token valid until 08:30 plus 8 hours.
optionExplanations.C: Revocation invalidates refresh tokens, so no new tokens can be obtained.
optionExplanations.D: The user revoked individual consent; that takes effect without an admin.

concept.title: Revoking consent and existing tokens
concept.line: Revoking consent invalidates refresh tokens and blocks new ones, but an issued access token keeps working until it expires (Auth Code: 8 hours).

topic: Send an envelope with Connected Fields
stem: Ridgeway Logistics has installed a connected fields extension app that verifies carrier tax IDs against its vendor master. Today senders drag the verified fields onto documents by hand in the Add Fields view. The team now wants its dispatch system to create and send these envelopes through the eSignature REST API, with each carrier's data already placed in the verified tabs. In the kickoff meeting a developer suggests moving the whole process into a Maestro workflow with a Data IO step instead. What is the correct API sequence?

options.text: Call Envelopes:create with plain text tabs and let the extension app verify them when the sender opens Add Fields.
Call TabInfo:GetConnectedFieldsTabGroups, put the data in each tab's extensionData, then call Envelopes:create.
Build a Maestro workflow with a connected fields step, then start it with a Workflow Builder API trigger call.
Call TabInfo:GetConnectedFieldsTabGroups, then send the carrier values in the envelope customFields on Envelopes:create.

answerText: Call TabInfo:GetConnectedFieldsTabGroups, put the data in each tab's extensionData, then call Envelopes:create.
explanation: The documented flow to send connected fields by API is: TabInfo:GetConnectedFieldsTabGroups, then place the data in each tab's extensionData, then Envelopes:create. The clue is 'through the eSignature REST API, with each carrier's data already placed in the verified tabs'.
whyNotOthers: B is right because connected field tabs carry their extension metadata in extensionData. The trap is D: it starts correctly but puts the values in envelope custom fields, which are not connected field tabs. A sends ordinary tabs with no link to the extension, and C fails because connected fields are not supported in Maestro.

optionExplanations.A: Plain text tabs have no extension data, and Add Fields is the manual UI path the team wants to replace.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. Get the connected field tab groups, fill each tab's extensionData, then create the envelope.
optionExplanations.C: Connected fields are not supported in Maestro workflows; Data IO in Maestro is a different extension.
optionExplanations.D: Envelope customFields hold envelope metadata; connected field data belongs in each tab's extensionData.

concept.title: Sending connected fields by API
concept.line: Call TabInfo:GetConnectedFieldsTabGroups, put data in each tab's extensionData, then Envelopes:create (not envelope customFields).

decode.prompt: What does the dispatch system need?

options.text: Let senders keep placing verified fields by hand before sending
Move the process into an orchestrated workflow instead of direct envelope creation
Carry the carrier values as envelope-level metadata rather than in fields
Create and send envelopes programmatically with verified app fields already populated, without any manual preparation step

decode.explanation: 'through the eSignature REST API, with each carrier's data already placed in the verified tabs' means fetching the connected fields tab definitions and filling their extension data before creating the envelope.
clues: 'through the eSignature REST API' -> Envelopes:create, not a Maestro workflow
'already placed in the verified tabs' -> data goes in each tab's extensionData
'suggests moving the whole process into a Maestro workflow' -> red herring
decode.needs: GetConnectedFieldsTabGroups, fill extensionData per tab, then Envelopes:create.

stem: A developer's integration key reached Review Passed, but he never selected a production account to promote it into. Four months later, what is the key's state?

options.text: Live, because Docusign promotes passed keys into the developer's default production account after 30 days
Review Expired; the review must be done again because the key was not submitted within 90 days
Still Review Passed, because the status does not change until a production account is selected
Declined; he must fill in the manual review form, which takes 24-48 hours to process

answerText: Review Expired; the review must be done again because the key was not submitted within 90 days
explanation: If a key that passed review is not submitted to a production account within 90 days, its status becomes Review Expired and the review must be done again.
whyNotOthers: B is right because four months is past the 90-day window. The trap is C: Review Passed does not last forever. A fails because Docusign never promotes a key automatically; you must choose the production account. D fails because Declined means the app needs manual review; it is not what happens when a passed review is left unused.

optionExplanations.A: Promotion is never automatic; the developer must confirm and select a production account where he is an admin.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. A passed review that is not submitted within 90 days expires and must be repeated.
optionExplanations.C: Review Passed lasts only 90 days without submission.
optionExplanations.D: Declined is the manual-review outcome of a review, not the result of leaving a passed review unused.

concept.title: Go-Live: Review Expired after 90 days
concept.line: A key that passed review but is not submitted to a production account within 90 days becomes Review Expired and must be reviewed again.

stem: Priya's JWT Grant claims service for Larch Mutual has just gone Live. She has already added an RSA key pair to the production copy of the key, and the claims system user has granted consent in production. Her code still contains the values she hard-coded during development: the developer API Account ID, the integration key GUID, account-d.docusign.com as the OAuth host and JWT aud value, and https://demo.docusign.net/restapi as the API base. Larch Mutual's production account is hosted in a data center she has not checked. Which two code changes are required? (Select two)

options.text: Change the OAuth host and the JWT aud claim from account-d.docusign.com to account.docusign.com
Replace the iss claim with the new GUID that Docusign issued for the production copy of the integration key
Replace demo.docusign.net with na1.docusign.net, because every production account shares that base URI
Call /oauth/userinfo with the production token and build API URLs from the returned account_id and base_uri
Keep the developer API Account ID, because Go-Live copies that account ID into the production account

answerText: Change the OAuth host and the JWT aud claim from account-d.docusign.com to account.docusign.com; Call /oauth/userinfo with the production token and build API URLs from the returned account_id and base_uri
explanation: After Go-Live the authentication host (and therefore the JWT aud) must be account.docusign.com, and API calls must use the production account's account_id and base_uri from /oauth/userinfo. The clue 'a data center she has not checked' rules out hard-coding any server.
whyNotOthers: A and D are right: the auth host changes to account.docusign.com, and the production account ID and base URI come from userinfo. The trap is C: production base URIs depend on the account's data center ({server}.docusign.net), so hard-coding na1 can be wrong. B fails because the promoted key keeps the same value, and E fails because the production account has its own account ID; nothing is copied from the developer account.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. Production OAuth and the JWT audience use account.docusign.com instead of account-d.docusign.com.
optionExplanations.B: The key is duplicated into production with the same value; iss does not change.
optionExplanations.C: Production base URIs vary by data center; the base_uri must come from userinfo (or Apps and Keys), not be assumed.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. userinfo returns the production account_id and base_uri used to build every API URL.
optionExplanations.E: The production account is a separate account with its own API Account ID; the developer ID is not copied.

concept.title: Production auth host and base URI
concept.line: After Go-Live use account.docusign.com as OAuth host and JWT aud; take account_id and base_uri from /oauth/userinfo, never hard-code a server.

decode.prompt: What must the code stop assuming after Go-Live?

options.text: Keep the developer account identifier because it carries over to production
Replace the integration key because production uses a different GUID
Hard-code a single production API server shared by all accounts
Point authentication at the production auth server and discover the production account and its server at runtime

decode.explanation: Production uses account.docusign.com for OAuth and the JWT aud, and 'a data center she has not checked' means the base URI and account ID must come from userinfo rather than being hard-coded.
clues: 'account-d.docusign.com as the OAuth host and JWT aud' -> must become account.docusign.com
'data center she has not checked' -> get base_uri from /oauth/userinfo
'developer API Account ID' -> production account has a different account_id
'integration key GUID' -> promotion keeps the same GUID
decode.needs: Production auth host and aud plus account_id and base_uri from /oauth/userinfo.

stem: Ana at Solano Credit Union embeds Maestro workflow instances in the member portal by placing the instance_url from Workflows:triggerWorkflow in an iframe. Her draft workflow is: Set Up Invite, Verify Someone's Identity configured for government photo ID verification, Collect Data with Web Forms, Send Documents for Signature with focused view display enabled, and a Store Files step to SharePoint. The start method is From an API call and the token includes aow_manage. Testing in the iframe shows problems in two steps. Which two changes align the workflow with the documented restrictions for embedded instances? (Select two)

options.text: Change the start method to From a Link, since API-triggered instances cannot be embedded
Configure the Verify Someone's Identity step to use Phone Authentication
Turn off focused view display for the Send Documents for Signature step
Set frameAncestors on the signing step so focused view can render inside the portal's iframe
Replace the iframe with the Docusign JS client SDK, which is required to render workflow instances

answerText: Configure the Verify Someone's Identity step to use Phone Authentication; Turn off focused view display for the Send Documents for Signature step
explanation: For embedded workflow instances, only the Phone Authentication method is supported in Verify Someone's Identity steps, and focused view display is not supported for Send Documents for Signature steps.
whyNotOthers: B and C are right because the two failing steps are the government ID check and focused-view signing, both restricted when an instance is embedded. The trap is D: frameAncestors belongs to focused view in eSignature embedded signing, but focused view itself is not supported inside an embedded workflow, so configuring it does not help. A is wrong because From an API call is a supported start method for embedding, and E is wrong because the instance_url is embedded with a plain iframe.

optionExplanations.A: Wrong. Both From a Link and From an API call are supported start methods for embedded instances.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. Only the Phone Authentication verification method is supported in embedded workflow instances.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. Focused view display of the agreement is not supported for Send Documents for Signature in embedded instances.
optionExplanations.D: Wrong. frameAncestors configures focused view embedding for eSignature; focused view is not supported in an embedded workflow at all.
optionExplanations.E: Wrong. The documented approach is to place the instance_url in an iframe (or redirect); the JS SDK is not required.

concept.title: Embedded workflow step restrictions
concept.line: Embedded workflow instances support only Phone Authentication in Verify Someone's Identity and do not support focused view in Send Documents for Signature.

decode.prompt: Which requirement decides the changes?

options.text: Allow the host page to frame the signing experience
Change how the workflow is started so it can be embedded
Render the instance through a dedicated client SDK instead of an iframe
Use only the step features that are supported when a workflow instance runs inside a host page's iframe

decode.explanation: API-triggered instances can be embedded via instance_url; the problems are in two steps, and embedded instances support only Phone Authentication for ID verification and do not support focused view in signing steps.
clues: 'embeds Maestro workflow instances ... in an iframe' -> embedded-instance restrictions apply
'government photo ID verification' -> only Phone Authentication is supported embedded
'focused view display enabled' -> not supported in embedded workflow signing steps
decode.needs: Phone Authentication in the ID step and focused view turned off in the signing step.

stem: An integration's JWT token requests the signature and impersonation scopes, and its eSignature calls work, but Workflows:triggerWorkflow is rejected as unauthorized. Which scope must be added to the token request?

options.text: extended
organization_read
user_read
aow_manage

answerText: aow_manage
explanation: Maestro API calls such as triggerWorkflow, pause, resume and cancel require the Maestro-specific aow_manage scope in addition to the normal eSignature scopes.
whyNotOthers: D is right because aow_manage is the Maestro scope named for trigger and instance-management calls. The trap is A: extended changes refresh token lifetime in Authorization Code Grant and grants no Maestro access. B and C are Admin API scopes for organization and user data that do not authorize workflow calls.

optionExplanations.A: Wrong. extended relates to refresh token lifetime; it adds no API permissions for Maestro.
optionExplanations.B: Wrong. organization_read is an Admin API scope for organization data, not for triggering workflows.
optionExplanations.C: Wrong. user_read is an Admin API user scope; it does not authorize Maestro endpoints.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. aow_manage is required to call Maestro endpoints such as triggerWorkflow.

concept.title: Maestro API scope: aow_manage
concept.line: Maestro API calls (trigger, pause, resume, cancel) need the aow_manage scope in addition to normal eSignature scopes, not extended.

topic: Listener design for retries and duplicates
stem: Oakline Telecom provisions a fiber line when an envelope-completed Connect message arrives. Its listener currently validates the message, writes three database tables and calls a slow provisioning API before returning 200, and during peak hours some calls take over a minute. Operations now sees occasional double provisioning for the same customer. The configuration has HMAC enabled and requireAcknowledgement set to true, and the team is happy with the JSON SIM payload. Which two changes follow Connect webhook best practices? (Select two)

options.text: Finish all database writes and the provisioning call before responding, so Docusign only records success after the work is done
Return a 2xx response as soon as the message is validated and stored in a queue, then process it asynchronously
Set requireAcknowledgement to false so slow responses are no longer retried by Connect
Make provisioning idempotent, for example keyed on envelope ID and event, so a redelivered message has no extra effect
Return an HTTP 500 when a duplicate message is detected so that Connect stops sending it

answerText: Return a 2xx response as soon as the message is validated and stored in a queue, then process it asynchronously; Make provisioning idempotent, for example keyed on envelope ID and event, so a redelivered message has no extra effect
explanation: Any non-2xx response or timeout counts as a failure and is retried, so the listener should acknowledge fast, process from a queue, and handle redelivered messages idempotently. The deciding clue is 'some calls take over a minute' combined with 'double provisioning'.
whyNotOthers: B and D are right: a fast 2xx avoids timeouts that trigger retries, and idempotent processing makes any redelivery harmless. The trap is A: it sounds safe, but long synchronous work causes timeouts, which Connect treats as failures and retries, creating the duplicates. C fails because it turns off automatic retries entirely, so genuinely failed messages would be lost; E fails because a non-2xx response is itself a failure that schedules another retry.

optionExplanations.A: Doing slow work before responding is what causes timeouts; Connect treats a timeout as a failure and retries, which produces the duplicate provisioning.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. Acknowledge quickly with 2xx after validating and queuing the message, then do the heavy work asynchronously so deliveries do not time out.
optionExplanations.C: requireAcknowledgement is what enables automatic retries; turning it off would stop retries for real failures too, so messages could be lost.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. Because retries can redeliver a message, processing must be idempotent so the same envelope event never provisions twice.
optionExplanations.E: Any non-2xx response counts as a failed delivery, so a 500 schedules another retry instead of stopping it.

concept.title: Connect listener: ack fast, idempotent
concept.line: Non-2xx or timeout triggers retries; return 2xx once validated and queued, process asynchronously, and make processing idempotent (e.g. envelope ID plus event).

decode.prompt: What is the listener design really missing?

options.text: Acknowledge each message quickly and tolerate repeated delivery of the same event without repeating side effects
Stop Docusign from retrying slow or failed deliveries
Confirm receipt only after all downstream work has completed
Signal Docusign to stop sending messages already seen

decode.explanation: Calls 'take over a minute' cause timeouts that Connect treats as failures and retries, which produces the 'double provisioning'; the fix is fast 2xx with queued processing plus idempotent handling.
clues: 'take over a minute' before returning 200 -> timeouts trigger retries
'double provisioning' -> redelivered messages must be idempotent
'HMAC enabled' and 'happy with the JSON SIM payload' -> not the problem
decode.needs: Return 2xx fast, process asynchronously from a queue, and make provisioning idempotent.

topic: Building trigger_inputs from the trigger requirements
stem: Tomasz maintains an integration at Harbourline Logistics that starts a published carrier-onboarding workflow through the Maestro API. Last week a process builder renamed two starting variables in Workflow Builder and republished. Since then, every POST to /v1/accounts/{accountId}/workflows/{workflowId}/actions/trigger returns 400 Bad Request, while his token, account ID and workflow ID are unchanged and other Maestro calls succeed. Tomasz wants his code to adapt automatically the next time variables change instead of hard-coding field names. What should the integration do before each trigger call?

options.text: Call Workflows:getWorkflowTriggerRequirements and build trigger_inputs from the trigger_input_schema it returns
Call getWorkflowInstance on the last successful instance and copy its input values into the new request
Append the starting variables as query parameters to the instance_url and open it instead of calling trigger
Call pauseNewWorkflowInstances and then resumePausedWorkflow so the new variable names are applied

answerText: Call Workflows:getWorkflowTriggerRequirements and build trigger_inputs from the trigger_input_schema it returns
explanation: getWorkflowTriggerRequirements returns the trigger configuration and the trigger_input_schema (field names, data types, defaults); trigger_inputs must match that schema, so reading it before each trigger keeps the request in step with renamed variables.
whyNotOthers: A is right because the 400 follows a change to the starting variables, and the trigger_input_schema from getWorkflowTriggerRequirements is the source of the field names trigger_inputs must use. The trap is B: getWorkflowInstance reports an existing instance's status and timing, not the current input schema, and old values carry the old names. C misuses the instance_url, which only exists after a trigger, and D only controls whether new instances can start.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. The trigger requirements expose the current trigger_input_schema, which trigger_inputs must match.
optionExplanations.B: Wrong. getWorkflowInstance describes an instance that already ran (status, times, started_by); it would reproduce the outdated variable names.
optionExplanations.C: Wrong. The instance_url is returned by a successful trigger to display the running instance; it is not a way to pass starting variables.
optionExplanations.D: Wrong. Pause and resume affect whether new instances can be created; they do not change the input schema or fix a malformed request.

concept.title: Build trigger_inputs from trigger schema
concept.line: Workflows:getWorkflowTriggerRequirements returns trigger_input_schema (names, types, defaults); build trigger_inputs from it, not from a past instance's inputs.

decode.prompt: What does Tomasz really need?

options.text: Discover the workflow's current required input fields at runtime so trigger requests always match the published definition
Start the workflow by link instead of through the API
Force the published workflow to reload its variables
Reuse input values from an earlier successful run

decode.explanation: The 400 started when starting variables were renamed, and 'adapt automatically' means reading the trigger input schema before each trigger instead of hard-coding names.
clues: 'renamed two starting variables' -> trigger_inputs field names no longer match
'adapt automatically the next time variables change' -> read the schema at runtime
'token, account ID and workflow ID are unchanged' -> not an auth or ID problem
decode.needs: Call getWorkflowTriggerRequirements and build trigger_inputs from trigger_input_schema.

stem: Priya builds a patient-intake portal for Harbor Clinics. Her server creates each envelope with status sent and a signer whose name is "Dr. Maria Lopez", email maria.lopez@harbor.example and clientUserId "pt-1001". The portal also stores an internal patient number and a returnUrl that is already registered as a redirect URI. When the patient clicks Sign, the portal calls EnvelopeViews:createRecipient with email maria.lopez@harbor.example, userName "Maria Lopez", clientUserId "pt-1001", authenticationMethod "none" and the returnUrl, and Docusign rejects the request saying the recipient cannot be found. What should Priya change?

options.text: Send userName exactly as the signer name used at envelope creation, "Dr. Maria Lopez"
Add the signer's recipientId to the request, because createRecipient locates the signer by recipientId
Set authenticationMethod to "email", because "none" is not accepted for an embedded recipient
Recreate the envelope with status created, because a view cannot be requested for a sent envelope

answerText: Send userName exactly as the signer name used at envelope creation, "Dr. Maria Lopez"
explanation: createRecipient finds the embedded signer by matching email, userName and clientUserId against the values set at envelope creation. Here the clue is userName "Maria Lopez" versus the creation name "Dr. Maria Lopez", so the lookup fails.
whyNotOthers: A is right because all three identity values must match the envelope recipient exactly. The trap is B: recipientId identifies a recipient inside the envelope, but the documented required matching values are email, userName and clientUserId, and the name mismatch would still break the lookup. C fails because authenticationMethod only records how your app authenticated the user. D fails because embedded signing requires status sent.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. email, userName and clientUserId must match the recipient defined in Envelopes:create; the name differs only by the "Dr." prefix.
optionExplanations.B: recipientId is not one of the documented matching values; adding it does not fix the userName mismatch.
optionExplanations.C: authenticationMethod only records your app's authentication on the certificate; it is not why the recipient is not found.
optionExplanations.D: Embedded signing requires the envelope to be sent; a draft (created) envelope cannot be signed.

concept.title: createRecipient must match exactly
concept.line: EnvelopeViews:createRecipient matches email, userName and clientUserId exactly as set at envelope creation; recipientId is not the lookup key.

decode.prompt: Why can Docusign not find the recipient?

options.text: Identify the embedded signer with exactly the same identifying values used when the envelope was created
Require an authentication method other than none for embedded signers
Request the signing view before the envelope is sent
Identify the signer by its position number in the envelope

decode.explanation: createRecipient matches email, userName and clientUserId; the request uses 'Maria Lopez' while the envelope has 'Dr. Maria Lopez', so the lookup fails.
clues: 'name is "Dr. Maria Lopez"' vs 'userName "Maria Lopez"' -> name mismatch
'clientUserId "pt-1001"' matches -> embedded signer is set up correctly
'returnUrl ... already registered' -> red herring
decode.needs: Send userName identical to the signer name at envelope creation.

topic: Choosing the Connect level (org vs account vs envelope)
stem: Harbor Freight Holdings runs four Docusign eSignature accounts, one per subsidiary, all under one Docusign organization. Developer Priya Nair must feed a single compliance data lake with status events. Two of the subsidiaries send most envelopes from a custom portal through Envelopes:create, but the legal teams in every subsidiary also receive NDAs from outside law firms, and those received envelopes must be captured too. The CIO wants one configuration to maintain, not one per account, and the data lake team has already written a JSON parser. Which Connect approach meets all of these requirements?

options.text: Add an eventNotification object to every Envelopes:create request sent by the custom portal
Create a custom account-level Connect configuration in each of the four accounts, all pointing to the data lake
Create one organization-level Connect configuration covering all four accounts, delivered in JSON SIM
Create a Recipient Connect configuration for the legal users in each subsidiary account

answerText: Create one organization-level Connect configuration covering all four accounts, delivered in JSON SIM
explanation: Organization-level Connect sends events for envelopes sent from or received by all or selected accounts in the organization, and it always uses JSON SIM. The deciding clues are 'one configuration, not one per account' and 'received envelopes must be captured too'.
whyNotOthers: C is right because a single org-level configuration spans every account and covers envelopes both sent and received. The trap is B: account-level configurations would capture sent and received envelopes, but it means four separate configurations, which the CIO ruled out. A fails because envelope-level webhooks only exist for envelopes your integration sends and cannot cover NDAs received from outside firms; D only targets specific receiving users per account and still needs per-account setup while missing portal-sent envelopes.

optionExplanations.A: Envelope-level eventNotification is set only when your own integration creates the envelope, so it can never cover envelopes received from outside law firms, and it skips anything not sent by the portal.
optionExplanations.B: Account-level Connect would capture sent and received envelopes, but it requires one configuration per account (four in total), violating the single-configuration requirement.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. An organization-level configuration covers envelopes sent from or received by all (or selected) accounts in the organization from one place, and it always delivers JSON SIM messages.
optionExplanations.D: Recipient Connect notifies when specific account users receive an envelope; it would miss the portal-sent envelopes and still has to be set up account by account.

concept.title: Organization-level Connect scope
concept.line: One org-level Connect configuration covers sent and received envelopes for all or selected accounts, always JSON SIM; no per-account configurations needed.

decode.prompt: Which requirement decides the Connect level?

options.text: Capture both sent and received envelopes across several accounts with a single configuration to maintain
Give each subsidiary account its own independently managed feed
Capture only envelopes created by the custom portal's API calls
Track only envelopes received by a specific group of users

decode.explanation: 'one configuration, not one per account' plus 'received envelopes must be captured too' across four accounts in one organization points to organization-level Connect, which uses JSON SIM.
clues: 'four Docusign eSignature accounts ... under one Docusign organization' -> org-level Connect
'received envelopes must be captured too' -> envelope-level eventNotification is not enough
'one configuration to maintain' -> not one per account
'already written a JSON parser' -> fits JSON SIM
decode.needs: One organization-level Connect configuration in JSON SIM covering all four accounts.

stem: A process builder wants to permanently delete a published workflow that still has active instances. Which sequence is allowed?

options.text: Delete it directly from the Workflows list; active instances are cancelled automatically
Unpublish it, then delete it once it shows as unpublished
Pause it, unpublish it once no instances are running, then delete it
Pause it, then delete it, since paused workflows no longer count toward the quota

answerText: Pause it, unpublish it once no instances are running, then delete it
explanation: Only a paused workflow with no running instances can be unpublished, and only an unpublished workflow can be deleted; deletion is permanent.
whyNotOthers: C is right because it follows pause, then unpublish with no running instances, then delete. The trap is B: unpublish requires the workflow to be paused first. A skips every precondition, and D is wrong twice: a paused workflow still counts toward the quota and cannot be deleted until it is unpublished.

optionExplanations.A: Wrong. A published workflow cannot be deleted directly; only unpublished workflows can be deleted.
optionExplanations.B: Wrong. You can only unpublish a workflow that has been paused.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. Pause, wait until no instances are running, unpublish, then delete permanently.
optionExplanations.D: Wrong. Paused workflows still count toward the quota, and deletion requires the unpublished state.

concept.title: Deleting a published workflow
concept.line: Pause it, unpublish once no instances run, then delete; only paused workflows with no running instances can be unpublished. Deletion is permanent.

stem: Harbor Logistics wants an extension app that writes signed bills of lading into its 15-year-old document repository. The repository exposes a SOAP endpoint that accepts and returns XML, sits inside the corporate network, and only accepts traffic from approved addresses. The team already uses OAuth 2.0 through Okta, which can issue tokens to Docusign with the right client ID, client secret, authorization URL and token URL. Some employees run browser ad blockers. Which two infrastructure tasks are needed so Docusign can call the service and admins can install the app? (Select two)

options.text: Add Docusign's origins to the CORS allowed origins list in Apps and Keys
Build and host an API proxy that maps Docusign's JSON action contract to the SOAP/XML interface
Add a CNAME record so the repository is reachable under a docusign.com subdomain
Change firewall (and ad blocker) configuration so Docusign can reach the service and the app can be installed
Submit a Go-Live request for an integration key that points to the repository

answerText: Build and host an API proxy that maps Docusign's JSON action contract to the SOAP/XML interface; Change firewall (and ad blocker) configuration so Docusign can reach the service and the app can be installed
explanation: The service speaks XML that does not conform to the Docusign action contract, so an API proxy is needed, and it only 'accepts traffic from approved addresses', so firewall and ad blocker configuration must allow Docusign requests and App Center installation.
whyNotOthers: B and D are right: Docusign lists an API proxy (when the API does not match the action contract) and network firewall/ad blocker changes as the infrastructure an extension app may need. The trap is A: CORS in Apps and Keys lets a browser single-page app call the eSignature API, it does nothing for server-to-server calls from Docusign to your service. C is not a Docusign requirement, and E belongs to API integrations using integration keys, not to extension apps, which are approved through review and publishing.

optionExplanations.A: CORS settings in Apps and Keys let a browser app call Docusign APIs; they do not let Docusign reach an external service.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. An API proxy translates Docusign's action requests and responses to the XML/SOAP format the repository understands.
optionExplanations.C: No DNS CNAME entry is required for extension apps; reachability is a firewall issue, not a naming issue.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. Firewall and ad blocker changes may be needed so Docusign can send requests to the API service and users can install the app.
optionExplanations.E: Go-Live promotes an integration key for API integrations; extension apps go through Developer Console review and publishing instead.

concept.title: Extension app infrastructure needs
concept.line: Non-conforming APIs need an API proxy mapping to the Docusign action contract; firewalls and ad blockers must allow Docusign requests and App Center install.

decode.prompt: What infrastructure gaps must be closed?

options.text: Allow browser cross-origin calls from Docusign pages
Promote a credential to production before installation
Host the service under a Docusign-owned domain name
Translate between Docusign's JSON action contract and a legacy XML service, and let Docusign traffic through the network restrictions

decode.explanation: 'SOAP endpoint that accepts and returns XML' needs an API proxy, and 'only accepts traffic from approved addresses' plus 'ad blockers' needs firewall and ad blocker changes.
clues: 'SOAP endpoint ... XML' -> API proxy to the JSON action contract
'only accepts traffic from approved addresses' -> firewall must allow Docusign
'browser ad blockers' -> can block App Center installation
'OAuth 2.0 through Okta' -> auth is already solved
decode.needs: An API proxy for SOAP/XML plus firewall and ad blocker configuration.

stem: A JWT Grant integration gets an access token at 09:00. How does it keep calling the eSignature REST API after that token expires?

options.text: It uses the refresh token returned with the JWT response, adding extended so it stays valid 30 days after each refresh
The token lasts 8 hours, so it calls /oauth/token with grant_type=refresh_token shortly before 17:00
The token lasts about 1 hour and no refresh token is issued, so it builds and signs a new JWT to get another token
The token lasts 1 hour, so it sends the original JWT assertion again, because an assertion stays valid for 30 days

answerText: The token lasts about 1 hour and no refresh token is issued, so it builds and signs a new JWT to get another token
explanation: JWT Grant access tokens last 1 hour and JWT Grant returns no refresh token; the app mints a new JWT (exp at most 1 hour after iat) and requests a new token.
whyNotOthers: C is right because JWT Grant never returns a refresh token. The trap is A: extended and rolling 30-day refresh tokens apply only to Authorization Code Grant. B uses the 8-hour Auth Code lifetime, and D fails because the assertion itself expires within an hour (exp is at most iat plus 3600).

optionExplanations.A: extended and refresh tokens belong to Authorization Code Grant; JWT returns no refresh token.
optionExplanations.B: 8 hours is the Auth Code access token lifetime, and JWT has no refresh token to use.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. 1-hour token, no refresh token: mint and sign a new JWT.
optionExplanations.D: The JWT assertion's exp is at most 1 hour after iat, so it cannot be reused for 30 days.

concept.title: JWT token: 1 hour, no refresh
concept.line: JWT Grant access tokens last 1 hour with no refresh token; mint a new JWT (exp at most 1 hour after iat).

stem: When you call Envelopes:create for a signer who will sign inside your application, which two values are always required in that request for embedded signing? (Select two)

options.text: returnUrl on the signer object
Envelope status set to sent
frameAncestors on the envelope definition
A non-null clientUserId on the signer
emailNotification set to suppress the email

answerText: Envelope status set to sent; A non-null clientUserId on the signer
explanation: Docusign University states that two parameters are always required when creating an envelope for embedded signing: status (sent) and clientUserId on the recipient.
whyNotOthers: B and D are right: status sent lets the signer act immediately, and any non-null clientUserId marks the recipient as embedded. The trap is A: returnUrl is required, but on the later createRecipient call, not on Envelopes:create. C also belongs to createRecipient (focused view only), and E does not make a recipient embedded.

optionExplanations.A: returnUrl is supplied on EnvelopeViews:createRecipient, not on Envelopes:create.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. Embedded signing requires an envelope status of sent so the signer can act right away.
optionExplanations.C: frameAncestors is a createRecipient parameter used only for focused view.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. Any non-null clientUserId tells Docusign the recipient will sign embedded.
optionExplanations.E: Turning off email does not make the recipient embedded; clientUserId does.

concept.title: Embedded signing required parameters
concept.line: Embedded signing envelopes always need status sent and a non-null clientUserId on the recipient; returnUrl is not one of the two required parameters.

stem: Fenwick Supply's renewal desk needs a nightly job that finds every agreement with the party Orion Freight whose expiration date falls within the next 90 days, together with its provisions, and pushes the results into the CRM. The Agreement Manager repository holds about 40,000 agreements, the account shares its hourly API limit with three other integrations, and the architect asks for the fewest calls possible. The CRM already stores some agreement IDs from an earlier pilot, but not all of them. Which approach fits?

options.text: Call GetAgreement for each agreement ID stored in the CRM and keep only those expiring within 90 days.
Call GetAgreementsList filtered on parties.name_in_agreement and a provisions.expiration_date range, paging with ctoken.
Call CreateAgreementSummary for Orion Freight's agreements and parse the expiration dates out of each summary.
Call Envelopes:listStatusChanges for Orion Freight envelopes and read expiration dates from envelope custom fields.

answerText: Call GetAgreementsList filtered on parties.name_in_agreement and a provisions.expiration_date range, paging with ctoken.
explanation: GetAgreementsList accepts filters such as parties.name_in_agreement and provisions.expiration_date (with operators like gte and lte) and returns each agreement's provisions, so one paged query answers the need. The clue is 'fewest calls' over 40,000 agreements.
whyNotOthers: B is right because the list operation filters server-side and already includes provisions. The trap is A: GetAgreement is one call per agreement and the CRM does not hold all IDs. C creates AI summaries (a POST per agreement) rather than querying dates, and D uses the eSignature API, which does not expose AI-extracted expiration dates.

optionExplanations.A: One call per agreement wastes the shared limit, and the CRM is missing some agreement IDs.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. Server-side filters on party and expiration date, results include provisions, ctoken pages through them.
optionExplanations.C: CreateAgreementSummary generates a summary of one agreement; it is not a search and costs a call per agreement.
optionExplanations.D: eSignature envelope data does not contain Agreement Manager's AI-extracted provisions such as expiration_date.

concept.title: Filtering agreements in one query
concept.line: GetAgreementsList filters on fields like parties.name_in_agreement and provisions.expiration_date (gte/lte) and pages with ctoken, avoiding per-agreement GetAgreement calls.

decode.prompt: Which requirement decides the approach?

options.text: Read expiration data from the signing transaction records
Retrieve a filtered set of agreements by party and expiration window, with their provisions, in as few calls as possible
Look up only the agreements whose IDs are already known
Generate natural-language overviews of each agreement

decode.explanation: 'fewest calls possible' over 40,000 agreements, filtered by party and an expiration date range with provisions, is a single filtered and paged list query.
clues: 'every agreement with the party Orion Freight' -> filter on parties
'expiration date within the next 90 days' -> provisions.expiration_date range
'fewest calls possible' -> one paged list query, not per-ID gets
'CRM already stores some agreement IDs' -> red herring, incomplete
decode.needs: GetAgreementsList with party and expiration filters, paging with ctoken.

stem: In the template reference model, which property of the Envelopes:create body assigns a real person to a recipient role defined in the template?

options.text: recipients.signers, matched to the template by recipientId
templateRoles, matched to the template by roleName
inlineTemplates, matched to the template by sequence
compositeTemplates.serverTemplates, matched by templateId

answerText: templateRoles, matched to the template by roleName
explanation: The template reference model uses templateId plus templateRoles; each templateRoles entry gives name and email and is matched to the template role by roleName.
whyNotOthers: B is right because templateRoles with roleName is how the template reference model fills roles. The trap is A: recipients.signers belongs to the direct documents model and does not map to template roles by recipientId. C and D are composite template constructs, not part of the template reference model.

optionExplanations.A: recipients.signers is the direct documents model structure, not role mapping for a template.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. templateRoles entries are matched to template roles by roleName.
optionExplanations.C: inlineTemplates and sequence belong to the composite templates model.
optionExplanations.D: serverTemplates is part of the composite templates model, not the template reference model.

concept.title: Template reference model roles
concept.line: The template reference model uses templateId plus templateRoles, each giving name and email and matched to the template by roleName.

stem: When Docusign validates an extension app manifest, which value must exactly match the name of an entry in the connections object?

options.text: The connectionsReference value inside each action definition
Each entry of the actionReferences array inside an extension
The template identifier of each action definition
The params.uri value of each action definition

answerText: The connectionsReference value inside each action definition
explanation: Each action points to the auth credentials it uses through connectionsReference, and that value must match a defined connection name, which is why connection names must be unique.
whyNotOthers: A is right because the action-to-connection link is made by connectionsReference. The trap is B: actionReferences is also a reference by name, but it links an extension to actions, not to connections. C names the Docusign-defined action contract and D is the external endpoint URL, neither of which refers to a connection.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. connectionsReference in an action links it to the connection (auth credentials) defined in the connections object.
optionExplanations.B: actionReferences links an extension to its action definitions, one level away from connections.
optionExplanations.C: The action template is a Docusign-predefined identifier of the action contract, not a connection name.
optionExplanations.D: params.uri is the external platform endpoint the action calls, not a reference to a connection.

concept.title: Manifest: connectionsReference
concept.line: Each action names its auth credentials via connectionsReference, which must match a defined connection name; hence connection names must be unique.

stem: Right after any Docusign OAuth flow returns an access token, where should the integration get the values used to build its eSignature REST API request URLs?

options.text: From the JWT sub claim for the account ID, with account-d.docusign.com as the API base path
From the API Account ID in Apps and Keys, combined with the account.docusign.com host
From GET /oauth/userinfo: the account_id and base_uri of the account where is_default is true
From the token response body, which returns account_id and base_uri next to access_token

answerText: From GET /oauth/userinfo: the account_id and base_uri of the account where is_default is true
explanation: For every flow, the app calls /oauth/userinfo with the bearer token and takes account_id and base_uri from the account where is_default is true.
whyNotOthers: C is right because userinfo is the source of account_id and base_uri. The trap is B: the API Account ID is a real account ID, but account.docusign.com is the authentication host, not the API base URI. A confuses the user ID (sub) with the account ID, and D fails because the token response does not carry account_id or base_uri.

optionExplanations.A: sub is the user ID, not the account ID, and account-d.docusign.com is the auth server.
optionExplanations.B: account.docusign.com is the OAuth host; the API base_uri comes from userinfo.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. userinfo, default account, account_id plus base_uri.
optionExplanations.D: The token response holds tokens and expiry, not account_id or base_uri.

concept.title: account_id and base_uri from userinfo
concept.line: For every flow, call /oauth/userinfo and use account_id and base_uri from the account where is_default is true.

stem: An existing JWT integration requests the signature and impersonation scopes and must now call GetAgreement. What must change?

options.text: Nothing, because the signature scope covers every Docusign API that accepts the same access token.
Add the aow_manage scope, which governs access to AI-extracted agreement data.
Move to Authorization Code Grant, because the Agreement Manager API does not accept JWT tokens.
Add the adm_store_unified_repo_read scope to the token request and obtain consent for it.

answerText: Add the adm_store_unified_repo_read scope to the token request and obtain consent for it.
explanation: Agreement Manager (Navigator) uses the same OAuth access tokens as eSignature, but the token must include a Navigator scope; getAgreement requires adm_store_unified_repo_read.
whyNotOthers: D is right because the token type is unchanged and only the Navigator read scope (with consent) is missing. The trap is B: aow_manage is the Maestro workflow scope. A fails because signature does not cover Navigator, and C fails because JWT, Authorization Code and Implicit tokens all work.

optionExplanations.A: The signature scope does not authorize Navigator endpoints; a Navigator scope is required.
optionExplanations.B: aow_manage is the Workflow Builder (Maestro) scope, not the agreement data scope.
optionExplanations.C: JWT Grant is supported; Navigator accepts the same token types as the eSignature REST API.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. Request adm_store_unified_repo_read (and obtain consent for the new scope) in the same JWT flow.

concept.title: Navigator scope for getAgreement
concept.line: Agreement Manager uses eSignature-style OAuth tokens but needs a Navigator scope; getAgreement requires adm_store_unified_repo_read (not aow_manage).

stem: Lena works for a regional credit union that is not a Docusign partner. Her extension app verifies member numbers against the credit union's core banking system and must be installable only by the credit union's three production accounts. She built and tested it in her developer account, which the Developer Console has already installed it into, and the review has just finished with the app in Approved status. Her manager asks her to 'make it live in the same way as the public apps we use'. What should Lena do next?
