options.text: Click the button that makes the app available to all customers, then limit it with publicationRegions
Submit a Go-Live request so the app's integration key is promoted to the three production accounts
Add the account IDs of the developer account and the demo accounts the testers used
Publish it privately by adding each production account ID (GUID) with an alias, then wait for each admin to accept it

answerText: Publish it privately by adding each production account ID (GUID) with an alias, then wait for each admin to accept it
explanation: The app is for 'only the credit union's three production accounts' and the org is 'not a Docusign partner', so it is a private app: after approval she adds each production account ID (GUID), and each account shows Pending until its admin accepts the app in the App Center.
whyNotOthers: D is right because private distribution is shared by listing production account IDs, and status stays Pending until the admin accepts. The trap is A: that is the public flow (which also requires partner status), and publicationRegions limits regions, not specific accounts. B confuses extension apps with API integration Go-Live, and C lists non-production accounts, while private apps are shared with production accounts.

optionExplanations.A: This is the public publishing flow; it exposes the app to every App Center customer, and publicationRegions applies to public apps only, by region, not by account.
optionExplanations.B: Go-Live is for integration keys of API integrations; extension apps become usable in production by being published after review.
optionExplanations.C: Private apps are shared with selected production accounts; the developer account already has the app for testing.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. For PRIVATE distribution she adds each production account ID (GUID) with an alias; status is Pending until that account's administrator accepts the app.

concept.title: Publishing a private app
concept.line: Private apps are shared by adding each production account ID (GUID) after approval; each shows Pending until its admin accepts in the App Center.

decode.prompt: Which requirement decides the next step?

options.text: Make an approved extension app available only to a few named customer accounts, which must each accept it
Promote an integration key from development to production
Make the app listed for every customer and then narrow it by region
Make the app available to the developer and test accounts

decode.explanation: 'installable only by the credit union's three production accounts' and 'not a Docusign partner' mean private publication by account ID, with each admin accepting the app.
clues: 'only by the credit union's three production accounts' -> private app
'not a Docusign partner' -> public listing is not the path
'Approved status' -> next step is publishing, not Go-Live
'same way as the public apps' -> misleading wording from the manager
decode.needs: Publish privately by adding each production account GUID with an alias; admins accept it.

stem: Lena is an administrator of her company's production Docusign account. She built an internal contract tool for her own colleagues and, this morning, created its integration key and made four test calls. She then selected Actions > Start Go live in Apps and Keys and logged in with her production credentials, but an error message appeared instead of a list of accounts to choose from. Her manager thinks the old minimum-call rule is to blame. Later Lena finds that a teammate, copying a partner tutorial, had set 'How will you use this integration?' to Public integration. What is the most likely cause of the error?

options.text: The key has not yet made the minimum of 20 successful API calls required before Go-Live can start
Lena is not an administrator of the production account that she logged into during Start Go live
The integration type chosen for the key does not match the type of account she logged into
The key's earlier review expired after 90 days, so it must be reviewed again before accounts are listed

answerText: The integration type chosen for the key does not match the type of account she logged into
explanation: Docusign documents that an error shown instead of the account list means the integration type set on the key does not match the account type you logged into. Lena's key is classified as Public integration, but it is an internal tool and she logged into an ordinary company account.
whyNotOthers: C is right because the clue 'error instead of a list of accounts' maps to a mismatch between the key's integration type and the account type. The trap is A: the 20-call requirement was removed, and Go-Live can start right after the key is set up. B fails because the stem says Lena is an admin of that account. D fails because the key was created this morning, so no review could have expired.

optionExplanations.A: Go-Live no longer requires 20 API calls; you can start right after creating the key.
optionExplanations.B: The stem says Lena is an administrator of the production account.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. An error instead of the account list means the key's integration type does not match the account type.
optionExplanations.D: Review Expired applies only when a passed review is not submitted within 90 days; this key is a day old.

concept.title: Go-Live error: integration type mismatch
concept.line: An error instead of the account list means the key's integration type does not match the type of account you logged into.

decode.prompt: What does the error really indicate?

options.text: The key has not yet been used enough times in development
The way the key is classified does not fit the kind of account being used to promote it
The person logging in lacks admin rights on the production account
An earlier review has lapsed and must be redone

decode.explanation: An error instead of the account list means a type mismatch, and the teammate set the internal tool's key to Public integration.
clues: 'error message appeared instead of a list of accounts' -> integration type mismatch
'set ... to Public integration' -> wrong classification for an internal tool
'old minimum-call rule' -> red herring
'administrator of her company's production account' -> admin rights are fine
decode.needs: Integration type on the key must match the account type logged into during Go-Live.

stem: MedLink's tablet check-in app creates an envelope for each patient with a clientUserId when the front desk registers them at 8 a.m., and in the same job it calls EnvelopeViews:createRecipient and caches the returned URL in the patient's record. The clinic uses focused view, Docusign JS loads correctly, and Connect already reports envelope status. Patients reach the signing station anywhere from 10 minutes to 3 hours later, and almost all of them get an expired-session error when the cached URL opens. Which change fixes the problem with the least rework?

options.text: Ask Docusign to extend the recipient view lifetime by passing a longer session timeout in the returnUrl query string
Void each envelope at the station and create a new envelope plus a new signing URL for the patient
Keep the 8 a.m. envelope, but call createRecipient only when the patient taps Start at the station
Create the envelope at 8 a.m. in draft status and change it to sent when the patient reaches the station

answerText: Keep the 8 a.m. envelope, but call createRecipient only when the patient taps Start at the station
explanation: The signing URL expires after about 5 minutes and is single-use, so it must be requested only when the user is ready to sign. The envelope itself does not expire in hours, so only the createRecipient call needs to move.
whyNotOthers: C is right because the clue is that the URL is cached at 8 a.m. and opened up to hours later. The trap is B: a new envelope plus URL would work but discards valid envelopes and adds needless calls; only the URL is stale. A fails because the returnUrl only controls where the user goes afterwards. D fails because the draft status was never the problem; the cached URL would still expire.

optionExplanations.A: The returnUrl is only the redirect destination; it cannot extend the short URL lifetime.
optionExplanations.B: It works but is wasteful: the envelope is still valid, only the short-lived URL expired.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. Generate the recipient view URL only when the signer is ready; reuse the existing sent envelope.
optionExplanations.D: Envelope status is not the cause; a URL generated early would still expire before use.

concept.title: Signing URL lifetime: 5 minutes
concept.line: The embedded signing URL is single-use and expires in about 5 minutes; call createRecipient only when the signer is ready.

decode.prompt: What is the actual timing requirement?

options.text: Delay sending the transaction until the patient arrives
Lengthen how long a signing session link stays valid
Obtain the signing session link only at the moment the patient is ready to sign, since that link is short-lived and single-use
Recreate the whole transaction when the patient arrives

decode.explanation: The URL is cached at 8 a.m. and used 10 minutes to 3 hours later, but recipient view URLs expire in about 5 minutes; the envelope itself is fine, so only the createRecipient call moves.
clues: 'caches the returned URL' -> signing URLs are single-use and short-lived
'10 minutes to 3 hours later' -> far beyond the URL lifetime
'least rework' -> keep the envelope, move only createRecipient
'Docusign JS loads correctly' -> not a front-end problem
decode.needs: Call createRecipient only when the patient taps Start at the station.

topic: Redirect after remote web form signing
stem: Pinecrest Credit Union sends membership applications as remote web form instances (sendOption set to now) created from a template-based configuration. Members open the form from an email link, submit it, and then sign the generated envelope remotely from Docusign's email. Compliance wants every member who finishes signing to land on the credit union's 'What happens next' contact page. One developer proposes adding a returnUrl to the Instances:createInstance body; another suggests editing the signing resource file. Neither the configuration nor its web form template is associated with any brand yet. What will reliably redirect these members after signing?

options.text: Associate a brand whose Destination URLs Signing Completed field holds the contact page, for example via brandId in createInstance.
Add a returnUrl to the Instances:createInstance request so Docusign redirects the member once the envelope is completed.
Upload a customized signing branding resource file that contains the contact page link to the account's default brand.
Turn on In-Session landing pages in the web form configuration so the contact page is shown right after submission.

answerText: Associate a brand whose Destination URLs Signing Completed field holds the contact page, for example via brandId in createInstance.
explanation: For remote web form instances a redirect after signing works only through branding: the web form template or instance must be associated with a brand whose Destination URLs include a Signing Completed URL. The clue is 'remote web form instances' plus 'not associated with any brand yet'.
whyNotOthers: A is right because remote instances redirect only via a brand's Signing Completed destination URL, and a brandId in createInstance applies that brand. The trap is B: returnUrl in createInstance is used for template-based instances with embedded signing, not remote delivery. C changes text elements of the signing experience, not the post-signing destination, and D is not a web form redirect feature.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. A brand with a Signing Completed destination URL is the documented redirect mechanism for remote web form instances.
optionExplanations.B: returnUrl in createInstance redirects users of template-based instances that use embedded signing, not remotely signed ones.
optionExplanations.C: Branding resource files customize labels and text of the experience; the redirect target lives in Destination URLs.
optionExplanations.D: Not the mechanism; without a brand post-signing URL a remote instance ends on a static Docusign-branded page.

concept.title: Remote web form redirect via brand
concept.line: Remote web form redirect after signing works only through a brand's Signing Completed destination URL (e.g. brandId), not returnUrl.

decode.prompt: Which requirement decides the redirect mechanism?

options.text: Redirect remote signers after signing, which for remote web form flows works only through account branding settings
Customize the signing page's resource file
Pass a return address on the API call that creates the instance
Show a landing page right after the form is submitted

decode.explanation: 'remote web form instances' signed from Docusign email have no returnUrl, so the redirect needs a brand with a Signing Completed destination URL; the 'not associated with any brand yet' clue confirms it.
clues: 'remote web form instances (sendOption set to now)' -> no embedded returnUrl
'sign ... remotely from Docusign's email' -> redirect comes from branding
'not associated with any brand yet' -> associate a brand with Destination URLs
decode.needs: A brand with a Signing Completed Destination URL associated with the instance or template.

stem: A developer calls Instances:getInstance for a submitted instance that was created from a standalone web form configuration. Which response is expected?

options.text: status SUBMITTED and an envelopes array holding the envelope generated when the user submitted the form.
status INPROGRESS, which stays until the generated envelope is completed by every recipient.
status SUBMITTED with the recipient authentication record properties echoed back for the certificate.
status SUBMITTED, the submitted formValues, and an envelopes array that is empty.

answerText: status SUBMITTED, the submitted formValues, and an envelopes array that is empty.
explanation: A standalone configuration collects data only and never generates an envelope, so a submitted instance shows status SUBMITTED, its formValues, and an empty envelopes array.
whyNotOthers: D is right because standalone means 'no envelope, data collection only'. The trap is A, which describes a template-based configuration where an envelope is generated. B ties status to an envelope that does not exist, and C fails because the authentication record properties are not supported for standalone configurations.

optionExplanations.A: Describes a template-based configuration; standalone instances never generate an envelope.
optionExplanations.B: INPROGRESS means the user is still filling the form; a standalone instance has no envelope to wait for.
optionExplanations.C: authenticationMethod, authenticationInstant, assertionId and securityDomain are not supported for standalone configurations.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. Submitted standalone instances return SUBMITTED, the formValues, and an empty envelopes array.

concept.title: Standalone web form results
concept.line: Standalone configurations only collect data and never create envelopes; a submitted instance has status SUBMITTED, formValues, and an empty envelopes array.

topic: Sending an envelope with connected fields by API (multi)
stem: Tomas maintains a loan origination portal that creates envelopes through the eSignature REST API. His company has installed and connected a private connected fields app that verifies account numbers against its ledger. Preparers who use the eSignature web app already see the App Fields, but Tomas must now add the same verified fields to envelopes his portal sends without any manual preparation, and keep his existing JSON SIM Connect listener. Which two steps belong to his API flow? (Select two)

options.text: Call TabInfo:GetConnectedFieldsTabGroups to retrieve the connected fields tab definitions for the installed app
Call the app's Get Type Definitions endpoint directly from the portal to build the tabs
Place the returned extension data in each tab's extensionData and then call Envelopes:create
Add the connected fields as a step in a Maestro workflow that the portal triggers
Create the envelope first and then call Get Type Names to attach the verification to it

answerText: Call TabInfo:GetConnectedFieldsTabGroups to retrieve the connected fields tab definitions for the installed app; Place the returned extension data in each tab's extensionData and then call Envelopes:create
explanation: The documented sequence for connected fields by API is TabInfo:GetConnectedFieldsTabGroups, then put the data in each tab's extensionData, then Envelopes:create.
whyNotOthers: A and C are right because the Connected Fields API returns the tab groups for installed apps and the integration copies that data into each tab's extensionData before creating the envelope. The trap is B: Get Type Definitions is an action Docusign calls on the extension app when the connection is created or refreshed, not something the portal calls to build tabs. D fails because connected fields are not supported in Maestro, and E reverses the flow by attaching verification after creation.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. TabInfo:GetConnectedFieldsTabGroups retrieves the connected fields tab groups available from installed apps.
optionExplanations.B: Get Type Definitions is called by Docusign on the external service during connection or refresh; the integration uses the Connected Fields API instead.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. Each tab's extensionData carries the connected field information, and then Envelopes:create sends the envelope.
optionExplanations.D: Connected fields are not currently supported in Maestro workflows.
optionExplanations.E: Get Type Names is a Docusign-to-app action run at connect or refresh time; verification data must be on the tabs when the envelope is created.

concept.title: Connected fields by API sequence
concept.line: Sequence: TabInfo:GetConnectedFieldsTabGroups, place data in each tab's extensionData, then Envelopes:create; do not call the app's endpoints directly.

decode.prompt: What does Tomas's portal need?

options.text: Build the field definitions by calling the extension service directly
Attach verification to an envelope after it has been created
Add verified app fields to API-created envelopes automatically, using the definitions Docusign holds for the installed app
Hand envelope creation over to an orchestrated workflow

decode.explanation: 'add the same verified fields to envelopes his portal sends without any manual preparation' is the connected fields by API flow: get the tab groups, fill extensionData, then create the envelope.
clues: 'creates envelopes through the eSignature REST API' -> stays on Envelopes:create
'same verified fields ... App Fields' -> connected fields tab groups
'keep his existing JSON SIM Connect listener' -> red herring
decode.needs: GetConnectedFieldsTabGroups, then extensionData in each tab, then Envelopes:create.

stem: Which statement correctly describes the default eSignature REST API hourly limit?

options.text: 3,000 calls per hour per account, shared by all integrations that call the account, resetting at the top of the hour
3,000 calls per hour per integration key, measured over a rolling 60-minute window for each key
1,000 calls per hour per account, after which extra calls are queued and run at the start of the next hour
500 calls per hour per integration key, plus a separate burst allowance of 200 calls every 30 seconds

answerText: 3,000 calls per hour per account, shared by all integrations that call the account, resetting at the top of the hour
explanation: The default hourly limit is 3,000 calls per hour per account. All integrations that call the account share it, and it resets on the hour.
whyNotOthers: A is right: 3,000 per account per hour, shared, resetting on the hour. The trap is B: the number is right, but the limit applies to the account, not to each key, and it resets on the hour rather than over a rolling window. C fails because the number is wrong and excess calls are blocked, not queued. D mixes up the burst limits (500 per 30 seconds in production, 200 in demo) with the hourly limit.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. The limit is 3,000 per hour per account, shared by all apps, and resets on the hour.
optionExplanations.B: The limit is per account and shared, not per integration key, and it resets on the hour.
optionExplanations.C: The default is 3,000, and calls over the limit are blocked, not queued.
optionExplanations.D: 500 per 30 seconds (production) and 200 (demo) are burst limits, not the hourly limit.

concept.title: Hourly API limit
concept.line: Default 3,000 calls per hour per account, shared by all integrations calling it, resetting at the top of the hour (not rolling per key).

stem: Harbor Lane Insurance embeds a claims intake web form in its customer portal. When a customer clicks Start Claim, the Node.js backend calls Instances:createInstance with a clientUserId and an expirationOffset of 72, caches the whole response, and the page renders the instance with Docusign JS. QA reports that customers who open the claim page, take a phone call, and click Start Claim again about ten minutes later get an error instead of the form, even though the instance itself still has days left before it expires. The team does not want duplicate instances per claim. What should the backend do before rendering the cached instance again?

options.text: Call Instances:createInstance again with a longer expirationOffset so the new instance outlives the session.
Call EnvelopeViews:createRecipient with the same clientUserId to obtain a fresh URL for the web form.
Call Instances:refreshToken with the cached instance id and render with the new instanceToken it returns.
Raise expirationOffset on the existing instance so that its instance token stays valid for the full 72 hours.

answerText: Call Instances:refreshToken with the cached instance id and render with the new instanceToken it returns.
explanation: The instance token returned by createInstance expires five minutes after it is generated and that period cannot be changed. The clue is 'about ten minutes later' while 'the instance itself still has days left': Instances:refreshToken with the instance id issues a new five-minute token for the same instance.
whyNotOthers: C is right because only the token expired, and refreshToken renews it for the existing instance. The trap is D: expirationOffset sets the lifetime of the instance, not of its token, which is fixed at five minutes. A creates the duplicate instance the team wants to avoid, and B is an eSignature signing view, not the way to render a web form instance.

optionExplanations.A: Creates a second instance for the same claim, which the team explicitly wants to avoid; the original instance was still valid.
optionExplanations.B: EnvelopeViews:createRecipient produces an eSignature signing URL for an envelope, not a web form instance URL.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. refreshToken takes the instance id and returns a new instanceToken (again valid five minutes) until the instance expires.
optionExplanations.D: expirationOffset controls when the instance expires; the instance token always expires after five minutes and cannot be extended.

concept.title: Web form instance token: 5 minutes
concept.line: The createInstance instanceToken expires after five minutes (fixed); Instances:refreshToken with the instance id issues a new token for the same instance.

decode.prompt: What has actually expired?

options.text: Extend the lifetime of the existing instance
Create a new instance with a longer lifetime
Renew the short-lived access token for an existing instance without creating a new instance
Obtain a signing session link for the form user

decode.explanation: 'about ten minutes later' while 'the instance itself still has days left' means the five-minute instance token expired, not the instance; refreshToken issues a new token for the same instance.
clues: 'caches the whole response' -> cached instanceToken goes stale
'about ten minutes later' -> instance tokens last five minutes
'instance itself still has days left' -> expirationOffset is not the issue
'does not want duplicate instances' -> no new createInstance
decode.needs: Call Instances:refreshToken with the cached instance id and render with the new token.

topic: Choosing connected fields vs data verification
stem: Meridian Mutual, an insurer, sends renewal agreements from eSignature. Its developer Kwame must check, while the policyholder is filling in the envelope, that the policy number, the vehicle VIN and the named driver together match one record in Meridian's own policy administration system, and show the signer a custom message telling them what to fix. A colleague suggests reusing the address-validation extension already installed for mailing addresses. Meridian also runs Maestro workflows for claims, but those are out of scope here. Which extension type and extension point should Kwame use?

options.text: Data verification extension, invoked at the eSignature Add Fields view and signing
Data IO extension, invoked from a read step in a Maestro workflow
Connected fields extension, invoked at the eSignature Add Fields view and signing
Connected fields extension, invoked from an extension step in a Maestro workflow

answerText: Connected fields extension, invoked at the eSignature Add Fields view and signing
explanation: The data is a proprietary multi-property policy record in Meridian's own system of record and must be checked 'while the policyholder is filling in the envelope', which is exactly the connected fields extension at the eSignature Add Fields and signing extension point.
whyNotOthers: C is right because connected fields verify any data against your own system of record during eSignature preparation and signing, and the response can carry custom messages. The trap is A: data verification has the same extension point but only verifies specific predefined data types (bank account, email, phone, SSN, postal address, business FEIN), not a proprietary policy record. B is a Maestro-only extension and D fails because connected fields are not supported in Maestro workflows.

optionExplanations.A: Right extension point, but data verification extensions verify fixed data types such as bank account or postal address, not a custom policy record in Meridian's own system.
optionExplanations.B: Data IO reads and writes a system of record from Maestro workflow steps; it is not invoked while a signer fills in an eSignature envelope.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. Connected fields verify custom data against the organization's system of record at the eSignature Add Fields and signing extension point and can return custom guidance messages.
optionExplanations.D: Right extension type, wrong extension point: connected fields are not currently supported in Maestro workflows.

concept.title: Connected fields for proprietary data
concept.line: Proprietary data in your own system of record, checked while filling the envelope, uses connected fields at Add Fields and signing.

decode.prompt: Which requirement decides the extension type?

options.text: Validate a single standard data type such as a mailing address
Read data into an orchestrated workflow step
Check values in a workflow step after signing
Verify a combination of values against the company's own system of record while the signer fills in the envelope

decode.explanation: 'together match one record in Meridian's own policy administration system' during envelope fill-in is a proprietary multi-property check at the eSignature Add Fields and signing point, which is connected fields.
clues: 'together match one record' -> multi-property concept, connected fields
'Meridian's own policy administration system' -> proprietary system of record
'while the policyholder is filling in the envelope' -> eSignature Add Fields and signing
'Maestro workflows ... out of scope' and 'address-validation' -> red herrings
decode.needs: Connected fields extension at the eSignature Add Fields and signing extension point.

topic: Start method for an API-triggered embedded workflow
stem: Priya at Kestrel Lending is wiring a 'Start application' button in the company's authenticated loan portal. Her Node.js server already holds a JWT access token with the aow_manage scope. When a logged-in customer clicks the button, the server must start a Docusign workflow, pass the customer's name, email and loan amount as starting variable values in trigger_inputs, and then show the returned instance URL inside an iframe on the portal page. The marketing team also wants a shareable URL for a future email campaign, but that is out of scope for this release. Which start method should Priya set on the workflow?

options.text: From a Link, because the instance will be displayed in an iframe on the portal
Manually in Docusign, so a user with Workflows: Prepare permission runs it for each applicant
From an API call, because the server triggers it and passes starting variables in trigger_inputs
From an Event, so the portal's button click is treated as a Docusign platform event

answerText: From an API call, because the server triggers it and passes starting variables in trigger_inputs
explanation: The server itself triggers the workflow with Workflows:triggerWorkflow and passes starting variable values in trigger_inputs; for that case Docusign recommends the From an API call start method, and API-call workflows can still be embedded via the returned instance URL.
whyNotOthers: C is right because the deciding clue is that the server triggers the instance and passes starting variables in trigger_inputs. The trap is A: From a Link is also supported for embedded instances, but it is meant for a participant opening a URL, and Docusign recommends From an API call when trigger_inputs carry starting values; the email-campaign link is explicitly out of scope. B needs an internal user to run every instance, and D is not driven by a button in your own application.

optionExplanations.A: Wrong. From a Link suits a participant opening a URL (website or email); with starting values passed in trigger_inputs, the recommended start method is From an API call.
optionExplanations.B: Wrong. Manually in Docusign means someone inside the organization clicks Run Workflow; it does not let the portal start instances for customers.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. A server-side trigger with trigger_inputs is the From an API call pattern, and the instance_url it returns can be embedded in an iframe.
optionExplanations.D: Wrong. An event-based start reacts to a Docusign event, not to a click in a custom application; the button maps to an API call.

concept.title: API-triggered workflow start method
concept.line: When a server triggers a workflow via triggerWorkflow with trigger_inputs, use From an API call; it can still be embedded via the returned URL.

decode.prompt: Which requirement decides the start method?

options.text: React to an occurrence inside Docusign
A server starts each run itself and passes starting variable values with the request
Display the running workflow inside the portal page
Have a Docusign user start each run by hand

decode.explanation: The server 'must start a Docusign workflow, pass ... starting variable values in trigger_inputs', which is the From an API call start method; embedding via instance URL also works with that method.
clues: 'server must start a Docusign workflow' -> triggerWorkflow call
'starting variable values in trigger_inputs' -> API-call start method
'inside an iframe' -> red herring, API-triggered instances can be embedded
'shareable URL ... out of scope' -> not From a Link
decode.needs: Start method From an API call.

stem: Quarry Point Capital is building an internal copilot that answers questions such as 'Which of our NDAs are governed by California law?' through retrieval-augmented generation over Agreement Manager data. Every answer must cite the agreement it came from. Contract admins sometimes correct AI-extracted values in the Agreement Manager UI, and the security team has asked that the copilot never modify the agreement repository itself. Which two design choices are appropriate? (Select two)

options.text: Use GetAgreementsList and GetAgreement to pull agreements with their parties and provisions as the data source.
Call CreateAgreementSummary for every agreement and index the summaries as the structured provisions.
Index each record in the retrieval store keyed by agreementId so answers can cite the source agreement.
Read each envelope's form data with the eSignature REST API, which exposes the same AI-extracted provisions.
Call DeleteAgreement after indexing so the copilot never retrieves stale or duplicate agreement records.

answerText: Use GetAgreementsList and GetAgreement to pull agreements with their parties and provisions as the data source.; Index each record in the retrieval store keyed by agreementId so answers can cite the source agreement.
explanation: The list and get operations return AI-extracted (and user-corrected) parties and provisions and are documented as a data source for RAG and copilots; keying the index by agreementId lets each answer cite its source.
whyNotOthers: A and C are right because they supply structured data and traceable citations. The trap is B: summaries are narrative text, not structured provisions, so filtering by governing law would be unreliable. D fails because the eSignature API does not surface AI-extracted provisions, and E deletes agreements from the repository, which the security team forbade.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. GetAgreementsList and GetAgreement return structured AI-extracted data and are intended for RAG and copilots.
optionExplanations.B: A summary is free text; the structured provisions needed for precise filtering come from list and get.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. Keying by agreementId keeps every retrieved chunk traceable to its source agreement.
optionExplanations.D: The eSignature API returns envelope data, not Agreement Manager's AI-extracted provisions.
optionExplanations.E: DeleteAgreement removes the agreement from the repository, which modifies it and destroys the source.

concept.title: Agreement data as RAG source
concept.line: GetAgreementsList/GetAgreement return AI-extracted and user-corrected parties and provisions, a documented RAG source; key the index by agreementId for citations.

decode.prompt: What do the copilot's constraints require?

options.text: Use AI-written prose overviews as the structured data
Use data captured during signing as the source
A read-only source of structured agreement data, indexed so each answer can point back to its agreement
Clean the repository after indexing to avoid duplicates

decode.explanation: 'cite the agreement it came from' needs indexing by agreementId, 'never modify the agreement repository' rules out deletes, and list and get return the corrected parties and provisions.
clues: 'retrieval-augmented generation over Agreement Manager data' -> list and get as data source
'must cite the agreement' -> key records by agreementId
'correct AI-extracted values' -> read provisions from Agreement Manager, not envelopes
'never modify the agreement repository' -> no DeleteAgreement
decode.needs: GetAgreementsList and GetAgreement as the source, indexed by agreementId.

stem: Harbor Logistics' operations dashboard shows signing progress. A background job calls Envelopes:get for every in-flight envelope every 5 minutes, and about 1,500 envelopes are usually in flight. Since go-live, the API Usage Center shows a poor efficiency score, and some calls fail with Hourly_Envelope_Polling_Limit_Exceeded. The team lead proposes that an admin use Update Hourly Limit to raise the account's limit, since the plan allows it. The business only needs the dashboard to change when an envelope or recipient status actually changes. What is the best fix?

options.text: Raise the account's hourly limit in the API Usage Center so the 5-minute polling job is no longer blocked
Subscribe to envelope and recipient events with Connect, drop per-envelope polling, and use listStatusChanges only for catch-up
Slow the job to check each envelope every 10 minutes, which keeps it under the per-envelope polling limit
Replace Envelopes:get with EnvelopeRecipients:list every 5 minutes, because recipient status checks are not polling

answerText: Subscribe to envelope and recipient events with Connect, drop per-envelope polling, and use listStatusChanges only for catch-up
explanation: The job breaks the rule of at most one status check per envelope every 15 minutes, which is what the per-envelope polling error reports. Connect pushes only real changes, and its messages do not count against API limits; listStatusChanges covers catch-up.
whyNotOthers: B is right because Connect removes the polling that causes both the error and the poor score. The trap is A: raising the hourly limit requires efficient apps, and the per-envelope polling limit would still be broken. C fails because 10 minutes is still more often than once per 15 minutes, and D fails because excessive recipient status requests are themselves an efficiency score factor.

optionExplanations.A: A higher hourly limit does not lift the per-envelope polling limit, and the limit can only be raised for apps that are efficient.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. Connect sends only real status changes and does not count against API limits; listStatusChanges handles catch-up.
optionExplanations.C: Polling every 10 minutes still exceeds the limit of one status check per envelope per 15 minutes.
optionExplanations.D: Excessive recipient status requests are a listed efficiency factor; this only moves the polling to another endpoint.

concept.title: Polling limit vs Connect
concept.line: Poll each envelope at most once per 15 minutes; use Connect for changes (not counted against limits) and listStatusChanges for catch-up.

decode.prompt: What does the business really need?

options.text: Check each envelope a little less often
Check status through a different resource on the same schedule
Allow the current per-envelope checking to continue unchanged
Learn about status changes when they happen instead of repeatedly asking about each envelope

decode.explanation: 'only needs the dashboard to change when an envelope or recipient status actually changes' is event-driven notification, and per-envelope polling every 5 minutes breaks the 15-minute rule regardless of the hourly limit.
clues: 'Hourly_Envelope_Polling_Limit_Exceeded' -> per-envelope polling rule, not the hourly limit
'every 5 minutes' -> more often than once per 15 minutes
'only ... when ... status actually changes' -> Connect events
'raise the account's limit' -> red herring
decode.needs: Connect for envelope and recipient events, with listStatusChanges only for catch-up.

topic: Identity verification in the eSignature API
stem: A developer must require government photo ID verification for one signer in an envelope created with eSignature REST API v2.1. What should be added to that signer?

options.text: An authenticationMethod value describing ID verification, passed when calling EnvelopeViews:createRecipient.
An idCheckConfigurationName value set to the account's ID Check configuration name.
An identityVerification object whose workflowId comes from IdentityVerifications:list.
The step ID of a Verify Someone's Identity step copied from a Workflow Builder workflow.

answerText: An identityVerification object whose workflowId comes from IdentityVerifications:list.
explanation: ID verification is requested on the recipient with identityVerification.workflowId, and the workflow IDs available to the account come from IdentityVerifications:list.
whyNotOthers: C is right because identityVerification.workflowId is how v2.1 enforces IDV for a recipient. The trap is A: authenticationMethod on createRecipient only records how your app authenticated the user; it enforces nothing. B configures KBA (ID Check), not photo ID, and D belongs to Workflow Builder, not to an eSignature envelope.

optionExplanations.A: authenticationMethod only records your app's own authentication on the certificate; it does not enforce IDV.
optionExplanations.B: idCheckConfigurationName (for example 'ID Check $') is knowledge-based authentication, US public-record questions.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. Add identityVerification with a workflowId retrieved from IdentityVerifications:list.
optionExplanations.D: Workflow Builder steps are not referenced from an eSignature recipient definition.

concept.title: ID verification on recipients
concept.line: Request ID verification with the recipient's identityVerification.workflowId; available workflow IDs come from IdentityVerifications:list.

stem: Orion Insurance sends policy renewals through its claims app. Sometimes an underwriter must change the premium field on a renewal that is already out for signature, and while the change is being made nobody may sign the old value. After the edit, the same envelope must continue to the same signer without being re-sent. The team already has Connect for status and must not create duplicate envelopes. Which approach should the developer implement?

options.text: Void the envelope with a voidedReason, update the tab, then change the status back to sent
Call EnvelopeRecipients:update to replace the signer, which pauses signing until the change is done
Set the envelope back to created status, update the tab, then set the status to sent again
Create an envelope lock with EnvelopeLocks:create, update the tab with EnvelopeRecipientTabs:update, then release the lock

answerText: Create an envelope lock with EnvelopeLocks:create, update the tab with EnvelopeRecipientTabs:update, then release the lock
explanation: A lock (correct status) temporarily prevents recipients from acting for a set duration or until it is released, which fits "nobody may sign the old value" while the envelope stays the same. The tab is then changed with EnvelopeRecipientTabs:update.
whyNotOthers: D is right because the requirement is a temporary hold on the same envelope. The trap is A: voiding stops signing, but it is permanent and voided is a terminal status, so the envelope cannot be changed or resumed. B replaces a recipient rather than holding the envelope. C is not the documented way to put a sent envelope on hold; locking is.

optionExplanations.A: voided is terminal: no further changes can be made and the envelope cannot be sent again.
optionExplanations.B: EnvelopeRecipients:update replaces a recipient; it is not a hold mechanism for editing.
optionExplanations.C: The documented way to hold a sent envelope while editing is a lock, not moving it back to draft.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. Locks are temporary (lockType, app name, duration in seconds); tabs are updated with EnvelopeRecipientTabs:update.

concept.title: Envelope lock for in-process edits
concept.line: To change an in-process envelope safely: EnvelopeLocks:create, EnvelopeRecipientTabs:update, then release; the lock blocks recipient action meanwhile.

decode.prompt: Which requirement decides the approach?

options.text: Change who the recipient is
Temporarily stop anyone acting on an in-flight envelope while a field value is edited, then let the same envelope continue
Cancel the envelope and send it again after the edit
Move the envelope back to a draft state

decode.explanation: 'nobody may sign the old value' while 'the same envelope must continue ... without being re-sent' is an envelope lock followed by a tab update, then release.
clues: 'nobody may sign the old value' -> lock the envelope
'same envelope must continue to the same signer' -> no void, no new envelope
'change the premium field' -> EnvelopeRecipientTabs:update
'already has Connect' -> red herring
decode.needs: EnvelopeLocks:create, EnvelopeRecipientTabs:update, then release the lock.

topic: Storing completed files from a workflow
stem: VaultCo sells a secure document vault and wants Docusign customers to drop their completed agreements into it automatically as the last step of their Maestro workflows, next to steps that already push deal status into Salesforce. VaultCo's architect proposes reusing the record-writing logic they built for the CRM integration, because 'a file is just another record'. A second engineer found an older sample built on the file archive extension and wants to copy it. Which extension should VaultCo build for this new app?

options.text: File output cloud storage extension (File IO), used from a Maestro workflow step
Data IO extension with a Create Record action that writes the agreement into the vault
File archive extension, because it is the extension Docusign recommends for new storage apps
Connected fields extension, used after the final signer completes the envelope

answerText: File output cloud storage extension (File IO), used from a Maestro workflow step
explanation: The requirement is to store completed agreement files from a Maestro workflow step, which is the file output cloud storage extension; the docs say file output cloud storage is for new apps and file archive is legacy.
whyNotOthers: A is right because writing files to a cloud storage system from a workflow is the File IO (file output cloud storage) extension. The trap is B: Data IO reads and writes structured records in a system of record, it does not deliver document files to storage. C fails because file archive is the legacy option, not the recommended one for new apps, and D verifies field values during signing and is not supported in Maestro.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. The file output cloud storage extension writes files to a cloud storage system and is invoked from Maestro workflows; it is the choice for new apps.
optionExplanations.B: Data IO actions such as Create Record handle structured record data in a system of record, not storing agreement documents.
optionExplanations.C: File archive is the legacy extension; Docusign recommends file output cloud storage for new apps.
optionExplanations.D: Connected fields verify signer-entered values against a system of record during signing; they do not store files and are not supported in Maestro.

concept.title: Storing files from a workflow
concept.line: Storing completed files from a Maestro step uses the file output cloud storage (File IO) extension; file archive is legacy.

decode.prompt: What kind of capability does VaultCo's app provide?

options.text: Write completed agreement files to external storage from a workflow step, using the current (not legacy) storage extension
Verify field values during signing
Write a business record into a system of record
Use the storage extension found in older samples

decode.explanation: 'drop their completed agreements into it ... as the last step of their Maestro workflows' is file storage from a workflow, which is file output cloud storage; file archive is legacy.
clues: 'drop their completed agreements into it' -> files, not records
'last step of their Maestro workflows' -> workflow step extension
'a file is just another record' -> misreading toward Data IO
'older sample built on the file archive extension' -> legacy
decode.needs: File output cloud storage (File IO) extension used from a Maestro workflow step.

stem: Kestrel HR sells a payroll SaaS product and wants to add contract signing inside it for hundreds of small-business customers. Most of these customers have never used Docusign and will not buy their own accounts. Kestrel will pay for one Docusign account that it owns and controls, and every envelope will be sent through that account on its customers' behalf. The product manager also mentions a possible App Center listing and partner referral revenue in a later year, but that is not part of this release. Under 'How will you use this integration?', which classification should Kestrel choose for this integration key?

options.text: Public integration, because the app serves many customers and Kestrel can earn referral revenue through the Partner Program
Private custom integration, because Kestrel's own Docusign account is the only account the key will call
Third-party integration key, because Kestrel's customers are third parties who never see the integration key
Embedded integration, which needs an ISV Embed partner license because customers use the features through Kestrel's account

answerText: Embedded integration, which needs an ISV Embed partner license because customers use the features through Kestrel's account
explanation: The deciding clue is that customers 'will not buy their own accounts' and use Docusign features through one account that Kestrel 'owns and controls'. That is the definition of an Embedded integration, which requires an ISV Embed partner license.
whyNotOthers: D is right because the customers have no Docusign accounts of their own and use Kestrel's account. The trap is A: a Public integration is for many Docusign customers who use their own accounts and authorize the app, and the referral revenue is explicitly out of scope for this release. B fails because Private custom integration is for an integration used directly by your or your clients' employees, not for offering Docusign features as a service inside a product. C fails because Third-party integration key is chosen by a customer who must supply its own key to a partner's integration.

optionExplanations.A: Public integration means customers use their own Docusign accounts and authorize the app; Kestrel's customers have no accounts.
optionExplanations.B: Private custom integration covers integrations used directly by your or your clients' employees, not offering Docusign features as a service in your product.
optionExplanations.C: Third-party integration key is for a customer who must supply its own key to a partner product, which is the reverse of this case.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. Embedding Docusign features in your product, delivered through your own account to customers without accounts, is an Embedded integration (ISV Embed license).

concept.title: Embedded integration classification
concept.line: Customers using Docusign through an account you own and control, without their own accounts, is an Embedded integration requiring an ISV Embed partner license.

decode.prompt: Which fact decides the classification?

options.text: The product serves many customers and may earn partner revenue
Customers never see the integration credentials
Only one Docusign account is ever called
Customers use signing features through one account owned and paid for by the software vendor, without their own accounts

decode.explanation: 'will not buy their own accounts' and one account Kestrel 'owns and controls' sending on customers' behalf define an Embedded integration, which needs an ISV Embed license.
clues: 'will not buy their own accounts' -> not Public integration
'one Docusign account that it owns and controls' -> Embedded integration
'on its customers' behalf' -> ISV Embed partner license
'App Center listing ... later year' -> red herring
decode.needs: Embedded integration classification with an ISV Embed partner license.

topic: Test prerequisites in the Developer Console
stem: In the Developer Console, which prerequisite is required before running functional tests but is NOT required before running integration tests?

options.text: Setting up an API proxy if the external API does not match the Docusign contract
Successful connection test and successful extension tests for each extension
An account with the authorization provider whose credentials you supply in the test
A registered extension app in the Developer Console

answerText: Successful connection test and successful extension tests for each extension
explanation: Functional tests require a successful connection test and successful extension tests for every extension; integration tests are those connection and extension tests themselves.
whyNotOthers: B is right because functional tests build on passed integration tests. The trap is A: an API proxy, when needed, is required for both integration and functional tests. C is also required for both, and D is required for every test type, including the App Center preview.

optionExplanations.A: Required for both integration and functional tests (not for App Center preview), so it is not what distinguishes them.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. A successful connection test and extension tests for each extension are prerequisites only for functional tests.
optionExplanations.C: Credentials for the authorization provider are needed for both integration and functional tests.
optionExplanations.D: Registration is required for integration tests, functional tests and the App Center preview alike.

concept.title: Functional test prerequisites
concept.line: Functional tests require a successful connection test and successful extension tests for every extension; those are the integration tests.

stem: Kestrel Lending generates loan agreements as PDFs whose clauses vary in length, so the signature line moves between pages 3 and 5. The direct documents model is used, and there is no template. A developer sets anchorString "Borrower Signature" with anchorUnits inches and anchorXOffset 1. Testing shows the signature tab now follows the moving signature line, but every envelope also gets a second signature tab on page 1, where the table of contents lists the "Borrower Signature" section. Which approach fixes this while keeping the placement dynamic?

options.text: Replace the anchors with xPosition and yPosition values calculated for page 3, the most common page
Add a unique hidden anchor string such as /sn1/ only at the signature line and anchor to it
Keep "Borrower Signature" and set anchorIgnoreIfNotPresent to true to suppress the extra match
Move the tab definition into a server template so its fixed tab placement is reused for every loan

answerText: Add a unique hidden anchor string such as /sn1/ only at the signature line and anchor to it
explanation: An anchor tab is placed at every occurrence of anchorString in the documents, so a phrase that also appears in the table of contents creates a second tab. A unique string (for example /sn1/, often in white text) placed only at the signature line keeps the dynamic placement and removes the duplicate.
whyNotOthers: B is right because the deciding clue is the second occurrence of the phrase on page 1. The trap is C: anchorIgnoreIfNotPresent only controls whether a missing anchor string causes an error; it does not reduce multiple matches. A and D both go back to fixed positions, which break when the text moves between pages.

optionExplanations.A: Fixed xPosition and yPosition break when the signature line moves between pages 3 and 5.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. Anchor tabs are added at each occurrence of the string, so use a string that appears only at the signature line.
optionExplanations.C: anchorIgnoreIfNotPresent only decides whether a missing string is an error; it does not remove extra matches.
optionExplanations.D: Fixed template placement has the same problem as absolute coordinates when the content shifts.

concept.title: Anchor tabs: use unique strings
concept.line: Anchor tabs are placed at every occurrence of anchorString; use a unique (often hidden white) string like /sn1/ at the target only.

decode.prompt: What does the placement really require?

options.text: Ignore a marker when it cannot be found
A reusable document definition with fixed field positions
A marker that occurs only at the signature line, so placement stays dynamic but matches once
Fixed coordinates on the most likely page

decode.explanation: Anchor tabs are placed at every occurrence of the anchor string, and 'Borrower Signature' also appears in the table of contents; a unique hidden string fixes the duplicate while keeping dynamic placement.
clues: 'signature line moves between pages 3 and 5' -> placement must stay dynamic
'second signature tab on page 1 ... table of contents' -> anchor matches every occurrence
'no template' and 'direct documents model' -> anchors in the request
decode.needs: A unique hidden anchor string such as /sn1/ placed only at the signature line.

stem: Kestrel Freight runs a containerized reconciliation service that, every night at 02:00, voids stale envelopes and downloads completed documents as a dedicated Docusign user named ops-sender. Nobody ever signs in as ops-sender and the service must never open a browser. Staff also use an internal Grafana dashboard through SSO, but it never calls Docusign. Last year the service was paused for 45 days during a data-center move and had to resume after restart with no human re-authorization. An administrator has already granted consent for the integration key. Which approach meets these requirements?

options.text: Confidential Authorization Code Grant with the extended scope, refreshing the refresh token on every nightly run
JWT Grant, building and signing a new assertion with the RSA private key whenever a fresh access token is needed
Public Authorization Code Grant with PKCE, keeping the refresh token in an encrypted volume between runs
Implicit Grant, requesting a new access token from the authorization endpoint at the start of each nightly run

answerText: JWT Grant, building and signing a new assertion with the RSA private key whenever a fresh access token is needed
explanation: JWT Grant is the flow for service integrations with no user present: after the one-time consent, the service signs a new JWT with its RSA private key whenever it needs a token, so a 45-day pause does not matter.
whyNotOthers: B is right because no one ever signs in and the service must survive a 45-day pause without re-authorization. The trap is A: extended makes the refresh token roll, but it still expires 30 days after the last refresh, so a 45-day pause forces a new interactive login (and the first token needs one too). C and D are user-interactive browser flows, and a Public refresh token lasts only up to 24 hours.

optionExplanations.A: Needs an interactive login to start, and an extended refresh token still expires 30 days after the last refresh, so the 45-day pause breaks it.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. JWT Grant needs no browser after consent; a new signed JWT gets a new 1-hour token at any time.
optionExplanations.C: Public Auth Code Grant is interactive and its refresh token lasts only up to 24 hours.
optionExplanations.D: Implicit Grant is a legacy browser flow that needs a user at the login page; it is not for headless services.

concept.title: JWT Grant for unattended services
concept.line: Service integrations with no user use JWT Grant: after one-time consent, sign a new JWT with the RSA private key whenever a token is needed.

decode.prompt: Which requirement decides the OAuth flow?

options.text: Authenticate from a client that cannot hold a secret
Obtain tokens repeatedly with no user or browser present, even after a long outage, from a server that can hold a private key
Let a signed-in person authorize in a browser and keep a refreshable token
Receive tokens directly in a browser redirect

decode.explanation: 'nobody ever signs in', 'must never open a browser' and 'resume after a 45-day pause with no human re-authorization' mean JWT Grant: sign a new assertion whenever a token is needed after one-time consent.
clues: 'nobody ever signs in as ops-sender' -> no user present
'must never open a browser' -> no Authorization Code flow
'paused for 45 days' -> refresh tokens would expire, JWT does not depend on them
'Grafana dashboard through SSO' -> red herring
decode.needs: JWT Grant, signing a new assertion with the RSA private key for each token.

topic: Request URL: base URI and account ID
stem: Lena's JWT integration works perfectly in the demo environment, where she hard-coded https://demo.docusign.net/restapi as the base path and put the user GUID from her JWT sub claim in the accounts segment of the URL. After go-live, the production account's users sit on a different server pod, and every Envelopes:create call fails even though tokens are issued correctly. Her integration key, consent and RSA key pair are all fine. Which change correctly builds the production request URL?

options.text: Keep the base path but replace the user GUID with the integration key in the accounts segment
Change only the host to www.docusign.net and keep the user GUID in the accounts segment
Call /oauth/userinfo and use the returned base_uri plus /restapi/v2.1/accounts/{account_id}/envelopes
Use the account base URI from Apps and Keys and keep the JWT sub value as the account identifier

answerText: Call /oauth/userinfo and use the returned base_uri plus /restapi/v2.1/accounts/{account_id}/envelopes
explanation: The request URL is {base_uri}/restapi/v2.1/accounts/{accountId}/envelopes, and both base_uri and the API account ID come from the userinfo endpoint after authentication. The clue is that she used the user GUID (sub) as the account and hard-coded a demo host.
whyNotOthers: C is right because it fixes both errors: the pod-specific base URI and the account ID. The trap is D: the account base URI is correct to use, but the JWT sub is a user ID, not the account ID. A uses the integration key, which identifies the app, not the account. B guesses a host and still uses the user GUID.

optionExplanations.A: The integration key identifies the app, not the account in the URL path.
optionExplanations.B: Production base URIs depend on the account's server, and the user GUID is still the wrong identifier.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. userinfo returns base_uri and account_id; build {base_uri}/restapi/v2.1/accounts/{account_id}/envelopes.
optionExplanations.D: The sub claim is the user ID; the path needs the API account ID.

concept.title: Building the request URL
concept.line: Request URL is {base_uri}/restapi/v2.1/accounts/{accountId}/...; both come from /oauth/userinfo, not the user GUID (sub) or a hard-coded host.

decode.prompt: What must the request URL be built from?

options.text: Use the integration key as the account in the path
Use the account's own server and API account identifier, both discovered after authentication
Switch to a single well-known production host
Use the user's identifier as the account in the path

decode.explanation: She used the user GUID (sub) as the account and hard-coded a demo host, while 'users sit on a different server pod'; userinfo returns base_uri and account_id for {base_uri}/restapi/v2.1/accounts/{account_id}.
clues: 'user GUID from her JWT sub claim in the accounts segment' -> wrong identifier
'hard-coded https://demo.docusign.net' -> wrong host after go-live
'different server pod' -> base_uri must come from userinfo
'tokens are issued correctly' -> auth is fine
decode.needs: base_uri and account_id from /oauth/userinfo to build the request URL.

stem: Imani, a developer at Lattice Health, is building a JWT Grant integration in the demo environment. She opened this URL, logged in as the user to be impersonated, and clicked Allow Access: https://account-d.docusign.com/oauth/auth?response_type=code&scope=signature&client_id={IK}&redirect_uri={registered URI}. Her JWT header uses RS256; in the payload, iss is the integration key, sub is the user's GUID, aud is account-d.docusign.com, exp is iat plus 3600, and scope is signature. The token request is still rejected because the required consent is missing. What should she change?

options.text: Add impersonation to the scope claim in the JWT payload and leave the consent URL as it is
Change aud to account.docusign.com, because consent is recorded on the production authentication server
Generate a new RSA key pair, because consent is bound to the key pair that existed when it was granted
Repeat consent with scope=signature%20impersonation in the URL, and keep only signature in the JWT payload scope

answerText: Repeat consent with scope=signature%20impersonation in the URL, and keep only signature in the JWT payload scope
explanation: JWT Grant needs consent that includes the impersonation scope (signature impersonation). Her consent URL requested only scope=signature; once impersonation consent exists, the JWT payload lists only the API scopes needed, such as signature.
whyNotOthers: D is right because the clue is the consent URL with scope=signature only. The trap is A: impersonation belongs in the consent request; putting it in the payload does not create consent that was never granted. B fails because demo apps use aud account-d.docusign.com, and C fails because consent is granted to the integration key for a user, not to a key pair.

optionExplanations.A: The payload cannot grant consent; impersonation must be in the consent request.
optionExplanations.B: In demo the aud must be account-d.docusign.com; switching to production would break the request.
optionExplanations.C: The RSA key signs the JWT; consent is not tied to a specific key pair.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. Consent must include signature impersonation; the payload then needs only signature.

concept.title: JWT consent needs impersonation
concept.line: JWT consent must include impersonation (scope=signature impersonation); the JWT payload scope then lists only API scopes like signature.

decode.prompt: What is the consent actually missing?

options.text: Replace the signing key pair
The user's one-time consent must include the right to be impersonated; the token request itself lists only the API scopes it needs
Point the token request at the production auth server
Put the impersonation right into each token request

decode.explanation: The consent URL used only scope=signature, but JWT Grant needs consent covering signature impersonation; the JWT payload scope can stay signature.
clues: 'scope=signature' in the consent URL -> impersonation consent missing
'aud is account-d.docusign.com' -> correct for demo
'required consent is missing' -> fix the consent, not the payload
decode.needs: Redo consent with scope=signature%20impersonation; keep signature in the JWT payload.

topic: Choosing the trigger event for intermediate document capture
stem: Westbrook Lending sends a two-signer loan agreement: the borrower signs first and the bank officer countersigns second. Regulators require the bank to archive a copy of the document immediately after the borrower signs and before the officer receives it, and the archive must also show who signed when. The integration already has an account-level JSON SIM configuration that posts envelope-sent and envelope-completed events, and the developer is under pressure to stay well within API limits. What should the developer add?

options.text: Poll EnvelopeRecipients:list every 15 minutes and download the document when the borrower's status changes to completed
Include documents in the existing envelope-completed event and archive the borrower's copy from that message
Subscribe to envelope-delivered and archive the document when the officer opens the envelope
Subscribe to the recipient-completed event with documents included and archive when the borrower's event arrives

answerText: Subscribe to the recipient-completed event with documents included and archive when the borrower's event arrives
explanation: recipient-completed fires for each recipient who finishes, so the borrower's signature produces its own message before the officer is routed the envelope. Connect is documented as the way to save a document after the first signer signs but before the second receives it.
whyNotOthers: D is right because recipient-completed is the per-recipient event and including documents gives the archive copy at the right moment without API calls. The trap is B: envelope-completed only fires after the officer has also signed, which is too late for the regulatory copy. A fails because polling uses API calls and, at 15-minute intervals, can easily miss the window before the officer receives the envelope; C fires when the officer opens the envelope, which is after they received it.

optionExplanations.A: Polling counts against API limits and a 15-minute interval cannot guarantee capture before the officer receives the envelope.
optionExplanations.B: envelope-completed fires only when every recipient has finished, so the copy would already include the officer's countersignature.
optionExplanations.C: envelope-delivered relates to the envelope being opened, which happens after the officer has already received it, missing the required window.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. recipient-completed fires as soon as the borrower finishes, and including documents in the message delivers the copy before the officer is routed the envelope.

concept.title: recipient-completed for intermediate capture
concept.line: recipient-completed fires as each recipient finishes, so Connect can save documents after the first signer, before the next; envelope-completed comes only at the end.

decode.prompt: Which requirement decides the trigger?

options.text: Get the document only when everyone has finished
Check periodically whether the first signer has finished
Detect when a later recipient opens the envelope
Get notified the moment one specific signer finishes, with the document, before the next signer is routed

decode.explanation: 'immediately after the borrower signs and before the officer receives it' needs a per-recipient completion event; 'stay well within API limits' rules out polling.
clues: 'immediately after the borrower signs' -> recipient-completed event
'before the officer receives it' -> envelope-completed is too late
'show who signed when' -> include documents and recipient data in the message
'well within API limits' -> no polling
decode.needs: Subscribe to recipient-completed with documents included.

stem: An organization administrator creates a custom organization-level Connect configuration through the Admin API. Which statement about that configuration is accurate?

options.text: It can be switched to legacy XML with aggregate delivery if the listener prefers fewer messages
Its settings always win over any account-level configuration that defines the same setting
It uses JSON SIM only, and logging and require-acknowledgement (automatic retries) are enabled automatically
It can be secured with Basic authentication, HMAC, mutual TLS or OAuth for Connect

answerText: It uses JSON SIM only, and logging and require-acknowledgement (automatic retries) are enabled automatically
explanation: Organization-level configurations support only the Connect 2.0 JSON SIM experience, and enable log and require acknowledgement (auto-retry) are auto-enabled for them.
whyNotOthers: C is right because org-level Connect is JSON SIM only with logging and auto-retry switched on. The trap is D: the security list looks complete, but org-level Connect supports HMAC, TLS and OAuth while Basic authentication is not supported. A fails because legacy XML and aggregate exist only at account and envelope level; B is reversed, because when both levels define a setting with different values the account-level value is used.

optionExplanations.A: Legacy XML and aggregate options are available only for account-level and envelope-level configurations; every org-level configuration uses JSON SIM.
optionExplanations.B: It is the reverse: if org-level and account-level configurations define the same setting differently, the account-level setting is used.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. Org-level configurations are JSON SIM only, and enable log plus require acknowledgement (automatic retries) are turned on automatically.
optionExplanations.D: Org-level Connect supports HMAC, TLS and OAuth, but Basic authentication is not supported at the organization level.

concept.title: Org-level Connect behaviour
concept.line: Organization-level Connect supports only JSON SIM, and logging and require acknowledgement (auto-retry) are enabled automatically.

stem: In an Envelopes:update request, which body permanently cancels a sent envelope that no recipient has finished signing?

options.text: status set to voided, with a voidedReason value
status set to correct, with a lock duration in seconds
status set to deleted, with a voidedReason value
status set to created, with a voidedReason value

answerText: status set to voided, with a voidedReason value
explanation: Voiding is done with Envelopes:update, setting status to voided and giving a voidedReason. Voiding is permanent and ends the lifecycle for all recipients.
whyNotOthers: A is right because voided is the documented permanent cancel. The trap is B: correct status puts the envelope on a temporary hold (lock) and does not cancel it. C uses deleted, which is not the cancel status. D tries to move a sent envelope back to draft, which does not cancel it.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. status voided plus voidedReason permanently terminates the envelope for all recipients.
optionExplanations.B: Correct status and locks are temporary holds; they do not cancel the envelope.
optionExplanations.C: deleted is not the status used to cancel an in-process envelope; voided is.
optionExplanations.D: created is the draft state, not a cancellation of a sent envelope.

concept.title: Voiding an envelope
concept.line: Void with Envelopes:update setting status voided plus a voidedReason; voiding is permanent and ends the lifecycle for all recipients.

stem: Omar, a developer at Brightline Credit, built a borrower portal that uses Confidential Authorization Code Grant. In the developer account he configured two redirect URIs, a secret key and a CORS origin. The Go-Live review passed, he selected the company's production account (where he is an admin), and the key now shows Live. He switched the auth host to account.docusign.com and kept the same integration key GUID in his config, but the production login now rejects his redirect and token requests fail. A colleague insists the key was moved and that the GUID must therefore have changed. What should Omar do?

options.text: Ask Docusign Support for the new production integration key GUID and replace the developer GUID in the app configuration
Resubmit the key for Go-Live review, because the review only copies the settings that his test calls actually exercised
In the production account's Apps and Keys page, add the redirect URIs and a new secret key to the promoted key, then update the app
Wait up to 48 hours, because redirect URIs and secrets are synchronized to production only after manual approval completes

answerText: In the production account's Apps and Keys page, add the redirect URIs and a new secret key to the promoted key, then update the app
explanation: When a key is promoted it is duplicated into production with the same value, but configuration parameters such as secrets and redirect URIs are not copied. Omar must add the redirect URIs and a secret on the production copy of the key in the production account's Apps and Keys page.
whyNotOthers: C is right because secrets and redirect URIs are never duplicated to production and must be added there. The trap is A: the colleague's 'moved' theory is wrong, the key is duplicated with the same value, so the GUID in Omar's config is already correct. B and D fail because no review or waiting period ever copies these settings; the key is already Live.

optionExplanations.A: The promoted key keeps the same value in production; there is no new GUID to obtain.
optionExplanations.B: Go-Live review does not copy any secrets or redirect URIs, whatever calls were made; re-review would not fix this.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. Secrets and redirect URIs are not copied at promotion; they must be added to the key in the production account.
optionExplanations.D: The key is already Live; there is no delayed synchronization of secrets or redirect URIs.

concept.title: Promoted key: config not copied
concept.line: Promotion duplicates the key with the same value, but secrets and redirect URIs are not copied; add them in production Apps and Keys.

decode.prompt: Why do redirects and token requests fail in production?

options.text: Wait for settings to synchronize automatically
Obtain a different key identifier for production
Recreate on the production copy of the key the settings that are not carried over by promotion
Have the key reviewed again

decode.explanation: Promotion copies the key with the same GUID, but redirect URIs and secrets are not copied, so they must be added on the production key in the production account's Apps and Keys.
clues: 'kept the same integration key GUID' -> correct, the GUID does not change
'production login now rejects his redirect' -> redirect URIs not copied
'token requests fail' -> secret key not copied
'GUID must therefore have changed' -> red herring
decode.needs: Add redirect URIs and a new secret key on the production key, then update the app.

topic: Prepare Document Template vs Prepare eSignature Template
stem: A workflow must produce an agreement whose clauses appear or disappear based on workflow variables (region and contract type) collected earlier. Which step pattern fits?

options.text: Prepare Document Template using conditional show/hide logic, followed by Send Documents for Signature
Prepare eSignature Template with one template for all instances, followed by Send Documents for Signature
Collect Data with Web Forms, followed directly by Send Documents for Signature with no prepare step
Prepare Document Template on its own, because it sends the generated document for signature itself

answerText: Prepare Document Template using conditional show/hide logic, followed by Send Documents for Signature
explanation: Prepare Document Template generates different document content from workflow variables using conditional show/hide logic; it, like Prepare eSignature Template, should be followed by Send Documents for Signature.
whyNotOthers: A is right because clauses vary with variables, which is the Prepare Document Template use case. The trap is B: Prepare eSignature Template is for a single template where the signed document is always exactly the same. C skips document preparation entirely, and D forgets that both prepare steps must be followed by the send step.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. Variable-driven content uses Prepare Document Template, then Send Documents for Signature.
optionExplanations.B: Wrong. Prepare eSignature Template fits when one fixed template serves every instance, not variable clauses.
optionExplanations.C: Wrong. A web form collects data but does not generate the agreement document to be signed.
optionExplanations.D: Wrong. A prepare step only prepares the document; Send Documents for Signature is still required.

concept.title: Prepare Document Template use
concept.line: Prepare Document Template generates varying document content from workflow variables with conditional show/hide; follow it with Send Documents for Signature.

topic: Public Auth Code Grant with PKCE
stem: Tomasz is building Parcelo, a React single-page application served from a CDN with no backend. Each warehouse supervisor signs in with their own Docusign credentials to send pick-list acknowledgements. Security review forbids any long-lived secret in the JavaScript bundle, and the app's Apps and Keys entry says it cannot securely store a client secret. To save time, the team lead suggests copying the token-request code from the company's older server-side portal, which uses Confidential Authorization Code Grant. Which two steps belong in Parcelo's authentication flow? (Select two)
