options.text: On the token request, send an Authorization: Basic header containing base64 of integrationKey:secretKey
On the /oauth/auth request, send a code_challenge made from a random string, with code_challenge_method S256
Request response_type=token so the access token comes back in the redirect and no code exchange is needed
On the /oauth/token request, send the original random string as code_verifier together with the authorization code
Request the extended scope so the refresh token stays valid for 30 days in the browser, as on the server portal

answerText: On the /oauth/auth request, send a code_challenge made from a random string, with code_challenge_method S256; On the /oauth/token request, send the original random string as code_verifier together with the authorization code
explanation: Public Auth Code Grant uses PKCE: the app hashes a random string with S256 and base64url-encodes it as code_challenge on /oauth/auth, then sends the original string as code_verifier on /oauth/token instead of a secret.
whyNotOthers: B and D are right because the app 'cannot securely store a client secret', so PKCE replaces the secret. The trap is A: the Basic integrationKey:secretKey header comes from the old Confidential portal, and Parcelo has no secret. C is the legacy Implicit Grant pattern, and E fails because a Public Auth Code refresh token lasts up to 24 hours, not 30 days.

optionExplanations.A: Basic integrationKey:secretKey is the Confidential flow; a public SPA has no secret.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. code_challenge (S256 hash, base64url) plus code_challenge_method S256 goes on /oauth/auth.
optionExplanations.C: response_type=token is the legacy Implicit Grant, which Docusign does not recommend.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. The code_verifier proves the same app that started the flow is finishing it.
optionExplanations.E: Public Auth Code Grant refresh tokens last up to 24 hours, not 30 days.

concept.title: PKCE in Public Auth Code Grant
concept.line: Send code_challenge (S256 hash of a random string) on /oauth/auth, then the original string as code_verifier on /oauth/token instead of a secret.

decode.prompt: Which requirement decides the authentication steps?

options.text: Receive the token directly in the browser redirect
Authenticate the token request with the app's client secret
Prove the token request comes from the same client that started login, without any stored secret
Keep a long-lived token in the browser

decode.explanation: A CDN-hosted SPA that 'cannot securely store a client secret' and forbids 'any long-lived secret in the JavaScript bundle' uses Public Auth Code Grant with PKCE: code_challenge on /oauth/auth, code_verifier on /oauth/token.
clues: 'no backend' and 'cannot securely store a client secret' -> public client
'forbids any long-lived secret' -> no Basic header, no extended refresh tokens
'copying ... Confidential Authorization Code Grant' -> red herring
decode.needs: PKCE: S256 code_challenge on the auth request, code_verifier on the token request.

topic: Pause new instances vs cancel one instance
stem: Brightwell Telecom runs a published 'Spring upgrade offer' workflow that customers start from an API call. Legal discovers a pricing error at 10:00. About 40 instances are already in progress and legal is happy for them to finish, because those customers saw the old, valid price. No customer may start a new instance until a corrected version is published. Separately, one in-progress customer, Mr. Osei, has asked to withdraw, so his instance must stop now while everything collected from him so far is kept. Which two Maestro API operations meet these requirements? (Select two)

options.text: pauseNewWorkflowInstances on the workflow
Unpublish the workflow so no new instances can be triggered
Edit the workflow steps and republish so running instances pick up the fix
cancelWorkflowInstance on Mr. Osei's instance

answerText: pauseNewWorkflowInstances on the workflow; cancelWorkflowInstance on Mr. Osei's instance
explanation: Pausing blocks new instances while active instances keep running, and cancelling a single instance stops further steps while keeping the data collected so far.
whyNotOthers: A and D are right: 'about 40 already in progress ... happy for them to finish' plus 'no new instance' is exactly what pause does, and cancelWorkflowInstance stops one instance and keeps its collected data. The trap is B: you can only unpublish a workflow that is already paused and has no running instances, so it cannot be the move here. C fails because editing never changes active instances; only new instances reflect the edit.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. Pausing stops new instances from being created while active instances continue to run.
optionExplanations.B: Wrong. Unpublishing requires the workflow to be paused first and no running instances, and 40 are still running.
optionExplanations.C: Wrong. Edits do not modify current active instances; only new instances reflect the changes.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. Cancelling an instance stops further steps for that instance; data collected up to that point is stored.

concept.title: Pause workflow vs cancel instance
concept.line: pauseNewWorkflowInstances blocks new instances while active ones run; cancelWorkflowInstance stops one instance's further steps, keeping collected data.

decode.prompt: What two separate controls are needed?

options.text: Block new runs of a workflow while letting current ones finish, and stop one specific run while keeping its data
Remove the workflow from use entirely
Apply the fix to runs already in progress
Stop all current runs at once

decode.explanation: 'No customer may start a new instance' while the 40 in progress finish is pausing new instances, and Mr. Osei's 'must stop now while everything collected ... is kept' is cancelling that one instance.
clues: 'legal is happy for them to finish' -> active instances keep running
'No customer may start a new instance' -> pause new instances
'his instance must stop now ... is kept' -> cancel that instance
decode.needs: pauseNewWorkflowInstances on the workflow and cancelWorkflowInstance on one instance.

stem: Brightway Logistics shows envelope status in a carrier portal. A scheduled job calls Envelopes:listStatus for every open envelope every five minutes, and the integration has started returning Hourly_Envelope_Polling_Limit_Exceeded errors. The go-live reviewer also flagged the polling pattern. The architect proposes an account-level Connect configuration and must justify it to management, who care most about API consumption and code complexity rather than message format. Which two statements are valid justifications? (Select two)

options.text: Connect messages are pushed by Docusign, so they do not count against the integration's API request limits
Having a Connect configuration raises the per-envelope allowance, so the five-minute status job becomes compliant
Messages arrive only when something changes, which removes the scheduling and re-query logic the job needs
A subscription to envelope-completed alone tells the portal each individual recipient's progress
After each message the listener calls Envelopes:get, which keeps status calls within the 15-minute rule

answerText: Connect messages are pushed by Docusign, so they do not count against the integration's API request limits; Messages arrive only when something changes, which removes the scheduling and re-query logic the job needs
explanation: Docusign documents three Connect advantages: messages do not count against API limits, they are delivered only when an envelope changes, and they remove cumbersome polling logic. Polling is limited to one GET per envelope every 15 minutes regardless of Connect.
whyNotOthers: A and C are right because they are the documented benefits: no API-limit consumption and event-driven delivery without polling logic. The trap is E: calling Envelopes:get after every message reintroduces API calls and is unnecessary because the message already carries the event data. B fails because the 15-minute per-envelope limit does not change when Connect is enabled; D fails because envelope-completed fires once for the whole envelope and cannot show per-recipient progress.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. Because Docusign pushes the data to the listener, Connect messages do not count against the API request limits.
optionExplanations.B: No setting raises the polling allowance; the limit stays at one GET per envelope every 15 minutes whether or not Connect is configured.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. Messages are delivered only when the envelope changes, so the app no longer needs custom logic deciding when to query again.
optionExplanations.D: envelope-completed fires only when the whole envelope is complete; per-recipient progress needs recipient events such as recipient-completed.
optionExplanations.E: The Connect message already contains the event data; calling Envelopes:get for every message adds API traffic and defeats the purpose of Connect.

concept.title: Connect advantages over polling
concept.line: Connect messages don't count against API limits, arrive only on change, and remove polling logic; polling stays limited to once per envelope per 15 minutes.

decode.prompt: What does management care about?

options.text: Keep querying status after each notification
Make the current polling schedule compliant
Track each recipient's progress with a single envelope event
Reduce API consumption and remove scheduling and re-query logic from the integration

decode.explanation: Management 'care most about API consumption and code complexity', which match the documented Connect advantages: messages do not count against limits and arrive only on change.
clues: 'API consumption' -> Connect messages do not count against API limits
'code complexity' -> no scheduling or re-query logic
'rather than message format' -> format is not the point
decode.needs: Justify Connect by no API-limit cost and change-only delivery.

stem: Lakeshore Legal is adding a Quick Read panel to its matter-management system. When counsel opens a vendor MSA, the panel must show a short plain-language overview of the document written by Docusign AI. The agreement's structured provisions, such as governing law and renewal terms, are already synced every night through another job. A teammate insists on calling a GET endpoint named getAgreementSummary so that the panel stays strictly read-only. Which Agreement Manager API call produces the overview?

options.text: CreateAgreementSummary, a POST to /v1/accounts/{accountId}/agreements/{agreementId}/ai/actions/summarize.
getAgreementSummary, a GET to /v1/accounts/{accountId}/agreements/{agreementId}/summary.
GetAgreement, whose provisions object includes the AI-written overview text for the agreement.
GetAgreementsList with an id filter, which returns a summary field for each matching agreement.

answerText: CreateAgreementSummary, a POST to /v1/accounts/{accountId}/agreements/{agreementId}/ai/actions/summarize.
explanation: The Agreement Manager API has exactly four agreement operations: GetAgreementsList, GetAgreement, DeleteAgreement and CreateAgreementSummary. An AI-generated summary comes only from CreateAgreementSummary, a POST to .../agreements/{agreementId}/ai/actions/summarize.
whyNotOthers: A is right because summarizing is an AI action exposed as a POST. The trap is B: there is no getAgreementSummary operation. C and D return structured fields (parties, provisions, metadata), not an AI-written narrative.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. CreateAgreementSummary is the only operation that produces an AI-generated summary of an agreement.
optionExplanations.B: No such operation exists; the API has only list, get, delete and create-summary operations for agreements.
optionExplanations.C: GetAgreement returns structured extracted data such as provisions and parties, not a narrative summary.
optionExplanations.D: GetAgreementsList returns agreement records with metadata and provisions, not AI-written summaries.

concept.title: AI agreement summary operation
concept.line: AI summaries come only from CreateAgreementSummary, POST .../agreements/{agreementId}/ai/actions/summarize; there is no GET summary endpoint.

decode.prompt: What output does the panel really need?

options.text: The agreement's structured extracted terms
A plain-language overview of one agreement generated by Docusign AI on request
Strictly read-only access to a precomputed summary
A summary attribute returned when listing agreements

decode.explanation: 'short plain-language overview ... written by Docusign AI' is only produced by CreateAgreementSummary; structured provisions are already synced and no GET summary endpoint exists.
clues: 'written by Docusign AI' -> CreateAgreementSummary
'structured provisions ... already synced' -> not GetAgreement
'getAgreementSummary ... read-only' -> red herring, no such endpoint
decode.needs: CreateAgreementSummary POST to .../ai/actions/summarize.

topic: Refreshing a connected fields data model
stem: Priya's private connected fields app has been accepted by her company's production account for three months and works well. Last week the back-end team added a new LoanPurpose property to the verifiable Loan concept in their Concerto model, and the extension test for Get Type Definitions now returns it correctly. However, in the eSignature Add Fields view, preparers still see the old list of App Fields without LoanPurpose. Nothing in the manifest changed, and the connection's OAuth tokens are still valid. What should Priya do so that preparers see the new field?

options.text: Resubmit the extension app for Docusign review so that the updated data model is approved
Refresh the extension app's connection in the App Center so Docusign calls Get Type Names and Get Type Definitions again
Delete the app from the account and re-add the account ID, then ask the administrator to accept it again
Add LoanPurpose to the actionReferences of the connected fields extension in the manifest

answerText: Refresh the extension app's connection in the App Center so Docusign calls Get Type Names and Get Type Definitions again
explanation: The data model changed 'after the extension app was connected', so the account still holds the old type definitions; refreshing the connection keeps it intact and makes Docusign execute Get Type Names and Get Type Definitions to retrieve the latest model.
whyNotOthers: B is right because Docusign reads the Concerto data model only when a connection is created or refreshed. The trap is C: removing and re-sharing would force a reconnect, but it is disruptive (admins are not notified of removal and the app is in use) and unnecessary when a refresh does the same. A fails because a data model change on the external service is not a manifest change that needs review, and D fails because actionReferences list actions, not data model properties.

optionExplanations.A: Review evaluates the registered app; the data model lives in the external service's responses and is picked up on connection refresh, not by re-review.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. Refreshing the connection in the App Center keeps it intact and makes Docusign re-run Get Type Names and Get Type Definitions to load the new property.
optionExplanations.C: This would eventually reload the model, but it removes an app that is in use without notifying the admin; a connection refresh is the intended fix.
optionExplanations.D: actionReferences in an extension point to action definitions such as Verify; data model properties are never listed there.

concept.title: Refreshing a connected fields model
concept.line: After the data model changes, refresh the app connection in the App Center so Docusign re-calls Get Type Names and Get Type Definitions.

decode.prompt: Why do preparers still see the old fields?

options.text: Change the app's manifest to declare the new field
Make Docusign re-read the app's data model for an existing connection, without reinstalling or re-reviewing
Remove and reinstall the app in the account
Have the changed app approved again

decode.explanation: The data model changed after the app was connected, so the account holds the old type definitions; refreshing the connection makes Docusign call Get Type Names and Get Type Definitions again.
clues: 'added a new LoanPurpose property' -> data model changed after connection
'extension test ... returns it correctly' -> back end is fine
'Nothing in the manifest changed' -> no review or manifest edit needed
'OAuth tokens are still valid' -> connection itself is fine
decode.needs: Refresh the extension app's connection in the App Center.

stem: Delta Bank's onboarding site, https://open.deltabank.example, uses focused view with Docusign JS loaded from js.docusign.com and is now going live in production. In testing on demo, the createRecipient request used frameAncestors ["https://open.deltabank.example", "https://apps-d.docusign.com"] and messageOrigins ["https://apps-d.docusign.com"]. The signer has a clientUserId, the envelope is sent, no ID verification is used, and the security team insists that no demo-environment value remains anywhere in the production configuration. Which two values must the production createRecipient request contain? (Select two)

options.text: frameAncestors ["https://open.deltabank.example", "https://apps-d.docusign.com"]
frameAncestors ["https://open.deltabank.example", "https://apps.docusign.com"]
messageOrigins ["https://apps.docusign.com"]
frameAncestors ["https://open.deltabank.example/", "https://apps.docusign.com/"]
messageOrigins ["https://open.deltabank.example"]

answerText: frameAncestors ["https://open.deltabank.example", "https://apps.docusign.com"]; messageOrigins ["https://apps.docusign.com"]
explanation: For focused view, frameAncestors must list your site's origin plus https://apps.docusign.com in production (apps-d in demo), and messageOrigins is a single-element array with https://apps.docusign.com in production.
whyNotOthers: B and C are right for production. The trap is A: that is the demo value and still names apps-d.docusign.com. D fails because frameAncestors accepts origins only, with no path or trailing slash. E fails because messageOrigins names the Docusign origin that sends the messages, not your own site.

optionExplanations.A: apps-d.docusign.com is for the developer (demo) environment, not production.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. Your site's origin plus https://apps.docusign.com for production.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. messageOrigins is https://apps.docusign.com in production.
optionExplanations.D: Origins must not include a path or a trailing slash.
optionExplanations.E: messageOrigins identifies the Docusign domain that sends the message, not your site.

concept.title: Focused view frameAncestors and messageOrigins
concept.line: frameAncestors lists your origin plus https://apps.docusign.com (apps-d in demo); messageOrigins is a single-element array with https://apps.docusign.com.

decode.prompt: What must change for production?

options.text: Allow the embedding site and the production Docusign app origin to frame and message, with no demo values
Add trailing slashes to make the origins explicit
Allow messages from the embedding site's own origin
Keep the values that worked in the demo environment

decode.explanation: 'no demo-environment value remains' means apps-d becomes apps.docusign.com in frameAncestors, and messageOrigins is the single production Docusign origin.
clues: 'going live in production' -> apps.docusign.com, not apps-d
'no demo-environment value remains' -> replace apps-d everywhere
'focused view' -> needs frameAncestors and messageOrigins
decode.needs: frameAncestors with site origin plus https://apps.docusign.com; messageOrigins https://apps.docusign.com.

stem: At Fenwick Legal, a Node.js server implements Confidential Authorization Code Grant. The redirect returns a fresh code, and the server posts to /oauth/token within ten seconds with grant_type=authorization_code and the code in the body. The token endpoint rejects the client. Logs show the header is Authorization: Basic followed by base64 of the integration key, a colon, a space, and the secret key. The developer also wonders whether a code_verifier is needed, but Apps and Keys says the app can store a secret and PKCE was not used. What fixes the request?

options.text: Add a code_verifier to the body, because every Authorization Code Grant token request needs one
Base64-encode only the integration key in the Basic header and send the secret key in the body
Rebuild the Basic header as base64 of integrationKey:secretKey, with no space after the colon
Replace Basic with Bearer and send the integration key as the bearer token value

answerText: Rebuild the Basic header as base64 of integrationKey:secretKey, with no space after the colon
explanation: The Confidential token request uses Authorization: Basic base64(integrationKey:secretKey) with a colon and no spaces; the logged value includes a space, so the credentials do not match.
whyNotOthers: C is right because the clue is the extra space after the colon. The trap is A: code_verifier is required only for Public Auth Code Grant (or Confidential with PKCE), and PKCE was not used. B splits the credentials in a format the token endpoint does not use, and D confuses the token request with API calls, where Bearer carries an access token.

optionExplanations.A: code_verifier is needed only when PKCE was used; here it was not.
optionExplanations.B: Both values go together in the Basic header as integrationKey:secretKey.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. base64(integrationKey:secretKey), colon, no spaces.
optionExplanations.D: Bearer carries an access token on API calls, not client credentials on /oauth/token.

concept.title: Confidential token Basic header
concept.line: Confidential token requests use Authorization: Basic base64(integrationKey:secretKey) with a colon and no spaces.

decode.prompt: Which requirement decides the fix here?

options.text: Send the client credentials in the exact Basic format a confidential client must use for the code exchange
Prove possession of a PKCE verifier because the client cannot hold a secret
Exchange the authorization code faster, before it expires
Identify the caller with a user token instead of client credentials

decode.explanation: The code is fresh, exchanged within ten seconds, and the app is confirmed to hold a secret without PKCE, so the only defect left is the malformed key:secret string in the Basic header.
clues: a colon, a space, and the secret key -> the Basic credential string is malformed
app can store a secret and PKCE was not used -> confidential client, no code_verifier needed
within ten seconds -> code expiry is not the problem
decode.needs: A correctly formatted Basic base64(integrationKey:secretKey) credential on the token request.

stem: Which two statements describe what happens when a running workflow instance is canceled? (Select two)

options.text: The workflow is paused so no new instances can start until it is resumed
Data collected up to the point of cancellation is stored
No further workflow steps are triggered for that instance
Any envelope the instance already sent is automatically voided and purged

answerText: Data collected up to the point of cancellation is stored; No further workflow steps are triggered for that instance
explanation: Cancelling an instance stores the data collected so far and stops any further steps for that instance.
whyNotOthers: B and C are right: cancel keeps collected data and triggers no further steps. The trap is A: stopping new instances is what pause does at the workflow level, not cancel on one instance. D invents automatic envelope voiding and purging, which is not part of instance cancellation.

optionExplanations.A: Wrong. Pausing the workflow blocks new instances; cancelling affects only one instance.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. Data collected up to that point is stored.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. No further workflow steps are triggered for the canceled instance.
optionExplanations.D: Wrong. Cancelling the instance is not described as voiding or purging envelopes; voiding is an eSignature envelope action.

concept.title: Effect of cancelling an instance
concept.line: Cancelling a workflow instance stores data collected so far and triggers no further steps for that instance; it does not pause the workflow.

topic: Reading a system of record in Maestro
stem: Aster Health is designing a Maestro patient intake workflow. Before the web form step, the workflow must look up the patient in Aster's proprietary records platform and prefill the form; after signing, it must write the updated insurance details back. A consultant proposes connected fields because 'they already map to our system of record and support autofill values'. Another engineer suggests the bank account verification extension already installed for billing. Which extension type should Aster's developer build to meet the requirement?

options.text: Connected fields extension, because it can return autofill values from the system of record
Data verification extension, because it can check the patient data before prefilling
File output cloud storage extension, writing the updated data back as a file
Data IO extension, invoked by read and write steps in the Maestro workflow

answerText: Data IO extension, invoked by read and write steps in the Maestro workflow
explanation: The lookup and the write-back both happen inside a Maestro workflow against a system of record, which is the Data IO extension; connected fields are not supported in Maestro.
whyNotOthers: D is right because Data IO reads data from and writes data to a system of record from Maestro read and write steps. The trap is A: connected fields do map to a system of record and can autofill, but only inside eSignature envelopes, and they are not supported in Maestro workflows. B verifies a fixed data type rather than reading and writing records, and C stores files, not field data.

optionExplanations.A: Connected fields autofill only in eSignature envelopes and are not currently supported in Maestro workflows.
optionExplanations.B: Data verification checks a specific data type such as a bank account; it does not read or write patient records.
optionExplanations.C: File output writes documents to cloud storage; it does not update structured fields in a system of record.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. Data IO reads from and writes to a system of record and is invoked from Maestro workflow steps.

concept.title: Data IO for system of record
concept.line: Reading and writing a system of record inside a Maestro workflow uses Data IO read/write steps; connected fields are not supported in Maestro.

decode.prompt: What does this scenario really require?

options.text: Verify a field value against the system of record while a signer fills in an eSignature envelope
Read from and write back to a proprietary system of record as steps inside a Maestro workflow
Verify a standard data type against an authoritative third-party provider
Archive the completed document as a file in external storage

decode.explanation: The lookup before the form and the write-back after signing both happen inside a Maestro workflow against Aster's own platform, which is structured read/write, not tab verification.
clues: Maestro patient intake workflow -> the extension point is Maestro, not eSignature tabs
look up the patient ... write the updated insurance details back -> structured read and write to a system of record
connected fields ... autofill values -> red herring; connected fields are not supported in Maestro
decode.needs: Structured read/write against a custom system of record from Maestro steps.

topic: Editing a workflow with active instances
stem: A process builder edits the participants and steps of a published workflow while 12 instances are active. What happens?

options.text: All 12 active instances restart from the first step with the new definition
The 12 active instances keep their original definition, and new instances reflect the changes
The edit is blocked until all 12 instances complete or are cancelled
The 12 active instances adopt the new steps from their current step onward

answerText: The 12 active instances keep their original definition, and new instances reflect the changes
explanation: Editing participants or steps does not modify current active instances; only new instances reflect the changes.
whyNotOthers: B is right per the Workflow Builder rules: active instances are not modified. The trap is D: it sounds like a graceful migration, but running instances are never changed by an edit. A and C invent restart and blocking behaviour that does not exist.

optionExplanations.A: Wrong. Active instances are not restarted by an edit.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. Current active instances are unchanged; new instances use the edited definition.
optionExplanations.C: Wrong. You can edit published workflows while instances run; edits are not blocked.
optionExplanations.D: Wrong. Active instances are not modified at all, not even from their current step.

concept.title: Editing workflow with active instances
concept.line: Editing participants or steps does not change active instances; only new instances reflect the changes.

topic: Recovering events after a long listener outage
stem: Northgate Insurance's Connect listener was broken for 20 days after a certificate expired; every delivery attempt during that time failed with a TLS error. The account-level JSON SIM configuration has requireAcknowledgement and logging enabled. After fixing the certificate, developer Tomas Berg notices that recent failed events are being redelivered on their own, but events from the first days of the outage never arrive. The claims system needs every missing envelope event. What should Tomas do?

options.text: Wait for the automatic exponential back-off retries, which continue daily until every failed event is delivered
Resend the affected envelopes with Envelopes:create using their original transactionId values so the events fire again
Use the Connect failure log to find the failed envelopes, then republish them with ConnectEvents:retryForEnvelopes
Schedule Envelopes:listStatus calls every five minutes for the affected envelopes until the claims system catches up

answerText: Use the Connect failure log to find the failed envelopes, then republish them with ConnectEvents:retryForEnvelopes
explanation: Automatic retries use exponential back-off and then once per day for a 15-day span, so events older than that will not be retried. The Connect failure log identifies the envelopes that failed to post, and retryForEnvelopes republishes them.
whyNotOthers: C is right because the 20-day outage exceeds the 15-day automatic retry window, so the oldest events must be republished from the failure log. The trap is A: retries do continue daily, but only for 15 days, which explains why the early events never arrive. B fails because transactionId only prevents duplicate envelope creation on a failed create call and does not replay events; D fails because five-minute polling violates the 15-minute per-envelope limit.

optionExplanations.A: Retries run on a back-off schedule and then once a day for 15 days only; events from the start of a 20-day outage have left the retry window.
optionExplanations.B: transactionId makes a retried create request idempotent; it does not republish Connect events for existing envelopes.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. The Connect failure log lists envelopes that failed to post, and ConnectEvents:retryForEnvelopes republishes them once the listener is fixed.
optionExplanations.D: Polling every five minutes breaks the one GET per envelope every 15 minutes rule and still does not redeliver the event messages.

concept.title: Recovering events after long outage
concept.line: Connect retries back off then run daily for 15 days only; use the failure log and ConnectEvents:retryForEnvelopes to republish older failures.

decode.prompt: What does this scenario really require?

options.text: Let the automatic retry mechanism finish redelivering the whole backlog
Regenerate the events by creating the envelopes again
Recover events that have aged out of Connect's automatic retry window, using the recorded failures
Poll envelope status continuously from now on

decode.explanation: The outage lasted 20 days, longer than the 15-day automatic retry span, so the oldest failures will never be retried and must be found in the failure log and republished.
clues: broken for 20 days -> longer than Connect's 15-day retry span
events from the first days of the outage never arrive -> automatic retries expired for them
requireAcknowledgement and logging enabled -> failures are recorded and can be republished
decode.needs: Find failed envelopes in the Connect failure log and republish them manually.

stem: Northgate University collects alumni address updates with a standalone web form configuration embedded through the Web Forms API; no envelope is involved. Marketing wants the alumni association's logo and colors on these forms. The developer looked up the brand with AccountBrands:list and added its brandId to the Instances:createInstance body, but the forms still show the default look. Another team, whose configuration is template-based, passes brandId the same way and sees its brand applied. How should the developer apply the brand to the alumni forms?

options.text: Add the brandId to the envelope with Envelopes:update after each form instance is submitted.
Keep the brandId but move it inside the formValues object of the createInstance request.
Select the brand under Branding on the Preview tab when editing the web form configuration.
Upload the logo in a signing branding resource file so it applies to every standalone instance.

answerText: Select the brand under Branding on the Preview tab when editing the web form configuration.
explanation: Applying a brand through an API request is not supported for instances created from standalone configurations; a brand selected under Branding on the configuration's Preview tab applies to web form instances and works for both standalone and template-based configurations.
whyNotOthers: C is right because the configuration-level Preview tab is the branding path that supports standalone forms. The trap is A: there is no envelope in a standalone flow. B misuses formValues, which only prefills form fields, and D changes resource text, not the brand applied to the form.

optionExplanations.A: Standalone configurations generate no envelope, so there is nothing to update.
optionExplanations.B: formValues prefills fields by name; it is not a place for configuration settings such as a brand.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. Branding on the configuration's Preview tab applies the brand to instances, including standalone ones.
optionExplanations.D: Resource files customize text in the signing, sending and email experiences; they do not brand a web form.

concept.title: Branding a standalone web form
concept.line: Standalone instances cannot get a brand via API; select the brand under Branding on the configuration's Preview tab (works for both configuration types).

decode.prompt: What does this scenario really require?

options.text: Apply a brand to the envelope generated after the form is submitted
Pass brand information as data when each instance is created
Change account-wide signing resource files
Apply a brand to standalone web form instances, where a brand cannot be applied through the API request

decode.explanation: The forms are standalone with no envelope, and API brandId only works for template-based configurations, so the brand must be set on the web form configuration itself.
clues: standalone web form configuration ... no envelope is involved -> envelope or API branding does not apply
template-based ... sees its brand applied -> API brandId works only for template-based
logo and colors on these forms -> brand chosen in the configuration's own Branding settings
decode.needs: Configuration-level branding selected in the web form editor.

stem: Rosa leads mobile development at Vantage Realty, whose iOS and Android app lets 900 agents send listing agreements while on site. Each agent must sign in with their own Docusign account so that envelopes appear in their own Sent folder. The app is a native binary distributed through public app stores, and the security team warns that anything compiled into it can be extracted. A separate backend exists, but it only receives anonymised analytics and never handles Docusign traffic. Which OAuth flow should the app use?

options.text: Public Authorization Code Grant with PKCE, with each agent signing in through the Docusign login page
Confidential Authorization Code Grant, with the secret key kept in the device keychain
JWT Grant impersonating each agent, with the RSA private key bundled into the app
Implicit Grant, with the access token returned directly in the redirect to the app

answerText: Public Authorization Code Grant with PKCE, with each agent signing in through the Docusign login page
explanation: A native app that cannot securely store a secret, with each user signing in individually, should use Public Authorization Code Grant, which uses PKCE instead of a secret.
whyNotOthers: A is right because the clue is that 'anything compiled into it can be extracted', so the app cannot keep a secret. The trap is B: a device keychain is still on the client, and the backend never handles Docusign calls, so no server holds the secret. C puts a private key in a public binary and removes per-user login, and D is the legacy flow Docusign recommends replacing with Public Auth Code Grant.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. Native app, no safe secret, individual users: Public Auth Code Grant with PKCE.
optionExplanations.B: Confidential Grant needs a server that can store the secret; the backend does not handle Docusign traffic.
optionExplanations.C: JWT is for service integrations; shipping the private key in a public app exposes it.
optionExplanations.D: Implicit Grant is legacy and not recommended; Public Auth Code Grant replaces it.

concept.title: Flow for native mobile apps
concept.line: Native apps that cannot securely store a secret, with individual user sign-in, use Public Authorization Code Grant with PKCE.

decode.prompt: What does this scenario really require?

options.text: Let each user sign in individually from an app that cannot keep any secret
Authenticate one service identity with no user interaction
Protect a client secret in secure storage on the device
Return tokens straight to the app without a code exchange

decode.explanation: Each agent signs in with their own account, and anything compiled into the native app can be extracted, so it is a public client needing a user sign-in flow without a secret.
clues: each agent must sign in with their own Docusign account -> interactive user authorization
native binary ... anything compiled into it can be extracted -> public client, no secret or private key
backend never handles Docusign traffic -> no server to hold a secret
decode.needs: A public-client user sign-in flow where PKCE replaces the secret.

stem: After go-live, an account admin wants to raise the account's hourly API limit. Which statement is accurate?

options.text: Use the API Dashboard in Apps and Keys, which lets any user with access to the integration change the limit
Use Update Hourly Limit in the API Usage Center; it works only if the plan allows it and the account's apps are efficient
Submit a new Go-Live request with a higher-tier classification, because the hourly limit is set during review
Raise the limit separately for each integration key in Apps and Keys, because each key has its own allowance

answerText: Use Update Hourly Limit in the API Usage Center; it works only if the plan allows it and the account's apps are efficient
explanation: The API Usage Center has an Update Hourly Limit option. The admin can use it only if the plan includes limit management, no limit set by Support is in effect, and the apps are efficient enough (flagged issues fixed first).
whyNotOthers: B is right: the API Usage Center is the place, and efficiency is a condition. The trap is A: the API Dashboard shows request history and failures for troubleshooting but does not change limits. C fails because classification and Go-Live review do not set the hourly limit. D fails because the hourly limit is per account and shared by all integration keys.

optionExplanations.A: The API Dashboard is for monitoring and troubleshooting requests; it does not change limits.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. Update Hourly Limit in the API Usage Center needs a plan that allows it and efficient apps.
optionExplanations.C: The hourly limit is not set by the Go-Live classification or review.
optionExplanations.D: The limit belongs to the account and is shared by all keys; there is no allowance per key.

concept.title: Raising the hourly limit
concept.line: Admins use Update Hourly Limit in the API Usage Center only if the plan allows it, no Support limit applies, and apps are efficient.

stem: Which two statements about an integration key that has been promoted to production are true? (Select two)

options.text: The key is moved to production, so the developer environment copy stops working
The same key value keeps working in the developer environment and now also works in production
The key's secrets and redirect URIs are duplicated with it, so the production copy works at once
The key can call only the production account it was promoted into, because that account owns it
The key is tied to the selected production account for management, but can call the API for any account

answerText: The same key value keeps working in the developer environment and now also works in production; The key is tied to the selected production account for management, but can call the API for any account
explanation: At Go-Live the key is duplicated rather than moved, so the same value works in both environments. It is tied to the selected production account for management, but after promotion it can make API calls against any account.
whyNotOthers: B and E are right: the key is duplicated, not moved, and the management account does not restrict which accounts it can call. The trap is D: the account you select only manages the key. A fails because the key is duplicated, not moved. C fails because secrets and redirect URIs are not copied.

optionExplanations.A: The key is duplicated, not moved; the developer copy keeps working.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. The key keeps the same value and works in both the developer and production environments.
optionExplanations.C: Secrets and redirect URIs are not copied and must be added in production.
optionExplanations.D: The production account only manages the key; the key can call the API for any account.
optionExplanations.E: Correct. The key is tied to the management account, but after promotion it can be used against any account.

concept.title: Integration key after promotion
concept.line: Go-Live duplicates the key: same value works in developer and production; tied to one production account for management but can call any account.

topic: Composite templates: document precedence and order
stem: Aster Supply sends vendor packets with composite templates. Object 1 in the compositeTemplates array contains a document property with a generated cover letter, a server template "MSA" (sequence 1, which has its own MSA document) and an inline template (sequence 2) with the signer. Object 2 contains a server template "NDA" (sequence 1, with its NDA document) and an inline template (sequence 2). The developer expected three documents. Which documents does the envelope contain, in which order?

options.text: Cover letter, then NDA
MSA, then cover letter, then NDA
MSA, then NDA
NDA, then cover letter

answerText: Cover letter, then NDA
explanation: Each composite template object contributes at most one document, and a document property takes precedence over any template documents in that object, so object 1 contributes the cover letter and the MSA document is ignored. Documents then follow the order of objects in the array.
whyNotOthers: A is right: document precedence (first in wins) plus array order. The trap is B: it assumes each template adds its own document, but one object contributes one document only. C wrongly lets the sequence-1 server template beat the document property. D reverses the array order, which is what controls document order.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. Object 1 contributes only the cover letter (document property wins); object 2 contributes the NDA.
optionExplanations.B: A composite template object contributes at most one document, so the MSA and cover letter cannot both come from object 1.
optionExplanations.C: The document property takes precedence over server template documents regardless of sequence.
optionExplanations.D: Document order follows the order of objects in the compositeTemplates array.

concept.title: Composite templates: document precedence
concept.line: Each composite template object contributes at most one document, and a document property overrides its templates' documents; order follows the array.

decode.prompt: Which rule decides the outcome here?

options.text: Count every document defined anywhere in the request
Know which single document each composite template object contributes and how objects are ordered
Order documents by the template sequence numbers across the whole array
Determine which template supplies the signer

decode.explanation: Each composite object yields at most one document, a document property overrides template documents in that object, and documents follow array order.
clues: Object 1 contains a document property ... and a server template MSA -> the document property wins for that object
Object 2 contains a server template NDA -> the second object contributes the NDA
expected three documents -> misreading; one document per object
decode.needs: One document per composite object, document property first, ordered by array position.

stem: In an extension app manifest, which element of an action determines its request and response contract and the extension points that can trigger it?

options.text: The connectionsReference that points to the connection
The params.uri that names the external endpoint
The template identifier, which Docusign predefines
The extension's actionReferences array that lists it

answerText: The template identifier, which Docusign predefines
explanation: An action's template identifier, predefined by Docusign, specifies the action contract: the request and response contract to be used and the extension points that trigger the action.
whyNotOthers: C is right because the action contract is set by the action's template property. The trap is D: actionReferences ties actions to an extension, but the extension's own template sets the extension contract, not each action's request/response shape. A links to auth credentials and B only gives the endpoint URL.

optionExplanations.A: connectionsReference links the action to the auth credentials in a connection; it does not define the contract.
optionExplanations.B: params.uri is where the call goes, not what request/response shape it uses or which extension points trigger it.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. The action's Docusign-predefined template identifier sets the action contract and the extension points that trigger it.
optionExplanations.D: actionReferences only lists which actions belong to an extension; it does not define each action's contract.

concept.title: Action template identifier
concept.line: An action's Docusign-predefined template identifier specifies its action contract: request/response contract and the extension points that trigger it.

stem: Granite Telecom wants a daily job that finds customer agreements expiring in the next 60 days and, for each one, starts an existing multi-step renewal process that prefills a new order form, routes it for internal approval, and collects signatures. The renewal workflow is already published in Workflow Builder with the API call start method. The integration already holds a token with the required scopes for every API involved. Which two building blocks should the job use? (Select two)

options.text: CreateAgreementSummary to identify which agreements fall within 60 days of their expiration.
GetAgreementsList with a provisions.expiration_date range filter to find the expiring agreements.
The Web Forms API createInstance call to start the multi-step renewal orchestration for each agreement.
The Workflow Builder API to trigger the published workflow for each agreement, passing its data as inputs.
A Connected Fields verification on the expiration date tab to launch the renewal process.

answerText: GetAgreementsList with a provisions.expiration_date range filter to find the expiring agreements.; The Workflow Builder API to trigger the published workflow for each agreement, passing its data as inputs.
explanation: The Agreement Manager API finds agreements by AI-extracted expiration date, and the Workflow Builder (Maestro) API triggers a published workflow that does the prefill, approval and signature steps.
whyNotOthers: B and D are right: one finds the agreements, the other starts the orchestration. The trap is C: the Web Forms API creates a single form instance, not a multi-step workflow. A generates summaries instead of filtering by date, and E validates a field during preparation or signing and cannot start a workflow.

optionExplanations.A: CreateAgreementSummary writes a narrative summary of one agreement; it is not a date query.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. GetAgreementsList supports a provisions.expiration_date range filter (gte, lte).
optionExplanations.C: A web form instance is one data-collection step, not the orchestration engine for approval and signing.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. The Workflow Builder API triggers the published workflow and passes trigger inputs.
optionExplanations.E: Connected fields verify field values in Add Fields and signing; they do not trigger workflows.

concept.title: Agreement-driven renewal orchestration
concept.line: Find expiring agreements with GetAgreementsList (provisions.expiration_date filter), then trigger a published Maestro workflow per agreement via the Workflow Builder API.

decode.prompt: What does this scenario really require?

options.text: Generate agreement summaries to work out their dates
Collect form data to begin each renewal
Find agreements by an extracted expiration date, then start an already-published multi-step orchestration for each
Validate a field value during signing to kick off the renewal

decode.explanation: The job needs a date-based query over agreement data and a way to start the renewal workflow that is already published with the API start method.
clues: agreements expiring in the next 60 days -> Agreement Manager query on the expiration provision
published in Workflow Builder with the API call start method -> trigger it through the Maestro API
prefills, routes for internal approval, and collects signatures -> the orchestration lives in the workflow
decode.needs: Agreement list filtered by expiration date plus a Maestro workflow trigger.

stem: Felix's payroll service posts Envelopes:create for year-end bonus letters through a corporate API gateway. Last week the gateway timed out after 30 seconds on several calls, the service retried, and some employees received two identical envelopes because the first call had actually succeeded. The service never received an envelopeId for the timed-out calls. Each letter already uses envelopeIdStamping and a signer with clientUserId for embedded signing. Which change lets the service safely retry a timed-out create without producing duplicates?

options.text: Reuse the same clientUserId on the retry so Docusign recognizes the signer and skips duplicates
Retry with the envelopeId from the first call so Docusign updates rather than recreates the envelope
Rely on envelopeIdStamping, which makes Docusign reject a second envelope with the same documents
Send a unique transactionId with each create and reuse the same value when retrying that letter

answerText: Send a unique transactionId with each create and reuse the same value when retrying that letter
explanation: transactionId is a sender-generated value that makes the create request safe to retry: resending the same transactionId does not create a second envelope. The clue is that no envelopeId came back from the timed-out calls.
whyNotOthers: D is right because transactionId is the duplicate-prevention parameter. The trap is B: an envelopeId would identify the envelope, but Docusign assigns it only after a successful create, and the service never received it. A fails because clientUserId only marks an embedded signer. C fails because envelopeIdStamping prints the envelope ID on documents and does not detect duplicates.

optionExplanations.A: clientUserId marks the recipient as embedded; it does not deduplicate envelopes.
optionExplanations.B: The envelopeId is returned only after success, and the timed-out calls never returned one.
optionExplanations.C: envelopeIdStamping only stamps the envelope ID on documents; it does not prevent duplicates.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. Reusing the same transactionId on retry prevents a duplicate envelope.

concept.title: Idempotent create with transactionId
concept.line: A sender-generated transactionId makes Envelopes:create safe to retry; resending the same value does not create a second envelope.

decode.prompt: What does this scenario really require?

options.text: Identify the embedded signer consistently across attempts
Update an envelope whose ID is already known
Detect duplicate envelopes by their document content
Make envelope creation safe to retry when the caller never learned whether the first attempt succeeded

decode.explanation: No envelopeId came back from the timed-out calls, so the service needs a sender-generated key that lets Docusign recognise a repeated create.
clues: never received an envelopeId -> nothing to reference; need a sender-generated key
the first call had actually succeeded -> duplicates come from blind retries
envelopeIdStamping and clientUserId -> red herrings unrelated to deduplication
decode.needs: An idempotency value (transactionId) sent on create and reused on retry.

topic: Redirect after embedded web form signing
stem: Copperline Bank embeds a template-based web form for loan pre-approval. The configuration's 'Initiate signing session from email' setting is off, so after submission the generated envelope opens for signing inside the bank's page. Product wants applicants sent to /preapproval/next when they finish signing; today they see the configuration's thank you page. The account has no custom brands, and the admin team will not create or edit brands this quarter. The app never calls EnvelopeViews because Docusign creates and displays the envelope automatically. What should the developer change?

options.text: Add a returnUrl to an EnvelopeViews:createRecipient call made right after the applicant submits the form.
Supply a returnUrl in the Instances:createInstance request that creates each applicant's instance.
Set a Signing Completed destination URL under the account brand's Destination URLs settings.
Switch the configuration to standalone so its thank you page can point to /preapproval/next.

answerText: Supply a returnUrl in the Instances:createInstance request that creates each applicant's instance.
explanation: For template-based instances with embedded signing (the 'Initiate signing session from email' setting off), the redirect after envelope completion is the returnUrl supplied in Instances:createInstance; without it the thank you page is shown.
whyNotOthers: B is right because the envelope is created and displayed automatically, so the redirect must be set when the instance is created. The trap is C: a brand Signing Completed URL is the remote-delivery mechanism and the admins will not touch brands. A adds a call the flow does not use, and D removes the envelope entirely and standalone configurations offer no redirect.

optionExplanations.A: The app does not create the signing view; Docusign displays the generated envelope automatically after submission.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. returnUrl in createInstance controls where embedded-signing users go after completing the envelope.
optionExplanations.C: Brand destination URLs are how remote instances redirect, and the stem rules out creating or editing brands.
optionExplanations.D: Standalone configurations generate no envelope and offer no redirect; Docusign shows the configured thank you page.

concept.title: Embedded web form redirect: returnUrl
concept.line: Template-based embedded-signing web form instances redirect via returnUrl in Instances:createInstance; without it the thank you page shows.

decode.prompt: What does this scenario really require?

options.text: Set the after-signing redirect for a template-based web form with embedded signing, per instance, without brands
Set the redirect on a signing session the app creates itself
Configure an account-wide redirect after signing
Change the thank you page of a standalone form

decode.explanation: Embedded signing is launched by the web form itself and brands are off the table, so the redirect must come from the instance creation request.
clues: 'Initiate signing session from email' setting is off -> embedded signing launched by the web form
never calls EnvelopeViews -> no recipient view returnUrl to set
will not create or edit brands -> brand destination URLs are ruled out
decode.needs: A returnUrl supplied when creating the web form instance.

topic: Connect write-back use case versus extension apps
stem: Marlow Utilities sends service agreements from its homegrown CRM using the eSignature REST API; no Maestro workflows are involved. Signers may correct their mailing address in a text tab while signing, and after the envelope is completed the CRM must be updated with the corrected address within seconds. The CRM is internal, not Salesforce, and the team wants to avoid adding API traffic. Which approach should the developer build?

options.text: A custom Connect configuration that posts envelope-completed messages including tab data to a listener that updates the CRM
A Data IO extension app that writes the corrected address back to the CRM when the signer finishes
The pre-built Connect for Salesforce integration, mapping the address tab to the CRM contact record
A scheduled job that calls EnvelopeTabs every ten minutes for completed envelopes and updates the CRM

answerText: A custom Connect configuration that posts envelope-completed messages including tab data to a listener that updates the CRM
explanation: Write-back of signer-updated data to a line-of-business system after completion is a documented custom Connect use case, and Connect pushes the data without consuming API calls.
whyNotOthers: A is right because a custom Connect listener receiving envelope-completed with tab data is the documented write-back pattern for internal systems. The trap is B: Data IO does write to external systems, but it runs as a step in a Maestro workflow, and this scenario has no Maestro workflow. C fails because the pre-built Salesforce connector only pushes to Docusign for Salesforce, not an internal CRM; D fails because polling adds API traffic, is not near real time, and violates the 15-minute per-envelope polling rule.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. A custom Connect configuration pushes envelope-completed messages with tab data to a listener that writes the corrected address into the internal CRM, with no polling.
optionExplanations.B: Data IO extension apps read and write external data as steps in Maestro workflows; with plain eSignature API sending there is no workflow step to run them.
optionExplanations.C: Connect for Salesforce pushes data to the Docusign for Salesforce app; it does not update a homegrown internal CRM.
optionExplanations.D: Polling every ten minutes adds API calls, misses the within-seconds requirement and breaks the one GET per envelope every 15 minutes rule.

concept.title: Connect for post-completion write-back
concept.line: Writing signer-updated data back to a business system after completion is a custom Connect use case (envelope-completed with tab data), using no API calls.

decode.prompt: What does this scenario really require?

options.text: Write data to a system of record from a Maestro workflow step
Push completed-envelope tab data to an internal non-Salesforce system within seconds, without polling
Use a prebuilt CRM connector
Periodically pull tab values from completed envelopes

decode.explanation: Plain eSignature sending with no Maestro, an internal CRM, near-real-time updates and no extra API traffic all point to a push-based custom listener.
clues: eSignature REST API; no Maestro workflows -> not a Data IO step
within seconds ... avoid adding API traffic -> push, not polling
internal, not Salesforce -> custom listener rather than a prebuilt connector
decode.needs: Custom Connect configuration including tab data, posting to a listener.

stem: A company wants signers sent to its own thank-you page after signing. Some signers sign remotely from an email link, others sign embedded in the company portal. What controls the redirect for each group?

options.text: returnUrl in Envelopes:create for remote signers; Brand Destination URLs for embedded signers
Brand Destination URLs for both groups, because they override any returnUrl value
returnUrl in EnvelopeViews:createRecipient for both groups, because it applies to every signer
Brand Destination URLs for remote signers; returnUrl in EnvelopeViews:createRecipient for embedded signers

answerText: Brand Destination URLs for remote signers; returnUrl in EnvelopeViews:createRecipient for embedded signers
explanation: For remote signing the post-signing destination comes from the brand's destination URLs; for embedded signing your app sets returnUrl when it calls EnvelopeViews:createRecipient.
whyNotOthers: D is right because each group uses a different mechanism. The trap is C: returnUrl is correct for embedded signers, but remote signers never go through createRecipient. A swaps the two mechanisms and puts returnUrl on the wrong call. B ignores that embedded signing returns to the returnUrl your app supplies.

optionExplanations.A: This swaps the mechanisms; returnUrl is not set on Envelopes:create for remote signers.
optionExplanations.B: Embedded signers are redirected to the returnUrl supplied on createRecipient.
optionExplanations.C: Remote signers do not use createRecipient, so a returnUrl there cannot redirect them.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. Brand Destination URLs for remote signing; returnUrl on createRecipient for embedded signing.

concept.title: Post-signing redirect: remote vs embedded
concept.line: Remote signers are redirected via brand Destination URLs; embedded signers via returnUrl set in EnvelopeViews:createRecipient.

topic: Implicit Grant vs Public Auth Code Grant
stem: Why does Docusign recommend Public Authorization Code Grant rather than Implicit Grant for a new single-page application?

options.text: Implicit returns the access token straight to the browser with no code exchange; Public Auth Code adds a PKCE-protected exchange
Implicit requires the client secret in the browser, while Public Auth Code Grant needs only the integration key
Implicit tokens can call only the Admin API, while Public Auth Code tokens can call the eSignature REST API
Implicit cannot use a registered redirect URI, so it cannot return the user to the single-page app

answerText: Implicit returns the access token straight to the browser with no code exchange; Public Auth Code adds a PKCE-protected exchange
explanation: Implicit Grant is a legacy flow that hands the token directly to the browser; Docusign recommends Public Auth Code Grant, where the code exchange is protected by PKCE (code_challenge and code_verifier).
whyNotOthers: A is right because PKCE is what makes Public Auth Code Grant the recommended choice for clients without a secret. The trap is B: neither flow uses a client secret, which is why both target SPAs. C invents an API restriction, and D fails because Implicit also returns to a registered redirect URI.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. No code exchange in Implicit; Public Auth Code adds PKCE to the exchange.
optionExplanations.B: Neither Implicit nor Public Auth Code Grant uses a client secret.
optionExplanations.C: No such API restriction exists; the problem is security, not reach.
optionExplanations.D: Implicit Grant also redirects to a registered redirect URI.

concept.title: Implicit vs Public Auth Code Grant
concept.line: Implicit (legacy) returns the token straight to the browser with no code exchange; Public Auth Code adds a PKCE-protected exchange and is recommended.

stem: Jonah builds an internal agreement dashboard as a single-page app hosted at https://dash.vela.example with no back end. Users sign in with Authorization Code Grant with PKCE, and tokens are issued correctly. When the browser calls Envelopes:listStatusChanges directly, the requests are blocked with cross-origin errors before Docusign returns any data. The same calls with the same token work from Postman. Focused view is not used, and the company does not want to build or host a back-end proxy. What should Jonah do?

options.text: Add https://dash.vela.example as an allowed origin in the integration key's CORS settings in Apps and Keys
Add an Access-Control-Allow-Origin header with the dashboard origin to each request the SPA sends
Request an additional OAuth scope for browser access when the user signs in
Add https://dash.vela.example to frameAncestors so Docusign trusts the dashboard's origin

answerText: Add https://dash.vela.example as an allowed origin in the integration key's CORS settings in Apps and Keys
explanation: CORS for the eSignature API is configured on the integration key in Apps and Keys, where you list the allowed origins (and methods). The clue is that calls work from Postman (no browser origin checks) but fail in the browser.
whyNotOthers: A is right because the origin allowlist is set by Docusign for the integration key. The trap is B: Access-Control-Allow-Origin is a response header the server sends, so the browser ignores it on the SPA's own requests. C fails because scopes control permissions, not allowed origins. D fails because frameAncestors only controls where focused view can be framed.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. Allowed CORS origins are configured on the integration key in Apps and Keys.
optionExplanations.B: Access-Control-Allow-Origin is a server response header; setting it on requests does nothing.
optionExplanations.C: OAuth scopes grant API permissions; they do not configure allowed browser origins.
optionExplanations.D: frameAncestors governs focused view framing, not cross-origin API calls.

concept.title: CORS for single-page apps
concept.line: eSignature CORS is configured on the integration key in Apps and Keys by listing allowed origins, not via headers the SPA sends.

decode.prompt: What does this scenario really require?

options.text: Obtain broader token permissions for the user
Allow Docusign content to be framed inside the dashboard
Allow a specific browser origin to call the eSignature API directly, without a proxy
Have the browser client declare its own origin as trusted

decode.explanation: The token works from Postman but the browser blocks the call, so the gap is cross-origin permission, which must be granted on Docusign's side.
clues: blocked with cross-origin errors -> CORS
work from Postman -> token and scopes are fine; only browser origin checks fail
does not want to build or host a back-end proxy -> CORS on the integration key
Focused view is not used -> framing settings are irrelevant
decode.needs: The dashboard origin listed in the integration key's CORS settings.

stem: Sofia at Arcadia Realty triggers a lease workflow that ends with three steps after signing: a Branching Rule on envelope status, a Store Files step that archives the lease to Google Drive, and a Writeback step to the property system. Her listener already receives JSON SIM messages. The property manager wants the lease marked 'Done' in the portal only when everything, including the archive and the writeback, has finished. A teammate proposes keying off envelope-completed because the lease is fully signed at that point. Which event should Sofia subscribe to for this status?

options.text: workflow-started
workflow-completed
envelope-completed
recipient-completed

answerText: workflow-completed
explanation: workflow-completed is published when all steps in the workflow are completed by all participants, which includes the archive and writeback steps that run after signing.
whyNotOthers: B is right because the clue is that 'Done' must wait for the archive and writeback steps after signing. The trap is C: envelope-completed fires when signing finishes, before the Store Files and Writeback steps run. A fires when execution begins, and D tracks a single recipient within the envelope.

optionExplanations.A: Wrong. workflow-started fires when the instance is triggered and execution begins.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. workflow-completed fires only when every step in the workflow has completed.
optionExplanations.C: Wrong. envelope-completed fires when signing is done, but the archive and writeback steps still follow.
optionExplanations.D: Wrong. recipient-completed tracks one recipient in the envelope, not the whole workflow.

concept.title: workflow-completed Connect event
concept.line: workflow-completed fires when all workflow steps are done by all participants, including steps after signing; envelope-completed does not cover those.

decode.prompt: What does this scenario really require?

options.text: Know when the document is fully signed
Know when each individual signer finishes
Know when the workflow has started
Know when every workflow step, including post-signing steps, has finished

decode.explanation: The portal status depends on the archive and writeback steps that run after signing, so only a workflow-level completion signal is late enough.
clues: only when everything, including the archive and the writeback, has finished -> workflow-level completion
Store Files and Writeback after signing -> envelope completion fires too early
teammate proposes envelope-completed -> red herring
decode.needs: Subscribe to the workflow-completed event.

stem: Northwind Clinics bought a scheduling product from a Docusign partner. The vendor's setup guide says each customer must create its own Docusign integration key, paste the key and its secret into the vendor's admin screen, and take the key through Go-Live. Northwind wrote none of the application code, and only Northwind's own staff will use the product. Northwind's developer, Ash, creates the key in a developer account and reaches 'How will you use this integration?'. The vendor's product does show Docusign signing inside its own screens. Which classification should Ash choose?

options.text: Private custom integration, because only Northwind's own employees will use the integration
Public integration, because the vendor's product is offered to many Docusign customers
Embedded integration, because the vendor's product shows Docusign signing inside its screens
Third-party integration key, because a partner integration requires Northwind to supply its own key

answerText: Third-party integration key, because a partner integration requires Northwind to supply its own key
explanation: Docusign's classification table maps 'you want to use a Docusign partner integration, and that integration requires you to provide your own integration key' to Third-party integration key. The deciding clues are that the vendor requires each customer's own key and that Northwind wrote none of the code.
whyNotOthers: D is right because Northwind is supplying its own key to a partner's product. The trap is A: Northwind's employees are the users, but Private custom integration is for an integration you build yourself, and Northwind wrote none of the code. B is the vendor's own classification for its multi-customer app, not the customer's. C fails because Embedded integration describes an ISV offering Docusign through its own account; showing signing in the UI (embedded signing) is a red herring.

optionExplanations.A: Private custom integration is for an integration you build for your own (or your clients') employees; Northwind only uses a partner product.
optionExplanations.B: Public integration is what the partner would choose for its multi-customer app; Northwind is not publishing an app.
optionExplanations.C: Embedded integration is an ISV Embed model where customers use the ISV's Docusign account; embedded signing in a UI is unrelated.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. Using a partner integration that requires your own integration key is the Third-party integration key classification.

concept.title: Third-party integration key
concept.line: Using a partner integration that requires you to supply your own integration key is classified as a Third-party integration key.

decode.prompt: What does this scenario really require?

options.text: Classify a key that the customer must supply to a partner's product it did not build
Classify an integration used only by the organization's own staff
Classify an integration offered to many Docusign customers
Classify the integration by how signing is displayed to users

decode.explanation: The vendor requires each customer to create and supply its own key, and Northwind wrote none of the code, which matches the third-party key row of the classification table.
clues: each customer must create its own integration key -> partner integration that requires the customer's key
Northwind wrote none of the application code -> not a custom integration
shows Docusign signing inside its own screens -> red herring
decode.needs: Third-party integration key classification.

topic: External admin consent: ID token coid
stem: Quillon Software sells a multi-tenant contract tool to hundreds of companies and uses JWT Grant. To spare customers from asking every employee for consent, Quillon sends each customer's administrator to /oauth/auth with scope=openid and admin_consent_scope=signature%20impersonation. The customer organizations have Access Management and claimed domains. Quillon's billing team now wants a reliable list of which customer organizations have granted this admin consent; the developer notes that userinfo only lists accounts for one user. Where should Quillon get this list?

options.text: From the accounts array returned by /oauth/userinfo for each impersonated user
From the sub claim of each JWT assertion that Quillon signs for customer users
From the Connected Apps page in Quillon's own Docusign Admin organization
From the coid claim of the ID token returned because openid was requested

answerText: From the coid claim of the ID token returned because openid was requested
explanation: Requesting openid returns an ID token whose coid claim lists the organizations that granted admin consent; this is the only way to get that list.
whyNotOthers: D is right because the clue is scope=openid in the admin consent URL, which returns an ID token. The trap is A: userinfo shows accounts for a single user, as the stem says, not consenting organizations. B is the user ID Quillon itself supplies, and C shows apps authorized in Quillon's own organization, not consent granted inside customer organizations.

optionExplanations.A: userinfo lists one user's accounts, not which organizations consented.
optionExplanations.B: sub is the user ID Quillon puts into the JWT; it says nothing about organizations.
optionExplanations.C: Quillon's own Connected Apps page covers its own organization, not its customers'.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. The ID token's coid claim lists consenting organization IDs.

concept.title: External admin consent: coid claim
concept.line: Requesting openid returns an ID token whose coid claim lists organizations that granted admin consent; this is the only way to get that list.

decode.prompt: What does this scenario really require?

options.text: List the accounts a single user can access
Obtain the list of customer organizations that granted admin consent
Identify which user each token impersonates
View the apps connected inside the vendor's own organization

decode.explanation: The question is about organization-level consent across customers, and the openid request returns an ID token that carries exactly that list.
clues: which customer organizations have granted this admin consent -> organization-level consent record
scope=openid -> an ID token is returned
userinfo only lists accounts for one user -> userinfo is the wrong level
decode.needs: The coid claim of the ID token.

stem: Ridgeway Talent's recruiting platform lets recruiters build offer packets. The recruiter must open the Docusign tagging screen inside the platform, drag signature and date fields onto the uploaded offer, review the candidate details, and click Send there. Candidates sign remotely by email and use no embedded signing. The platform authenticates recruiters with Authorization Code Grant, already registers a return URL, and receives envelope status from an account-level Connect listener. Which API sequence should the developer implement?

options.text: Create the envelope with status sent, then call EnvelopeViews:createSender for the recruiter
Create the envelope with status created, then call EnvelopeViews:createSender for the recruiter
Create the envelope with a clientUserId on the candidate, then call EnvelopeViews:createRecipient
Create the envelope with status created and a clientUserId on the recruiter, then call createRecipient

answerText: Create the envelope with status created, then call EnvelopeViews:createSender for the recruiter
explanation: Embedded sending uses EnvelopeViews:createSender on a draft (status created) envelope, so the user can edit tabs, documents and recipients and send from inside the app. The clue is that the recruiter tags and clicks Send in the platform while candidates sign remotely.
whyNotOthers: B is right because the sender view needs a draft envelope. The trap is A: it uses the right view, but a sent envelope has already been sent, so the recruiter cannot prepare and send it. C embeds the candidate's signing, which the scenario rules out. D uses the recipient (signing) view, which does not provide the tagging and sending screen.

optionExplanations.A: Once sent, the envelope is no longer a draft the recruiter can prepare and send.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. createSender on a created (draft) envelope gives the embedded tagging and sending experience.
optionExplanations.C: That is embedded signing for the candidate, who signs remotely in this scenario.
optionExplanations.D: createRecipient opens a signing session, not the sender's tagging view.

concept.title: Embedded sending with createSender
concept.line: Embedded sending: create the envelope as draft (status created), then EnvelopeViews:createSender so the user edits and sends in-app.

decode.prompt: What does this scenario really require?

options.text: Let the signer sign inside the app
