Let the app user act as an embedded signing recipient
Let an app user prepare, tag and send an envelope from inside the app while signers sign remotely
Create and send the envelope automatically with no user editing

decode.explanation: The recruiter tags fields and clicks Send in the platform while candidates sign by email, which is embedded sending on a draft envelope.
clues: drag signature and date fields ... click Send there -> embedded sending (sender view)
candidates sign remotely by email -> no recipient view needed
return URL and Connect listener -> already handled, not decisive
decode.needs: A sender view on an envelope created in draft status.

topic: Promoting a workflow from demo to production
stem: Imani at Northbay Utilities built and tested a service-transfer workflow in her developer (demo) account. It uses a Collect Data with Web Forms step, a Prepare eSignature Template step with several field mappings, and is triggered by her app at https://api-d.docusign.com/v1. The production account has none of these web forms or templates yet, and the go-live review for her integration key is already approved. A teammate offers to rebuild the workflow by hand in production. Which two actions follow Docusign's documented approach for moving it? (Select two)

options.text: Rebuild the field mappings manually after import, because import keeps steps but drops mappings
Recreate the web form and eSignature template in production before importing, because import omits them
Export the workflow from demo and import it into production; referenced web forms and templates are added
Keep the api-d.docusign.com/v1 base path, because the Maestro API uses one global host
Point the app's Maestro calls at https://api.docusign.com/v1 for production

answerText: Export the workflow from demo and import it into production; referenced web forms and templates are added; Point the app's Maestro calls at https://api.docusign.com/v1 for production
explanation: Docusign recommends creating and testing in demo, exporting, then importing into production; import preserves step configuration and field mappings and adds referenced Web Forms and eSignature templates. Production Maestro calls use https://api.docusign.com/v1.
whyNotOthers: C and E are right: export/import carries the steps, mappings and referenced resources, and production calls go to api.docusign.com/v1 instead of api-d. The trap is B: it sounds prudent, but import adds the referenced web forms and eSignature templates itself. A is wrong because field mappings are preserved, and D is wrong because demo and production have different base paths.

optionExplanations.A: Wrong. All field mappings configured in workflow steps are preserved on import.
optionExplanations.B: Wrong. Resources referenced in steps, including Web Forms and eSignature templates, are added when the workflow is imported.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. Export from demo and import into production is the documented best practice, and referenced resources come along.
optionExplanations.D: Wrong. Demo uses api-d.docusign.com/v1 and production uses api.docusign.com/v1.
optionExplanations.E: Correct. Production Maestro API calls use the https://api.docusign.com/v1 base path.

concept.title: Promoting a workflow to production
concept.line: Export from demo and import into production (keeps configuration and mappings, adds referenced web forms/templates); production Maestro base is https://api.docusign.com/v1.

decode.prompt: What does this scenario really require?

options.text: Rebuild the workflow and its assets by hand in production
Repeat the integration's go-live review for the workflow
Keep the same API host because the workflow itself is unchanged
Move a tested workflow and its dependencies from demo to production and repoint the app to the production host

decode.explanation: Docusign's documented path is export from demo and import into production, which brings referenced assets, and production calls must use the production Maestro host.
clues: built and tested ... in her developer (demo) account -> export/import path
production account has none of these web forms or templates -> import adds referenced assets
triggered at api-d.docusign.com -> must switch to the production host
decode.needs: Export/import the workflow and call api.docusign.com/v1 in production.

topic: Least-privilege scopes for consent and JWT
stem: Sana builds a JWT Grant service for Corvid Energy that sends envelopes through the eSignature REST API and starts Maestro workflows through the Maestro API, which needs aow_manage. Least privilege is mandatory and consent will be collected once. In the design review, one engineer argues the consent request should list only signature, because impersonation 'can be added later in the token', and another wants extended so the service can refresh its tokens. Which two choices are correct? (Select two)

options.text: Consent URL scope: signature impersonation, then add aow_manage only to the JWT payload once Maestro calls begin
Consent URL scope: signature aow_manage impersonation
JWT payload scope: signature aow_manage impersonation extended
JWT payload scope: signature aow_manage
Consent URL scope: signature, with a JWT payload scope of signature aow_manage impersonation

answerText: Consent URL scope: signature aow_manage impersonation; JWT payload scope: signature aow_manage
explanation: Consent must cover every scope the service will use plus impersonation (signature aow_manage impersonation); the JWT payload then requests only the API scopes it needs (signature aow_manage).
whyNotOthers: B and D are right. The trap is A: the payload cannot request aow_manage if consent never covered it. C adds impersonation, which is no longer needed after consent, and extended, which is for Authorization Code Grant only (JWT returns no refresh token). E repeats the engineer's mistake: impersonation must be part of consent, not added in the token.

optionExplanations.A: aow_manage was never consented, so the token request cannot include it.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. Consent covers both APIs plus impersonation.
optionExplanations.C: impersonation is not needed in the payload after consent, and extended does not apply to JWT.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. The payload lists only the API scopes the service calls.
optionExplanations.E: Consent without impersonation cannot be fixed by adding impersonation in the payload.

concept.title: Least-privilege consent and JWT scopes
concept.line: Consent must cover all scopes used plus impersonation (signature aow_manage impersonation); the JWT payload requests only API scopes (signature aow_manage).

decode.prompt: What does this scenario really require?

options.text: Collect consent once for every scope the service will ever use plus impersonation, then request only needed API scopes per token
Consent to the minimum now and add scopes later in the assertion
Obtain refresh tokens for a server-to-server flow
Use identical scope lists in the consent request and the assertion

decode.explanation: Consent collected once must already cover signature, aow_manage and impersonation, while least privilege means the JWT asks only for the API scopes it needs.
clues: consent will be collected once -> consent must include signature, aow_manage and impersonation
least privilege is mandatory -> the JWT payload lists only the API scopes
extended so the service can refresh -> JWT Grant has no refresh tokens; red herring
decode.needs: Consent: signature aow_manage impersonation; JWT scope: signature aow_manage.

stem: Mireille at Cobalt Realty promoted her integration key, set up the production OAuth settings and switched to the production base URI from userinfo. Her app creates envelopes by referring to server templates by ID. In production, envelope creation now fails with template-not-found errors. In addition, a Data Verification step that validated addresses in the developer account is not available in the production account, which runs on the company's existing entry-level plan. Her lead suggests going through Go-Live again. Which two tasks remain? (Select two)

options.text: Resubmit Go-Live with the template IDs listed, so that the review copies those templates into production
Recreate or migrate the templates in the production account and update the app to use their production template IDs
Confirm that the production plan includes every feature the app used in development, such as Basic Data Verification, and upgrade if not
Point the template calls back at demo.docusign.net, because templates stay in the developer account after promotion
Wait up to 48 hours for the settings sync that copies developer templates and features into production

answerText: Recreate or migrate the templates in the production account and update the app to use their production template IDs; Confirm that the production plan includes every feature the app used in development, such as Basic Data Verification, and upgrade if not
explanation: Production account data and settings are separate from the developer account: templates must be migrated and their new production IDs used. Developer accounts may include features that the production plan lacks, so the plan must include everything the app relied on, for example Basic Data Verification.
whyNotOthers: B and C are right: templates get new IDs in production, and the entry-level plan is the clue that a feature is missing. The trap is A: Go-Live copies only the integration key, never templates or settings. D fails because production envelopes must be created in the production account; templates in a developer account cannot be used there. E fails because no sync copies templates or features.

optionExplanations.A: Go-Live duplicates only the integration key; templates are never copied by a review.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. Templates must be added to the production account, and the production template IDs are different.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. The production plan must include every feature the app used in development; developer accounts can have features the plan lacks.
optionExplanations.D: Developer-account templates cannot be used by envelopes in the production account.
optionExplanations.E: There is no automatic sync of templates or features from developer to production.

concept.title: Data and plan after Go-Live
concept.line: Production is separate: migrate templates and use their production IDs, and confirm the production plan has every feature used in development.

decode.prompt: What does this scenario really require?

options.text: Repeat the go-live review
Recreate account data in production and confirm the production plan has the features used, since promotion copies neither
Wait for an automatic sync from the developer account
Keep using resources in the developer account

decode.explanation: Template-not-found errors and a missing Data Verification step both come from the production account being separate from demo in data and plan features.
clues: template-not-found errors -> templates exist only in the developer account
Data Verification ... not available ... entry-level plan -> the production plan lacks the feature
going through Go-Live again -> red herring
decode.needs: Migrate templates and use their production IDs; ensure the plan includes all features used.

topic: Rendering an embedded web form instance
stem: Solano Realty creates embedded web form instances from its Next.js backend for home buyers. A junior developer saves only the formUrl from each Instances:createInstance response in the database and later loads that URL in an iframe for the buyer. Buyers do not get their own prefilled instance, although formValues and clientUserId were sent correctly and every instance shows status INITIATED. During review the team lead points out that formUrl is identical for all instances created from the same configuration. What is the recommended way to render each buyer's instance?

options.text: Call EnvelopeViews:createRecipient with the buyer's clientUserId and frame the URL it returns.
Append the buyer's clientUserId to formUrl as a query parameter so the form loads that buyer's instance.
Call Configurations:getForm for the configuration and frame the instance URL that it returns.
Pass formUrl and the instanceToken to Docusign JS, which builds the instance URL and mounts the form.

answerText: Pass formUrl and the instanceToken to Docusign JS, which builds the instance URL and mounts the form.
explanation: createInstance returns formUrl (the same for every instance of a configuration) and an instanceToken unique to the user's session; the instance URL is formUrl#instanceToken=..., and Docusign JS builds it automatically. The clue is 'formUrl is identical for all instances'.
whyNotOthers: D is right because the token is what makes the URL unique and secure, and Docusign JS is the recommended renderer. The trap is A: createRecipient creates an eSignature signing view, not a web form instance view. B uses the wrong identifier (clientUserId is not part of the URL), and C returns the configuration's field definitions, not an instance URL.

optionExplanations.A: EnvelopeViews:createRecipient returns a signing URL for an envelope recipient, not a web form instance.
optionExplanations.B: The instance is identified in the URL by its instanceToken, not by clientUserId.
optionExplanations.C: Configurations:getForm describes the configuration's fields (used for prefill names); it returns no instance URL.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. Docusign JS combines formUrl and instanceToken into the secure instance URL and embeds the form.

concept.title: Rendering an embedded web form
concept.line: createInstance returns a shared formUrl and a per-session instanceToken; Docusign JS builds formUrl#instanceToken=... and mounts the form.

decode.prompt: What does this scenario really require?

options.text: Render an envelope signing session for a recipient
Identify the user by adding their ID to the shared URL
Render a specific user's web form instance rather than the shared configuration URL
Retrieve the configuration's form definition

decode.explanation: formUrl is the same for every instance, so something unique to each session must be combined with it to open that buyer's instance.
clues: formUrl is identical for all instances -> the URL alone does not identify an instance
each buyer's instance -> needs the per-session instanceToken
formValues and clientUserId sent correctly, status INITIATED -> data is fine; rendering is the gap
decode.needs: formUrl plus instanceToken, mounted with Docusign JS.

topic: Choosing data verification for a standard data type
stem: Corvid Supply onboards new vendors with an eSignature template. Its compliance lead, Ines, needs the vendor's business entity and federal employer identification number (FEIN) checked against authoritative records while the vendor fills in the agreement, with signing blocked until the value is corrected. Corvid has no internal registry of FEINs and does not want to model its own data types; a provider exists whose API supports Docusign's business entity verification contract. Corvid's CRM sync runs in Maestro separately. Which extension should Ines use?

options.text: Connected fields extension with a custom Concerto model of the vendor record
Data verification extension for business entity (FEIN), used in eSignature
Data IO extension that searches the provider's records from a Maestro step
Connected fields extension invoked from the CRM sync workflow in Maestro

answerText: Data verification extension for business entity (FEIN), used in eSignature
explanation: The data is a standard verifiable type (business FEIN), checked 'while the vendor fills in the agreement', and Corvid has 'no internal registry' and no wish to model data types, which points to the data verification extension at the eSignature extension point.
whyNotOthers: B is right because data verification extensions verify specific common data types, including business FEIN, in eSignature. The trap is A: connected fields also verify during signing, but they are meant for custom data in your own system of record and require a custom Concerto data model, which Corvid explicitly does not want. C and D place the check in Maestro, which is not where signers fill in envelopes, and connected fields are not supported in Maestro.

optionExplanations.A: Connected fields work at the same point but are designed for custom data against your own system of record, needing a custom data model Corvid does not have.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. Business FEIN verification is one of the data verification extensions and runs in eSignature while the signer completes fields.
optionExplanations.C: Data IO reads and writes a system of record from Maestro steps; it does not verify values while a vendor fills in an envelope.
optionExplanations.D: Connected fields are not supported in Maestro workflows, and the check must happen during signing.

concept.title: Data verification for standard types
concept.line: Standard verifiable types (e.g. business FEIN) without your own registry use the data verification extension at the eSignature extension point.

decode.prompt: What does this scenario really require?

options.text: Verify a field against the company's own records using a custom data model
Read and write records from a Maestro workflow step
Sync CRM data as part of an orchestration
Verify a standard business data type against an authoritative provider while the signer fills in an eSignature envelope

decode.explanation: The FEIN check happens during eSignature filling against an external provider, and Corvid has no registry or custom data model, which fits the verification extension for business entities.
clues: while the vendor fills in the agreement ... signing blocked -> eSignature extension point, verification
no internal registry ... does not want to model its own data types -> not connected fields
provider supports Docusign's business entity verification contract -> standard verification type
CRM sync runs in Maestro separately -> red herring
decode.needs: A data verification extension for business entity (FEIN) in eSignature.

stem: Cedar Valley County's procurement team receives signed bids from external vendors, who send envelopes from their own Docusign accounts to the county's buyers. Developer Anika Shah must notify the county ERP whenever a bid envelope reaches a buyer. She has API access with an admin user, the ERP accepts JSON, and security asks for HMAC on whatever is built. Four designs are proposed. Which design will NOT deliver the required events?

options.text: Have the county app add an eventNotification object to envelopes using Envelopes:create
Create a custom account-level Connect configuration on the county account through the ConnectConfigurations API
Create an organization-level Connect configuration that covers the county's account
Create an account-level Connect configuration in eSignature Admin limited to the buyers' users

answerText: Have the county app add an eventNotification object to envelopes using Envelopes:create
explanation: Envelope-level webhooks can only be configured when an envelope is sent, so they are not available for envelopes received by account members from external parties. The bids are sent from the vendors' accounts, so the county never creates them.
whyNotOthers: A is the design that fails, because the county never calls Envelopes:create for envelopes that vendors send. The trap is D: limiting an account-level configuration to selected users seems too narrow, but account-level Connect supports all or selected users and covers envelopes they receive. B and C both work because account-level and organization-level configurations cover envelopes sent from or received by the account or organization.

optionExplanations.A: Correct (this design fails). eventNotification is set only on envelopes your integration sends, so it cannot cover envelopes received from external vendors.
optionExplanations.B: This works: an account-level configuration, created in the UI or via the ConnectConfigurations API, covers envelopes received by the account.
optionExplanations.C: This works: organization-level Connect covers envelopes sent from or received by the accounts in the organization.
optionExplanations.D: This works: account-level Connect can be scoped to all users or selected users, and it includes envelopes those users receive.

concept.title: Envelope-level webhook limitation
concept.line: Envelope-level webhooks (eventNotification) are configured only when sending, so they cannot cover envelopes received from external parties.

decode.prompt: Which constraint rules out one of the designs?

options.text: Events are needed for envelopes the county receives but never creates
Events are needed only for envelopes the county itself sends
The decisive constraint is HMAC signing, which some designs cannot provide
Events must be limited to specific users in the account

decode.explanation: The bids come from vendors' own accounts, so any design that depends on the county creating the envelope cannot see them.
clues: vendors send envelopes from their own Docusign accounts -> the county never calls Envelopes:create for them
whenever a bid envelope reaches a buyer -> events for received envelopes
security asks for HMAC -> supported by every Connect option, not decisive
decode.needs: Account or organization Connect, since envelope-level webhooks only cover envelopes you send.

stem: Bayview Homes wants the two buyers of a duplex to receive a purchase web form by email, fill it in, and then sign the generated envelope. The developer calls Instances:createInstance on a template-based configuration with sendOption set to now and a recipients array listing signer1 and signer2 with names and emails. The security team asks whether the portal's own login can be recorded on the certificate of completion, and the product owner asks how the integration will tell instances apart later. Which two statements about this request are correct? (Select two)

options.text: clientUserId is required on this request and is limited to 100 characters.
authenticationMethod and authenticationInstant can be added so the portal login appears on the certificate.
The two buyers are differentiated by the roleName values in the recipients array.
The envelope is created only after the first buyer submits the web form instance.
tags can be added so instances can be identified in getInstance and listInstances responses.

answerText: The two buyers are differentiated by the roleName values in the recipients array.; tags can be added so instances can be identified in getInstance and listInstances responses.
explanation: Remote instances identify users by roleName in recipients (clientUserId is not required), and the tags array adds metadata that is returned by getInstance and listInstances.
whyNotOthers: C and E are right. The trap is B: the recipient authentication record properties work only for embedded signing of template-based forms and are not supported for remote instances. A is true only for embedded instances, and D is the embedded timing; a remote instance's envelope is created when createInstance is processed.

optionExplanations.A: clientUserId is required for embedded instances; remote instances identify users by roleName.
optionExplanations.B: Recording authentication properties is not supported for remote web form instances.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. roleName in the recipients array distinguishes the users of a remote instance.
optionExplanations.D: For remote delivery the envelope is created when createInstance is processed, not on first submission.
optionExplanations.E: Correct. tags values are stored with the instance and returned by getInstance and listInstances.

concept.title: Remote web form instance request
concept.line: Remote instances identify users by roleName in recipients (no clientUserId needed); tags add metadata returned by getInstance and listInstances.

decode.prompt: What does this scenario really require?

options.text: Treat the request as embedded, which needs app-side user identifiers
Know how a remote web form instance identifies its participants and carries metadata for later lookup
Capture the portal's own login as signer evidence
Control when envelope generation happens

decode.explanation: The buyers receive the form by email, so this is a remote instance where recipients are told apart by role, and instances are told apart by metadata returned by later reads.
clues: receive a purchase web form by email -> remote instance, not embedded
recipients array listing signer1 and signer2 -> roleName distinguishes participants
tell instances apart later -> tags returned by getInstance and listInstances
decode.needs: Remote instance: roleName in recipients, tags for instance metadata.

stem: A Confidential Authorization Code Grant app requests the scopes signature and extended. What does extended change?

options.text: The access token lasts 30 days instead of 8 hours
The refresh token expires 30 days after the last successful refresh, not 30 days after first issue
The refresh token never expires, as long as the user does not revoke consent
The integration key can also obtain refresh tokens when it uses JWT Grant

answerText: The refresh token expires 30 days after the last successful refresh, not 30 days after first issue
explanation: With extended, the refresh token expires 30 days from the last successful refresh (rolling); without it, 30 days from the original issue date.
whyNotOthers: B is right because extended only makes the refresh token window roll. The trap is C: the window rolls but still ends if the app does not refresh for 30 days. A applies the 30 days to the wrong token, and D fails because extended is for Authorization Code Grant only and JWT never returns a refresh token.

optionExplanations.A: The access token stays at 8 hours; extended affects the refresh token.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. Rolling 30-day window measured from the last refresh.
optionExplanations.C: It still expires if 30 days pass without a successful refresh.
optionExplanations.D: JWT Grant never returns a refresh token; extended is Auth Code only.

concept.title: extended scope: rolling refresh
concept.line: With extended, the refresh token expires 30 days after the last successful refresh; without it, 30 days after original issue.

topic: Regional availability of a public app
stem: Northwind Signals, a Docusign partner, has an approved extension app that verifies phone numbers using a carrier data provider. Its licence with that provider covers only North America and Australia, so customer accounts in other regions must not be able to install the app. Northwind expects thousands of customer accounts and cannot list them individually. The product manager also asks whether the OAuth scopes in the connection could be narrowed to block other regions. How should Northwind control availability?

options.text: Set distribution to PRIVATE and add the account ID of every customer account in those regions
Narrow the connection's OAuth scopes so installs from other regions fail
Set distribution to PUBLIC and choose only the permitted regions in publicationRegions
Publish to the App Center for all regions and reject unwanted installs in the API proxy

answerText: Set distribution to PUBLIC and choose only the permitted regions in publicationRegions
explanation: The app is for 'thousands of customer accounts' from a Docusign partner, so it is public, and publicationRegions (public apps only) controls from which regions the app can be installed in the production App Center.
whyNotOthers: C is right because publicationRegions restricts where a public app can be installed. The trap is A: private distribution does limit access, but only to individually listed production accounts, which Northwind says it cannot maintain. B fails because OAuth scopes govern what Docusign may access in the external API, not who may install, and D lets everyone install and then breaks their envelopes instead of controlling availability.

optionExplanations.A: Private apps are shared with individually listed account IDs, which does not scale to thousands of customers.
optionExplanations.B: OAuth scopes define access to the external API, not which Docusign accounts can install the app.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. For public apps, publicationRegions defines the regions in which the app can be installed in production.
optionExplanations.D: This makes the app installable everywhere and fails at runtime rather than controlling availability in the App Center.

concept.title: Public app regional availability
concept.line: Public apps use publicationRegions (public only) to control which regions can install the app from the production App Center.

decode.prompt: What does this scenario really require?

options.text: Restrict installs to a named list of accounts
Restrict what the app can access once installed
Restrict where a widely distributed app can be installed, by region, at scale
Filter unwanted installs at runtime in the app's own service

decode.explanation: Thousands of accounts mean public distribution, and the licence limit is geographic, so availability must be controlled by publication region.
clues: thousands of customer accounts ... cannot list them individually -> public, not private
licence covers only North America and Australia -> region-based availability
narrow the OAuth scopes -> red herring; scopes govern access, not region
decode.needs: PUBLIC distribution with publicationRegions.

stem: Bayview Insurance's quoting service currently sends policies with the template reference model. A new rule says each envelope must contain two existing server templates, Policy Terms and State Disclosures, plus a premium schedule PDF that the service generates for each quote, and everything must be created in a single API call. Signers and anchors are already defined in the templates, and the team wants an envelope structure that is easy to extend later. Which approach should the developer use?

options.text: Keep the template reference model and pass both template IDs in templateId with one templateRoles list
Use the direct documents model and reference both server templates from the documents array
Use the composite templates model, with one composite template object for each template and the PDF
Send from one template with the template reference model, then add the rest with EnvelopeDocuments:update

answerText: Use the composite templates model, with one composite template object for each template and the PDF
explanation: Only composite templates can apply multiple server templates and extra documents in one envelope per API call. The clue is "two server templates plus a generated PDF" and "a single API call".
whyNotOthers: C is right because composite templates combine server templates, inline templates and documents. The trap is D: adding documents later could work, but it takes several calls and still cannot apply the second template's roles and tabs. A fails because the template reference model takes a single template. B fails because the direct documents model does not reference server templates.

optionExplanations.A: The template reference model includes a single template; it cannot combine two.
optionExplanations.B: The direct documents model supplies documents directly and does not apply server templates.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. Composite templates are the only model that combines multiple server templates and a document in one call.
optionExplanations.D: This needs several calls and does not bring in the second template's recipients and tabs.

concept.title: Choosing composite templates
concept.line: Only composite templates apply multiple server templates plus extra documents in one envelope in a single API call.

decode.prompt: What does this scenario really require?

options.text: Send from a single template with role assignments
Upload documents only, without templates
Build the envelope incrementally over several calls
Combine several server templates with a generated document in one envelope in a single call

decode.explanation: Two server templates plus a per-quote PDF in one create call, with room to extend, requires the envelope model that layers multiple templates and documents.
clues: two existing server templates ... plus a premium schedule PDF -> multiple templates plus an extra document
created in a single API call -> no follow-up update calls
easy to extend later -> a modular envelope structure
decode.needs: Composite templates model.

stem: Sofia leads a partner team preparing to submit its first public extension app, which archives data to a cloud service. During development the registration pointed to a sandbox host, and the team has run connection, extension and functional tests in its developer account. Marketing has already prepared the icon, four screenshots and the listing text, and the support team wants to know how much control it will keep over customer installs afterwards. A new team member drafts a checklist for the release. Which two statements on the checklist are accurate? (Select two)

options.text: Once the review passes, the app automatically appears in the App Center for all customers
The review evaluates the business, technical, security and functional aspects of the app
The review requires a minimum number of successful eSignature API calls from the app
Production URLs must be in the registration before the public app is submitted for review
Account administrators are notified automatically if the team later removes the app from an account

answerText: The review evaluates the business, technical, security and functional aspects of the app; Production URLs must be in the registration before the public app is submitted for review
explanation: Docusign's review evaluates business, technical, security and functional aspects, and for a public app the production URLs must be supplied in the registration before submitting for review.
whyNotOthers: B and D are right per the build and test guidance. The trap is A: after a successful review the app is only in Approved status, and the developer must still click Publish to App Center (and, for public apps, make it available). C invents a call quota, and E is the opposite of the documented warning that admins are not notified when an app is removed.

optionExplanations.A: Approval leaves the app in Approved status; the developer must still publish it to the App Center.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. The review covers business, technical, security and functional aspects.
optionExplanations.C: No minimum API call count is part of the extension app review.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. For a public app, supply production URLs in the registration before submitting it for review.
optionExplanations.E: The account administrator is not notified when an app is removed, which is why removal must be done carefully.

concept.title: App review and publishing facts
concept.line: Review covers business, technical, security and functional aspects; public apps need production URLs in the registration before review.

decode.prompt: What does this scenario really require?

options.text: Know what public app review assesses and what must be in place before submitting
Know the usage thresholds the app must reach before review
Know what happens automatically once review passes
Know how customer administrators are told about later changes

decode.explanation: The registration still points to a sandbox host, so the team needs the pre-submission requirements and the scope of Docusign's review.
clues: registration pointed to a sandbox host -> production URLs needed before submission
connection, extension and functional tests -> review covers technical and functional aspects
icon, four screenshots and the listing text -> listing assets ready; not decisive
decode.needs: Production URLs in the registration; review covers business, technical, security and functional aspects.

stem: Ridgeline Bank sends envelopes whose tabs use Connected Fields to verify account numbers against its core banking system. Its compliance team wants each verification result pushed to an audit service in real time. The account's only Connect configuration is a legacy XML configuration in aggregate mode that feeds an old document vault, which must keep working. The audit service is newly built, sits behind HTTPS, and can parse any format. What should the developer do?

options.text: Add the extension-executed event to the existing XML aggregate configuration and forward it to the audit service
Create a separate JSON SIM configuration for the audit service that subscribes to the extension-executed event
Subscribe the audit service to recipient-completed and read the verification outcome from the tab values
Build a Data IO extension app that writes the verification results to the audit service during signing

answerText: Create a separate JSON SIM configuration for the audit service that subscribes to the extension-executed event
explanation: Connected Fields verification results arrive through the Connect extension-executed event, which is available only with JSON SIM. A separate configuration keeps the XML aggregate feed for the vault untouched.
whyNotOthers: B is right because extension-executed requires JSON SIM, and a second configuration avoids breaking the legacy vault feed. The trap is A: reusing the existing configuration seems simplest, but XML aggregate cannot deliver extension-executed. C fails because recipient-completed reports the signer finishing, not the verification result; D fails because Data IO is a Maestro workflow extension for reading and writing records, not the channel that reports Connected Fields results.

optionExplanations.A: The extension-executed event is available only with JSON SIM, so it cannot be added to an XML aggregate configuration.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. A dedicated JSON SIM configuration subscribed to extension-executed receives Connected Fields verification results while the XML vault feed stays unchanged.
optionExplanations.C: recipient-completed reports that a recipient finished; it is not the event that carries the Connected Fields verification result.
optionExplanations.D: Data IO extension apps read and write data in Maestro workflows; they do not report Connected Fields verification outcomes during eSignature signing.

concept.title: Connected fields results via Connect
concept.line: Connected fields verification results arrive via the extension-executed event, JSON SIM only; add a separate configuration rather than changing an XML feed.

decode.prompt: What does this scenario really require?

options.text: Extend the existing legacy configuration with new events
Stream connected-fields verification results in real time without disturbing an existing legacy feed
Derive verification outcomes from signer completion data
Write results to an external system from inside an extension

decode.explanation: Verification results are published as an event that only the JSON SIM format supports, and the old XML feed must stay as is.
clues: Connected Fields ... each verification result -> the extension-executed event
legacy XML configuration in aggregate mode ... must keep working -> leave it untouched
can parse any format -> JSON SIM is acceptable and required
decode.needs: A separate JSON SIM Connect configuration subscribed to extension-executed.

stem: Fenwick Legal's Connect listener returns HTTP 200 for every message and then puts it on an internal queue. For about three hours, a bug in the queue consumer silently discarded those messages; Connect logged no delivery failures because every message was acknowledged. About 1,800 envelopes may have changed status during that time. The team wants to resynchronize without hurting the integration's efficiency score or breaking the polling rules. A developer proposes looping over all 1,800 envelopes with Envelopes:get, spaced out to stay under the burst limit. What should the team do?

options.text: Loop over the envelopes with Envelopes:get, spacing calls so the job stays under the 500-per-30-seconds burst limit
Wait for Connect to retry the discarded messages, because Connect re-sends any message the listener failed to process
Call EnvelopeRecipients:list for each envelope, because recipient status requests do not count toward API limits
Call Envelopes:listStatusChanges with a from_date slightly before the outage began, then update records from the results

answerText: Call Envelopes:listStatusChanges with a from_date slightly before the outage began, then update records from the results
explanation: Docusign's recommended catch-up after missed Connect messages is Envelopes:listStatusChanges with an overlapping time window. A few list calls replace 1,800 individual requests.
whyNotOthers: D is right because one ranged listStatusChanges query recovers every changed envelope efficiently. The trap is B: Connect retries only failed deliveries, and here every message was acknowledged with HTTP 200, so nothing is retried. A fails because 1,800 single-envelope requests count as excessive envelope requests even when they stay under the burst limit. C fails because recipient status requests do count, and excessive ones lower the efficiency score.

optionExplanations.A: Staying under the burst limit does not stop 1,800 per-envelope calls from counting as excessive envelope status requests.
optionExplanations.B: Connect retries only failed deliveries; these messages were acknowledged with HTTP 200, so Connect treats them as delivered.
optionExplanations.C: Recipient status requests count toward limits, and excessive ones are an efficiency score factor.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. listStatusChanges with a time window that overlaps the outage is the recommended catch-up method.

concept.title: Catch-up with listStatusChanges
concept.line: After missed Connect messages, call Envelopes:listStatusChanges with a from_date overlapping the outage; a few list calls replace many individual GETs.

decode.prompt: What does this scenario really require?

options.text: Re-fetch each affected envelope individually at a safe pace
Rely on Connect to resend the lost messages
Catch up on status changes missed during a time window with as few calls as possible
Use endpoints that do not count toward API limits

decode.explanation: Connect saw every message acknowledged so nothing will be resent, and the efficiency score rules out 1,800 single gets, leaving a time-window catch-up query.
clues: Connect logged no delivery failures because every message was acknowledged -> no retries will happen
without hurting the efficiency score or breaking the polling rules -> avoid per-envelope gets
for about three hours -> a bounded time window to query
decode.needs: Envelopes:listStatusChanges with from_date just before the outage.

stem: Ashford Retail's analytics service calls GetAgreementsList with limit=100 to copy all agreement records into a data warehouse. The account holds about 2,300 agreements, but the warehouse only ever receives the first 100. One colleague suggests switching to the start_position and count parameters used by eSignature list calls; another wants to fetch every agreement individually with GetAgreement. The account's hourly API limit is shared with several other integrations. Which change retrieves the full set efficiently?

options.text: Replace limit with start_position and count, raising start_position by 100 on each call.
Call GetAgreement for every agreement ID listed in the first page, then repeat the list call.
Remove limit entirely, because GetAgreementsList then returns every agreement in one response.
Keep limit=100 and pass the continuation token (ctoken) from each response into the next request.

answerText: Keep limit=100 and pass the continuation token (ctoken) from each response into the next request.
explanation: GetAgreementsList pages its results: limit sets the page size and ctoken, an opaque continuation token, retrieves the next page.
whyNotOthers: D is right because ctoken paging walks the whole result set in about 23 calls. The trap is A: start_position and count belong to eSignature list endpoints, not to this API. B multiplies calls and still never reaches records past the first page, and C fails because the list is paginated whether or not limit is sent.

optionExplanations.A: start_position and count are eSignature paging parameters; GetAgreementsList uses limit and ctoken.
optionExplanations.B: Per-agreement GET calls waste the shared limit and never discover agreements beyond the first page.
optionExplanations.C: The list endpoint is paginated; removing limit does not return all 2,300 agreements at once.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. limit sets page size and ctoken continues to the next page.

concept.title: Paging GetAgreementsList with ctoken
concept.line: GetAgreementsList pages with limit (page size) and ctoken, an opaque continuation token for the next page.

decode.prompt: What does this scenario really require?

options.text: Use the paging parameters of the eSignature API
Fetch every record in one unbounded call
Retrieve every record individually by ID
Page through a large Agreement Manager result set using that API's own paging mechanism

decode.explanation: Only the first page arrives because the next-page token is ignored, and the shared hourly limit rules out per-record calls.
clues: warehouse only ever receives the first 100 -> paging is not being followed
start_position and count used by eSignature list calls -> the wrong API's convention
hourly API limit is shared -> avoid per-agreement calls
decode.needs: Follow the ctoken continuation token with limit=100.

stem: Which two statements about HMAC security for Docusign Connect are correct? (Select two)

options.text: HMAC encrypts the Connect message body, so the listener no longer needs an HTTPS endpoint
With two active HMAC keys, each message carries X-DocuSign-Signature-1 and X-DocuSign-Signature-2, and matching either one verifies it
HMAC is available only for organization-level configurations, not for account-level or envelope-level ones
The listener verifies the header by decrypting it with a public key that Docusign publishes
Each header holds an HMAC-SHA256 hash of the message body, which proves both authenticity and integrity

answerText: With two active HMAC keys, each message carries X-DocuSign-Signature-1 and X-DocuSign-Signature-2, and matching either one verifies it; Each header holds an HMAC-SHA256 hash of the message body, which proves both authenticity and integrity
explanation: Each defined HMAC key (up to one hundred) adds its own X-DocuSign-Signature-N header containing the body hashed with HMAC-SHA256, and any one of them can be used to verify that the message came from Docusign and was not altered.
whyNotOthers: B and E are right: one header per key, any header may be used, and the hash proves the message is from Docusign and unchanged. The trap is D: it describes asymmetric signing, while HMAC uses shared secret keys known only to Docusign and your app. A fails because HMAC hashes rather than encrypts, so HTTPS is still needed; C fails because HMAC is available for all types of Connect configuration.

optionExplanations.A: HMAC produces a hash for verification; it does not encrypt the body, so the listener still needs HTTPS for confidentiality.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. Each defined key adds its own X-DocuSign-Signature-N header, and validating against any one of them is sufficient.
optionExplanations.C: HMAC is available for all Connect configuration types, including account-level and envelope-level.
optionExplanations.D: HMAC is symmetric: the listener recomputes the hash with its shared secret key; there is no public key involved.
optionExplanations.E: Correct. The header is the message body hashed with HMAC-SHA256 using a secret key, verifying authenticity (sent by Docusign) and integrity (unchanged).

concept.title: Multiple HMAC keys and headers
concept.line: Each HMAC key (up to 100) adds an X-DocuSign-Signature-N header with HMAC-SHA256 of the body; matching any one proves authenticity and integrity.

stem: An agreement was imported into Agreement Manager by mistake and must be removed through the API. Which request is correct?

options.text: DELETE /v1/accounts/{accountId}/agreements/{agreementId} (DeleteAgreement).
PUT /restapi/v2.1/accounts/{accountId}/envelopes/{envelopeId} with status set to voided.
PUT /v1/accounts/{accountId}/agreements/{agreementId} with status set to deleted.
POST /v1/accounts/{accountId}/agreements/{agreementId}/actions/purge.

answerText: DELETE /v1/accounts/{accountId}/agreements/{agreementId} (DeleteAgreement).
explanation: DeleteAgreement is a DELETE on /v1/accounts/{accountId}/agreements/{agreementId}; it is one of the four agreement operations (list, get, delete, create summary).
whyNotOthers: A is right. The trap is B: voiding cancels an in-flight eSignature envelope and does not remove an imported agreement from the repository. C and D are not operations of the Agreement Manager API, which has no update or purge action.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. DeleteAgreement removes a specific agreement.
optionExplanations.B: Voiding is an eSignature envelope action; an imported agreement is not an in-flight envelope.
optionExplanations.C: There is no update operation on agreements; deletion is a DELETE request.
optionExplanations.D: No purge action exists; the only agreement action endpoint is ai/actions/summarize.

concept.title: Deleting an agreement
concept.line: DeleteAgreement is DELETE /v1/accounts/{accountId}/agreements/{agreementId}; one of four agreement operations (list, get, delete, create summary).

stem: Quantis offers an identity-matching service. Its CTO wants Docusign customers to use the service inside their own envelopes and Maestro workflows, discovered and installed by account admins, with no code deployed or hosted by the customer. A solutions engineer proposes giving each customer a Quantis-built eSignature API integration with its own integration key, Go-Live review and JWT consent. Another suggests asking customers to register Connect webhooks pointing at Quantis. Which approach matches the CTO's goal?

options.text: Build an extension app registered in the Developer Console and published to the Docusign App Center
Build an eSignature API integration and promote its integration key to each customer's production account
Ask each customer to configure an account-level Connect listener that calls the Quantis service
Publish a Maestro workflow template that calls the Quantis API from an eSignature API step

answerText: Build an extension app registered in the Developer Console and published to the Docusign App Center
explanation: The goal is functionality used 'inside their own envelopes and Maestro workflows, discovered and installed by account admins, with no code' on the customer side, which is what extension apps published to the App Center provide.
whyNotOthers: A is right because extension apps execute on the Docusign platform, are installed from the App Center and work within the Docusign user experience, extending reach to Docusign's customer base. The trap is B: an API integration is self-contained and hosted by its developer, and Go-Live promotes an integration key, not an installable in-product feature. C only pushes event notifications out of Docusign after the fact, and D still requires per-customer building rather than an installable app.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. Extension apps are published to the App Center, installed by admins, and run inside envelopes and workflows.
optionExplanations.B: API integrations are self-contained apps hosted by their developers; they do not add installable features inside customers' Docusign experience.
optionExplanations.C: Connect sends event notifications outward; it does not add a service that runs inside envelopes or workflow steps.
optionExplanations.D: This still relies on each customer building workflows around a raw API call instead of an installable, reviewed app.

concept.title: Extension app vs API integration
concept.line: No-code functionality inside customers' envelopes and Maestro workflows, installed by admins, is an extension app published to the App Center.

decode.prompt: What does this scenario really require?

options.text: Deliver a provider's capability that customers discover and install inside Docusign, with no customer-hosted code
Give each customer its own API integration to operate
Have customers forward envelope events to the provider
Distribute a workflow customers configure to call the provider

decode.explanation: Use inside envelopes and workflows, discovery and install by admins, and no customer code together describe a published extension app.
clues: inside their own envelopes and Maestro workflows -> Docusign extension points
discovered and installed by account admins -> App Center listing
no code deployed or hosted by the customer -> not an API integration or Connect listener
decode.needs: An extension app registered in the Developer Console and published to the App Center.

stem: Luca at Ferro Motors triggers a vehicle-finance workflow from the dealership CRM through the Maestro API. The CRM must show, for each deal record, whether that customer's workflow is still running, completed or canceled, who started it and when it ended. Luca stored the response of each triggerWorkflow call in the deal record. A colleague proposes polling the eSignature EnvelopeRecipients endpoint because a signing step exists, and another suggests listing every workflow on the account each hour. Which approach returns the required details for a single deal most directly?

options.text: Call GetWorkflowsList hourly and match each deal by workflow name
Call EnvelopeRecipients:list for the envelope the workflow created and infer the instance status
Call getWorkflowInstance with the workflowId and the instance ID saved from the trigger response
Call getWorkflowInstancesList and read the trigger_input_schema for each instance

answerText: Call getWorkflowInstance with the workflowId and the instance ID saved from the trigger response
explanation: The trigger response returns the instance ID; getWorkflowInstance on /workflows/{workflowId}/instances/{instanceId} returns that instance's status, start and end times and started_by.
whyNotOthers: C is right because the stored trigger response contains the instance ID, and getWorkflowInstance returns status, times and started_by for that one instance. The trap is B: recipient status covers only the signing step, not whether the whole workflow completed or was canceled. A returns workflow definitions, not instance status, and D lists instances but the trigger_input_schema belongs to the trigger requirements, not instance status.

optionExplanations.A: Wrong. GetWorkflowsList returns workflow definitions and their input schemas, not the status of a deal's instance.
optionExplanations.B: Wrong. Envelope recipient status shows only the signing step, not instance status, started_by or end time.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. getWorkflowInstance with the saved instance ID returns status, start and end times and started_by.
optionExplanations.D: Wrong. trigger_input_schema describes required trigger inputs; it is not instance status data.

concept.title: Tracking a triggered instance
concept.line: Save the instance ID from the trigger response; getWorkflowInstance returns its status, start/end times and started_by.

decode.prompt: What does this scenario really require?

options.text: Infer workflow progress from signing activity
Get the status and details of one specific workflow instance whose ID is already known
Scan all workflows on the account
Read a workflow's input definition

decode.explanation: The trigger response already holds the instance ID, and the CRM needs one instance's status, starter and end time.
clues: for each deal record -> a single instance
stored the response of each triggerWorkflow call -> the instance ID is available
who started it and when it ended -> instance-level details
decode.needs: getWorkflowInstance with the workflowId and the stored instance ID.

stem: Tomas runs a nightly JWT Grant service for Alder Insurance that voids expired envelopes as a system user. After the key went Live in the production account, he changed the OAuth host and the aud claim to account.docusign.com, cached base_uri from userinfo, and kept signing assertions with the private key he generated in the developer account's Apps and Keys page. The system user has already granted consent in production, and the scopes are unchanged. Token requests are still rejected. A teammate suspects the key value changed during promotion. What should Tomas do?

options.text: Add an RSA key pair to the integration key in the production account's Apps and Keys and sign the JWT with its private key
Replace the iss claim with the new integration key GUID that Docusign generated for the production copy of the key
Change the aud claim back to account-d.docusign.com, because JWT assertions are always validated by the demo server
Add the extended scope so the token response includes a refresh token that can be reused in production

answerText: Add an RSA key pair to the integration key in the production account's Apps and Keys and sign the JWT with its private key
explanation: RSA key pairs, secrets and redirect URIs are not duplicated when the key is promoted. The private key 'generated in the developer account' has no matching public key on the production key, so Tomas must add an RSA key pair in production and sign with it.
whyNotOthers: A is right because RSA key pairs must be added to the production copy of the key. The trap is B: the key is duplicated with the same value, so iss stays the same. C fails because the production audience is account.docusign.com. D fails because JWT Grant never returns a refresh token (extended applies only to Authorization Code Grant).

optionExplanations.A: Correct. RSA key pairs are not copied at promotion; add one to the production key and sign with its private key.
optionExplanations.B: The integration key keeps the same value in production; iss does not change.
optionExplanations.C: In production the aud value must be account.docusign.com.
optionExplanations.D: JWT Grant does not return refresh tokens; the extended scope applies only to Authorization Code Grant.

concept.title: JWT RSA keys after promotion
concept.line: RSA key pairs are not copied on promotion; add one to the production key in Apps and Keys; sign with its private key.

decode.prompt: What does this scenario really require?

options.text: Use a different integration key identifier in production
Have assertions validated by the demo authorization server
Sign assertions with a key registered on the production integration key, since keys are not copied at promotion
Obtain long-lived reusable tokens

decode.explanation: Host, aud, consent and scopes are all correct; the remaining gap is the private key created in the developer account, which has no matching public key in production.
clues: private key he generated in the developer account's Apps and Keys page -> no matching public key in production
changed the OAuth host and aud, consent granted, scopes unchanged -> the rest is correct
teammate suspects the key value changed -> red herring; the GUID stays the same
decode.needs: Add an RSA key pair in production and sign with its private key.

stem: Okafor Logistics runs a Confidential Authorization Code Grant integration. To avoid interrupting users, a scheduler refreshes the tokens every 7 hours and saves the new refresh token. A separate reporting microservice, however, cached the access token when it started and keeps reusing it. Right after each scheduled refresh, the reporting service starts getting authentication errors, even though less than 8 hours have passed since its token was issued. Engineers have confirmed that the scopes, base_uri and account ID are all correct. What explains the errors?

options.text: The refresh was sent without the extended scope, so it cut every access token down to 1 hour
Refreshing revokes the user's consent, which must be granted again after each refresh
A refresh returns a new access token and a new refresh token, and the previous access token is no longer valid
Confidential Auth Code access tokens last only 7 hours, so the cached token simply expired

answerText: A refresh returns a new access token and a new refresh token, and the previous access token is no longer valid
explanation: Refreshing returns a new access token and a new refresh token, and the previous access token is no longer valid, so the cached token fails right after each refresh.
whyNotOthers: C is right because the errors start 'right after each scheduled refresh' with less than 8 hours elapsed. The trap is D: the 7-hour schedule tempts you, but Auth Code access tokens last 8 hours. A misuses extended, which only changes the refresh token lifetime, and B is false because refreshing does not touch consent.

optionExplanations.A: extended affects the refresh token's 30-day window, not the access token lifetime.
optionExplanations.B: Refreshing does not revoke consent; revocation is a separate user or admin action.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. The refresh replaces both tokens and the old access token stops working.
optionExplanations.D: Auth Code access tokens last 8 hours, and the errors match the refresh times, not expiry.

concept.title: Refresh token behaviour
concept.line: A refresh returns a new access token and new refresh token, and the previous access token is no longer valid.

decode.prompt: What does this scenario really require?

options.text: Understand how long access tokens last
Understand how consent behaves on refresh
Understand how scopes affect token lifetime
Understand what happens to existing access tokens when a refresh occurs

decode.explanation: Errors begin right after each refresh and before the 8-hour lifetime, so the refresh itself must be invalidating the cached token.
clues: right after each scheduled refresh -> the refresh is the trigger
less than 8 hours have passed -> not normal expiry
cached the access token ... keeps reusing it -> a stale token after refresh
decode.needs: A refresh issues new tokens and invalidates the previous access token, so every service must use the new one.

stem: Copperline Credit embeds loan signing with classic view. After signing, Docusign redirects the borrower to https://loans.copperline.example/done?app=7781, and the current code marks the loan as signed and starts funding whenever that page loads. Auditors found loans funded for borrowers who had closed the session or declined. The company already has an account-level Connect listener using JSON SIM that receives envelope events for every loan envelope. Which two changes follow Docusign's guidance? (Select two)

options.text: Read the event query parameter on the returnUrl and treat only signing_complete as a finished signature
Poll Envelopes:get every minute after the redirect until the envelope shows completed
Start funding only after Connect confirms the envelope is completed, not from the redirect alone
Replace the returnUrl with Brand Destination URLs so declined borrowers are redirected elsewhere
Treat ttl_expired as completed, because it means the session ended after signing

answerText: Read the event query parameter on the returnUrl and treat only signing_complete as a finished signature; Start funding only after Connect confirms the envelope is completed, not from the redirect alone
explanation: Docusign appends event={type} (signing_complete, cancel, decline, ttl_expired, and so on) to the returnUrl, so the app must read it. Because the redirect alone is not proof, the final status should be confirmed through Connect, which the company already has.
whyNotOthers: A and C are right. The trap is B: it checks status, but polling once a minute breaks the one-request-per-envelope-every-15-minutes limit, and Connect is already in place. D fails because Brand Destination URLs control redirects for remote signing, not embedded signing. E fails because ttl_expired means the session expired, not that the borrower signed.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. The event parameter tells you what the signer did; only signing_complete means they signed.
optionExplanations.B: Polling every minute breaks the 15-minute polling limit; Connect is already available.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. Do not rely on the returnUrl alone; confirm completion through Connect before funding.
optionExplanations.D: Brand Destination URLs apply to remote signing redirects; embedded signing uses returnUrl.
optionExplanations.E: ttl_expired means the signing session timed out, not that signing finished.

concept.title: returnUrl event parameter
concept.line: Docusign appends event=... (signing_complete, cancel, decline, ttl_expired) to returnUrl; read it, but confirm final status via Connect, not the redirect.

decode.prompt: What does this scenario really require?

options.text: Determine the real signing outcome instead of trusting the redirect alone
Send declined users to a different page
Treat any end of session as completion
Poll envelope status frequently after the redirect

decode.explanation: The redirect fires for cancel and decline too, so the app must check the outcome on the redirect and confirm final status through the existing Connect feed.
clues: marks the loan as signed whenever that page loads -> the redirect happens on any session end
closed the session or declined -> different event values on the returnUrl
already has an account-level Connect listener -> confirm completion from Connect
decode.needs: Check event=signing_complete and fund only after Connect confirms completion.

stem: Where in Docusign can a connected fields extension check a field value against an external system of record?

options.text: In Maestro workflow steps, alongside Data IO read and write actions.
In the eSignature Add Fields view and during signing.
Only after completion, through the Connect extension-executed event.
Only in the eSignature API, through Envelopes:create without a sender view.

answerText: In the eSignature Add Fields view and during signing.
explanation: The connected fields extension point is the eSignature Add Fields view and signing; verification runs when the signer completes the required fields.
whyNotOthers: B is right. The trap is C: the extension-executed Connect event reports verification results, it is not where verification happens. A fails because connected fields are not supported in Maestro, and D fails because connected fields also work in the sender's Add Fields view, not only through the API.

optionExplanations.A: Connected fields are not supported in Maestro; Data IO is the extension used in workflows.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. Connected fields use the eSignature Add Fields view and signing as their extension point.
optionExplanations.C: The extension-executed event delivers results (JSON SIM only); it is not the verification point.
optionExplanations.D: API sending is possible, but senders also place connected fields in the Add Fields view, so 'only' is wrong.

concept.title: Where connected fields verify
concept.line: Connected fields verify data in the eSignature Add Fields view and during signing, when the signer completes required fields.

topic: When the envelope is created (remote instance)
stem: For a remote web form instance created from a template-based configuration, when is the envelope created?

options.text: When the Instances:createInstance request is processed.
When the first recipient submits the web form instance.
When the app calls Envelopes:create with the submitted formValues.
Never, because remote instances only collect form data.

answerText: When the Instances:createInstance request is processed.
explanation: For template-based configurations the envelope timing depends on delivery: remote instance, the envelope is created when createInstance is processed; embedded instance, when the first user submits.
whyNotOthers: A is right for remote delivery. The trap is B, which is the timing for embedded instances. C is wrong because Docusign generates the envelope itself, and D describes standalone configurations, not template-based ones.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. A remote instance's envelope is created when the createInstance request is processed.
optionExplanations.B: This is the timing for embedded instances, where the envelope is created when the first user submits.
optionExplanations.C: The app makes no Envelopes:create call; Docusign generates the envelope from the web form template.
optionExplanations.D: Only standalone configurations produce no envelope; this configuration is template-based.

concept.title: Web form envelope creation timing
concept.line: Template-based web forms: remote instance creates the envelope when createInstance is processed; embedded instance creates it when the first user submits.

stem: A back-office system must record the outcome of every connected fields verification that happens during signing. How should it receive the results?

options.text: Subscribe to the extension-executed event using the XML Aggregated message format
Poll Get Type Definitions on the extension app after each envelope completes
Implement a Connect listener for the extension-executed event using JSON SIM
Add an eventNotification for the recipient-completed event to each envelope

answerText: Implement a Connect listener for the extension-executed event using JSON SIM
explanation: Verification results can be retrieved programmatically through the Connect extension-executed event, which is supported only with the JSON SIM event model; they also appear in envelope history and the certificate of completion.
whyNotOthers: C is right because extension-executed is the event that carries verification results, and it is JSON SIM only. The trap is A: right event, but XML Aggregated is not supported for it. B calls a data model action that returns types, not results, and D signals that a recipient finished, not the verification outcome.

optionExplanations.A: Right event, wrong format: extension-executed is supported only with JSON SIM.
optionExplanations.B: Get Type Definitions returns the data model, not verification results.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. A Connect listener for extension-executed in JSON SIM receives the verification results.
optionExplanations.D: recipient-completed reports a recipient's completion, not the result of a connected fields verification.

concept.title: Verification results via extension-executed
concept.line: Verification results are retrieved programmatically via the Connect extension-executed event, JSON SIM only; also shown in envelope history and certificate.

stem: Daniel's extension app is registered once in the Developer Console and points at his company's staging API. Integration tests pass. Before submitting the app for public review, he must point the same registration at the production API, which uses a different OAuth client and different hostnames, while keeping the same extension types, actions and App Center listing. He will edit the downloaded manifest and upload it again. Which two sets of values must he change? (Select two)

options.text: The connection's clientId, clientSecret and authorization settings in customConfig
The template identifier of each action, so it targets the production contract
The publicationRegions list, so the app is installable in production
The params.uri of each action (and capability) so requests go to production URLs
The connectionsReference of each action, so it points to a new production connection name

answerText: The connection's clientId, clientSecret and authorization settings in customConfig; The params.uri of each action (and capability) so requests go to production URLs
explanation: Docusign's guidance for switching environments is to update the connection settings (clientId, clientSecret and authorization settings in customConfig) and the params.uri of each action and capability; public apps must have production URLs before review.
whyNotOthers: A and D are right because only credentials/authorization settings and endpoint URLs are environment-specific. The trap is E: connectionsReference would only change if he renamed or added a connection, but he is editing the existing connection's values. B is a Docusign-predefined contract identifier that does not differ by environment, and C controls in which regions the public app can be installed, not which API it calls.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. Environment-specific credentials and authorization settings live in the connection's customConfig.
optionExplanations.B: Action templates are Docusign-defined contract identifiers; they are the same for staging and production.
optionExplanations.C: publicationRegions controls where a public app can be installed, not which external API it calls.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. params.uri holds the endpoint URL for each action and capability and must point to production.
optionExplanations.E: He updates the existing connection's values, so the connection name and every connectionsReference can stay the same.

concept.title: Switching extension app environment
concept.line: Update connection settings (clientId, clientSecret, auth settings in customConfig) and each action's and capability's params.uri to production URLs.

decode.prompt: What does this scenario really require?

options.text: Change the contract or extension type identifiers
Change only environment-specific connection credentials and endpoint URLs, keeping the extension definitions
Change distribution or listing settings
Create new named connections for production

decode.explanation: Only the OAuth client and hostnames differ while extension types, actions and listing stay the same, so only credentials and URIs change.
clues: different OAuth client -> connection clientId, clientSecret and authorization settings
different hostnames -> params.uri of each action and capability
keeping the same extension types, actions and App Center listing -> do not touch templates or regions
decode.needs: Update customConfig credentials and each params.uri.

stem: After go-live, an app that sends with the template reference model gets template-not-found errors in production, although it worked in demo. What must the developer do?

options.text: Nothing in the account; re-run the go-live review so templates are copied with the integration key
Switch the app to composite templates, because server templates are not referenced in production
Make the template available in the production account and update the app to use its production template ID
Keep the demo template ID and change only the base URI, since template IDs are global

answerText: Make the template available in the production account and update the app to use its production template ID
explanation: Go-live promotes the integration key, not templates. The template must exist in the production account, which gives it a new template ID, and the app must reference that ID.
whyNotOthers: C is right because template IDs differ between demo and production. The trap is D: the base URI does change, but template IDs are not global, so the demo ID still fails. A fails because go-live does not copy templates. B fails because the template reference model works in production.

optionExplanations.A: Go-live promotes the integration key only; templates are not copied.
optionExplanations.B: Server templates and the template reference model are fully supported in production.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. Put the template in the production account and reference its new production template ID.
optionExplanations.D: Template IDs are environment-specific; changing the base URI alone does not help.

concept.title: Templates after go-live
concept.line: Go-live promotes the key, not templates; the template must exist in production, with a new template ID the app must use.

stem: Westgate Property Management wants prospective tenants to start a rental pre-qualification workflow themselves from a button on the company's public marketing website and from an automatic email reply. The website is a static site hosted by an agency, with no server-side code and no place to store OAuth credentials. The workflow collects applicant data with a web form, verifies identity, and routes a disclosure for signature. Leasing agents sometimes ask whether they could also start it on behalf of walk-in applicants, but management says that is not needed. Which start method should the process builder choose?

options.text: From a Link, copying the workflow URL into the website button and the email reply
From an API call, with the static site calling Workflows:triggerWorkflow when the button is clicked
Manually in Docusign, so leasing agents with Workflows: Prepare start each application
Collect Data with Web Forms as the first step, embedded on the site with the Docusign JS client SDK

answerText: From a Link, copying the workflow URL into the website button and the email reply
explanation: From a Link is meant for workflows initiated by a participant opening a URL, such as a link on a website or in an automatic email response, and it needs no server or token.
whyNotOthers: A is right because the participant starts it from a public site and an email, and the clue 'no server-side code and no place to store OAuth credentials' rules out an API trigger. The trap is B: triggerWorkflow needs an access token with aow_manage held by a backend. C is for people inside the organization, which management said is not needed, and D is a step, not a start method, and embeds only a form rather than starting the multi-step workflow.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. From a Link gives a URL to place on a website or in an automated email for self-service starts.
optionExplanations.B: Wrong. An API trigger requires a server holding an OAuth token with aow_manage; the static site has none.
optionExplanations.C: Wrong. Manually in Docusign is for someone in your organization to run the workflow, not applicants.
optionExplanations.D: Wrong. This is a step choice, not a start method, and embedding a single web form does not start the workflow.

concept.title: From a Link start method
concept.line: From a Link suits participant-initiated workflows via a URL on a website or auto-email, needing no server or token.

decode.prompt: What does this scenario really require?

options.text: Start the workflow from code that calls the API
Let staff start it on behalf of applicants
Let members of the public start the workflow themselves from a URL, with no server or stored credentials
Embed a form on the site with a client SDK

decode.explanation: Tenants start it from a website button and an email reply on a static site with nowhere to store credentials, so the start must need no token.
clues: static site ... no server-side code and no place to store OAuth credentials -> no API call
button on the public website and an automatic email reply -> a shareable link
leasing agents ... management says that is not needed -> red herring
decode.needs: The From a Link start method.

topic: Envelope-level webhook for an ISV integration
stem: Quillpoint, an ISV, sells a contract tool that sends envelopes through each customer's Docusign account using Envelopes:create and JWT Grant.
