Every envelope the tool creates must report its events to a tenant-specific Quillpoint URL that changes per customer, and customers' Docusign administrators refuse to let Quillpoint change account settings or Connect pages. Envelopes users send manually from the web app are out of scope. The tool already uses transactionId to avoid duplicate sends. How should Quillpoint receive the events?

options.text: Ask each customer to create an account-level Connect configuration whose urlToPublishTo is the tenant URL
Create one organization-level Connect configuration in Quillpoint's own organization covering all customers
Configure a Recipient Connect configuration for the users who authorize Quillpoint's integration key
Include an eventNotification object with the tenant URL and events in each Envelopes:create request

answerText: Include an eventNotification object with the tenant URL and events in each Envelopes:create request
explanation: An envelope-level webhook is defined by the eventNotification property on Envelopes:create; it is API-only, needs no account-level Connect configuration, and can point each envelope at its own URL. The clue is 'only envelopes the tool creates' plus 'administrators refuse account-setting changes'.
whyNotOthers: D is right because eventNotification travels with each API-created envelope and can name the tenant URL without touching account settings. The trap is A: account-level Connect would work technically, but it requires the very admin changes customers refused and would also report manually sent envelopes. B fails because an org-level configuration only covers accounts inside the organization that owns it, not customer accounts; C fails because Recipient Connect is about envelopes received by specific users, not envelopes sent by the tool.

optionExplanations.A: Account-level Connect requires administrator setup in every customer account, which the customers refused, and it would also report out-of-scope manual envelopes.
optionExplanations.B: An organization-level configuration covers only the accounts in that organization; customer accounts are not part of Quillpoint's organization.
optionExplanations.C: Recipient Connect notifies when specific account users receive envelopes, which does not match tracking the envelopes the tool sends.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. The eventNotification object on Envelopes:create sets an envelope-level webhook per envelope through the API, with its own URL and events, and needs no account configuration change.

concept.title: Envelope-level webhook via eventNotification
concept.line: eventNotification on Envelopes:create is API-only envelope-level Connect, needs no account configuration, and can point each envelope to its own URL.

decode.prompt: What does this scenario really require?

options.text: Configure each customer's account to send events
Centralize events in the vendor's own organization
Capture events for envelopes users send manually
Route events per envelope to a tenant-specific URL without touching customer account settings

decode.explanation: Only envelopes the tool creates matter, the URL varies per tenant, and admins refuse account changes, so the webhook must travel with each create request.
clues: every envelope the tool creates ... tenant-specific URL -> per-envelope webhook
refuse to let Quillpoint change account settings or Connect pages -> no account-level Connect
envelopes sent manually are out of scope -> envelope-level is enough
decode.needs: eventNotification on each Envelopes:create.

topic: Data IO read and writeback in a workflow
stem: Orchard Wholesale's sales operations team wants a Maestro workflow that, at the start of each renewal, reads the customer's current credit limit and payment terms from the company's own order management system, uses them in a generated renewal agreement, and after signing writes the new contract status back to that same system. An architect suggests Connected Fields because the company already uses it to verify account numbers during signing, and IT also mentions its existing Connect listener. Which extension type should the developer build or install for the read and write steps?

options.text: Connected Fields, reusing the existing verification connection inside the workflow
File IO, using a Store Files step to move the data in and out of the system
A Docusign Connect listener that receives envelope-completed events and writes the status back
Data IO, exposed in Workflow Builder as Read and Writeback apps steps

answerText: Data IO, exposed in Workflow Builder as Read and Writeback apps steps
explanation: Data IO extension apps read and write structured data to and from a system of record and are used in Maestro workflows as read and writeback steps.
whyNotOthers: D is right because the workflow must read structured fields at the start and write status back later, which is the Data IO use case. The trap is A: Connected Fields works at the eSignature Add Fields and signing extension points and is not supported in Maestro workflows. B moves files, not structured field values, and C is an outbound notification channel that cannot read data into a workflow.

optionExplanations.A: Wrong. Connected Fields is an eSignature extension point and is not currently supported in Maestro workflows.
optionExplanations.B: Wrong. File IO and Store Files steps handle documents, not reading credit limits into workflow variables.
optionExplanations.C: Wrong. Connect pushes event notifications out; it does not read data into the workflow and is not a workflow step.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. Data IO apps provide read and writeback steps against a system of record inside Maestro workflows.

concept.title: Data IO Read and Writeback steps
concept.line: Data IO extension apps read and write structured system-of-record data, appearing in Workflow Builder as Read and Writeback steps.

decode.prompt: What does this scenario really require?

options.text: Read and write structured data with the company's own system of record as steps in a Maestro workflow
Verify field values while a signer fills in an envelope
Move files in and out of a storage service
React to envelope events from outside the workflow

decode.explanation: Reading credit terms at the start and writing contract status back at the end are workflow steps against a system of record, not signing-time verification.
clues: Maestro workflow ... reads ... writes the new contract status back -> read and writeback steps
Connected Fields ... verify account numbers during signing -> red herring
existing Connect listener -> outside the workflow, not a step
decode.needs: Data IO extension used as Read and Writeback steps.

stem: Greenleaf Wealth is designing an account-update workflow. The first form a client sees is pre-filled with sensitive data from the client's file (tax ID and account balances), so compliance insists that the client's identity is confirmed before that form is ever displayed. After the client reviews and corrects the form, an updated mandate is sent for signature. A business analyst points to an onboarding workflow from last year that collected data first and verified identity afterwards, and suggests copying it. Which step sequence meets the compliance requirement?

options.text: Collect Data with Web Forms, Set Up Invite, Verify Someone's Identity, Send Documents for Signature
Send Documents for Signature, Verify Someone's Identity, Collect Data with Web Forms
Collect Data with Web Forms, then a Branching Rule on Validated = True, then Send Documents for Signature
Set Up Invite, Verify Someone's Identity, Collect Data with Web Forms, Send Documents for Signature

answerText: Set Up Invite, Verify Someone's Identity, Collect Data with Web Forms, Send Documents for Signature
explanation: Steps can be sequenced as needed, including an ID verification step before a web form step so a participant's identity is verified before sensitive pre-filled data is shown; the course pairs Set Up Invite with Verify Someone's Identity.
whyNotOthers: D is right because compliance requires identity to be confirmed before the pre-filled form is displayed. The trap is A: it copies last year's collect-then-verify order, which would show the sensitive data before verification. B signs before the data is reviewed, and C has no identity verification step at all, so Validated has nothing to evaluate.

optionExplanations.A: Wrong. This order displays the pre-filled sensitive form before identity is verified.
optionExplanations.B: Wrong. It sends the mandate before the client has reviewed and corrected the data.
optionExplanations.C: Wrong. There is no identity verification step, so the branch on Validated has nothing to test.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. Invite and verify identity first, then show the pre-filled form, then send for signature.

concept.title: Verify identity before revealing data
concept.line: Steps can be sequenced so Verify Someone's Identity (after Set Up Invite) precedes a web form showing sensitive pre-filled data.

decode.prompt: What does this scenario really require?

options.text: Confirm identity at any point before signing
Confirm the participant's identity before any sensitive prefilled data is shown
Validate the collected data after the form
Reuse the order of an earlier onboarding workflow

decode.explanation: Compliance requires verification before the first form is displayed, so identity checks must come ahead of the web form step.
clues: confirmed before that form is ever displayed -> identity verification precedes the web form
collected data first and verified identity afterwards -> red herring
updated mandate is sent for signature -> the signature step comes last
decode.needs: Set Up Invite, Verify Someone's Identity, Collect Data with Web Forms, Send for Signature.

stem: Tidewater Energy syncs Agreement Manager data into its ERP. Last week the AI extracted a renewal_notice_period of P60D for a supplier agreement. A contract manager reviewed the value against the document in the Agreement Manager UI and changed it to P90D. The integration calls GetAgreement every night with the same JWT token flow and has not changed its code or scopes. The ERP owner wants to know which value will flow downstream tonight. What will tonight's GetAgreement response contain for renewal_notice_period?

options.text: P60D, because the API always returns the original AI-extracted value and UI edits stay in the UI.
Both values, with the original AI value flagged as superseded by the reviewer's edit.
P90D, because user-updated values replace the AI-extracted values in later GET responses.
No value until CreateAgreementSummary is called to re-run the extraction for the agreement.

answerText: P90D, because user-updated values replace the AI-extracted values in later GET responses.
explanation: Schema values come from AI extraction and from user input; after a user reviews and modifies a value in the UI, subsequent GET requests return the user-updated value instead of the original AI-extracted one.
whyNotOthers: C is right because the reviewed value overwrites the AI value in the data the API returns. The trap is A, which assumes UI edits are cosmetic. B invents a dual-value response, and D misreads CreateAgreementSummary, which writes an AI summary and does not re-run or gate extraction.

optionExplanations.A: UI corrections update the stored agreement data, so the API no longer returns the original AI value.
optionExplanations.B: The response holds one value per field; there is no superseded-value flag.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. Later GET responses return the user-updated value, so the review loop feeds the ERP automatically.
optionExplanations.D: CreateAgreementSummary produces an AI summary; it does not control whether provision values are returned.

concept.title: User-corrected extraction values
concept.line: After a user modifies an AI-extracted value in the UI, later GET requests return the user-updated value, not the original extraction.

decode.prompt: What does this scenario really require?

options.text: Know whether the integration must change its scopes
Know how to re-run AI extraction
Know whether a reviewer's edit in the UI replaces the AI-extracted value in API responses
Know how value history is exposed by the API

decode.explanation: A user corrected the value in the UI and the integration is unchanged, so the question is simply which value later GET calls return.
clues: changed it to P90D -> a user-updated value
has not changed its code or scopes -> nothing for the integration to change
which value will flow downstream tonight -> what GetAgreement returns
decode.needs: GET returns the user-updated value.

stem: Ravi's connected fields app verifies wire transfers against his bank's ledger. The Get Type Definitions response defines a TransferAuthorization concept marked as verifiable, with properties AccountNumber, RoutingNumber and Memo. In the Add Fields view all three appear under App Fields, but none shows an asterisk, so preparers keep sending envelopes without AccountNumber and the Verify call never has enough data. The connection test and the Get Type Names extension test both pass. Which change to the data model fixes this?

options.text: Add the IsRequiredForVerifyingType decorator to the AccountNumber and RoutingNumber properties
Add the VerifiableType decorator to the AccountNumber and RoutingNumber properties
Move AccountNumber and RoutingNumber into a separate concept returned by Get Type Names
Mark the Memo property as optional so the other two become required

answerText: Add the IsRequiredForVerifyingType decorator to the AccountNumber and RoutingNumber properties
explanation: Properties with the IsRequiredForVerifyingType decorator appear with an asterisk because they are required to verify the object; the concept is already 'marked as verifiable', so the missing piece is the property-level required decorator.
whyNotOthers: A is right because IsRequiredForVerifyingType marks a property as required for verifying the type, which shows the asterisk. The trap is B: VerifiableType is the decorator that makes an object verifiable from envelopes, it belongs on the concept (already done), not on individual properties to make them required. C would change the structure without marking anything required, and D does not make other properties required.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. IsRequiredForVerifyingType on a property marks it required for verification and shows it with an asterisk in Add Fields.
optionExplanations.B: VerifiableType marks an object (concept) as verifiable; it is already on TransferAuthorization and does not make properties required.
optionExplanations.C: Splitting the concept does not mark any property as required for verification.
optionExplanations.D: Making Memo optional does not add the required decorator to the other properties.

concept.title: IsRequiredForVerifyingType decorator
concept.line: IsRequiredForVerifyingType marks properties required to verify an object (shown with an asterisk); add it per property on an already-verifiable concept.

decode.prompt: What does this scenario really require?

options.text: Mark the whole concept as verifiable
Restructure which concepts are exposed to the app
Fix the app's connection
Mark specific properties as mandatory for verification so the UI enforces them

decode.explanation: The concept is already verifiable and the tests pass, but no field shows an asterisk, so the property-level required marker is missing.
clues: concept marked as verifiable -> the concept-level setting is fine
none shows an asterisk -> property-level required decorator missing
connection test and Get Type Names test both pass -> not a connection problem
decode.needs: IsRequiredForVerifyingType on AccountNumber and RoutingNumber.

stem: Delmar Bank's month-end job creates about 600 envelopes by sending all create requests in parallel, and it finishes in about 20 seconds. In the developer account even more calls failed, so the team blamed the demo environment and went live anyway. In production about a hundred create calls still fail, even though the account made only about 900 calls that hour and the job never checks envelope status. The team is considering asking for a higher hourly limit. Which limit is being hit, and what should the job do?

options.text: The hourly limit of 3,000 calls per account; ask an admin to raise it with Update Hourly Limit in the API Usage Center
The per-envelope polling limit; wait 15 minutes between requests that touch the same envelope
The production burst limit of 500 calls per 30 seconds; throttle the job and back off using the X-RateLimit headers
The demo burst limit of 200 calls per 30 seconds, which still applies until the key passes another review

answerText: The production burst limit of 500 calls per 30 seconds; throttle the job and back off using the X-RateLimit headers
explanation: About 600 calls in 20 seconds is more than the production burst limit of 500 calls per 30 seconds, which explains about a hundred failures. More failed in demo because the demo burst limit is 200.
whyNotOthers: C is right because the clue '600 calls in 20 seconds' with only 900 calls that hour points to the burst limit. The trap is A: 900 calls is far below the 3,000 hourly limit, so raising it changes nothing. B fails because the job creates envelopes and never polls them. D fails because the demo burst limit of 200 applies only in the developer environment; about a hundred failures in production match 500, not 200.

optionExplanations.A: About 900 calls is well under the 3,000 hourly limit, so the hourly limit is not the cause.
optionExplanations.B: The polling limit applies to repeated status checks on an envelope; this job only creates envelopes.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. 600 calls in 20 seconds exceeds the production burst limit of 500 per 30 seconds; throttle and watch the rate-limit headers.
optionExplanations.D: The 200-per-30-seconds burst limit applies to demo; production uses 500.

concept.title: Burst limit
concept.line: Burst limit is 500 calls per 30 seconds in production (200 in demo), distinct from the hourly limit; throttle and back off using X-RateLimit headers.

decode.prompt: What does this scenario really require?

options.text: Stay within a short-window request rate by throttling the job
Raise the hourly call allowance
Respect the per-envelope polling frequency
Wait for environment-specific limits to change

decode.explanation: About 600 calls in 20 seconds exceeds a 30-second burst cap while the hourly total is far below its limit.
clues: about 600 envelopes ... in parallel ... about 20 seconds -> burst over 500 per 30 seconds
only about 900 calls that hour -> hourly limit not reached
never checks envelope status -> polling rules are irrelevant
even more calls failed in demo -> the demo burst limit is lower
decode.needs: Throttle under the production burst limit and back off using X-RateLimit headers.

stem: When the final signer completes an envelope, which Connect setup delivers the recipient-completed and envelope-completed events as a single combined message to the listener?

options.text: An organization-level configuration in JSON SIM with both events selected
An envelope-level eventNotification in JSON SIM with the envelope summary included
An account-level configuration in XML SIM, which sends one message for each event
An account-level configuration in XML format using the aggregate delivery option

answerText: An account-level configuration in XML format using the aggregate delivery option
explanation: The aggregate option, available only for configurations using the XML data type at account or envelope level, combines similar events such as recipient complete and envelope complete into one message.
whyNotOthers: D is right because aggregation requires XML and combines the final recipient and envelope completion into one delivery. The trap is C: it is XML, but SIM mode by definition sends an individual message per event. A and B fail because JSON SIM always sends one message per event; including the envelope summary enlarges a message but does not merge events.

optionExplanations.A: Organization-level configurations always use JSON SIM, which sends an individual message for each event, never an aggregated one.
optionExplanations.B: JSON SIM sends one message per event; including the envelope summary adds data to each message but does not combine events.
optionExplanations.C: XML SIM still sends individual messages for each event; only the aggregate option combines them.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. In an XML configuration (account or envelope level), the aggregate option combines recipient complete and envelope complete into a single message.

concept.title: Aggregate Connect message mode
concept.line: The aggregate option, XML only at account or envelope level, combines similar events (e.g. recipient and envelope complete) into one message.

stem: Which two envelope statuses are terminal, so that tabs can no longer be added to the envelope through the API? (Select two)

options.text: sent
declined
correct
voided
delivered

answerText: declined; voided
explanation: Docusign University lists completed, declined and voided as terminal statuses; no further API modifications, including adding tabs, can be made on them.
whyNotOthers: B and D are right because declined and voided are terminal. The trap is C: correct stops signing, but it is a temporary lock, and the envelope can be edited and resumed. A and E are normal in-progress states where changes are still possible.

optionExplanations.A: sent is in progress; the envelope can still be modified.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. declined is a terminal status.
optionExplanations.C: correct is a temporary hold (lock), not a terminal status.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. voided is a terminal status; voiding is permanent.
optionExplanations.E: delivered means recipients have viewed the envelope; it is still in progress.

concept.title: Terminal envelope statuses
concept.line: Completed, declined and voided are terminal: no further API modifications such as adding tabs; correct is not terminal.

stem: Ravi at Copperline Clinics calls POST /v1/accounts/{accountId}/workflows/{workflowId}/actions/trigger from a scheduler. The token was obtained with JWT Grant and includes signature and aow_manage, and the same token successfully calls getWorkflowInstancesList on that workflow. The trigger call returns 400 Bad Request. His request body is {"name": "Clinic 42 intake", "inputs": {"clinicEmail": "ops@example.com"}}. The workflow's start method is From an API call and it is published and not paused. What is the most likely fix?

options.text: Send instance_name and trigger_inputs, with trigger_inputs keys matching the workflow's trigger_input_schema
Request a new token that adds the aow_manage scope, because 400 indicates a missing Maestro permission
Call resumePausedWorkflow before triggering so the workflow accepts new instances
Change the start method to From a Link, because API triggers cannot accept starting variable values

answerText: Send instance_name and trigger_inputs, with trigger_inputs keys matching the workflow's trigger_input_schema
explanation: The TriggerWorkflow body requires instance_name and trigger_inputs, whose key-value pairs must match the trigger_input_schema; Ravi's body uses name and inputs.
whyNotOthers: A is right because the body uses the wrong property names, and a malformed body is what a 400 Bad Request signals. The trap is B: a missing scope produces an authorization failure (401/403), and the token already includes aow_manage and works on another Maestro call. C is irrelevant because the workflow is not paused, and D is backwards: trigger_inputs exists precisely to pass starting values through the API.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. instance_name and trigger_inputs are both required, and inputs must match the trigger_input_schema.
optionExplanations.B: Wrong. The token already has aow_manage and works on another Maestro call; a scope problem is 401/403, not 400.
optionExplanations.C: Wrong. The workflow is published and not paused, so resuming changes nothing.
optionExplanations.D: Wrong. API triggers pass starting variables in trigger_inputs; From a Link is not required for that.

concept.title: triggerWorkflow request body
concept.line: TriggerWorkflow body needs instance_name and trigger_inputs, with keys matching trigger_input_schema; wrong field names (name, inputs) cause the 400.

decode.prompt: What does this scenario really require?

options.text: Obtain additional permissions for the token
Send the trigger request body with the field names and shape the workflow trigger expects
Make the workflow accept new instances
Use a different workflow start method

decode.explanation: A 400 with a token that already works and a published, unpaused workflow means the request body is malformed.
clues: returns 400 Bad Request -> malformed request, not authorization
same token successfully calls getWorkflowInstancesList -> scopes are fine
published and not paused -> workflow state is fine
body uses name and inputs -> wrong field names
decode.needs: instance_name and trigger_inputs matching trigger_input_schema.

stem: Northwind Payroll has completed go-live for its JWT Grant integration and is switching the token code to production. The impersonated user is payroll-bot, whose production user ID differs from its demo user ID, and payroll-bot has already granted consent with signature impersonation in production. The team reuses the code that builds the assertion and changes only claim values. A reviewer notes that the key was first created in the developer account and asks whether that affects any claim. Which two claim values must the production JWT carry? (Select two)

options.text: iss set to payroll-bot's production user ID, since iss identifies the impersonated user
aud set to account-d.docusign.com, because the integration key was created in the developer account
sub set to payroll-bot's production user ID (GUID)
sub set to payroll-bot's email address, so one value works in both environments
exp set to no more than 3600 seconds after iat

answerText: sub set to payroll-bot's production user ID (GUID); exp set to no more than 3600 seconds after iat
explanation: A production JWT has iss = integration key, sub = the impersonated user's ID (GUID) in that environment, aud = account.docusign.com, and exp no more than 1 hour after iat. Of the options, only C and E state correct values.
whyNotOthers: C and E are right. The trap is B: where the key was created does not matter; production tokens need aud account.docusign.com. A swaps iss and sub: iss is the integration key, the user ID goes in sub. D fails because sub is the user ID GUID, not an email address.

optionExplanations.A: iss is the integration key; the impersonated user's ID belongs in sub, so this swaps the two claims.
optionExplanations.B: In production aud must be account.docusign.com; account-d is the demo server.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. sub is the impersonated user's ID GUID in the target environment.
optionExplanations.D: sub takes the user ID GUID, not an email address.
optionExplanations.E: Correct. A JWT assertion may be valid for at most 1 hour.

concept.title: Production JWT claims
concept.line: Production JWT: iss = integration key, sub = impersonated user's production GUID, aud = account.docusign.com, exp at most 3600 s after iat.

decode.prompt: What does this scenario really require?

options.text: Keep the environment where the key was created as the audience
Use one user identifier that works in both environments
Use claim values that identify the key and the user as they exist in production, within the token time limit
Reuse the demo claim values because only the host changes

decode.explanation: The user's production ID differs from demo, and where the key was first created does not affect production claims, so the claims must carry production values and respect the expiry rule.
clues: production user ID differs from its demo user ID -> sub must be the production GUID
key was first created in the developer account -> red herring; production aud is account.docusign.com
changes only claim values -> iss stays the integration key, exp at most one hour after iat
decode.needs: iss = integration key, sub = production user GUID, exp within 3600 seconds of iat.

stem: Maple Health's referral app creates envelopes with three signers in routing order and includes an eventNotification object in Envelopes:create, because only these referral envelopes, not the whole account, should go to its listener. The nurse dashboard must show a check mark as soon as each individual signer finishes. Today the listener receives a single message when the whole envelope finishes. The listener already returns 200 quickly and uses HMAC. What should the developer change?

options.text: Add an account-level Connect configuration that publishes recipient events for all envelopes
Add the recipient-completed event to the eventNotification in the Envelopes:create request
Poll EnvelopeRecipients:list for each open referral so the dashboard sees each signer's status
Keep only envelope-completed and read each signer's status from that final message

answerText: Add the recipient-completed event to the eventNotification in the Envelopes:create request
explanation: An eventNotification on Envelopes:create is envelope-level Connect for just that envelope. Subscribing it to recipient-completed sends a message as each signer finishes; the clue is "only these referral envelopes" and "as soon as each individual signer finishes".
whyNotOthers: B is right because it adds per-recipient events while keeping the envelope-level scope. The trap is D: envelope-completed fires only once, after all signers are done, so it cannot show progress in real time. A breaks the requirement to keep this scoped to these envelopes. C polls, which counts against API limits and is restricted to once per 15 minutes per envelope.

optionExplanations.A: Account-level Connect covers every envelope, which the requirement rules out.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. Subscribing the envelope-level eventNotification to recipient-completed gives per-signer messages.
optionExplanations.C: Polling counts against API limits and is restricted to once per 15 minutes per envelope.
optionExplanations.D: envelope-completed arrives only after the last signer, so per-signer progress is lost.

concept.title: Per-signer events via eventNotification
concept.line: Add recipient-completed to an Envelopes:create eventNotification to get a message as each signer finishes, for that envelope only.

decode.prompt: What does this scenario really require?

options.text: Receive events for every envelope in the account
Derive each signer's status from the final envelope message
Pull signer status on a schedule
Receive per-signer completion events only for the envelopes the app creates

decode.explanation: Only the referral envelopes should notify, and the dashboard needs a message per signer, so the existing envelope-level webhook must subscribe to a recipient event.
clues: eventNotification ... only these referral envelopes -> envelope-level Connect
as soon as each individual signer finishes -> recipient-completed
single message when the whole envelope finishes -> only envelope-level completion is subscribed
decode.needs: Add recipient-completed to the eventNotification on Envelopes:create.

stem: A listener shares an account-level configuration and receives some event types it has no use for. Following Docusign's listener guidance, how should it respond to those messages?

options.text: Return HTTP 200 and then discard the message
Return HTTP 400 so Connect stops sending that event
Return HTTP 404 so Connect marks the event not applicable
Leave the request unanswered so it times out quietly

answerText: Return HTTP 200 and then discard the message
explanation: Docusign's guidance is to always return 200 after receiving a message; if the app does not need it, it acknowledges with 200 and discards it.
whyNotOthers: A is right because any non-2xx response or timeout counts as a failure and is retried. The trap is B: a 400 sounds like telling Connect 'not wanted', but Connect treats it as a failed delivery and retries it. C and D fail for the same reason: errors and timeouts trigger retries and show up as failures.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. Acknowledge every message with 200; drop the ones the app does not need after acknowledging.
optionExplanations.B: Connect has no 'unsubscribe by status code' behavior; a 400 is a failure and the event is retried.
optionExplanations.C: A 404 is also a non-2xx response, so the event is recorded as failed and retried.
optionExplanations.D: A timeout is a failure; the listener should answer within about five seconds.

concept.title: Always acknowledge with 200
concept.line: Any non-2xx or timeout is a failure that Connect retries; acknowledge unneeded messages with 200 and discard them.

topic: Request URL: base URI per account
stem: Atlas Payroll sells a SaaS product in which each customer company connects its own Docusign account through Authorization Code Grant. The first customers were in North America, and every call worked with a hard-coded https://na3.docusign.net host. A new customer in Germany connects, and every eSignature call for that customer fails, although the access token and the customer's account ID are correct. Some customers' users also belong to other companies' Docusign accounts. The German customer also prints on A4 paper. What should the developer do?

options.text: After login, call userinfo, pick the customer's account, and build each call from its base_uri followed by /restapi/v2.1/accounts/{accountId}
Keep the na3 host but put the German account ID in the path, because the host only routes traffic and any Docusign data center can serve any account
Switch to the account-d.docusign.com host for this customer, because the authentication host also serves eSignature REST calls for every region
After login, call userinfo, take the first account in the accounts list, and build each call from its base_uri followed by /restapi/v2.1/accounts/{accountId}

answerText: After login, call userinfo, pick the customer's account, and build each call from its base_uri followed by /restapi/v2.1/accounts/{accountId}
explanation: Each account lives on a specific base URI, returned per account by the userinfo endpoint; the request URL is {base_uri}/restapi/v2.1/accounts/{accountId}/... The clue is 'token and account ID are correct' but the host is hard-coded.
whyNotOthers: A is right because the base URI must come from userinfo for the specific account being used. The trap is D: userinfo is correct, but users who belong to other companies' accounts may have a different account listed first, so the app must select the customer's account rather than the first entry. B fails because an account must be called on its own base URI, which for this customer is not na3. C confuses the demo authentication host with an eSignature API host.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. userinfo returns each account's base_uri; append /restapi/v2.1/accounts/{accountId}.
optionExplanations.B: An account must be called on its own base URI; a hard-coded host fails for accounts in other data centers.
optionExplanations.C: account-d.docusign.com is the demo authentication server, not an eSignature API host.
optionExplanations.D: userinfo is the right source, but a user can belong to several accounts; the first one listed is not necessarily the customer's account, so its base_uri and ID may be wrong.

decode.needs: Build URLs from userinfo base_uri
clues: each customer connects its own account -> different accounts on different base URIs
token and account ID are correct but calls fail -> wrong host
users also belong to other companies' accounts -> pick the right account from userinfo, not the first one
A4 paper -> red herring

concept.title: Discover base_uri per account
concept.line: Never hard-code the API host; call userinfo and use the selected account's base_uri with its account ID.

stem: The Riverside Rowing Association wants its 3,000 members to update their emergency contact details each season. No signature is involved, and the board does not want any agreement or signing record created for this exercise. The developer built a standalone web form configuration and now calls Instances:createInstance with sendOption set to now and a recipients array so each member gets the form by email, but the request fails. The member portal already has single sign-on, and the club emails its newsletter through its own mailing tool. Which approach fits?

options.text: Recreate the form as a template-based configuration so that remote delivery is allowed, and let Docusign email each member a link to their own form instance.
Keep the standalone configuration and retry createInstance with a clientUserId added next to sendOption and the recipients array for each member.
Keep the standalone configuration, create an embedded instance with a clientUserId when a member opens the portal page, and email members a link to that page.
Set the configuration's allowSending property to true through the Web Forms API and keep sending the same createInstance request with sendOption.

answerText: Keep the standalone configuration, create an embedded instance with a clientUserId when a member opens the portal page, and email members a link to that page.
explanation: Standalone configurations collect data without generating an envelope, but they are not eligible for remote (emailed) delivery; they support embedded delivery with a clientUserId. Emailing a portal link with the club's own tool meets 'no agreement or signing record'.
whyNotOthers: C is right because embedded delivery is supported for standalone forms and the club can send its own link. The trap is A: template-based configurations do allow remote delivery, but every submission then generates an eSignature envelope, which the board ruled out. B still asks for remote delivery, and D fails because allowSending is a read-only indicator in Configurations responses; a standalone form must be recreated as template-based to send remotely.

optionExplanations.A: Template-based forms generate an envelope on submission, which the board does not want.
optionExplanations.B: Adding clientUserId does not change the fact that standalone configurations cannot be delivered remotely.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. Standalone plus embedded delivery collects the data with no envelope, and the club emails its own link to the portal.
optionExplanations.D: allowSending is reported by Configurations:getForm and listForms; it is not switched on by an API call, and standalone forms never allow sending.

decode.needs: Standalone web form, embedded instance with clientUserId, no envelope, own email with a link.
clues: 'no agreement or signing record' -> standalone configuration (no envelope)
'sendOption... recipients... request fails' -> standalone is not eligible for remote delivery
'portal with single sign-on' -> embedded instance with clientUserId
'own mailing tool' -> the club can send the link itself

concept.title: Standalone forms are embedded only
concept.line: Standalone web forms collect data with no envelope and support embedded delivery only; remote email delivery needs a template-based configuration.

topic: Retrieving ID images for an archive
stem: Northline Bank's compliance archive must keep the front and back images of each customer's photo ID after an account-opening envelope with ID Verification completes. A headless nightly job will collect them, about 200 envelopes per night, and an auditor will later spot-check that the stored images match each signer. The admin has confirmed that the IDV configuration is set to save the front and back side of the ID. The job already holds a JWT access token that it renews every hour. Which retrieval sequence fits?

options.text: Per recipient, read the recipientIdGuid from EnvelopeRecipients:list, get a resource token from POST .../identity_proof_token, then call ID Evidence events and media with it.
Request one resource token with POST .../identity_proof_token at the start of the job and reuse it for all recipients, calling the ID Evidence events list and media URLs for each one.
Call the ID Evidence events list for each recipient with the JWT access token as the bearer token, then download the ID images from the media URLs listed in that response.
Download each envelope's certificate of completion with EnvelopeDocuments:get, because it embeds the verified ID images once ID Evidence storage is enabled.

answerText: Per recipient, read the recipientIdGuid from EnvelopeRecipients:list, get a resource token from POST .../identity_proof_token, then call ID Evidence events and media with it.
explanation: The ID Evidence API takes a resource token, created per envelope recipient with EnvelopeRecipients:createRecipientProofFileResourceToken (POST .../recipients/{recipientIdGuid}/identity_proof_token) and valid for only 2 minutes; it is then used for Events:list and the media URLs.
whyNotOthers: A is right because each recipient needs its own short-lived resource token. The trap is B: the resource token is issued for one recipient and expires after 2 minutes, so it cannot serve a whole nightly batch. C skips the resource token, which the ID Evidence API requires instead of the OAuth token, and D fails because the certificate of completion does not carry the ID images.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. recipientIdGuid, then a per-recipient resource token, then events and media from the ID Evidence API.
optionExplanations.B: A resource token is tied to one envelope recipient and is valid for 2 minutes only.
optionExplanations.C: The OAuth token is used to request the resource token; the ID Evidence calls need the resource token.
optionExplanations.D: ID images are retrieved through the ID Evidence media endpoint, not from the certificate of completion.

decode.needs: Per recipient: recipientIdGuid, identity_proof_token resource token, ID Evidence events and media.
clues: 'front and back images of each customer's photo ID' -> ID Evidence media
'IDV configuration saves front and back side' -> ID Evidence storage enabled
'headless nightly job, JWT renewed hourly' -> OAuth token only to request resource tokens
'about 200 envelopes' -> red herring

concept.title: ID Evidence resource tokens
concept.line: Get ID evidence with a per-recipient resource token (valid 2 minutes) from identity_proof_token, then call the ID Evidence events and media.

stem: Orchard Foods sends its annual code-of-conduct acknowledgment to 8,000 employees from its HR platform. The document carries low legal risk, but internal audit wants a second factor beyond the emailed link, so that someone holding a forwarded email cannot sign in an employee's name. Finance has refused any per-transaction verification charges, and about a third of staff work outside the United States. Every employee can already see a personal PIN on the HR intranet, which uses single sign-on. Which recipient authentication approach fits?

options.text: Require phone authentication by SMS for every employee, because a one-time code sent to a mobile number is the lightest second factor that Docusign enforces.
Require knowledge-based authentication for every employee, because public-record questions stop a forwarded email from being used without any extra setup.
Record authenticationMethod on each recipient to show that employees signed in to the intranet, which adds the second factor to the certificate of completion.
Set an accessCode on each recipient equal to the employee's intranet PIN, so the code reaches employees through a separate channel with no per-use fee.

answerText: Set an accessCode on each recipient equal to the employee's intranet PIN, so the code reaches employees through a separate channel with no per-use fee.
explanation: An access code is the lightest enforced method and is shared out of band (here the intranet PIN). Phone, KBA and IDV carry per-use fees, which conflicts with 'refused any per-transaction verification charges'.
whyNotOthers: D is right because the access code is enforced, delivered by a separate channel and has no per-use fee. The trap is A: SMS phone authentication is a real second factor but incurs per-use fees, and SMS can cost extra. B also has a fee and relies on US public records, which fails a third of the staff. C only records an authentication on the certificate and enforces nothing.

optionExplanations.A: Phone authentication incurs a per-use fee (and SMS may cost more), which finance refused.
optionExplanations.B: KBA incurs a per-use fee and uses US public records, so non-US staff cannot pass it; it is heavy for a low-risk acknowledgment.
optionExplanations.C: authenticationMethod records your app's authentication on the certificate; it does not enforce a second factor.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. accessCode is enforced, uses an out-of-band channel (the intranet PIN) and has no per-use fee.

decode.needs: An enforced, fee-free second factor shared out of band: recipient accessCode.
clues: 'second factor beyond the emailed link' -> enforced recipient authentication
'refused any per-transaction verification charges' -> excludes phone, KBA, IDV
'personal PIN on the HR intranet' -> out-of-band access code
'third of staff outside the United States' -> rules out KBA

concept.title: Match authentication to risk
concept.line: Access code is the lightest enforced factor with no per-use fee; phone, KBA and IDV add fees and friction for stronger assurance.

topic: Enforcing bank account verification during signing
stem: Lakeside Credit Union sends auto loan disbursement forms in which the borrower types a US checking account number and ABA routing number. Compliance requires that the borrower cannot finish signing unless those details pass a check with the credit union's bank-data provider. Who owns the account is not part of this check, because identity is confirmed in a separate know-your-customer step earlier in the process. Loan officers send the forms from the eSignature web app, and each envelope also carries a rate disclosure PDF. Which two choices meet the requirement? (Select two)

options.text: Select Must verify to sign on the verification fields so the borrower cannot complete the envelope until the bank-data check succeeds
Leave Must verify to sign unchecked, because verification still runs and prompts the borrower to correct invalid details before completing
Use the bank account owner verification extension so the provider confirms both the account details and that the borrower owns the account
Add a Data IO read step to a Maestro workflow that searches the bank-data provider for the account number before the envelope is sent out
Use bank account verification extension fields on the template so the account and routing number are checked as they are entered

answerText: Select Must verify to sign on the verification fields so the borrower cannot complete the envelope until the bank-data check succeeds; Use bank account verification extension fields on the template so the account and routing number are checked as they are entered
explanation: Bank account verification (Verify.Version3.BankAccount) checks the account and routing details in real time during signing, and Must verify to sign makes successful verification a condition of completing. 'Cannot finish signing unless' is the enforcement clue; 'who owns the account is not part of this check' rules out the owner extension.
whyNotOthers: A and E are right: the bank account verification extension performs the check, and Must verify to sign enforces it. The trap is B: if Must verify to sign is left unchecked, verification still occurs but successful verification is not required to complete signing, so it only records rather than enforces. C adds an ownership check the stem explicitly excludes, and D runs in a Maestro workflow before sending, not while the borrower signs, and Data IO is not a verification extension.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. Must verify to sign requires successful verification of the supplied data before the signing process can be completed.
optionExplanations.B: Unchecked, verification still occurs, but completing the envelope no longer depends on it; the requirement is enforcement.
optionExplanations.C: Bank account owner verification also confirms ownership or authorized signatory, which the stem says is handled elsewhere and is not required.
optionExplanations.D: Data IO reads or writes a system of record in Maestro workflows; it does not check what the borrower types during signing.
optionExplanations.E: Correct. The bank account verification extension checks US ABA account details in real time as the recipient fills in the fields.

decode.needs: Bank account verification fields with Must verify to sign selected
clues: cannot finish signing unless the check passes -> Must verify to sign
who owns the account is not part of the check -> bank account verification, not owner verification
sent from the web app, extra disclosure PDF -> red herrings

concept.title: Must verify to sign enforces verification
concept.line: Data verification runs either way; selecting Must verify to sign makes successful verification a condition for completing signing.

stem: An operations team wants its Connect listener to raise an alert whenever a step in a running workflow instance fails. Which event should the configuration subscribe to?

options.text: workflow-started
workflow-completed
extension-executed
workflow-failed

answerText: workflow-failed
explanation: workflow-failed is published when a workflow step fails, which matches 'whenever a step ... fails'.
whyNotOthers: D is right because it is the Maestro event for a failed step. The trap is B: workflow-completed only fires when every step is completed by all participants, so a failure never produces it. A fires when an instance starts, and C is the eSignature event for verification extension results (also JSON SIM), not a workflow step event.

optionExplanations.A: Published when an instance is triggered and its steps begin, not when a step fails.
optionExplanations.B: Published only when all steps are completed by all participants.
optionExplanations.C: An eSignature Connect event that reports the result of a verification extension on an envelope; it does not report a failed workflow step.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. Published when a workflow step fails (delivered in JSON SIM format).

concept.title: Maestro Connect event names
concept.line: Maestro Connect events are workflow-started, workflow-failed and workflow-completed, delivered only in JSON SIM format.

stem: A developer calls TabInfo:GetConnectedFieldsTabGroups for an account to build envelopes with verified fields, but the response contains no data types. What is the most likely cause?

options.text: No connected fields or data verification extension app is installed and connected in the account.
The request must include the ID of the template whose documents will carry the connected fields.
Connected field definitions are returned only after the envelope has been created as a draft.
The access token lacks the extended scope that connected fields discovery requires.

answerText: No connected fields or data verification extension app is installed and connected in the account.
explanation: GetConnectedFieldsTabGroups returns the field types that the account's installed connected fields or data verification extension apps can verify; if the account has neither, it returns no data types.
whyNotOthers: A is right because discovery depends on an installed and connected extension app. The trap is B: discovery is per account, not per template, and the result is used to build tabs before the envelope exists, which also rules out C. D fails because extended is the Authorization Code Grant refresh-token scope, unrelated to connected fields.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. Without an installed and connected connected fields or data verification app there are no types to return.
optionExplanations.B: Discovery describes the account's verifiable data types; it is not tied to a template.
optionExplanations.C: The tab groups are fetched first and then placed in each tab's extensionData when the envelope is created.
optionExplanations.D: The extended scope only governs reusable refresh tokens in Authorization Code Grant.

concept.title: Connected fields need installed apps
concept.line: Connected fields discovery returns types only from connected fields or data verification extension apps installed and connected in the account.

stem: Beacon Staffing is building an onboarding workflow in which the candidate's profile is pulled from the company's HR platform to prefill an intake form before the offer letter is signed. The HR platform is the system of record, and the information security review will reject any app registration that declares the ability to write back to it: data may flow out of HR, never in. The workflow runs in the company's own account, and the HR vendor exposes a REST API. How should the developer implement the extension app?

options.text: Implement all five Data IO actions and have Create Record and Patch Record return an error, so that any write attempted at runtime is rejected by the HR platform
Implement Get Type Names, Get Type Definitions and Create Record, because the type actions describe the HR data and Create Record returns it to the workflow
Register a connected fields extension so the intake form fields are autofilled from the HR platform at the moment the candidate opens the form
Register a Data IO extension with the Data Read option, implementing only Search Records, Get Type Names and Get Type Definitions

answerText: Register a Data IO extension with the Data Read option, implementing only Search Records, Get Type Names and Get Type Definitions
explanation: Data input can be implemented on its own: a read-only Data IO app implements only Search Records, Get Type Names and Get Type Definitions (Data Read in the form). Because the review rejects 'any registration that declares the ability to write', write actions must not be declared at all.
whyNotOthers: D is right because Data IO supports read-only registration with just the three read actions, so no write capability is declared. The trap is A: erroring at runtime still declares the write actions, which the stated security review rejects. B misuses Create Record, which writes a new record rather than reading one, and C is wrong because connected fields work in eSignature envelopes, not in prefilling workflow forms from a system of record.

optionExplanations.A: Declaring all five actions declares write capability, which is exactly what the security review rejects; runtime errors do not change the registration.
optionExplanations.B: Create Record creates entries in the system of record; reading data uses Search Records.
optionExplanations.C: Connected fields verify and autofill eSignature envelope fields; reading a system of record into a workflow is the Data IO extension.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. Data input is a standalone capability: Search Records plus the two type actions (Data Read) read without declaring any write.

decode.needs: A Data IO extension registered for reading only
clues: prefill an intake form inside the workflow from HR -> Data IO data read step
review rejects any registration declaring write -> do not implement Create or Patch Record
HR vendor exposes REST -> red herring

concept.title: Data IO can be read-only
concept.line: A read-only Data IO app implements only Search Records, Get Type Names and Get Type Definitions; writing requires all five actions.

stem: Kestrel Pharma wants AI-extracted renewal terms checked before they drive its procurement ERP. The plan is an external review queue that compares each agreement's extracted renewal_notice_period and expiration_date with the ERP's own records, and a contract analyst who resolves any mismatch. The integration has read access to Agreement Manager, and IT has asked that the ERP never act on a value nobody has confirmed. Which two design elements match what the Agreement Manager API supports today? (Select two)

options.text: Pull each agreement with GetAgreement and compare its provisions with the ERP's values to build the analyst's mismatch queue.
Write the analyst's corrected value back with a PUT on the agreement so the repository and the ERP stay aligned automatically.
Call CreateAgreementSummary on a mismatched agreement so Docusign AI re-runs the extraction with the corrected value.
Have the analyst correct the value in the Agreement Manager UI, and let the next GetAgreement sync pick up the user-updated value.
Delete the mismatched agreement with DeleteAgreement and upload it again so the AI produces a fresh extraction of its terms.

answerText: Pull each agreement with GetAgreement and compare its provisions with the ERP's values to build the analyst's mismatch queue.; Have the analyst correct the value in the Agreement Manager UI, and let the next GetAgreement sync pick up the user-updated value.
explanation: The API reads provisions (GetAgreement) but has no update operation; reviewers correct values in the Agreement Manager UI, and later GET responses return the user-updated values instead of the AI ones.
whyNotOthers: A and D are right: read and compare through the API, correct in the UI, and the next sync sees the fix. The trap is B: writing values back sounds natural, but the API has no update operation today. C returns an AI overview and does not re-extract or accept corrections, and E destroys the record and simply re-runs the AI, which can produce the same error.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. GetAgreement returns the provisions needed to compare against the ERP.
optionExplanations.B: There is no update operation in the Agreement Manager API; values are corrected in the UI.
optionExplanations.C: CreateAgreementSummary produces a summary; it does not re-run extraction or take corrected values.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. UI edits replace the AI-extracted values in later GET responses.
optionExplanations.E: Deleting and re-uploading only repeats the AI extraction and loses the record; nobody confirms the value.

decode.needs: External review via GetAgreement, human correction in the UI, re-sync picks up the edit.
clues: 'external review queue compares' -> read provisions with GetAgreement
'analyst resolves any mismatch' -> correction in the Agreement Manager UI
'supports today' -> no update operation in the API

concept.title: Review extractions: read via API
concept.line: Read extracted provisions through the API for external review; corrections are made in the Agreement Manager UI and flow back on the next GET.

stem: Novalis Pharma's release pipeline publishes approved workflow changes without a person clicking through Workflow Builder. The pipeline first calls the publish endpoint with isPreRunCheck=true. Today the automated pre-publication check failed with a consent error, and the response contains a consentUrl. The token already includes the signature and aow_manage scopes, and the workflow's web form and template were imported from the demo account last week. The release manager wants the fix that unblocks this and future releases. What should the team do to get the workflow published?

options.text: Call the publish endpoint again without isPreRunCheck right away, because the actual publish call grants any consent that the check found missing
Add the impersonation scope to the pipeline's JWT request and repeat the check, because a consent error in the check means the token is missing a scope
Have the user open the consentUrl and provide consent, repeat the check, then publish by calling again with the isPreRunCheck=true parameter removed
Have the user open the consentUrl and provide consent, then call again with isPreRunCheck=true still set, because that parameter is what publishes it

answerText: Have the user open the consentUrl and provide consent, repeat the check, then publish by calling again with the isPreRunCheck=true parameter removed
explanation: If the pre-publication check fails with consent errors, open the consentUrl, have the user consent and call again; once the check passes, publish by calling again without isPreRunCheck=true.
whyNotOthers: C is right because consent is granted through the consentUrl and the real publish omits isPreRunCheck. The trap is D: granting consent is right, but isPreRunCheck=true only runs the check and never publishes. A fails because publishing does not grant consent, and B misreads the error: the response points to consentUrl, not to a missing token scope.

optionExplanations.A: The publish call does not grant consent; the check fails until the user consents through consentUrl.
optionExplanations.B: The error is about user consent and comes with a consentUrl; adding a scope to the token does not resolve it.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. Consent through consentUrl, then publish by calling again without isPreRunCheck=true.
optionExplanations.D: isPreRunCheck=true runs only the automated review; the publish call must omit it.

decode.needs: Resolve consent via consentUrl, then publish by calling without isPreRunCheck=true.
clues: automated pre-publication check -> isPreRunCheck=true
consent error with consentUrl -> user must open it and consent
web form and template imported from demo -> red herring

concept.title: Consent first, then real publish
concept.line: A consent failure in the pre-publication check returns consentUrl; consent, then publish by calling again without isPreRunCheck=true.

topic: Data IO action when no record matches
stem: A Maestro data write step runs, but its query finds no matching record in the system of record. Which Data IO action does Docusign invoke to store the data?

options.text: Patch Record
Create Record
Search Records
Get Type Definitions

answerText: Create Record
explanation: Create Record runs when a data output step is executed and no query is provided or the query does not find a record to update.
whyNotOthers: B is right because Create Record handles the 'nothing found' case of a write step. The trap is A: Patch Record runs only when the query finds an existing record. C is the lookup that came back empty, not the write, and D runs when a connection is established or refreshed.

optionExplanations.A: Patch Record updates an existing entry and runs only when the query finds a record.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. With no query or no match, the write step creates a new entry with Create Record.
optionExplanations.C: Search Records performs the lookup that found nothing; it does not store data.
optionExplanations.D: Get Type Definitions runs when a connection is created or refreshed to describe the data model.

concept.title: Create versus Patch in Data IO
concept.line: A data write step patches the record its query finds; with no query or no match, it creates a new record.

stem: A legal-tech startup's matter-intake widget is pure browser JavaScript with no server of its own. Today it sends attorneys to /oauth/auth with response_type=token and reads the access token straight from the redirect. A penetration test flagged this, and the CTO wants the flow Docusign recommends for this kind of app, while each attorney still signs in with their own Docusign login and nothing secret may ship to the browser. The widget is embedded in the firm's WordPress site. What should the team do?

options.text: Keep response_type=token but add a random state value to every request, which Docusign treats as enough hardening for browser-only apps
Switch to Confidential Authorization Code Grant, placing the secret key in an obfuscated JavaScript bundle so the widget can call the token endpoint
Switch to JWT Grant impersonating each attorney after consent, so the widget never has to send an attorney to the login page again
In Apps and Keys, mark the app as unable to store a secret and as a single-page app, then use Public Authorization Code Grant with PKCE
In Apps and Keys, keep the default confidential setting, then use Authorization Code Grant with PKCE, sending only a code_verifier and no secret

answerText: In Apps and Keys, mark the app as unable to store a secret and as a single-page app, then use Public Authorization Code Grant with PKCE
explanation: A browser-only app ("no server of its own") that cannot hold a secret, with each attorney signing in, should use Public Authorization Code Grant with PKCE, configured in Apps and Keys by stating the app cannot store a client secret and is a single-page app.
whyNotOthers: D is right because Docusign recommends Public Auth Code Grant with PKCE instead of Implicit for SPAs and configures it in Apps and Keys. The trap is E: PKCE is right, but the default confidential setting expects a secret on the token request; the code_verifier replaces the secret only when the app is configured as public. A keeps the legacy Implicit flow, B leaks the secret to every browser, and C has no secure place for a private key.

optionExplanations.A: state adds CSRF protection but keeps the legacy Implicit flow the pen test flagged.
optionExplanations.B: Any secret in browser JavaScript is exposed, however obfuscated.
optionExplanations.C: JWT needs a private key on a secure server and is for acting without the user; this widget has no server.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. Configure the app as public (cannot store a secret, SPA) and use Public Auth Code Grant with PKCE.
optionExplanations.E: With the confidential setting the token request must carry the secret; only a public app sends code_verifier instead.

decode.needs: Public Authorization Code Grant with PKCE, configured as a single-page app in Apps and Keys.
clues: response_type=token -> legacy Implicit Grant
pure browser JavaScript with no server -> cannot store a secret
each attorney signs in -> user-present flow
WordPress site -> red herring

concept.title: SPAs use Public Auth Code
concept.line: Browser-only apps that cannot keep a secret should be configured as public in Apps and Keys and use Auth Code Grant with PKCE.

stem: Which extension points support the phone verification extension?

options.text: eSignature Add Fields view and Signing only
eSignature Add Fields view and Signing, and Maestro workflows
Web Forms only
eSignature Add Fields view and Signing, and Web Forms

answerText: eSignature Add Fields view and Signing, and Web Forms
explanation: Phone verification, like email address verification, is supported at the eSignature Add Fields view and Signing and also in Web Forms.
whyNotOthers: D is right because phone and email verification are the two data verification extensions that also work in Web Forms. The trap is A: that is the extension point for the other verification types such as bank account, SSN, FEIN and postal address. B swaps Web Forms for Maestro workflows, which are the extension point for Data IO and file output, and C drops eSignature.

optionExplanations.A: This is true for bank account, SSN, FEIN and postal address verification, but phone verification is also available in Web Forms.
optionExplanations.B: Maestro workflows are the extension point for Data IO and file output cloud storage; phone verification's second extension point is Web Forms.
optionExplanations.C: Phone verification also works in eSignature Add Fields view and Signing.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. Phone and email verification support eSignature Add Fields view and Signing plus Web Forms.

concept.title: Email and phone verification reach Web Forms
concept.line: Email and phone verification work in eSignature and Web Forms; other data verification types are eSignature only.

stem: The trigger URL returned by Workflows:getWorkflowTriggerRequirements contains two query parameters that Maestro generates when the workflow is published, used to authenticate the request and identify a valid workflow. Which are they?

options.text: mtid and mtsec
code and state
client_id and client_secret
workflowId and accountId

answerText: mtid and mtsec
explanation: The trigger URL includes the mtid and mtsec query parameters, generated by Maestro at publication to authenticate the request and identify the workflow.
whyNotOthers: A is right because mtid and mtsec are the Maestro-generated trigger parameters. The trap is C: client ID and secret sound like authentication values, but they belong to the integration key and OAuth, not to the trigger URL. B are OAuth authorization code grant parameters, and D are path values in API endpoints, not query parameters generated at publication.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. Maestro generates mtid and mtsec when the workflow is published.
optionExplanations.B: code and state belong to the OAuth Authorization Code Grant redirect.
optionExplanations.C: Integration key credentials used for OAuth, not trigger URL parameters.
optionExplanations.D: These appear in API paths; they are not generated at publication.

concept.title: Trigger URL carries mtid and mtsec
concept.line: Maestro generates mtid and mtsec at publish time; they appear on the trigger URL to authenticate the call and identify the workflow.

stem: Pellucid Wealth's advisor portal runs on its own web servers and uses Confidential Authorization Code Grant with the signature and extended scopes. Advisors sign in only now and then, so a background token keeper renews each advisor's session before the access token lapses, without ever sending the advisor back to a login screen. The keeper does not use PKCE. The portal is hosted in Azure and ships its logs to Splunk. Which two elements must the keeper's renewal request to the Docusign authentication service include? (Select two)

options.text: A body with grant_type=refresh_token and the most recently issued refresh token, so the service returns a new token pair without any advisor interaction
An Authorization header of Bearer followed by the access token that is about to expire, so the service can tell which advisor session is being extended
A body with grant_type=authorization_code and the code from the advisor's original sign-in, so the service re-issues tokens from that original consent
An Authorization header of Basic followed by the base64 of integrationKey:secretKey, so the service can authenticate the confidential client sending the request
A code_verifier in the body that matches the original code challenge, so the service can prove the app renewing the session is the one that started it

answerText: A body with grant_type=refresh_token and the most recently issued refresh token, so the service returns a new token pair without any advisor interaction; An Authorization header of Basic followed by the base64 of integrationKey:secretKey, so the service can authenticate the confidential client sending the request
explanation: Renewing without the user means POST /oauth/token with grant_type=refresh_token and the refresh token, and because the portal is a confidential server app ("runs on its own web servers", "does not use PKCE") the request carries the Basic header built from integrationKey:secretKey.
whyNotOthers: A and D are right because a Confidential refresh call is the token endpoint with grant_type=refresh_token plus the Basic client header. The trap is B: a Bearer header is how you call the APIs and userinfo, not how you authenticate a token refresh. C fails because an authorization code is single-use and valid for only 120 seconds. E fails because code_verifier replaces the secret only in PKCE flows, and the stem says no PKCE.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. Refresh requests use grant_type=refresh_token with the latest refresh token (each refresh returns a new one).
optionExplanations.B: Bearer plus the access token is used for API and userinfo calls, not to authenticate a refresh request.
optionExplanations.C: The authorization code is single-use and expires after 120 seconds; it cannot be replayed weeks later.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. Confidential Auth Code Grant authenticates token requests with Basic base64(integrationKey:secretKey).
optionExplanations.E: code_verifier is sent only when PKCE was used (always for Public); this keeper does not use PKCE.

decode.needs: The exact contents of a Confidential Auth Code Grant refresh request to /oauth/token.
clues: runs on its own web servers -> confidential client that holds a secret
without sending the advisor back to a login screen -> refresh token, not a new authorization code
does not use PKCE -> no code_verifier
Azure, Splunk -> red herrings

concept.title: Confidential refresh request contents
concept.line: A Confidential refresh posts grant_type=refresh_token and the refresh token to /oauth/token with a Basic header of integrationKey:secretKey.

stem: Lakeshore Credit Union closes joint mortgages in which each of two co-borrowers must sign their own copy of the same Borrower Certification server template. That template defines one role, borrower, with its tabs. The loan officer also wants a rate-lock letter that the loan system generates as a PDF included in the same envelope, and everything must be created in one API call. The credit union is also moving to a new core banking vendor next quarter. How should the developer structure the request?

options.text: Use the template reference model with the template ID once and two templateRoles entries named borrower, one per co-borrower, and add the rate-lock PDF in documents
Use one composite template object holding the server template plus two inline templates, sequence 2 and 3, each mapping a different co-borrower to the borrower role
Use one composite template object per co-borrower, each with the server template and an inline template mapping that person to borrower, plus one for the PDF
Use the direct documents model, upload the certification PDF twice, and rely on the server template's anchor settings to place the borrower tabs for each signer

answerText: Use one composite template object per co-borrower, each with the server template and an inline template mapping that person to borrower, plus one for the PDF
explanation: Composite templates can apply the same server template more than once with a different recipient for each instance, but each composite template object contributes only one document. The clue 'each co-borrower must sign their own copy' needs two objects, plus one for the generated PDF.
whyNotOthers: C is right because each copy of the certification needs its own composite template object with its own inline recipient mapping. The trap is B: one object contributes a single document, and the inline template with the higher sequence overwrites the lower one, so only one copy and one borrower survive. A cannot mix a template with an extra document or duplicate the template, and D loses the template's tabs because direct documents do not use server template settings.

optionExplanations.A: The template reference model applies one template once; it cannot duplicate the template or add the generated PDF.
optionExplanations.B: One object yields one document, and attributes from higher sequences overwrite lower ones, so the two mappings collide.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. Separate objects give two copies of the template, each mapped to a different co-borrower, plus an object for the letter.
optionExplanations.D: Direct documents ignore server template tabs, so the borrower fields would have to be rebuilt by hand.

decode.needs: Composite templates: one object per template instance plus one for the generated document
clues: each co-borrower signs their own copy of the same template -> same server template applied twice
generated PDF in the same envelope, one API call -> composite templates
new core banking vendor -> red herring

concept.title: One document per composite object
concept.line: To reuse a server template for several recipients, give each instance its own composite template object with an inline template mapping the role.

stem: Orchard Freight's CIO says the company's Docusign account keeps nearing its shared hourly API allowance. Three internal apps call Docusign: a dispatch app, a billing app and a driver-onboarding app. Before anyone asks for a higher limit, she wants a per-app view showing which integration behaves inefficiently, the specific negative factors behind it, and Docusign's recommendations for fixing each one. The billing app was written by a contractor who has since left. Which approach fits best?

options.text: Open the API Usage Center and, for each app, select Actions > View Efficiency Score to see its score, negative factors and linked recommendations
Open the API Dashboard under Apps and Keys and compare each app's 90-day timeline of successful and failed requests to find the worst one
Turn on API request logging for each app's user and compare the last 50 downloaded requests from each app to spot wasted calls
Open a Docusign Support case for a per-app call report, because efficiency analysis is available only to Docusign staff on request

answerText: Open the API Usage Center and, for each app, select Actions > View Efficiency Score to see its score, negative factors and linked recommendations
explanation: The API Usage Center shows an efficiency score per app, and Actions > View Efficiency Score lists the negative factors with recommendations, matching 'specific negative factors' and 'recommendations for fixing each one'.
whyNotOthers: A is right because only the Usage Center scores efficiency and links fixes for each factor. The trap is B: the API Dashboard shows a 90-day timeline and failed-request details, but no efficiency score or recommendations. C gives raw samples of at most 50 requests per user, not a per-app analysis. D fails because admins can see efficiency scores themselves.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. The API Usage Center scores each app, and View Efficiency Score lists its negative factors with recommendations.
optionExplanations.B: The API Dashboard shows request timelines and failures, but no efficiency score, factors or recommendations.
optionExplanations.C: Request logging captures at most 50 raw requests per user and does not analyse efficiency.
optionExplanations.D: Efficiency scores are available to admins in the API Usage Center; no support case is needed.

decode.needs: Use the API Usage Center efficiency score to find inefficient apps.
clues: nearing its shared hourly allowance -> per-account limit, check app efficiency
negative factors and recommendations per app -> API Usage Center, View Efficiency Score
contractor who has since left -> red herring

concept.title: Efficiency score per app
concept.line: The API Usage Center shows each app's efficiency score, negative factors and recommendations; fix these before raising the hourly limit.

topic: Multi Branch Rule vs Branching Rule
stem: Meridian Freight onboards new carriers through a workflow that starts with a web form. One form answer, operating region, has four possible values: North America, EU, APAC and LATAM. Each region must sign a different carrier agreement countersigned by a different legal entity, and the EU route also needs an extra identity check before signing. The process builder wants a single decision point right after the form that sends each carrier down the route for its region, and the carriers' fleet size question on the same form does not affect routing. Which design fits?
