options.text: Add a Multi Branch Rule step on the region variable after the form, with one path per region holding that region's template, signing and, for EU, verification steps
Add a Branching Rule step on the region variable after the form and define four conditions, because a Branching Rule creates one path for each condition defined
Use one Prepare Document Template step with show/hide logic on the region variable, so each region's agreement content is generated from a single shared document
Build four workflows and add a Send an Email step after the form that sends the carrier the start link of the workflow that matches their region

answerText: Add a Multi Branch Rule step on the region variable after the form, with one path per region holding that region's template, signing and, for EU, verification steps
explanation: A Multi Branch Rule step creates several paths from one decision point, which fits 'single decision point ... four possible values', and each path can contain different steps (the EU identity check).
whyNotOthers: A is right because one Multi Branch Rule splits into a path per region. The trap is B: a Branching Rule is an if/else split into exactly two paths, so it cannot route four values in a single step. C varies document content but cannot add an extra verification step or change countersigners per region, and D splits the process into separate instances instead of routing within one workflow.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. A Multi Branch Rule creates multiple paths from one step, and each path can hold its own steps.
optionExplanations.B: A Branching Rule is an if/else step with only two paths.
optionExplanations.C: Show/hide logic changes document content only; it cannot add the EU-only verification step or change the route.
optionExplanations.D: This makes carriers restart in another workflow instead of routing within one instance at a single decision point.

decode.needs: Use a Multi Branch Rule step to split into more than two paths with different steps per path.
clues: four possible values, single decision point -> Multi Branch Rule (not two-way Branching Rule)
EU route needs an extra identity check -> paths differ in steps, not just document content
fleet size question -> red herring

concept.title: More than two paths: Multi Branch
concept.line: A Branching Rule splits into two paths (if/else); a Multi Branch Rule creates several paths, each with its own steps.

stem: At Pemberton Credit Union, a member-services agent who is not a Docusign administrator and has no access to the account's integrations reports that some envelopes sent under her user from the loan system fail with an error. The development team asks her to capture the raw API requests and responses made under her user so they can compare them with a working colleague's. She works the afternoon shift on a shared branch computer. Which tool should she use?

options.text: The API Dashboard in Admin > Apps and Keys, filtered by response code for the loan system's integration key
The efficiency score page for the loan system's key in the API Usage Center, which lists its failed calls
The Connect failure log for the account's Connect configuration, which records each failed request
API request logging, enabled under My Preferences, which keeps up to 50 requests that she can download

answerText: API request logging, enabled under My Preferences, which keeps up to 50 requests that she can download
explanation: API request logging is available to all users, is turned on in My Preferences, and keeps up to 50 request logs that can be downloaded; the agent has 'no access to the account's integrations'.
whyNotOthers: D is right because request logging works for any user and captures raw requests and responses. The trap is A: the API Dashboard shows failed-request details, but only to users who have access to the integrations. B shows efficiency factors and recommendations, not raw requests, and is an admin tool. C covers webhook deliveries, not API calls.

optionExplanations.A: The API Dashboard is available only to users with access to the API integrations; she has none.
optionExplanations.B: The efficiency score shows negative factors and recommendations, not raw request and response bodies, and it is an admin view.
optionExplanations.C: Connect logs record webhook deliveries from Docusign, not the API requests the loan system sends.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. Request logging is off by default, is enabled in My Preferences by any user, and keeps up to 50 downloadable logs.

decode.needs: Pick the debugging tool available to a non-admin user without integration access.
clues: not an administrator, no access to integrations -> API Dashboard is not available to her
raw API requests and responses under her user -> API request logging
afternoon shift, shared branch computer -> red herring

concept.title: Request logging versus API Dashboard
concept.line: API request logging (My Preferences, 50 logs) is for any user; the API Dashboard is only for users with access to the integrations.

stem: Which two are requirements for an eSignature app to pass the Go-Live review and be promoted? (Select two)

options.text: The app uses OAuth 2.0 authentication configured on its integration key
The key has made at least 20 successful API calls in the developer account
The production account uses the same email address as the developer account
The secret and redirect URIs are already configured in the production account
A paid or partner production account in which the submitter is an administrator

answerText: The app uses OAuth 2.0 authentication configured on its integration key; A paid or partner production account in which the submitter is an administrator
explanation: The eSignature Go-Live review needs OAuth 2.0 authentication and a paid (or partner) production account that the submitter administers.
whyNotOthers: A and E are right because the review checks OAuth 2.0 and needs a production management account where you are an admin. The trap is B: the 20-call rule used to apply, but it was removed, so you can start Go-Live right after creating the key. C fails because the production account may use a different email; D fails because the key does not exist in production until it is promoted.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. OAuth 2.0 authentication is required (or a policy exception).
optionExplanations.B: The old 20-call requirement was removed; Go-Live can start right after the key is set up.
optionExplanations.C: The production account can use a different email address from the developer account.
optionExplanations.D: Secrets and redirect URIs are added in production after promotion, because the key is only duplicated there at Go-Live.
optionExplanations.E: Correct. A paid or partner production account is needed, and the submitter must be its administrator.

concept.title: Go-Live review requirements
concept.line: Go-Live needs OAuth 2.0 plus a paid or partner production account administered by the submitter; the 20-call rule no longer exists.

stem: OAuth for Docusign Connect lets a listener confirm that webhook messages really come from Docusign. Which OAuth grant does Docusign use with the customer's authorization server to obtain the token it sends?

options.text: JWT Grant
Client Credentials
Authorization Code Grant
Implicit Grant

answerText: Client Credentials
explanation: OAuth for Connect uses the Client Credentials grant: Docusign sends the client ID, secret and custom parameters to the customer's token URL and passes the returned token in the Authorization header of each message.
whyNotOthers: B is right because OAuth for Connect is a server-to-server Client Credentials flow against the customer's own IdP. The trap is A: JWT Grant is what server integrations use to call Docusign APIs, not how Connect authenticates itself to a listener. C and D are user-interactive grants and need a browser.

optionExplanations.A: JWT Grant is used by your integration to get Docusign access tokens for API calls; OAuth for Connect works in the opposite direction.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. Docusign uses the Client Credentials grant against your authorization server and sends the token as a Bearer value in the Authorization header.
optionExplanations.C: Authorization Code Grant requires a user to log in through a browser, which does not fit Docusign calling a listener.
optionExplanations.D: Implicit Grant is a browser-based user flow and is not used for server-to-server webhook authentication.

concept.title: OAuth for Connect uses Client Credentials
concept.line: Docusign obtains a token from the customer's IdP with Client Credentials and sends it as a Bearer token with every Connect message.

topic: Connection grant type for an internal-only app
stem: Orchard Freight wants signers to have their shipment rate codes checked against the company's in-house rates service, which sits behind the corporate identity provider. The information security team allows only machine-to-machine access to that service: no person may ever sign in interactively to authorize a connection. The app will be used only by Orchard's own two production accounts and will never be offered to other companies. The service is written in Java and hosted in a private cloud. Which registration choices should the developer make?

options.text: Set the distribution to PUBLIC and choose the Client Credentials grant for the connection, limiting the publication regions to those where Orchard's accounts are hosted
Set the distribution to PRIVATE and choose the Authorization Code grant, asking the identity team for a service user that an admin signs in as once when connecting
Set the distribution to PRIVATE and choose the Client Credentials grant for the connection, then share the live app with Orchard's two production accounts
Set the distribution to PRIVATE and leave the connection unauthenticated, letting the rates service trust calls signed with Orchard's Docusign integration key

answerText: Set the distribution to PRIVATE and choose the Client Credentials grant for the connection, then share the live app with Orchard's two production accounts
explanation: The connection grant type can be Authorization Code or Client Credentials, and Client Credentials can be selected only when the distribution is Private. 'Only machine-to-machine access' plus 'only Orchard's own accounts' therefore means Private with Client Credentials.
whyNotOthers: C is right because Client Credentials gives the no-interactive-login connection the security team demands, and it is only available for privately distributed apps. The trap is A: Client Credentials is not available with PUBLIC distribution, and limiting regions does not change that. B breaks the rule that no person signs in interactively, and D is wrong because the connection is how Docusign obtains authorization to the external service; a Docusign integration key plays no part in it.

optionExplanations.A: Client Credentials can only be selected when the distribution type is Private, and a public listing is not what Orchard wants anyway.
optionExplanations.B: Authorization Code requires someone to sign in to authorize the connection, which the security team forbids.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. Private distribution unlocks the Client Credentials grant, which needs no interactive sign-in, and sharing limits use to Orchard's accounts.
optionExplanations.D: The connection holds the authorization details for the external service; a Docusign integration key does not authenticate Docusign's calls to it.

decode.needs: A private extension app whose connection uses the Client Credentials grant
clues: only machine-to-machine access, no person signs in -> Client Credentials grant
only our own two production accounts -> PRIVATE distribution
Java, private cloud -> red herring

concept.title: Client Credentials requires private distribution
concept.line: Extension app connections use Authorization Code or Client Credentials; Client Credentials is selectable only for privately distributed apps.

topic: Recipient Connect for envelopes received from outside
stem: Harlow and Finch, a mid-size law firm, wants its matter-management system to log the moment a partner finishes signing an engagement letter. The letters are prepared and sent by clients from the clients' own Docusign accounts, usually from the web app, so the firm has no say in how they are created. The firm's Docusign organization has claimed the firm's email domain, and every partner is a user in the firm's linked account. The firm's own outbound fee agreements are already tracked by an existing integration. The records team wants each update within a minute, refuses any scheduled job, and its listener accepts only JSON messages. Which approach fits?

options.text: Ask each client to add an eventNotification object pointing to the firm's listener whenever they create an engagement letter, so the envelope reports to the firm
Create an organization-level Connect configuration for the firm's linked account, delivering XML aggregate messages for the partners' recipient-completed events
Create a Recipient Connect configuration (customrecipient) for the partners' users, subscribed to recipient-completed, so envelopes they receive are reported
Run a job every 15 minutes that calls Envelopes:listStatusChanges for the partners and posts any newly signed engagement letters to the matter system

answerText: Create a Recipient Connect configuration (customrecipient) for the partners' users, subscribed to recipient-completed, so envelopes they receive are reported
explanation: Recipient Connect notifies your listener when a domain user of your organization is a recipient (signer or CC) of an envelope, even one sent from another account. The clues are "sent by clients from the clients' own accounts" and "the organization has claimed the firm's email domain".
whyNotOthers: C is right because Recipient Connect is built for envelopes your users receive rather than send, its prerequisites (organization, claimed domain, linked account) are met, and its messages are always JSON. The trap is B: an organization-level configuration sounds like it covers everything, but organization-level Connect delivers only JSON SIM, never XML aggregate messages, and the listener accepts only JSON. A fails because clients mostly use the web app and the firm cannot control envelope creation; D is polling and a scheduled job, which the records team refuses.

optionExplanations.A: Envelope-level Connect is set by whoever creates the envelope through the API; clients sending from the web app cannot add it, and the firm has no control over their process.
optionExplanations.B: Organization-level Connect supports only JSON SIM, so it cannot deliver XML aggregate messages, and the firm's listener accepts only JSON anyway.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. Recipient Connect (configurationType customrecipient) fires when a claimed-domain user of the organization is a recipient, which is exactly the partners' situation.
optionExplanations.D: This is polling on a schedule; the records team refuses scheduled jobs and wants updates within a minute, which Connect push delivers.

decode.needs: Event notifications for envelopes in which org users are recipients, sent from other accounts.
clues: sent by clients from the clients' own accounts -> the firm is the recipient, not the sender
organization has claimed the firm's email domain -> Recipient Connect prerequisite is met
refuses any scheduled job -> no polling
listener accepts only JSON -> rules out any XML delivery
outbound fee agreements already tracked -> red herring

concept.title: Recipient Connect covers received envelopes
concept.line: Account-level Connect tracks envelopes your users send; Recipient Connect tracks envelopes your claimed-domain users receive as signer or CC.

stem: Besides completed agreements, what else can Workflow Builder Store Files steps automatically store in a cloud repository?

options.text: Web form drafts
Connect event logs
Workflow activity logs
ID Evidence data

answerText: ID Evidence data
explanation: Store Files steps automate the storage of completed agreements and ID Evidence data.
whyNotOthers: D is right because the course lists completed agreements and ID Evidence data as what Store Files steps save. The trap is C: the activity log gives visibility of actions across workflows, but it is viewed in Docusign and is not what a Store Files step archives. A and B are not outputs that a Store Files step handles.

optionExplanations.A: Web form drafts are not something a Store Files step archives.
optionExplanations.B: Connect messages go to your listener; they are not stored by a workflow step.
optionExplanations.C: Activity logs are viewed in Workflow Builder; Store Files steps do not archive them.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. Store Files steps store completed agreements and ID Evidence data.

concept.title: Store Files saves agreements and evidence
concept.line: Store Files apps steps (Google Drive, Box, Dropbox, OneDrive, SharePoint, Salesforce) store completed agreements and ID Evidence data.

stem: Halcyon Group runs two subsidiaries, Halcyon Marine and Halcyon Rail, from a single Docusign account. Each subsidiary's line-of-business app sends contracts through the eSignature REST API on behalf of its own staff. Marketing wants every counterparty to see the right subsidiary's logo and colors and to land on that subsidiary's website after signing. Compliance insists that Marine staff can never send with Rail's look by mistake, and the reverse. Both apps already use JWT with the same integration key, and volume is about 5,000 envelopes a month. Which approach fits?

options.text: Create one brand per subsidiary, leave both brands available to every sender in the account, and pass the matching brandId in every Envelopes:create request from that subsidiary's app.
Create one brand per subsidiary, assign each brand to that subsidiary's user group, and pass the matching brandId in every Envelopes:create request from that subsidiary's app.
Create one brand per subsidiary and mark both as the account's default brand, so Docusign chooses the right one from the sender's group without any brandId in the request.
Create one brand per subsidiary and put the post-signing website in each brand's sending settings, because the sending view decides where counterparties land after signing.

answerText: Create one brand per subsidiary, assign each brand to that subsidiary's user group, and pass the matching brandId in every Envelopes:create request from that subsidiary's app.
explanation: Separate brands carry separate logos, colors and the post-signing redirect URL; assigning a brand to a group means only that group's users can use it ('Marine staff can never send with Rail's look'), and brandId on Envelopes:create applies it.
whyNotOthers: B is right because per-subsidiary brands, group assignment and brandId cover look, redirect and the access restriction. The trap is A: it gets the look and redirect right, but leaving both brands available to every sender means a wrong brandId is accepted, so 'never by mistake' is not enforced; assigning brands to groups is what limits which brands each group's members can use. C fails because the account has one default brand, and D fails because the redirect URL is a signing-brand setting, not a sending one.

optionExplanations.A: Separate brands and brandId give the right look and redirect, but with both brands open to all senders nothing stops a Marine sender from passing Rail's brandId, so the compliance rule is not enforced.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. One brand per subsidiary, restricted to that subsidiary's group, applied with brandId on each envelope.
optionExplanations.C: An account has a single default brand; the default is meant for all envelopes, not chosen per group.
optionExplanations.D: The sending view brand covers colors, logo and footer links; the post-signing redirect belongs to the signing experience.

decode.needs: Two signing brands, each assigned to a group, applied with brandId in Envelopes:create.
clues: 'right logo and colors... land on the website after signing' -> signing brand: logo, colors, redirect URL
'Marine staff can never send with Rail's look' -> assign each brand to that subsidiary's group; brandId alone does not restrict anyone
'same integration key, 5,000 envelopes' -> red herring

concept.title: Brands, groups and brandId
concept.line: Use one brand per business identity, restrict it by assigning it to groups, and apply it per envelope with brandId.

stem: Varden Analytics copies Agreement Manager data into a data lake every night. The first full load is done, and the architect now wants each nightly run to pick up only the agreements added to the repository since the previous run. The legal team is still uploading contracts that were signed years ago, and many agreements have effective dates in the future. The account's hourly API limit is shared with a CPQ integration, and the data lake team prefers small nightly batches. Which request pattern fits?

options.text: Call GetAgreementsList with a provisions.execution_date filter of gte the last run time, following ctoken until the final page has been read.
Call GetAgreementsList with a metadata.created_at filter of gte the last run time, following ctoken until the final page has been read.
Call GetAgreementsList with a provisions.effective_date filter of gte the last run time, following ctoken until the final page has been read.
Call GetAgreementsList with no filter every night and compare each returned id with the data lake, following ctoken until the final page has been read.

answerText: Call GetAgreementsList with a metadata.created_at filter of gte the last run time, following ctoken until the final page has been read.
explanation: metadata.created_at is when the agreement record was created in the repository and accepts gte with an ISO 8601 date, so it returns exactly what was 'added since the previous run', whatever the contract's own dates.
whyNotOthers: B is right because only the record creation timestamp tracks additions to the repository. The trap is A: execution_date is when the contract was signed, so legacy contracts 'signed years ago' but uploaded yesterday would be missed. C uses a contractual date that can lie in the future, and D works but re-reads the whole repository each night, wasting the shared hourly limit.

optionExplanations.A: execution_date is the contract's signing date; old contracts uploaded today fall outside the filter.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. metadata.created_at with gte the last run time returns agreements added since then.
optionExplanations.C: effective_date is a contract term; future-dated agreements would be picked up repeatedly and others missed.
optionExplanations.D: Returns the same results with far more calls against the shared hourly limit.

decode.needs: GetAgreementsList filtered on metadata.created_at gte last run, paged with ctoken.
clues: 'added to the repository since the previous run' -> record creation timestamp
'contracts that were signed years ago' -> execution_date would miss them
'effective dates in the future' -> effective_date is the wrong clock
'hourly API limit is shared' -> avoid full re-reads

concept.title: Filter on record creation date
concept.line: For incremental sync filter GetAgreementsList on metadata.created_at; provision dates describe the contract, not when it entered the repository.

stem: Larkspur Analytics sells a cloud procurement platform to mid-size manufacturers. Each manufacturer already pays for its own Docusign subscription, and Larkspur wants a buyer at any of these companies to connect the platform to their company's Docusign account with a one-time authorization and then send purchase agreements from it. Larkspur has enrolled in the Docusign Partner Program and expects referral revenue as its customers' signing volume grows. The platform runs in Larkspur's own cloud, and the sales team mentions a European data center rollout next year. Which classification should Larkspur choose for the platform's integration key?

options.text: Private custom integration, because the platform is a custom build that its customers' employees use directly with their own Docusign logins
Public integration, because many separate Docusign customers authorize the platform against their own accounts and Larkspur earns partner referral revenue
Embedded integration, because Larkspur builds the signing features into its own product and offers them to its customers as part of the service
Third-party integration key, because each manufacturer is a third party that connects an outside partner's platform to its own Docusign account

answerText: Public integration, because many separate Docusign customers authorize the platform against their own accounts and Larkspur earns partner referral revenue
explanation: Public integration fits an app built for multiple Docusign customers who 'connect ... their company's Docusign account with a one-time authorization', with Partner Program membership and referral revenue.
whyNotOthers: B is right because many customers authorize the app against their own accounts and Larkspur is a partner earning referral revenue. The trap is A: Private custom also mentions customers' employees, but it is for an integration used by your own or one customer's staff, not a multi-customer product with referral revenue. C fails because Embedded means customers use the vendor's Docusign account and do not need their own. D fails because Third-party integration key is chosen by the customer who must supply its own key to a partner's app, not by the vendor.

optionExplanations.A: Private custom suits an app used directly by your own or a customer's employees; a multi-customer partner product with referral revenue is Public.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. Multiple Docusign customers authorize the app with their own accounts, and Partner Program membership with referral revenue marks a Public integration.
optionExplanations.C: Embedded is for ISV Embed partners whose customers use the vendor's own Docusign account; here every manufacturer has its own subscription.
optionExplanations.D: Third-party integration key is chosen by a customer that must provide its own key to a partner app, not by the vendor building the app.

decode.needs: Choose the classification for a multi-customer partner app where customers use their own accounts.
clues: each manufacturer already pays for its own Docusign subscription -> customers use their own accounts (not Embedded)
one-time authorization -> customers consent to the vendor's app (Public pattern)
Partner Program and referral revenue -> Public integration
European data center rollout -> red herring

concept.title: Public integration classification
concept.line: A product used by many Docusign customers with their own accounts, built by a Partner Program member earning referral revenue, is a Public integration.

topic: Fixing an app that is in review
stem: Amara submitted the first version of her company's extension app for Docusign review yesterday, and the Developer Console shows it as In Review. This morning QA found that one action still points at the old endpoint path in its params.uri. Amara wants the version that Docusign eventually approves and publishes to contain the corrected endpoint. Her manager suggests waiting until approval and fixing it afterwards to avoid delays, and the team has already prepared App Center screenshots. Which two steps should Amara take? (Select two)

options.text: Create a new draft version that contains the fix alongside the In Review version, and ask Docusign to review the newer draft instead
Cancel the publishing request so the version reverts to Draft status, and then correct the params.uri value in the registration
Edit the params.uri value directly on the In Review version, because the reviewers always evaluate the most recently saved registration details
Resubmit the corrected version for review, because after cancelling, the version is a Draft that cannot be published unreviewed
Delete the In Review version and register a separate app with the corrected endpoint under the same app name before resubmitting

answerText: Cancel the publishing request so the version reverts to Draft status, and then correct the params.uri value in the registration; Resubmit the corrected version for review, because after cancelling, the version is a Draft that cannot be published unreviewed
explanation: A version that is In Review cannot be updated or deleted until the publishing process is cancelled, which reverts it to Draft; after updating it, it must be resubmitted for review before it can be published.
whyNotOthers: B and D are right because cancelling returns the version to Draft so it can be edited, and the edited Draft must be resubmitted for review. The trap is A: you cannot create a new draft version while another version is in Draft, In Review, Approved or Rejected status. C fails because updating is prohibited in In Review, and E fails because deleting is also prohibited in In Review and app names must be unique.

optionExplanations.A: Only one version can be in Draft, In Review, Approved or Rejected at a time, so a new draft cannot be created alongside the In Review version.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. Cancelling the publishing process reverts the version to Draft, which is the only way to update it.
optionExplanations.C: Updating a version is prohibited while it is In Review; the version must first revert to Draft.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. After updating the reverted Draft, it must be resubmitted for review before it can be published.
optionExplanations.E: Deleting is prohibited in In Review, and a second registration with the same unique app name is not allowed.

decode.needs: Cancel publishing to return to Draft, edit, then resubmit
clues: shows In Review and needs a fix -> cancel the publishing process first
the approved version must contain the fix -> resubmit for review
manager's wait-and-fix idea, screenshots ready -> red herrings

concept.title: Cancel review to edit a version
concept.line: An In Review, Approved or Rejected version must be cancelled back to Draft to edit, then resubmitted for review.

topic: Reducing calls per envelope under the hourly limit
stem: Every weekday at 09:00, Brightmoor Lettings' tenancy system sends about 2,000 renewal agreements to tenants within one hour. The integration builds each agreement in five steps: create a draft, upload the document, add the tenant, add the signature fields, then change the status to sent. Since go-live the run stops partway through with hourly-limit errors, and a separate accounting app on the same Docusign account also starts failing during that hour. The account's plan does not include hourly limit management, and the office manager notes that most tenants sign on their phones. What change best fixes the problem?

options.text: Have an account administrator use Update Hourly Limit in the API Usage Center before tomorrow, so the five-step pattern fits within the hour
Move the renewal run to a new integration key of its own, so it receives a separate hourly allowance and stops affecting the accounting app
Build each agreement in one Envelopes:create request carrying document, recipient, tabs and status sent, and pace the run using the X-RateLimit headers
Send all 2,000 create requests in parallel at the start of the hour, so the run finishes before the accounting app becomes busy

answerText: Build each agreement in one Envelopes:create request carrying document, recipient, tabs and status sent, and pace the run using the X-RateLimit headers
explanation: Five calls per agreement means about 10,000 calls against a default account limit of 3,000 per hour that 'a separate accounting app on the same Docusign account' also uses; one create-and-send call per envelope plus header-based pacing fixes the cause.
whyNotOthers: C is right because it cuts the run to about 2,000 calls and watches the remaining allowance. The trap is A: Update Hourly Limit in the API Usage Center exists, but it requires a plan that includes limit management (this one does not) and efficient apps, so the call pattern must be fixed instead. B fails because the hourly limit applies per account, shared by all keys. D fails because firing everything at once breaks the 500-calls-per-30-seconds burst limit.

optionExplanations.A: Update Hourly Limit is offered only when the plan includes limit management and the apps are efficient; this plan lacks it, and the five-call pattern would still be inefficient.
optionExplanations.B: The hourly limit belongs to the account and is shared by every integration key, so a new key adds no allowance.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. One create request with status sent cuts calls fivefold, and the X-RateLimit headers let the run slow down before it is blocked.
optionExplanations.D: Parallel sending breaks the production burst limit of 500 calls per 30 seconds and still uses the same hourly allowance.

decode.needs: Reduce calls per envelope and respect the shared per-account hourly limit.
clues: five steps per agreement x 2,000 -> about 10,000 calls against a 3,000/hour default
separate accounting app on the same account also fails -> the limit is shared per account
plan does not include hourly limit management -> no self-service limit increase
tenants sign on their phones -> red herring

concept.title: Fewer calls per envelope
concept.line: Create and send an envelope in one request (aim for five calls or fewer), pace with X-RateLimit headers; the hourly limit is shared per account.

stem: Ridgeway Manufacturing's internal procurement bot uses JWT Grant to send purchase agreements as procurement lead Dana, whose address is in Ridgeway's claimed domain; an organization administrator originally granted consent for the bot in Docusign Admin. Dana is moving to a new role, and the compliance team wants the bot's ability to act as her withdrawn. Dana opened Manage Profile > Connected Apps herself but could not revoke the app. The bot runs every 30 minutes on a Linux VM. What should happen?

options.text: Dana asks the eSignature account administrator to remove the app in Apps and Keys, which immediately invalidates every access token already issued for her
An organization administrator revokes the consent in Docusign Admin; no new tokens are issued, but a token already issued works until its one-hour expiry
An organization administrator revokes the consent in Docusign Admin, which immediately invalidates the access token the bot holds and blocks any new tokens
Dana retries in Manage Profile > Connected Apps after the bot's current token expires, because individual revocation is blocked only while a token is live
The team rotates the RSA key pair in Apps and Keys, because consent that an administrator granted can only be withdrawn by invalidating the signing key

answerText: An organization administrator revokes the consent in Docusign Admin; no new tokens are issued, but a token already issued works until its one-hour expiry
explanation: Consent granted by an administrator for reserved-domain users is revoked in Docusign Admin ("could not revoke" herself), and revoking stops new tokens while live access tokens, including JWT ones (1 hour), stay valid until they expire.
whyNotOthers: B is right because admin-granted consent is revoked by an organization administrator in Docusign Admin, and live tokens expire naturally. The trap is C: the right person and place, but revocation does not kill tokens already issued. A is the wrong place and wrong effect, D fails because reserved-domain users can never revoke admin-granted consent themselves, and E would break the bot for every user and is not how consent is withdrawn.

optionExplanations.A: Apps and Keys is not where consent is revoked, and revocation never kills tokens already issued.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. Admin-granted consent is revoked in Docusign Admin; live tokens run until they expire (JWT: 1 hour).
optionExplanations.C: Revocation blocks new tokens and refresh tokens, but live access tokens keep working until they expire.
optionExplanations.D: Reserved-domain users cannot revoke admin-granted consent individually at any time.
optionExplanations.E: Rotating the key stops the bot for every user and is not the consent revocation mechanism.

decode.needs: Org admin revokes consent in Docusign Admin; existing JWT token lives until its 1-hour expiry.
clues: claimed domain, organization administrator granted consent -> admin consent
could not revoke herself -> reserved-domain users cannot revoke admin consent
withdrawn -> revocation blocks new tokens only
Linux VM every 30 minutes -> red herring

concept.title: Revoking admin-granted consent
concept.line: Admin-granted consent is revoked in Docusign Admin; new tokens stop, but live access tokens work until they expire.

topic: Choosing a flow for lobby tablets
stem: Lakeshore Credit Union is putting tablets in every branch lobby so walk-in members can sign account-opening agreements on the spot. Members have no Docusign accounts, and branch staff must never sign in to Docusign on the tablets; every agreement must be sent under the credit union's shared new-accounts sender. The tablets talk to a back-end service the credit union hosts in its own data center. Branch managers want the rollout finished before the spring savings campaign. The tablets are iPads managed through Intune. How should the integration authenticate to Docusign?

options.text: Public Authorization Code Grant with PKCE on each tablet, with branch staff signing in once a day as the new-accounts sender so nothing secret sits on the device
JWT Grant on each tablet, with the RSA private key bundled in the managed app so every device can mint tokens for the new-accounts sender directly
JWT Grant on the hosted back-end service, impersonating the new-accounts sender after one-time consent, with the tablets calling that service instead of Docusign
Confidential Authorization Code Grant on the hosted back-end service, with each member signing in through the Docusign login page before the agreement appears
Implicit Grant on each tablet, so the token arrives straight in the browser and no secret or private key ever needs to be stored on the device

answerText: JWT Grant on the hosted back-end service, impersonating the new-accounts sender after one-time consent, with the tablets calling that service instead of Docusign
explanation: No one signs in ("staff must never sign in", members have no accounts) and everything is sent as one shared sender, so the back end uses JWT Grant to impersonate that sender; the private key stays on the server the credit union hosts.
whyNotOthers: C is right because JWT Grant is the flow for acting as a consenting user who is not present, and its private key must live on a secure server. The trap is B: JWT is the right flow, but shipping the RSA private key inside an app on lobby devices exposes it. A fails because staff must not sign in. D fails because members have no Docusign accounts. E fails because Implicit is legacy and still needs a user to sign in.

optionExplanations.A: Requires a person to sign in to Docusign on the tablet, which the stem forbids.
optionExplanations.B: Right flow, wrong place: the RSA private key must be kept on a secure server, not bundled in a device app.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. A hosted service with JWT Grant impersonates the shared sender with no interactive sign-in.
optionExplanations.D: Members have no Docusign accounts, so they cannot sign in to an Auth Code flow.
optionExplanations.E: Implicit Grant is legacy and still needs an interactive Docusign sign-in.

decode.needs: JWT Grant on a secure server, impersonating one sender user.
clues: staff must never sign in -> no Authorization Code flow
shared new-accounts sender -> impersonate one user
back-end service in its own data center -> where the private key belongs
iPads managed through Intune -> red herring

concept.title: No sign-in means server-side JWT
concept.line: When nobody can sign in, a secure back end uses JWT Grant to impersonate a consenting sender; keep the private key off devices.

stem: Halvorsen Group runs a contract portal used by staff in three subsidiaries. Each subsidiary has its own production Docusign account: one is hosted in North America, one in the EU and one in Australia. The portal uses Authorization Code Grant, and its integration key has just gone Live, managed from the parent company's production account. During development the team put https://demo.docusign.net/restapi into a configuration file. The architect wants each user's envelopes to go to the right subsidiary account without per-subsidiary code or extra keys. The portal's front end is being redesigned at the same time. How should the portal determine the API base path in production?

options.text: Copy the Account Base URI shown on the parent company's Apps and Keys page into the configuration file, because that account manages the promoted key
Create a separate integration key for each subsidiary and store each one with that subsidiary's base URI, so each request goes to its own data center
Have each subsidiary's administrator grant admin consent to the portal, because the consent response tells the portal which data center the account uses
After each user first signs in, call /oauth/userinfo, take the base_uri of the account to use, and cache it for that user's later API calls

answerText: After each user first signs in, call /oauth/userinfo, take the base_uri of the account to use, and cache it for that user's later API calls
explanation: The base path depends on the account's data center, so the portal should read base_uri from /oauth/userinfo after the user first authenticates and cache it; this works for 'three subsidiaries' in different regions with one key.
whyNotOthers: D is right because userinfo returns the account_id and base_uri of each account the user can reach, whatever the data center. The trap is A: the Account Base URI on Apps and Keys is correct only for the parent's own account, and a promoted key can call any account, so the EU and Australian users would hit the wrong host. B adds keys the architect ruled out and is unnecessary. C fails because consent grants permission but does not return the base URI.

optionExplanations.A: The Apps and Keys Account Base URI belongs to the managing account only; the subsidiaries in other data centers have different base URIs.
optionExplanations.B: Unneeded: one promoted key can call any production account, and the stem rules out extra keys.
optionExplanations.C: Consent authorizes the app but does not supply the account's base URI.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. userinfo returns base_uri per account; call it once after first authentication and cache it.

decode.needs: Use /oauth/userinfo base_uri per user and account instead of a hard-coded base path.
clues: three subsidiaries in North America, EU and Australia -> different data centers, different base URIs
managed from the parent company's account -> management account, not the only account the key can call
no per-subsidiary code or extra keys -> one key, base path discovered at runtime
front end being redesigned -> red herring

concept.title: Discover base URI from userinfo
concept.line: In production, read base_uri for the user's account from /oauth/userinfo once after first login and cache it; never hard-code one data center.

stem: Harborview Credit Union is adding a 'Change my beneficiaries' journey to the web view inside its mobile banking app. The app's backend already holds an access token with the aow_manage scope and knows the member's name, email and account number, which must reach the workflow as starting values so the member never retypes them. The workflow has a web form, a phone authentication check and a signing step. The product owner insists that when the member finishes, they are still inside the banking app so it can show its own 'What happens next' page. Which two design decisions fit? (Select two)

options.text: Set the start method to From a Link and append the member's details to the link, because links are the recommended start method whenever values are prefilled
Set the start method to From an API call, because the backend passes the member's details as starting variables in trigger_inputs on Workflows:triggerWorkflow
Redirect the member's browser to the instance_url from the trigger response, so they complete the steps on Docusign and come back to the app when finished
Create a recipient view with EnvelopeViews:createRecipient for the workflow and display it in focused view, so the member stays inside the banking app
Load the instance_url from the trigger response in an iframe inside the app's page, so the app stays visible and can route the member onward when finished

answerText: Set the start method to From an API call, because the backend passes the member's details as starting variables in trigger_inputs on Workflows:triggerWorkflow; Load the instance_url from the trigger response in an iframe inside the app's page, so the app stays visible and can route the member onward when finished
explanation: Docusign recommends From an API call when the trigger request passes starting variables in trigger_inputs, and embedding the instance_url in an iframe keeps the app around the workflow so it can route the member afterwards ('still inside the banking app').
whyNotOthers: B and E are right. The trap is C: redirecting to instance_url does run the workflow, but the member remains on the Docusign platform after completing it and is not returned to the app. A fails because From an API call, not From a Link, is recommended when trigger_inputs carry starting values, and D fails because workflows are embedded through instance_url, and focused view is not supported for signing steps in embedded workflows.

optionExplanations.A: Docusign recommends From an API call, not From a Link, when the integration passes starting variable values in trigger_inputs.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. The backend triggers the workflow and supplies starting variables in trigger_inputs, which is the recommended start method for this case.
optionExplanations.C: With a redirect, the member stays on the Docusign platform after finishing instead of returning to the app.
optionExplanations.D: A workflow instance is displayed through its instance_url, not an eSignature recipient view, and focused view is not supported for signing in embedded workflows.
optionExplanations.E: Correct. An iframe keeps the app's UI visible, and when the workflow ends the app can send the member to its own next page.

decode.needs: Trigger via API with trigger_inputs, then embed the returned instance_url in an iframe.
clues: backend holds aow_manage token and passes member details -> From an API call with trigger_inputs
still inside the banking app when finished -> iframe, not redirect
phone authentication check -> red herring, the one IDV method supported when embedded

concept.title: Embed instance_url in an iframe
concept.line: Pass starting values through trigger_inputs (From an API call) and show instance_url in an iframe; a redirect leaves the user on Docusign.

stem: A log shows POST https://demo.docusign.net/restapi/v2.1/accounts/{accountId}/envelopes/{envelopeId}/views/recipient. What did the integration request?

options.text: A URL that lets a sender tag and send a draft envelope
The list of recipients and their current status
A URL for an embedded signer's signing session
A new recipient added to the sent envelope

answerText: A URL for an embedded signer's signing session
explanation: POST .../envelopes/{envelopeId}/views/recipient is EnvelopeViews:createRecipient, which returns the embedded signing (recipient view) URL. The demo host shows the developer environment.
whyNotOthers: C is right because /views/recipient creates the recipient view. The trap is A: the sender view is also under /views, but its path ends in /views/sender. B is a GET on /recipients, and D is a POST on /recipients, not /views/recipient.

optionExplanations.A: The sender view path ends in /views/sender.
optionExplanations.B: Listing recipients is GET .../envelopes/{envelopeId}/recipients.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. /views/recipient is EnvelopeViews:createRecipient, the embedded signing URL.
optionExplanations.D: Adding a recipient is POST .../envelopes/{envelopeId}/recipients.

concept.title: Decode the request path
concept.line: Base URI, /restapi/v2.1/accounts/{accountId}, then resource path; /views/recipient is embedded signing, /views/sender is embedded sending.

stem: A wealth management firm's onboarding service sent an account-opening envelope an hour ago. The first signer, the client, has not received it because the advisor mistyped the client's email address; the second signer, the advisor's manager, is later in routing order. Compliance wants the original envelope and its audit trail kept, and the client must receive the invitation at the corrected address now. What should the service do?

options.text: Void the envelope with a voidedReason and create a new one with the corrected address, because a sent envelope's recipients can no longer be changed
Call EnvelopeRecipients:update with the corrected email for that recipient and set the resend_envelope query parameter to true
Call EnvelopeRecipients:update with only the corrected email for that recipient, relying on Docusign to notify the client at the new address
Call Envelopes:update with status sent and the corrected email in the body, so that the same envelope is reissued to the client

answerText: Call EnvelopeRecipients:update with the corrected email for that recipient and set the resend_envelope query parameter to true
explanation: A recipient's email can be corrected on a sent envelope with EnvelopeRecipients:update. Because the client is the current recipient, the envelope is not resent by default, so resend_envelope=true forces the new notification. The clue is 'keep the original envelope' and 'must receive the invitation now'.
whyNotOthers: B is right because it corrects in place and forces the resend. The trap is C: the update succeeds, but for a recipient at or before the envelope's current routing order the envelope is not resent unless resend_envelope is true, so the client would not be notified. A throws away the original envelope and audit trail, and D uses the wrong endpoint; Envelopes:update does not change recipient addresses.

optionExplanations.A: Voiding discards the original envelope, which compliance wants to keep; recipient email can be corrected after sending.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. Update the email and force the resend with resend_envelope=true.
optionExplanations.C: The address is corrected, but a recipient at the current routing order is not re-notified unless resend_envelope=true is set.
optionExplanations.D: Recipient details are changed through EnvelopeRecipients:update, not by re-sending the envelope status.

decode.needs: EnvelopeRecipients:update with resend_envelope=true
clues: mistyped email on a sent envelope -> correct the recipient in place
keep the original envelope and audit trail -> do not void and recreate
must receive the invitation now -> force a resend

concept.title: Correct and resend a recipient
concept.line: Fix a sent envelope's recipient with EnvelopeRecipients:update; add resend_envelope=true to force a new notification.

stem: A developer at Tessaro Insurance creates an account-level configuration with POST /v2.1/accounts/{accountId}/connect. The body sets configurationType to custom, allUsers to true, deliveryMode to SIM, eventData.version to restv2.1, enableLog to true, and an events array with lowercase names such as envelope-completed. The call succeeds and returns a connectId, and the listener URL answers test posts from the team's own tools. Yet after several claims envelopes are completed, nothing reaches the listener and the Connect log shows no delivery attempts at all. What is the most likely cause?

options.text: The events values must be written in sentence case, such as Envelope-completed, before the configuration will fire
The body did not set allowEnvelopePublish to true, so the configuration was created in a disabled state
The body did not set requiresAcknowledgement, so the failed deliveries are hidden from the Connect log
allUsers must be false with a userIds list of senders for an account-level configuration to fire

answerText: The body did not set allowEnvelopePublish to true, so the configuration was created in a disabled state
explanation: The create endpoint makes a disabled configuration by default; allowEnvelopePublish must be true (or the configuration enabled in the UI). The clue is "no delivery attempts at all" despite a successful create.
whyNotOthers: B is right because a configuration created without allowEnvelopePublish=true does not publish anything. The trap is A: sentence case is required only for the legacy envelopeEvents and recipientEvents properties; the JSON SIM events array uses lowercase names. C fails because missing acknowledgement settings would not stop delivery attempts; D fails because allUsers=true is a valid way to cover every user.

optionExplanations.A: Sentence case applies to envelopeEvents and recipientEvents (legacy models); JSON SIM's events array uses lowercase values like envelope-completed.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. By default the endpoint creates a disabled configuration; set allowEnvelopePublish to true or enable it in the UI.
optionExplanations.C: requiresAcknowledgement affects retries and error data, but the configuration would still attempt deliveries and log them.
optionExplanations.D: Either allUsers=true or a non-empty userIds array is valid; allUsers=true already covers every sender.

decode.needs: Recognize that ConnectConfigurations:create makes a disabled configuration by default.
clues: call succeeds and returns a connectId -> the request body was valid
no delivery attempts at all -> the configuration is not publishing
lowercase names in the events array -> correct for JSON SIM, a distractor

concept.title: New configurations start disabled
concept.line: A configuration created through the API is disabled unless allowEnvelopePublish is true; check this first when nothing is sent.

stem: Which list contains only operations that exist in the Agreement Manager (Navigator) API?

options.text: GetAgreementsList, GetAgreement, UpdateAgreement, DeleteAgreement
GetAgreementsList, GetAgreement, getAgreementSummary, DeleteAgreement
GetAgreementsList, GetAgreement, DeleteAgreement, CreateAgreementSummary
GetAgreementsList, CreateAgreement, DeleteAgreement, CreateAgreementSummary

answerText: GetAgreementsList, GetAgreement, DeleteAgreement, CreateAgreementSummary
explanation: The API has exactly four agreement operations: GetAgreementsList, GetAgreement, DeleteAgreement and CreateAgreementSummary (POST .../agreements/{agreementId}/ai/actions/summarize).
whyNotOthers: C is right because it lists the four real operations. The trap is B: there is no getAgreementSummary; the summary is produced by the POST CreateAgreementSummary. A invents UpdateAgreement (extracted values are corrected in the UI), and D invents CreateAgreement.

optionExplanations.A: There is no UpdateAgreement; corrections to extracted values are made in the Agreement Manager UI.
optionExplanations.B: There is no getAgreementSummary; the AI summary is requested with the POST CreateAgreementSummary.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. These are the four agreement operations of the API.
optionExplanations.D: There is no CreateAgreement operation in the API.

concept.title: Four Agreement Manager operations
concept.line: The Agreement Manager API offers GetAgreementsList, GetAgreement, DeleteAgreement and CreateAgreementSummary, and nothing that updates agreements.

topic: Confidential Auth Code with optional PKCE
stem: Marrow County Health is building an HR onboarding site that runs on servers in its own locked-down data center, where credentials are kept in a secrets vault. Each HR coordinator signs in with their own Docusign login so offer letters go out under their own name. The security architect wants extra proof that the app completing each sign-in is the same app that started it, and coordinators should not have to sign in again more often than about once a month. The site is written in .NET 8 behind a web application firewall. Which approach fits best?

options.text: Public Authorization Code Grant with PKCE, because the code challenge gives the requested proof and no secret has to be kept anywhere in the solution
Confidential Authorization Code Grant plus the optional PKCE code challenge, keeping the secret in the vault so refresh tokens last up to 30 days
JWT Grant impersonating each coordinator, with the RSA private key held in the vault so that no coordinator ever needs to sign in again
Confidential Authorization Code Grant without PKCE, relying on the state parameter to prove the app finishing the sign-in is the one that started it
Implicit Grant with a short-lived token, because the server can silently repeat the sign-in whenever a coordinator's token expires

answerText: Confidential Authorization Code Grant plus the optional PKCE code challenge, keeping the secret in the vault so refresh tokens last up to 30 days
explanation: A server that can "keep credentials in a secrets vault" and users who sign in personally means Confidential Auth Code Grant, and Docusign lets it optionally add a PKCE challenge, which is exactly the proof that "the app completing each sign-in is the same app that started it".
whyNotOthers: B is right because Confidential Auth Code Grant supports an optional PKCE challenge and gives refresh tokens of up to 30 days. The trap is A: PKCE gives the proof, but Public Auth Code refresh tokens last only 24 hours, so coordinators would re-sign in daily, and a server that can store a secret should use the confidential flow. D fails because state defends against CSRF, not same-app proof. C and E fail because JWT means acting for absent users and Implicit is a legacy browser flow.

optionExplanations.A: Public refresh tokens last only 24 hours, breaking the once-a-month requirement; Public is for apps that cannot store a secret.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. Confidential Auth Code Grant can optionally use PKCE and its refresh tokens last up to 30 days.
optionExplanations.C: JWT is for service integrations that act for absent users; here each coordinator is present and signs in.
optionExplanations.D: state is a random value that prevents CSRF; proving the same app finished the flow is what PKCE does.
optionExplanations.E: Implicit Grant is legacy, issues no refresh token, and cannot silently re-run a sign-in.

decode.needs: Confidential Authorization Code Grant with the optional PKCE code challenge.
clues: servers in its own data center, secrets vault -> can store a client secret
own Docusign login -> user-present Authorization Code Grant
same app that started it -> PKCE
not more often than once a month -> 30-day refresh token, not 24-hour Public

concept.title: PKCE is optional for Confidential
concept.line: Confidential Auth Code Grant may add a PKCE challenge for extra security while keeping its 30-day refresh tokens.

stem: Glenmoor Foods runs its order system on servers inside the head-office data center. The business wants a supplier contract to trigger order setup as soon as it is fully signed, but the network team will not open any inbound port or add any allowlist rule on the corporate firewall; outbound HTTPS from the data center is permitted. The company already uses AWS for its online store, and the CFO notes that contract volumes double each December. Connect is available on the account. Which design meets the requirement?

options.text: Poll Envelopes:listStatusChanges from the data center every 15 minutes, because outbound calls need no firewall change and stay within the polling rule
Expose the order system's listener through the corporate firewall and secure it with mutual TLS, so that only Docusign's certificate is let through
Add an eventNotification object with the order system's internal URL to each envelope, so the messages travel to the data center over the private network
Host a small serverless listener in AWS that writes each Connect message to a cloud queue, and let an internal worker pull the queue over outbound HTTPS

answerText: Host a small serverless listener in AWS that writes each Connect message to a cloud queue, and let an internal worker pull the queue over outbound HTTPS
explanation: A cloud listener plus a cloud queue lets the on-premises worker receive messages through an outbound connection, so "no inbound port or allowlist rule" is respected while events still arrive "as soon as" the contract is signed.
whyNotOthers: D is right because Docusign recommends a PaaS listener and queue so workers behind the firewall pull messages outbound with no firewall changes. The trap is B: mutual TLS authenticates Docusign, but it still requires opening the firewall to inbound traffic, which the network team forbids. A is polling and adds up to 15 minutes of delay; C fails because a Connect listener must be reachable on the public internet.

optionExplanations.A: Polling avoids the firewall but delays order setup by up to 15 minutes per envelope, so it is not 'as soon as fully signed', and Connect is preferred over polling.
optionExplanations.B: Mutual TLS controls who may connect, but the listener would still need an inbound opening in the firewall, which is refused.
optionExplanations.C: Connect always posts to a URL on the public internet; an internal URL cannot be reached, whatever the configuration level.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. A cloud listener and queue accept Docusign's posts, and the internal worker reads the queue over outbound HTTPS, so no firewall change is needed.

decode.needs: A public Connect listener without any inbound firewall change.
clues: no inbound port or allowlist rule -> listener cannot live inside the data center
outbound HTTPS permitted -> worker can pull from a cloud queue
volumes double in December -> red herring (a queue also absorbs peaks)

concept.title: Cloud queue for firewalled listeners
concept.line: When inbound traffic is blocked, host the listener and a queue in the cloud and let internal workers pull messages outbound.

stem: Harborview Food Bank renews about 900 annual pledge agreements every January. A headless nightly job reads the donor roster from the CRM, and every donor must receive their own agreement to sign. The compliance team wants a dry run that proves the roster lines up with the agreement's signer roles before anything is released, and the fundraising director wants the emails to use the organization's purple branding. Which sequence of eSignature API calls should the job use?

options.text: Create the bulk send list, create the envelope with status sent so its roles are fixed, run createBulkSendTestRequest, then call createBulkSendRequest and keep the batchId
Create the bulk send list, create the envelope as a draft with status created, run createBulkSendTestRequest and check canBeSent, then call createBulkSendRequest
Create the envelope as a draft with status created, call createBulkSendRequest with the roster inline, then run createBulkSendTestRequest on the returned batchId
Create the bulk send list, run createBulkSendTestRequest against the list on its own, then call Envelopes:create with status sent and the listId to release it

answerText: Create the bulk send list, create the envelope as a draft with status created, run createBulkSendTestRequest and check canBeSent, then call createBulkSendRequest
explanation: The v2.1 bulk flow is: create the list, create a draft envelope (status created), optionally test it against the list (canBeSent true), then send the batch. The clue 'dry run that proves the roster lines up with the signer roles' is the optional test step.
whyNotOthers: B is right because the envelope used for bulk send must be a draft and the test is run before the send. The trap is A: the order looks right, but an envelope created with status sent goes to its own placeholder recipients and is not the sendable draft the bulk send needs. C runs the test after the batch is already released and puts the roster in the wrong call; D tests without an envelope and releases the batch through the wrong method.

optionExplanations.A: Status sent sends the envelope itself immediately; bulk send needs a draft (created) envelope or a template.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. List, draft envelope, optional test returning canBeSent, then createBulkSendRequest, which returns the batchId.
optionExplanations.C: The roster belongs in the bulk send list, and testing after the send cannot stop a bad batch.
optionExplanations.D: The test checks a list against an envelope or template, and the batch is released with createBulkSendRequest, not Envelopes:create.

decode.needs: Bulk send v2.1: list, draft envelope, test, send
clues: headless nightly job, own agreement per donor -> bulk send, one envelope per copy
dry run that proves the roster lines up -> createBulkSendTestRequest returning canBeSent
purple branding -> red herring

concept.title: Bulk send v2.1 call order
concept.line: Create list, create draft envelope (status created), optionally test for canBeSent, send the batch, optionally check batch status.

stem: Which /oauth/auth query parameter should carry a random value that the app checks on the redirect to defend against cross-site request forgery?

options.text: state
code_challenge
login_hint
client_id
code_challenge_method

answerText: state
explanation: Docusign says to include a state parameter with a random string to prevent CSRF attacks; the app checks the same value comes back on the redirect.
whyNotOthers: A is right because state exists for CSRF protection. The trap is B: code_challenge is also a random-derived value on the same request, but it proves that the app exchanging the code is the one that started the flow (PKCE). C pre-fills the email, D identifies the app, and E is always S256.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. A random state value, checked on the redirect, prevents CSRF.
optionExplanations.B: PKCE value: proves the app finishing the flow started it; it is not the CSRF defence.
optionExplanations.C: Pre-fills the user's email on the login page.
optionExplanations.D: The integration key that identifies the application.
optionExplanations.E: Names the hashing method for the PKCE challenge (always S256).

concept.title: state prevents CSRF
concept.line: Send a random state value on /oauth/auth and verify it on the redirect; PKCE serves a different purpose.

stem: When a private extension app becomes Live, with up to how many production accounts can the developer share it?
explanation: For a private extension app, the developer provides a list of up to 20 production accounts to share the live app with.
whyNotOthers: C is right: private sharing is capped at 20 production accounts. The trap is B, a common guess for a small allow-list; A and D are not documented limits either.

optionExplanations.A: Not the documented limit; private apps can be shared with more accounts than this.
optionExplanations.B: Plausible but wrong; the documented limit is higher.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. A private app can be shared with up to 20 production accounts.
optionExplanations.D: Exceeds the documented limit for private sharing.

concept.title: Private apps: up to 20 accounts
concept.line: A Live private extension app is shared with a list of up to 20 production accounts, each approved by its admin.

topic: ID verification in the envelope request
stem: Brightwater Lending's loan-origination system creates closing envelopes with eSignature REST API v2.1. Regulators require that the primary borrower prove their identity with a government-issued photo ID before opening the documents; the co-borrower only needs the normal email link. The account admin has already created and activated an ID Verification configuration in eSignature Settings, and the integration uses JWT with the signature and impersonation scopes. Which two steps must the developer add to the envelope request flow? (Select two)

options.text: Set idCheckConfigurationName to 'ID Check $' on the primary borrower so Docusign checks the borrower's identity before access.
Add identityVerification with the workflowId to both borrowers, because the setting applies to every signer in the envelope.
Call IdentityVerifications:list (GET .../accounts/{accountId}/identity_verification) to look up the configuration's workflowId.
Set authenticationMethod to the ID verification method on the primary borrower so the certificate shows that photo ID was required.
Add an identityVerification object with that workflowId to the primary borrower's signer object in the Envelopes:create request.

answerText: Call IdentityVerifications:list (GET .../accounts/{accountId}/identity_verification) to look up the configuration's workflowId.; Add an identityVerification object with that workflowId to the primary borrower's signer object in the Envelopes:create request.
explanation: IDV is required per recipient by adding identityVerification.workflowId to that signer, and the workflowId comes from IdentityVerifications:list. The clue 'only the primary borrower' means only that signer gets it.
whyNotOthers: C and E are right: look up the workflowId, then put it on the borrower's signer object. The trap is D: authenticationMethod only records an authentication your own app performed on the certificate; it enforces nothing. A is knowledge-based authentication (public-record questions), not photo ID, and B ignores that the co-borrower needs only the email link; workflow IDs are set per recipient.

optionExplanations.A: 'ID Check $' is knowledge-based authentication with public-record questions, not a government photo ID check.
optionExplanations.B: identityVerification is a recipient-level setting; the co-borrower must not get it.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. IdentityVerifications:list returns the account's workflow IDs, including the IDV configuration.
optionExplanations.D: authenticationMethod only records your app's own authentication on the certificate; Docusign does not enforce it.
optionExplanations.E: Correct. identityVerification.workflowId on the signer makes Docusign require that verification before access.

decode.needs: Look up the IDV workflowId and set identityVerification.workflowId on that one signer.
clues: 'government-issued photo ID' -> ID Verification, not KBA
'only the primary borrower' -> recipient-level setting
'admin already created the configuration' -> it has a workflowId to look up

concept.title: IDV via workflowId
concept.line: Require IDV or phone auth per recipient with identityVerification.workflowId, found through IdentityVerifications:list; authenticationMethod only records.

stem: Brightline Staffing's recruiting app builds each offer packet on the server, then lets the recruiter open Docusign inside the app to drag fields and press Send. Nothing may reach the candidate until the recruiter presses Send. The server calls Envelopes:create with status sent and then EnvelopeViews:createSender, which returns 400 with errorCode ENVELOPE_INVALID_STATUS. The recruiters work across three time zones. What should the developer change?

options.text: Lock the envelope with EnvelopeLocks:create before calling createSender, so that the sender view is allowed to edit the envelope that has already been sent
Keep status sent and call EnvelopeViews:createCorrect instead, because the correct view opens the same tagging screen for envelopes that are already in flight
Add a clientUserId to the recruiter as a sender recipient, so that Docusign treats the sender view as embedded and accepts the envelope that was sent
Create the envelope with status created and then call createSender, so the recruiter places the fields and sends it from the embedded sender view

answerText: Create the envelope with status created and then call createSender, so the recruiter places the fields and sends it from the embedded sender view
explanation: The sender view can be created only for an envelope in the created (draft) state; otherwise the call returns ENVELOPE_INVALID_STATUS. The clue 'nothing may reach the candidate until the recruiter presses Send' also rules out sending at creation.
whyNotOthers: D is right because embedded sending starts from a draft that the user tags and sends. The trap is B: the correct view does work on sent envelopes, but the envelope would already have reached the candidate, breaking the requirement. A misunderstands locking, which holds an in-flight envelope for edits but does not make a sent envelope a draft, and C misuses clientUserId, which belongs to embedded recipients.

optionExplanations.A: A lock does not turn a sent envelope back into a draft; the sender view still refuses it.
optionExplanations.B: The correct view needs a sent envelope, so the candidate would already have been notified.
optionExplanations.C: clientUserId marks embedded recipients; it does not change which envelope status the sender view accepts.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. createSender requires status created; the recruiter tags and sends from the view.

decode.needs: Embedded sending on a draft envelope
clues: drag fields and press Send inside the app -> embedded sending with createSender
nothing may reach the candidate until Send -> envelope status created
three time zones -> red herring

concept.title: Sender view needs a draft
concept.line: EnvelopeViews:createSender works only on envelopes in created status; otherwise it returns ENVELOPE_INVALID_STATUS.

stem: Tessera Analytics, a small software vendor that has never joined the Docusign partner program, has built an address-cleansing extension app with a team of three developers. Its business goal is for any Docusign customer in the United States to discover the app while browsing the App Center and install it without contacting Tessera first. The app passes its connection, extension and functional tests in Tessera's developer account. The product owner wants the route that reaches that goal without having to re-register the app later. Which approach fits best?

options.text: Register the app with PUBLIC distribution and submit it for review; Docusign onboards Tessera into the partner program as part of that submission
Register the app with PRIVATE distribution now, then switch the distribution to PUBLIC after the first live release, once partner onboarding has been completed
Register the app with PRIVATE distribution and share the live app with each customer's production account as that customer asks to use it
Give each customer the app manifest so their administrator can register a copy in the Developer Console and install it in their own account

answerText: Register the app with PUBLIC distribution and submit it for review; Docusign onboards Tessera into the partner program as part of that submission
explanation: Publishing a public app requires being a Docusign partner, and if you are not yet a partner Docusign works with you on partner program onboarding when you submit the app for review. 'Any customer can discover it in the App Center' means PUBLIC distribution.
whyNotOthers: A is right because public distribution is what makes the app discoverable by every customer, and partner onboarding happens with the review submission. The trap is B: the distribution type cannot be changed once the app is Live, so this would force a new registration. C requires manual sharing (up to 20 production accounts, each admin approving) and gives no browsing discovery, and D is not how customers obtain apps; they install them from the App Center.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. Public distribution gives App Center discovery to all customers, and Docusign handles partner onboarding when a non-partner submits for review.
optionExplanations.B: Distribution cannot be modified once the app is Live, so switching later would mean registering a new app.
optionExplanations.C: Private apps are shared with a limited list of production accounts whose admins must approve them; customers cannot discover them by browsing.
optionExplanations.D: Customers install apps from the App Center; handing out a manifest to re-register is not the distribution model.

decode.needs: PUBLIC distribution, with partner onboarding at review submission
clues: any customer can discover and install it -> PUBLIC distribution
never joined the partner program -> onboarding happens at review submission
without re-registering later -> distribution cannot change once Live
three developers -> red herring

concept.title: Public apps need the partner program
concept.line: Public App Center listing requires Docusign partnership; non-partners are onboarded when they submit for review, and distribution is fixed once Live.

stem: A native desktop app uses Public Authorization Code Grant with PKCE. At most, how long is the refresh token it receives valid?

options.text: 8 hours
1 hour
30 days
24 hours
120 seconds

answerText: 24 hours
explanation: Docusign states the refresh token is valid for up to 30 days for Confidential Auth Code Grant and 24 hours for Public Auth Code Grant.
whyNotOthers: D is right because Public Auth Code refresh tokens last 24 hours. The trap is C: 30 days is the Confidential lifetime. A is the access token lifetime in Auth Code Grant, B is the JWT access token lifetime, and E is the authorization code lifetime.

optionExplanations.A: 8 hours is the Auth Code access token lifetime.
optionExplanations.B: 1 hour is the JWT Grant access token lifetime.
optionExplanations.C: 30 days applies to Confidential Auth Code Grant refresh tokens.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. Public Auth Code Grant refresh tokens are valid for up to 24 hours.
optionExplanations.E: 120 seconds is how long the authorization code is valid.

concept.title: Public refresh tokens last 24 hours
concept.line: Refresh tokens last up to 30 days for Confidential and 24 hours for Public Auth Code Grant.

stem: Brookline Savings opens accounts on a tablet in the branch: the customer signs in person, and the branch app waits for the completion event before printing the welcome kit while the customer is still at the desk. Lately that wait has grown to tens of seconds. The account-level JSON SIM configuration subscribes to recipient-completed and envelope-completed and includes the envelope summary and all documents in every message, although the welcome kit needs only the envelope ID and status; the signed PDF is archived later by an overnight job. HMAC is enabled on the configuration. What change should the developer make?

options.text: Switch the configuration to aggregate delivery, so that recipient-completed and envelope-completed arrive together as one message to the branch app
Disable HMAC on this configuration, because computing the signature over such a large payload is what delays each message to the branch app
Turn off requiresAcknowledgement, so that slow deliveries are no longer retried and the branch app receives each completion message sooner
Stop including the envelope summary and documents, and let the overnight job download the signed PDF through the API when it runs

answerText: Stop including the envelope summary and documents, and let the overnight job download the signed PDF through the API when it runs
