explanation: Including the envelope summary and documents increases payload size and can delay delivery; Docusign advises against it where delivery speed is critical, such as in-person signing. The welcome kit "needs only the envelope ID and status".
whyNotOthers: D is right because a lean JSON SIM message arrives faster, and the archive job can fetch the PDF itself. The trap is A: combining events sounds efficient, but aggregate is a legacy mode that sends periodically and reflects status at send time, which does not speed things up. B fails because HMAC is not the source of the delay; C would remove retries and risk losing events without shrinking the payload.

optionExplanations.A: Aggregate mode is legacy and groups messages for periodic sending; it does not make the completion message reach the branch faster.
optionExplanations.B: HMAC adds a header computed over the body; the delay comes from the large payload itself, and dropping HMAC weakens security.
optionExplanations.C: Turning off acknowledgement only stops retries, so failed events can be lost; the large payload is unchanged.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. Smaller event-focused messages deliver faster; the overnight job can retrieve documents through the API.

decode.needs: Remove envelope summary and documents from the JSON SIM payload.
clues: tablet in the branch, customer still at the desk -> in-person, speed-critical
needs only the envelope ID and status -> no need for summary or documents
PDF archived later by an overnight job -> documents can be fetched via API
HMAC enabled -> red herring

concept.title: Keep speed-critical payloads lean
concept.line: Envelope summary and documents enlarge JSON SIM messages and slow delivery; omit them when speed matters and fetch data via API.

topic: Embedded and remote signers in one envelope
stem: Pinewood Auto Finance closes car loans at the dealership. The buyer signs on a tablet in the finance office as soon as the paperwork is ready, while the co-signer, usually a parent in another city, signs whenever convenient. The dealership portal has already logged the buyer in, and the finance manager does not want the buyer to receive any Docusign email. Both signers are in one envelope, buyer first, and the dealership uses a dark-blue theme. How should the developer define the signers?

options.text: Give only the buyer a clientUserId and request the buyer's signing URL at the tablet; leave the co-signer without one so Docusign emails the co-signer
Give both signers a clientUserId, then email the co-signer the URL returned by createRecipient so the portal controls every signing link from one place
Give only the co-signer a clientUserId so the remote signer is handled by the portal, and open the buyer's session at the tablet from the envelope's sender view
Leave both signers without a clientUserId and let the buyer open the Docusign email on the tablet, because one envelope cannot mix embedded and remote signers

answerText: Give only the buyer a clientUserId and request the buyer's signing URL at the tablet; leave the co-signer without one so Docusign emails the co-signer
explanation: clientUserId marks a signer as embedded (no Docusign email; your app requests the signing URL), and signers without it are remote and receive email. The clue 'buyer on the tablet, co-signer whenever convenient' means mixed recipients in one envelope.
whyNotOthers: A is right because embedded and remote signers can coexist, and only the embedded one gets a clientUserId. The trap is B: it sounds centralised, but a recipient view URL is single-use and expires in minutes, so it cannot be emailed for later signing. C reverses the roles and uses the sender view, which is for preparing and sending, and D wrongly claims mixing is impossible and ignores the no-email requirement.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. Embedded buyer via clientUserId and createRecipient; remote co-signer notified by Docusign email.
optionExplanations.B: Recipient view URLs are short-lived and single-use, so emailing one for later signing fails.
optionExplanations.C: Roles are reversed, and the sender view does not create a signing session for a recipient.
optionExplanations.D: An envelope can mix embedded and remote signers, and the buyer would receive an email.

decode.needs: clientUserId only on the in-app signer; the other signer stays remote
clues: tablet in the finance office, already logged in -> embedded signer with clientUserId
signs whenever convenient in another city -> remote signer by email
dark-blue theme -> red herring

concept.title: Mixing embedded and remote signers
concept.line: Set clientUserId only on signers who sign inside your app; others stay remote and get Docusign email.

topic: Testing an app served from a laptop
stem: Kenji is prototyping a postal address verification app on his laptop before the hosting team provisions a server. The external provider's OAuth service is cloud hosted, so the connection test in the Developer Console succeeds, but every extension test fails because the endpoint cannot be reached. Each action's params.uri currently points at http://localhost:3000. His laptop runs Chrome with the corporate VPN switched off, and the provider's responses already match the Docusign action contract. What should Kenji do to keep testing locally?

options.text: Keep localhost in params.uri and run the extension tests from a browser on the same laptop, because the Developer Console sends the test requests from the browser
Expose the local service through a tunnel such as ngrok and put the public HTTPS tunnel URL in each action's params.uri, because Docusign's servers make the calls
Reinstall the app in his developer account after each change so that the updated params.uri values are picked up before he reruns the extension tests
Build an API proxy on the laptop that maps requests to the Docusign action contract, and point each action's params.uri at the proxy's localhost port

answerText: Expose the local service through a tunnel such as ngrok and put the public HTTPS tunnel URL in each action's params.uri, because Docusign's servers make the calls
explanation: Extension tests are executed from the Docusign platform directly to the external endpoints, so Docusign servers need a public URL. Docusign recommends a tunnel such as ngrok to expose a locally running app while developing.
whyNotOthers: B is right because a tunnel gives Docusign a public URL that reaches the laptop. The trap is A: extension tests are not sent from the browser but from the Docusign platform, so localhost is unreachable. C fails because registration updates are applied automatically to the installed app, and D is unnecessary because the responses already match the contract and a localhost proxy is still unreachable.

optionExplanations.A: Extension tests run from the Docusign platform to the endpoint, so localhost on Kenji's laptop is never reachable.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. A tunnel such as ngrok exposes the local app at a public URL that Docusign's servers can call.
optionExplanations.C: Updates to the registration are applied automatically to the installed version; reinstalling does not fix reachability.
optionExplanations.D: A proxy is needed only when the API does not match the action contract, and a localhost proxy is just as unreachable.

decode.needs: A public URL (tunnel) for the locally running endpoints
clues: connection test passes but extension tests cannot reach the endpoint -> endpoint not publicly reachable
before the hosting team provisions a server -> keep running locally, so tunnel
responses already match the contract -> no API proxy needed
Chrome, VPN off -> red herrings

concept.title: Docusign must reach a public endpoint
concept.line: Docusign servers call extension endpoints directly, so local development needs a public tunnel URL such as ngrok.

topic: Freeing workflow quota: pause vs unpublish
stem: Summit Tax Advisors runs a 'Year-end client organizer' workflow every January to April. In May the account has reached its workflow quota, and the operations lead needs a free slot to publish a new engagement-letter workflow. She wants the organizer back next January exactly as it is, without rebuilding it. A handful of late clients still have organizer instances in progress, and their partners want those clients to finish rather than start over. The firm's billing system is unaffected by this change. Which approach meets all of this?

options.text: Pause the organizer now; a paused workflow accepts no new instances and is released from the quota until it is resumed next January
Pause the organizer now, let the remaining instances finish, then unpublish it; unpublished workflows do not count toward the quota and can be published again
Unpublish the organizer right away; the late clients' instances keep running to completion while the workflow no longer counts toward the quota
Cancel the late clients' instances and delete the organizer; deletion frees the slot, and the workflow can be restored from the activity log next January

answerText: Pause the organizer now, let the remaining instances finish, then unpublish it; unpublished workflows do not count toward the quota and can be published again
explanation: A paused workflow still counts toward the quota; only an unpublished workflow does not, and you can unpublish only a paused workflow with no running instances. The clues are 'needs a free slot', 'late clients ... finish' and 'back next January'.
whyNotOthers: B is right because pause, then unpublish once instances finish, frees the slot and keeps the workflow for republishing. The trap is A: pausing does stop new instances, but a paused workflow still counts toward the quota. C fails because you cannot unpublish while instances run or before pausing, and D fails because canceling breaks the partners' requirement and a deleted workflow cannot be recovered.

optionExplanations.A: A paused workflow still counts toward the workflow quota, so no slot is freed.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. Unpublishing requires a paused workflow with no running instances; unpublished workflows do not count toward the quota and can be published at any time.
optionExplanations.C: Only a paused workflow with no running instances can be unpublished.
optionExplanations.D: Canceling contradicts the partners' wish, and a deleted workflow cannot be recovered.

decode.needs: Pause, wait for running instances to finish, then unpublish to release quota while keeping the workflow.
clues: needs a free slot -> only unpublished workflows leave the quota
late clients should finish -> cannot unpublish while instances run
back next January unchanged -> unpublish (republishable), not delete

concept.title: Paused still counts; unpublished does not
concept.line: Pause stops new instances but still counts toward quota; unpublish (after pausing and no running instances) frees quota and can be republished.

topic: Linking agreements to their source envelope
stem: Pellham Insurance syncs Agreement Manager records into its CRM so account managers see agreement types, parties and renewal terms. Agreements reach the repository in two ways: completed envelopes sent from the CRM itself, and scanned legacy contracts uploaded by the legal team. Account managers want a View original envelope button on agreements that came from eSignature, matched against the envelope IDs the CRM already stores. The nightly sync uses GetAgreementsList with ctoken paging. How should the sync match agreements to the CRM's envelope records?

options.text: Treat each agreement's id as the envelope ID, because Agreement Manager reuses the envelope GUID as the agreement identifier for completed envelopes.
Read related_agreement_documents.parent_agreement_document_id, which points back to the envelope that produced the agreement in eSignature.
Call CreateAgreementSummary for each agreement and read the originating envelope ID from the AI summary text that the call returns.
Read source_name to see which system the agreement came from and source_id for its identifier in that system, then match it to the stored envelope ID.

answerText: Read source_name to see which system the agreement came from and source_id for its identifier in that system, then match it to the stored envelope ID.
explanation: Each agreement record carries source_name (the originating system, such as Docusign eSign), source_id (the record's identifier in that system) and source_account_id; this is what links an agreement to the envelope it came from, while uploaded legacy contracts show a different source.
whyNotOthers: D is right because the source fields identify the originating system and record. The trap is A: the agreement id is Agreement Manager's own GUID, separate from the source envelope ID. B describes a link to a parent agreement document (for example an amendment's master), not to an envelope, and C returns an AI-written overview of the document, not system identifiers.

optionExplanations.A: The agreement id is Agreement Manager's own identifier; the envelope reference is kept in the source fields.
optionExplanations.B: parent_agreement_document_id relates an agreement to a parent agreement document, not to an envelope.
optionExplanations.C: The summary is an AI-written overview of the content and does not carry source system IDs.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. source_name tells eSignature from uploads, and source_id carries the identifier in that source system.

decode.needs: Use the agreement's source_name and source_id to link back to the originating envelope.
clues: 'completed envelopes... and scanned legacy contracts' -> different sources
'View original envelope button' -> needs the source record ID
'ctoken paging' -> red herring

concept.title: Source fields trace origin
concept.line: Agreement records carry source_name, source_id and source_account_id to trace each agreement back to the system and record it came from.

stem: Which two statements about bulk send with eSignature REST API v2.1 are true? (Select two)

options.text: Each copy in the bulk send list becomes a separate envelope for that copy's recipients
All copies go out as one envelope in which each recipient sees only their own documents
The envelope or template being bulk sent must already have the status sent
A send request is queued as a whole batch; partial acceptance generally does not occur
The test request sends one sample envelope to the first copy so the sender can preview it

answerText: Each copy in the bulk send list becomes a separate envelope for that copy's recipients; A send request is queued as a whole batch; partial acceptance generally does not occur
explanation: Bulk send creates an individual envelope for each copy in the list, and createBulkSendRequest queues the entire batch or fails; partial success generally does not occur.
whyNotOthers: A and D are right because each recipient gets their own agreement and the batch is queued as a unit. The trap is E: the test call sounds like a preview send, but it only checks compatibility and returns canBeSent without sending anything. B describes one shared envelope, which is not how bulk send works, and C is wrong because the envelope must be a draft.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. Every copy in the list produces its own envelope.
optionExplanations.B: Bulk send does not build one shared envelope; each copy is its own envelope.
optionExplanations.C: The bulk envelope must be a draft (status created), not sent.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. The whole batch is queued for asynchronous processing or the call fails; partial success generally does not occur.
optionExplanations.E: The test sends nothing; it returns canBeSent or the compatibility errors.

concept.title: Bulk send creates separate envelopes
concept.line: Each bulk list copy becomes its own envelope; the batch is queued as a whole; the test only validates compatibility.

topic: Private extension app missing from Apps steps
stem: Ironbridge Insurance's developers built an in-house extension app that writes claim decisions back to the company's legacy claims platform. It is registered in the Developer Console and has passed its connection and extension tests. The app must only ever be used by Ironbridge's own account, and the security team will not let it be listed for other Docusign customers. When a process builder opens the Apps tab of the Add New Step panel in Workflow Builder, the extension does not appear. What should the team do so that it appears as a step?

options.text: Submit the app for App Center review with public distribution, because only publicly listed extension apps can be offered as steps in workflows
Publish the app with private distribution, then have an Ironbridge admin install it from the App Center and connect it to the account
Add the aow_manage scope to the app's connection settings in the manifest, because Workflow Builder lists only extensions whose connection holds that scope
Publish the workflow first, because extension steps appear in the Add New Step panel only for workflows that have already passed review and publishing

answerText: Publish the app with private distribution, then have an Ironbridge admin install it from the App Center and connect it to the account
explanation: An extension step does not appear unless the extension app is installed and connected to the account, and private distribution is the choice for an app used only by your own organization ('only ever be used by Ironbridge's own account').
whyNotOthers: B is right because a privately distributed app, once installed and connected, shows up as an Apps step. The trap is A: publishing the app does make it installable, but public distribution lists it for every customer, which security forbids, and private apps work in workflows too. C and D fail because aow_manage is a Maestro API token scope, not an app connection setting, and steps are added while the workflow is a draft, before it is published.

optionExplanations.A: Public distribution would list the app for all customers, and private apps can also be used as workflow steps.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. Private distribution keeps the app org-only, and installing and connecting it makes its extensions available as workflow steps.
optionExplanations.C: aow_manage is a scope for calling the Maestro API; it does not control which extensions Workflow Builder lists.
optionExplanations.D: Steps are added while building the workflow; publishing does not affect which extensions are listed.

decode.needs: Distribute the extension app privately, install it from the App Center and connect it so its steps appear.
clues: only Ironbridge's own account -> private distribution
does not appear in the Apps tab -> app not installed and connected in the account
passed connection and extension tests -> red herring, the build is fine

concept.title: Install and connect before using
concept.line: An extension appears as a workflow step only once the app is installed and connected to the account; org-only apps use private distribution.

stem: An integration key's Go-Live status in Apps and Keys shows Declined. What does this status mean?

options.text: The app requires manual review; submit the linked form with more account details, usually completed within 24-48 hours
The app passed review but was not promoted within 90 days, so the review expired and must be run again
The app is permanently rejected, so a new integration key must be created and taken through Go-Live again
The app passed the automated review and is waiting for you to select a production account to promote into

answerText: The app requires manual review; submit the linked form with more account details, usually completed within 24-48 hours
explanation: Declined means the app 'requires manual review': you fill in the form linked to the status, and the manual review should finish within 24-48 hours.
whyNotOthers: A is right because Declined points you to a manual-review form. The trap is C: the word Declined sounds final, but the key is not discarded. B describes Review Expired and D describes Review Passed.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. Declined means manual review is needed; complete the linked form and expect the review within 24-48 hours.
optionExplanations.B: This is Review Expired: the review passed but the key was not promoted within 90 days.
optionExplanations.C: Declined is not a permanent rejection; the same key continues through manual review.
optionExplanations.D: This is Review Passed: the next step is selecting a production account.

concept.title: Go-Live status meanings
concept.line: Under Review, Review Passed, Review Expired after 90 days unpromoted, Declined means manual review via form within 24-48 hours.

stem: In JWT Grant, which grant_type value does the integration post to /oauth/token together with the signed assertion?

options.text: authorization_code
client_credentials
refresh_token
urn:ietf:params:oauth:grant-type:saml2-bearer
urn:ietf:params:oauth:grant-type:jwt-bearer

answerText: urn:ietf:params:oauth:grant-type:jwt-bearer
explanation: The JWT token request body is grant_type=urn:ietf:params:oauth:grant-type:jwt-bearer and assertion=the signed JWT.
whyNotOthers: E is right because that is the grant type Docusign documents for JWT Grant. The trap is D: it has the same URN form but names a SAML assertion, which Docusign does not use. A and C belong to Authorization Code Grant (code exchange and refresh), and B is a generic OAuth grant Docusign does not use.

optionExplanations.A: Used to exchange an authorization code in Authorization Code Grant.
optionExplanations.B: Not a Docusign grant type; JWT Grant uses the jwt-bearer URN.
optionExplanations.C: Used to renew tokens in Authorization Code Grant; JWT Grant issues no refresh token.
optionExplanations.D: Same URN shape but for SAML assertions, which Docusign does not accept.
optionExplanations.E: Correct. JWT Grant posts grant_type=urn:ietf:params:oauth:grant-type:jwt-bearer with the assertion.

concept.title: JWT grant_type value
concept.line: A JWT Grant token request posts grant_type urn:ietf:params:oauth:grant-type:jwt-bearer and the signed JWT as assertion.

stem: In a v2.1 bulk send, which value in the createBulkSendTestRequest response confirms that the list and the envelope are compatible?

options.text: A batchId for the test batch
The listId of the bulk list
A queued count of 0
canBeSent set to true

answerText: canBeSent set to true
explanation: createBulkSendTestRequest returns canBeSent: true when the list is compatible with the envelope or template; otherwise it returns the errors found.
whyNotOthers: D is right because canBeSent is the Boolean the test call returns. The trap is A: batchId is returned only by createBulkSendRequest when the batch is actually queued. B is returned by createBulkSendList, and C (queued, sent, failed counts) comes from getBulkSendBatchStatus.

optionExplanations.A: batchId comes from createBulkSendRequest, the real send, not from the test.
optionExplanations.B: listId is returned when you create the bulk send list.
optionExplanations.C: Queued, sent and failed counts come from getBulkSendBatchStatus.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. A successful test returns canBeSent true.

concept.title: Bulk send return values
concept.line: createBulkSendList returns listId; test returns canBeSent; send returns batchId; batch status returns sent, queued and failed counts.

stem: Meridian Logistics' HR department must collect a signed safety-policy acknowledgement from 1,800 warehouse staff in one run started by an unattended back-office job. Each employee gets their own agreement, and HR wants the HRIS updated as each person signs without the job hammering the API. The HR director wants the email subject to read Annual Safety Policy. Which two practices should the developer adopt? (Select two)

options.text: Submit all 1,800 copies in a single bulk send list, because the account's queue of 2,000 in-flight envelopes can hold the whole run
Split the staff into two bulk send lists of no more than 1,000 copies each and release each list as its own batch
Poll Envelopes:get for every envelope once a minute until it completes, then update the employee's HRIS record
Create the envelope to be bulk sent with status sent, so that Docusign can copy its recipients and tabs into each copy
Use a Connect configuration to push envelope status events to the HRIS instead of polling individual envelopes

answerText: Split the staff into two bulk send lists of no more than 1,000 copies each and release each list as its own batch; Use a Connect configuration to push envelope status events to the HRIS instead of polling individual envelopes
explanation: A bulk send list may hold at most 1,000 copies (BULK_SEND_ENVELOPE_LIST_CONTAINS_TOO_MANY_COPIES), so 1,800 staff need two lists, and Connect pushes status changes so the job does not poll. The clue 'without hammering the API' points to Connect.
whyNotOthers: B and E are right because they respect the per-list copy limit and replace polling with webhooks. The trap is A: the in-flight queue limit is real, but it is a separate account-wide limit; a single list over 1,000 copies is rejected. C breaks the polling guideline of at most once per 15 minutes per envelope, and D uses a sent envelope where bulk send needs a draft.

optionExplanations.A: The queue limit is separate; a list above 1,000 copies is rejected regardless of queue space.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. Each bulk send list is limited to 1,000 copies, so split the run.
optionExplanations.C: Polling each envelope every minute breaks the once-per-15-minutes guideline and wastes the hourly limit.
optionExplanations.D: The bulk envelope must be a draft (status created), not sent.
optionExplanations.E: Correct. Connect pushes envelope events, which the bulk send course recommends over polling.

decode.needs: Respect the 1,000-copy list limit and use Connect
clues: 1,800 staff, each their own agreement -> bulk send above one list's limit
without hammering the API -> Connect, not polling
email subject wording -> red herring

concept.title: Bulk send limits and status tracking
concept.line: Keep each bulk list at 1,000 copies or fewer, mind the account queue, and track status with Connect rather than polling.

topic: Manual start method and Prepare permission
stem: Lakeshore Property Group wants to automate its lease packet. Applicants are screened in a separate tenant-screening tool, and only after a leasing agent has met the applicant and approved them should the lease packet go out. The agent decides when to start, types in the approved tenant's name and email, and the tenant then completes a form and signs. Prospective tenants must never be able to start the process on their own, and the company has no developers, so nothing can be built or coded. The leasing agents should not be able to change the workflow design. Which start method and permission setup fits?

options.text: Set the start method to From a Link and have agents email the copied workflow URL to each approved tenant, so the tenant starts the process when ready
Set the start method to From an API call so the screening tool starts an instance automatically with the tenant's details as soon as the applicant is approved
Set the start method to Manually in Docusign and give agents Workflows: Prepare, so they use Run Workflow and enter the tenant as participant before the invite goes out
Set the start method to Manually in Docusign and give agents Workflows: Create, because only users who can create workflows are able to start them with Run Workflow

answerText: Set the start method to Manually in Docusign and give agents Workflows: Prepare, so they use Run Workflow and enter the tenant as participant before the invite goes out
explanation: Run Workflow (Manually in Docusign) is for workflows started by someone in your organization who supplies participant details, and anyone with Workflows: Prepare can run published workflows. The clues are 'the agent decides when to start, types in the tenant's details' and 'agents should not change the workflow design'.
whyNotOthers: C is right because Prepare lets agents start any published workflow without editing rights. The trap is D: the start method is correct, but Create is the permission for building and editing workflows, not a requirement to run them, and it would let agents change designs. A fails because a link is a self-service start the tenant controls, and B needs an integration the company cannot build.

optionExplanations.A: A link is meant for self-service starts by the participant; anyone holding the URL could start an instance, which the stem forbids.
optionExplanations.B: From an API call needs code in the screening tool, and the company has no developers.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. Manually in Docusign with Run Workflow lets the agent start the instance and enter participant details; Workflows: Prepare is enough to run published workflows.
optionExplanations.D: Create is for building and editing workflows; users with Prepare can already run published workflows, and Create would let agents change the design.

decode.needs: Staff-initiated start (Manually in Docusign, Run Workflow) with the Workflows: Prepare permission.
clues: agent decides when to start and types tenant details -> Run Workflow, starter supplies participants
tenants must never start it themselves -> not From a Link
no developers -> not From an API call
agents must not change the design -> Prepare, not Create

concept.title: Manual start needs Prepare permission
concept.line: Manually in Docusign suits staff-initiated workflows; users with Workflows: Prepare can run published workflows, while Create is for building and editing.

stem: Pinewood Credit Union's security architect is reviewing the listener that receives signing events for its loan origination system. Two requirements must be met: every inbound call must carry a bearer token issued by the credit union's own Microsoft Entra ID tenant, which the existing API gateway already validates, and the loan system must be able to prove that each message body was not altered after it left Docusign. The listener is an account-level JSON SIM configuration on HTTPS, and the gateway team mentions that most traffic arrives at month-end. Which two measures together meet both requirements? (Select two)

options.text: Add Basic authentication to the same configuration as well, so the gateway can check a username and password next to the bearer token on each call
Enable OAuth for Connect with the Entra ID token URL, client ID and secret, so Docusign obtains a token and sends it in the Authorization header
Register the integration key for JWT Grant in the Entra ID tenant, so that Docusign signs each Connect message with the integration's RSA private key
Rely on the HTTPS channel alone, because TLS encryption already proves to the loan system that the stored body matches what Docusign sent
Enable HMAC with a secret key and have the listener recompute HMAC-SHA256 over the raw body and compare it with the X-DocuSign-Signature-1 header

answerText: Enable OAuth for Connect with the Entra ID token URL, client ID and secret, so Docusign obtains a token and sends it in the Authorization header; Enable HMAC with a secret key and have the listener recompute HMAC-SHA256 over the raw body and compare it with the X-DocuSign-Signature-1 header
explanation: OAuth for Connect delivers a token from the customer's own IdP ("bearer token issued by the credit union's own Entra ID tenant"), and HMAC proves integrity ("prove that each message body was not altered"). Docusign recommends HMAC plus OAuth for production listeners.
whyNotOthers: B and E are right: OAuth for Connect satisfies the token requirement and HMAC satisfies the integrity requirement. The trap is A: Basic authentication sounds like extra protection, but it cannot be used together with OAuth for Connect and does not prove integrity. C confuses JWT Grant (calling Docusign APIs) with Connect security; D fails because TLS protects data only in transit and proves nothing about the body after the gateway.

optionExplanations.A: Basic authentication is available for account-level and Recipient Connect, but it cannot be combined with OAuth for Connect on a configuration, and it does not prove integrity.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. OAuth for Connect uses Client Credentials against the customer's IdP and sends the resulting token as a Bearer value in the Authorization header of every message.
optionExplanations.C: JWT Grant is for your app to call Docusign APIs; Connect messages are not signed with an integration key's RSA key.
optionExplanations.D: TLS encrypts the channel in transit only; it gives the loan system no end-to-end proof that the body is unchanged.
optionExplanations.E: Correct. HMAC-SHA256 over the raw body with a shared secret proves both authenticity and integrity of each message.

decode.needs: OAuth for Connect (IdP token) plus HMAC (integrity).
clues: bearer token issued by the credit union's own Entra ID tenant -> OAuth for Connect (Client Credentials)
prove each body was not altered -> HMAC signature headers
most traffic at month-end -> red herring

concept.title: OAuth plus HMAC for production
concept.line: OAuth for Connect proves the sender with the customer's IdP token; HMAC proves integrity. Basic auth cannot be combined with OAuth for Connect.

topic: Consent for users outside the claimed domain
stem: Brookfield Group runs a headless nightly job that sends supplier attestations as the procurement sender of each business unit. It uses JWT Grant, and an organization administrator granted admin consent covering the group's claimed domain, brookfield.com. After an acquisition, a subsidiary's sender whose email is at northvale.co.uk, a domain Brookfield has not claimed, was added; the token request now fails only when sub is that user's ID, while the other senders still work. The RSA key pair was rotated last month. What should the team do?

options.text: Have the subsidiary's sender open the consent URL with scope=signature impersonation and allow access once, then rerun the job unchanged
Add impersonation to the scope claim of the JWT payload for that sender only, so the token request carries the permission the new user is missing
Have the organization administrator re-authorize the app in Docusign Admin, which extends the existing consent to every user in the organization
Generate a separate RSA key pair for the subsidiary, because users outside the claimed domain must be impersonated with their own signing key
Change the aud claim for that sender to the subsidiary's base URI, because users in another domain are served by a different authentication host

answerText: Have the subsidiary's sender open the consent URL with scope=signature impersonation and allow access once, then rerun the job unchanged
explanation: Admin consent covers only users in the claimed domain; the new sender is at "a domain Brookfield has not claimed", so that user must grant individual consent once with scope=signature impersonation.
whyNotOthers: A is right because individual consent is the fallback for users outside reserved domains, and the JWT itself needs no change. The trap is C: admin consent applies to users in the claimed domains, not to every user of the organization, so re-authorizing does not reach northvale.co.uk. B fails because the payload scope does not grant consent. D and E fail because the key and aud are the same for every user, and the other senders prove they work.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. A user outside the claimed domain grants individual consent once; the existing JWT code then works.
optionExplanations.B: The JWT payload scope lists API scopes only; it cannot substitute for consent the user never gave.
optionExplanations.C: Admin consent covers users in claimed (reserved) domains only, so it does not reach northvale.co.uk.
optionExplanations.D: One RSA key pair per integration key signs JWTs for every impersonated user.
optionExplanations.E: aud is the authentication host (account-d or account.docusign.com), the same for all users.

decode.needs: Individual consent (signature impersonation) for the one user outside the claimed domain.
clues: headless nightly job -> JWT Grant
domain Brookfield has not claimed -> admin consent does not apply
fails only when sub is that user -> per-user consent missing
RSA key rotated last month -> red herring

concept.title: Admin consent covers claimed domains only
concept.line: Admin consent applies to users in claimed domains; any other user must grant individual consent before JWT works.

topic: Token for the ID Evidence API
stem: Which call returns the bearer token that an app passes to the ID Evidence API to read a recipient's verification events?

options.text: POST /oauth/token with an identity evidence scope added to the JWT assertion
POST .../envelopes/{envelopeId}/recipients/{recipientIdGuid}/identity_proof_token
GET .../accounts/{accountId}/identity_verification to read the configuration's workflowId
GET .../envelopes/{envelopeId}/recipients with include_extended set to true

answerText: POST .../envelopes/{envelopeId}/recipients/{recipientIdGuid}/identity_proof_token
explanation: EnvelopeRecipients:createRecipientProofFileResourceToken (POST .../identity_proof_token) returns a resource token valid for 2 minutes, which is the bearer token for ID Evidence events and media calls.
whyNotOthers: B is right because the ID Evidence API takes a resource token issued per recipient. The trap is A: an OAuth access token is needed to request the resource token, but it is not itself accepted by the ID Evidence API for this purpose. C returns workflow IDs for sending, and D lists recipients (useful to find the recipientIdGuid) but issues no token.

optionExplanations.A: The OAuth token is only used to request the resource token; there is no special evidence scope flow here.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. identity_proof_token issues the 2-minute resource token for that recipient.
optionExplanations.C: IdentityVerifications:list returns workflow IDs used when sending, not an evidence token.
optionExplanations.D: EnvelopeRecipients:list gives the recipientIdGuid but no token.

concept.title: ID Evidence resource tokens
concept.line: Read ID Evidence with a per-recipient resource token from identity_proof_token, valid 2 minutes, not with the OAuth access token.

stem: A university's financial aid office runs a headless job that bulk sends award letters every evening. Tonight, while an earlier batch of several thousand letters is still being processed, the job's next createBulkSendRequest fails with BULK_SEND_ACCOUNT_HAS_TOO_MANY_QUEUED_ENVELOPES. The new list has only 400 copies and passed its test call yesterday. The registrar asks for the fix that will actually let tonight's letters go out. What should the developer do?

options.text: Split the 400 copies into four lists of 100 copies and send them one after another, so each smaller batch fits within the per-list limit
Run createBulkSendTestRequest again right before the send, because a passing test reserves space in the queue for the following batch
Move the job to the legacy v2 bulk recipients method, because that older method uses a separate queue from v2.1 bulk send lists
Wait until the earlier batch has drained, tracked with getBulkSendBatchStatus or Connect, then retry tonight's send request

answerText: Wait until the earlier batch has drained, tracked with getBulkSendBatchStatus or Connect, then retry tonight's send request
explanation: This error means the account already has the maximum number of in-flight bulk envelopes waiting to be processed; the documented fix is to try again later (or ask Docusign Support for a higher tier). The clue is 'an earlier batch of several thousand letters is still being processed'.
whyNotOthers: D is right because the limit is account-wide queued envelopes, which only drains with time. The trap is A: splitting fixes the per-list copy limit, but 400 copies are already under it and smaller lists still add to the same full queue. B is wrong because a test reserves nothing, and C relies on an invented separate queue for a legacy method.

optionExplanations.A: The list is already under the 1,000-copy limit; smaller lists still hit the same full account queue.
optionExplanations.B: The test checks compatibility only; it reserves no queue capacity.
optionExplanations.C: There is no documented separate queue to escape to; the account limit still applies.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. The account queue is full; wait for it to drain and retry.

decode.needs: Account queue full: wait and retry
clues: earlier batch of several thousand still being processed -> account in-flight queue full
only 400 copies -> not the per-list limit
passed its test yesterday -> red herring

concept.title: Queue limit is account-wide
concept.line: BULK_SEND_ACCOUNT_HAS_TOO_MANY_QUEUED_ENVELOPES means the account queue is full; wait and retry, unlike the per-list 1,000-copy limit.

stem: Cobalt Dental's front-office web app runs on its own server and uses Confidential Authorization Code Grant. Receptionists sign in with their own Docusign accounts only to send treatment consent forms through the eSignature REST API, and the app never acts for them while they are away. Practice managers complain that staff who use the app every week are still asked to sign in again each month, and the security officer insists on least privilege. The app is written in PHP. Which scope request fits best?

options.text: Request signature only, keeping the default refresh lifetime of 30 days from first issue, since least privilege rules out any additional scope
Request signature and extended, so each successful refresh restarts the 30-day refresh lifetime and regular users are not sent back to sign in
Request signature and impersonation, so the server can renew tokens on a receptionist's behalf without the receptionist being present
Request signature, impersonation and extended, combining rolling refresh tokens with the ability to act for receptionists when they are away
Request openid and signature, so the ID token returned at sign-in can be exchanged for a fresh access token whenever one is needed

answerText: Request signature and extended, so each successful refresh restarts the 30-day refresh lifetime and regular users are not sent back to sign in
explanation: The monthly re-login comes from the refresh token expiring 30 days after first issue; extended makes it expire 30 days after the last successful refresh, and signature covers eSignature calls. Nothing else is needed for "never acts for them while they are away".
whyNotOthers: B is right because signature plus extended is the minimum that removes the monthly sign-in. The trap is A: it is least privilege, but keeps the 30-day from-issue limit that causes the complaint. C and D add impersonation, a JWT consent scope the app does not need, and E fails because the ID token is never used to obtain access tokens or call APIs.

optionExplanations.A: Without extended the refresh token dies 30 days after first issue, which is the monthly re-login being complained about.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. extended makes the refresh token expire 30 days after the last refresh, and signature covers eSignature.
optionExplanations.C: impersonation is for JWT Grant consent; refreshing never needs it.
optionExplanations.D: Adds impersonation, violating least privilege for an app that never acts while users are away.
optionExplanations.E: The ID token identifies the user and cannot be exchanged for access tokens.

decode.needs: Scopes signature + extended on the Auth Code consent request.
clues: asked to sign in again each month -> refresh token expiring 30 days from issue
never acts while they are away -> no impersonation
least privilege -> only signature and extended
PHP -> red herring

concept.title: extended gives rolling refresh
concept.line: Add extended to Auth Code scopes so refresh tokens expire 30 days after the last refresh; impersonation is only for JWT.

stem: Verity Health licenses a third-party credentialing product whose integration key belongs to the vendor, not to Verity. The vendor's service uses JWT Grant and needs consent for about 2,000 Verity clinicians, all with addresses in Verity's claimed domain; Verity's Docusign plan includes Access Management. Verity's eSignature account administrator looked through the account settings and found no way to approve the vendor's app. The vendor's support team says the app is already live in production. The contract renews in March. How should consent be granted?

options.text: Verity's eSignature account administrator grants consent in Apps and Keys on behalf of every user who belongs to the eSignature account
A Verity organization administrator authorizes the vendor's app in Docusign Admin under Connected Apps, the same way as for an in-house app
A Verity organization administrator opens the vendor's /oauth/auth link with scope=openid and admin_consent_scope=signature impersonation
Each clinician opens the vendor's consent link with scope=signature impersonation once, because external apps cannot receive admin consent
The vendor's own organization administrator grants consent in its Docusign Admin, which covers Verity users because the vendor owns the key

answerText: A Verity organization administrator opens the vendor's /oauth/auth link with scope=openid and admin_consent_scope=signature impersonation
explanation: The key is owned by another company ("belongs to the vendor"), so this is admin consent for an external app: an organization administrator (not an eSignature account admin) goes to the authorization URI with scope=openid and admin_consent_scope listing the scopes.
whyNotOthers: C is right because external apps get admin consent through the openid plus admin_consent_scope request, made by an organization administrator. The trap is B: Docusign Admin's Connected Apps authorization works only for internal apps whose key the organization owns; external consent cannot be granted from the UI. A uses the wrong kind of administrator, D is possible but unnecessary since admin consent is available, and E fails because consent comes from the users' own organization.

optionExplanations.A: Admin consent is granted by an organization administrator, not an eSignature account administrator.
optionExplanations.B: Connected Apps authorization in Docusign Admin applies only to internal apps whose integration key the org owns.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. External-app admin consent uses /oauth/auth with scope=openid and admin_consent_scope, by an org admin.
optionExplanations.D: External apps can receive admin consent; with Access Management and a claimed domain, 2,000 individual consents are unnecessary.
optionExplanations.E: Consent must come from Verity's organization, which owns the users, not from the key owner.

decode.needs: Admin consent for external applications by a Verity organization administrator.
clues: integration key belongs to the vendor -> external application
claimed domain, Access Management -> admin consent possible
eSignature account administrator found no way -> wrong kind of admin
contract renews in March -> red herring

concept.title: Admin consent for external apps
concept.line: For an app whose key another company owns, an org admin grants consent via /oauth/auth with openid and admin_consent_scope.

stem: Crestline Insurance's records team archives every completed policy in its document management system. The archivist wants exactly one PDF per envelope containing every signed document plus the certificate of completion, so auditors open a single file. Envelopes contain between two and six documents, and some were signed on phones. Which call should the archiving job make after completion?

options.text: EnvelopeDocuments:get with documentId archive, which includes the certificate
EnvelopeDocuments:get for each documentId, then certificate
EnvelopeDocuments:get with documentId combined and certificate=true
EnvelopeDocuments:get with documentId certificate

answerText: EnvelopeDocuments:get with documentId combined and certificate=true
explanation: documentId combined returns all documents as a single PDF, and the certificate query parameter set to true includes the certificate of completion in that PDF. The clue is 'exactly one PDF'.
whyNotOthers: C is right because combined plus certificate=true gives one PDF with everything. The trap is A: archive also includes all documents and the certificate, but as a ZIP file, not a single PDF. B returns several files, and D returns only the certificate.

optionExplanations.A: archive returns a ZIP containing the PDFs and certificate, not one PDF.
optionExplanations.B: Separate calls produce several files and use more API calls.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. combined returns one PDF; certificate=true adds the certificate of completion.
optionExplanations.D: certificate returns only the certificate of completion.

decode.needs: documentId combined with certificate=true
clues: exactly one PDF per envelope -> combined, not archive
plus the certificate of completion -> certificate=true
signed on phones -> red herring

concept.title: Special documentId keywords
concept.line: combined = one PDF (certificate optional), archive = ZIP with documents and certificate, certificate = certificate only.

stem: Tidewater Logistics will license a new contract product to customers of every size; some customers have Docusign Access Management and a claimed domain, many do not. The product will run as an unattended back-office service that sends agreements as a designated user at each customer. In the architecture review the team must record the drawbacks that Docusign itself lists for JWT Grant before choosing it, and the security lead wants them stated precisely rather than as generic OAuth folklore. Which two are genuine drawbacks of JWT Grant? (Select two)

options.text: Each impersonated user must be signed in at the moment the integration asks for a new token
No refresh token is issued, so a new JWT must be built and exchanged when the one-hour token expires
The access token lasts eight hours, so a user whose consent is revoked stays reachable for a working day
The RSA key pair is weaker than a client secret, so Docusign requires rotating it every hour
Individual consent must be supported alongside admin consent, since not every customer has Access Management

answerText: No refresh token is issued, so a new JWT must be built and exchanged when the one-hour token expires; Individual consent must be supported alongside admin consent, since not every customer has Access Management
explanation: Docusign lists among JWT drawbacks that the token expires after one hour with no refresh token, and that integrations must support several consent methods, including individual consent, because not all users are under a claimed domain or have Access Management.
whyNotOthers: B and E are right because both appear in Docusign's JWT drawbacks. The trap is C: revocation lag is real, but the JWT access token lasts one hour, not eight (eight hours is the Auth Code access token). A describes Authorization Code Grant, and D is false because Docusign calls the RSA key pair excellent security.

optionExplanations.A: After consent, JWT Grant needs no user present; that is the point of the flow.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. JWT access tokens last one hour and no refresh token is issued; mint a new JWT.
optionExplanations.C: The JWT access token lasts one hour; eight hours is the Authorization Code access token.
optionExplanations.D: Docusign lists the RSA key pair as an advantage (excellent security); there is no hourly rotation rule.
optionExplanations.E: Correct. Admin consent needs Access Management and a claimed domain, so individual consent must also be supported.

decode.needs: Recall Docusign's documented disadvantages of JWT Grant.
clues: some customers have Access Management, many do not -> individual consent fallback needed
drawbacks Docusign itself lists -> documented trade-offs, not generic OAuth lore

concept.title: JWT Grant trade-offs
concept.line: JWT drawbacks: no refresh token (new JWT hourly), several consent paths, a stored user ID and crypto library; advantage: no user present.

stem: During a pilot, a branch manager collected loan agreements signed through the company's Docusign developer account. What is their legal standing?

options.text: Binding, because the same signing ceremony and audit trail are produced in both environments
Not legally binding, because only envelopes sent from a production account are legally binding
Binding once the integration key is promoted, because Go-Live converts earlier developer envelopes
Binding only for signers who completed access-code authentication during the signing session

answerText: Not legally binding, because only envelopes sent from a production account are legally binding
explanation: eSignature transactions in a developer account are not legally binding; they become binding only once the integration runs in production.
whyNotOthers: B is right because developer-account envelopes are never legally binding. The trap is A: the signing experience looks the same, but the environment decides the legal standing. C fails because Go-Live duplicates the key, not past envelopes, and D fails because authentication does not make a developer envelope binding.

optionExplanations.A: Similar-looking signing and audit trails do not make developer-account envelopes binding.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. Only production envelopes are legally binding.
optionExplanations.C: Go-Live duplicates the integration key; it does not change envelopes already sent from the developer account.
optionExplanations.D: Recipient authentication does not change the non-binding status of developer-account envelopes.

concept.title: Developer envelopes not legally binding
concept.line: Envelopes sent from a developer account are not legally binding; a production account is required for legally binding signatures.

topic: Default regions for a public app
stem: A public extension app is published without any additional regions being specified. Which accounts can install it from the production App Center?

options.text: Only accounts based in the US
Accounts in every Docusign region
Only accounts the developer lists at publication
Only accounts in the developer's own region

answerText: Only accounts based in the US
explanation: By default, published extension apps are available only to US customers on the production App Center; other regions must be added explicitly.
whyNotOthers: A is right because availability defaults to the US. The trap is B: global availability is not the default, so regions beyond the US must be specified. C describes private distribution, and D is not how the default is defined.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. Published extension apps default to US customers only; other regions must be added.
optionExplanations.B: Additional regions must be specified explicitly; they are not included by default.
optionExplanations.C: Listing specific accounts is how private apps are shared, not public ones.
optionExplanations.D: The default is the US, not the developer's own region.

concept.title: Public apps default to US only
concept.line: A published public extension app is installable only by US accounts unless additional publication regions are specified.

stem: Riverside Bank's branch staff open account agreements on a tablet while the customer sits at the desk. Staff often create the envelope when the appointment is booked in the morning, and customers sometimes step away during signing and come back later. Product owners also want the core banking record flagged as signed reliably. The branch Wi-Fi is slow at peak hours. Which two practices should the developer follow? (Select two)

options.text: Request the signing URL when the appointment is booked and store it, so the tablet opens the session instantly when the customer arrives
Call createRecipient only when the customer is at the tablet, and call it again for a fresh URL if the session must restart
Keep the first signing URL and reload it if the customer steps away, because the URL stays valid until the envelope is completed
Confirm completion through Connect or the envelope status rather than relying only on the event value in the returnUrl
Create the envelope with status created so no email goes out, and request the signing URL for that draft at the tablet

answerText: Call createRecipient only when the customer is at the tablet, and call it again for a fresh URL if the session must restart; Confirm completion through Connect or the envelope status rather than relying only on the event value in the returnUrl
explanation: Signing URLs expire after about 5 minutes and are single-use, so request them only when the signer is ready and request a new one to restart. The returnUrl can be spoofed or skipped, so confirm status through Connect or the API.
whyNotOthers: B and D are right because they respect the URL lifetime and the rule not to trust the returnUrl alone. The trap is C: reusing the same URL sounds efficient, but a used or old URL returns ttl_expired. A creates the URL hours early, and E fails because embedded signing needs a sent envelope; clientUserId already suppresses email.

optionExplanations.A: The URL expires within minutes, so one created at booking time is dead when the customer arrives.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. Request the URL just in time and generate a new one to resume.
optionExplanations.C: The URL is single-use and short-lived; reloading it gives ttl_expired.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. The returnUrl can be skipped or spoofed, so verify with Connect or the envelope status.
optionExplanations.E: Recipient views require a sent envelope; clientUserId, not draft status, stops the email.

decode.needs: Just-in-time signing URLs and verified completion
clues: created when the appointment is booked -> URL would expire
steps away and comes back -> request a fresh URL
flagged as signed reliably -> do not trust returnUrl alone
slow Wi-Fi -> red herring

concept.title: Signing URLs are short-lived
concept.line: Request the recipient view only when the signer is ready, regenerate it to resume, and verify completion via Connect or status.

stem: Halcyon runs an append-only compliance ledger: entries are never edited once written. Its Maestro onboarding workflow must add one new ledger entry each time an onboarding finishes, and nothing is ever read back into the workflow. To cut development time, the developer proposes declaring as few Data IO actions as possible. The ledger exposes a JSON API that already matches the Docusign contracts, and the app will be private. The workflow already includes an identity verification step before signing. What should the developer implement?

options.text: Only Create Record, Get Type Names and Get Type Definitions, because a create-only extension never searches for or patches an existing record
All five Data IO actions, with full logic in Create Record, while Patch Record must still be defined but does not need to contain any code
Search Records, Get Type Names and Get Type Definitions with the Data Read option, and send each new entry in the body of the search request
Create Record, Patch Record, Get Type Names and Get Type Definitions, omitting Search Records because no existing entry is ever looked up

answerText: All five Data IO actions, with full logic in Create Record, while Patch Record must still be defined but does not need to contain any code
explanation: Data output cannot be standalone because it uses the data input actions to find records, so writing requires all five Data IO actions. If the app only creates records, only Create Record needs a full implementation; Patch Record must still be defined but needs no code.
whyNotOthers: B is right because a writing Data IO app must declare all five actions, with Patch Record allowed to be an empty definition for a create-only system. The trap is D: Search Records cannot be omitted because data output relies on the input actions. A omits both Search and Patch, and C is a read-only registration that cannot write at all.

optionExplanations.A: Writing requires all five actions; Search Records and Patch Record cannot be dropped.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. All five actions are declared; for create-only, Create Record is fully implemented and Patch Record can be an empty definition.
optionExplanations.C: Data Read registers a read-only app; Search Records does not create entries.
optionExplanations.D: Data output uses the data input actions to find records, so Search Records must be implemented.

decode.needs: All five Data IO actions, with Patch Record as an empty definition
clues: append-only ledger, entries never edited -> create-only, Patch Record needs no code
add one new entry per onboarding -> data output (write) requires all five actions
JSON API matches contracts, private app -> red herrings

concept.title: Data IO writes need all five actions
concept.line: Data output cannot be standalone; a create-only app implements all five actions, with Patch Record defined but code-free.

stem: Cobalt Energy sends about 600 supplier rate-confirmation agreements each quarter in one bulk send run. Each agreement must carry the supplier's vendor number as hidden metadata so the ERP can match the signed copy when it comes back. The bulk list already gives every copy its recipients and an envelope-level custom field named vendorNumber, but createBulkSendTestRequest reports a custom field error. The agreements use the company's standard NDA wording. What should the developer change?

options.text: Remove vendorNumber from the bulk send list and add it to each envelope afterwards with EnvelopeCustomFields:create once the batch has finished
Move vendorNumber into a text tab assigned to the signer, because a bulk send list cannot carry any envelope-level custom field values
Define a custom field named vendorNumber with a placeholder value on the draft envelope, and keep the per-copy values in the bulk send list
Add vendorNumber to the createBulkSendRequest body instead, because envelope custom fields are applied only when the batch is released

answerText: Define a custom field named vendorNumber with a placeholder value on the draft envelope, and keep the per-copy values in the bulk send list
explanation: Each envelope-level custom field in the bulk send list must correspond to a custom field defined in the envelope definition; Docusign advises placeholder values for such fields on the draft. The clue is 'the test reports a custom field error' while the list already carries vendorNumber.
whyNotOthers: C is right because the draft envelope must declare the field so each copy's value can override it. The trap is B: tabs can hold data, but it would be visible to signers and bulk lists can carry envelope custom fields. A needs hundreds of extra calls after sending, and D puts the field in a request that only takes the list and envelope IDs.

optionExplanations.A: This adds hundreds of follow-up calls and leaves envelopes unmatched until they are patched.
optionExplanations.B: Bulk lists do carry envelope custom fields, and a signer tab is not hidden metadata.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. Declare vendorNumber on the draft envelope; the list supplies each copy's value.
optionExplanations.D: createBulkSendRequest identifies the list and envelope or template; it does not carry per-copy custom fields.

decode.needs: Declare the custom field on the draft envelope
clues: vendor number as hidden metadata for the ERP -> envelope custom field
test reports a custom field error -> list field has no match in the envelope definition
standard NDA wording -> red herring

concept.title: Bulk list fields must exist on envelope
concept.line: Every envelope-level custom field in a bulk send list must match a custom field defined, with a placeholder, on the draft envelope.

topic: Refreshing a known set of agreements
stem: Every morning, Saltmarsh Logistics' treasury dashboard refreshes 30 strategic supplier agreements whose Agreement Manager ids it already stores, showing each one's parties, expiration date and payment terms. The hourly API limit is shared with four other integrations, so the architect wants as few calls as possible. Agreements are never added to or removed from this list during the quarter, and the dashboard is read-only and shows one tile per agreement. Which approach fits?

options.text: Call GetAgreementsList once with an id filter listing the 30 stored ids with the in operator, and read parties and provisions from the records.
Call GetAgreement once for each of the 30 stored ids, so each dashboard tile reads the parties and provisions of exactly one agreement record.
Call GetAgreementsList with no filter and keep only the 30 stored ids, because the list call cannot filter by agreement id at all.
Call CreateAgreementSummary for each of the 30 stored ids and read the expiration date and payment terms from each returned summary.

answerText: Call GetAgreementsList once with an id filter listing the 30 stored ids with the in operator, and read parties and provisions from the records.
explanation: GetAgreementsList accepts an id filter with a comma-separated list and the in operator, and list records include parties and provisions, so one call (plus paging if needed) covers 'as few calls as possible'.
whyNotOthers: A is right because the list call filters by id with the in operator and its records include parties and provisions. The trap is B: GetAgreement per id would work and maps neatly to one tile per agreement, but 30 calls are not 'as few calls as possible'. C ignores the id filter and reads the whole repository, and D returns AI prose rather than the structured fields a dashboard needs.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. One filtered list call returns the 30 agreements with parties and provisions.
optionExplanations.B: Works and returns the same parties and provisions, but it costs 30 calls against a shared hourly limit, while one filtered list call returns all 30 records.
optionExplanations.C: GetAgreementsList does support an id filter (= or in with comma-separated UUIDs).
optionExplanations.D: Summaries are AI-written overviews, not structured provision values, and need 30 POST calls.

decode.needs: One GetAgreementsList call with an id in-filter.
clues: 'ids it already stores' -> id filter
'as few calls as possible' -> one list call, not 30 gets
'parties, expiration date and payment terms' -> provisions in list records
'one tile per agreement', 'never added or removed during the quarter' -> red herrings

concept.title: Filter the list by id
concept.line: To read a known set of agreements efficiently, filter GetAgreementsList on id with the in operator; list records include parties and provisions.

stem: Which bulk send call returns the batchId used to track a run?

options.text: BulkSend:createBulkSendList
BulkSend:createBulkSendRequest
BulkSend:createBulkSendTestRequest
BulkSend:getBulkSendBatchStatus

answerText: BulkSend:createBulkSendRequest
explanation: createBulkSendRequest queues the envelopes and returns the batchId; getBulkSendBatchStatus then takes that batchId.
whyNotOthers: B is right because the batch exists only once the send request is accepted. The trap is D: getBulkSendBatchStatus uses the batchId as input and returns sent, queued and failed counts. A returns listId and C returns canBeSent.

optionExplanations.A: Creating the list returns listId.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. The send request returns the batchId.
optionExplanations.C: The test returns canBeSent or errors.
optionExplanations.D: Batch status takes the batchId as input and returns the counts.

concept.title: Bulk send return values
concept.line: listId from the list, canBeSent from the test, batchId from the send, counts from the batch status.

stem: How long do agreement documents stored in Agreement Manager persist in a Docusign developer account?

options.text: They are purged every month, like eSignature envelopes in the developer environment.
They persist until an administrator deletes the developer account.
They are purged 30 days after AI extraction has completed for them.
They persist only until the integration key passes Go-Live review.

answerText: They persist until an administrator deletes the developer account.
explanation: Unlike eSignature documents in the developer environment, documents stored in Agreement Manager (Navigator) are not purged monthly; they persist until the admin deletes the account.
whyNotOthers: B is right per the Navigator concepts documentation. The trap is A: monthly purging applies to eSignature envelopes in demo, not to Agreement Manager documents. C and D describe retention rules that do not exist.

optionExplanations.A: Monthly purging is the eSignature demo behaviour, explicitly not Agreement Manager's.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. Agreement Manager documents in demo persist until the admin deletes the account.
optionExplanations.C: No such 30-day retention rule exists.
optionExplanations.D: Go-Live copies the integration key to production; it does not delete demo data.

concept.title: Demo agreement data persists
concept.line: Agreement Manager documents in a developer account are not purged monthly like eSignature envelopes; they stay until the account is deleted.

topic: Handling the hourly limit with rate-limit headers
stem: Linfield Utilities runs an unattended nightly job that archives completed service contracts from Docusign into its records system. Most nights it finishes quietly, but on month-end nights it starts receiving 'maximum number of hourly API invocations has been exceeded' errors at about 02:40, and every call after that fails. No one is at the keyboard, and the job's retry logic currently gives up after three attempts. The records system is due for a database upgrade next quarter. How should the job be changed?

options.text: Read X-RateLimit-Remaining and X-RateLimit-Reset on each response, pause when the allowance runs low, and resume once the limit resets at the top of the hour
Retry each blocked call immediately in a tight loop, because the hourly window rolls continuously and capacity frees up again within a few seconds
Run the month-end calls against the developer environment instead, because calls made there do not count toward the production account's hourly limit
Spread the job across three new integration keys, so each key draws on its own 3,000-call hourly allowance and the job no longer hits the limit

answerText: Read X-RateLimit-Remaining and X-RateLimit-Reset on each response, pause when the allowance runs low, and resume once the limit resets at the top of the hour
explanation: The hourly allowance resets at the top of each hour, and the X-RateLimit-Remaining and X-RateLimit-Reset headers tell the 'unattended nightly job' when to pause and when it can resume.
whyNotOthers: A is right because it reads the headers and waits for the reset instead of failing. The trap is D: extra keys seem to add capacity, but the hourly limit is per account and shared by every integration. B fails because the limit resets on the hour, not on a rolling window, so tight retries keep failing. C fails because the developer environment cannot reach production envelopes.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. Use the rate-limit headers to slow down and resume after the hourly reset.
optionExplanations.B: The hourly limit resets at the top of each hour, so immediate retries keep failing and waste calls.
optionExplanations.C: Production contracts live in the production account; the developer environment cannot archive them.
optionExplanations.D: The hourly limit applies per account and is shared by all integration keys, so new keys add no capacity.

decode.needs: Back off using rate-limit headers when the per-account hourly limit is reached.
clues: unattended nightly job, no one at the keyboard -> the code must handle limits itself
maximum number of hourly API invocations exceeded -> per-account hourly limit, resets on the hour
database upgrade next quarter -> red herring

concept.title: Back off with rate-limit headers
concept.line: Watch X-RateLimit-Remaining and X-RateLimit-Reset, pause near zero and resume at the hourly reset; extra keys do not raise the account limit.

stem: A GetAgreementsList request must return only agreements with a term of three years or more. In which format does the provisions.term_length filter expect its value?

options.text: An integer number of months, such as 36
An integer number of days, such as 1095
A plain-language duration, such as 3 years
An ISO 8601 duration, such as P3Y

answerText: An ISO 8601 duration, such as P3Y
explanation: term_length filters take an ISO 8601 duration string such as P1Y or P3Y, combined with operators like gte.
whyNotOthers: D is right because Agreement Manager stores durations as ISO 8601 (for example term_length P3Y, renewal_notice_period P90D). The trap is A: 36 months is the same length, but the filter does not take integers. B and C are likewise not the expected format.

optionExplanations.A: Durations are not expressed as integer months.
optionExplanations.B: Durations are not expressed as integer days.
optionExplanations.C: Plain-language text is not accepted as a duration filter.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. ISO 8601 durations such as P3Y, used with operators such as gte.

concept.title: ISO 8601 durations
concept.line: Agreement Manager durations such as term_length and renewal_notice_period use ISO 8601 duration strings like P3Y or P90D.

stem: Which two are factors that lower an app's efficiency score in the API Usage Center? (Select two)

options.text: Using Connect instead of polling to track envelope status
Excessive requests for envelopes that do not exist
Calling listStatusChanges with overlapping time windows
Excessive document retrieval requests
Creating and sending each envelope in a single API call

answerText: Excessive requests for envelopes that do not exist; Excessive document retrieval requests
explanation: The efficiency score factors include excessive requests for nonexistent envelopes and excessive document retrieval requests.
whyNotOthers: B and D are right because both are on the efficiency factor list. The trap is C: it looks like wasted calls, but overlapping time spans in listStatusChanges are the recommended way to catch up without missing changes. A and E are best practices that reduce calls.

optionExplanations.A: Connect is the recommended alternative to polling and reduces API calls.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. Excessive requests for nonexistent envelopes is an efficiency score factor.
optionExplanations.C: Overlapping listStatusChanges time spans are the recommended catch-up pattern, not an efficiency factor.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. Excessive document retrieval requests is an efficiency score factor.
optionExplanations.E: Creating and sending in one call is the efficient pattern Docusign recommends.

concept.title: Efficiency score factors
concept.line: Factors include blocked calls, exceeded limits, excessive document, envelope, status and nonexistent-envelope requests, and low call activity.

topic: Per-instance brand on a web form
stem: Lumen Credit Union runs a template-based web form for auto-loan applications, embedded in its website, and the configuration already uses the credit union's own brand. For a three-month co-marketing campaign, applications that start from a car dealer partner's landing page must show the partner's co-branded logo and colors on both the form pages and the loan envelope signed afterwards; every other application keeps the normal look. The co-branded brand already exists in the account, and the backend creates one instance per applicant. Which approach fits?

options.text: Select the co-branded brand in the web form template's Advanced Options, so that both the form pages and the envelope use it for campaign applicants.
Select the co-branded brand under Branding on the configuration's Preview tab, so that campaign instances show the partner's logo on every page.
Pass the co-branded brand's brandId in Instances:createInstance for campaign applicants only, which brands both the form instance and its envelope.
Pass the co-branded brand's brandId in Envelopes:create after each campaign form is submitted, which re-brands the envelope the instance generated.

answerText: Pass the co-branded brand's brandId in Instances:createInstance for campaign applicants only, which brands both the form instance and its envelope.
explanation: A brandId in Instances:createInstance applies to both the web form instance and its envelope and overrides the configuration's brand, so it can be set per applicant ('applications that start from a partner's page').
whyNotOthers: C is right because only the request-level brandId is per instance and covers both the form and the envelope. The trap is A: a brand chosen in the web form template's Advanced Options affects envelopes only and applies to every applicant. B affects instances only, again for everyone, and D fails because the envelope is generated automatically on submission; the app does not call Envelopes:create.

optionExplanations.A: Web form template Advanced Options brand the envelopes only, and for every instance of the configuration.
optionExplanations.B: The Preview tab brand applies to instances only, not envelopes, and to all applicants.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. brandId in createInstance brands the instance and its envelope and overrides the configuration's brand.
optionExplanations.D: Docusign creates the envelope on submission with no Envelopes:create call from the app.

decode.needs: Per-instance brandId in Instances:createInstance for template-based forms.
clues: 'both the form pages and the loan envelope' -> brand must cover instance and envelope
'every other application keeps the normal look' -> per-instance override
'template-based' -> request-level brandId is supported (not for standalone)

concept.title: Branding web forms per instance
concept.line: brandId in createInstance brands instance and envelope and overrides configuration brands; template brand affects envelopes, Preview brand affects instances.

stem: Crestline Dental Group's new-patient intake workflow was published with the From a Link start method, and the link was placed on the clinic website and in an automatic email reply. The IT team has since switched the start method to From an API call and republished, so the practice-management system now starts instances with the patient's details. Nobody has removed the old button from the website yet, and the clinic's branding was refreshed in the same release. What is true about the old link?

options.text: It stopped working when the start method changed, because a workflow can only be started through the start method currently configured for it
It now asks the visitor to sign in to Docusign first, because a workflow set to From an API call requires an OAuth access token for every start
It can still open instances that were already in progress, but it can no longer create new instances once the start method has been changed
It still starts new instances, because the configured start method does not stop the workflow from being started in any of the other ways

answerText: It still starts new instances, because the configured start method does not stop the workflow from being started in any of the other ways
