explanation: The start method only surfaces shortcuts; it does not prevent starting the workflow in other ways, so a previously copied link can still trigger the workflow after the method changes to API.
whyNotOthers: D is right because a copied trigger link keeps working regardless of the configured start method. The trap is A: it sounds logical that the start method controls access, but the documentation explicitly says an existing link can still be used after switching to API. B fails because the trigger link is an unauthenticated endpoint, and C invents a rule about existing instances.

optionExplanations.A: The start method does not block other ways of starting the workflow; the existing link still works.
optionExplanations.B: The trigger link is an unauthenticated endpoint; it does not ask for a sign-in.
optionExplanations.C: There is no such rule; opening the link starts a new instance.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. Changing the start method does not prevent the workflow from being started in other ways, including the old link.

decode.needs: A start method is a configuration shortcut; an existing trigger link still starts instances after switching.
clues: switched start method to From an API call -> does not disable other start ways
old button still on the website -> link still creates new instances
branding refresh -> red herring

concept.title: Start method does not lock others
concept.line: The selected start method does not prevent starting a workflow in other ways; a previously copied trigger link still starts instances.

stem: In Authorization Code Grant, what is the correct order of the three required steps before calling the APIs?

options.text: Get user info, get an authorization code, exchange it for tokens
Get an authorization code, get user info, exchange it for tokens
Get an authorization code, exchange it for tokens, get user info
Exchange credentials for tokens, get an authorization code, get user info
Get an authorization code, exchange it for tokens, refresh the tokens

answerText: Get an authorization code, exchange it for tokens, get user info
explanation: The three required steps, in order, are acquire an authorization code, acquire tokens, then acquire user information; refreshing is an optional fourth step.
whyNotOthers: C is right because userinfo needs the access token, which needs the code. The trap is E: refreshing is a real step but optional, and it skips userinfo, which supplies the account_id and base_uri. A and B call userinfo before having a token, and D has no code to exchange.

optionExplanations.A: /oauth/userinfo needs a bearer token, so it cannot come first.
optionExplanations.B: userinfo needs the access token, which only exists after the code exchange.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. Code, then tokens, then userinfo (refresh is optional).
optionExplanations.D: Tokens are obtained by exchanging the authorization code, so the code must come first.
optionExplanations.E: Refresh is optional and this sequence skips userinfo, which supplies account_id and base_uri.

concept.title: Auth Code step order
concept.line: Authorization Code Grant: get code, exchange for tokens, call userinfo; refresh tokens is an optional later step.

stem: In which status can an extension app version be deleted directly in the Developer Console?

options.text: Draft
Rejected
Approved
Live

answerText: Draft
explanation: An extension app version can only be deleted when it is in Draft status.
whyNotOthers: A is right: only Draft versions can be deleted. The trap is B: a Rejected version must first have its publishing request cancelled so it reverts to Draft. C has the same restriction, and a Live version cannot be deleted at all.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. Deletion is allowed only in Draft status.
optionExplanations.B: Rejected is still part of the review process; cancel publishing to revert to Draft before deleting.
optionExplanations.C: Approved versions must be cancelled back to Draft before they can be deleted.
optionExplanations.D: Live versions cannot be deleted; removing a live app requires help through the Developer Community.

concept.title: Only Draft versions can be deleted
concept.line: Delete only Draft versions; cancel publishing to revert In Review, Approved or Rejected versions; Live versions cannot be deleted.

stem: A back-office script updates the same envelope with many separate PUT requests spread over one hour (not in a short burst). Which error is it most likely to receive?

options.text: Hourly_Envelope_Polling_Limit_Exceeded
Burst_APIInvocation_Envelope_Limit_Exceeded
Hourly_APIInvocation_Envelope_Limit_Exceeded
Burst_Envelope_Polling_Limit_Exceeded

answerText: Hourly_APIInvocation_Envelope_Limit_Exceeded
explanation: Too many PUT requests for one envelope in an hour returns Hourly_APIInvocation_Envelope_Limit_Exceeded; the Polling codes are for GET requests.
whyNotOthers: C is right because the requests are PUTs spread over an hour. The trap is A: it is also an hourly per-envelope code, but it is for GET (polling) requests. B is the PUT code for a 30-second burst, and D is the GET code for a burst.

optionExplanations.A: This code is for too many GET requests on one envelope in an hour, not PUTs.
optionExplanations.B: This is the PUT code for a 30-second burst; the stem says the calls are spread over an hour.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. Too many PUT requests for one envelope within an hour return this code.
optionExplanations.D: This is the GET (polling) code for a 30-second burst.

concept.title: Per-envelope limit codes
concept.line: Polling codes cover GET requests and APIInvocation codes cover PUT requests on one envelope; Hourly and Burst give the time window.

stem: Calder Mutual's team has finished building a claims-settlement app in its developer account and must launch it next month. The project manager wants a launch checklist in the right order, and the finance team has asked whether the review itself will be invoiced. The app uses Authorization Code Grant with a secret key and two redirect URIs, and the developer who built it is also an administrator of Calder's paid production account. Claims handlers will start using it on the first business day after launch. Which sequence should the checklist follow?

options.text: Make 20 successful calls with the key, choose Start Go live, select the production account, then set the key's classification once it appears in production and add the secret

Set the key's classification in the developer account, confirm a paid production account where the submitter is admin, choose Start Go live and select it, then add the secret and redirect URIs in production
Set the key's classification, sign in to the production account and choose Start Go live from its Apps and Keys page, after which the secret and redirect URIs carry over
Add the secret and redirect URIs in the production account first, set the key's classification, then choose Start Go live in the developer account and select the production account

answerText: Set the key's classification in the developer account, confirm a paid production account where the submitter is admin, choose Start Go live and select it, then add the secret and redirect URIs in production
explanation: Classification must be chosen before Go-Live, the submitter must administer a paid production account, Start Go live runs from the developer account's Apps and Keys, and secrets and redirect URIs are not copied, so they are added in production afterwards.
whyNotOthers: B is right because it follows create and classify, production account, submit, then configure production. The trap is C: it has the right steps in a plausible order, but Start Go live is chosen in the developer account, and secrets and redirect URIs are not duplicated. A uses the retired 20-call rule and classifies too late. D fails because the key does not exist in production until it is promoted.

optionExplanations.A: The 20-call rule was removed, and the classification must be chosen before Go-Live, not afterwards.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. Classify, have an admin on a paid production account, Start Go live from the developer account, then add the secret and redirect URIs in production.
optionExplanations.C: Start Go live is chosen from the developer account's Apps and Keys, and secrets and redirect URIs are not copied to production.
optionExplanations.D: The production copy of the key exists only after promotion, so its secret and redirect URIs cannot be added first.

decode.needs: Order the Go-Live steps from classification to production configuration.
clues: launch checklist in the right order -> Go-Live sequence
secret key and two redirect URIs -> must be re-created in production after promotion
will the review be invoiced -> red herring (submitting Go-Live has no cost)

concept.title: Go-Live step order
concept.line: Classify the key, secure an admin seat on a paid production account, Start Go live from the developer account, then configure secrets and redirects in production.

stem: Which two statements about Basic authentication for Docusign Connect are correct? (Select two)

options.text: It is available only for account-level and Recipient Connect configurations
It proves that the message body was not changed after Docusign sent it
It cannot be combined with OAuth for Connect on the same configuration
It can be added to an envelope-level eventNotification in Envelopes:create
It is the legacy username and password login retired by the OAuth rules

answerText: It is available only for account-level and Recipient Connect configurations; It cannot be combined with OAuth for Connect on the same configuration
explanation: Basic authentication adds a username and password header; it is available only for account-level and Recipient Connect and cannot be used with OAuth for Connect.
whyNotOthers: A and C are right per the Connect security guidance. The trap is D: HMAC works at every level, so it is tempting to assume Basic auth does too, but Basic auth is limited to account-level and Recipient Connect. B describes HMAC (integrity), and E confuses Basic auth for Connect with the retired legacy API login; it remains usable.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. Basic authentication applies to account-level and Recipient Connect configurations only.
optionExplanations.B: Integrity proof comes from HMAC; Basic auth only checks a shared username and password.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. A configuration cannot use Basic authentication together with OAuth for Connect.
optionExplanations.D: Envelope-level Connect is not among the configurations that support Basic authentication.
optionExplanations.E: Basic auth for Connect is separate from legacy username/password API authentication and can still be used.

concept.title: Basic auth limits for Connect
concept.line: Basic authentication works only for account-level and Recipient Connect, cannot be combined with OAuth for Connect, and gives no integrity proof.

stem: Which request sends an existing draft envelope?

options.text: POST .../envelopes/{envelopeId}/send with an empty body
PUT .../envelopes/{envelopeId} with status set to sent
PUT .../envelopes/{envelopeId}/recipients?resend_envelope=true
POST .../envelopes with the draft's envelopeId and status sent

answerText: PUT .../envelopes/{envelopeId} with status set to sent
explanation: A draft (status created) is sent with Envelopes:update, a PUT on the envelope with status sent in the body.
whyNotOthers: B is right because changing the status to sent releases the draft. The trap is C: resend_envelope forces a resend to recipients of an envelope already sent; it does not send a draft. A is not an eSignature endpoint, and D creates a new envelope.

optionExplanations.A: There is no /send endpoint on an envelope in the eSignature API.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. Envelopes:update with status sent sends the draft.
optionExplanations.C: resend_envelope re-notifies recipients of a sent envelope; it does not send a draft.
optionExplanations.D: POST /envelopes creates a new envelope rather than sending the existing draft.

concept.title: Send a draft with Envelopes:update
concept.line: Create with status created for a draft, then PUT the envelope with status sent; voiding uses the same call with status voided.

stem: Alder & Finch Consulting's engagement workflow has two Send Documents for Signature steps: one for the mutual NDA and, later, one for the master services agreement. The firm's records team wants both signed envelopes archived automatically to its cloud storage, using a storage extension app that an admin has installed and connected. Each envelope is a few megabytes today, but the MSA template is about to have large exhibits added. Separately, account managers sometimes send a side letter directly from eSignature outside the workflow. Which two statements describe a valid configuration? (Select two)

options.text: Add a separate file output step for each envelope, one for the NDA envelope and one for the MSA envelope, so each signed envelope is written to the storage
Add one file output step that selects both Send Documents for Signature steps, so both signed envelopes are written to storage in a single Write File action
Add the account managers' side letters to the same file output step by entering their envelope IDs, so all client paperwork lands in one folder
Keep each template's signed envelope at no more than 10 MB, because that is the maximum file size the cloud storage file output step supports
Skip a dedicated step and let the installed app archive every completed envelope in the account automatically, since it is connected at the account level

answerText: Add a separate file output step for each envelope, one for the NDA envelope and one for the MSA envelope, so each signed envelope is written to the storage; Keep each template's signed envelope at no more than 10 MB, because that is the maximum file size the cloud storage file output step supports
explanation: If several envelopes must be stored, the process builder defines a separate file output step for each one, and the maximum supported file size is 10 MB ('large exhibits added').
whyNotOthers: A and D are right. The trap is B: it sounds efficient, but a file output step writes one envelope, so two envelopes need two steps. C fails because only envelopes generated by a workflow Send Documents for Signature step can be written, and E fails because the extension runs only when a workflow step invokes it.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. Each envelope to be stored needs its own file output step.
optionExplanations.B: A single step does not write several envelopes; define one step per envelope.
optionExplanations.C: Only envelopes generated by the workflow's Send Documents for Signature steps can be written to cloud storage.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. The file output step supports files up to 10 MB, so the template must stay within that limit.
optionExplanations.E: The extension acts only when a running instance reaches a file output step; it is not an account-wide archive.

decode.needs: One file output step per workflow envelope, each file within 10 MB.
clues: two signing steps, both archived -> two file output steps
large exhibits about to be added -> 10 MB file limit
side letter sent directly from eSignature -> not a workflow envelope, cannot be written

concept.title: One storage step per envelope
concept.line: File output steps store only workflow-generated envelopes, one step per envelope, with a 10 MB maximum file size.

stem: Pinnacle Bank's online banking site will start an account-update workflow for customers who are already logged in. The site already knows each customer's name, email and account number, and the first step is a web form that should open with those three fields already filled in so the customer only reviews them. The bank's marketing team also wants a campaign code recorded, but that is optional and can wait for a later release. How should the process builder set up the workflow so the site's values reach the form?

options.text: Define step variables on the Collect Data with Web Forms step, and have the banking site write the customer's values into those step variables at the moment it starts the workflow
Skip the web form and map the customer's values directly to the agreement's fields in a Prepare eSignature Template step, so the customer reviews them during signing
Define starting variables in the workflow settings with the start method, pass the customer's values when the workflow is triggered, and map them to the web form's fields
Create a separate web form instance with the Web Forms API and prefill it there, then have the workflow pick up that instance in its first step afterwards

answerText: Define starting variables in the workflow settings with the start method, pass the customer's values when the workflow is triggered, and map them to the web form's fields
explanation: Starting variables are defined with the start method in workflow settings and receive values before the instance is created, for example from an external system such as a bank website; they are then mapped to fields used in a step such as a web form.
whyNotOthers: C is right because starting variables carry external values into the instance. The trap is A: step variables also hold data, but they are defined and populated by the steps themselves, not by the system that starts the workflow. B removes the required form review step, and D creates a form outside the workflow that the workflow cannot adopt.

optionExplanations.A: Step variables are populated by workflow steps, not passed in by the starting system.
optionExplanations.B: Removes the web form the stem requires the customer to review first.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. Starting variables receive values at trigger time and are mapped to web form fields.
optionExplanations.D: A standalone web form instance is not part of the workflow instance; prefill belongs in starting variables.

decode.needs: Use starting variables defined with the start method and map them to web form fields.
clues: site already knows customer values at start -> starting variables
web form opens already filled in -> map starting variables to form fields
campaign code optional later -> red herring

concept.title: External values use starting variables
concept.line: Starting variables are defined with the start method and filled when the workflow is triggered; step variables are filled by steps.

stem: Every night an unattended job in Orbis Wholesale's ERP finds contracts due for renewal within 60 days. For each one, a published workflow must run that reads the contract record, emails the account manager a reminder and writes a renewal flag back to the ERP; no step asks anyone to fill in or sign anything. The ERP must store, against each contract, an identifier for that night's run and later its final status, without anyone checking screens. The job runs in the company's data center and already uses JWT Grant for other Docusign calls. Which design fits?

options.text: Use From an API call: the job gets a token with aow_manage, calls triggerWorkflow with trigger_inputs, saves the returned instance ID, and later checks getWorkflowInstance
Use From an API call: the job calls triggerWorkflow, then loads each returned instance_url in an iframe on an operations dashboard so that each run can progress
Use From a Link: the job opens the workflow link for each contract with its values, and staff read each run's status from the workflow activity log each morning
Use Manually in Docusign: a back-office user with Workflows: Prepare runs Run Workflow for each due contract that the nightly job lists in a report

answerText: Use From an API call: the job gets a token with aow_manage, calls triggerWorkflow with trigger_inputs, saves the returned instance ID, and later checks getWorkflowInstance
explanation: An unattended system should start the workflow with triggerWorkflow, which returns an instance ID that can be stored and checked with getWorkflowInstance ('identifier for that night's run and later its final status'). With no UI steps, embedding is not recommended.
whyNotOthers: A is right because the API trigger returns the instance ID needed for automated tracking. The trap is B: the trigger call is right, but embedding is not recommended when no step has a UI, and the instance runs without anyone viewing it. C fails the 'without anyone checking screens' requirement, and D needs a person, but the job is unattended.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. aow_manage token, triggerWorkflow with trigger_inputs, store the instance ID, then track status with getWorkflowInstance.
optionExplanations.B: Docusign does not recommend embedding instances that have no UI steps; displaying them adds nothing.
optionExplanations.C: Relies on people reading logs, which breaks the requirement for automatic status in the ERP.
optionExplanations.D: Requires a human to start each run, but the process is an unattended nightly job.

decode.needs: Trigger via Maestro API from the unattended job and track each instance by ID; do not embed when there are no UI steps.
clues: unattended nightly job -> From an API call with an aow_manage token
identifier and final status stored in the ERP -> instance ID from trigger response, getWorkflowInstance
no step asks anyone to fill in or sign -> no reason to embed instance_url
already uses JWT Grant -> red herring, just add aow_manage

concept.title: No UI steps: do not embed
concept.line: Start unattended workflows with triggerWorkflow, store the returned instance ID and poll getWorkflowInstance; embedding is pointless without UI steps.

stem: Vantage Mutual's Connect listener sits behind a corporate API gateway that terminates TLS and forwards each request over the internal network to the claims service. Auditors want the claims service itself to prove that each event body is exactly what Docusign sent and that it came from Docusign. The platform team also has no appetite for a control that must be reworked whenever Docusign renews its certificate, roughly once a year. The configuration is account-level JSON SIM, and the claims service is written in Java. Which control should the developer implement?

options.text: Mutual TLS on the gateway, requesting Docusign's client certificate during the handshake so that only Docusign can connect to the listener
Basic authentication, validating the username and password that the gateway forwards in a header on every request to the claims service
HMAC, defining a secret key in Connect and having the claims service recompute HMAC-SHA256 of the body and compare it with the header
OAuth for Connect, validating the bearer token from the company's authorization server on every request before it reaches the claims service

answerText: HMAC, defining a secret key in Connect and having the claims service recompute HMAC-SHA256 of the body and compare it with the header
explanation: HMAC gives end-to-end authenticity and integrity that survive TLS termination at the gateway, and its shared secret is not tied to Docusign's certificate renewal. Docusign recommends it over mutual TLS for these reasons.
whyNotOthers: C is right because only HMAC lets the claims service itself verify that the body is unchanged and came from Docusign. The trap is A: mutual TLS does authenticate Docusign, but only at the gateway that terminates TLS, it gives no end-to-end integrity, and it must be updated when the certificate is renewed. B and D authenticate the caller but do not prove the body was not altered.

optionExplanations.A: Mutual TLS authenticates Docusign only at the TLS endpoint (the gateway), offers no message integrity check, and needs updating on certificate renewal.
optionExplanations.B: Basic authentication checks a shared username and password; it proves nothing about the body's integrity.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. HMAC-SHA256 over the body with a secret key proves authenticity and integrity end to end, independent of TLS termination or certificates.
optionExplanations.D: OAuth for Connect proves the caller with a token but does not prove that the body is unchanged.

decode.needs: HMAC validated by the back-end service.
clues: gateway terminates TLS -> transport-level checks stop at the gateway
prove the body is exactly what Docusign sent -> integrity -> HMAC
no rework when Docusign renews its certificate -> not mutual TLS
written in Java -> red herring

concept.title: HMAC gives end-to-end integrity
concept.line: HMAC proves sender and unchanged body end to end; mutual TLS authenticates only at the TLS endpoint and needs certificate maintenance.

stem: Northgate Archives sells a cloud vault and is building an extension app so customers can save completed agreements into it as a step in their Maestro workflows. Customer feedback is clear: when configuring the step, workflow designers want to pick the target drive and then browse to a folder, instead of typing a storage path by hand. Many of these customers also sync deal data with Salesforce. Northgate is a new app, not an update of an existing one. How should Northgate design the extension?

options.text: Use the file output cloud storage extension with only its required write-file action, because Maestro discovers the provider's drives and folders on its own
Use the file archive extension, because it is the file extension type that lets the workflow designer browse destinations in the storage provider
Use a Data IO extension whose Search Records action returns folders as records, so the designer can search for the destination while configuring the step
Use the file output cloud storage extension with its required write-file action plus the optional ListDrives and ListDirectoryContents capabilities

answerText: Use the file output cloud storage extension with its required write-file action plus the optional ListDrives and ListDirectoryContents capabilities
explanation: File output cloud storage is the extension for new apps that write documents to cloud storage from Maestro workflows. Capabilities are optional extras; the List Drives capability returns the storage drives so the workflow preparer can select one, and List Directory Contents supports browsing folders.
whyNotOthers: D is right because the required write action stores the file, and the optional capabilities give designers the drive and folder pickers they asked for. The trap is A: capabilities are optional, so without them nothing provides the drive list. B fails because file archive is the legacy extension that new apps should not use, and C misuses Data IO, which reads and writes system-of-record data rather than storing files.

optionExplanations.A: Capabilities are optional and must be implemented; without List Drives there is nothing for the designer to pick from.
optionExplanations.B: File archive is legacy; new extension apps should use file output cloud storage.
optionExplanations.C: Data IO moves structured data to and from a system of record; it is not the file storage extension.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. The write-file action is required, and the ListDrives and ListDirectoryContents capabilities let the preparer pick a drive and folder.

decode.needs: File output cloud storage with ListDrives and ListDirectoryContents capabilities
clues: save completed agreements as a workflow step -> file output cloud storage in Maestro
pick the drive and browse to a folder -> optional capabilities
new app -> not the legacy file archive extension
Salesforce sync -> red herring

concept.title: Capabilities add optional extension features
concept.line: Extensions require their contract actions; optional capabilities, like List Drives for file output, add features such as destination pickers.

stem: Northbay Property Management sends lease renewals from a server template that already defines the tenant role, the signature field and a text field with the data label monthlyRent. The leasing app must pre-fill each tenant's new rent and send the lease in a single Envelopes:create call, and the template must not be changed because the legal team owns it. The app also stores each tenant's parking space number, which is not on the lease. What should the request contain?

options.text: templateId plus a templateRoles entry for the tenant whose tabs include a textTabs item with tabLabel monthlyRent and the rent value
templateId plus templateRoles for the tenant, and a textCustomFields entry named monthlyRent so the template's field picks up that value
compositeTemplates with an inline template whose documents property re-uploads the lease PDF with the new rent already printed on it
templateId with status created, then EnvelopeRecipientTabs:update to set monthlyRent before a second call changes the status to sent

answerText: templateId plus a templateRoles entry for the tenant whose tabs include a textTabs item with tabLabel monthlyRent and the rent value
explanation: In the template reference model, templateRoles can carry tabs; a tab whose tabLabel matches the template field's data label receives the supplied value. The clue is 'single Envelopes:create call' with a template that must not change.
whyNotOthers: A is right because the value travels with the role mapping in one call. The trap is B: envelope custom fields are metadata about the envelope and do not populate document fields, even with a matching name. C replaces the template's document with a reprinted one and best practice puts documents on the composite document property; D works but needs extra calls, breaking the single-call requirement.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. templateRoles.tabs with a matching tabLabel pre-fills the template field.
optionExplanations.B: Envelope custom fields do not populate a document's text tabs.
optionExplanations.C: Reprinting the lease bypasses the template field and is not how values are pre-filled.
optionExplanations.D: This takes three calls instead of the single Envelopes:create required.

decode.needs: templateRoles tabs matched by tabLabel
clues: text field with data label monthlyRent -> tabLabel to match
single Envelopes:create call -> no follow-up tab updates
parking space number -> red herring

concept.title: Pre-fill template tabs by tabLabel
concept.line: With templateId and templateRoles, include tabs whose tabLabel matches the template field's data label to set its value.

stem: When a Connect delivery fails, Docusign retries with exponential back-off (5, 10, 20 and 40 minutes, then 1 hour, 2 hours and 1 day). For how long do the once-a-day retries continue before the event must be republished manually?

options.text: 24 hours
7 days
15 days
30 days

answerText: 15 days
explanation: After the back-off steps, Connect retries once per day for a 15-day span; events still failing after that must be republished.
whyNotOthers: C is right: the retry schedule ends with daily attempts over a 15-day span. The trap is D: 30 days is the default Connect Dashboard view period, not the retry window. A and B are shorter than the documented span.

optionExplanations.A: One day is only the last back-off step before the daily retries begin.
optionExplanations.B: Seven days is not a documented Connect limit; daily retries continue longer.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. Daily retries continue for a 15-day span; after that, republish the event.
optionExplanations.D: Thirty days is the Connect Dashboard's default time range, not the retry window.

concept.title: Retries run for 15 days
concept.line: Connect retries failed deliveries with exponential back-off, then daily for 15 days; after that, events must be republished manually.

stem: Copperline Telecom's customer care dashboard shows each step of a contract's journey: sent, opened by the customer, signed and completed. The integration uses an account-level Connect configuration in JSON aggregate mode that a contractor set up years ago. Agents complain that when a customer opens and signs within a minute, the opened step never appears, and the developer confirms there are no delivery failures in the Connect Dashboard. The dashboard team prefers JSON, and the listener already verifies HMAC. Which change resolves the gap?

options.text: Keep aggregate mode and sort incoming messages by their TimeGenerated value, so the dashboard can rebuild the opened step from the later message
Switch the configuration to XML aggregate mode, which keeps one message for every status change instead of folding statuses together
Add an eventNotification object to each new envelope, while keeping the account-level aggregate configuration that feeds the dashboard
Switch the configuration to JSON SIM, so each subscribed event, such as recipient-delivered, is sent as its own message when it occurs

answerText: Switch the configuration to JSON SIM, so each subscribed event, such as recipient-delivered, is sent as its own message when it occurs
explanation: In aggregate modes each message reflects the envelope status when the message is sent, so quick changes are folded into a later status. JSON SIM sends each event individually at the time it occurs, so "opened" (recipient-delivered) is never lost.
whyNotOthers: D is right because JSON SIM is event-focused and reports every subscribed event as it happens. The trap is A: TimeGenerated lets you order aggregate messages, but it cannot recover a status that was never sent because aggregation already moved to the later one. B fails because XML aggregate behaves the same way; C fails because the dashboard still reads the aggregate configuration.

optionExplanations.A: Ordering by TimeGenerated helps sequence messages, but aggregate messages carry the status at send time, so the opened step is simply not there to sort.
optionExplanations.B: XML aggregate uses the same aggregation behavior as JSON aggregate and also breaks the team's JSON preference.
optionExplanations.C: Envelope-level messages may help, but the dashboard keeps reading the aggregate configuration, so the gap remains unless that is changed.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. JSON SIM sends one message per event at the moment it occurs, including recipient-delivered for the opened step.

decode.needs: Move from aggregate to JSON SIM.
clues: opened step never appears when customers act within a minute -> aggregation folds quick status changes
no delivery failures -> not a retry problem
set up years ago by a contractor -> legacy mode
listener verifies HMAC -> red herring

concept.title: SIM reports every event
concept.line: Aggregate messages reflect status at send time and can fold quick changes; JSON SIM sends each event individually when it occurs.

stem: What does the Set Up Invite step do in a workflow?

options.text: It defines the participant roles available to later workflow steps
It sends an automated status email to someone about the agreement
It sends email workflow invitations so participants can do their steps
It displays a message telling a participant their tasks are complete

answerText: It sends email workflow invitations so participants can do their steps
explanation: Set Up Invite sends email workflow invitations to participants so they can complete their part of the workflow.
whyNotOthers: C is right because inviting participants by email is the purpose of Set Up Invite. The trap is B: it also sends email, but that describes the Send an Email step, which notifies people about status. A describes defining participants in the workflow settings, and D is the Show a Confirmation Screen step.

optionExplanations.A: Participants are defined in the workflow setup, not by Set Up Invite.
optionExplanations.B: That is the Send an Email step, used for status notifications.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. Set Up Invite emails workflow invitations to participants.
optionExplanations.D: That is the Show a Confirmation Screen step.

concept.title: Set Up Invite emails participants
concept.line: Set Up Invite emails workflow invitations to participants; Send an Email sends notifications; Show a Confirmation Screen displays messages.

topic: Envelope-level Connect on a limited plan
stem: Ridgeway Solar, a 12-person installer, sends every installation contract from its own scheduling app through Envelopes:create. Its Docusign plan does not include account-level Connect, and an upgrade is not in the budget. The operations manager wants residential contracts to report only their completion, while commercial contracts must also report each signer's progress, and both must update the scheduling app without any timed status checks. The app already stores the envelope ID returned at creation. Which design fits?

options.text: Add an eventNotification object to each Envelopes:create request, choosing the events per contract type so each envelope reports only what it needs
Create two account-level custom configurations, one for the residential and one for the commercial senders, each subscribed to its own set of events
Create a Recipient Connect configuration for the sales users, so that signer progress is reported for every contract those users send out
Call Envelopes:get once per envelope every 15 minutes from the scheduling app, which stays within the polling limit for both contract types

answerText: Add an eventNotification object to each Envelopes:create request, choosing the events per contract type so each envelope reports only what it needs
explanation: Envelope-level Connect (eventNotification) is available on all plans and lets each envelope request different events and data. The clues are "plan does not include account-level Connect" and different events per contract type.
whyNotOthers: A is right because the app creates every envelope through the API and can attach a tailored eventNotification. The trap is B: two account-level configurations would separate the event sets, but the plan does not include account-level Connect. C fails because Recipient Connect covers envelopes users receive, not send; D is a timed status check, which the manager ruled out.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. Envelope-level Connect is available on all plans and supports different events and data per envelope.
optionExplanations.B: Account-level Connect is available only on specific plans, and this plan does not include it.
optionExplanations.C: Recipient Connect reports envelopes that claimed-domain users receive, not the contracts the sales users send.
optionExplanations.D: Polling every 15 minutes is compliant but is exactly the timed status check the manager does not want.

decode.needs: Envelope-level Connect via eventNotification on Envelopes:create.
clues: plan does not include account-level Connect -> envelope-level is available on all plans
residential vs commercial report different events -> per-envelope settings
every contract sent from its own app through Envelopes:create -> app controls envelope creation
12-person installer -> red herring

concept.title: Envelope-level Connect for per-envelope needs
concept.line: Use eventNotification when your app creates envelopes via API and needs different events per envelope or lacks account-level Connect.

stem: Ashgrove Health's procurement assistant shows buyers a short AI-written overview of each supplier contract. It also blocks purchase orders when a contract has expired or its payment terms exceed 60 days. The product owner proposes using one source for both features to keep the code simple. Legal reminds the team that blocking decisions must rest on data that contract reviewers can confirm, and that an AI overview is not a statement of the binding terms. Which design fits?

options.text: Use CreateAgreementSummary for both features, and parse the expiration date and payment terms out of the summary text with the assistant's own language model.
Use GetAgreement provisions for both features, and compose the buyer overview from those provisions instead of requesting any Docusign AI summary.
Use CreateAgreementSummary only for the overview, and base the blocking rules on the expiration_date and payment_terms_due_date provisions.
Drive the blocking rules from GetAgreement provisions, and get the overview with a GET request to .../agreements/{agreementId}/summary for each contract.

answerText: Use CreateAgreementSummary only for the overview, and base the blocking rules on the expiration_date and payment_terms_due_date provisions.
explanation: CreateAgreementSummary gives an AI overview that may not capture all details or legal nuances, while provisions are structured values that reviewers can confirm or correct in the UI, which matches 'blocking decisions must rest on data that reviewers can confirm'.
whyNotOthers: C is right because each feature uses the source built for it. The trap is D: provisions for the rules is correct, but there is no GET summary endpoint; the overview comes from the POST CreateAgreementSummary. A builds blocking rules on unconfirmed AI prose, and B drops the AI-written overview the buyers asked for.

optionExplanations.A: Parsing AI prose bases blocking decisions on text that is not a reviewed statement of terms.
optionExplanations.B: Meets the rule but no longer gives buyers the AI-written overview the feature requires.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. Summary for reading, structured provisions for decisions.
optionExplanations.D: There is no GET summary endpoint; the summary is created with POST .../ai/actions/summarize.

decode.needs: Summary via CreateAgreementSummary; rules on GetAgreement provisions.
clues: 'AI-written overview' -> CreateAgreementSummary (POST)
'blocks purchase orders' -> structured provisions
'data that contract reviewers can confirm' -> provisions, reviewable in the UI

concept.title: Summaries inform, provisions decide
concept.line: Use CreateAgreementSummary for human-readable overviews and structured provisions from GetAgreement for automated business rules.

topic: Two applicants on an embedded web form
stem: Granary Bank opens joint savings accounts on a tablet in the branch. A banker starts an embedded instance of a template-based web form configured for two recipients, primary applicant and co-applicant, and the bank expects both applicants, sitting together, to fill in the form on the same tablet and then sign one account agreement. The configuration's Initiate signing session from email setting is off, and the branch Wi-Fi is reliable. Branch staff are measured on how quickly accounts are opened. What should the team plan for?

options.text: Create the instance with two clientUserId values, one per applicant, so that the tablet shows each applicant's part of the form in turn before signing.
Create one embedded instance per applicant on the tablet, so that each one fills in the form there and both sign the same account agreement afterwards.
Turn on Initiate signing session from email, which lets both applicants complete the form and then sign together on the tablet in one session.
Only the primary applicant completes the embedded instance on the tablet; the co-applicant reaches the form through a link in an envelope email.

answerText: Only the primary applicant completes the embedded instance on the tablet; the co-applicant reaches the form through a link in an envelope email.
explanation: An embedded instance is completed by a single user in the embedded view; additional recipients access the form through a link in the envelope email. The clue 'both applicants... on the same tablet' is the expectation the team must correct.
whyNotOthers: D is right because embedded delivery covers only the primary recipient. The trap is B: each web form instance generates its own envelope, so two instances produce two agreements, not one. A fails because clientUserId identifies one primary user per instance, and C switches the signing to email, which moves signing off the tablet rather than adding the co-applicant.

optionExplanations.A: clientUserId identifies the single primary user of an embedded instance; there is no second one.
optionExplanations.B: Each instance generates its own envelope, so the applicants would sign two separate agreements.
optionExplanations.C: That setting sends the submitter a signing link by email; it does not bring other recipients into the embedded session.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. Only the primary recipient uses the embedded view; additional recipients get an envelope email.

decode.needs: Embedded instance serves only the primary recipient; others get an envelope email.
clues: 'tablet in the branch' -> embedded instance
'two recipients... same tablet' -> only the primary recipient is embedded
'sign one account agreement' -> one instance, one envelope
'Wi-Fi is reliable' -> red herring

concept.title: Embedded web forms: one user
concept.line: An embedded web form instance is completed by one primary user; other recipients reach the form and envelope by email, one envelope per instance.

topic: Functional test for a Data IO app
stem: Pinewood Insurance's QA lead must reproduce what a real end user will experience with the company's new Data IO extension app before it is submitted for review. The app reads policyholder details from the policy administration system to prefill a form and writes any changes back. Connection and extension tests have already passed in the developer account. The policy team keeps its standard forms as eSignature templates, and the QA lead has a budget of two days. Which approach should the QA lead take?

options.text: Add the app's fields to an eSignature template, send an envelope to herself, and fill in the fields as a signer would to trigger the read and write actions
Build a Maestro workflow with a web form derived from the policy eSignature template between a data read step and a data write step, then run an instance
Create and publish a Maestro workflow with a data read step, a standalone web form step and a data write step, then execute an instance of the workflow
Rerun the extension tests for Search Records, Create Record and Patch Record from App Testing, since they replay the end-user flow for each action

answerText: Create and publish a Maestro workflow with a data read step, a standalone web form step and a data write step, then execute an instance of the workflow
explanation: Functional tests simulate the end-user experience, and for Data IO the supported functional test is a Maestro workflow test. The web form used in that workflow must be standalone; web forms derived from eSignature templates cannot be used in workflows.
whyNotOthers: C is right because Data IO is tested functionally through a workflow instance with read, standalone web form and write steps. The trap is B: it uses the right test type, but a web form derived from an eSignature template cannot be used in a workflow. A fails because the envelope test is not supported for Data IO, and D fails because extension tests are integration tests that call endpoints directly rather than simulating the end user.

optionExplanations.A: The envelope functional test is not supported for Data IO; Data IO runs in Maestro workflows.
optionExplanations.B: Right test type, but web forms derived from eSignature templates cannot be used in workflows; the form must be standalone.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. A workflow instance with read, standalone web form and write steps is the Data IO functional test.
optionExplanations.D: Extension tests call endpoints from the Docusign platform directly; they do not simulate the end-user experience.

decode.needs: A Maestro workflow functional test with a standalone web form
clues: reproduce what a real end user will experience -> functional test, not integration test
reads to prefill a form and writes back -> Data IO read and write steps in Maestro
standard forms kept as eSignature templates -> template-derived web forms cannot be used in workflows
two-day budget -> red herring

concept.title: Data IO functional tests use workflows
concept.line: Data IO and file output are functionally tested in Maestro workflows; connected fields and data verification in envelopes.

stem: Corvid Mutual is choosing recipient authentication for high-value claim settlement releases sent to claimants in the United States, Canada and Germany. The claims platform is being built against a Docusign developer account first and will go live in about four months, after a pilot with one regional claims office. Claimants log in to the claims portal before they are sent the release. The risk team wants a short list of facts before it picks a method. Which two statements are accurate? (Select two)

options.text: Phone authentication confirms the claimant's legal identity against a government record before the documents open.
Recording authenticationMethod on the recipient makes Docusign enforce the claims portal login before signing.
Knowledge-based authentication relies on US public records, so it does not suit the Canadian and German claimants.
Every authentication method, including ID Verification, is enabled by default in the developer environment for testing.
Phone authentication, knowledge-based authentication and ID Verification each carry a per-use fee in production.

answerText: Knowledge-based authentication relies on US public records, so it does not suit the Canadian and German claimants.; Phone authentication, knowledge-based authentication and ID Verification each carry a per-use fee in production.
explanation: KBA uses US public-record questions, so it only fits US recipients, and phone, KBA and ID Verification all incur per-use fees. The clue 'Canada and Germany' rules KBA out for most claimants.
whyNotOthers: C and E are right. The trap is D: every method except ID Verification is enabled in the developer environment; IDV must be requested from Docusign. A overstates phone authentication, which proves access to a phone number, not legal identity, and B describes a record on the certificate that Docusign does not enforce.

optionExplanations.A: Phone authentication proves access to the phone number by a code; it is not a government ID check.
optionExplanations.B: authenticationMethod only records the app's own authentication; nothing is enforced by Docusign.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. KBA questions come from US public records, so non-US claimants cannot use it.
optionExplanations.D: ID Verification is the one method not enabled by default in the developer environment.
optionExplanations.E: Correct. Phone, KBA and IDV each incur a per-use fee.

decode.needs: Know the limits and costs of each recipient authentication method.
clues: 'United States, Canada and Germany' -> KBA is US only
'developer account first' -> IDV not enabled by default in demo
'log in to the claims portal' -> authenticationMethod only records it

concept.title: Authentication trade-offs
concept.line: Access code is free and light; phone proves phone access; KBA is US only; IDV checks government ID, is not on in demo; phone/KBA/IDV cost per use.

stem: Ridgeview Health has contracted Coastal Integrators, a Docusign partner, to build an extension app that checks patient record numbers against the hospital's proprietary clinical system while forms are signed. Only Ridgeview's US production accounts will ever use it, so it will be a private app. Coastal's project manager writes down the assumptions for the rollout plan, noting that the hospital's own IT team also wants to try the app in its developer account. Which two assumptions are correct? (Select two)

options.text: Because the app is private, it can be published without any Docusign review, since that review applies only to apps listed for all customers
Docusign must still approve the private app before publication, although the approval guidelines are less stringent than for public apps
After publication, Coastal can also share the private app with the hospital's developer accounts so the IT team can try it there
If other hospitals ask for the app later, Coastal can switch the Live app's distribution to public without registering it again
An administrator of each shared production account must approve the private app before any user there can install and use it

answerText: Docusign must still approve the private app before publication, although the approval guidelines are less stringent than for public apps; An administrator of each shared production account must approve the private app before any user there can install and use it
explanation: Private extension apps still need Docusign approval before publication (with less stringent guidelines), and each production account's administrator must approve the shared app before its users can install it.
whyNotOthers: B and E are right: review still applies to private apps, and account admins approve shared private apps. The trap is C: private apps can be shared with additional production accounts but not with additional developer accounts. A is wrong because publishing still requires approval, and D is wrong because distribution cannot be changed once the app is Live.

optionExplanations.A: Private apps are not visible to all customers, but Docusign still must approve them before publication.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. Private apps go through Docusign approval, with guidelines less stringent than for public apps.
optionExplanations.C: Private apps can be shared with additional production accounts, not with additional developer accounts.
optionExplanations.D: Distribution type cannot be modified once the app is Live.
optionExplanations.E: Correct. An administrator of each production account must approve the private app before anyone in the account can use it.

decode.needs: Private distribution rules: review, admin approval, production accounts only
clues: only the hospital's own production accounts -> private distribution
built by a contracted partner -> partners can build private apps for customers
IT team wants it in its developer account -> private apps cannot be shared with other developer accounts

concept.title: Private apps: review plus admin approval
concept.line: Private apps still pass Docusign review, are shared only with production accounts, and each account admin must approve them.

stem: In a new developer account, GET /restapi/v2.1/accounts/{accountId}/identity_verification returns an empty array. What does this indicate?

options.text: No identity verification is configured for the account, so it must be enabled before testing.
The access token lacks a scope, so the endpoint hides configurations the account already has.
Workflows are listed only after an envelope with identity verification has been sent.
The v2 endpoint must be used, because v2.1 lists phone authentication workflows only.

answerText: No identity verification is configured for the account, so it must be enabled before testing.
explanation: Docusign states that if IDV is not configured for the account, the identity_verification call returns an empty array; ID Verification is not enabled by default in developer accounts.
whyNotOthers: A is right because an empty array means there is no configuration to return. The trap is B: a missing scope would produce an authorization error, not a silently empty list. C reverses the order (the workflowId is needed before sending), and D fails because identity verification by workflowId is a v2.1 feature.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. Empty means no identity verification configuration; IDV is not on by default in demo.
optionExplanations.B: Authorization problems return an error status, not an empty successful list.
optionExplanations.C: The workflowId is needed to send an envelope with verification, so it must be listed beforehand.
optionExplanations.D: identityVerification.workflowId is a REST v2.1 feature; v2 is not the fix.

concept.title: IDV must be configured first
concept.line: IdentityVerifications:list returns an empty array when IDV is not configured; IDV is not enabled by default in developer accounts.

topic: Connected field that must pass verification
stem: When an envelope with connected fields is created through the eSignature REST API, which extensionData property makes a field pass verification before the signer can complete the document?

options.text: actionInputKey
requiredForExtension
extensionGroupId
extensionContract

answerText: requiredForExtension
explanation: requiredForExtension is the boolean that indicates whether the field must pass verification to sign the document.
whyNotOthers: B is right because requiredForExtension controls whether verification must succeed. The trap is A: actionInputKey is required too, but it names the input data key used for verification, not whether it must pass. C groups tabs that belong to the same model, and D names the template that defines the extension.

optionExplanations.A: actionInputKey identifies the input data key used for the verification request.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. When true, the field must pass verification before the document can be signed.
optionExplanations.C: extensionGroupId ties together tabs that belong to the same data model or concept.
optionExplanations.D: extensionContract indicates the template that defines the extension.

concept.title: Connected fields extensionData
concept.line: Connected fields tabs carry extensionData from discovery; requiredForExtension decides whether verification must pass before signing.

stem: In Public Authorization Code Grant, what does the app send to /oauth/token in place of a Basic header built from a secret key?

options.text: The code_challenge in the request body
The state value in the request body
The code_verifier in the request body
The integration key alone in a Basic header
The code_challenge_method in a request header

answerText: The code_verifier in the request body
explanation: For Public Auth Code Grant the Basic header is not used; instead the body carries the code_verifier, the random string from which the code_challenge was derived.
whyNotOthers: C is right because the token endpoint hashes the code_verifier and compares it with the code_challenge sent earlier. The trap is A: the code_challenge went on the /oauth/auth request; sending it again would prove nothing. B is the CSRF value checked by the app itself, D is not how Docusign authenticates public clients, and E belongs on /oauth/auth and is always S256.

optionExplanations.A: The challenge was already sent on /oauth/auth; the token request must reveal the original verifier.
optionExplanations.B: state is checked by the app on the redirect, not sent to the token endpoint.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. Public clients send the code_verifier in the body instead of a secret-based Basic header.
optionExplanations.D: There is no secret-less Basic header; public clients prove themselves with the code_verifier.
optionExplanations.E: code_challenge_method (S256) is sent on /oauth/auth, not on the token request.

concept.title: Verifier replaces the secret
concept.line: Public clients send code_challenge on /oauth/auth and the original code_verifier on /oauth/token instead of a secret.

topic: Direct vs remote signing in a workflow
stem: Westfield Auto Finance runs its loan workflow on a tablet at the dealership desk. The buyer, who is at the desk, must sign the retail installment contract on the tablet right away without leaving to check email. The co-buyer, the buyer's spouse, is at work across town and signs next, and the dealership's finance manager countersigns last from the back office. The contract template has three signer roles, and the dealership uses its own branded tablet stand. How should the Send Documents for Signature step be configured?

options.text: Use a direct signing session for all three signers in turn on the dealership tablet, so every signature is captured during the same visit
Use remote signing for the buyer so the invitation arrives on the tablet's mail app, and direct signing for the co-buyer and the finance manager
Make the finance manager the first signer in a direct session at the desk, then send the buyer and the co-buyer remote email invitations to sign
Make the buyer the first signer in a direct signing session on the tablet, then have the co-buyer and finance manager sign through email notifications

answerText: Make the buyer the first signer in a direct signing session on the tablet, then have the co-buyer and finance manager sign through email notifications
explanation: In a Send Documents for Signature step, only the first signer can use direct (embedded) or remote signing; all later signers must access their sessions through email notifications. The buyer 'must sign on the tablet right away', so the buyer is first and direct.
whyNotOthers: D is right because the buyer signs directly as first signer and the others follow by email. The trap is A: a direct session sounds ideal at a kiosk, but signers after the first must use email notifications. B fails because the buyer would have to open email, and C puts the wrong person first and sends the buyer away to email.

optionExplanations.A: Only the first signer can use a direct session; later signers must use email notifications.
optionExplanations.B: The buyer must not depend on email, and later signers cannot use direct signing.
optionExplanations.C: The buyer, not the finance manager, must sign immediately on the tablet.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. First signer direct on the tablet, subsequent signers by email notification.

decode.needs: First signer uses a direct signing session; subsequent signers receive email notifications.
clues: buyer signs on the tablet right away -> first signer, direct (embedded) session
spouse across town and back-office countersigner -> later signers via email
branded tablet stand -> red herring

concept.title: Only first signer can be direct
concept.line: In Send Documents for Signature, the first signer can sign direct or remote; every subsequent signer accesses signing through email.

stem: A finance department wants every completed vendor contract copied to its OneDrive automatically. No developer is available, so the account administrator must set it up alone in eSignature Admin. What should they use?

options.text: A custom account-level Connect configuration that posts envelope-completed events to OneDrive
The preset (pre-built) OneDrive Connect configuration in eSignature Admin
An envelope-level eventNotification with documents included on each vendor contract
A Recipient Connect configuration for the finance users with documents included

answerText: The preset (pre-built) OneDrive Connect configuration in eSignature Admin
explanation: Docusign offers preset Connect configurations that send envelope documents and data to Box, OneDrive, Salesforce and eOriginal without custom code, which fits "no developer is available".
whyNotOthers: B is right because the preset OneDrive configuration is set up by an administrator and needs no listener. The trap is A: a custom configuration also sends envelope-completed events, but it needs a listener app to receive them and upload the file, which means code. C requires API changes to every send; D covers envelopes the finance users receive, not completed vendor contracts in general, and still needs a listener.

optionExplanations.A: A custom configuration posts messages to a listener you must build; OneDrive does not process Connect messages by itself.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. Preset Connect configurations push documents to Box, OneDrive, Salesforce and eOriginal without development.
optionExplanations.C: eventNotification is set in Envelopes:create through the API, which requires a developer.
optionExplanations.D: Recipient Connect is for envelopes your users receive and still delivers to a custom listener.

concept.title: Preset Connect for common targets
concept.line: Pre-built Connect configurations push documents to Box, OneDrive, Salesforce and eOriginal; custom Connect needs your own listener.

stem: Tamsin, the only developer at Rowan Insurance, created the company's developer account and its integration keys under her own work email, and she plans to submit the claims app for Go-Live this week. Rowan's production Docusign account is run by the IT operations team. Her manager worries that if Tamsin leaves, nobody will be able to manage the keys or their production settings. Rowan also plans a second app next quarter and recently changed its email provider. What should the team do before submitting?

options.text: Submit from Tamsin's developer account and select her personal production user, then hand her password to IT operations if she ever leaves the company
Wait until IT operations opens its own developer account, because the production account chosen at Go-Live must use the same email as the developer account
Promote the key into Rowan's production account and then close Tamsin's developer account, because a live key no longer depends on the developer copy
Use a shared team mailbox for the developer account and for the production account that will manage the keys, with an administrator on that production account

answerText: Use a shared team mailbox for the developer account and for the production account that will manage the keys, with an administrator on that production account
explanation: Docusign recommends a shared email alias or mailbox for both the developer account and the production account that manages the keys, so access survives staff changes; the submitter still needs admin rights there.
whyNotOthers: D is right because a shared mailbox keeps ownership with the team rather than with Tamsin. The trap is B: it sounds like a rule, but you may select a production account with a different email from the developer account. A depends on sharing a personal password. C fails because the developer copy of the key stays in use for regression testing, and closing it removes the place where the key is maintained.

optionExplanations.A: Tying keys to a personal user and sharing passwords is fragile and against good practice; a shared team mailbox avoids this.
optionExplanations.B: The production account selected at Go-Live may use a different email address from the developer account.
optionExplanations.C: The developer key stays in use after Go-Live, for example for regression testing, so closing that account loses it.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. A shared mailbox for both the developer account and the managing production account keeps key ownership with the team.

decode.needs: Keep integration key management independent of one employee.
clues: only developer, keys under her own email -> single point of failure
nobody able to manage the keys if she leaves -> use a shared team mailbox for the developer and managing production accounts
changed email provider, second app next quarter -> red herrings

concept.title: Shared mailbox for key management
concept.line: Use a team email alias for the developer account and the production account that manages keys; the production account email may differ.

topic: Extension template value for Data IO
stem: In an app manifest for a Data IO app, which value belongs in extensions.template?

options.text: DataIO.Version6.SearchRecords
DataIO.Version6.GetTypeDefinitions
DataIO.Version6.DataInputOutput
FileIO.Version1.FileOutputCloudStorage

answerText: DataIO.Version6.DataInputOutput
explanation: For a Data IO app registered by manifest, extensions.template is DataIO.Version6.DataInputOutput; values such as DataIO.Version6.SearchRecords go in actions.template.
whyNotOthers: C is right because the extension contract for Data IO is DataIO.Version6.DataInputOutput. The trap is A: SearchRecords is an action contract value used in actions.template, not the extension template. B is also an action value, and D is the extension template for file output cloud storage.

optionExplanations.A: This is an action contract value used in actions.template.
optionExplanations.B: This is an action contract value used in actions.template.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. DataIO.Version6.DataInputOutput is the Data IO extension contract set in extensions.template.
optionExplanations.D: This is the extension template for file output cloud storage, not Data IO.

concept.title: Extension template versus action template
concept.line: extensions.template names the extension contract; actions.template names an action contract, such as DataIO.Version6.SearchRecords.

stem: Tidewater Utilities has a workflow with a writeback step from its own extension app that updates the customer's service order in the billing platform. In test instances, the web form and signing steps complete, but the Connect listener (configured for JSON SIM) receives workflow-failed when the instance reaches the writeback step. The workflow published without errors last week, and the billing team recently rotated its firewall rules. The developer needs detailed error messages about why the call to the billing platform fails. What is the best next step?

options.text: Run the pre-publication check again with isPreRunCheck=true, because it lists the error each step returned during the failed test instances
Run the extension app's connection and extension tests in the Developer Console, which return detailed error messages for the calls to the external system
Change the Connect configuration's message format to JSON SIM with extension data included, so the workflow-failed event carries the billing error
Cancel the failed test instance with cancelWorkflowInstance and trigger a new one using a token that includes the aow_manage scope to retry the step

answerText: Run the extension app's connection and extension tests in the Developer Console, which return detailed error messages for the calls to the external system
explanation: When an extension is not invoked successfully, run the Developer Console connection and extension tests for the extension app to get detailed error messages; the failure is at the call to the billing platform ('rotated its firewall rules').
whyNotOthers: B is right because the Developer Console tests exercise the app's connection and actions against the external system and report detailed errors. The trap is A: the pre-publication check validates configuration and consent before publishing, not runtime calls made by past instances. C fails because the listener is already on JSON SIM and the event does not report the external API's error, and D retries without diagnosing anything.

optionExplanations.A: The pre-publication check reviews configuration and consent; it does not report runtime errors from earlier instances.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. Developer Console connection and extension tests give detailed error messages for the extension's external calls.
optionExplanations.C: The listener already uses JSON SIM; changing format settings does not diagnose the external call.
optionExplanations.D: Canceling and retriggering repeats the failure without revealing its cause; the trigger already worked.

decode.needs: Diagnose a failing extension step with the Developer Console connection and extension tests.
clues: workflow-failed at the writeback step -> extension call to the external system fails
rotated firewall rules -> external connectivity, test the app's connection
published without errors last week -> pre-publication check is not the tool

concept.title: Test the extension, not the workflow
concept.line: When an extension step fails at runtime, run the app's Developer Console connection and extension tests for detailed error messages.

stem: Which two capabilities need the composite templates model rather than the template reference model? (Select two)

options.text: Assigning recipients to the template's roles by matching roleName
Creating the envelope as a draft with status created
Combining two different server templates in one envelope
Pre-filling a template's text field with a value when creating it
Reusing one server template twice with a different recipient each

answerText: Combining two different server templates in one envelope; Reusing one server template twice with a different recipient each
explanation: The template reference model uses one template; combining templates, or applying the same template several times with different recipients, needs composite templates.
whyNotOthers: C and E are right because only composite templates hold several template instances. The trap is D: pre-filling sounds advanced, but templateRoles can carry tabs with matching tabLabels in the template reference model. A and B are available in both models.

optionExplanations.A: templateRoles maps people to roles by roleName in the template reference model too.
optionExplanations.B: Any model can create a draft with status created.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. Combining several server templates requires composite templates.
optionExplanations.D: templateRoles tabs can pre-fill values in the template reference model.
optionExplanations.E: Correct. Reusing one template for several recipients needs separate composite template objects.

concept.title: When composite templates are required
concept.line: Use composite templates to combine templates, reuse a template several times, or add documents; simple role mapping and tab values work with templateRoles.

stem: Which value goes in the alg field of the JWT header that an integration signs for Docusign JWT Grant?

options.text: HS256
ES256
PS256
RS256

answerText: RS256
explanation: The JWT header is {"alg": "RS256", "typ": "JWT"}, signed with the RSA private key created in Apps and Keys.
whyNotOthers: E is right because Docusign JWTs are signed with the app's RSA private key using RS256. The trap is B: S256 is the PKCE code_challenge_method, not a JWT signing algorithm. A is a shared-secret HMAC algorithm, and C and D are other asymmetric algorithms Docusign does not use for this.

optionExplanations.A: HMAC with a shared secret; Docusign JWTs are signed with an RSA private key.
optionExplanations.B: S256 is the PKCE code_challenge_method, not a JWT signing algorithm.
optionExplanations.C: Elliptic-curve signing; Docusign keys are RSA.
optionExplanations.D: An RSA-PSS variant that Docusign does not specify for JWT Grant.
optionExplanations.E: Correct. The header uses alg RS256 with typ JWT.

concept.title: JWT signed with RS256
concept.line: Docusign JWT assertions use header alg RS256, signed with the RSA private key from Apps and Keys.

topic: Auth Code vs JWT for named users
stem: At Orchard Mutual, about 250 underwriters use an in-house underwriting workbench, hosted on company servers, to send policy documents. Each underwriter must send from their own Docusign account so envelopes sit in their own Sent folder and the audit trail names them. An architect proposes JWT Grant impersonating every underwriter so nobody ever sees a Docusign login, but the CISO refuses to give the workbench standing power to act as people who are not at the keyboard. Underwriters accept signing in now and then. The workbench runs on Kubernetes. Which approach fits best?

options.text: JWT Grant with admin consent for internal apps so underwriters never see a login, accepting impersonation because every underwriter is in the claimed domain
Public Authorization Code Grant with PKCE, because avoiding impersonation means the workbench must not hold any client secret on its servers
JWT Grant impersonating one shared sender account, so only a single consent is needed and the workbench never acts as individual underwriters
Confidential Authorization Code Grant with signature and extended scopes, so each underwriter signs in personally and the server renews tokens quietly
Confidential Authorization Code Grant with signature and impersonation scopes, so each underwriter signs in once and the server can act for them later

answerText: Confidential Authorization Code Grant with signature and extended scopes, so each underwriter signs in personally and the server renews tokens quietly
explanation: Users are present ("accept signing in now and then"), each sends as themselves, the server can hold a secret, and impersonation is ruled out, so Confidential Auth Code Grant fits; extended keeps refresh tokens rolling so sign-ins stay rare.
whyNotOthers: D is right because Docusign advises Auth Code Grant when an integration does not need impersonation, and extended limits re-login. The trap is A: it matches the convenience wish but grants exactly the impersonation the CISO refused. E adds impersonation, which serves only JWT. C breaks the own-Sent-folder requirement, and B wrongly ties avoiding impersonation to giving up a server-side secret.

optionExplanations.A: Admin consent still grants JWT impersonation, which the CISO explicitly refused.
optionExplanations.B: A server-hosted app can store a secret; avoiding impersonation does not require the public flow.
optionExplanations.C: A shared sender puts every envelope in one account, breaking the own-Sent-folder and audit requirement.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. Confidential Auth Code with signature and extended: personal sign-in, rolling refresh, no impersonation.
optionExplanations.E: impersonation is the consent scope for JWT Grant; it adds the standing power the CISO refused.

decode.needs: Confidential Authorization Code Grant, signature + extended scopes.
clues: own Sent folder, audit trail names them -> each user authenticates as themselves
no standing power to act as people not at the keyboard -> no JWT impersonation
hosted on company servers -> can store a secret
Kubernetes -> red herring

concept.title: Skip JWT without impersonation need
concept.line: If users are present and impersonation is not needed, Docusign recommends Authorization Code Grant over JWT Grant.

stem: Brightline, a Docusign partner, has a Live public extension app installed by about 300 customer accounts. Product management wants to add a phone verification extension to the same app. Customers must keep using the current app without interruption while the change goes through, and should not have to do anything to receive the new version. Brightline's sales team also wants to announce the feature at a conference next month, and the support desk is preparing a short help article. Which approach should Brightline follow?

options.text: Edit the Live version in place; registration changes to a Live app apply immediately to installed accounts, so customers get the new extension with no further review
Delete the Live version and register a new app that contains both extensions, then ask the 300 customers to install the new listing from the App Center
Update the registration, which creates a new Draft version; after review and publishing, the old version is Discontinued and each customer admin reinstalls the new one
Update the registration to create a new Draft version; once reviewed and published, the old version is Discontinued and installs upgrade automatically

answerText: Update the registration to create a new Draft version; once reviewed and published, the old version is Discontinued and installs upgrade automatically
explanation: Updating a Live app's registration creates a new Draft version that must be reviewed and published. On publication the new version becomes Live, the previous one becomes Discontinued, and accounts that had it installed are automatically upgraded.
whyNotOthers: D is right because versioning keeps the current Live version running during review and upgrades installed accounts automatically. The trap is C: it describes the same flow but wrongly requires admins to reinstall, which contradicts 'should not have to do anything'. A skips the new version and review, and B is impossible because a Live version cannot be deleted and would force customers to reinstall.
