optionExplanations.A: Updating a Live app creates a new Draft version that must pass review; nothing changes in place.
optionExplanations.B: Live versions cannot be deleted, and customers would have to reinstall a new listing.
optionExplanations.C: Same versioning flow, but installed accounts are upgraded automatically; admins do not need to reinstall.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. The new version goes through review and publishing, the old one becomes Discontinued, and installed accounts are upgraded automatically.

decode.needs: Extension app versioning: new Draft, review, publish, automatic upgrade
clues: add an extension to a Live app -> update registration, new Draft version
keep using it without interruption -> Live version stays until the new one is published
should not have to do anything -> installed accounts are upgraded automatically
conference next month -> red herring

concept.title: Live app updates create new versions
concept.line: Updating a Live app creates a Draft version; once published, the old version is Discontinued and installs upgrade automatically.

stem: Summit Fitness lets new members join on a tablet at the front desk. The membership agreement, embedded in the club's web app, includes a payment field that charges the first month's dues by card during signing. Marketing wants the signing area to sit neatly inside the club's branded page, and the IT lead has already prototyped focused view with Docusign JS. The club has 40 locations. Which approach should the developer use for this agreement?

options.text: Use focused view with frameAncestors and messageOrigins set correctly, because focused view supports payment fields once Docusign JS is loaded
Keep focused view for signing and send the payment as a separate remote envelope by email after the member has signed the agreement
Replace the envelope with a standalone web form, because web forms collect card payments and need no envelope at the front desk
Use classic view for this embedded signing session, because payment fields are among the features that focused view does not support

answerText: Use classic view for this embedded signing session, because payment fields are among the features that focused view does not support
explanation: Focused view is recommended for basic embedded signing, but classic view is required for payment tabs (also ID verification, some SBS providers, AI-Assisted Review and 21 CFR Part 11). The clue is 'payment field that charges the first month's dues during signing'.
whyNotOthers: D is right because the payment field rules out focused view. The trap is A: frameAncestors and messageOrigins are required for focused view, but no configuration makes it support payment tabs. B breaks the requirement to charge during signing, and C drops the envelope, while a standalone web form has no signing step at all.

optionExplanations.A: Correct configuration of focused view still does not enable payment tabs.
optionExplanations.B: Splitting payment into a later email breaks 'charge during signing' and adds friction.
optionExplanations.C: A standalone web form produces no envelope and no signature.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. Payment tabs need classic view.

decode.needs: Embedded signing in classic view because of payment
clues: payment field that charges dues during signing -> payment tab
IT already prototyped focused view -> red herring that tempts A
40 locations -> red herring

concept.title: Classic view for payments
concept.line: Choose focused view for simple embedded signing; use classic view for payment tabs, IDV, some SBS providers or Part 11.

stem: Lucia is preparing the Developer Console integration testing plan for her team's connected fields app, which verifies customer IDs against their CRM. The CRM's OAuth server and API are both reachable on public HTTPS endpoints, and the app has been installed to her developer account. The plan will be reviewed by an architect who often asks why the order matters. She will change the registration several times while testing, and the CRM team wants the results by Friday. Which two statements belong in her plan? (Select two)

options.text: After every change to the registration, uninstall and reinstall the app in the developer account so the tests use the updated values
Run the extension tests before configuring the connection, because they only check that each action endpoint answers on its configured URL
Run the connection test first, signing in with the authorization provider's credentials, because extension tests reuse that authorization
Treat passing extension tests as proof of the signer's experience, because they call the endpoints from inside a test envelope
Expect extension tests to call each action's params.uri from the Docusign platform and confirm the response format

answerText: Run the connection test first, signing in with the authorization provider's credentials, because extension tests reuse that authorization; Expect extension tests to call each action's params.uri from the Docusign platform and confirm the response format
explanation: A connection test obtains authorization using the provider credentials you supply, and extension tests use that authorization, so the connection test must pass first. Extension tests call each action's endpoint from the Docusign platform and confirm the response format.
whyNotOthers: C and E are right because they describe the required order and what extension tests actually check. The trap is A: updates to the registration are applied automatically to the installed version, so no reinstall is needed. B reverses the required order, and D confuses integration tests with functional tests, which are the ones that exercise envelopes or workflows.

optionExplanations.A: Registration updates are applied automatically to the installed app; reinstalling is unnecessary.
optionExplanations.B: A successful connection test is required before extension tests can run.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. The connection test obtains authorization with the provider credentials, and extension tests reuse it.
optionExplanations.D: Extension tests call endpoints directly; the signer experience is checked by functional tests.
optionExplanations.E: Correct. Extension tests send requests to each params.uri from the Docusign platform and check the response format.

decode.needs: The integration test order and what each test checks
clues: why the order matters -> extension tests reuse the connection test's authorization
will change the registration several times -> updates apply automatically, no reinstall
public HTTPS endpoints -> red herring here, endpoints are reachable

concept.title: Connection test before extension tests
concept.line: Connection tests obtain authorization that extension tests reuse; registration updates apply automatically to the installed app.

stem: Which workflow step type is not supported when an integration embeds workflow instances in its own web application?

options.text: Collect Data with Web Forms
Collect Data from an ID
Send an Email
Show a Confirmation Screen

answerText: Collect Data from an ID
explanation: All step types are supported in embedded workflow instances except Collect Data from an ID.
whyNotOthers: B is right because Collect Data from an ID is the single step type excluded from embedded instances. The trap is A: a web form step also collects data, but it is supported when embedded. C and D are supported too, although a workflow made only of non-UI steps is not worth embedding.

optionExplanations.A: Supported in embedded instances.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. The only step type not supported with embedded workflow instances.
optionExplanations.C: Supported; it runs without a UI, so it does not affect embedding.
optionExplanations.D: Supported; often the last step a participant sees.

concept.title: Embedded: no Collect Data from ID
concept.line: Embedded workflow instances support all step types except Collect Data from an ID; identity checks are limited to Phone Authentication.

stem: An embedded signer clicks Finish Later in the signing session. Which event value does Docusign append to the returnUrl?

options.text: cancel
decline
session_timeout
ttl_expired

answerText: cancel
explanation: event=cancel means the recipient decided to finish later.
whyNotOthers: A is right because Finish Later is reported as cancel. The trap is B: decline means the recipient refused to sign, which ends the envelope. C means the signer did not finish in time (20 minutes), and D means the signing URL token was not used in time or was already used.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. cancel = the recipient chose to finish later.
optionExplanations.B: decline = the recipient refused to sign.
optionExplanations.C: session_timeout = the signer did not finish within the session timeout.
optionExplanations.D: ttl_expired = the URL token expired or was already used.

concept.title: returnUrl event meanings
concept.line: signing_complete, cancel (finish later), decline, session_timeout, ttl_expired (URL unused in time or reused), viewing_complete.

stem: Westbrook Consulting, a systems integrator, has been hired by Halden Hospitals to build an onboarding portal that Halden's HR staff will use to send employment contracts. Halden has its own production Docusign account and will be the only organization that ever uses the portal; Westbrook hands over the code when the project ends. Westbrook is not a Docusign partner and has no plans to sell the portal to anyone else. The portal will be hosted in Halden's Azure tenant. Which classification should be selected for the portal's integration key?

options.text: Public integration, because an outside vendor is building the app for a customer that signs in with its own Docusign account
Third-party integration key, because Halden is adopting an app that an outside firm built and must provide its own key for it
Private custom integration, because the portal will be used directly by the employees of one customer organization
Embedded integration, because Westbrook is building Docusign signing into a product that it delivers to its client

answerText: Private custom integration, because the portal will be used directly by the employees of one customer organization
explanation: Private custom integration covers an integration used directly by your employees or your customers' employees; here Halden's HR staff are the only users and the portal is a one-off build.
whyNotOthers: C is right because a single organization's employees use a custom-built app. The trap is B: Third-party integration key is for a Docusign partner's integration that asks you for your own key, and Westbrook 'is not a Docusign partner'. A fails because Public is a multi-customer product from a Partner Program member. D fails because Embedded means customers use the vendor's Docusign account, and Halden uses its own.

optionExplanations.A: Public needs a multi-customer product and Partner Program membership; this portal serves one organization and Westbrook is not a partner.
optionExplanations.B: Third-party integration key applies to a Docusign partner integration that asks for your own key; this is a custom build for one client.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. The portal is used directly by one customer's employees, which is a Private custom integration.
optionExplanations.D: Embedded is for ISV Embed partners whose customers use the vendor's account; Halden uses its own account.

decode.needs: Classify a custom app built for and used by a single organization's staff.
clues: only organization that ever uses the portal -> not a multi-customer product
HR staff will use it -> used directly by the customer's employees (Private custom)
not a Docusign partner, no plans to sell -> not Public or Third-party
hosted in Halden's Azure tenant -> red herring

concept.title: Private custom integration classification
concept.line: An app used directly by your own or a client's employees, not sold to many Docusign customers, is a Private custom integration.

stem: Ashford Property Management's leasing team ran a bulk send of 40,000 lease renewals this morning. Its account-level JSON SIM configuration includes documents in every message, and the listener, a single virtual machine, is now overloaded and failing requests. The infrastructure team needs about four hours to add servers and does not want to lose any lease events or change the configuration's settings. requiresAcknowledgement is already true and the listener validates HMAC. What should the developer do?

options.text: Pause the configuration until the servers are added; retries skipped while paused are not lost and resume at the next scheduled retry
Set requiresAcknowledgement to false until the servers are added, so that Connect stops retrying and the listener has room to recover
Delete the configuration and recreate it with identical settings once the servers are added, then republish the morning's envelopes
Switch the configuration to aggregate mode for the afternoon, so Connect groups the lease events into fewer and larger messages

answerText: Pause the configuration until the servers are added; retries skipped while paused are not lost and resume at the next scheduled retry
explanation: Pausing (pausePublish) halts processing without changing settings or resetting the retry schedule; skipped retries are not lost and resume at the next scheduled interval. It requires requiresAcknowledgement=true, which is already set.
whyNotOthers: A is right because a pause fits "do not lose any events or change settings" for a four-hour window well inside the 15-day retry span. The trap is B: turning off acknowledgement does ease the load, but failed events are then not retried and are effectively lost. C changes and rebuilds the configuration and forces manual republishing; D changes settings and moves to a legacy mode.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. Account- and org-level configurations can be paused; retries scheduled during the pause are skipped but not lost and resume afterwards.
optionExplanations.B: Without acknowledgement, failed deliveries are not retried, so events during the overload would be lost.
optionExplanations.C: Deleting and recreating changes the setup and loses the retry history, forcing manual republishing.
optionExplanations.D: Aggregate is a legacy mode and changing the delivery mode is a settings change the team ruled out.

decode.needs: Pause the Connect configuration (pausePublish) temporarily.
clues: listener overloaded after a bulk send -> temporary halt needed
do not lose any events or change settings -> pause, not acknowledgement off or rebuild
about four hours -> well inside the retry window
listener validates HMAC -> red herring

concept.title: Pause instead of dropping events
concept.line: Pausing a Connect configuration halts processing without losing events; retries resume at the next scheduled interval after unpausing.

stem: A successful Workflows:triggerWorkflow call returns which two values that an integration typically keeps?

options.text: The new instance's ID and the workflow instance URL
The envelope ID and the recipient signing URL
The workflow ID and the trigger input schema
The instance's ID and a consentUrl to approve it

answerText: The new instance's ID and the workflow instance URL
explanation: The trigger response returns the new instance's identifier and a workflow instance URL that can be used to interact with or embed the instance.
whyNotOthers: A is right because the instance ID and instance URL come back from the trigger. The trap is C: the workflow ID and trigger input schema relate to triggering, but they come from getWorkflowTriggerRequirements before the trigger call. B belongs to eSignature embedded signing, and D mixes in consentUrl, which comes from a failed pre-publication check.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. The instance ID for tracking and the instance URL for display or embedding.
optionExplanations.B: These come from eSignature envelope creation and recipient views.
optionExplanations.C: The input schema comes from getWorkflowTriggerRequirements, called before triggering.
optionExplanations.D: consentUrl is returned by a failed pre-publication consent check, not by the trigger.

concept.title: Trigger returns instance ID and URL
concept.line: triggerWorkflow returns the new instance ID and instance URL; getWorkflowTriggerRequirements supplies the trigger URL and input schema beforehand.

topic: Save and resume a long web form
stem: Applicants for Riverbend University's graduate scholarships complete a long template-based web form embedded in the applicant portal, which renders it with Docusign JS. Many applicants need to look up transcripts and references, so the admissions office wants them to be able to stop halfway, close the browser, and continue another day without retyping anything. Applicants already authenticate to the portal with the university's single sign-on. How should the developer implement this?

options.text: Store the entered values in the portal's database from Docusign JS events, then create a new instance next time with those stored values in formValues.
Create remote instances with sendOption now so that applicants can reopen the form from the envelope email whenever they want to continue.
Set hideWelcomePage to true in webFormOptions so the saved instance reopens on the last page the applicant viewed when it is rendered again.
Set showFinishLater to true in webFormOptions, then later refresh the same instance's token and render it so Docusign restores the saved values.

answerText: Set showFinishLater to true in webFormOptions, then later refresh the same instance's token and render it so Docusign restores the saved values.
explanation: showFinishLater adds a Finish Later button that saves partial values; rendering the same instance again after refreshing its token restores them. The clue is 'stop halfway ... continue another day without retyping'.
whyNotOthers: D is right because Finish Later is the built-in save-and-resume feature of embedded instances. The trap is A: it rebuilds a new instance from copied data, which is custom work the feature already provides. B changes the delivery model away from the portal, and C only hides the welcome page.

optionExplanations.A: Possible but unnecessary custom storage; Finish Later already saves values on the same instance.
optionExplanations.B: Remote delivery moves the form out of the portal and does not add a save-for-later function.
optionExplanations.C: hideWelcomePage only skips the welcome page; it does not save or restore values.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. showFinishLater saves the partial form; refreshToken plus rendering the same instance restores it.

decode.needs: Built-in save and resume of an embedded instance: showFinishLater, then refreshToken on the same instance.
clues: 'stop halfway ... continue another day' -> Finish Later
'renders it with Docusign JS' -> webFormOptions are available
'single sign-on' -> red herring

concept.title: Finish Later for web forms
concept.line: showFinishLater in Docusign JS saves a partial instance (status INPROGRESS); refresh its token and render it again to resume.

stem: A colleague needs to edit and republish workflows that she has built herself, not only start workflows that others have published. Which workflow permission does she need?

options.text: Workflows: Prepare
Workflows: Create
Workflows: Use
Workflows: Publish
eSignature Sender

answerText: Workflows: Create
explanation: Users with Workflow Create permission can edit and republish any workflows they created; Prepare lets users initiate published workflows.
whyNotOthers: B is right because editing and republishing your own workflows is the Create permission. The trap is A: Prepare sounds like setup work, but it only lets a user start published workflows (Run Workflow). C is paired with Create for managing running instances, D is not a listed workflow permission, and E is an eSignature role.

optionExplanations.A: Prepare lets a user initiate published workflows, not edit or republish them.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. Workflows: Create lets users edit and republish workflows they created.
optionExplanations.C: Use is combined with Create to manage running instances; it does not grant editing.
optionExplanations.D: Not a workflow permission named in the course.
optionExplanations.E: An eSignature sending role, unrelated to workflow authoring.

concept.title: Create versus Prepare permission
concept.line: Workflows: Create lets users edit and republish their own workflows; Workflows: Prepare lets users start published workflows.

topic: Connection provider value in the manifest
stem: In an extension app manifest, to which value is the provider property inside a connection's params set?

options.text: OAUTH2
DOCUSIGN
CUSTOM
EXTERNAL
CLIENT_CREDENTIALS

answerText: CUSTOM
explanation: In the connections params the developer sets clientId and clientSecret from the external platform, provider to CUSTOM, scopes, grantType and customConfig (tokenUrl, authorizationUrl and related settings).
whyNotOthers: C is right. The trap is A: the connection uses OAuth 2, but that is expressed through grantType and customConfig, not provider. B, D and E are not valid provider values (E confuses provider with grantType).

optionExplanations.A: OAuth 2 is the protocol used, but it is not the provider value.
optionExplanations.B: The connection points to the external platform or identity provider, not Docusign.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. The manifest guidance says provider should be set to CUSTOM.
optionExplanations.D: Not a documented value for provider.
optionExplanations.E: Client credentials is a grantType value (client_credentials), not the provider.

concept.title: Connection provider is CUSTOM
concept.line: An extension app connection sets provider to CUSTOM and holds clientId, clientSecret, scopes, grantType and customConfig URLs.

topic: Folder picker missing in a Store Files step
stem: Quarry Lane Architects' in-house developers built a file output cloud storage extension app that writes signed client agreements to the firm's document vault through an API proxy. The app is installed and connected to the account, and its Store Files step appears in Workflow Builder. When the process builder configures the step, she can choose the drive, but there is no control for choosing a folder, so every agreement lands at the drive's root. The vault's folder structure was reorganized by IT last month. What is the most likely cause?

options.text: The app was published with private distribution, and private file output apps can only write files to the root of whichever drive is selected
The app registration does not implement List Drives, which the step needs before it can show the folders on the drive that was selected
Store Files steps support only the cloud providers listed in App Center, so in-house storage targets always receive files at the root
The app's Write File action is failing silently and the step falls back to the root folder, so the Developer Console tests will show it
The app registration does not implement List Directory Contents, so the step configuration page cannot display folder selection controls

answerText: The app registration does not implement List Directory Contents, so the step configuration page cannot display folder selection controls
explanation: If an app registration does not include List Directory Contents, the step configuration UI does not display folder selection controls; List Drives only drives the drive selector, which she can already see.
whyNotOthers: E is right because the drive picker works but the folder picker is missing. The trap is B: List Drives is the sibling capability, but it controls the drive selector, which is already shown. A and C invent restrictions on private or in-house apps, and D describes a runtime failure, while the missing control appears at configuration time.

optionExplanations.A: Distribution type does not limit where a file output app can write.
optionExplanations.B: List Drives controls the drive selector, which she can already use.
optionExplanations.C: Custom file output apps are supported; the step is already available for this app.
optionExplanations.D: The symptom is a missing configuration control, not a runtime write failure.
optionExplanations.E: Correct. Without List Directory Contents the configuration page shows no folder selection controls.

decode.needs: App must implement List Directory Contents for folder selection
clues: can choose the drive -> List Drives is implemented
no control for choosing a folder -> List Directory Contents missing
folder structure reorganized -> red herring

concept.title: File output capabilities shape the UI
concept.line: List Drives enables the drive picker and List Directory Contents the folder picker in a Store Files step; Write File runs at execution.

stem: Brackenridge Health's unattended claims-intake service runs on a container platform and impersonates one of 40 regional coordinators, depending on which region a claim belongs to. It caches each coordinator's access token until it expires, but before processing every single claim it calls /oauth/userinfo to rediscover the base URI. At month end the service handles tens of thousands of claims an hour and starts receiving HTTP 429 responses with the error principal_throttled. The containers restart about once a week for patching. What is the best fix?

options.text: Call /oauth/userinfo each time a coordinator's token is renewed instead of per claim, because the base URI can change whenever Docusign issues a new token
Call /oauth/userinfo once per impersonated coordinator after each service restart, cache the returned base URI, and reuse it for all of that coordinator's claims
Ask an administrator to raise the account's hourly API limit in the API Usage Center, because user info requests count against that hourly allowance
Switch the service to Authorization Code Grant so that user info is requested only when a coordinator signs in interactively at the start of a shift

answerText: Call /oauth/userinfo once per impersonated coordinator after each service restart, cache the returned base URI, and reuse it for all of that coordinator's claims
explanation: Docusign limits /oauth/userinfo requests per user and per integration key and returns 429 principal_throttled when they are exceeded. For JWT apps the guideline is to call userinfo once per impersonated user per application restart; the clue 'before every single claim' is the problem.
whyNotOthers: B is right because it follows the JWT guideline and base URIs change rarely, so caching is safe. The trap is A: it sounds disciplined, but Docusign says JWT apps should not call userinfo each time a new token is obtained. C fails because the userinfo limits are separate from the account's eSignature hourly limit, and D fails because the service is unattended, so no coordinator is there to sign in.

optionExplanations.A: For JWT Grant, Docusign says not to call userinfo every time a new token is obtained; once per user per restart is enough.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. One userinfo call per impersonated user per restart, with the base URI cached, is the documented pattern.
optionExplanations.C: principal_throttled comes from the separate userinfo limits, which the API Usage Center hourly limit does not raise.
optionExplanations.D: An unattended service has no person to sign in, so Authorization Code Grant does not fit.

decode.needs: Reduce /oauth/userinfo calls: once per impersonated user per restart for JWT; cache base_uri.
clues: 429 principal_throttled -> userinfo request limit exceeded
userinfo before every claim -> far too frequent
unattended service, 40 coordinators -> JWT Grant with several impersonated users
weekly restarts -> a natural point to refresh the cached base URI

concept.title: Userinfo once per user
concept.line: JWT apps call /oauth/userinfo once per impersonated user per restart and cache base_uri; overuse returns 429 principal_throttled.

stem: Ashgrove Bank's connected fields app verifies wire-transfer authorization codes against its payments hub while customers sign. Every Verify call writes an audit entry that the compliance team reconciles each month. Auditors found occasional duplicate entries for the same signer and the same field values, always on days when the payments hub was slow to answer or returned an internal server error. The hub runs on-premises behind an API proxy, and the audit database has no unique constraints. How should the developer stop the duplicate audit entries?

options.text: Deduplicate on the envelope ID alone, because Docusign sends exactly one Verify request per envelope however often the signer edits the fields.
Return HTTP 404 from the proxy whenever a duplicate arrives, so Docusign treats the request as complete and sends no further retries.
Turn off automatic retries for the extension in the Developer Console integration settings, so a failed Verify request is never resent.
Write the audit entries from a Connect listener for the extension-executed event instead, because Verify requests are retried but Connect never redelivers.
Use the idempotencyKey in each Verify request to detect resubmissions, because Docusign resends the same key when it retries after an error or a timeout.

answerText: Use the idempotencyKey in each Verify request to detect resubmissions, because Docusign resends the same key when it retries after an error or a timeout.
explanation: The clue is that duplicates appear only when the hub is 'slow to answer or returned an internal server error': Docusign retries Verify up to three times on a 500 or timeout, reusing the same idempotencyKey so the external system can detect the resubmission.
whyNotOthers: E is right because the idempotency key identifies retried Verify requests. The trap is A: it sounds like a simple dedupe, but Verify is sent again whenever the signer modifies a required field, so it would drop real events. B breaks the signer's result, C invents a setting, and D relies on a false claim about Connect.

optionExplanations.A: Verify runs again whenever the signer changes a required connected field value, so envelope ID alone would hide legitimate re-verifications.
optionExplanations.B: 404 signals a processing error, and the signer would see a failure instead of the original verification result.
optionExplanations.C: There is no such setting; retries are part of Docusign's defined behaviour for connected fields actions.
optionExplanations.D: Connect also retries failed deliveries, and the question is about recognising Docusign's own Verify retries, which the idempotency key is designed for.
optionExplanations.E: Correct. On a 500 or no response, Docusign retries up to three times with the same idempotencyKey so the external system can recognise a resubmitted request.

decode.needs: Use the Verify request's idempotencyKey to recognise Docusign retries after 500 errors or timeouts.
clues: 'slow to answer or internal server error' -> Docusign retry behaviour
'same signer and same values' duplicated -> resubmitted request
'behind an API proxy' -> red herring

concept.title: Retries reuse the idempotency key
concept.line: Docusign retries a failed or timed-out Verify up to three times with the same idempotencyKey so the back-end can detect resubmissions.

topic: Firewall planning for regions and environments (multi)
stem: Larkspur Payroll, a Docusign partner, is preparing a public extension app that writes payroll setup data into its platform from Maestro workflows. The app will be offered to customers whose Docusign accounts are in the US and EU data centers. Larkspur runs separate development, test and production environments of its platform, each behind its own firewall that only admits approved source addresses. The product owner also wants a dark-mode version of the listing icon. Which two network actions should the infrastructure team take? (Select two)

options.text: Add the Docusign endpoint IP addresses only to the production firewall, because demo-environment testing traffic comes from the Developer Console in the tester's browser.
Allow the Docusign endpoint IP addresses listed for North America-based and demo accounts, and also those listed for European Union-based accounts.
Allow only the European Union-based Docusign addresses, because Docusign sends requests from the data center region of the account that is calling the app.
Enable CORS on the API service for the App Center domain so that installations and action calls from Docusign are not blocked by the browser.
Add the Docusign endpoint IP addresses to the firewalls of the development, test and production environments, since each may receive requests from Docusign.

answerText: Allow the Docusign endpoint IP addresses listed for North America-based and demo accounts, and also those listed for European Union-based accounts.; Add the Docusign endpoint IP addresses to the firewalls of the development, test and production environments, since each may receive requests from Docusign.
explanation: Docusign needs to reach every environment it will call ('development, test and production environments, each behind its own firewall'), and the allow-list must include North America/demo addresses plus the addresses for each extra production region ('US and EU data centers').
whyNotOthers: B and E are right: allow NA/demo plus EU addresses, on every environment's firewall. The trap is A: it sounds efficient, but Developer Console tests are executed by Docusign servers against the dev and test environments. C forgets that US customers and demo testing use North America addresses, and D confuses browser CORS with network allow-listing. The dark-mode icon is a red herring.

optionExplanations.A: Integration and functional tests are sent by Docusign's servers, not the tester's browser, so development and test firewalls must allow Docusign too.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. North America and demo addresses are always needed (development, testing and US production users), and EU addresses are needed because the app will be offered to EU-based accounts.
optionExplanations.C: The region does decide which addresses are used, but US customers and all demo testing use the North America addresses, so EU alone is not enough.
optionExplanations.D: Docusign's calls to the API are server-to-server; CORS is a browser mechanism and does not open the firewall.
optionExplanations.E: Correct. The docs say to add the addresses to all firewalls in all environments that may receive requests from extension apps.

decode.needs: Allow Docusign endpoint IPs for every region served (NA/demo always, plus EU) on every environment's firewall.
clues: 'accounts in the US and EU data centers' -> NA (incl. demo) and EU IP ranges
'separate development, test and production environments, each behind its own firewall' -> allow-list on all of them
'only admits approved source addresses' -> firewall allow-list, not CORS

concept.title: Allow Docusign IPs everywhere needed
concept.line: Allow North America/demo Docusign IPs always, add each production region served, and configure every environment's firewall that Docusign calls.

topic: Starting Maestro from a CLM workflow
stem: Valemont Logistics' legal operations team already runs its supplier contract process in Docusign CLM, including CLM's WhatsApp and SMS delivery options, which many of its regional haulage partners prefer over email. The team now wants a Workflow Builder workflow (web form intake, identity check, then signature) to run as part of that same automated CLM process, so the haulage partners get the CLM delivery options and the Maestro steps in a single flow. The team has no developers available this quarter, and the partner portal is being redesigned. How should the Maestro workflow be started?

options.text: Trigger the Maestro workflow from within the CLM workflow, which is meant for starts inside Docusign and keeps CLM delivery options such as WhatsApp and SMS in one process
Set the start method to From a Link and have CLM text the copied workflow URL to each partner, so that partners start their own instance from their phone whenever they choose
Set the start method to From an API call and have CLM post to the trigger URL with trigger_inputs, so that each supplier record starts an instance with that partner's details
Set the start method to Manually in Docusign so a legal ops user with Workflows: Prepare runs each instance from Run Workflow after the CLM step for that partner finishes
Rebuild the intake, identity check and signing as CLM steps and retire the Maestro workflow, because Maestro steps cannot run inside the same automated CLM process

answerText: Trigger the Maestro workflow from within the CLM workflow, which is meant for starts inside Docusign and keeps CLM delivery options such as WhatsApp and SMS in one process
explanation: Docusign lets a Maestro workflow be triggered from within a CLM workflow, which is meant for starts inside Docusign and lets you use CLM options such as WhatsApp or SMS delivery alongside Maestro 'in a single automated process'.
whyNotOthers: A is right because the stem asks for the Maestro steps inside 'that same automated CLM process' with CLM's delivery options and no developers. The trap is B: a link can start the workflow, but each partner would start a separate, self-service instance outside the CLM process. C needs developer work and an API design, D adds a manual step per partner, and E is false because the CLM start option exists precisely to combine the two.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. Starting from a CLM workflow is the documented option for combining CLM delivery options (WhatsApp, SMS) with Maestro in one automated process.
optionExplanations.B: Self-service link starts happen outside the CLM process; the partner decides when, and the flows are not one automated process.
optionExplanations.C: From an API call needs an integration that posts to the trigger URL; there are no developers, and CLM can start Maestro directly.
optionExplanations.D: Manual starts by a Prepare user are not automated and add a person to every partner's process.
optionExplanations.E: False premise: a CLM workflow can trigger a Maestro workflow, so nothing needs to be rebuilt.

decode.needs: Trigger the Maestro workflow from inside the CLM workflow
clues: already runs in Docusign CLM -> start option from a CLM workflow
WhatsApp and SMS delivery -> CLM delivery options kept in the same process
no developers available -> no API trigger code
portal redesign -> red herring

concept.title: CLM workflow as a start option
concept.line: A Maestro workflow can be triggered from within a CLM workflow, combining CLM options like WhatsApp or SMS delivery with Maestro steps.

stem: An Agreement Manager integration built against the developer environment is moving to production. Which base path should its production calls use?

options.text: https://api.docusign.com/v1
https://api-d.docusign.com/v1
https://na3.docusign.net/restapi/v1
https://account.docusign.com/v1

answerText: https://api.docusign.com/v1
explanation: The Agreement Manager (Navigator) API uses https://api-d.docusign.com/v1 in the developer environment and https://api.docusign.com/v1 in production.
whyNotOthers: A is right because production uses api.docusign.com. The trap is C: the account's eSignature base URI from userinfo is for eSignature calls, not for Agreement Manager. B is the developer host, and D is the authentication server.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. Production Agreement Manager calls go to https://api.docusign.com/v1/accounts/{accountId}/agreements.
optionExplanations.B: This is the developer (demo) host that the integration is moving away from.
optionExplanations.C: An eSignature base URI of the account; Agreement Manager calls do not use the restapi host.
optionExplanations.D: account.docusign.com is the OAuth authentication server, not an API host.

concept.title: Agreement Manager hosts
concept.line: Agreement Manager calls use api-d.docusign.com/v1 for developer and api.docusign.com/v1 for production, not the eSignature base URI.

topic: Embedded views: correcting a sent envelope
stem: Northgate's procurement app sends purchase agreements to suppliers. Yesterday a buyer sent one with the signature field on the wrong page and the supplier contact's email slightly wrong; the supplier has not opened it. The buyer wants to open Docusign's own correction screen inside the procurement app, fix the field and the email, and resume the same envelope, without leaving the app or starting over. The app authenticates buyers with Authorization Code Grant. Which call should the app make?

options.text: EnvelopeViews:createSender for the sent envelope, then show the returned URL so the buyer can re-tag and send it
EnvelopeViews:createConsole, then let the buyer find the envelope in the Docusign web app and correct it there
Envelopes:update with status voided, then create a corrected copy as a draft and open EnvelopeViews:createSender
EnvelopeViews:createCorrect for the sent envelope, then show the returned URL to the buyer inside the app

answerText: EnvelopeViews:createCorrect for the sent envelope, then show the returned URL to the buyer inside the app
explanation: The correction view (EnvelopeViews:createCorrect) is the embedded view for an envelope that 'has already been sent'. The clue is 'correction screen inside the app ... resume the same envelope'.
whyNotOthers: D is right because it opens the correction UI for this sent envelope. The trap is A: createSender is the embedded sending view, which works on drafts, not on envelopes already sent. B opens the general web app rather than this envelope's correction screen, and C voids and restarts, which the buyer ruled out.

optionExplanations.A: The sender view is for preparing a draft (status created) envelope before sending; it is not the correction view for a sent envelope.
optionExplanations.B: The console view embeds the whole web app; it works but does not take the buyer to the correction screen of this envelope, which is the stated need.
optionExplanations.C: Voiding ends the envelope; the buyer wants to resume the same envelope, not start over.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. createCorrect returns a URL for the correction view of an envelope that has already been sent.

decode.needs: Embedded correct view: EnvelopeViews:createCorrect
clues: already sent, supplier has not opened it -> in-process envelope can still be corrected
Docusign's own correction screen inside the app -> embedded correct view
resume the same envelope, not start over -> no void and resend
Authorization Code Grant -> red herring

concept.title: Sender view vs correct view
concept.line: createSender embeds tagging and sending of a draft; createCorrect embeds correction of an envelope that has already been sent.

topic: Remote instance with an omitted role
stem: Thornbury Lettings sends a tenancy-renewal web form by email from its property system. The template-based configuration has two roles: tenant (primary, fills in the form and signs) and guarantor (signs only), and the web form template has no fixed name or email for the guarantor role. The developer's Instances:createInstance request includes sendOption now and a recipients array with only the tenant's roleName, name and email, because 'the guarantor can be added later'. What happens?

options.text: The request fails, because every role in the configuration must appear in the recipients array of a remote instance request.
The tenant gets the email, and the envelope is held after the tenant signs until the property system adds the guarantor by API.
The tenant gets the email, and the guarantor is removed from the envelope process together with the tabs assigned to that role.
The tenant gets the email, and the guarantor's tabs are reassigned to the tenant so that the tenant completes both roles.

answerText: The tenant gets the email, and the guarantor is removed from the envelope process together with the tabs assigned to that role.
explanation: Only the primary recipient's values are mandatory; a role with no values in the request and none hard-coded in the template is removed from the envelope process with its tabs. The clue is 'no fixed name or email for the guarantor role'.
whyNotOthers: C is right because Docusign drops recipients whose information is not supplied. The trap is A: only the primary role is required, so the request succeeds. B fails because nothing holds the envelope for a later addition, and D fails because tabs are removed, not reassigned.

optionExplanations.A: Only the primary recipient's name and email are required; other roles can be omitted.
optionExplanations.B: The envelope is not held; the omitted role is removed when the instance is created.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. Roles without supplied or hard-coded values are removed along with their tabs.
optionExplanations.D: Tabs of omitted recipients are removed, not moved to another role.

decode.needs: Understand which recipient values a remote createInstance must carry and what happens to omitted roles.
clues: 'sends ... by email' -> remote instance, sendOption now
'no fixed name or email for the guarantor' -> nothing hard-coded to fall back on
'can be added later' -> false assumption, the role is dropped

concept.title: Remote instance recipient values
concept.line: Remote instances need values for the primary role; other roles without supplied or hard-coded values are removed with their tabs.

stem: An eligible administrator is raising the account's hourly API limit in the API Usage Center. What can she do about the 30-second burst limit shown in the same API Limit panel?

options.text: Nothing there; the burst limit cannot be changed
It rises in proportion to the new hourly limit
It can be raised in steps of 100 calls
It can be raised only in the production environment

answerText: Nothing there; the burst limit cannot be changed
explanation: The API Limit panel shows both values, but only the hourly limit can be updated; Docusign states that you cannot change the burst limit.
whyNotOthers: A is right because the burst limit is fixed (500 per 30 seconds in production, 200 in the developer environment). The trap is B: it sounds logical that a higher hourly limit raises the burst, but it does not. C and D invent controls that do not exist.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. The burst limit is displayed but cannot be changed through limit management.
optionExplanations.B: Raising the hourly limit does not change the burst limit.
optionExplanations.C: There is no burst-limit slider; only the hourly limit changes, in steps of 500.
optionExplanations.D: The burst limit cannot be changed in either environment.

concept.title: Burst limit is fixed
concept.line: API limit management changes only the hourly call limit; the 30-second burst limit cannot be changed.

stem: Halden Mutual has acquired a regional insurer whose 6,000 legacy vendor contracts exist only as scanned PDFs on a file share. Procurement wants the AI-extracted renewal dates and payment terms of all vendor contracts in its ERP, and from next month every new vendor contract will be signed through Docusign eSignature. The legal team insists that the legacy contracts must not be re-signed or altered in any way. An offshore team has already been booked for the migration, and the ERP sync job already holds a token with the Agreement Manager read scope. Which two statements describe a correct migration plan? (Select two)

options.text: Call GetAgreementsList with the file-share path as a filter so Agreement Manager pulls the scanned PDFs into the repository overnight.
Send each scanned PDF as an eSignature envelope to an internal signer so that completing the envelope places the contract in the repository.
Import the scanned PDFs into Agreement Manager as legacy agreements, not as envelopes, so AI extraction runs on them without re-signing.
After the import, call CreateAgreementSummary on each contract so that Docusign AI extracts its parties, dates and provisions for the ERP.
Expect new contracts completed through eSignature to reach the repository automatically, so only the legacy scans need a one-time import.

answerText: Import the scanned PDFs into Agreement Manager as legacy agreements, not as envelopes, so AI extraction runs on them without re-signing.; Expect new contracts completed through eSignature to reach the repository automatically, so only the legacy scans need a one-time import.
explanation: Legacy agreements are imported into Agreement Manager (not sent as envelopes), and AI extraction runs automatically on import, which respects 'must not be re-signed or altered'. Completed eSignature envelopes reach the repository automatically, which covers 'every new vendor contract signed through eSignature'.
whyNotOthers: C and E are right: legacy files are imported once, and new eSignature agreements arrive automatically. The trap is A: GetAgreementsList is the API's search call, but it only reads existing agreements and cannot import files. B re-signs the contracts, which legal forbids, and D creates a prose summary; extraction already runs on import.

optionExplanations.A: GetAgreementsList only reads agreements already in the repository; it cannot pull files from a file share or import anything.
optionExplanations.B: Routing old contracts through a new signing ceremony alters and re-signs them, which the legal team explicitly ruled out.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. Importing the legacy PDFs into Agreement Manager adds them to the repository and AI extraction runs automatically, with no re-signing.
optionExplanations.D: CreateAgreementSummary returns an AI-written overview; extraction of type, parties and provisions already runs automatically when agreements are imported.
optionExplanations.E: Correct. Completed eSignature envelopes are added to the repository and analyzed by AI automatically, so only the legacy backlog needs importing.

decode.needs: A one-time import of non-Docusign contracts plus automatic ingestion of completed envelopes, then API reads.
clues: scanned PDFs on a file share -> legacy (non-Docusign) agreements that must be imported
signed through Docusign eSignature from next month -> completed envelopes reach the repository automatically
must not be re-signed or altered -> rules out pushing old contracts through new envelopes
offshore team booked -> red herring

concept.title: Import legacy, envelopes arrive automatically
concept.line: Legacy files are imported through Agreement Manager because the API cannot upload; completed eSignature envelopes enter the repository and get AI extraction automatically.

stem: A Connect configuration can deliver JSON or XML, and send events individually (SIM) or in aggregate. Which of these four data models is deprecated and meant for legacy apps only?

options.text: XML SIM
XML aggregate
JSON aggregate
JSON SIM

answerText: XML SIM
explanation: The ConnectConfigurations:create reference lists four data models and marks XML SIM as deprecated (legacy apps only); JSON SIM is the recommended model.
whyNotOthers: A is right because XML SIM is the one model flagged as deprecated. The trap is B: aggregate mode is a legacy option too, but XML aggregate is still a supported data model, not the deprecated one. C is a supported JSON variant, and D is the model Docusign recommends for all apps.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. The API reference states that the XML SIM model is deprecated and should be used by legacy apps only.
optionExplanations.B: XML aggregate is a legacy option that combines similar events into one message, but it is still listed as a supported data model.
optionExplanations.C: JSON aggregate is supported (deliveryMode aggregate with eventData.version restv2.1); it is not the deprecated model.
optionExplanations.D: JSON SIM (Connect 2.0) is the recommended model for all apps.

concept.title: Four Connect data models
concept.line: Connect supports JSON SIM (recommended), JSON aggregate, XML aggregate and XML SIM, which is deprecated.

topic: Account-level configuration limited to selected users
stem: Kestrel Brokerage has one Docusign account with about 120 users. Its 14 commercial underwriters send policy binders from the Docusign web app using shared templates, and operations wants the ERP updated within minutes whenever one of those binders is fully signed. Envelopes sent by HR, marketing and the claims team must never reach the ERP's listener, which is hosted in Azure. There is no custom sending application, and the IT team holds Docusign administrator rights. Which approach meets the requirement?

options.text: Add an eventNotification object to each binder envelope so that only the underwriters' envelopes report to the ERP listener and other teams are unaffected
Create an account-level custom configuration that lists only the underwriters' user IDs instead of all users, so binders they send from the web app are reported automatically
Create an organization-level configuration limited to the brokerage's single account, so one configuration managed in Org Admin captures the underwriters' binders
Create an account-level custom configuration for all users and have the ERP listener return 200 and discard messages for envelopes sent by other teams
Create a Recipient Connect configuration for the underwriters' users, so events on envelopes in which they take part are reported to the ERP listener

answerText: Create an account-level custom configuration that lists only the underwriters' user IDs instead of all users, so binders they send from the web app are reported automatically
explanation: The binders are sent from the web app ("no custom sending application"), so the webhook must come from a standing configuration, and an account-level configuration can be scoped to selected users so other teams' envelopes "never reach" the listener.
whyNotOthers: B is right because an account-level configuration can list specific users, which captures web-app sending and excludes other teams. The trap is D: returning 200 and discarding is correct listener behaviour, but the stem says other teams' envelopes must never reach the listener. A fails because eventNotification is API-only and cannot be added from the web app; C fails because organization-level scope is chosen by account, not by user, so HR envelopes would be included; E fails because the underwriters are senders, not recipients.

optionExplanations.A: eventNotification can only be set through Envelopes:create in the API; the underwriters send from the web app, so there is nowhere to add it.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. Account-level configurations cover all users or selected users (allUsers false plus userIds), and they work for envelopes sent from the web app.
optionExplanations.C: Organization-level configurations select all or selected accounts, not individual users, so every user in the brokerage's one account would be reported.
optionExplanations.D: Discarding after a 200 is the right way to handle unneeded events, but HR and marketing envelopes would still be delivered to the ERP listener, which the stem forbids.
optionExplanations.E: Recipient Connect reports envelopes that domain users receive as signers or carbon copies; the underwriters are the senders here.

decode.needs: Account-level custom configuration with selected users (userIds), not envelope-level or organization-level
clues: send from the Docusign web app, no custom sending application -> envelope-level eventNotification is impossible
only the 14 underwriters, other teams must never reach the listener -> scope by user, not by account
listener hosted in Azure -> red herring, does not change the configuration level

concept.title: Scope account Connect to users
concept.line: Account-level Connect can cover all users or a selected list of users and works for web-app sending, unlike envelope-level webhooks.

topic: Reading a request URL: recipient tabs
stem: A log shows GET https://eu.docusign.net/restapi/v2.1/accounts/{accountId}/envelopes/{envelopeId}/recipients/2/tabs. What did the integration request?

options.text: Recipient 2's tabs in that envelope, in a developer (demo) account in the EU
The envelope's recipient list, filtered to the tab types they can fill
Recipient 2's tabs in that envelope, in a production account on the EU site
The tabs of role 2 in the server template the envelope came from

answerText: Recipient 2's tabs in that envelope, in a production account on the EU site
explanation: The path segments read as: production site eu, REST API v2.1, account, envelope, recipient 2, tabs. This is the EnvelopeRecipientTabs:list call.
whyNotOthers: C is right. The trap is A: the resource is right but demo uses demo.docusign.net, not eu. B misreads the path as the recipients list, and D confuses the envelope with a template.

optionExplanations.A: Demo accounts use demo.docusign.net; eu is a production site.
optionExplanations.B: The path ends in /recipients/2/tabs, which targets one recipient's tabs, not the recipient list.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. This is EnvelopeRecipientTabs:list, and eu.docusign.net is a production site.
optionExplanations.D: The path is under /envelopes/{envelopeId}, so it reads the envelope's recipient, not a template role.

concept.title: Reading eSignature request URLs
concept.line: Host shows the environment and site, then /restapi/v2.1/accounts/{accountId}, then the resource path from envelope down to recipient and tabs.

stem: The corporate secretary of Vantor Holdings must collect a unanimous written consent from the nine board members for a new share plan. Every director signs the same resolution, the directors may sign in any order, and the general counsel wants a single completed record that shows all nine signatures together for the minute book. The board portal already stores each director's email, and the resolution is a two-page PDF. Which approach fits?

options.text: Use bulk send with a list of nine copies, one per director, so each director gets the resolution at the same time and the batch status shows when all have signed
Create one envelope with nine signers numbered routingOrder 1 to 9, so each director signs in turn and the last signature completes the record
Create one envelope with the resolution and nine signers who all share routingOrder 1, so the directors sign in parallel and one completed envelope holds every signature
Create nine envelopes in a loop from the portal, one per director, and merge the nine signed PDFs into the minute book afterwards

answerText: Create one envelope with the resolution and nine signers who all share routingOrder 1, so the directors sign in parallel and one completed envelope holds every signature
explanation: Bulk send is for sending the same agreement separately to many recipients. Here a fixed number of parties sign one document and the counsel wants 'a single completed record', so one envelope with parallel signers is the fit.
whyNotOthers: C is right because one envelope with shared routing order yields one record and allows any order. The trap is A: bulk send gives each director their own envelope. B gives one record but imposes sequential signing, and D creates nine envelopes by hand.

optionExplanations.A: Bulk send creates a separate envelope for each copy, so there would be nine completed records, not one with all signatures.
optionExplanations.B: This produces one record, but sequential routing forces an order the stem says is not needed and slows completion.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. A fixed group signing the same document belongs in one envelope; the same routing order lets them sign in parallel.
optionExplanations.D: Nine envelopes give nine separate records and certificates; merging PDFs afterwards is not a single completed agreement.

decode.needs: One envelope, multiple signers with the same routingOrder
clues: same resolution, single completed record -> one envelope, not bulk send
sign in any order -> same routingOrder (parallel)
nine directors -> fixed number of parties, not a mass mailing
two-page PDF -> red herring

concept.title: One envelope or bulk send
concept.line: A fixed set of parties signing the same document uses one envelope; bulk send gives each recipient their own separate envelope.

stem: Copperline, a Docusign partner, has a Live public extension app that archives agreements to a storage product it will shut down at year end. Leadership wants the App Center listing removed entirely, with no replacement version, and asks the developer to simply take it down from the Developer Console before the next billing cycle starts. The app currently has no Draft, In Review or Approved version. A separate team is building an unrelated app for the same storage brand. What should the developer do?

options.text: Cancel the publishing request on the Live version so that it reverts to Draft status, and then delete that Draft version from the App Versions page of the app.
Delete the Live version from the My Apps kebab menu, which removes the listing and uninstalls the app from customer accounts.
Reach out through the Docusign Developer Community for assistance, because a Live version cannot be deleted or unpublished in the Developer Console.
Create a new version with distribution set to Private and an empty account list, then publish it so the public listing disappears.
Publish a new version with publicationRegions set to an empty array so that no region can install the app any longer.

answerText: Reach out through the Docusign Developer Community for assistance, because a Live version cannot be deleted or unpublished in the Developer Console.
explanation: The clue is 'removed entirely, with no replacement version': Live versions cannot be deleted or unpublished in the Developer Console, so the developer must ask for help through the Developer Community.
whyNotOthers: C is right because the Console cannot delete a Live version. The trap is A: cancelling publication is the correct move for a version In Review, Approved or Rejected, but not for a Live version. B only works for Drafts, D would change distribution after Live, and E fails validation and tries to remove regions. The unrelated app is a red herring.

optionExplanations.A: Cancelling publication reverts In Review, Approved or Rejected versions to Draft; it does not apply to a Live version.
optionExplanations.B: Delete is only possible for Draft versions; a Live version cannot be deleted.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. Live versions cannot be deleted, and the docs direct you to the Developer Community to remove a live app without replacing it.
optionExplanations.D: The distribution type cannot be changed once an app has been Live.
optionExplanations.E: An empty publicationRegions array causes a validation error, and regions cannot be removed from a published app.

decode.needs: Know that a Live extension app version cannot be deleted in the Developer Console.
clues: 'removed entirely, no replacement version' -> delete a Live app
'no Draft, In Review or Approved version' -> nothing to cancel or delete
'unrelated app for the same brand' -> red herring

concept.title: Live versions cannot be deleted
concept.line: Only Draft versions can be deleted; removing a Live app without replacement needs Docusign help via the Developer Community.

topic: CORS: authentication for a single-page app
stem: Ostara Labs built an internal single-page app that calls the eSignature API from the browser through CORS. It was written two years ago with Implicit Grant. The security team now asks the developers to move to the flow Docusign recommends for single-page apps, without adding a back-end server, and to keep the app's existing CORS origins. The app is hosted on a content delivery network. What should the developers do?

options.text: Create a new integration key set to Public Authorization Code Grant with CORS configured, enable CORS for OAuth calls, request the signature and cors scopes, and update the app to use the new key
Change the existing integration key's authentication method from Implicit Grant to Public Authorization Code Grant, enable CORS for OAuth calls, and request the signature and cors scopes
Keep Implicit Grant but add the cors scope to the authorization request, because Implicit Grant is the only flow that runs entirely in the browser
Switch to JWT Grant and build the assertion in the browser with the RSA private key, so no user login is needed

answerText: Create a new integration key set to Public Authorization Code Grant with CORS configured, enable CORS for OAuth calls, request the signature and cors scopes, and update the app to use the new key
explanation: Docusign recommends Public Authorization Code Grant (no secret) for SPAs. To move from Implicit Grant you create a new integration key with that method, allow CORS for OAuth calls, and request signature plus cors.
whyNotOthers: A is right because it follows the documented migration path. The trap is B: the settings are right, but the existing key cannot just be switched; a new key is required. C keeps the flow the security team wants to retire, and D exposes a private key in the browser.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. Moving from Implicit Grant to Public Authorization Code Grant requires a new integration key; that method also needs the option to allow CORS for OAuth calls.
optionExplanations.B: The method of an existing SPA key cannot simply be switched; Docusign says to create a new integration key for Public Authorization Code Grant.
optionExplanations.C: Implicit Grant still works with CORS, but the recommended flow for SPAs is Public Authorization Code Grant, which the security team asked for.
optionExplanations.D: A private key in browser code is exposed to every user; JWT is for confidential server-side apps.

decode.needs: SPA + CORS: Public Authorization Code Grant on a new integration key, cors scope
clues: move to the flow Docusign recommends for SPAs -> Public Authorization Code Grant (PKCE, no secret)
written with Implicit Grant -> changing method needs a new integration key
no back-end server -> CORS, not a proxy
hosted on a CDN -> red herring

concept.title: CORS SPA authentication
concept.line: SPAs using CORS should use Public Authorization Code Grant with signature and cors scopes; moving from Implicit Grant needs a new integration key.

stem: Each night at 01:00, an unattended archiving job at Glenmore Bank collects ID Verification evidence for the previous day's account openings, around 400 recipients. The job lists recipients for each envelope, requests one identity proof resource token at start-up, caches it, and then loops through all recipients calling the ID Evidence API. The first few recipients succeed, but after that every call returns 401 Unauthorized. The bank's OAuth access token is valid for eight hours. What should the developer change?

options.text: Request a new resource token from identity_proof_token for each recipient just before calling the ID Evidence API, because a resource token is valid for only 2 minutes.
Refresh the OAuth access token before each recipient and send it to the ID Evidence API directly, because that API accepts the eSignature access token as its bearer token.
Request one resource token per envelope instead of per run, because a resource token is bound to an envelope and expires when the job moves to the next envelope.
Process the 400 recipients in parallel threads so that every ID Evidence call is made while the single cached resource token is still within its lifetime.

answerText: Request a new resource token from identity_proof_token for each recipient just before calling the ID Evidence API, because a resource token is valid for only 2 minutes.
explanation: Resource tokens are created per recipient (the path includes the recipientIdGuid) and are valid for only 2 minutes. The clue is 'one ... resource token at start-up, caches it' followed by 401 errors after a few recipients.
whyNotOthers: A is right because the job must request a fresh token per recipient right before the call. The trap is C: it shortens the reuse window but the token belongs to one recipient, not an envelope, and its lifetime is time-based. B fails because the ID Evidence API takes the resource token, not the OAuth token, and D still reuses one token across recipients.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. Resource tokens are per recipient and expire after 2 minutes.
optionExplanations.B: The ID Evidence API needs the resource token as the bearer token, not the OAuth access token.
optionExplanations.C: The token is requested for a specific recipient and expires after 2 minutes, not at an envelope boundary.
optionExplanations.D: A token requested for one recipient cannot serve all recipients, and racing the clock is not a fix.

decode.needs: Fetch a short-lived resource token per recipient immediately before each ID Evidence call.
clues: 'unattended archiving job' -> server-side batch, no user present
'one resource token at start-up, caches it' -> token reuse is the bug
'OAuth access token is valid for eight hours' -> red herring, a different token

concept.title: ID Evidence resource tokens
concept.line: Request a resource token per recipient from identity_proof_token just before calling ID Evidence; it is valid for 2 minutes.

stem: Fernhill Library Services is building a browser-only volunteer-agreement app: plain JavaScript served from a static website, with no server code at all. Each branch coordinator signs in with their own Docusign login, and the scripts call the eSignature REST API directly from the browser to send agreements. The integration key is set up for Public Authorization Code Grant, allowed origins and HTTP methods are configured on the key, and the account administrator has left CORS enabled for all apps. Most branches use Chromebooks. What should the authorization request ask for in its scope parameter?

options.text: signature cors, so the token covers the eSignature endpoints and is allowed to make requests from browser scripts
signature extended, so the token covers the eSignature endpoints and the browser can keep refreshing it for 30 days
signature impersonation, so the browser scripts can act for the coordinator without needing any server
signature only, because the allowed origins on the integration key are what permit requests from browsers
cors only, because the cors scope already includes the eSignature endpoints that have an account ID in the path

answerText: signature cors, so the token covers the eSignature endpoints and is allowed to make requests from browser scripts
explanation: An app that sends eSignature requests from browser scripts must be configured for CORS and must request the cors scope in addition to signature.
whyNotOthers: A is right because CORS needs both the app configuration and the cors scope. The trap is D: allowed origins are necessary but not sufficient; without the cors scope the browser calls are rejected. B is wrong because a Public Auth Code refresh token lasts only up to 24 hours, C confuses the JWT consent scope with a browser flow, and E drops signature, which the eSignature endpoints require.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. signature covers most eSignature endpoints and cors is the scope required to send CORS requests.
optionExplanations.B: extended does not give a Public (browser) app 30-day refresh tokens, and it does not enable browser requests.
optionExplanations.C: impersonation is the consent scope for JWT Grant service integrations, not for a browser sign-in.
optionExplanations.D: Allowed origins are required, but the app must also request the cors scope.
optionExplanations.E: cors does not replace signature; the eSignature endpoints still need signature.

decode.needs: Request signature and cors in the Public Authorization Code Grant scope
clues: 'no server code at all, scripts call the API from the browser' -> CORS request, needs the cors scope
'allowed origins already configured' -> necessary but not sufficient
'Chromebooks' -> red herring

concept.title: Scopes for CORS apps
concept.line: A browser app calling the eSignature API directly needs CORS configured on the key and must request both signature and cors.

stem: Quarry Health's QA team and its development team want to test the same connected fields app at the same time: QA against the staging patient-index service and developers against a sandbox, each with its own OAuth client and hostnames. Re-editing a single registration every time a team switches has caused clashes, with each team breaking the other's tests mid-run. Both teams work in one Docusign developer account and share a Git repository, and the release manager wants no further lost test days. Which approach fits?

options.text: Keep one registration and add a second connection for the sandbox, then point each action's connectionsReference at whichever of the two connections the team needs for that day's test run.
Keep one registration and rely on the automatic reinstall after each edit, scheduling test windows so that the two teams never edit it at the same time.
Share the Live private app with a second developer account for the developers, so each team installs its own copy pointing at its own environment.
Download the manifest and create a separate registration per environment, each with a unique name and its own clientId, clientSecret, customConfig and params.uri values.
Keep one registration and list both hostnames in each action's params.uri, separated by commas, so Docusign falls back to the sandbox when staging fails.

answerText: Download the manifest and create a separate registration per environment, each with a unique name and its own clientId, clientSecret, customConfig and params.uri values.
explanation: The clue is 'at the same time' with different OAuth clients and hostnames: a registration supports one external environment, so the documented option is separate registrations per environment with a unique name and environment-specific connection and params.uri values.
whyNotOthers: D is right because separate registrations let each team test its own environment concurrently. The trap is A: multiple connections sound neat, but a registration supports one environment's connection properties and switching is still an edit. B is valid only when teams test one after another, C relies on unsupported developer-account sharing, and E invents a fallback list. The shared Git repository is a red herring.

optionExplanations.A: A registration currently supports connection properties for a single external service environment, and changing connectionsReference is still an edit that clashes.
optionExplanations.B: This is the supported 'update the registration' method, but it cannot let both teams test at the same time, which is the requirement.
optionExplanations.C: Private apps cannot be shared with additional developer accounts, and a shared copy would still point at the same endpoints.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. Docusign documents separate registrations per environment, named to reflect the environment, as the alternative to editing one registration back and forth.
optionExplanations.E: params.uri holds a single endpoint URL; there is no fallback list.

decode.needs: Maintain separate extension app registrations (unique names) for each external environment.
clues: 'at the same time' -> editing one registration does not work
'each with its own OAuth client and hostnames' -> connection and params.uri differ per environment
'share a Git repository' -> red herring

concept.title: One registration, one environment
concept.line: A registration supports one external environment; to test environments in parallel, keep separate uniquely named registrations.

stem: Lumen Telecom embeds contract signing in its responsive website with focused view and Docusign JS. Customers report two problems: the agreement takes several seconds to appear after they press Review contract, and on small phones the agreement is cut off at the side. Customers are otherwise happy with the signing experience itself. The marketing team has also asked for the brand's teal colour on the Finish button. Which two changes address the two reported problems? (Select two)

options.text: Load the Docusign JS script asynchronously when the page loads, before the signing URL is ready for loadDocuSign
Trigger the next steps from the sessionEnd event handler instead of waiting for the returnUrl redirect
Set the container div to the default 400px height and full width so the agreement keeps its designed size
Size the div that holds the agreement as a percentage of the screen rather than a fixed number of pixels
Open the signing URL in a new browser tab instead of an iframe on mobile browsers

answerText: Load the Docusign JS script asynchronously when the page loads, before the signing URL is ready for loadDocuSign; Size the div that holds the agreement as a percentage of the screen rather than a fixed number of pixels
explanation: The two problems map to two focused view best practices: load the script asynchronously before the URL is ready ('takes several seconds to appear') and scale the container by percentage ('cut off on small phones').
whyNotOthers: A and D are right because they target load time and screen fit. The trap is B: event handlers are good practice but do not fix either reported problem. C keeps the fixed size that causes the cut-off, and E is classic view guidance.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. Loading the script early and asynchronously is the recommended way to improve focused view load time.
optionExplanations.B: This is a real focused view best practice, but it handles what happens after signing; it fixes neither the load delay nor the cut-off.
optionExplanations.C: Fixed pixel sizing is what causes the poor fit; Docusign recommends overriding the defaults to fit the page.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. Percentage sizing makes the focused view fit any screen size.
optionExplanations.E: This is the classic view advice for mobile; focused view is rendered with Docusign JS in a div, not by redirecting to a tab.

decode.needs: Focused view best practices: async script loading and percentage-sized container
clues: takes several seconds to appear -> load Docusign JS asynchronously early
cut off on small phones -> size the div by percentage
teal Finish button -> red herring (style settings)

concept.title: Focused view performance and fit
concept.line: Load Docusign JS asynchronously before the URL exists, size the container by percentage, and use event handlers for next steps.

topic: Connected fields Verify response for a mismatch
stem: Fenwick Mutual's private connected fields app checks a member number and date of birth against the society's membership ledger while members sign their annual renewal. When a member mistypes the date of birth, the back-end currently answers with HTTP 400 BAD_REQUEST and the text 'Date of birth does not match'. Members complain that the signing screen shows a generic failure instead of telling them what to fix. The service runs in the society's Azure tenant behind an API gateway. How should the back-end respond when its matching logic runs successfully but the values do not match?

options.text: Return HTTP 400 with a more descriptive message, because Docusign shows the message text of a 400 response to the signer in the signing screen as guidance on what to fix.
Return HTTP 404 NOT_FOUND with a code and message, because no ledger record matches both the member number and the date of birth.
