Return HTTP 500 so that Docusign retries the Verify request up to three times, giving the member time to correct the value in the meantime.
Return a normal Verify response with verified set to false, and supply verifyResponseMessage and verifyFailureReason that tell the member what to correct.
Return a Verify response with verified set to true and suggested values that autofill the correct date of birth from the ledger.

answerText: Return a normal Verify response with verified set to false, and supply verifyResponseMessage and verifyFailureReason that tell the member what to correct.
explanation: The clue is 'its matching logic runs successfully but the values do not match': that is a verification result, so the back-end returns a Verify response with verified false and a verifyResponseMessage and verifyFailureReason, which Docusign displays in the signing UI.
whyNotOthers: D is right because a mismatch is reported in the Verify response, not as an HTTP error. The trap is A: a descriptive 400 sounds like the fix, but the contract reserves 400, 404 and 500 for requests that could not be processed. B and C misuse error codes (C only causes retries), and E bypasses the control.

optionExplanations.A: HTTP 400, 404 and 500 are for errors that prevent the request from being processed; the docs say not to use them when the logic ran and found the values invalid.
optionExplanations.B: 404 is for processing errors such as an unknown type; a non-matching value is a verification result, not an error.
optionExplanations.C: A 500 triggers retries of the same values and ends as a failed request; it gives the member no guidance.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. When the verification logic ran and found invalid values, the contract says to return a Verify response with verified false plus the message and failure reason, which the signing UI shows.
optionExplanations.E: Passing verification and autofilling the ledger's date of birth would defeat the check and expose member data to whoever typed the member number.

decode.needs: Return verified=false with a response message and failure reason in the connected fields Verify response.
clues: 'matching logic runs successfully but values do not match' -> verification result, not an error
'show what to fix' -> verifyResponseMessage and verifyFailureReason
Azure tenant and API gateway -> red herring

concept.title: Invalid value is not an error
concept.line: When verification logic runs and values are invalid, return verified false with message and reason; HTTP 400/404/500 are only for processing errors.

stem: Which set lists the four required JSON body properties of an Envelopes:create request that uses the direct documents model?

options.text: emailSubject, documents, templateRoles, status
emailSubject, documents, recipients, routingOrder
emailBlurb, documents, recipients, status
emailSubject, documents, recipients, status

answerText: emailSubject, documents, recipients, status
explanation: The course lists emailSubject, documents, recipients and status as the required properties for a direct documents request.
whyNotOthers: D is right. The trap is A: templateRoles is required only in the template reference model, where there is no recipients array. B swaps status for a recipient-level setting and C swaps emailSubject for the optional body text.

optionExplanations.A: templateRoles belongs to the template reference model; direct documents define recipients.
optionExplanations.B: routingOrder is a per-recipient setting, not a required envelope-level property; status is required.
optionExplanations.C: emailBlurb is optional message text; the required property is emailSubject.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. These are the four required properties for the direct documents model.

concept.title: Direct documents required properties
concept.line: Direct documents requests need emailSubject, documents, recipients and status; template reference needs status, templateId and templateRoles.

stem: Which Docusign Connect event is published when a workflow instance has been successfully triggered and execution of its steps begins?

options.text: workflow-completed
workflow-triggered
envelope-sent
workflow-step-started
workflow-started

answerText: workflow-started
explanation: workflow-started is published when a workflow instance is successfully triggered and execution of workflow steps begins (JSON SIM only).
whyNotOthers: E is right because it is the documented Maestro start event. The trap is B: 'triggered' describes the action, but the event name is workflow-started. A fires when all steps are done, C is an eSignature envelope event, and D is not a Maestro Connect event.

optionExplanations.A: Published when all steps are completed by all participants, not at the start.
optionExplanations.B: Not an event name; the start event is workflow-started.
optionExplanations.C: An eSignature envelope event, not a workflow instance event.
optionExplanations.D: No per-step start event is listed for Maestro; the documented events are started, failed and completed.
optionExplanations.E: Correct. workflow-started fires when the instance is triggered and step execution begins.

concept.title: Maestro Connect events
concept.line: Maestro Connect events (JSON SIM only): workflow-started, workflow-failed, workflow-completed.

stem: Corvane Energy's 'Winter fixed-rate switch' workflow is started by the customer website through the Maestro API. In October an engineer's script called pauseNewWorkflowInstances while a tariff was re-approved; instances already in progress finished normally. The tariff has now been approved without any change to the workflow itself, and marketing wants new sign-ups to work again tonight, driven from the company scheduler, with nobody logging in to Workflow Builder. The scheduler's configuration already holds the workflow ID and a token with the aow_manage scope. Which call should the scheduler make?

options.text: POST to the workflow's trigger URL from GetWorkflowTriggerRequirements, because the first new trigger automatically lifts the pause on new instances
POST to /v1/accounts/{accountId}/workflows/{workflowId}/actions/resume (resumePausedWorkflow), which returns the workflow to active for new instances
POST to the publish endpoint with isPreRunCheck=true and then again without it, because a paused workflow must be republished before it accepts instances
POST to /workflows/{workflowId}/instances/{instanceId}/actions/resume for each paused instance, so that the sign-ups paused in October can continue
POST to /v1/accounts/{accountId}/workflows/{workflowId}/actions/pause a second time, because the pause endpoint toggles between paused and active

answerText: POST to /v1/accounts/{accountId}/workflows/{workflowId}/actions/resume (resumePausedWorkflow), which returns the workflow to active for new instances
explanation: resumePausedWorkflow (POST .../workflows/{workflowId}/actions/resume) resumes the creation of new instances of a paused workflow and returns status 'active'.
whyNotOthers: B is right because the pause only blocked new instances and the workflow is unchanged, so resuming is all that is needed. The trap is D: it sounds precise, but pausing never stopped running instances (they 'finished normally'), and there is no per-instance resume. A would be rejected while paused, C republishes an unchanged workflow for no reason, and E invents toggle behaviour.

optionExplanations.A: Triggering does not lift a pause; new instances are blocked until the workflow is resumed.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. resumePausedWorkflow re-enables new instances; the sample response shows status 'active'.
optionExplanations.C: Nothing changed in the workflow, so a republish is unnecessary; the documented action is resume.
optionExplanations.D: Pause affects new instances only, so no instance was paused; the Maestro API has no instance-level resume.
optionExplanations.E: Pause and resume are separate endpoints; calling pause again does not reactivate the workflow.

decode.needs: Call resumePausedWorkflow on the workflow
clues: new sign-ups to work again -> resume creation of new instances
instances already in progress finished normally -> pause never touched running instances
no change to the workflow -> no republish needed
driven from the scheduler -> API call, not Workflow Builder

concept.title: Pause and resume affect new instances
concept.line: pauseNewWorkflowInstances blocks new instances; resumePausedWorkflow re-enables them. Running instances are never paused.

stem: Velden Legal, a Dutch law firm, will move its share-purchase agreements to qualified electronic signatures so signers authenticate through a qualified trust service provider. Today, counterparties use Markup to propose wording changes, the firm's notaries hold remote notarization sessions for some deeds, every document carries a 'Confidential' watermark, and signers occasionally return a wet-signed page. The managing partner asks which current practices will no longer be available once these envelopes use standards-based signatures. (Select two)

options.text: Counterparties proposing wording changes with Markup
The Confidential watermark on every document
Signers returning a wet-signed page
Remote notarization sessions run by the firm's notaries
Free-form signing after the first signer has signed

answerText: Counterparties proposing wording changes with Markup; Remote notarization sessions run by the firm's notaries
explanation: Markup and Notary are listed as not compatible with standards-based signatures. The clue is 'no longer be available', which separates incompatible features from those that only work differently.
whyNotOthers: A and D are right because Markup and Notary cannot be used with SBS envelopes. The trap is E: free-form signing still works, but only signature and initials fields can be added after someone has signed. B and C also still work differently: watermarks become annotations and wet-signed documents are added as new documents.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. Markup is not compatible with standards-based signatures.
optionExplanations.B: Watermarks still work with SBS; they are added as annotations.
optionExplanations.C: Wet signing still works with SBS; the wet-signed documents are added as new documents.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. Notary is not compatible with standards-based signatures.
optionExplanations.E: Free-form signing still works, limited to signature and initials fields after the first signature.

decode.needs: Separate features that SBS blocks (Markup, Notary) from features SBS only changes.
clues: 'qualified electronic signatures ... trust service provider' -> standards-based signatures (QES)
'no longer be available' -> incompatible, not merely different
'Dutch law firm' -> red herring, the rule is the same everywhere

concept.title: SBS incompatible features
concept.line: Standards-based signatures exclude Markup, Notary, fax attachments and legacy digital signatures; watermarks, wet signing and free-form signing work differently.

stem: Helix Trials runs a patient-consent web app for clinical studies that must meet 21 CFR Part 11. Docusign has configured the production account for Part 11, and SMS authentication is enabled. The developers built embedded signing with focused view because the UX team likes its clean look, and they added an identityVerification object to the signer, but the consent sessions do not work. The study sponsor also asked for the sponsor's colours on the signing button. What should the team change?

options.text: Keep SMS identityVerification on the signer and switch the session to classic view, since identityVerification is not supported in focused view
Keep focused view and change the identityVerification to use SMS, then add the sponsor's colours through the Docusign JS style settings
Keep focused view and replace identityVerification with an accessCode texted to each patient, which Part 11 accepts as identity verification
Keep focused view and remove all tabs from the consent so it runs as a click-to-agree experience, which avoids needing the identity check at all

answerText: Keep SMS identityVerification on the signer and switch the session to classic view, since identityVerification is not supported in focused view
explanation: For 21 CFR Part 11 the course requires a Part 11-configured account, SMS identity verification through identityVerification, and classic view, because identityVerification cannot be used with focused view.
whyNotOthers: A is right because the failure comes from using identityVerification in focused view. The trap is B: it fixes a detail that was not the problem and keeps the unsupported view. C swaps in a method that is not the Part 11 one, and D removes the identity check altogether.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. Part 11 embedded signing needs identityVerification with SMS on a Part 11 account, and that parameter works only with classic view.
optionExplanations.B: SMS is the right method, but identityVerification is not supported with focused view, so the session still fails.
optionExplanations.C: Part 11 embedded signing requires identityVerification with SMS; an access code is not the specified Part 11 method.
optionExplanations.D: Dropping identity verification breaks the Part 11 requirement; click-to-agree is not a compliance workaround.

decode.needs: Part 11 embedded signing = identityVerification (SMS) + Part 11 account + classic view
clues: 21 CFR Part 11 -> identityVerification with SMS, Part 11 account
focused view ... sessions do not work -> identityVerification is classic-view only
sponsor colours on the button -> red herring

concept.title: Part 11 needs classic view
concept.line: 21 CFR Part 11 embedded signing uses identityVerification with SMS on a Part 11 account and works only with classic view.

stem: Westmoor Credit Union members log in to online banking with a password and a push approval before they open a loan-modification request built on a template-based web form. The credit union's auditors want the certificate of completion for each resulting agreement to show that the member was already authenticated by the bank's own login, including when and by which identity domain. The marketing team also asks for the credit union's colors on the form. Which delivery design supports this record?

options.text: Create remote instances with sendOption now and add authenticationMethod, authenticationInstant, assertionId and securityDomain to the Instances:createInstance request.
Create embedded instances with the Initiate signing session from email setting enabled, and pass the four authentication record properties in Instances:createInstance.
Create embedded instances from a standalone copy of the configuration, and pass the four authentication record properties in Instances:createInstance.
Create embedded instances with the Initiate signing session from email setting disabled, and pass the four authentication record properties in Instances:createInstance.

answerText: Create embedded instances with the Initiate signing session from email setting disabled, and pass the four authentication record properties in Instances:createInstance.
explanation: The authentication record properties work only when the generated envelope is signed in an embedded signing view, which needs 'Initiate signing session from email' turned off. The clue is 'certificate of completion ... already authenticated by the bank's own login'.
whyNotOthers: D is right because the record of recipient authentication is supported only for embedded signing of template-based web forms. The trap is B: the instance is embedded, but with the email setting enabled the envelope is not signed in an embedded view. A fails because remote instances do not support these properties, and C fails because standalone configurations create no envelope or certificate.

optionExplanations.A: Remote web form instances do not support the authentication record properties.
optionExplanations.B: With Initiate signing session from email enabled, signing is not embedded, so the record is not supported.
optionExplanations.C: Standalone configurations generate no envelope, so there is no certificate to record anything on.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. Embedded signing of a template-based instance supports the four authentication record properties.

decode.needs: Record the portal's own login on the certificate: embedded template-based instance, embedded signing, authentication record properties.
clues: 'already authenticated by the bank's own login' -> record, not enforce, the app's authentication
'certificate of completion' -> an envelope must exist, so template-based
'credit union's colors' -> red herring

concept.title: Web form authentication record
concept.line: authenticationMethod and related properties in createInstance only record your own login, and only for embedded signing of template-based forms.

topic: Production account for a public integration
stem: Quillon, a four-person startup, has built a contract-review add-on that it will offer to many Docusign customers, who will each connect it to their own accounts. The key is already classified correctly and the founders want to launch in six weeks. Quillon has no Docusign production account of any kind. The CTO suggests signing up for a free trial production account this afternoon so that he can press Start Go live today. The add-on is written in Python and hosted on a managed cloud platform. What should Quillon do?

options.text: Sign up for the free trial production account, make the CTO its administrator, and promote the key into it, since any production account in which he is an admin can manage a promoted key
Apply to the Partner Program now, as joining can take weeks, and promote the key into the complimentary partner account, or a paid one, where the submitter is an admin
Promote the key into the developer account Quillon already has, because a public integration is managed from the developer environment until its first customer connects
Skip the production account for now, because Docusign promotes public integrations on the partner's behalf once the listing is approved, so no management account is needed

answerText: Apply to the Partner Program now, as joining can take weeks, and promote the key into the complimentary partner account, or a paid one, where the submitter is an admin
explanation: Each production key must belong to a paid or partner production account in which the submitter is an administrator, and a public integration requires the Partner Program, whose complimentary partner account can manage the key. The clue 'six weeks' matters because joining the program can take several weeks.
whyNotOthers: B is right because it meets both the account rule and the partner requirement in time. The trap is A: being an admin is necessary, but a free trial is not a paid or partner production account. C fails because promotion always goes into a production account, and D invents an automatic promotion that does not exist.

optionExplanations.A: A free trial is neither a paid nor a partner production account, so it cannot manage the promoted key.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. Partner Program members get a complimentary partner production account to manage keys; apply early because it can take weeks.
optionExplanations.C: Go-Live promotes the key into a production account; the developer account cannot be the target.
optionExplanations.D: Every promoted key needs a paid or partner production management account; Docusign does not promote it for you.

decode.needs: Have a paid or partner production account (submitter is admin) before Go-Live; public apps need the Partner Program.
clues: many customers connect their own accounts -> public integration, Partner Program required
no production account, free trial idea -> must be paid or partner production account
launch in six weeks -> partner enrolment can take weeks, so apply early
Python, managed cloud -> red herrings

concept.title: Paid or partner production account
concept.line: A promoted key must be managed by a paid or partner production account in which the submitter is an administrator.

topic: Mutual TLS at the load balancer
stem: Halvorsen Bank's network standard says every inbound partner connection to the DMZ must be authenticated by the F5 load balancer during the TLS handshake, using a client certificate that chains to an approved certificate authority; a caller that cannot present one must be dropped before any HTTP request reaches an application. The Connect listener is written in Java and receives JSON SIM messages, and the application team has no budget to change listener code this quarter. Which approach satisfies the standard?

options.text: Enable HMAC and have the load balancer hash each body with the secret and compare it with X-DocuSign-Signature-1, so unauthenticated calls are dropped early
Enable mutual TLS on the Connect configuration and have the Java listener read and validate Docusign's client certificate in its request handler, updating trust on renewal
Enable mutual TLS on the Connect configuration and have the F5 request and validate Docusign's client certificate in the handshake, updating trust when Docusign renews it
Enable OAuth for Connect, so Docusign obtains a token from the bank's authorization server and the load balancer validates it before forwarding the request
Restrict the DMZ firewall to Docusign's published IP ranges, so that only Docusign can open a TLS connection to the listener and others are refused

answerText: Enable mutual TLS on the Connect configuration and have the F5 request and validate Docusign's client certificate in the handshake, updating trust when Docusign renews it
explanation: Only mutual TLS authenticates the caller "during the TLS handshake" with a client certificate: the listener's server sends a certificate request and validates Docusign's certificate, with no listener code change.
whyNotOthers: C is right because mutual TLS validated by the F5 authenticates Docusign with a certificate inside the handshake, with no listener code change. The trap is B: it uses mutual TLS too, but the certificate is checked in the Java listener's request handler, after the request reaches the application and only by changing listener code. A (HMAC) and D (OAuth) are HTTP-level checks after the handshake, and E filters by IP address rather than authenticating a certificate.

optionExplanations.A: HMAC is checked on the HTTP body after the TLS session is set up and uses a shared secret, so it cannot meet a certificate-in-the-handshake rule.
optionExplanations.B: Mutual TLS is the right mechanism, but validating the certificate in the Java request handler happens after the request reaches the application and needs a listener code change, which the standard and the budget rule out.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. With mutual TLS the server requests Docusign's certificate during the handshake and validates it; the trust setup must be maintained when Docusign renews its certificate, roughly yearly.
optionExplanations.D: OAuth for Connect puts a bearer token in the Authorization header, again an HTTP-level check after the handshake.
optionExplanations.E: IP allowlisting restricts sources but does not authenticate a client certificate, which the standard requires.

decode.needs: Mutual TLS on the Connect configuration, validated by the F5
clues: authenticated during the TLS handshake with a client certificate -> mutual TLS
dropped before any HTTP request reaches an application -> header-based checks (Basic, OAuth, HMAC) are too late
no budget to change listener code -> the F5 validates the certificate, not the Java listener
written in Java, JSON SIM -> red herrings

concept.title: Mutual TLS authenticates at handshake
concept.line: Mutual TLS lets the listener's server request and validate Docusign's client certificate during the TLS handshake, before any HTTP request is processed.

stem: The architecture board at Quarry Point Energy must approve a design in which an unattended back-office service sends royalty statements on behalf of the land agent responsible for each lease, using JWT Grant. Most agents have addresses in the company's claimed domain, but some contract land agents use their own agency domains. The company has Access Management, and the service will run in a Kubernetes cluster managed by a partner. The board asks for an accurate list of the drawbacks it is accepting with this flow. Which two statements belong on that list? (Select two)

options.text: The service must keep a client secret on a secure web server and send it in a Basic header on every token request
Each access token lasts one hour with no refresh token, so the service must build and exchange a new JWT each time
The refresh token expires 30 days after issue unless extended is requested, so each agent must sign in again every month
Admin consent will not reach agents outside the claimed domain, so the service also needs an individual consent path
Each impersonated agent must be signed in to Docusign whenever the service starts a sending run for their leases

answerText: Each access token lasts one hour with no refresh token, so the service must build and exchange a new JWT each time; Admin consent will not reach agents outside the claimed domain, so the service also needs an individual consent path
explanation: The documented JWT drawbacks include a one-hour token with no refresh token, and the need to support individual consent for users that admin consent cannot cover, such as contractors outside the claimed domain.
whyNotOthers: B and D are right: the contract agents on agency domains are the deciding clue for D. The trap is C: refresh tokens and the extended scope belong to Authorization Code Grant; JWT Grant issues no refresh token at all. A describes the Confidential Auth Code secret (JWT uses an RSA key pair) and E contradicts the point of JWT, which needs no user present after consent.

optionExplanations.A: JWT Grant signs an assertion with an RSA private key; the Basic header with a secret belongs to Confidential Auth Code Grant.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. A JWT access token lasts one hour and no refresh token is provided.
optionExplanations.C: JWT Grant issues no refresh token, so this Authorization Code rule does not apply.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. Users outside the claimed domain need individual consent, so the integration must support it too.
optionExplanations.E: After consent, JWT Grant does not need the impersonated user to be present.

decode.needs: Identify the documented disadvantages of JWT Grant
clues: 'unattended back-office service on behalf of each land agent' -> JWT impersonating many users
'contract agents on their own agency domains' -> outside admin consent, need individual consent
'Kubernetes cluster managed by a partner' -> red herring

concept.title: JWT Grant trade-offs
concept.line: JWT: no user needed after consent, but one-hour tokens with no refresh, possible individual-consent fallback, RSA key handling and high trust.

topic: Publishing changes to a paused workflow
stem: At Osterley Rentals, a process builder paused the 'Tenant renewal' workflow last week so that no new renewals could start while legal rewrote one clause. Twelve renewals already in progress kept running. She has now swapped the revised template into the Prepare eSignature Template step and saved the draft, but Review & Publish will not let her publish the change. The workflow's start method is From a Link, and the link is printed on paper renewal letters. What explains this, and what is the right next step?

options.text: Changes made to a paused workflow cannot be published, so she should resume the workflow first and then publish the revised version
A workflow with running instances cannot be republished, so she must cancel the twelve active renewals before publishing the revised version
She must unpublish the paused workflow first and then publish the draft, because only unpublished workflows can accept edited versions
Workflows started From a Link cannot be republished, so she should change the start method to From an API call before publishing
The template swap needs a fresh consent grant, so she should open the consentUrl from the pre-publication check and then publish again

answerText: Changes made to a paused workflow cannot be published, so she should resume the workflow first and then publish the revised version
explanation: The course states that 'changes made to a paused workflow can not be published' and that a paused workflow can be resumed at any time; resuming first lets the revised version be published.
whyNotOthers: A is right because the deciding detail is that the workflow is paused. The trap is B: running instances matter for unpublishing, but editing and republishing leaves active instances on their original definition, so they need not be cancelled. C would require no running instances and is not needed, D invents a start-method restriction, and E applies only when the pre-publication check returns a consent error, which the stem does not describe.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. Paused workflows cannot have changes published; resume, then publish the revised version.
optionExplanations.B: Active instances keep their original definition when a workflow is edited; they do not block publishing.
optionExplanations.C: Unpublish is for freeing quota and needs no running instances; it is not the path to publish edits.
optionExplanations.D: The start method does not block republishing.
optionExplanations.E: Only a consent error returns a consentUrl; nothing in the stem shows one.

decode.needs: Resume the paused workflow, then publish the edited version
clues: paused so no new renewals could start -> workflow state is paused
will not let her publish -> paused workflows cannot publish changes
twelve renewals kept running -> active instances are unaffected by edits
link printed on letters -> red herring

concept.title: Paused workflows block publishing
concept.line: Changes to a paused workflow cannot be published; resume the workflow first. Active instances keep their original definition.

stem: Calder Mutual's policyholder portal lets customers sign renewal documents inside the portal right after they log in with the portal's two-step login. About a third of customers close the browser before signing. The business wants Docusign to send those customers a reminder email, but the link in that email must bring them back through the portal's login before the documents open, because the compliance team relies on that login as the identity check. The portal runs on a new cloud host. What should the envelope request contain for each customer?

options.text: Keep the clientUserId and set embeddedRecipientStartURL to the portal's signing page, so the Docusign email routes the customer through the portal, which requests a new recipient view
Keep the clientUserId on the customer and set embeddedRecipientStartURL to SIGN_AT_DOCUSIGN, so the Docusign email opens the embedded signing session directly for the customer
Remove the clientUserId when the customer leaves, so the customer becomes a remote signer and receives the standard Docusign email with a link that opens the documents to sign
Store the recipient view URL created at login and email it from the portal to customers who leave, so they can resume the same signing session later from that link

answerText: Keep the clientUserId and set embeddedRecipientStartURL to the portal's signing page, so the Docusign email routes the customer through the portal, which requests a new recipient view
explanation: embeddedRecipientStartURL makes Docusign email an embedded recipient while routing the link back to your own URL, so your app can authenticate the user before calling createRecipient. The deciding clue is 'must bring them back through the portal's login'.
whyNotOthers: A is right because the email link is redirected to the portal, which keeps control of authentication. The trap is B: SIGN_AT_DOCUSIGN does send an email, but it opens signing directly at Docusign and bypasses the portal login. C turns the customer into a remote signer outside the portal, and D reuses a URL that expires within minutes.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. With clientUserId and embeddedRecipientStartURL set, Docusign emails the embedded recipient and the link redirects through Docusign to your URL, where your app authenticates the user and requests the signing session.
optionExplanations.B: SIGN_AT_DOCUSIGN sends the recipient straight to signing at Docusign and bypasses the sending application and its authentication, which the stem forbids.
optionExplanations.C: A remote signer signs from the email link at Docusign without passing through the portal login, so the compliance requirement is lost.
optionExplanations.D: Recipient view URLs are short-lived and single-use, so a stored URL fails with ttl_expired; it also skips the portal login.

decode.needs: clientUserId + embeddedRecipientStartURL pointing to the app (not SIGN_AT_DOCUSIGN)
clues: sign inside the portal -> embedded signer with clientUserId
Docusign should send a reminder email -> embeddedRecipientStartURL makes Docusign email an embedded recipient
link must come back through the portal's login -> URL of your app, not SIGN_AT_DOCUSIGN
new cloud host -> red herring

concept.title: Email link for embedded signers
concept.line: embeddedRecipientStartURL lets Docusign email an embedded recipient; your URL keeps your authentication, SIGN_AT_DOCUSIGN bypasses it.

topic: Flow selection: interactive users plus nightly batch
stem: Harbor & Pine, a furniture wholesaler, runs a dealer-relations portal on its own application servers, where credentials live in a hardware-backed vault. During the day about 120 account managers sign in to the portal and send dealer agreements that must show each manager as the sender, and the security office insists the portal must never act for a manager who is not personally signed in. Every night an unattended reconciliation job on the same servers downloads completed agreements account-wide as a service user named recon-svc. The portal's screens were recently rebuilt in Vue. Which authentication design fits best?

options.text: JWT Grant for both parts, impersonating each account manager by user ID during the day and recon-svc at night, after one admin consent
Confidential Authorization Code Grant for both parts, with recon-svc signing in once and the nightly job reusing its stored extended refresh token
Confidential Authorization Code Grant for the managers' sessions and JWT Grant as recon-svc for the nightly job, both credentials on one key
Public Authorization Code Grant with PKCE for the managers because the screens are a Vue app, and JWT Grant as recon-svc for the nightly job
Implicit Grant for the managers' browser sessions so no secret is stored, and JWT Grant as recon-svc for the nightly job

answerText: Confidential Authorization Code Grant for the managers' sessions and JWT Grant as recon-svc for the nightly job, both credentials on one key
explanation: Managers sign in personally on a server that can keep a secret in a vault, so Confidential Authorization Code Grant fits them; the job with no human at the keyboard needs JWT Grant. One integration key can hold both a secret key and an RSA key pair.
whyNotOthers: C is right because the daytime part is interactive and server-hosted while the nightly part is unattended. The trap is D: the Vue front end is a red herring, because the server does the token exchange and can protect a secret, so Confidential is preferred over Public. A breaks the rule that the portal never acts for a manager who is not signed in; B makes a headless job depend on one interactive login and a refresh token; E uses the legacy Implicit Grant.

optionExplanations.A: JWT would let the portal act for managers who are not signed in, which the security office forbids.
optionExplanations.B: An unattended job should not depend on one interactive login and a refresh token chain; JWT is the flow for a service user.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. Confidential for the signed-in managers on a secret-capable server, JWT for the headless job; both credentials can live on one integration key.
optionExplanations.D: Public Auth Code is for apps that cannot keep a secret; this portal's servers have a vault, so the Vue UI does not change the choice.
optionExplanations.E: Implicit Grant is legacy and less secure; it is not recommended for a server that can store a secret.

decode.needs: Confidential Authorization Code Grant for signed-in users plus JWT Grant for the unattended service user
clues: 'never act for a manager who is not personally signed in' -> user-present flow, not JWT impersonation
'credentials live in a hardware-backed vault' -> the app can keep a secret: Confidential
'unattended reconciliation job as recon-svc' -> JWT Grant
'rebuilt in Vue' -> red herring; token exchange still happens on the server

concept.title: Mixing flows on one key
concept.line: Interactive users on a secret-capable server use Confidential Auth Code; unattended jobs use JWT. One integration key can carry both a secret and an RSA key pair.

stem: Copperline Insurance uses one integration key for two integrations: a claims-adjuster web portal on company servers that uses Confidential Authorization Code Grant, and a headless overnight batch that uses JWT Grant to impersonate a claims-mailroom user. During a credential clean-up, an engineer deleted the key's only secret key but left its RSA key pair untouched. The change was made from a contractor's laptop while most adjusters were mid-shift. Assuming nothing else changes, what happens to new token requests from the two integrations?

options.text: Both integrations fail, because every /oauth/token request is authenticated with the integration key's secret key
The portal can't exchange codes or refresh tokens, as its Basic header needs the secret; the batch keeps working
The batch can no longer get tokens, because its JWT is signed with the secret key; the portal keeps working with user logins
Neither integration is affected, because the secret key is only checked when the integration key is promoted at go-live
The portal keeps working until its refresh tokens expire in 30 days, while the batch fails at its next run tonight

answerText: The portal can't exchange codes or refresh tokens, as its Basic header needs the secret; the batch keeps working
explanation: Confidential Authorization Code Grant sends a Basic header built from integration key and secret on the code exchange and on refreshes; JWT Grant signs its assertion with the RSA private key, so it does not need the secret.
whyNotOthers: B is right because only the Confidential flow depends on the secret key. The trap is A: both flows call /oauth/token, but JWT requests carry an RSA-signed assertion, not a Basic header. C reverses the credentials, D invents a go-live-only check, and E is wrong because refreshing itself needs the Basic header with the secret.

optionExplanations.A: JWT token requests are authenticated by the RSA-signed assertion, not by the secret.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. Code exchange and refresh need the Basic integrationKey:secretKey header; the JWT batch only needs its RSA private key.
optionExplanations.C: The JWT is signed with the RSA private key, not with the secret key.
optionExplanations.D: The secret is used on every Confidential token and refresh request, not only at go-live.
optionExplanations.E: A Confidential refresh request also needs the Basic header, so refreshing fails too; the JWT batch is unaffected.

decode.needs: Know which credential each flow sends to /oauth/token
clues: 'deleted the only secret key' -> Confidential Auth Code token and refresh requests fail
'RSA key pair untouched' -> JWT Grant still works
'contractor's laptop, mid-shift' -> red herrings

concept.title: Secret key versus RSA key
concept.line: Confidential Auth Code authenticates token requests with integration key plus secret; JWT Grant authenticates with an assertion signed by the RSA private key.

stem: When a Confidential Authorization Code Grant app posts the authorization code to /oauth/token, which Content-Type must the request use?

options.text: application/json
multipart/form-data
application/jwt
text/plain
application/x-www-form-urlencoded

answerText: application/x-www-form-urlencoded
explanation: The /oauth/token endpoint requires Content-Type application/x-www-form-urlencoded, with grant_type and code in the form body.
whyNotOthers: E is right because the token endpoint takes form-encoded parameters. The trap is A: most Docusign REST calls use JSON, but the OAuth token request does not. B, C and D are not accepted formats for this endpoint.

optionExplanations.A: JSON is used by the eSignature REST API bodies, not by the /oauth/token request.
optionExplanations.B: The token request is not a multipart upload.
optionExplanations.C: There is no application/jwt content type for this request; even JWT Grant sends the assertion as a form field.
optionExplanations.D: Plain text is not the documented format.
optionExplanations.E: Correct. The documented Content-Type for /oauth/token is application/x-www-form-urlencoded.

concept.title: Token endpoint content type
concept.line: POST /oauth/token takes form-encoded parameters (application/x-www-form-urlencoded), not a JSON body.

topic: Locate an agreement from an envelope ID
stem: Corvane Logistics' service desk tool shows a customer's signed contract whenever an agent opens a ticket. The CRM stores the Docusign envelope ID of each contract it sent for signature, but it has never stored any Agreement Manager identifiers. Agents now want the contract's AI-extracted payment terms and renewal notice period on the ticket screen. The desk handles about 400 tickets a day, the CRM is hosted in a separate EU region, and the account's hourly API limit is shared with a billing integration. How should the tool look up the agreement?

options.text: Call GetAgreement with the stored envelope ID as the agreementId, because a completed envelope keeps its envelope ID as its agreement ID.
Call GetAgreementsList filtered on related_agreement_documents.parent_agreement_document_id set to the stored envelope ID, then read the provisions.
Call the eSignature Envelopes:get endpoint with the stored envelope ID and read the AI-extracted provisions from the envelope's custom fields.
Call GetAgreementsList filtered on source_id set to the stored envelope ID, then read the payment terms and renewal notice period from the record.

answerText: Call GetAgreementsList filtered on source_id set to the stored envelope ID, then read the payment terms and renewal notice period from the record.
explanation: source_id holds the record's identifier in the originating system (for eSignature, the envelope ID) and GetAgreementsList can filter on it, so one call turns 'the envelope ID the CRM stores' into the agreement and its provisions.
whyNotOthers: D is right because the source_id filter bridges the envelope ID to the agreement record. The trap is A: the agreement id is Agreement Manager's own GUID, not the envelope ID, so GetAgreement would not find it. B uses the link from an amendment to its parent document, and C fails because eSignature does not expose AI-extracted provisions.

optionExplanations.A: The agreement id is a separate GUID generated by Agreement Manager; the envelope ID lives in source_id, so this lookup fails.
optionExplanations.B: parent_agreement_document_id links a child agreement (such as an amendment) to its parent document, not to an eSignature envelope.
optionExplanations.C: The eSignature API returns envelope data; AI-extracted payment terms and notice periods come only from the Agreement Manager API.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. GetAgreementsList accepts a source_id filter, and source_id carries the originating envelope ID for eSignature agreements.

decode.needs: Find the agreement record from an envelope ID by filtering GetAgreementsList on source_id.
clues: stores the envelope ID, never any Agreement Manager identifiers -> the agreementId is unknown
AI-extracted payment terms and renewal notice period -> provisions from the Agreement Manager record
EU region, 400 tickets a day -> red herrings

concept.title: source_id links agreement to envelope
concept.line: An agreement's source_id is its identifier in the originating system; filter GetAgreementsList on it when only the envelope ID is known.

topic: Sharing a private app with developer accounts
stem: A private extension app is Live and shared with the company's production account. A contractor working in a separate Docusign developer account asks to install it there for testing. What applies?

options.text: It cannot be shared with additional developer accounts; private sharing targets production accounts only.
Add the contractor's developer account ID with an alias, just like a production account.
It appears automatically in every developer account that belongs to the same organization.
Publish it to the demo App Center as public for testing while keeping it private in production.
The contractor's admin accepts it from a Pending notification in the demo App Center.

answerText: It cannot be shared with additional developer accounts; private sharing targets production accounts only.
explanation: Docs: a private app is automatically available in your own developer account, and you can share it (once published) with additional production accounts, but you cannot share it with additional developer accounts.
whyNotOthers: A is right because private sharing is only for production accounts. The trap is B: adding an account ID with an alias is the real sharing mechanism, but only for production accounts. C, D and E invent sharing paths that do not exist.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. A private app is available automatically in your own developer account, and once published it can be shared with production accounts, but not with additional developer accounts.
optionExplanations.B: The account list for a private app takes production account IDs; additional developer accounts are not supported.
optionExplanations.C: Only the developer account that registered the app sees it automatically.
optionExplanations.D: An app has one distribution type for all versions; you cannot be public in demo and private in production.
optionExplanations.E: Pending and Accepted statuses apply to the production accounts on the sharing list, not to developer accounts.

decode.needs: Know the sharing scope of a private extension app.
clues: 'separate Docusign developer account' -> not a valid sharing target

concept.title: Private sharing is production only
concept.line: A private app is visible in its own developer account and can be shared only with listed production accounts, never other developer accounts.

stem: Corvane Lettings runs a tenant-screening portal. While an application waits for signatures, a background timer asks Docusign for that agreement's status every 10 minutes so leasing agents see near-real-time progress. Every one of these calls succeeds and the account stays far below its hourly allowance, yet the Go-Live review of the portal's integration key flags the app. The portal is written in .NET and hosted in Azure, and the agents work from three regional offices. What should the team change before resubmitting?

options.text: Leave the timer as it is, because every call succeeds and the account stays well under its 3,000-per-hour allowance, and ask Docusign Support for a manual review of the key instead
Keep the 10-minute timer but raise the account's hourly limit in the API Usage Center, so that the status calls are no longer treated as excessive during the review
Receive status changes through Connect notifications instead of the timer, and if a fallback check must remain, space it at least 20 minutes apart for each agreement
Change the timer to 15 minutes per agreement, and also poll immediately whenever an agent clicks Refresh, so agents still see near-real-time progress

answerText: Receive status changes through Connect notifications instead of the timer, and if a fallback check must remain, space it at least 20 minutes apart for each agreement
explanation: Apps may make only one status GET per envelope per 15 minutes; extra calls do not fail but are flagged as rate-limit violations that can fail the Go-Live review. The clue 'every 10 minutes' with 'calls succeed' points to this rule; Docusign recommends Connect, or polling at 20-minute intervals.
whyNotOthers: C is right because Connect pushes each change without counting against limits, and any fallback check stays well inside the polling rule. The trap is D: a 15-minute timer looks compliant, but the on-demand Refresh polls bring the frequency back above one call per envelope per 15 minutes. A ignores the flagged polling pattern, and B fails because raising the hourly limit does not change the per-envelope polling rule.

optionExplanations.A: Succeeding calls and a low hourly total do not matter: exceeding one status GET per envelope per 15 minutes is flagged even though the request succeeds.
optionExplanations.B: The hourly account limit and the per-envelope polling rule are separate; raising one does not excuse the other.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. Connect pushes status changes without polling; any fallback poll should run at 20-minute intervals.
optionExplanations.D: The 15-minute timer alone would respect the rule, but the extra on-demand Refresh polls break the one-status-call-per-envelope-per-15-minutes limit again; Connect gives near-real-time updates without polling.

decode.needs: Stop per-envelope status polling more often than every 15 minutes; use Connect (fallback poll at 20 minutes).
clues: timer every 10 minutes per agreement -> violates one status GET per envelope per 15 minutes
calls succeed but review flags the app -> polling violations are flagged, not rejected
.NET, Azure, three offices -> red herrings

concept.title: Polling rule and Go-Live review
concept.line: One status GET per envelope per 15 minutes; excess calls succeed but are flagged and can fail Go-Live. Use Connect or 20-minute polls.

topic: Migrating users and Connect after Go-Live
stem: Ferncliff Water's billing platform went live last week with JWT Grant. The team added an RSA key pair to the production copy of the key, changed the OAuth host, and now builds API URLs from userinfo. Two problems remain. Token requests fail because the JWT's sub still holds the user ID of 'billing-svc', the user it impersonated in the sandbox. And although invoices now go out from production, the finance system never hears about completed invoices; in testing it did, through an account-wide webhook the team set up in the sandbox's admin settings. Which two actions fix these problems? (Select two)

options.text: Add the finance system's listener URL to the production key's redirect URIs, because redirect URIs are not copied by Go-Live and also govern where webhook messages may be sent
Create the billing-svc user in the production account (or pick an existing production user), put that user's production user ID in sub, and obtain that user's consent in production
Run Start Go live again for the same key, because a second promotion copies the sandbox's users and their consent records into the production account
Wait for the nightly synchronisation between the environments, which copies account settings such as Connect configurations into production within 24 hours
Recreate the account-level Connect configuration in the production account's admin settings, pointing at the finance system's listener with the same events selected

answerText: Create the billing-svc user in the production account (or pick an existing production user), put that user's production user ID in sub, and obtain that user's consent in production; Recreate the account-level Connect configuration in the production account's admin settings, pointing at the finance system's listener with the same events selected
explanation: Production account settings and data are separate from the developer account, so users and settings such as Connect configurations must be migrated after Go-Live. The clues 'sub still holds the sandbox user ID' and 'webhook set up in the sandbox's admin settings' show what was never moved.
whyNotOthers: B and E are right: the production user has a different user ID that needs its own consent, and an account-level Connect configuration lives in the account where it was created. The trap is A: redirect URIs really are not copied, but they are OAuth return addresses and have nothing to do with where Connect posts. C fails because Go-Live copies only the key, and D fails because no synchronisation between environments exists.

optionExplanations.A: Redirect URIs are OAuth settings for returning users after sign-in; Connect delivery is set in the Connect configuration.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. Users must be migrated; sub must be the production user's ID, and consent must be granted in production.
optionExplanations.C: Go-Live duplicates only the integration key; it never copies users or consent.
optionExplanations.D: There is no synchronisation of settings between developer and production accounts.
optionExplanations.E: Correct. Account settings such as Connect configurations must be recreated in the production account.

decode.needs: Migrate users (new production user ID plus consent) and recreate account settings like Connect in production.
clues: sub still holds the sandbox user ID -> production users have different IDs
account-wide webhook set up in the sandbox admin -> account-level Connect configuration stays in the developer account
RSA key and OAuth host already done -> those are not the remaining problems

concept.title: Migrate users and settings
concept.line: After Go-Live, production users, consent and account settings such as Connect configurations must be set up separately.

topic: Moving a Maestro integration to production
stem: Fenwick Health's developers have finished a referral-intake integration in their developer account. Their scheduling app triggers a published workflow through the Maestro API, and one workflow step is a Writeback step from the company's own private extension app that updates the referral in the clinical scheduling system. Everything passes in demo. The project manager asks what must be in place before the app can run the workflow against the production account; the go-live date was set by the board. Which two items are required? (Select two)

options.text: Create a new integration key in the production account and use it with JWT Grant, because developer integration keys cannot be promoted to production
Pass the Go-Live review for the app's integration key, so the key is copied into production and can call the production API endpoints
Add the scheduling system's base URL to the production account's Connect configuration so the Writeback step can reach the external system
Make sure the private extension app used by the Writeback step is published, and that the workflow the app triggers is published in production
Request aow_manage through a separate production consent form, because Maestro scopes are not available to keys that went live for eSignature

answerText: Pass the Go-Live review for the app's integration key, so the key is copied into production and can call the production API endpoints; Make sure the private extension app used by the Writeback step is published, and that the workflow the app triggers is published in production
explanation: Docusign's Publishing and Go-Live guidance lists: publish the workflows the app invokes, make sure any extension apps used in workflow steps are published, and promote the integration key from the developer account through a Go-Live review.
whyNotOthers: B and D are right because production needs a promoted integration key and published workflow and extension app. The trap is A: it sounds safe to start fresh, but integration keys are promoted to production by passing Go-Live, after which the same key calls production endpoints. C confuses Connect (outbound notifications) with how an extension reaches its system, and E invents a separate consent form for Maestro scopes.

optionExplanations.A: The documented path is Go-Live review, which copies the existing integration key into production.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. A Go-Live review promotes the integration key so the app can call the production endpoints.
optionExplanations.C: Connect sends event notifications to listeners; an extension app reaches its external system through its own connection.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. The workflow the app invokes and any extension apps used in its steps must be published.
optionExplanations.E: aow_manage is requested in the normal OAuth flow like other scopes; no separate production form exists.

decode.needs: Go-Live review for the key plus published workflow and extension app
clues: before the app can run against production -> Go-Live requirements
private extension app in a Writeback step -> extension app must be published
board set the date -> red herring

concept.title: Maestro go-live checklist
concept.line: Production needs the integration key promoted through Go-Live, the workflow published, and every extension app used in steps published.

stem: Larchmont Health's JWT Grant service must rotate its RSA key pair every 90 days under a new security policy, with no window in which token requests fail. The team plans to generate a new key pair on the integration key, deploy the new private key to the service in all three regions, confirm that tokens are being issued, and only then delete the old pair. A reviewer points out that the integration key already holds four RSA key pairs left over from earlier experiments and asks how many the key can hold. What is the documented maximum number of RSA key pairs per integration key?

options.text: One
Two
Three
Ten
Five

answerText: Five
explanation: An integration key can hold a maximum of 5 RSA key pairs; with four defined, one more can be added before the old pair is deleted.
whyNotOthers: E is right: the documented limit is five, and when five exist one must be deleted before another is created. The trap is B: rotation is often pictured as one active plus one pending key, but Docusign allows up to five. A, C and D are not the documented limit.

optionExplanations.A: The key can hold more than one pair, which is what makes overlap during rotation possible.
optionExplanations.B: Two is a common mental model for rotation, but the limit is five.
optionExplanations.C: Three is not the documented limit.
optionExplanations.D: Ten exceeds the limit.
optionExplanations.E: Correct. Up to 5 RSA key pairs; delete one before creating a sixth.

decode.needs: Know the RSA key pair limit on an integration key
clues: 'rotate with no failure window' -> add new pair before deleting old
'already holds four pairs' -> one more is still allowed
'three regions' -> red herring

concept.title: RSA key pairs per key
concept.line: An integration key holds up to five RSA key pairs, which allows overlap when rotating JWT signing keys.

topic: Default brand for an unchangeable integration
stem: Tamsin Foods is rolling out a new corporate identity next month. Its procurement suite, a vendor-hosted system the company cannot modify, creates about 900 supplier contracts a week through the eSignature REST API on behalf of one service user, and its requests never name a brand. The HR team, which sends from the web app using templates, has already switched its templates to the new brand. Marketing wants every supplier who receives a contract from the procurement suite to see the new logo and colors from launch day. What should the Docusign administrator do?

options.text: Select the new brand on every template in the account, so that any envelope created from those templates, including supplier contracts, carries the new identity.
Ask the vendor to add the new brand's brandId to each Envelopes:create request, so every supplier contract explicitly names the brand it should use.
Set the new brand as the account's default brand, so that envelopes created without a brandId, such as the procurement suite's contracts, use it automatically.
Assign the new brand to a group and add the procurement service user to that group, so that the service user is permitted to send with the new brand.

answerText: Set the new brand as the account's default brand, so that envelopes created without a brandId, such as the procurement suite's contracts, use it automatically.
explanation: A brand set as the account default is used for envelopes that do not name a brand. The clues are 'a system the company cannot modify' and 'its requests never name a brand'.
whyNotOthers: C is right because the default brand covers envelopes created without a brandId, with no code change. The trap is D: assigning a brand to a group only controls which users may use it; the suite still sends no brandId. B needs a code change in a system that cannot be modified, and A fails because the suite does not send from templates (the HR templates are a red herring).

optionExplanations.A: The procurement suite sends without templates, so template brands never reach its contracts.
optionExplanations.B: brandId on Envelopes:create works, but the vendor-hosted suite cannot be changed.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. The account default brand applies to envelopes that do not specify a brand.
optionExplanations.D: Group assignment controls who may use a brand; it does not apply it to envelopes that name no brand.

decode.needs: Make the brand apply without any brandId in the API request: set it as the account default brand.
clues: 'vendor-hosted system the company cannot modify' -> no brandId can be added
'its requests never name a brand' -> needs a brand applied by default
'HR team ... switched its templates' -> red herring, the suite does not use templates

concept.title: Account default brand
concept.line: Envelopes that do not specify a brandId use the account's default brand; group assignment only limits who may use a brand.

stem: A field agent's mobile app uses Public Authorization Code Grant and ships with no secret. At the token step, how does Docusign confirm that the app redeeming the authorization code is the one that started the flow?

options.text: It checks that the code_challenge sent again in the token request matches the one sent to /oauth/auth
It verifies the code_verifier's signature with the public key registered on the integration key
It decrypts the code_challenge with the integration key and compares it with the authorization code
It hashes the code_verifier with S256, base64url-encodes it and compares the result with the earlier code_challenge
It compares the code_verifier with the random state value that the app sent to /oauth/auth

answerText: It hashes the code_verifier with S256, base64url-encodes it and compares the result with the earlier code_challenge
explanation: The app sends the unhashed code_verifier to /oauth/token; Docusign hashes it with S256, base64url-encodes it and checks that it matches the code_challenge from the authorization request.
whyNotOthers: D is right because PKCE proves possession of the original random string. The trap is A: the challenge is sent only on /oauth/auth; at the token step the app sends the verifier, never the challenge again. B and C invent key operations PKCE does not use, and E confuses PKCE with the CSRF state parameter.

optionExplanations.A: The token request carries the code_verifier, not the code_challenge again.
optionExplanations.B: PKCE involves no signature or public key; that is JWT Grant.
optionExplanations.C: Nothing is decrypted; the verifier is hashed and compared.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. S256 hash of the verifier, base64url-encoded, must equal the stored code_challenge.
optionExplanations.E: state protects against CSRF on the redirect; it plays no part in PKCE.

concept.title: How PKCE proves the caller
concept.line: Send code_challenge (S256 hash of a random verifier) on /oauth/auth; send the raw code_verifier to /oauth/token, where Docusign re-hashes and compares.

stem: Brightwell Partners wants an internal chat assistant for its sales directors. A director types questions such as 'Which of our reseller agreements with Novatek expire before the end of June?' and gets an answer that names the agreements. Contract admins correct AI-extracted dates in Agreement Manager several times a day, and directors must see a correction as soon as it is saved. The information security team will not approve any copy of agreement data stored outside Docusign, and the assistant runs on the company's existing large language model platform. Which design fits?

options.text: Copy every agreement nightly into a vector store with GetAgreementsList, and let the model answer each question from that store while citing each agreementId.
Call CreateAgreementSummary for each agreement at question time, and let the model read the expiration dates and party names out of the returned summaries.
Let the model turn each question into a GetAgreementsList call filtered on parties.name_in_agreement and provisions.expiration_date, then answer.
Let the model search completed envelopes with the eSignature listStatusChanges call and read expiration dates from each envelope's document fields.

answerText: Let the model turn each question into a GetAgreementsList call filtered on parties.name_in_agreement and provisions.expiration_date, then answer.
explanation: Docusign documents copilot integrations where the model constructs Agreement Manager queries from a natural-language question and interprets the returned data. Querying live at question time satisfies 'see a correction as soon as it is saved' and 'no copy stored outside Docusign'.
whyNotOthers: C is right because a filtered live query returns current, user-corrected values without storing a copy. The trap is A: an indexed RAG store is a valid pattern in general, but a nightly copy is both stale and forbidden here. B produces AI prose per agreement, which is slow and unstructured, and D uses eSignature, which has no AI-extracted expiration dates.

optionExplanations.A: A nightly copy is stale for up to a day and stores agreement data outside Docusign, both ruled out by the stem.
optionExplanations.B: Summaries are narrative text generated per agreement; they are not a reliable or efficient way to filter by party and date.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. The model maps the question to party and expiration_date filters and answers from current records, so corrections show immediately.
optionExplanations.D: Envelope status calls do not return AI-extracted provisions such as expiration_date.

decode.needs: Live, filtered Agreement Manager queries generated by the LLM, with no external index.
clues: see a correction as soon as it is saved -> user-updated values must be read live, not from a snapshot
no copy of agreement data stored outside Docusign -> rules out a vector store or data lake
reseller agreements with Novatek expire before June -> parties.name_in_agreement plus expiration_date filters
existing large language model platform -> red herring

concept.title: Copilot builds filtered queries live
concept.line: A copilot can translate questions into GetAgreementsList filters at answer time, giving current, user-corrected data without keeping a copy.

topic: Redirect versus iframe for an instance URL
stem: Brightmoor Credit Union's members start a loan-deferral request from the online banking portal. The portal's server already triggers the published workflow with the member's details and receives the instance URL. In the pilot, developers simply sent the member's browser to that URL: members completed the web form and the signature without trouble, but afterwards they were left on a Docusign page, and many called the contact centre asking how to get back to their accounts. The product owner wants members to see the portal's navigation throughout and land on the portal's next-steps page when they finish. The portal also runs a chat widget. What should change?

options.text: Keep redirecting the browser to the instance URL, but pass the next-steps page as a return URL in trigger_inputs so the workflow sends members back after the last step
Switch the start method to From a Link and place the workflow link on a portal page, so that each member opens the workflow from inside the portal instead of being redirected
Create an eSignature recipient view with a returnUrl for the signing step only, and keep redirecting the browser to the instance URL for the web form and other steps
Load the instance URL in an iframe on a portal page, so the portal interface stays visible during every step and the portal routes the member onward when the workflow ends
Add a Show a Confirmation Screen step whose message links back to the portal, because a workflow instance cannot be displayed inside another web application

answerText: Load the instance URL in an iframe on a portal page, so the portal interface stays visible during every step and the portal routes the member onward when the workflow ends
explanation: With a redirect, the user 'remains at the Docusign platform' after finishing; embedding the instance URL in an iframe keeps the web application visible, and when the workflow finishes the browser still shows the application, which can route the member onward.
whyNotOthers: D is right because the deciding clues are 'see the portal's navigation throughout' and 'land on the next-steps page'. The trap is A: it sounds like eSignature's returnUrl, but trigger_inputs carry starting variable values, not a redirect target, and a redirected user stays on Docusign. B still navigates away when the link opens, C mixes in an eSignature view the workflow does not need, and E is false because instance URLs are designed to be framed.

optionExplanations.A: trigger_inputs hold starting variable values; there is no documented return URL there, and a redirected member stays on Docusign.
optionExplanations.B: Opening a workflow link still takes the member to Docusign; it also drops the server-side trigger with the member's details.
optionExplanations.C: The signing step runs inside the workflow instance; a separate eSignature recipient view does not fix the redirect for the whole journey.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. In an iframe the portal stays visible, and after the last step the browser still shows the portal, which routes the member to next steps.
optionExplanations.E: Embedding the instance URL in an iframe is the documented option, so the premise is wrong.

decode.needs: Embed the triggered instance URL in an iframe instead of redirecting
clues: left on a Docusign page -> the redirect option
see the portal's navigation throughout -> iframe embedding
land on the portal's next-steps page -> app routes the user after completion
chat widget -> red herring

concept.title: Embed instance URL in iframe
concept.line: Redirecting to an instance URL leaves users on Docusign afterwards; an iframe keeps your app visible and lets it route users when done.

topic: Back-filling a new listener with historical envelopes
stem: Corvid Energy launched a contract analytics listener today. Analysts also need data for about 2,000 envelopes that were completed during the last quarter, before the listener existed, delivered to the same listener in the same JSON format as live events. The account already has an XML configuration that feeds an old archive system, and the archive team will not allow any change to it. A new JSON SIM configuration for the analytics listener was created this morning. What is the best way to deliver the historical envelopes?

options.text: Use the Connect failure log and ConnectEvents:retryForEnvelopes to republish the quarter's envelopes so they are posted to the analytics listener
Temporarily point the existing XML configuration at the analytics listener and republish the quarter's envelopes from the Connect logs, then restore it
Run a job that calls Envelopes:get for each of the 2,000 envelopes and posts each response body to the analytics listener as if it were a Connect event
Rely on the new JSON SIM configuration, which automatically sends completion events for envelopes completed before it was created within the 15-day window
Submit the envelope IDs to the historical envelope publish endpoint with an ad hoc JSON configuration naming the analytics URL, and track progress in the Bulk Actions Log

answerText: Submit the envelope IDs to the historical envelope publish endpoint with an ad hoc JSON configuration naming the analytics URL, and track progress in the Bulk Actions Log
explanation: The historical envelope publish endpoint (POST /connect/envelopes/publish/historical) submits a batch of existing envelopes to a URL using an ad hoc configuration, always in JSON, without touching existing configurations; progress appears in the Bulk Actions Log.
whyNotOthers: E is right because historical publish is built for sending existing envelopes to a webhook without changing any configuration. The trap is A: retryForEnvelopes republishes failed deliveries, but these envelopes never failed and the analytics listener did not exist. B changes the protected XML configuration, and Connect logs keep only recent entries; C produces API responses rather than Connect messages and wastes calls; D is false because a new configuration only reports events that happen after it exists.

optionExplanations.A: Retry republishes failures from a configuration's failure log; these envelopes were never sent to the analytics listener, so there is nothing to retry.
optionExplanations.B: This changes the archive team's protected configuration, and the Connect logs hold only the most recent 100 entries for 15 days.
optionExplanations.C: Envelopes:get returns the REST envelope resource, not a Connect JSON SIM message, and makes 2,000 extra API calls.
optionExplanations.D: A configuration reports only events that occur after it is created; it does not replay older completions.
optionExplanations.E: Correct. Historical publish sends existing envelopes to the urlToPublishTo in an ad hoc JSON configuration and reports status in the Bulk Actions Log.

decode.needs: Historical envelope publish (POST /connect/envelopes/publish/historical) with an ad hoc JSON configuration
clues: completed before the listener existed -> nothing failed, so no retry
same JSON format as live events -> historical publish always sends JSON
archive team will not allow any change to the XML configuration -> ad hoc configuration, not editing the existing one

concept.title: Historical envelope republish
concept.line: To send existing envelopes to a webhook, use the historical publish endpoint with an ad hoc JSON configuration instead of changing a live configuration.

topic: Branching on envelope status after signing
stem: Harlow Mutual's renewals team is automating its home-policy renewal packet. A web form collects the policyholder's updated details, a fixed renewal agreement is prepared from a template, and it goes out for remote signature. Compliance wants the signed packet filed in the company's SharePoint library only when the policyholder actually finishes signing. If the envelope ends any other way, for example declined or voided, the assigned agent must be emailed a notice so they can call the customer. The team also plans to refresh the packet's logo next quarter. Which design should the process builder add after the signing step?

options.text: Add a Store Files step directly after signing and then a Send an Email step to the agent, so every instance archives the packet and also alerts the agent
Add a Multi Branch Rule step on the policyholder's state from the web form, with one path that archives to SharePoint and one path that emails the assigned agent
Add a Branching Rule step on envelope status equals completed, with a Store Files step to SharePoint on the true path and a Send an Email step on the false path
Add a Branching Rule step on envelope status equals completed, with a Store Files step on the true path and a Show a Confirmation Screen step on the false path
Add a Writeback step that records the envelope status in SharePoint, and have the agent check that library each morning for declined or voided packets

answerText: Add a Branching Rule step on envelope status equals completed, with a Store Files step to SharePoint on the true path and a Send an Email step on the false path
explanation: Two outcomes hang on one condition ('only when the policyholder actually finishes signing', otherwise 'emailed a notice'), so a Branching Rule on envelope status = completed with Store Files on the true path and Send an Email on the false path fits, exactly as in the course's offer-letter example.
whyNotOthers: C is right because the archive and the notice are mutually exclusive outcomes of the envelope status. The trap is D: the branch is right, but a Show a Confirmation Screen step displays a message to a participant in the session; it does not email the agent. A archives and alerts on every instance, B branches on the wrong variable, and E replaces the automatic notice with a manual check.

optionExplanations.A: Archives even unsigned packets and alerts the agent every time; there is no condition.
optionExplanations.B: Branches on the policyholder's state, which has nothing to do with whether the envelope was completed.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. A Branching Rule on envelope status = completed gives a true path (Store Files to SharePoint) and a false path (Send an Email to the agent).
optionExplanations.D: The false path shows an on-screen message to a participant; it does not email the agent, who is not in the session.
optionExplanations.E: A Writeback step updates a system of record; a daily manual check is not the required automatic notice.

decode.needs: Branching Rule on envelope status = completed; Store Files on true, Send an Email on false
clues: only when the policyholder actually finishes signing -> condition on envelope status completed
declined or voided -> the false path
agent must be emailed a notice -> Send an Email step, not a confirmation screen
logo refresh next quarter -> red herring

concept.title: Branching Rule for two outcomes
concept.line: Use a Branching Rule on a step result (such as envelope status) when one condition decides between a true path and a false path.

stem: A branch tablet app reloads one envelope's details, documents and recipients in a tight loop while a customer waits, sending dozens of GET requests for that single envelope within a few seconds. Which error is it most likely to receive?

options.text: Hourly_Envelope_Polling_Limit_Exceeded
Burst_APIInvocation_Envelope_Limit_Exceeded
Hourly_APIInvocation_Envelope_Limit_Exceeded
Burst_Envelope_Polling_Limit_Exceeded

answerText: Burst_Envelope_Polling_Limit_Exceeded
explanation: Too many GET requests for one envelope (including its documents and recipients) within a 30-second burst period return Burst_Envelope_Polling_Limit_Exceeded. The clues are GET and 'within a few seconds'.
whyNotOthers: D is right because the calls are GETs in a short burst. The trap is B: it is a burst error too, but APIInvocation errors are for PUT requests. A and C are hourly errors, and C is also for PUTs.

optionExplanations.A: This is the hourly GET error; the calls here happen within seconds.
optionExplanations.B: APIInvocation errors count PUT requests; these are GETs.
