optionExplanations.C: This is the hourly PUT error; wrong method and wrong time window.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. Too many GETs for one envelope within 30 seconds produce this burst polling error.

concept.title: Per-envelope error codes
concept.line: Polling errors count GETs per envelope; APIInvocation errors count PUTs. Burst means 30 seconds, Hourly means one hour.

stem: Ledgerline, a payroll software vendor, onboards about 300 client companies, each with its own Docusign account. During onboarding, Ledgerline's service creates a Connect configuration in each client account that points to Ledgerline's multi-tenant listener running on Kubernetes. Ledgerline's security team wants every client's messages signed with Ledgerline's own HMAC secrets, managed in one place, and does not want any client administrator to generate keys or handle secrets. Clients are spread across three time zones. How should Ledgerline create the client configurations?

options.text: Ask each client administrator to enable HMAC on their Connect page and send the generated secret to Ledgerline's support team through a secure vault
Enable OAuth for Connect in each client account with Ledgerline's identity provider, because a bearer token on each call proves that messages come from Docusign
Create each client configuration on the client's Connect page in eSignature Admin with HMAC and the integrator-managed option selected, reusing the main account's keys
Create each configuration with ConnectConfigurations:create, setting includeHMAC and integratorManaged to true, using a token for Ledgerline's main account so its HMAC keys sign the messages
Create each configuration through the API with includeHMAC set to true using the client administrator's token, so the client account's own HMAC keys are applied automatically

answerText: Create each configuration with ConnectConfigurations:create, setting includeHMAC and integratorManaged to true, using a token for Ledgerline's main account so its HMAC keys sign the messages
explanation: Integrator-managed HMAC lets a partner use its main account's HMAC keys for client configurations: set includeHMAC and integratorManaged to true in ConnectConfigurations:create, and the access token identifies the main account whose keys are used. This meets "Ledgerline's own HMAC secrets, managed in one place".
whyNotOthers: D is right because integratorManaged with includeHMAC signs client messages with the main account's keys, and the token identifies that main account. The trap is C: the integrator-managed option exists, but it can currently be configured only through the API, not the Connect page. A and E use the clients' own keys, which the stem rules out; B swaps HMAC for OAuth, which does not meet the requirement for HMAC signatures.

optionExplanations.A: This makes every client generate and hand over secrets, which the security team explicitly does not want.
optionExplanations.B: OAuth for Connect is a different mechanism; the requirement is HMAC signatures with Ledgerline's own secrets.
optionExplanations.C: Integrator-managed configurations can currently be set up only with the API, so this UI path is not available.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. includeHMAC plus integratorManaged set to true, called with a token from the main account, makes Connect sign client events with the main account's HMAC keys.
optionExplanations.E: With the client administrator's token and no integratorManaged flag, the client account's own keys would be used, and clients would have to create them.

decode.needs: ConnectConfigurations:create with includeHMAC and integratorManaged set to true, using the main account's token
clues: Ledgerline's own HMAC secrets, managed in one place -> integrator-managed HMAC
no client administrator handles keys -> not per-client HMAC keys
service creates the configuration during onboarding -> API route, which integrator-managed requires
Kubernetes, three time zones -> red herrings

concept.title: Integrator-managed HMAC
concept.line: A partner can create client Connect configurations through the API with includeHMAC and integratorManaged true so its main account's HMAC keys sign them.

topic: Bank account owner vs bank account verification
stem: Harrow Commercial Lending pays out equipment loans by depositing funds into the borrower's business checking account. The loan agreement is sent from the eSignature web app, and the person signing types in the company's US account number and ABA routing number. The fraud team says it is not enough to know that the account exists and is open: before any money moves, they need confirmation that the individual signing actually holds that account or is an authorized signatory on it. The credit team also wants the envelope to keep its existing branding theme. Which approach meets the fraud team's requirement?

options.text: Add bank account verification fields from an installed data verification app (Verify.Version3.BankAccount) so the account number and routing number are checked against the provider while the borrower signs.

Add bank account owner verification fields from an installed data verification app (Verify.Version1.BankAccountOwner) so the provider confirms during signing that the signer owns or may sign on the account.
Add a Data IO read step to a Maestro workflow before signing that searches the bank-data provider for the account and saves the owner's name in a variable for the fraud team.
Build a connected fields app with the Verify action so the account number and routing number are compared with records in the lender's own loan servicing system during signing.
Require ID Verification for the signer so a government photo ID is checked before the agreement opens, which proves the signer is the account holder.

answerText: Add bank account owner verification fields from an installed data verification app (Verify.Version1.BankAccountOwner) so the provider confirms during signing that the signer owns or may sign on the account.
explanation: The deciding clue is that the fraud team needs to know the signer 'holds that account or is an authorized signatory', not just that the account is valid. That is the bank account owner verification extension (Verify.Version1.BankAccountOwner), used at the eSignature Add Fields view and signing.
whyNotOthers: B is right because bank account owner verification confirms the owner or authorized signatory. The trap is A: bank account verification is also a bank-data check during signing, but it only validates the account details, which the fraud team said is not enough. C and D use the wrong extension (workflow data access or the lender's own records), and E proves identity, not account ownership. The branding theme is a red herring.

optionExplanations.A: Bank account verification only confirms that the account details are valid; the fraud team explicitly said that knowing the account exists is not enough.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. Bank account owner verification checks the identity of the account owner or authorized signatory, which is exactly the fraud team's need ('holds that account or is an authorized signatory'), and it supports US ABA routing numbers.
optionExplanations.C: Data IO reads a system of record from a Maestro workflow; it does not verify the signer against the account during signing, and the agreement is sent from the eSignature web app.
optionExplanations.D: Connected fields verify against the organization's own system of record; the lender's loan system cannot prove who owns an account at another bank.
optionExplanations.E: ID Verification proves who the signer is, not that this person owns or may sign on the stated bank account.

decode.needs: A data verification extension that confirms the signer owns or is an authorized signatory on a US bank account, during eSignature signing.
clues: 'holds that account or is an authorized signatory' -> bank account owner verification
'not enough to know the account exists' -> rules out plain bank account verification
'sent from the eSignature web app' -> extension point is Add Fields view and signing, not Maestro

concept.title: Account validity vs account ownership
concept.line: Bank account verification checks the account details are valid; bank account owner verification checks the signer owns or may sign on the account.

topic: Composite templates: dynamic document with a server template
stem: Bramwell & Tate, a law firm, generates a different engagement letter PDF for every new client from its practice-management system, because fee terms and scope paragraphs change each time. The signature block, date and initials fields are already laid out in a server template called Engagement Sign Block, which the knowledge team maintains in the web app. The partners want the fields from that template applied to the freshly generated letter, and the template's own placeholder PDF must not appear in the client's envelope. The firm's logo was recently updated. How should the integration build the request?

options.text: Use two composite template objects: the first carries the generated PDF in its document property with an inline recipient, the second references Engagement Sign Block, so the template's fields join the envelope

Use one composite template object: put the generated PDF in its document property, reference Engagement Sign Block in serverTemplates with sequence 1, and map the client to the role in an inlineTemplate with sequence 2
Use the template reference model with templateId set to Engagement Sign Block, templateRoles for the client, and a documents array holding the generated PDF so it replaces the sample
Use one composite template object with the generated PDF inside the inline template's documents, giving the inline template sequence 1 and Engagement Sign Block sequence 2

answerText: Use one composite template object: put the generated PDF in its document property, reference Engagement Sign Block in serverTemplates with sequence 1, and map the client to the role in an inlineTemplate with sequence 2
explanation: Only composite templates can apply a server template's fields to a document supplied at send time. Putting the letter in the composite object's document property makes it the only document for that object ('placeholder PDF must not appear'), and sequence 1 for the server template lets the inline template map the client to an existing role.
whyNotOthers: B is right because the document property takes precedence over the template's own document in the same object. The trap is A: two objects means two documents, so the placeholder PDF would be in the envelope and the fields would land on it. C fails because the template reference model cannot replace the template's document, and D reverses the sequence and hides the PDF in the inline template.

optionExplanations.A: Each composite object contributes its own document, so the second object would add the template's placeholder PDF, and its fields would sit on that PDF, not on the letter.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. The document property supplies the one document for that object and wins over the template's document, while the server template contributes the fields and the inline template maps the client.
optionExplanations.C: The template reference model applies one template as is; it cannot swap in or add a dynamically supplied document. That needs composite templates.
optionExplanations.D: The lowest sequence that supplies a document wins, and attributes apply in sequence order, so the role would not exist when the inline template maps the client; the document property is also the recommended place for the PDF.

decode.needs: Composite template: document property + serverTemplate (seq 1) + inlineTemplate (seq 2) in one object
clues: different letter for every client -> document supplied dynamically
fields already laid out in a server template -> serverTemplates reference
placeholder PDF must not appear -> one composite object whose document property overrides the template document
logo was recently updated -> red herring

concept.title: Server template fields on a new document
concept.line: Within one composite object the document property supplies the document and overrides template documents, while server and inline templates supply roles and tabs.

stem: Tidewater Logistics' listener went down on 1 March after a failed deployment, so deliveries from its account-level JSON SIM configuration (requiresAcknowledgement enabled) began failing and retrying. On 5 March the operations lead paused the configuration while the team rebuilt the listener across its three warehouses' environments. The configuration was unpaused on 18 March, 13 days later, and the new listener is healthy. Some events first failed on 1 and 2 March; others first failed on 4 March. What should the team expect, and what must it do?

options.text: Events still inside their 15-day window continue at their next scheduled retry, while events whose window ended during the pause have expired and must be republished manually
Every skipped event is retried immediately on unpause, because pausing holds events in a queue and releases them all as soon as processing resumes
Because the configuration stayed paused for more than ten days, Docusign disabled it, so every event must be republished after re-enabling it
Unpausing restarts each event's schedule from the first five-minute retry, so all events, including the oldest, are delivered within a few hours
Events skipped during the pause were discarded, so the team must send every March envelope again through the historical envelope publish endpoint

answerText: Events still inside their 15-day window continue at their next scheduled retry, while events whose window ended during the pause have expired and must be republished manually
explanation: Pausing skips retries without losing them or resetting the schedule; after unpause, events resume at their next scheduled retry. Events that reached the end of their 15-day window while paused (first failed on 1 and 2 March) expire and must be republished manually.
whyNotOthers: A is right because unpaused events resume at the next scheduled retry and only those past the 15-day window need manual republishing. The trap is B: skipped events are not lost, but they wait for the next scheduled retry rather than being sent at once. C uses the wrong threshold (auto-disable happens after 14 consecutive paused days, and this pause was 13); D is false because pausing does not reset retry schedules; E is false because skipped events are not discarded.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. Events from 4 March are still within 15 days and resume at their next scheduled (daily) retry; events from 1 and 2 March passed day 15 during the pause and must be republished.
optionExplanations.B: Skipped events are kept, but processing resumes at the next scheduled retry interval, not immediately.
optionExplanations.C: A paused configuration is disabled automatically only after 14 consecutive days; 13 days does not trigger it.
optionExplanations.D: Pausing does not reset retry schedules, so there is no restart from the five-minute step.
optionExplanations.E: Skipped events are bypassed, not discarded; most of them continue retrying on their own.

decode.needs: Know the pause rules: skipped not lost, next scheduled retry, 15-day expiry, 14-day auto-disable
clues: paused 13 days -> below the 14-day automatic disable
first failed on 1 and 2 March, unpaused 18 March -> beyond the 15-day retry window, manual republish
first failed on 4 March -> still in window, resumes on schedule
three warehouses, failed deployment -> red herrings

concept.title: Pause skips, never resets
concept.line: Pausing skips scheduled retries without losing events; after unpause they resume at the next scheduled retry, but events past 15 days must be republished.

topic: Advantages of JSON SIM over legacy formats
stem: Which two are advantages of the JSON SIM (Connect 2.0) message format over the legacy Connect formats? (Select two)

options.text: Messages are event-focused and smaller, carrying data about the triggering event rather than a full envelope summary by default
Every message carries the complete envelope summary by default, so the listener never needs a follow-up API call
The payload follows the eSignature SOAP object model, so existing SOAP-based parsers can be reused unchanged
More event types can be subscribed to, and each notification is sent at the time its event occurs
Similar events are combined into a single delivery, reducing the number of messages the listener must handle

answerText: Messages are event-focused and smaller, carrying data about the triggering event rather than a full envelope summary by default; More event types can be subscribed to, and each notification is sent at the time its event occurs
explanation: Docusign lists three JSON SIM benefits: smaller event-focused messages (envelope summary optional), more event types, and notification at the time each event occurs.
whyNotOthers: A and D are right because they are the documented JSON SIM benefits. The trap is B: JSON SIM can include an envelope summary, but only if you choose it, and it is not sent by default because it slows delivery. C describes the legacy XML format, and E describes aggregate mode, which is the opposite of sending individual messages.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. By default a JSON SIM message carries data about the triggering event, so it is smaller and easier to process.
optionExplanations.B: The envelope summary is optional in JSON SIM and not returned by default; adding it increases payload size and delivery time.
optionExplanations.C: Reusing the SOAP object model is a reason to choose the legacy XML format, not a JSON SIM advantage.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. JSON SIM supports more event types and sends each notification when the event happens.
optionExplanations.E: Combining similar events into one delivery is the legacy aggregate option, not JSON SIM.

concept.title: JSON SIM benefits
concept.line: JSON SIM sends smaller event-focused messages, supports more event types and notifies at the time each event occurs; the envelope summary is optional.

stem: Besides the action that verifies an address, which other action does the postal address verification extension define?

options.text: Address Typeahead (Typeahead.Version1.PostalAddress)
Get Type Definitions (DataIO.Version6.GetTypeDefinitions)
Search Records (DataIO.Version6.SearchRecords)
Autofill Address (Verify.Version1.AddressAutofill)
List Directory Contents (FileIO.Version1.ListDirectoryContents)

answerText: Address Typeahead (Typeahead.Version1.PostalAddress)
explanation: The postal address verification extension (template Verify.Version1.PostalAddress) has two actions: Verify Postal Address and Address Typeahead (Typeahead.Version1.PostalAddress).
whyNotOthers: A is right. The trap is B: type definitions are used by extensions with a Concerto data model (connected fields, Data IO), while postal address verification has a fixed contract. C, D and E belong to other extensions or do not exist.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. The extension has two actions: Verify Postal Address and Address Typeahead.
optionExplanations.B: Get Type Definitions belongs to connected fields and Data IO, not the fixed postal address contract.
optionExplanations.C: Search Records is a Data IO action used by Maestro read and write steps.
optionExplanations.D: Not a real action; autofill suggestions are a connected fields Verify feature.
optionExplanations.E: This is an optional capability of the file output cloud storage extension.

concept.title: Postal address has typeahead
concept.line: Postal address verification defines Verify Postal Address and Address Typeahead; Concerto type actions belong to connected fields and Data IO.

stem: A tester opens an embedded signing URL, closes the tab, and pastes the same URL into a new tab two minutes later. Which event does Docusign append to the returnUrl?

options.text: session_timeout
ttl_expired
cancel
exception

answerText: ttl_expired
explanation: Recipient view URLs are single-use. Opening one again reports ttl_expired ('the token has already been accessed'), even within the five-minute lifetime.
whyNotOthers: B is right because the URL had already been redeemed. The trap is A: session_timeout is about inactivity inside an open session, not reuse of the link. C is Finish Later and D is an error event.

optionExplanations.A: session_timeout means the signer did not finish within the session timeout (20 minutes) of an active session.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. ttl_expired means the token was not used within the timeout period or had already been accessed.
optionExplanations.C: cancel is sent when the signer chooses Finish Later.
optionExplanations.D: exception reports an error during the signing session, not reuse of a URL.

concept.title: Signing URLs are single-use
concept.line: A recipient view URL used twice or after its short lifetime returns ttl_expired; request a fresh URL instead.

stem: Tidewater Systems sells a cloud property-management suite to hundreds of letting agencies. Every agency already pays for its own Docusign subscription. Tidewater wants each agency's office manager to authorize the suite once against the agency's own Docusign account; after that, tenancy agreements are signed inside the suite's own screens through embedded signing, with no email links. Tidewater has joined the Docusign Partner Program and expects referral revenue as agency usage grows. Its developers are based in two countries. Which classification should Tidewater choose for the integration key?

options.text: Embedded integration, because tenancy agreements are signed inside the suite's own screens through embedded signing instead of through links in Docusign emails
Private custom integration, because the office managers who use the suite are employees of Tidewater's customers rather than members of the public
Third-party integration key, because each agency must authorize Tidewater's suite before it can send agreements from the agency's own account
Public integration, because many separate Docusign customers connect the suite to accounts they own, which is the partner model that earns referral revenue

answerText: Public integration, because many separate Docusign customers connect the suite to accounts they own, which is the partner model that earns referral revenue
explanation: A public integration serves many Docusign customers who authorize it against their own accounts, and it earns referral revenue through the Partner Program. The clues 'own Docusign subscription', 'authorize once' and 'referral revenue' decide it; embedded signing is a signing experience, not a classification.
whyNotOthers: D is right because the agencies use their own accounts and Tidewater is a referral partner. The trap is A: 'Embedded integration' means customers without accounts use features through the ISV's own account under an ISV Embed licence, which has nothing to do with embedded signing. B fails because a multi-customer product with referral revenue is public, and C fails because a third-party key is one a customer creates to plug into someone else's partner app.

optionExplanations.A: Embedded integration is the ISV Embed model where customers have no accounts and use the ISV's account; embedded signing does not decide the classification.
optionExplanations.B: Private custom fits apps built for your own or one customer's employees, not a product many Docusign customers authorize for referral revenue.
optionExplanations.C: A third-party integration key is created by a customer who must supply its own key to a partner's app.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. Many Docusign customers authorize the suite against their own accounts, and Tidewater earns referral revenue as a partner.

decode.needs: Classify a multi-customer product whose customers use their own Docusign accounts: Public integration.
clues: each agency pays for its own subscription -> customers use their own accounts
authorize the suite once -> customers connect the integration to their accounts
referral revenue, Partner Program -> Public integration
signed inside the suite's screens -> embedded signing, a red herring for classification

concept.title: Embedded signing is not classification
concept.line: Public integration: many customers authorize it on their own accounts. Embedded integration: customers lack accounts and use yours.

stem: An organization wants a single administrator action to give its in-house JWT Grant app consent for all of its employees. Which two conditions must be true? (Select two)

options.text: The organization has Docusign Access Management as part of its plan
The person granting consent is an eSignature account administrator
The employees' email domain has been claimed by the organization
The integration key has completed go-live and is in production
The app requests the extended scope so the consent does not lapse

answerText: The organization has Docusign Access Management as part of its plan; The employees' email domain has been claimed by the organization
explanation: Admin consent requires the Access Management product and a claimed domain; it then covers the users in that claimed domain.
whyNotOthers: A and C are right because admin consent needs Access Management and a claimed domain. The trap is B: consent is granted by an organization administrator in Docusign Admin, not by an eSignature account administrator. D is not a prerequisite (admin consent works in the developer environment too) and E is wrong because extended only affects Authorization Code refresh tokens.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. Access Management is required for admin consent.
optionExplanations.B: The documentation says an organization administrator, not an eSignature account administrator, grants admin consent.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. Admin consent applies to users whose addresses are in the organization's claimed domain.
optionExplanations.D: Go-live is not a prerequisite for admin consent.
optionExplanations.E: extended changes refresh token lifetime in Authorization Code Grant; it has nothing to do with consent or JWT.

concept.title: Admin consent prerequisites
concept.line: Admin consent needs Access Management and a claimed domain, and is granted by an organization administrator, not an eSignature account admin.

stem: A connected fields app's Get Type Definitions response includes a property whose Concerto type is an enumeration. How is that property rendered in eSignature envelopes?

options.text: As a dropdown list
As radio buttons
As a text field with validation
As a checkbox group
It is not supported in envelopes

answerText: As radio buttons
explanation: The data model reference states that Concerto enumerations are rendered in eSignature envelopes as radio buttons, while in Maestro read and write steps they are not supported.
whyNotOthers: B is right. The trap is A: a dropdown is the usual way to show a list of values, but Docusign renders enumerations as radio buttons. E mixes up envelopes with Maestro steps, where enumerations are not supported; C and D are wrong control types.

optionExplanations.A: Plausible UI choice, but the data model page states radio buttons.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. Concerto enumerations are rendered in eSignature envelopes as radio buttons.
optionExplanations.C: Enumerations are not rendered as free text.
optionExplanations.D: Checkboxes would allow several values; an enumeration is one choice rendered as radio buttons.
optionExplanations.E: Enumerations are not supported in Maestro read and write steps, but they are supported in envelopes.

concept.title: Enumerations render as radio buttons
concept.line: Concerto enumerations appear as radio buttons in eSignature envelopes and are not supported in Maestro read and write steps.

stem: Oakfield Equipment Finance creates lease agreements from its loan-origination system with eSignature REST API v2.1. The lessee's director must prove identity with a government photo ID, while the personal guarantor only needs a one-time code that Docusign sends to his mobile phone. Both verification types are configured and active in the account. A teammate proposes one setting for the whole envelope to keep the request simple. How should the envelope request be built?

options.text: Set one identityVerification object at the envelope level with the ID Verification workflowId, which Docusign then applies to every signer in routing order.
Add identityVerification with the ID Verification workflowId to the director, and set idCheckConfigurationName to ID Check on the guarantor.
Add identityVerification with the ID Verification workflowId to the director, and set an accessCode on the guarantor that the system texts to him.
Add identityVerification to each signer, using the ID Verification workflowId for the director and the Phone Authentication workflowId for the guarantor.

answerText: Add identityVerification to each signer, using the ID Verification workflowId for the director and the Phone Authentication workflowId for the guarantor.
explanation: identityVerification is a recipient property, and different workflow IDs from IdentityVerifications:list can be set per recipient. The clue is 'one-time code that Docusign sends to his mobile phone', which is phone authentication.
whyNotOthers: D is right because each signer gets its own workflowId. The trap is C: an access code texted by the lender's system is not a code Docusign sends. A fails because the setting is per recipient, not per envelope, and B uses ID Check, which is knowledge-based authentication.

optionExplanations.A: identityVerification is set on recipients, not on the envelope.
optionExplanations.B: ID Check is knowledge-based authentication, not a code sent to a phone.
optionExplanations.C: The access code would be sent by the lender's system, not by Docusign.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. Each signer carries identityVerification with its own workflowId.

decode.needs: Two signers, two verification workflows, each set on its own recipient.
clues: 'government photo ID' -> ID Verification workflow
'one-time code that Docusign sends to his mobile' -> Phone Authentication workflow
'one setting for the whole envelope' -> red herring, there is no envelope-level option

concept.title: Per-recipient identity verification
concept.line: Set identityVerification with a workflowId from IdentityVerifications:list on each recipient; workflow IDs can differ per recipient.

topic: Flow selection: SPA front end with a server back end
stem: Saltmarsh Credit's loan-officer workspace has a React front end, but every call to Docusign goes through the bank's own Node.js API layer in its data center, where credentials sit in a managed secrets vault; the browser only ever holds the bank's own session cookie. Each of 300 loan officers signs in with their own Docusign login so that disclosures go out under their name. A front-end developer argues that because the UI is a single-page app, the key should be registered as unable to keep a secret. Which flow should the bank use?

options.text: Confidential Authorization Code Grant, with the Node.js layer exchanging the code using the vaulted secret and holding tokens
Public Authorization Code Grant with PKCE, because the user interface is a React single-page application that runs in the browser
JWT Grant from the Node.js layer, impersonating each loan officer so that none of them ever sees a Docusign login page
Implicit Grant, letting the React front end read the access token from the redirect and pass it on to the Node.js layer
Public Authorization Code Grant without PKCE, because the Node.js layer already protects the token exchange from interception

answerText: Confidential Authorization Code Grant, with the Node.js layer exchanging the code using the vaulted secret and holding tokens
explanation: The token exchange happens in a server layer that can protect a secret, and each officer signs in personally, so Confidential Authorization Code Grant is the recommended flow.
whyNotOthers: A is right because 'every call goes through the Node.js layer' with a vault means the app can keep a secret. The trap is B: Public is for apps with no secure place for a secret, and here the React UI never touches Docusign tokens. C removes the personal sign-in the bank wants, D is the legacy Implicit Grant, and E is wrong because Public Auth Code always uses PKCE.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. Server-side code exchange with a vaulted secret and individual logins is Confidential Auth Code Grant.
optionExplanations.B: The React UI is a red herring; the server layer, not the browser, talks to Docusign and can store a secret.
optionExplanations.C: JWT impersonation is for service integrations, not for officers who sign in individually.
optionExplanations.D: Implicit Grant is legacy and exposes the token in the browser.
optionExplanations.E: Public Authorization Code Grant always uses PKCE; it is never 'without PKCE'.

decode.needs: Confidential Authorization Code Grant run by the server-side API layer
clues: 'every call goes through our Node.js layer, credentials in a vault' -> can keep a secret
'each officer signs in with their own Docusign login' -> user-present Auth Code flow
'React front end' -> red herring

concept.title: Where the token exchange runs
concept.line: If a server you control performs the token exchange and can protect a secret, use Confidential Auth Code even when the UI is an SPA.

stem: Halden Bank's back-office service already sends account-opening envelopes through the eSignature REST API, using JWT Grant with an integration key that has passed Go-Live. The team now wants the same service to start a published Maestro workflow for business customers. A junior architect proposes registering a second integration key and building a separate OAuth flow, 'because Maestro is a different API host'. The service runs in the bank's Frankfurt data centre, and the architect also wants to keep the service's existing token cache. What is the correct approach?

options.text: Keep the same integration key and JWT flow and request the signature scope plus aow_manage, because Maestro uses the same OAuth tokens as eSignature
Register a second integration key for Maestro and request only aow_manage with it, because Maestro tokens cannot also carry any eSignature scopes at all
Keep the same integration key but switch to Authorization Code Grant, because Maestro calls must be made by a user who is present to consent
Keep the same token and scopes, and use the mtid and mtsec values from the trigger URL as the bearer credential for every Maestro call
Keep the same integration key and request aow_manage only, because adding the signature scope to a Maestro token makes trigger calls fail

answerText: Keep the same integration key and JWT flow and request the signature scope plus aow_manage, because Maestro uses the same OAuth tokens as eSignature
explanation: Maestro OAuth access tokens are the same ones used for the eSignature REST API; you request the signature scope and one or more Maestro scopes, such as aow_manage, with any of the recommended grant types including JWT.
whyNotOthers: A is right because the existing key and grant work once aow_manage is added. The trap is E: aow_manage is required, but the how-to says to request signature plus the Maestro scope, so dropping signature is wrong. B duplicates the key for no reason, C wrongly rules out JWT, and D misuses the trigger URL parameters, which only authenticate the trigger request.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. Same key and JWT flow; request signature plus aow_manage.
optionExplanations.B: A second key is unnecessary; Maestro tokens carry signature and Maestro scopes together.
optionExplanations.C: JWT Grant is one of the supported grant types for Maestro.
optionExplanations.D: mtid and mtsec authenticate the trigger URL request; they are not a bearer token for other calls.
optionExplanations.E: The documented scopes are signature plus aow_manage; signature is not harmful.

decode.needs: Same integration key and grant; add aow_manage alongside signature
clues: already uses JWT with a live integration key -> reuse it
different API host -> different base path, same OAuth
Frankfurt data centre -> red herring

concept.title: Maestro uses eSignature tokens
concept.line: Maestro calls use the same OAuth tokens as eSignature; request signature plus a Maestro scope such as aow_manage.

topic: What the API proxy does with credentials
stem: Bramwell Logistics will put an API proxy in front of its legacy freight system so that Docusign's Data IO requests and the system's responses match the Data IO contract. Bramwell's security architect asks what the proxy must do with the credentials on each incoming request, given that the extension app's connection uses Authorization Code Grant against Bramwell's own identity provider. The proxy will run on the same VM cluster as the company intranet and will be monitored by the network operations team. What should the design specify?

options.text: Validate an HMAC signature computed with a Connect secret key, because Docusign signs every extension action request in the same way that it signs Connect webhook messages.
Validate a Docusign-issued JWT on each request against Docusign's public key, because Docusign signs every extension request with its own key.
Accept requests without checking credentials, because the firewall allow-list of Docusign IP addresses already proves that the caller is Docusign.
Validate the access token that Bramwell's identity provider issued during authorization, which each request carries, before forwarding the call to the freight system.
Exchange the Docusign integration key found in each request for a freight-system session, then forward the call with that session token.

answerText: Validate the access token that Bramwell's identity provider issued during authorization, which each request carries, before forwarding the call to the freight system.
explanation: The clue is that the connection uses Authorization Code Grant against Bramwell's identity provider: Docusign sends that access token with each request, and the API proxy should validate it before passing the request to the freight system.
whyNotOthers: D is right because the proxy validates the access token from the connection. The trap is A: HMAC sounds like the Docusign security answer, but it belongs to Connect webhooks. B invents a Docusign-signed JWT, C skips token validation, and E invents an integration key exchange. The VM cluster is a red herring.

optionExplanations.A: HMAC with a Connect key is how Connect messages are verified; extension requests carry the OAuth access token from the connection.
optionExplanations.B: Extension requests are authorized with the token from the app's own connection, not a Docusign-signed JWT.
optionExplanations.C: IP allow-listing is a network control; the docs still say the proxy should validate the token.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. Requests through a proxy include the access token returned by the external service or identity provider, and the proxy should validate it before passing the request on.
optionExplanations.E: Requests do not carry a Docusign integration key for exchange; they carry the access token from Bramwell's identity provider.

decode.needs: API proxy validates the OAuth access token (from the external IdP) carried by each extension request.
clues: 'Authorization Code Grant against Bramwell's own identity provider' -> request carries that IdP's access token
'what to do with credentials on each request' -> validate the token before forwarding
'same VM cluster as the intranet' -> red herring

concept.title: Proxy validates the access token
concept.line: Extension requests through an API proxy carry the access token from the connection's authorization; the proxy validates it before forwarding.

stem: Glenmoor Utilities is writing the runbook for a new unattended meter-dispute service that sends notices as the Docusign user disputes-desk through the eSignature REST API. The RSA private key is mounted into the service's container from a secrets store, and the account's base URI differs between the developer and production environments. A consultant drafted several sequences, and the on-call team wants the one that is correct from first setup through ongoing operation. The service also posts a daily summary to the team's chat channel. Which sequence should go in the runbook?

options.text: Build and sign a JWT; post it to /oauth/token; have disputes-desk consent once; call /oauth/userinfo; call the API; build a new JWT on expiry
Have disputes-desk consent once; build and sign a JWT; post it to /oauth/token; call /oauth/userinfo; call the API; use the refresh token on expiry
Have disputes-desk consent once; request an authorization code; post the code with the JWT to /oauth/token; call /oauth/userinfo; call the API
Have disputes-desk consent once; build and sign a JWT; post it to /oauth/token; call /oauth/userinfo; call the API; build a new JWT on expiry
Build a JWT signed with the secret key; post it to /oauth/token; call /oauth/userinfo; call the API; have disputes-desk consent again each hour

answerText: Have disputes-desk consent once; build and sign a JWT; post it to /oauth/token; call /oauth/userinfo; call the API; build a new JWT on expiry
explanation: JWT Grant starts with one-time consent, then the service signs a JWT with the RSA private key, exchanges it at /oauth/token, reads account_id and base_uri from /oauth/userinfo, and builds a new JWT when the one-hour token expires.
whyNotOthers: D is right because it orders consent, JWT, token, userinfo, API and renews by building a new JWT. The trap is B: its steps match D until renewal, but JWT Grant issues no refresh token, so ongoing operation needs a new JWT. A requests a token before consent, which fails with consent_required. C mixes in an authorization code exchange, and E signs with the secret and repeats consent needlessly.

optionExplanations.A: Consent must come before the first token request; without it /oauth/token returns consent_required, so the order is wrong even though the renewal step is right.
optionExplanations.B: Every step is right except renewal: JWT Grant issues no refresh token, so the service must build and sign a new JWT when the one-hour token expires.
optionExplanations.C: JWT Grant does not exchange an authorization code; the token request carries only the signed assertion.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. Consent once, sign JWT, exchange, userinfo, call the API, and build a new JWT when the token expires.
optionExplanations.E: The JWT is signed with the RSA private key, and consent is a one-time step, not hourly.

decode.needs: Order the JWT Grant steps and renew without a refresh token
clues: 'unattended service sends as disputes-desk' -> JWT Grant
'base URI differs between environments' -> must call /oauth/userinfo
'from first setup through ongoing operation' -> order of consent and how renewal works (new JWT, no refresh token)
'daily summary to chat' -> red herring

concept.title: JWT Grant step order
concept.line: Consent once, sign JWT with RSA private key, POST /oauth/token, GET /oauth/userinfo, call API; on expiry build a new JWT.

stem: In Confidential Authorization Code Grant, after the user signs in and allows access, what does Docusign add to the redirect URI?

options.text: An access_token value in the URL fragment, ready to use as a bearer token
A code query parameter, plus the state value if the app sent one
An id_token query parameter that carries the account_id and base_uri
A refresh_token query parameter that the app exchanges for an access token
An assertion parameter that the app signs and returns to /oauth/token

answerText: A code query parameter, plus the state value if the app sent one
explanation: Docusign redirects to the redirect_uri with a code query string parameter (and echoes state), which the app then exchanges at /oauth/token.
whyNotOthers: B is right because Authorization Code Grant returns a short-lived code, not a token. The trap is A: returning the access token directly in the redirect is Implicit Grant (response_type=token). C, D and E describe values that are not returned on this redirect: account_id and base_uri come from /oauth/userinfo, refresh tokens come from /oauth/token, and assertions belong to JWT Grant.

optionExplanations.A: That is Implicit Grant behaviour.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. The redirect carries the authorization code (and the state value).
optionExplanations.C: account_id and base_uri come from /oauth/userinfo, not the redirect.
optionExplanations.D: Refresh tokens are returned by /oauth/token, never on the redirect.
optionExplanations.E: An assertion is the signed JWT in JWT Grant.

concept.title: What the redirect returns
concept.line: Auth Code Grant redirects with a code (and state); Implicit Grant returns the access token directly.

stem: Brightwater Telecom's online sign-up flow shows each new customer a clickwrap agreement that the legal team designs and maintains in the Docusign web app. The integration only needs to present that existing clickwrap to new customers and check whether a customer has already agreed. It runs as an unattended service using JWT Grant, it also sends contracts through the eSignature REST API, and the CISO requires least privilege. Marketing wants the clickwrap restyled next quarter, which legal will do in the web app. Which scope list should the one-time consent request?

options.text: signature click.manage impersonation
signature click.send impersonation
signature click.manage click.send extended
signature click.send
signature click.send extended impersonation

answerText: signature click.send impersonation
explanation: click.send is the Click API scope required to send a clickwrap or check for a previously sent one; signature covers the eSignature calls and impersonation is needed for JWT consent.
whyNotOthers: B is right because the service only sends and checks clickwraps, so click.send meets least privilege. The trap is A: click.manage enables all elastic template operations, including creating and updating them, which legal does in the web app. C and E add extended, which is an Authorization Code scope, and D omits impersonation, which JWT consent requires.

optionExplanations.A: click.manage grants create and update rights the service does not need, so it breaks least privilege.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. signature for eSignature, click.send for presenting and checking clickwraps, impersonation for JWT consent.
optionExplanations.C: Includes unneeded click.manage and the Authorization Code-only extended scope, and lacks impersonation.
optionExplanations.D: Without impersonation the consent does not allow JWT Grant to act as the user.
optionExplanations.E: extended has no role in JWT Grant; it adds nothing and should not be requested.

decode.needs: Consent scopes: signature click.send impersonation
clues: 'present existing clickwrap and check whether already agreed' -> click.send only
'legal designs it in the web app' -> no click.manage needed
'unattended service using JWT' -> impersonation in consent, no extended
'restyled next quarter' -> red herring

concept.title: Least privilege across APIs
concept.line: Request only the scopes the calls need: click.send to send or check clickwraps, click.manage only to build or edit them.

stem: At Pellham Insurance, when a large commercial policy is fully signed, up to 30 underwriters, brokers and auditors open it from the policy system within the first hour. Each click makes the policy system fetch the envelope's combined PDF straight from Docusign. Since go-live, many of these clicks fail with API_REQUEST_IS_THROTTLED and 'GetDocument call blocked', even though the account used only about a third of its hourly allowance. The policy system already receives Connect messages. What should the team do?

options.text: Ask an administrator to raise the account's hourly API limit in the API Usage Center, so that the extra document requests fit inside a larger allowance
Switch the policy system from the combined PDF to the ZIP archive option, which is counted separately, and keep fetching the file from Docusign on every click
Download the completed documents once when the completion message arrives, store them in the policy system, and serve every later viewer from that stored copy
Add a retry loop that repeats each blocked download every few seconds until Docusign returns the file, so that every viewer eventually sees the document

answerText: Download the completed documents once when the completion message arrives, store them in the policy system, and serve every later viewer from that stored copy
explanation: Docusign limits concurrent downloads of the same document (for the combined option, three in progress per hour) and blocks the excess with API_REQUEST_IS_THROTTLED. The clues 'same envelope, 30 viewers in an hour' and 'only a third of the hourly allowance' point to the per-document download limit, which caching solves.
whyNotOthers: C is right because one download per completed envelope removes the repeated requests. The trap is B: archive downloads are counted separately, but they have their own limit of 10 per hour, so 30 viewers would still be blocked. A fails because the hourly limit is not the cause, and D adds more blocked calls, which also lowers the efficiency score.

optionExplanations.A: The account is far below its hourly limit; this is the per-document download limit.
optionExplanations.B: The archive type has its own counter but still allows only 10 in-progress downloads per hour, so 30 viewers fail.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. Fetch the documents once, triggered by Connect, and serve viewers from your own store.
optionExplanations.D: Retrying blocked downloads only produces more blocked calls and hurts efficiency.

decode.needs: Avoid repeated downloads of the same document: download once on completion and cache it.
clues: GetDocument call blocked, API_REQUEST_IS_THROTTLED -> document download limit
30 viewers of the same envelope in an hour -> concurrent downloads of one document
a third of the hourly allowance -> not the account hourly limit
already receives Connect messages -> use the completion event as the trigger

concept.title: Cache completed documents
concept.line: Downloads of the same document are capped per hour; fetch completed documents once and serve users from your system.

topic: When the legacy XML format is justified
stem: Granite Mutual's claims mainframe team built a parser eight years ago against the eSignature SOAP object model, and its vendor contract requires that the inbound payload never change. The mainframe only needs envelope completion events for one account, whose adjusters send claim forms from the Docusign web app. No workflow or extension events are needed. An architect proposes managing everything from the organization level, as the company does for its other two accounts. Which configuration should the developer create for the mainframe?

options.text: An organization-level configuration in XML format, so the mainframe feed is managed centrally alongside the configurations for the other accounts
An account-level JSON SIM configuration, with the mainframe team rewriting the parser, since JSON SIM is mandatory for every new configuration
A Recipient Connect configuration in XML for the adjusters' users, so that the SOAP object model reaches the mainframe for each completed claim
An account-level configuration in the legacy XML format, since a stable SOAP-model payload is a documented reason to choose it and only envelope events are needed
An envelope-level eventNotification in XML on each claim form, since envelope-level webhooks are the only level where the XML format remains available

answerText: An account-level configuration in the legacy XML format, since a stable SOAP-model payload is a documented reason to choose it and only envelope events are needed
explanation: Docusign recommends JSON SIM for all apps but documents the legacy XML format for teams that want the SOAP object model or a payload that never changes; legacy formats are available only at account and envelope level.
whyNotOthers: D is right because the stem gives the documented reasons for the legacy format, and account level supports it while covering web-app sending. The trap is A: central management sounds sensible, but organization-level configurations always use JSON SIM. B overstates the guidance (JSON SIM is recommended, not mandatory); C fails because Recipient Connect is JSON-only and adjusters are senders; E fails because envelope-level webhooks need the API, and the adjusters use the web app.

optionExplanations.A: Organization-level configurations always use the JSON SIM model, so XML is not possible there.
optionExplanations.B: JSON SIM is recommended for all apps but not mandatory; legacy XML is still supported at account and envelope level.
optionExplanations.C: Recipient Connect always sends JSON and reports envelopes that users receive, not ones they send.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. Wanting the SOAP object model and a payload that never changes are the documented reasons for legacy XML, which account-level configurations support.
optionExplanations.E: Envelope-level webhooks need Envelopes:create in the API, and XML is also available at account level.

decode.needs: Account-level configuration in legacy XML format
clues: parser built against the SOAP object model, payload must never change -> documented reasons for legacy XML
send from the Docusign web app -> envelope-level eventNotification is impossible
manage from the organization level -> organization configurations are JSON SIM only

concept.title: Legacy XML only at account/envelope
concept.line: Legacy XML suits SOAP-model parsers or a never-changing payload, and exists only at account and envelope level; organization level is always JSON SIM.

stem: An integration needs the custom attributes that an agreement carried over from eSignature, such as a sender's envelope custom field. Which property of the Agreement Manager agreement record is documented to hold custom attributes originating from eSignature?

options.text: custom_provisions
additional_user_defined_data
additional_custom_esign_data
additional_custom_clm_data

answerText: additional_custom_esign_data
explanation: The agreement schema separates custom data by origin: additional_custom_esign_data holds custom attributes originating from eSign.
whyNotOthers: C is right because it is the eSign-origin property. The trap is B: user-defined data sounds generic enough to fit, but it holds user-defined attributes added to the agreement, not eSign-origin data. A extends the standard provisions of the agreement type, and D holds attributes that came from CLM.

optionExplanations.A: custom_provisions holds user-defined provisions that extend the standard provision set for the agreement type.
optionExplanations.B: additional_user_defined_data holds user-defined attributes included in the agreement, not data that came from eSignature.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. additional_custom_esign_data is documented as custom attributes originating from eSign.
optionExplanations.D: additional_custom_clm_data holds custom attributes that originated in CLM.

concept.title: Custom data properties by origin
concept.line: Agreement records keep custom data in separate properties by origin: eSign, CLM, user-defined data, and custom provisions.

stem: A process builder publishes a workflow, later edits it, and publishes it a second time. Which version number does the second publication receive?

options.text: 1.0.0 plus a saved draft

explanation: Maestro workflows support major versioning only: the first publish is 1.0.0 and each new publish adds 1.0.0, so the second is 2.0.0.
whyNotOthers: B is right because only major versions are used. The trap is A: a minor bump feels natural for a small edit, but minor and patch versioning are not supported. C is a patch bump, D describes an unpublished edit (a single draft), and E mixes major and minor.

optionExplanations.A: Minor versioning is not supported; each publish increases the major number.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. Second publication = 2.0.0.
optionExplanations.C: Patch versioning is not supported.
optionExplanations.D: A saved but unpublished edit is a draft; here the edit was published.
optionExplanations.E: Minor numbers are not used; the version is 2.0.0.

concept.title: Major-only workflow versions
concept.line: Each publish of a workflow increments the major version (1.0.0, 2.0.0, ...); only one draft exists per workflow.

stem: Larkspur Insurance runs a template-based web form for roadside-assistance enrollment. Instances are created by three line-of-business apps owned by other teams, and no code release is possible this quarter. A designer opened the web form template in the Web Forms builder, chose the company brand under Advanced Options, and saved the change. Customers now see the company logo on the agreement they sign after submitting, but the form pages themselves still show the default look. What is the smallest change that brands the form pages for every instance?

options.text: Select the brand under Branding on the configuration's Preview tab, which brands the form instances while the template brand keeps covering envelopes.
Pass the brand's brandId in every Instances:createInstance request, which brands both the form instance and its envelope and overrides the configuration's brand.
Select the brand again under Advanced Options in the web form template, because that setting reaches form pages only after the configuration is reactivated.
Set the brand as the account default brand, because web form instances always use the account default and ignore brands chosen in the Web Forms builder.

answerText: Select the brand under Branding on the configuration's Preview tab, which brands the form instances while the template brand keeps covering envelopes.
explanation: A brand chosen in the web form template's Advanced Options affects envelopes only; the Branding option on the configuration's Preview tab affects the instances. The clue is 'no code release is possible'.
whyNotOthers: A is right because the Preview tab brand covers form pages without any API change. The trap is B: brandId in createInstance would brand both, but it needs code changes in three apps. C misunderstands the template setting, which never brands instances, and D is false because builder-level brands are applied.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. Preview tab Branding applies to instances; the template brand already covers envelopes.
optionExplanations.B: Works technically, but requires code changes in apps that cannot be released this quarter.
optionExplanations.C: The web form template brand affects envelopes only, however often it is reselected.
optionExplanations.D: Brands selected in the configuration or template are applied; instances do not ignore them.

decode.needs: Brand the form pages with a configuration setting, not code: Preview tab Branding.
clues: 'no code release is possible' -> no brandId in createInstance
'Advanced Options' in the web form template -> envelopes only
'form pages ... still show the default look' -> the instance brand is missing

concept.title: Web form brand levels
concept.line: Template brand affects envelopes, Preview tab brand affects instances, brandId in createInstance affects both and overrides.

topic: Data IO search with no matching record
stem: Mapleford Credit's Maestro onboarding workflow uses a Data IO app to look up an applicant in its loan origination system before showing a prefilled web form. For first-time applicants the lookup finds nothing, and the developer's endpoint answers with HTTP 404 and the message 'No record found'. Operations sees these runs flagged as errors even though a first-time applicant is the normal case, and the later write step that should add the applicant does not behave as designed. The endpoint runs on Kubernetes behind a load balancer. How should the Search Records endpoint answer when no applicant matches?

options.text: Return HTTP 404 with code NOT_FOUND and a message, because the Data IO contract reserves 404 for searches that match no record.
Return a successful response with one placeholder record whose fields are blank, so the web form renders and the write step patches that placeholder.
Return HTTP 500 so that Docusign retries the search, giving the origination system time to finish indexing the new applicant.
Return HTTP 204 No Content, because Docusign reads an empty body as zero matches and then calls Create Record in the write step.
Return a successful response with an empty records array, because under the Data IO contract a search that finds no matching record is not an error.

answerText: Return a successful response with an empty records array, because under the Data IO contract a search that finds no matching record is not an error.
explanation: The clue is that 'a first-time applicant is the normal case': no match is a valid search result, and the contract says to return an empty records array rather than 404. The write step then calls Create Record because its query finds no record to patch.
whyNotOthers: E is right because an empty search is a normal result. The trap is A: 404 NOT_FOUND looks natural, but the contract explicitly says not to return it for a search with no matches. B misleads the write step into Patch Record, C causes pointless retries and errors, and D is not the documented response. Kubernetes is a red herring.

optionExplanations.A: The contract uses 404 for errors such as an unknown record ID in a request, and explicitly says not to return it for an empty search.
optionExplanations.B: A fake record would make the write step call Patch Record on a record that does not exist instead of Create Record.
optionExplanations.C: 500 signals a processing failure; a first-time applicant will never appear, so retries only produce an error.
optionExplanations.D: The Search Records contract expects a records array in the response; 204 with no body is not the documented answer.
optionExplanations.E: Correct. The Data IO contract says a 404 should not be returned when Search Records finds no match; return an empty records array instead.

decode.needs: Search Records returns an empty records array (not 404) when nothing matches.
clues: 'lookup finds nothing ... normal case' -> empty result, not an error
'write step should add the applicant' -> Create Record when the query finds no record
Kubernetes and load balancer -> red herring

concept.title: Empty search is not 404
concept.line: Data IO Search Records returns an empty records array when nothing matches; error codes are only for failed processing.

topic: Changing regions of a Live public app (multi)
stem: Tidewell, a Docusign partner, has a Live public phone-verification extension app published for the United States and Canada. A new data licence now covers the European Union but, from next quarter, will no longer cover Canada. Product asks the developer to make the app installable by EU-based accounts and to stop Canadian accounts from installing it. Tidewell's API sits behind a firewall that admits only approved source addresses, and marketing also wants fresh screenshots. Which two statements describe what the developer can do? (Select two)

options.text: Update the registration to add the EU region to publicationRegions; the update creates a new version that goes Live after Docusign review and publication.
In the same update, remove Canada from publicationRegions so that the new Live version stops Canadian accounts from installing the app.
Allow the Docusign endpoint IP addresses for European Union-based accounts on Tidewell's firewall so that requests from EU accounts reach the API.
Omit publicationRegions from the updated manifest so the default of US applies, which drops Canada while keeping the US region.
Change the distribution to Private and list the EU production accounts, since a Live app's regions cannot be changed in any way.

answerText: Update the registration to add the EU region to publicationRegions; the update creates a new version that goes Live after Docusign review and publication.; Allow the Docusign endpoint IP addresses for European Union-based accounts on Tidewell's firewall so that requests from EU accounts reach the API.
explanation: The clues are 'make the app installable by EU-based accounts' (add a region, which is allowed after Live) and 'firewall that admits only approved source addresses' (allow EU Docusign IPs). Removing Canada is not supported in the Console.
whyNotOthers: A and C are right: regions can be added in a new version, and the EU IP addresses must be allowed. The trap is B: removing a region looks like the obvious second half of the request, but published apps can add regions, not remove them. D misreads the default (only for new manifests) and E relies on changing distribution, which is locked after Live.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. Regions can be added to a published app; updating a Live app creates a new Draft version that is reviewed and then published.
optionExplanations.B: Regions cannot be removed from a published app in the Developer Console; it needs a case-by-case request through the Developer Community.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. Adding a region means allowing that region's Docusign IP addresses on the firewall.
optionExplanations.D: The US default applies only to a new manifest; on an update, omitting the property keeps the published value.
optionExplanations.E: Distribution cannot change after Live, and regions can be added.

decode.needs: Add a region via a new reviewed version and allow that region's Docusign IPs; regions cannot be removed after publishing.
clues: 'make installable by EU-based accounts' -> add EU to publicationRegions
'stop Canadian accounts' -> removal is not supported in the Console
'firewall that admits only approved addresses' -> allow EU Docusign IPs
'fresh screenshots' -> red herring

concept.title: Add regions, never remove
concept.line: After an app is Live you can add publicationRegions through a new version but cannot remove regions or change distribution.

stem: Halden Wealth sends account-transfer forms from the eSignature web app; advisers in the branch prepare and send each one. Clients type their portfolio number, and the firm wants the form to check it against Halden's in-house client master while the client is signing, show a tailored message when it fails, and then fill in the client's registered address from the client master so the client does not retype it. Halden has no workflow licence, and the client master is reachable only by Halden. Which solution fits?

options.text: Build a private Data IO app with a read step that looks up the client in the client master and prefills the registered address before the agreement is sent for signing.
Build a private connected fields app whose Verify response returns the result, a custom message and suggested values that autofill the address fields during signing.
Install a postal address verification app so the address the client enters is checked and reformatted against an authoritative address source.
Build a public connected fields app so that any adviser account can install it, exposing the client master through an API proxy.
Use the eSignature API from the advisers' desktops to read the client master and prefill the address tabs when each envelope is created.

answerText: Build a private connected fields app whose Verify response returns the result, a custom message and suggested values that autofill the address fields during signing.
explanation: The clues are 'check it against Halden's in-house client master while the client is signing', 'tailored message' and 'fill in the registered address': connected fields return verification results, custom messages and autofill suggestions, and an internal system calls for private distribution.
whyNotOthers: B is right because connected fields verify against the in-house system during signing and can autofill values. The trap is A: Data IO also reads the system of record to prefill data, but it runs in Maestro (no licence) and before signing. C checks the wrong thing, D uses the wrong distribution, and E does not verify during signing.

optionExplanations.A: Data IO runs in Maestro workflows, which Halden does not have, and it cannot react to the portfolio number the client types while signing.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. Connected fields verify any data against the organization's system of record during signing, return custom messages, and can return autofill values; private suits an in-house system.
optionExplanations.C: This verifies that an address exists and is deliverable; it does not check the portfolio number against Halden's client master.
optionExplanations.D: The connected fields part is right, but an in-house client master used only by Halden fits private distribution, not public.
optionExplanations.E: Advisers send from the web app, and prefilling at creation time does not verify what the client types while signing.

decode.needs: Private connected fields app: Verify during signing with custom messages and autofill suggestions.
clues: 'while the client is signing' -> eSignature signing extension point
'in-house client master' -> custom verification (connected fields), private distribution
'fill in the registered address' -> autofill values in the Verify response
'no workflow licence' -> rules out Data IO in Maestro

concept.title: Connected fields verify and autofill
concept.line: Connected fields verify signer data against your own system during signing, show custom messages and can autofill values.

topic: Bulk send from a server template
stem: Every March, Pellucid Foods must collect a signed food-safety pledge from about 700 franchise owners. The pledge already exists as a server template with a single role named franchisee, and the operations director does not want developers to rebuild or copy the document each year. A headless scheduled job reads the owner list from the franchise database. The pledge was translated into Spanish last year. How should the job send the pledges?

options.text: Create a bulk send list, create an envelope from the template with status sent to the first owner, then call createBulkSendRequest with that envelope's ID as the source
Loop through the 700 owners and call Envelopes:create with templateId, templateRoles for the owner and status sent for each one
Create a bulk send list mapping each owner to the franchisee role, test it with the template ID as envelopeOrTemplateId, then call createBulkSendRequest with that ID
Create one envelope from the template with 700 signers mapped to the franchisee role in templateRoles, so every owner signs the same pledge in a single run

answerText: Create a bulk send list mapping each owner to the franchisee role, test it with the template ID as envelopeOrTemplateId, then call createBulkSendRequest with that ID
explanation: The bulk send test and send requests take envelopeOrTemplateId, so an existing server template can be the source ('does not want developers to rebuild the document'). Each copy in the list becomes its own envelope.
whyNotOthers: C is right because it reuses the template directly. The trap is A: using an envelope is valid, but only a draft one; status sent dispatches it to the first owner. B works but wastes calls and ignores bulk send, and D puts everyone on one agreement.

optionExplanations.A: The envelope used for bulk send must be a draft; an envelope created with status sent goes to that owner immediately.
optionExplanations.B: This works but makes 700 separate API calls under the hourly limit; bulk send is the designed way to send one agreement to many recipients.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. Bulk send v2.1 accepts an envelope or a template as envelopeOrTemplateId, so the existing template can be used without building a draft envelope.
optionExplanations.D: One envelope would make all owners sign one shared agreement; each owner needs their own pledge.

decode.needs: Bulk send with envelopeOrTemplateId = existing template ID
clues: 700 owners each sign their own pledge -> bulk send
pledge already exists as a server template -> envelopeOrTemplateId can be the template
headless scheduled job -> API-only bulk send flow
translated into Spanish -> red herring

concept.title: Bulk send source envelope or template
concept.line: createBulkSendTestRequest and createBulkSendRequest take envelopeOrTemplateId, so a draft envelope or a template can be the source.

stem: Which statement best describes the role of an extension app on the Docusign IAM platform?

options.text: It brings a third-party service into Docusign agreement processes, invoked at defined extension points such as signing or a Maestro step.
It lets a third-party application call Docusign APIs to create and manage agreements from outside Docusign.
It receives Docusign event notifications by webhook so external systems learn about envelope status changes.
It embeds the Docusign signing session inside a third-party web page by using a recipient view URL.
It packages Docusign templates and workflows so they can be copied between accounts through the App Center.

answerText: It brings a third-party service into Docusign agreement processes, invoked at defined extension points such as signing or a Maestro step.
explanation: Extension apps connect third-party services into Docusign (verify data, read and write a system of record, write files to storage), invoked at extension points, and are distributed through the App Center.
whyNotOthers: A is right. The trap is B: both involve a third party and Docusign, but API integrations bring Docusign into your app, whereas extension apps bring your service into Docusign. C, D and E describe Connect, embedded signing and a non-existent template marketplace.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. Extension apps connect third-party services into Docusign and are invoked at extension points.
optionExplanations.B: That describes an API integration (Docusign into your app), the opposite direction.
optionExplanations.C: That is Docusign Connect.
optionExplanations.D: That is embedded signing through the eSignature API.
optionExplanations.E: The App Center distributes extension apps, not templates or workflows.

concept.title: Extension apps extend Docusign inward
concept.line: Extension apps bring external services into Docusign at extension points; API integrations bring Docusign into your own applications.

stem: After an internal audit, the compliance officer of Brightline Pharma Distribution requires that no counterparty can open any document sent from the company's Docusign account without passing an authentication check. Envelopes come from six integrations built by different agencies, plus about 40 staff who send from the web app. The officer does not want to depend on every integration adding the right recipient properties, and the deadline is next week. What is the most reliable approach?

options.text: Ask each agency to add an accessCode to every signer in its Envelopes:create requests and verify compliance with a monthly envelope report.
Create a phone authentication identity verification configuration and make it the only active one, so every envelope automatically uses it.
Have an eSignature administrator use the account's Security Settings to require that all recipients pass authentication before opening documents.
Configure an account-level Connect listener that voids any envelope whose recipients lack an authentication method as soon as it is sent.

answerText: Have an eSignature administrator use the account's Security Settings to require that all recipients pass authentication before opening documents.
explanation: An eSignature administrator can require that all recipients pass an authentication or identity verification check before accessing any document sent from the account. The clue is 'not ... depend on every integration'.
whyNotOthers: C is right because the account setting enforces authentication for every sender without code changes. The trap is B: activating a configuration only makes it available for senders to choose; it does not apply it to recipients. A depends on every integration, which the officer rejects, and D reacts after sending instead of preventing access.

optionExplanations.A: Relies on six agencies changing code and only detects gaps afterwards.
optionExplanations.B: Active configurations are options senders can choose; they are not applied automatically.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. The account Security Settings can require authentication for all recipients.
optionExplanations.D: Voiding after sending is a workaround; the counterparty may already have received the envelope.

decode.needs: An account-level enforcement of recipient authentication that does not rely on integrations.
clues: 'any document sent from the company's Docusign account' -> account-wide setting
'not ... depend on every integration' -> no per-request properties
'deadline is next week' -> admin setting, no development

concept.title: Account-wide recipient authentication
concept.line: Administrators can require authentication for all recipients in Security Settings, independent of how envelopes are sent.

stem: Merrow Shipping's ERP pulls agreement data from Agreement Manager every night. Hundreds of vessel charter contracts arrive with the agreement type Other and without the vessel name or cargo type the chartering desk needs, because no standard agreement type covers charter contracts. The chartering manager wants charters classified correctly and both values captured by AI rather than typed in by clerks. The ERP vendor has offered to add a free-text notes field for the clerks if needed. Which two configuration steps address the need? (Select two)

options.text: Create a custom Charter Contract agreement type, then set up, activate and test its AI detection so that charters stop landing in Other.
Have the nightly job change the type of each Other agreement to Charter Contract through the Agreement Manager API once a clerk confirms it.
Call CreateAgreementSummary for each Other agreement and let the ERP parse the vessel name and cargo type out of the AI summary text.
Add Vessel Name and Cargo Type as custom fields on that agreement type and enable AI so their values are detected and surfaced.
Delete the Other agreements with DeleteAgreement and import them again, so the AI re-runs and places them in a standard type.

answerText: Create a custom Charter Contract agreement type, then set up, activate and test its AI detection so that charters stop landing in Other.; Add Vessel Name and Cargo Type as custom fields on that agreement type and enable AI so their values are detected and surfaced.
explanation: Agreements whose type cannot be determined are typed Other; custom agreement types with AI detection reduce that, and custom fields with AI enabled capture organization-specific values. That matches 'classified correctly' and 'captured by AI rather than typed in'.
whyNotOthers: A and D are right because a custom type fixes classification and AI-enabled custom fields capture the extra values. The trap is B: writing the type back sounds efficient, but the API has no update operation. C turns structured needs into parsing AI prose, and E only re-runs the same classification, which still has no matching standard type.
