optionExplanations.A: Correct. A custom agreement type with activated, tested AI detection is the documented way to reduce agreements classified as Other.
optionExplanations.B: The Agreement Manager API cannot update agreements; it offers only list, get, delete and create summary.
optionExplanations.C: Summary text is unstructured and not a substitute for extracted fields that the ERP can map.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. Custom fields added to an agreement type, with AI enabled, surface organization-specific values such as vessel name.
optionExplanations.E: Re-importing repeats the same classification; with no standard charter type, the contracts would land in Other again.

decode.needs: Configure custom extractions (custom agreement type plus AI-enabled custom fields) in Agreement Manager.
clues: type Other -> AI could not determine a standard type
no standard agreement type covers charters -> custom agreement type
captured by AI rather than typed in -> enable AI detection on custom fields
free-text notes field -> red herring

concept.title: Custom types and fields reduce Other
concept.line: Create custom agreement types with AI detection and add AI-enabled custom fields to capture data that standard types do not cover.

stem: Ashgrove Property Management's lease portal runs on a cluster of company web servers behind a load balancer and uses Confidential Authorization Code Grant so that each leasing agent sends from their own Docusign account. A penetration tester objected that the current build returns the access token and refresh token to the browser, which saves them in localStorage and attaches the access token to every AJAX call back to the portal. The portal also writes a nightly CSV export of lease statuses for finance. Where should the tokens be kept?

options.text: In localStorage, but encrypted with a key that is embedded in the portal's JavaScript bundle
In a browser cookie readable by JavaScript, so that any server node can read it from each request
In sessionStorage, so the tokens are discarded automatically as soon as the agent closes the browser tab
In IndexedDB, wrapped with the Web Crypto API so that page scripts cannot read the raw token value
On the server, bound to the agent's session in a store shared by every node behind the load balancer

answerText: On the server, bound to the agent's session in a store shared by every node behind the load balancer
explanation: In Confidential Authorization Code Grant the tokens are kept on the server; binding them to a server-side session store shared by all nodes keeps them out of the browser and works behind a load balancer.
whyNotOthers: E is right because the Confidential flow exists so that secrets and tokens stay on a secure server. The trap is C: sessionStorage shortens exposure but still leaves both tokens readable by browser scripts. A, B and D all keep the tokens in the browser, where an XSS flaw or the embedded key exposes them.

optionExplanations.A: A key embedded in the JavaScript bundle is visible to anyone, so the encryption protects nothing.
optionExplanations.B: A JavaScript-readable cookie still exposes the tokens to browser scripts.
optionExplanations.C: sessionStorage is still browser storage readable by scripts on the page.
optionExplanations.D: The tokens still live in the browser and the refresh token remains at risk.
optionExplanations.E: Correct. Server-side storage bound to the user's session, shared across the load-balanced nodes.

decode.needs: Store Confidential Auth Code tokens on the server, tied to the session
clues: 'returns tokens to the browser, localStorage' -> the flaw to fix
'cluster behind a load balancer' -> the session store must be shared
'nightly CSV export' -> red herring

concept.title: Keep tokens server-side
concept.line: Confidential Auth Code apps store access and refresh tokens on the server, bound to the user's session, never in browser storage.

stem: Where do you choose an integration key's classification, which must be set before the key can complete Go-Live?

options.text: In the production account, while selecting it during Start Go live
On the developer key, under 'How will you use this integration?'
In the review form Docusign emails after the automated review
In the API Usage Center, on the key's efficiency details page

answerText: On the developer key, under 'How will you use this integration?'
explanation: When you add an app and integration key in the developer account, you select an option under 'How will you use this integration?'; Go-Live cannot complete without it.
whyNotOthers: B is right because classification is part of the key's settings in the developer account. The trap is A: you do pick the production account during Start Go live, but the classification is already set by then, and a mismatch with the account type causes an error. C and D are not places where classification is set.

optionExplanations.A: Selecting the production account happens after classification; a mismatch there produces an error.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. The classification is chosen on the key under 'How will you use this integration?' in the developer account.
optionExplanations.C: No emailed form sets the classification.
optionExplanations.D: The API Usage Center shows efficiency, not classification.

concept.title: Classification set in developer account
concept.line: Choose the classification under 'How will you use this integration?' on the developer key before Go-Live.

topic: Amendments linked to a master agreement
stem: Ostara Biotech's legal operations portal shows each master services agreement together with every amendment and change order signed under it. Amendments are titled inconsistently ('Addendum 2', 'Variation Letter', 'Change Order - Q3'), and the same suppliers also appear on many unrelated contracts. Each amendment's record in Agreement Manager links back to its master through its related agreement documents. The portal is rebuilt every Monday morning by a headless job, and the legal team has asked for a dark theme on the page. Which query should the job use to collect the amendments of one master agreement?

options.text: Call GetAgreementsList filtered on title with the words Amendment, Addendum and Change Order, and keep the records naming the master's supplier.
Call GetAgreementsList filtered on related_agreement_documents.parent_agreement_document_id set to the master's document ID, paging with ctoken.
Call GetAgreementsList filtered on parties.name_in_agreement set to the master's supplier, and treat every record returned as an amendment.
Call GetAgreementsList filtered on source_id set to the master's agreement ID, because an amendment records its master as its source.

answerText: Call GetAgreementsList filtered on related_agreement_documents.parent_agreement_document_id set to the master's document ID, paging with ctoken.
explanation: related_agreement_documents.parent_agreement_document_id is the documented link from a child agreement to its parent, and GetAgreementsList can filter on it. The clue is 'links back to its master through its related agreement documents'.
whyNotOthers: B is right because the parent link selects exactly the amendments of one master. The trap is A: title filtering looks practical, but the titles are inconsistent, so amendments would be missed. C returns every contract with that supplier, including unrelated ones, and D misuses source_id, which identifies the record in its originating system.

optionExplanations.A: Titles such as 'Variation Letter' would be missed, so a title filter cannot reliably collect all amendments.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. The parent_agreement_document_id filter returns the records linked to the master, whatever they are titled.
optionExplanations.C: The supplier appears on many unrelated contracts, so a party filter over-collects.
optionExplanations.D: source_id holds the identifier in the originating system (for example an envelope ID), not a link to a master agreement.

decode.needs: Filter GetAgreementsList on the parent agreement document link.
clues: titled inconsistently -> a title filter is unreliable
same suppliers on unrelated contracts -> a party filter over-collects
links back through related agreement documents -> parent_agreement_document_id
dark theme -> red herring

concept.title: Parent link finds child agreements
concept.line: Use the related_agreement_documents.parent_agreement_document_id filter to retrieve agreements linked to a parent, instead of guessing from titles or parties.

stem: Halvard Freight's nightly settlement job was written years ago and authenticates by sending a service user's email and password in an X-DocuSign-Authentication header. Nobody is at the keyboard when it runs at 02:00. The company is moving the job to a new integration key, and the key fails the Go-Live review with a message about authentication. The job runs on Linux and handles about 400 envelopes a night. What is the best way to get the key through review?

options.text: Keep the header-based login but move the stored password into a secrets vault, because the review fails only on credentials that are kept in plain text
Resubmit the key with a smaller nightly volume, because the review rejects legacy authentication only when the job sends hundreds of envelopes per run
Move the job to Authorization Code Grant, so that an operator signs in once before 02:00 and the job then uses that access token for the night's run
Move the job to JWT Grant with an RSA key pair and one-time consent from the service user, since review requires OAuth 2.0 and no person is present

answerText: Move the job to JWT Grant with an RSA key pair and one-time consent from the service user, since review requires OAuth 2.0 and no person is present
explanation: Go-Live requires REST integrations to use OAuth 2.0 (or obtain a policy exception), so the legacy header login must go. The clue 'nobody is at the keyboard' makes JWT Grant the right OAuth flow.
whyNotOthers: D is right because JWT Grant is OAuth 2.0 and needs no person after the one-time consent. The trap is C: it is also OAuth 2.0, but it depends on an operator signing in every night, which does not fit an unattended job. A and B keep legacy authentication, which the review rejects whatever the storage or volume.

optionExplanations.A: Legacy header authentication fails the review however the password is stored; OAuth 2.0 is required.
optionExplanations.B: Volume does not matter; legacy authentication is rejected outright.
optionExplanations.C: Authorization Code Grant is OAuth 2.0, but it needs a person to sign in, which an unattended 02:00 job lacks.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. JWT Grant satisfies the OAuth 2.0 requirement and suits a job with no user present.

decode.needs: Replace legacy header authentication with OAuth 2.0; unattended job -> JWT Grant.
clues: X-DocuSign-Authentication with email and password -> legacy authentication
fails Go-Live review about authentication -> OAuth 2.0 is required
nobody at the keyboard at 02:00 -> JWT Grant
Linux, 400 envelopes -> red herrings

concept.title: OAuth 2.0 required
concept.line: Go-Live requires OAuth 2.0; legacy header authentication fails review unless a policy exception is granted.

topic: JWT with admin consent for many users
stem: Rowan & Sable, a national accountancy, wants its practice-management system to send engagement letters from each partner's own Docusign account so that every letter sits in that partner's Sent folder. All 900 partners are on the firm's claimed domain, the firm has Access Management, and the managing partner has ruled that partners must never be shown a Docusign login or consent page, not even once. The system is hosted on the firm's servers and can protect an RSA private key. Partners also work heavily in Microsoft Teams. What should the integration do?

options.text: Use Confidential Authorization Code Grant with the extended scope, so each partner signs in once and the refresh token keeps rolling
Use JWT Grant impersonating one firm-wide sender, and put each partner's name in the email subject so the letter appears to come from them
Use Public Authorization Code Grant with PKCE inside a Teams tab, so partners authenticate with their existing Microsoft session
Have an organization administrator grant admin consent, then use JWT Grant with each partner's user ID as sub, looked up by email
Use JWT Grant impersonating each partner, sending every partner the individual consent URL once during their onboarding

answerText: Have an organization administrator grant admin consent, then use JWT Grant with each partner's user ID as sub, looked up by email
explanation: Admin consent for an internal app covers every partner in the claimed domain without anyone seeing a consent page, and JWT Grant with each partner's user ID as sub sends from that partner's account.
whyNotOthers: D is right because 'never shown a login or consent page, not even once' rules out every flow that needs the partner in a browser. The trap is E: JWT impersonation is right, but individual consent shows each partner a consent page once. A and C need partners to sign in, and B sends from one shared account, so letters would not sit in each partner's Sent folder.

optionExplanations.A: Each partner would still have to sign in at least once.
optionExplanations.B: Letters would sit in the shared sender's folder, not each partner's.
optionExplanations.C: Partners would still go through a Docusign sign-in; Teams is a red herring.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. Admin consent covers the claimed domain, and JWT with each partner's user ID impersonates them with no page shown.
optionExplanations.E: Individual consent shows each partner a consent page, which the managing partner forbade.

decode.needs: Admin consent for the claimed domain, then JWT Grant impersonating each partner
clues: 'from each partner's own account, own Sent folder' -> impersonate each user, sub = their user ID
'never shown a login or consent page, not even once' -> admin consent, not individual
'claimed domain, Access Management' -> admin consent is available
'Microsoft Teams' -> red herring

concept.title: Admin consent plus per-user JWT
concept.line: To act as many domain users with no prompts, combine admin consent with JWT Grant using each user's ID as sub.

stem: Penrose Insurance is building an internal admin console where operations staff choose which published workflow the claims system should start for each claim type. The console must list every available workflow in the Docusign account with its name and ID and, for the one chosen, show what input data a trigger has to supply, so staff no longer ask developers for IDs. The console already authenticates with JWT Grant and the aow_manage scope, and it uses the company's corporate colour theme. Which call should populate the picker list?

options.text: getWorkflowInstancesList, which returns every workflow in the account together with the instances that each one is currently running in the account
GetWorkflowTriggerRequirements without a workflowId, which returns the trigger URL and input schema for every published workflow
GetWorkflowsList, which returns each available workflow's id, name and description together with the input schema needed to trigger it
getWorkflowInstance for each workflow, which returns the workflow's name, status and started_by details for the account's admin view
eSignature Templates:list, because every published workflow is stored in the account as an eSignature template with a workflow ID

answerText: GetWorkflowsList, which returns each available workflow's id, name and description together with the input schema needed to trigger it
explanation: GetWorkflowsList (GET /v1/accounts/{accountId}/workflows) returns each available workflow's id, name and description, plus its trigger input schema, which is exactly what a picker needs.
whyNotOthers: C is right because the console must list 'every available workflow' with name, ID and input data. The trap is B: GetWorkflowTriggerRequirements does return the input schema, but it is called per workflow with a workflowId, so it cannot build the list. A and D work at instance level and need a workflow or instance ID first, and E confuses workflows with eSignature templates.

optionExplanations.A: Instance listing is per workflow (/workflows/{workflowId}/instances); it does not list workflows.
optionExplanations.B: Its path is /workflows/{workflowId}/trigger-requirements; it needs a workflowId and returns one workflow.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. GetWorkflowsList returns all available workflows with id, name, description and trigger input schema.
optionExplanations.D: Returns one instance's details and needs an instance ID; it does not enumerate workflows.
optionExplanations.E: Workflows are not stored as eSignature templates.

decode.needs: Call GetWorkflowsList to enumerate workflows
clues: list every available workflow with name and ID -> account-level workflow list
what input data a trigger has to supply -> input schema in the list entries
corporate colour theme -> red herring

concept.title: GetWorkflowsList for discovery
concept.line: GetWorkflowsList enumerates an account's workflows with IDs and input schemas; trigger requirements are fetched per workflow.

topic: Tracking a co-signer after embedded submission
stem: Copperfield Motors embeds a template-based web form for vehicle finance in its dealer website. The buyer fills in the form and signs in focused view on the dealer's tablet; a co-buyer named in the form signs the generated agreement later from an emailed link. The website already listens to Docusign JS events. The finance team's dashboard must show when each co-buyer has signed, and the dealership wants push updates rather than scheduled checks. What should the developer use?

options.text: A Docusign Connect listener subscribed to envelope and recipient events, because Docusign JS events reflect envelope activity only for the instance submitter.
The Docusign JS envelope events already handled by the website, because they report signing activity for every recipient of the generated envelope.
Instances:getInstance on a schedule, reading the co-buyer's instanceRecipientStatus, because it changes to SUBMITTED when the co-buyer signs the agreement.
Envelopes:listStatusChanges every few minutes from the dashboard, because it reports each recipient's status, including recipients outside the embedded session.

answerText: A Docusign Connect listener subscribed to envelope and recipient events, because Docusign JS events reflect envelope activity only for the instance submitter.
explanation: Docusign JS events only reflect envelope activity for the web form instance submitter; other recipients are tracked with Connect or Envelopes:listStatusChanges. The clue is 'push updates rather than scheduled checks'.
whyNotOthers: A is right because Connect pushes envelope and recipient events for every recipient. The trap is B: the JS events only cover the buyer who submitted the instance. C polls and tracks form submission, not signing, and D polls, which the dealership ruled out.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. Connect pushes events for all recipients; JS events cover only the submitter.
optionExplanations.B: Docusign JS events reflect envelope activity only for the instance submitter.
optionExplanations.C: Scheduled polling, and instanceRecipientStatus tracks the form view, not envelope signing.
optionExplanations.D: listStatusChanges can report recipient status, but it is polling on a schedule, which the dealership rejected in favour of push updates; Connect provides the push.

decode.needs: Push notifications about the co-signer's signing of the generated envelope.
clues: 'co-buyer ... from an emailed link' -> recipient outside the embedded session
'push updates rather than scheduled checks' -> Connect, not polling
'already listens to Docusign JS events' -> tempting but limited to the submitter

concept.title: Tracking web form envelopes
concept.line: Docusign JS events cover only the instance submitter; track other recipients with Connect or Envelopes:listStatusChanges.

stem: Larchfield Council publishes a 'Pothole damage claim' workflow that residents start themselves From a Link on the council website, so the council's systems never receive an instance ID. The highways team wants a nightly report in its case-management tool listing every instance of that workflow, running or completed, with who started it, when it was last modified and how many steps are done. The nightly job already has a token with the aow_manage scope and knows the workflow ID. Residents can also report potholes by phone. Which approach fits?

options.text: Call getWorkflowInstance nightly for each instance, using the instance IDs that the website link passes back to the case-management tool each day
Subscribe a Connect configuration in XML SIM format to workflow-started and workflow-completed events and build the report from them
Call GetWorkflowsList nightly and read the instance count and step progress that each entry returns for the pothole claim workflow
Call cancelWorkflowInstance in a dry-run mode for each instance, which returns the current status without stopping the instance
Call getWorkflowInstancesList for the workflow ID nightly, which lists its instances with status, timestamps, starter and steps completed

answerText: Call getWorkflowInstancesList for the workflow ID nightly, which lists its instances with status, timestamps, starter and steps completed
explanation: getWorkflowInstancesList (GET .../workflows/{workflowId}/instances) returns every instance of the workflow with its id, status, timestamps and metadata such as who started it, when it was last modified and how many steps are completed; only the workflow ID is needed.
whyNotOthers: E is right because the job knows only the workflow ID ('never receive an instance ID'). The trap is A: getWorkflowInstance gives rich detail, but it needs an instance ID per call, and link starts do not return IDs to the council. B fails because Maestro events are delivered only in JSON SIM, C lists workflows not instances, and D invents a dry-run mode.

optionExplanations.A: Needs instance IDs, which a self-service link start never hands back to the council.
optionExplanations.B: Maestro Connect events are available only in JSON SIM format, not XML.
optionExplanations.C: GetWorkflowsList describes workflows and their input schemas, not their instances.
optionExplanations.D: Cancel stops an instance; there is no dry-run mode.
optionExplanations.E: Correct. The instance list needs only the workflow ID and returns status, timestamps, starter and steps completed.

decode.needs: getWorkflowInstancesList for the workflow
clues: residents start it from a link -> no instance IDs returned to your system
every instance, running or completed -> list of instances for one workflow
who started it, last modified, steps done -> instance list metadata
phone reports -> red herring

concept.title: Instance list when IDs are unknown
concept.line: getWorkflowInstancesList needs only the workflow ID; getWorkflowInstance needs a known instance ID, such as one returned by a trigger.

topic: Native mobile embedded signing: returnUrl handling
stem: Arbor Bank's Android app shows loan agreements for signing inside an in-app WebView using classic view. When the borrower finishes, the app must close the WebView and show its own confirmation screen instead of loading any web page. The developers want to follow Docusign's native mobile guidance, and the product owner insists that no Docusign or bank web page flashes on screen after the borrower taps Finish. The app also has an iPad version built by a separate team. What should the Android team do?

options.text: Use a custom host such as https://arborloans/ as the returnUrl and handle it in WebViewClient.shouldOverrideUrlLoading, returning false so the WebView loads the return page before closing
Use the public website's thank-you page as the returnUrl and close the WebView after the page has finished loading
Render the agreement with focused view and add the app's package name to frameAncestors so the WebView can host it
Use a custom host such as https://arborloans/ as the returnUrl and handle it in WebViewClient.shouldOverrideUrlLoading, returning true when the URL matches that host and reading the event parameter

answerText: Use a custom host such as https://arborloans/ as the returnUrl and handle it in WebViewClient.shouldOverrideUrlLoading, returning true when the URL matches that host and reading the event parameter
explanation: For native apps Docusign recommends a custom host for the returnUrl and returning true when a URL change matches that host; on Android this is done in WebViewClient.shouldOverrideUrlLoading.
whyNotOthers: D is right because it intercepts the redirect before any page loads. The trap is A: the same approach, but returning false lets the WebView navigate. B loads a real web page, and C misuses frameAncestors and changes the view.

optionExplanations.A: Returning false lets the WebView load the URL; the guidance is to return true for URLs that match your host so the app handles the event.
optionExplanations.B: This loads a web page, which the app wants to avoid, and does not follow the custom host guidance.
optionExplanations.C: frameAncestors lists web origins allowed to frame focused view; it is not how a native app detects completion, and the bank uses classic view.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. Docusign's guidance for native apps: custom returnUrl host, return true for URLs that match it, and for Android handle it in shouldOverrideUrlLoading.

decode.needs: Native mobile: custom returnUrl host intercepted in shouldOverrideUrlLoading (return true)
clues: Android app WebView -> WebViewClient.shouldOverrideUrlLoading
close the WebView instead of loading any page -> intercept the custom host and return true
iPad version by a separate team -> red herring (WKWebView is the iOS route)

concept.title: returnUrl in native apps
concept.line: Native apps use a custom returnUrl host, intercept it (Android shouldOverrideUrlLoading, iOS WKWebView) and return true to handle the event.

stem: Rowan Foods requires an expiration date on every supplier contract before its ERP will release a purchase order. After the legal team imported a batch of old scanned contracts into Agreement Manager, the nightly sync finds that some records come back without a usable expiration_date, because the date is not stated clearly or the scan is poor. Purchasing complains that orders are blocked, and a developer proposes deriving the date from effective_date plus term_length inside the ERP. The controller wants every date in the ERP to be traceable to a reviewed value in Agreement Manager. Which review step fits?

options.text: Queue the agreements that lack a usable expiration_date for a contract analyst, who enters the date in Agreement Manager before the next sync.
Compute each missing date in the ERP from effective_date plus term_length, and flag the ERP record as reviewed so purchase orders are released at once.
Call CreateAgreementSummary for each agreement without a date, and store the expiration date the summary mentions as the reviewed value in the ERP.
Delete each agreement without a date with DeleteAgreement and import it again, so the AI extraction runs a second time and fills in the date.

answerText: Queue the agreements that lack a usable expiration_date for a contract analyst, who enters the date in Agreement Manager before the next sync.
explanation: When AI finds no value, a business user reviews the agreement and enters it in Agreement Manager; later GET responses return the user-entered value. That keeps every ERP date 'traceable to a reviewed value in Agreement Manager'.
whyNotOthers: A is right because the correction is made at the source and flows to the ERP on the next sync. The trap is B: the derived date may be correct, but it exists only in the ERP and nobody reviewed it in Agreement Manager. C relies on unreviewed AI prose, and D repeats the same extraction on the same poor scan.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. An external queue finds the gaps and an analyst fills them in Agreement Manager, whose user-entered values the next GET returns.
optionExplanations.B: The derived value lives only in the ERP and was never reviewed in Agreement Manager, which breaks the controller's traceability rule.
optionExplanations.C: An AI summary is not a reviewed value and may omit or misstate the date.
optionExplanations.D: Re-importing the same poor scan re-runs the same extraction and still leaves no reviewed value.

decode.needs: An external review queue for missing values, with the fix made in Agreement Manager so the API returns it.
clues: records come back without a usable expiration_date -> AI found no value to extract
traceable to a reviewed value in Agreement Manager -> the correction must be made in Agreement Manager, not the ERP
derive from effective_date plus term_length -> tempting shortcut that bypasses review

concept.title: Fill extraction gaps at the source
concept.line: When AI extraction leaves a value empty, route it to a reviewer who enters it in Agreement Manager; later API reads return the user value.

topic: Legacy event values in the wrong case
stem: A developer at Pellham Freight keeps an existing XML parser and creates an account-level configuration with POST /v2.1/accounts/{accountId}/connect. The body sets configurationType to custom, allUsers to true, allowEnvelopePublish to true, enableLog to true and deliveryMode to aggregate, with no eventData version, and lists envelopeEvents as completed and declined. The call returns 201, but no messages arrive when test envelopes are completed, even though the listener answers webhook test tools correctly. What should the developer change?

options.text: Set allowEnvelopePublish to true, because configurations created through the API are disabled until it is set
Replace envelopeEvents with an events array of lowercase names such as envelope-completed while keeping the aggregate XML model
Write the envelopeEvents values in sentence case, such as Completed and Declined, because lowercase values in that property do not match
Set allUsers to false and list the shipping clerks' user IDs, because allUsers applies only to organization-level configurations
Enable requiresAcknowledgement, because Connect does not deliver legacy XML messages to a listener unless acknowledgement is required

answerText: Write the envelopeEvents values in sentence case, such as Completed and Declined, because lowercase values in that property do not match
explanation: The create reference's troubleshooting list says that when you use envelopeEvents or recipientEvents, the values must be sentence case, not lowercase; the body already enables publishing and covers all users.
whyNotOthers: C is right because legacy envelopeEvents values must be sentence case. The trap is B: lowercase hyphenated names are correct, but in the events property used by JSON SIM, not in a legacy XML aggregate configuration. A is already set in the body, D is false because allUsers applies to account-level configurations, and E is false because acknowledgement controls retries, not first delivery.

optionExplanations.A: The body already sets allowEnvelopePublish to true, so the configuration is enabled.
optionExplanations.B: The events array with names such as envelope-completed belongs to the JSON SIM model; legacy XML uses envelopeEvents or recipientEvents.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. The troubleshooting guidance says envelopeEvents and recipientEvents values must be sentence case, not lowercase.
optionExplanations.D: allUsers true (or a non-empty userIds list) is exactly what an account-level configuration needs.
optionExplanations.E: requiresAcknowledgement governs retries of failed deliveries; it is not a precondition for sending messages.

decode.needs: Fix the case of the legacy envelopeEvents values
clues: deliveryMode aggregate, no eventData version -> legacy XML model, so envelopeEvents applies
envelopeEvents completed and declined in lowercase -> must be sentence case
allowEnvelopePublish true, allUsers true -> already correct, ruling out the usual suspects
listener answers test tools -> red herring, the listener is fine

concept.title: Legacy events need sentence case
concept.line: Legacy configurations use envelopeEvents or recipientEvents in sentence case; JSON SIM uses an events array of lowercase hyphenated names.

stem: Kestrel Robotics' HR system must send offer letters from a document generation template that already contains the candidate name, job title, start date and salary placeholders, plus a relocation clause that appears only when relocation is offered. Recruiters never touch Docusign; an unattended back-office job sends each offer as soon as the hiring manager approves it in the HR system. The letters use the company's new font. Which sequence of calls should the job use?

options.text: Envelopes:create (templateId, templateRoles, status sent); getEnvelopeDocGenFormFields; updateEnvelopeDocGenFormFields with the values so the letter is complete
Envelopes:create (templateId, templateRoles, status created); getEnvelopeDocGenFormFields; updateEnvelopeDocGenFormFields with the values; Envelopes:update to status sent
Envelopes:create with templateId, status created and templateRoles whose textTabs carry the values by tabLabel; Envelopes:update with status sent
Envelopes:create with compositeTemplates and an inline template holding the values; updateEnvelopeDocGenFormFields; Envelopes:update to status sent

answerText: Envelopes:create (templateId, templateRoles, status created); getEnvelopeDocGenFormFields; updateEnvelopeDocGenFormFields with the values; Envelopes:update to status sent
explanation: A document generation template is sent in four steps: create a draft (status created), get the docGenFormFields, update them with values (conditional content such as the relocation clause is applied here), then set status to sent.
whyNotOthers: B is right because the fields must be filled while the envelope is still a draft. The trap is A: the calls are right but the envelope is already sent before the values are added. C uses the standard-template tabLabel technique, and D puts the data in the wrong structure and skips reading the field names.

optionExplanations.A: With status sent the envelope goes out before the fields are filled; the document generation flow requires a draft created with status created.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. Document generation needs a draft envelope, then the field list, then the values (where conditional content is applied), then the send.
optionExplanations.C: Pre-filling tabs by tabLabel is for standard templates; document generation fields are filled through the docGenFormFields endpoints.
optionExplanations.D: The course flow starts from the template reference request with status created and reads the field names first; values go into docGenFormFields, not an inline template.

decode.needs: Doc gen: create draft -> get docGenFormFields -> update docGenFormFields -> status sent
clues: document generation template with placeholders -> docGenFormFields endpoints
clause appears only when relocation is offered -> conditional content applied at the update step
unattended back-office job -> fully API-driven, no sender UI
new font -> red herring

concept.title: Document generation send flow
concept.line: Create the envelope as a draft, read and fill docGenFormFields, then change status to sent.

topic: Extension step labels in Workflow Builder
stem: On the Apps tab of the Add New Step panel, which app manifest properties supply the name and description shown for an installed and connected extension app's step?

options.text: connections.name and connections.description
actions.name and actions.description
The manifest's top-level name and description
extensions.name and extensions.description
distribution.listingName and distribution.summary

answerText: extensions.name and extensions.description
explanation: The Add New Step panel displays the values of the extensions.name and extensions.description properties from the app manifest.
whyNotOthers: D is right because the step represents an extension defined in the registration. The trap is C: the app's own name and description describe the App Center listing, not the individual step. A describes authentication to the external system, B describes the endpoints called, and E is invented.

optionExplanations.A: Connections define how Docusign authenticates to the external system.
optionExplanations.B: Actions define the external endpoints that are called.
optionExplanations.C: The top-level app name and description describe the app, not the step label.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. extensions.name and extensions.description label the step.
optionExplanations.E: Not manifest properties used for the step label.

concept.title: Step labels come from extensions
concept.line: In Workflow Builder, an extension app's step shows the manifest's extensions.name and extensions.description.

stem: Rowan Motors runs a vehicle-handover workflow on a tablet in each showroom. Its Send Documents for Signature step uses a direct signing session, and the buyer's name and email are mapped from workflow variables collected in the web form. After go-live a sales manager reports a 'bug': buyers sign on the tablet without trouble, but none of them ever receives a Docusign signing email at the address they typed in. The showroom Wi-Fi was upgraded the same week. What is the correct explanation?

options.text: The email variable is mapped incorrectly, because a direct signing session always emails the signing link to the buyer as a backup to the tablet
The showroom network blocks the step's outbound email, so the step has failed and a workflow-failed event should appear in the Connect log
The Set Up Invite step is missing, because a direct signing session sends its signing email only after an invite step has run earlier
This is expected: with a direct signing session Docusign does not send an email to the supplied address, whereas remote signing would
Direct signing sessions cannot use workflow variables, so the step falls back to the template's default recipient and emails that address

answerText: This is expected: with a direct signing session Docusign does not send an email to the supplied address, whereas remote signing would
explanation: With a direct signing session, Docusign does not send an email to the supplied address when executing workflow instances; the signer signs in the session itself. Remote signing is the option that notifies by email.
whyNotOthers: D is right because 'buyers sign on the tablet without trouble' shows the step works as designed. The trap is C: Set Up Invite does send workflow invitations, but a direct signing session is meant for someone present and does not email a signing link. A and E invent behaviour, and B describes a failure, yet the signing completes.

optionExplanations.A: Direct signing does not email the signer at all; there is no backup email.
optionExplanations.B: Signing completes, so the step has not failed; Wi-Fi is a red herring.
optionExplanations.C: Set Up Invite sends workflow invitations; it does not make a direct signing session email a signing link.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. A direct signing session sends no email to the supplied address; remote signing would.
optionExplanations.E: Name and email can come from workflow variables in a direct signing session.

decode.needs: Expected behaviour of a direct signing session
clues: tablet in each showroom -> signer present, direct signing session
never receives a signing email -> direct signing sends none
Wi-Fi upgrade -> red herring

concept.title: Direct signing sends no email
concept.line: In a workflow, a direct signing session signs in-session with no email to the signer; remote signing notifies by email.

stem: Rothwell Bank's document-generation service went live yesterday. It uses JWT Grant to act as a dedicated system user. The developer has added a new RSA key pair to the production copy of the key, changed the OAuth host and the aud claim to account.docusign.com, and set sub to the system user's production user ID. Token requests now fail with consent_required. In the developer sandbox, the system user granted consent months ago. Rothwell's Docusign organization has a claimed domain and an organization administrator. What should the team do?

options.text: Run Start Go live again, so that the consent granted in the developer sandbox is copied across to the production copy of the integration key
Generate another RSA key pair in production, because consent_required means the JWT was signed with a key that production does not recognise
Obtain consent in production, either as admin consent for the key's scopes from the organization administrator or as the system user's own consent
Change the aud claim back to account-d.docusign.com, because consent is always recorded against the developer authentication service

answerText: Obtain consent in production, either as admin consent for the key's scopes from the organization administrator or as the system user's own consent
explanation: Production and developer OAuth settings are separate, so consent given in the sandbox does not apply to production. The clue 'consent_required' after the RSA key, host and sub are fixed leaves consent; with a claimed domain, the organization administrator can grant admin consent proactively.
whyNotOthers: C is right because consent must exist in production. The trap is A: it assumes Go-Live copies OAuth state, but it copies only the key value. B fails because a key-pair problem is a different error and the pair is already in production, and D would send production tokens to the developer service.

optionExplanations.A: Go-Live duplicates only the key; no consent or other OAuth settings are copied, and repeating it changes nothing.
optionExplanations.B: consent_required is about missing consent, and a production RSA key pair is already in place.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. Consent must be granted in production; an org admin with a claimed domain can grant admin consent.
optionExplanations.D: Production requires account.docusign.com; the developer host would not issue production tokens.

decode.needs: After Go-Live, grant consent again in production (admin consent or individual consent).
clues: consent_required after RSA, host, aud and sub are fixed -> consent missing in production
consented in the sandbox months ago -> sandbox consent does not carry over
claimed domain, organization administrator -> admin consent is possible

concept.title: Consent does not carry over
concept.line: Developer and production OAuth settings are separate; JWT users must grant consent again in production.

stem: Pellham Freight's private connected fields extension app verifies customer account numbers against its billing platform. Last sprint, the billing team added a 'credit hold' property to the verified customer object in the external data model and redeployed the service. Senders now report that the new field does not appear among the app's fields when preparing envelopes, although verification of the existing fields still works. Reinstalling the app in production would delete live connections. What should the team do?

options.text: Republish the extension app manifest with a new version number so that the App Center review adds the new property to the field list for all accounts.
Refresh the extension app's connection in the App Center so that Docusign calls Get Type Names and Get Type Definitions again and loads the updated model.
Uninstall and reinstall the extension app on the Developer Console Testing page and then run a new connection test to rebuild the list of fields.
Add the new property to each envelope's tabs through extensionData by API, because the Add Fields view lists only properties that existed at installation.

answerText: Refresh the extension app's connection in the App Center so that Docusign calls Get Type Names and Get Type Definitions again and loads the updated model.
explanation: When a connection is created or refreshed, Docusign calls Get Type Names and Get Type Definitions to load the data model. The clue is 'added a property ... does not appear', with existing connections that must survive.
whyNotOthers: B is right because refreshing keeps the connection intact and reloads the model. The trap is C: reinstalling in the Developer Console would rebuild the list but deletes all existing connections, which the stem rules out. A is not needed for a data model change, and D is wrong because a refreshed model shows in Add Fields.

optionExplanations.A: The data model is read from the external service at connection time, not from a new manifest version.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. A connection refresh re-runs Get Type Names and Get Type Definitions.
optionExplanations.C: Reinstalling deletes existing connections, which the stem says must be avoided.
optionExplanations.D: The Add Fields view shows new properties once the connection is refreshed.

decode.needs: Reload an extension's data model without breaking live connections: refresh the connection.
clues: 'added a property ... does not appear' -> stale data model
'verification of existing fields still works' -> connection is healthy
'would delete live connections' -> rules out reinstalling

concept.title: Refreshing a connected fields model
concept.line: Changes to the external data model appear after the connection is refreshed, which re-runs Get Type Names and Get Type Definitions.

topic: Classification: private custom with outside signers
stem: Ashgrove Mortgage's in-house team has built a loan-origination tool used only by Ashgrove's own underwriters and loan processors. The tool sends disclosures to thousands of outside borrowers each month, and some borrowers sign on a tablet in the branch. Ashgrove pays for its own Docusign production account, has no plans to sell the tool, and does not belong to any partner program. When creating the integration key, which option should the developer pick under 'How will you use this integration?'

options.text: Private custom integration, because the tool is used directly by Ashgrove's own employees, whoever the people signing the documents may be
Public integration, because the disclosures are signed by thousands of members of the public who are outside the Ashgrove organization
Embedded integration, because some borrowers sign inside Ashgrove's own branch tablet experience instead of opening an email link
Third-party integration key, because the borrowers are third parties to Ashgrove and the key is registered on their behalf

answerText: Private custom integration, because the tool is used directly by Ashgrove's own employees, whoever the people signing the documents may be
explanation: Classification follows who uses the integration and the business model: a tool used directly by your own employees is a private custom integration. The clue 'used only by Ashgrove's own underwriters and loan processors' decides; who signs is irrelevant.
whyNotOthers: A is right because the users are Ashgrove's employees and nothing is sold. The trap is B: 'public' describes an integration offered to many Docusign customers through the Partner Program, not one whose signers are members of the public. C fails because Ashgrove is not an ISV Embed partner offering its account to customers, and D fails because a third-party key is one you supply to someone else's partner app.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. The tool is used directly by Ashgrove's employees, which is the private custom integration case.
optionExplanations.B: Public integration means many Docusign customers authorize your product on their own accounts; signers do not count.
optionExplanations.C: Embedded integration is the ISV Embed licence model; in-person or embedded signing does not decide it.
optionExplanations.D: A third-party integration key is created to plug into a partner's app; borrowers are just signers.

decode.needs: Classify by who uses the integration: own employees -> Private custom integration.
clues: used only by Ashgrove's own underwriters -> employees are the users
thousands of outside borrowers sign -> signers do not change the classification
tablet in the branch -> in-person or embedded signing, a red herring
no partner program, not sold -> not public or embedded

concept.title: Classify by users, not signers
concept.line: Classification depends on who uses the integration and the business model, not on who signs the documents.

topic: Multi Branch Rule with a fallback path
stem: Tavistock Engineering is automating onboarding for new contractors. After the offer letter is signed, the process depends on the work country captured in the intake form: UK contractors must verify their identity before signing a UK contract, contractors in any other country must be handed to their local HR partner by email, and if an instance somehow arrives with no recognisable country, the central HR coordinator must be told that it could not be routed. The intake form is available in English and Welsh. Which two design choices meet this? (Select two)

options.text: Add a Multi Branch Rule step on the country variable with a UK path, an Other path and the No Conditions Met path
Add a Branching Rule step on country equals UK, with identity verification on true and the HR partner email on false
On the No Conditions Met path, add a Show a Confirmation Screen step telling the contractor to contact HR
Add a Set Up Invite step for the HR partner at the start so the partner is invited for every contractor
On the No Conditions Met path, add a Send an Email step telling the central HR coordinator routing failed

answerText: Add a Multi Branch Rule step on the country variable with a UK path, an Other path and the No Conditions Met path; On the No Conditions Met path, add a Send an Email step telling the central HR coordinator routing failed
explanation: Three outcomes (UK, other, unrecognised) need a Multi Branch Rule with UK, Other and No Conditions Met paths, and the coordinator 'must be told', which is a Send an Email step on the No Conditions Met path, as in the course's onboarding example.
whyNotOthers: A and E are right because the unrecognised case needs its own path and an email to the coordinator. The trap is B: a Branching Rule handles UK versus not-UK, but its false path would treat an unrecognised country as 'other' and email an HR partner instead of telling the coordinator. C informs the wrong person on screen, and D invites the HR partner to every instance instead of only non-UK ones.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. A Multi Branch Rule gives separate UK, Other and No Conditions Met paths.
optionExplanations.B: Only two paths: an unrecognised country would fall into the false path and go to an HR partner.
optionExplanations.C: A confirmation screen tells the contractor; the coordinator must be informed.
optionExplanations.D: Invites the partner for every contractor, including UK ones; it is not routing.
optionExplanations.E: Correct. A Send an Email step on No Conditions Met tells the coordinator the instance could not be routed.

decode.needs: Multi Branch Rule (UK / Other / No Conditions Met) with an email on the fallback path
clues: UK, any other country, no recognisable country -> three outcomes
must be told it could not be routed -> No Conditions Met path with Send an Email
English and Welsh form -> red herring

concept.title: Multi Branch Rule fallback path
concept.line: A Multi Branch Rule gives one path per value plus a No Conditions Met path for unexpected values; a Branching Rule has only two.

stem: Which two are prerequisites for using Recipient Connect? (Select two)

options.text: Each envelope must be sent with an eventNotification object that names the recipient organization's listener URL
The organization must have claimed the email domain of the users who will be monitored as recipients
The configuration must use the legacy XML format, because Recipient Connect reuses the SOAP envelope model
The accounts that send the envelopes must be linked to the receiving organization in Docusign Admin
The accounts that will receive the envelopes must be linked to an organization in Docusign Admin

answerText: The organization must have claimed the email domain of the users who will be monitored as recipients; The accounts that will receive the envelopes must be linked to an organization in Docusign Admin
explanation: Recipient Connect needs an organization in Docusign Admin, a claimed domain for the monitored users, and the receiving accounts linked to that organization.
whyNotOthers: B and E are right because Recipient Connect works for domain users of your own organization whose accounts are linked to it. The trap is D: linking accounts is a prerequisite, but it is the receiving accounts, not the outside senders' accounts, that must be linked. A fails because the sender controls the envelope and no eventNotification is needed; C fails because Recipient Connect messages are always JSON.

optionExplanations.A: Recipient Connect is a standing configuration on the receiving side; the outside sender does not add anything to the envelope.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. Monitored users must belong to a domain claimed by the organization (Access Management with SSO).
optionExplanations.C: Recipient Connect messages are always sent in JSON, never XML.
optionExplanations.D: Senders are often outside companies that cannot be linked to your organization; only the receiving accounts need linking.
optionExplanations.E: Correct. The accounts that receive envelopes and trigger the notifications must be linked to the organization.

concept.title: Recipient Connect prerequisites
concept.line: Recipient Connect needs an organization, a claimed domain for monitored users, and the receiving accounts linked to the organization.

stem: Saltmarsh Solar's quoting tool sends price quotes for signature. Because panel prices change, sales leadership wants every quote to expire 14 days after it is sent, with a reminder email every 3 days until then. Other departments that send from the same Docusign account need the account's default reminder and expiration settings to stay as they are. The quotes are generated as PDFs from the pricing engine. How should the integration handle this?

options.text: Ask the account administrator to change the account's default reminder and expiration settings to 3 and 14 days for all senders
Schedule a job that calls Envelopes:update with resend_envelope every 3 days and sets status voided after 14 days
Add a notification object to each request with useAccountDefaults false, reminders every 3 days and expiration after 14 days
Add a notification object to each request with useAccountDefaults true and the reminder and expiration values set inside it

answerText: Add a notification object to each request with useAccountDefaults false, reminders every 3 days and expiration after 14 days
explanation: The notification object in Envelopes:create sets reminders and expirations for one envelope; useAccountDefaults must be false for those values to apply. The clue is that other departments must keep the defaults.
whyNotOthers: C is right because it scopes the settings to each quote. The trap is D: the structure looks the same, but useAccountDefaults true makes Docusign use the account settings. A changes every department's envelopes, and B replaces built-in features with costly custom calls.

optionExplanations.A: This changes the behaviour for every department on the account, which the stem rules out.
optionExplanations.B: This rebuilds reminders and expiry with many extra API calls, and voiding is not the same as an expiration setting.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. The envelope-level notification object overrides reminders and expiration for that envelope only.
optionExplanations.D: With useAccountDefaults true the account settings apply and the per-envelope values are ignored.

decode.needs: Envelope-level notification object with useAccountDefaults false
clues: expire 14 days, remind every 3 days -> expirations and reminders
other departments keep defaults -> envelope-level, not account-level
PDFs from the pricing engine -> red herring

concept.title: Per-envelope reminders and expiration
concept.line: Set reminders and expirations in the envelope's notification object with useAccountDefaults false to override account defaults for that envelope only.

stem: Tessaly sells a single-page scheduling app to clinics. The app calls the eSignature API from the browser through CORS, its integration key lists the app's origin and the needed HTTP methods, and it requests the signature and cors scopes. Clinics that have used it for months work fine, but a new clinic group, whose users consented to the app last week, gets 403 errors on every CORS request, while a non-CORS test call made with the same key from a server succeeds for that group. The new clinic group uses a different email provider. What is the most likely fix?

options.text: Add the new clinic group's own website domain to the integration key's allowed origins list
Add the cors scope again and ask every user in the new clinic group to grant consent a second time
Add OPTIONS and DELETE to the integration key's allowed HTTP methods so the browser preflight succeeds
Ask the new clinic group's account administrator to allow CORS for all apps or for this app

answerText: Ask the new clinic group's account administrator to allow CORS for all apps or for this app
explanation: CORS settings exist at two levels: the app (origins, methods) and the account (admin enables or disables CORS for all or specific apps). Only the new account fails, and non-CORS calls work, so the account-level setting is off.
whyNotOthers: D is right because the account administrator controls whether CORS requests from apps are accepted for that account. The trap is A: origins are the app's script origin, not the customer's site. B repeats steps that already work, and C changes app settings that work for every other clinic.

optionExplanations.A: Allowed origins are the origins of the script making the calls, which is the app's origin, already listed; the clinic's website is irrelevant.
optionExplanations.B: The app already requests cors and the users have consented; the server-side test shows authentication works.
optionExplanations.C: The same methods work for the other clinics, so the app-level method list is not what differs for this account.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. Docusign checks both the app's CORS settings and the account-level setting; if the user's account admin has not enabled CORS, CORS requests are rejected.

decode.needs: Account admin must enable CORS for the app in that account
clues: only the new clinic group fails -> account-specific setting
non-CORS call with the same key succeeds -> auth is fine, CORS is blocked
app origin and methods already configured -> app-level settings are fine
different email provider -> red herring

concept.title: Two levels of CORS settings
concept.line: An app defines CORS origins and methods; each customer account admin must also allow CORS for that app, or requests get 403/400.

stem: Juniper Docs' marketing team supplied the App Center icon for the company's new extension app as an animated GIF with a transparent background, sized 300 x 120 pixels to match the corporate logo banner. The developer is about to submit the app for review and wants to avoid a rejection on listing assets. The team also plans to add three screenshots taken from its staging environment using realistic customer-style data, and legal has approved the listing text. What should the developer do with the icon?

options.text: Keep the animated GIF but pad it to a 1:1 aspect ratio, because animation and transparency are accepted by review as long as the image is square.
Replace it with a transparent PNG at 300 x 120 pixels, because App Center rescales icons automatically and only animation causes a rejection.
Replace it with a square 1:1 PNG, JPG or SVG of about 100 x 100 pixels with no transparency, supplied as Base64 in icon.data with its mediaType.
Provide the icon as a public URL in icon.data so the App Center loads the current logo from Juniper's CDN without needing a new version.
Upload the GIF as the first screenshot instead, because only screenshots are checked in review and the icon defaults to the publisher logo.

answerText: Replace it with a square 1:1 PNG, JPG or SVG of about 100 x 100 pixels with no transparency, supplied as Base64 in icon.data with its mediaType.
explanation: The listing guidelines recommend a 1:1 PNG, JPG or SVG at 100 x 100 pixels; GIF and transparent PNG files may not render well and will be rejected. In the manifest the image goes into icon.data as Base64 with icon.mediaType.
whyNotOthers: C is right because it meets format, ratio and transparency guidance. The trap is A: making the image square fixes the ratio but keeps the GIF format and transparency that cause rejection. B keeps transparency, D puts a URL where Base64 is required, and E invents a default icon. The screenshots detail is a red herring.

optionExplanations.A: GIF and transparent images may not render well and will be rejected for publishing, whatever their shape.
optionExplanations.B: Transparent PNGs are also rejected, and the recommended aspect ratio is square.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. Best practices recommend PNG, JPG or SVG, 1:1, 100 x 100 pixels; GIF and transparent PNG files may be rejected. The manifest takes Base64 in icon.data plus icon.mediaType.
optionExplanations.D: icon.data must contain the Base64 representation of the image, not a URL.
optionExplanations.E: The icon is part of the listing and is reviewed; there is no default publisher-logo icon.

decode.needs: Supply a square, non-transparent PNG/JPG/SVG icon (about 100 x 100) as Base64 in icon.data.
clues: 'animated GIF with transparent background' -> both are rejection causes
'300 x 120' -> not the recommended 1:1
'avoid a rejection on listing assets' -> App Center publishing guidelines

concept.title: Icon format for App Center
concept.line: Use a square 100 x 100 PNG, JPG or SVG without transparency, Base64 encoded in icon.data; GIFs and transparent PNGs get rejected.

topic: Replacing on-demand polling in a mobile app
stem: Arbor Solar's field reps use a phone app, built in React Native, that lists customer proposals awaiting signature. Each time a rep opens the list, the app calls Envelopes:get for every one of that rep's 40 or so open envelopes, and reps open the list dozens of times a day. The go-live reviewer flagged the pattern, and sales management wants a proposal to show as signed within a minute of the customer signing. Proposals are sent by API from templates. What is the best redesign?

options.text: Keep the per-envelope calls but cache each result on the phone for five minutes, so that each rep's device sends fewer status requests per hour
Have Connect push signing events to a backend listener that updates the proposal database, and let the phone app read status from that database
Replace the per-envelope calls with one Envelopes:listStatusChanges call each time the list opens, covering the rep's envelopes since the start of the day
Add an eventNotification to each proposal that points at the rep's phone, so status reaches the device directly without any server in between
Have the app poll each open envelope every 15 minutes in the background, whether or not the rep opens the list, so the limit is never exceeded

answerText: Have Connect push signing events to a backend listener that updates the proposal database, and let the phone app read status from that database
explanation: Connect pushes events only when something changes, does not count against API limits and arrives in near real time, so a backend listener feeding the app's database meets both the review and the "within a minute" goal.
whyNotOthers: B is right because push events give near real-time status with no polling. The trap is C: listStatusChanges is the right call for occasional catch-up, but calling it on every app open is still frequent polling of the same envelopes. A still polls far more often than once per 15 minutes; D fails because a listener must be a public HTTPS endpoint, not a phone; E respects the limit but can leave a status up to 15 minutes old, missing the one-minute goal.

optionExplanations.A: A five-minute cache still checks each envelope up to three times as often as the 15-minute rule allows.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. Connect messages are pushed when status changes, do not count against API limits and remove the polling logic.
optionExplanations.C: listStatusChanges suits periodic reconciliation, but running it dozens of times a day per rep is still polling and does not fix the review finding.
optionExplanations.D: Connect posts to a listener available on the public internet over HTTPS; a rep's phone cannot act as that endpoint.
optionExplanations.E: Polling every 15 minutes is allowed but wasteful, and a signature could take up to 15 minutes to appear.

decode.needs: Connect to a backend listener that stores status; the app reads its own database
clues: go-live reviewer flagged the pattern -> polling rule violation
signed within a minute -> push, not 15-minute polling
phone app -> cannot be the webhook endpoint
React Native, templates -> red herrings

concept.title: Push status instead of polling
concept.line: Use Connect to push status into your own data store and have clients read that store, instead of polling Docusign on demand.

stem: The Larchmont Food Bank collects volunteer availability with a standalone web form embedded on its website; nothing is signed. The board now asks for changes: volunteers should upload a scan of their safeguarding certificate; the form should keep the food bank's logo and colors; returning volunteers should see their name and phone number prefilled; and the coordinator wants Docusign to email the form to volunteers who registered by phone. Which two requirements force a move to a template-based configuration? (Select two)

options.text: Keeping the food bank's logo and colors on the form
Uploading a scan of the safeguarding certificate
Prefilling name and phone number for returning volunteers
Docusign emailing the form to volunteers who registered by phone
Embedding the form in the food bank's website

answerText: Uploading a scan of the safeguarding certificate; Docusign emailing the form to volunteers who registered by phone
explanation: Attachment fields and remote (emailed) delivery are supported only with template-based configurations. The clues are 'upload a scan' and 'Docusign to email the form'.
whyNotOthers: B and D are right because standalone configurations support neither attachment fields nor remote delivery. The trap is A: branding feels like a template feature, but a brand can be applied to standalone forms on the configuration's Preview tab. C and E work with standalone embedded instances through formValues and Docusign JS.

optionExplanations.A: A brand can be applied to standalone configurations on the Preview tab.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. Attachment fields need a template-based configuration.
optionExplanations.C: Prefill with formValues works for standalone embedded instances.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. Remote delivery needs a template-based configuration.
optionExplanations.E: Standalone configurations support embedded delivery.

decode.needs: Identify which needs exceed a standalone configuration: attachments and emailed delivery.
clues: 'upload a scan' -> attachment field, template-based only
'Docusign to email the form' -> remote instance, template-based only
'logo and colors' -> possible on standalone, a trap

concept.title: Standalone configuration limits
concept.line: Standalone forms lack envelopes, routing, envelope custom fields, attachments, authentication records and remote delivery.

stem: Each quarter, Marlowe Energy's billing platform sends updated terms to about 900 business customers. The run attaches the same 4 MB terms-and-conditions PDF to every envelope and uses 100 parallel workers; each Envelopes:create call takes about 20 seconds to upload and process, so the run stays well inside the burst limit. Partway through, some requests fail with UNSPECIFIED_ERROR and the message 'PDF validation failed', yet the same PDF opens fine and succeeds when it is resent later on its own. What is the most likely cause and fix?

options.text: Too many in-progress uploads of identical document bytes; keep concurrent uploads of that one file under 70 by using fewer workers
The PDF is larger than the API allows for a single upload; compress it below the limit and resend all 900 requests in parallel again
The account hit its 30-second burst limit; read X-BurstLimit-Remaining and pause the workers whenever it gets close to zero before continuing
The account's hourly API limit was exceeded mid-run; ask an administrator to raise it with Update Hourly Limit in the API Usage Center

answerText: Too many in-progress uploads of identical document bytes; keep concurrent uploads of that one file under 70 by using fewer workers
explanation: Docusign allows at most 70 in-progress uploads of the same document bytes within an hour (and within six hours); excess uploads are blocked with UNSPECIFIED_ERROR 'PDF validation failed'. The clues 'same PDF', '100 parallel workers' and 'succeeds when resent later' identify it.
whyNotOthers: A is right because the error is the same-document upload limit, fixed by limiting concurrency. The trap is C: throttling is the right instinct, but the stem says the run stays inside the burst limit, and burst errors look different. B fails because 4 MB is far below the 32 MB API upload limit, and D fails because hourly-limit errors say the hourly invocations were exceeded.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. More than 70 in-progress uploads of identical bytes are blocked with 'PDF validation failed'.
optionExplanations.B: 4 MB is well below the 32 MB per-upload API limit, and the same file succeeds later.
optionExplanations.C: The stem rules out the burst limit, and burst errors are not reported as 'PDF validation failed'.
optionExplanations.D: Exceeding the hourly limit returns a 'maximum number of hourly API invocations' error, not a PDF error.

decode.needs: Limit concurrent uploads of the same document bytes (max 70 in progress).
clues: same 4 MB PDF in every envelope -> identical document bytes
100 parallel workers, 20 seconds each -> about 100 in-progress uploads of one file
PDF validation failed, fine when resent alone -> upload limit, not a broken file
well inside the burst limit -> not a rate limit

concept.title: Same-document upload limit
concept.line: At most 70 in-progress uploads of the same document bytes; excess calls fail with 'PDF validation failed'.

stem: Which two response headers tell an app how close the account is to its 30-second call ceiling? (Select two)

options.text: X-BurstLimit-Limit
X-RateLimit-Remaining
X-RateLimit-Reset
X-BurstLimit-Remaining
X-RateLimit-Limit

answerText: X-BurstLimit-Limit; X-BurstLimit-Remaining
explanation: The burst limit is reported by X-BurstLimit-Limit (200 developer, 500 production) and X-BurstLimit-Remaining for the current 30-second span.
whyNotOthers: A and D are right because they are the burst headers. The trap is B: it also reports remaining calls, but for the hourly limit. C and E also belong to the hourly limit.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. X-BurstLimit-Limit gives the 30-second maximum for all apps on the account.
optionExplanations.B: X-RateLimit-Remaining counts what is left of the hourly limit, not the burst limit.
optionExplanations.C: X-RateLimit-Reset is the timestamp when the hourly limit resets.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. X-BurstLimit-Remaining gives the calls left in the current 30-second span.
optionExplanations.E: X-RateLimit-Limit is the hourly limit (3,000 by default).

concept.title: RateLimit vs BurstLimit headers
concept.line: X-RateLimit-* headers describe the hourly limit; X-BurstLimit-Limit and -Remaining describe the 30-second burst limit.

stem: In JWT Grant, a user opens the consent URL, signs in and clicks Allow Access, and the browser is redirected with a code parameter. What should the integration do with that code?

options.text: Exchange it at /oauth/token within 120 seconds to obtain the first access token
Put it in the JWT payload as proof that the user granted consent
Nothing; the redirect parameters are not used in JWT Grant, so the service now builds and signs its JWT
Store it as the refresh token that renews JWT access tokens each hour
Send it as the assertion parameter together with the jwt-bearer grant_type

answerText: Nothing; the redirect parameters are not used in JWT Grant, so the service now builds and signs its JWT
explanation: In the JWT flow the consent redirect only records consent; the returned parameters such as code are not used. The service then builds a JWT and exchanges it.
whyNotOthers: C is right because the documentation states the returned parameters are not used in the JWT flow. The trap is A: exchanging a code within 120 seconds is Authorization Code Grant. B, D and E misplace the code: the JWT payload has no consent claim, JWT issues no refresh token, and the assertion is the signed JWT itself.

optionExplanations.A: That is the Authorization Code Grant step; in JWT the code is ignored.
optionExplanations.B: The JWT payload holds iss, sub, aud, iat, exp and scope, not a consent code.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. Consent is recorded by Docusign; the integration ignores the code and moves on to the JWT.
optionExplanations.D: JWT Grant never issues a refresh token.
optionExplanations.E: The assertion is the signed JWT, not the code.

concept.title: Consent redirect in JWT
concept.line: In JWT Grant the consent redirect only records consent; its code is not used. Tokens come from posting a signed JWT.

stem: Which two are documented disadvantages of Confidential Authorization Code Grant compared with the other Docusign grant types? (Select two)

options.text: It issues no refresh token, so users must sign in again whenever the access token expires
Its access token lasts only one hour, so users must sign in several times a day
The user must be present to authenticate, so autonomous applications cannot use it
It cannot be combined with a PKCE code challenge for added protection
The app must be able to keep a client secret secure, typically on a web server

answerText: The user must be present to authenticate, so autonomous applications cannot use it; The app must be able to keep a client secret secure, typically on a web server
explanation: The documented disadvantages are that the user must be present (no autonomous use) and that the app must be able to secure a client secret.
whyNotOthers: C and E are right. The trap is B: one-hour tokens belong to JWT Grant; Confidential Auth Code access tokens last 8 hours. A is wrong because Confidential returns a refresh token (up to 30 days), and D is wrong because PKCE is an optional extra for Confidential.

optionExplanations.A: Confidential Auth Code Grant does return a refresh token.
optionExplanations.B: Its access token lasts 8 hours by default; one hour is the JWT token.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. A user must be present, so it cannot serve autonomous applications.
optionExplanations.D: PKCE can optionally be added to Confidential Auth Code Grant.
optionExplanations.E: Correct. Unlike Public Auth Code Grant, it requires a secured client secret.

concept.title: Confidential Auth Code drawbacks
concept.line: Confidential Auth Code needs a present user and a securely stored secret; it gives 8-hour tokens and refresh tokens.

stem: Without Connect, an integration checks envelope status by polling. What polling frequency does the eSignature REST API allow for an envelope?

options.text: Once per envelope every 5 minutes
Once per envelope every hour
Once per envelope every 15 minutes
Once per account every 15 minutes, across all envelopes

answerText: Once per envelope every 15 minutes
explanation: Docusign limits status GET requests to one per envelope every 15 minutes, and an application that violates the polling rules will not be approved at go-live.
whyNotOthers: C is right because the limit is one status check per envelope every 15 minutes. The trap is D: it uses the right interval but the wrong scope, because the limit applies per envelope (or other API object), not per account. A is too frequent and B is stricter than the rule.

optionExplanations.A: Five minutes is three times more frequent than the rule allows.
optionExplanations.B: The rule allows once every 15 minutes; once per hour is stricter than required.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. Polling is limited to one GET per envelope every 15 minutes, which is why Connect is preferred.
optionExplanations.D: The 15-minute interval is right, but it applies to each envelope or API object, not to the account as a whole.

concept.title: Polling limit per envelope
concept.line: Status polling is limited to one request per envelope every 15 minutes; violating it blocks go-live approval.

topic: Composite templates: sequence rules for documents and attributes
stem: A developer at Brightwater Leasing reviews one composite template object in an envelope request. It has no document property. It contains a server template with sequence 1, which supplies the lease PDF and defines the lessee role and its tabs, and an inline template with sequence 2, which supplies a different PDF in its documents array and maps a recipient to the lessee role. The finance team wants to know what the resulting envelope will contain. Which two statements are true? (Select two)

options.text: The inline template's PDF replaces the lease PDF, because the higher sequence overrides what came before
Both PDFs appear in the envelope, one after the other, because each template in the object adds its own document
The lease PDF from the server template is the document contributed by this object, because the lowest sequence that supplies a document wins
The request is invalid, because sequence values must be unique across every composite template object in the envelope
The recipient from the inline template is assigned to the lessee role and its tabs, because later sequences overlay attributes

answerText: The lease PDF from the server template is the document contributed by this object, because the lowest sequence that supplies a document wins; The recipient from the inline template is assigned to the lessee role and its tabs, because later sequences overlay attributes
explanation: Within one composite object, documents follow 'first in wins' (document property, else lowest sequence that supplies one) while recipients and tabs follow 'last in wins'.
whyNotOthers: C and E are right because documents and attributes are prioritised in opposite directions. The trap is A: it applies the attribute rule to documents. B ignores the one-document-per-object rule, and D misstates the scope of sequence uniqueness.

optionExplanations.A: Last in wins applies to attributes such as recipients and tabs; documents follow first in wins.
optionExplanations.B: Each composite template object contributes only one document.
