optionExplanations.C: Correct. With no document property, the template with the lowest sequence that supplies a document contributes it.
optionExplanations.D: Sequence values must be unique within a composite template object; numbering can restart at 1 in each object.
optionExplanations.E: Correct. Attributes follow last in wins, so the inline template's recipient is applied after the server template defines the role.

decode.needs: Composite priority rules: documents first in wins, attributes last in wins
clues: no document property -> lowest sequence supplying a document wins
inline template seq 2 maps a recipient -> attributes overlay in sequence order
two PDFs in one object -> only one is contributed

concept.title: Composite document and attribute priority
concept.line: Per composite object: document property first, else lowest sequence document; recipients and tabs from higher sequences overwrite lower ones.

stem: Which two request headers does the course list as required for an Envelopes:create call? (Select two)

options.text: Accept: application/json
Authorization: Bearer followed by the OAuth access token
Authorization: Basic with the base64 integration key and secret
X-DocuSign-Authentication with the user's name and password
Content-Type: application/json (or multipart for binary documents)

answerText: Authorization: Bearer followed by the OAuth access token; Content-Type: application/json (or multipart for binary documents)
explanation: A request to create an envelope must include the Authorization header (Bearer plus the access token) and the Content-Type header.
whyNotOthers: B and E are the two required headers. The trap is A: Accept appears in many samples but is not required. C belongs to the token request, and D is legacy authentication.

optionExplanations.A: Common in samples, but not one of the two required headers.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. The Authorization header carries Bearer plus a valid access token.
optionExplanations.C: Basic credentials are used at the OAuth token endpoint, not on eSignature API calls.
optionExplanations.D: Legacy header authentication is not the OAuth Bearer header the course requires.
optionExplanations.E: Correct. Content-Type is the second required header.

concept.title: Envelope request headers
concept.line: eSignature calls need Authorization: Bearer {token} and Content-Type; Basic credentials are for the OAuth token endpoint.

topic: In-person signing hosted by an employee
stem: At Corbel Credit Union branches, an employee hands a tablet to a walk-in member who has no email address, and the audit trail must show which employee hosted the signing. Which recipient setup fits?

options.text: An inPersonSigner with the employee as host (hostName, hostEmail) and the member as signerName
A signer with a clientUserId and the employee's email, so the member signs on the tablet
A carbon copy for the employee and a remote signer for the member at a branch mailbox
An agent recipient for the employee, who then names the member as signer by email

answerText: An inPersonSigner with the employee as host (hostName, hostEmail) and the member as signerName
explanation: In person signing is designed for a host who facilitates the session for a signer in the same location; hostName and hostEmail identify the employee and signerName the member.
whyNotOthers: A is right because it records the host and needs no member email. The trap is B: embedded signing on a tablet sounds right, but the identity recorded would be the employee's. C needs an email the member lacks, and D misuses the agent role.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. In person signing lets a host facilitate a session for a signer who is physically present, and records the host.
optionExplanations.B: The member would sign as the employee, and the record would not show a hosted session for the member.
optionExplanations.C: The member has no email, and a carbon copy does not host the session.
optionExplanations.D: An agent chooses the next recipient by email; it does not host a face-to-face session for someone without email.

concept.title: Hosted in-person signing
concept.line: Use an inPersonSigner with host details when an employee hosts signing for someone physically present.

topic: File output endpoints in a form-registered app
stem: Rowan Vault's developer registered a new extension app using the form-based experience and selected File Input Output, then File Output Cloud Storage. On the integration details page she cannot find where to enter the URL of the write-file endpoint or of the optional drive-listing endpoint, so the extension tests cannot run. Her manager suggests switching to the file archive extension, which his team used two years ago in another product, because he remembers that the form handled everything. What should she do?

options.text: Switch the extension to file archive, because file archive actions can be fully defined in the form and it remains the recommended extension for storing completed files.
Delete the registration and recreate it by editing the manifest, because an app created with the form can never be edited as a manifest afterward.
Install the app into her developer account first, after which the endpoint URI fields for file output appear on the integration details page.
Enter the endpoint URLs in the App Center listing's support URL field, which the form-based experience uses to route file output requests.
Edit the app manifest to define the write-file action and any list-drives capability with their params.uri values, because the form does not yet support these endpoint details.

answerText: Edit the app manifest to define the write-file action and any list-drives capability with their params.uri values, because the form does not yet support these endpoint details.
explanation: The clue is 'form-based experience' plus 'File Output Cloud Storage': Docusign states that for this extension the actions and capabilities must be defined by editing the app manifest (template, name, connectionsReference and params.uri), as the form does not yet support it.
whyNotOthers: E is right because file output endpoints are defined in the manifest. The trap is A: file archive is familiar and was form-friendly, but it is legacy and new apps should use file output cloud storage. B is unnecessary, C invents an unlock, and D confuses listing metadata with endpoints.

optionExplanations.A: File archive is legacy; new apps should use file output cloud storage.
optionExplanations.B: A form-registered app has a manifest that can be edited; there is no need to delete and recreate it.
optionExplanations.C: Installation does not unlock the fields; the form simply does not support defining file output endpoints yet.
optionExplanations.D: The support URL is listing metadata shown to customers; endpoints are defined in each action's params.uri.
optionExplanations.E: Correct. For file output cloud storage, actions and capabilities must be defined by editing the app manifest; the form-based UI does not yet support them.

decode.needs: Define file output cloud storage actions/capabilities by editing the app manifest.
clues: 'registered using the form-based experience' + 'File Output Cloud Storage' -> endpoints must be set in the manifest
'switch to file archive' -> legacy, not for new apps
'two years ago in another product' -> red herring

concept.title: File output needs manifest editing
concept.line: File output cloud storage actions and capabilities are defined in the app manifest; the form cannot set them, and file archive is legacy.

stem: In the production base URI https://{site}.docusign.net/restapi, what does {site} identify?

options.text: The region chosen for the integration key during the go-live review
The Docusign site that hosts the account, such as na3, eu or au
The organization's claimed email domain in Docusign Admin
The REST API version used by the integration

answerText: The Docusign site that hosts the account, such as na3, eu or au
explanation: In production the host is {site}.docusign.net, where {site} is the site hosting the account (na3, eu, au). Development uses demo.docusign.net.
whyNotOthers: B is right. The trap is A: go-live promotes the key, but the host depends on the account's site. C and D confuse the host with an Admin setting and with the version segment.

optionExplanations.A: Integration keys are not tied to a site segment in this URI; the account's site decides it.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. The site is where the account lives; read it from base_uri in the userinfo response.
optionExplanations.C: Domains are an Admin concept and do not appear in the API host.
optionExplanations.D: The version is the /v2.1 segment after /restapi, not the host.

concept.title: Production base URI
concept.line: Production calls go to https://{site}.docusign.net/restapi, where site is the account's host site; demo uses demo.docusign.net.

stem: Garrow & Pike's HR team starts a 'Contract extension' workflow manually in Docusign with Run Workflow, dozens of times a week. In the workflow's instance list every run shows the same generic name, so coordinators cannot tell which instance belongs to which employee without opening each one. The coordinators want each new instance to be named with the employee's name and the extension date automatically, with no extra typing and no developer work. The workflow's emails use the company letterhead. Which change should the process builder make?

options.text: Set instance_name in the trigger request body to the employee's name and date, so that each run started from Run Workflow is labelled automatically
Add a Show a Confirmation Screen step whose title includes the employee's name, since the instance list displays the last confirmation title shown
Define the naming convention for the workflow's instances during Review & Publish, including the employee name and extension date, then republish
Rename the workflow itself to include the employee's name, because each instance in the list inherits the workflow's name at the time it starts
Ask coordinators to type the employee's name into a free-text participant field in Run Workflow, which the instance list shows as its name

answerText: Define the naming convention for the workflow's instances during Review & Publish, including the employee name and extension date, then republish
explanation: At Review & Publish you can define the naming convention of your workflow instances so they meet your requirements; republishing applies it to new instances started with Run Workflow.
whyNotOthers: C is right because the workflow is started manually and the team wants automatic names without developers. The trap is A: instance_name does label an instance, but only in an API trigger request, and these instances come from Run Workflow with no code. B and D invent behaviour, and E needs extra typing, which the stem rules out.

optionExplanations.A: instance_name belongs to the Maestro API trigger request; Run Workflow starts send no API body and the team has no developers.
optionExplanations.B: Confirmation screens show a message to participants; they do not name instances.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. The instance naming convention is defined at Review & Publish and applies to new instances.
optionExplanations.D: A workflow has one name; renaming it cannot give each instance a different employee name.
optionExplanations.E: Adds manual typing, which the coordinators explicitly do not want.

decode.needs: Instance naming convention set during Review & Publish
clues: started manually with Run Workflow -> no API request body
named automatically, no extra typing -> naming convention
no developer work -> workflow setting, not code
letterhead -> red herring

concept.title: Instance naming at publish
concept.line: The instance naming convention is set during Review & Publish; API triggers can also pass instance_name per run.

stem: Logging is enabled on a Connect configuration. According to the ConnectEvents reference, how many Connect log entries are kept, and for how long?

options.text: The most recent 100 entries, deleted after 15 days
The most recent 50 entries, deleted after 30 days
The most recent 100 entries, kept until an administrator deletes them
The most recent 1,000 entries, deleted after 15 days

answerText: The most recent 100 entries, deleted after 15 days
explanation: The ConnectEvents resource stores the most recent 100 Connect logs and deletes them after 15 days, so logs suit recent troubleshooting, not long-term audit.
whyNotOthers: A is right because the reference states 100 logs kept and deleted after 15 days. The trap is B: 50 is the limit of the eSignature API request log (Clear # of 50 Logs), a different feature. C ignores the 15-day deletion, and D has the wrong count.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. The most recent 100 Connect logs are stored and are deleted after 15 days.
optionExplanations.B: 50 entries belongs to the API request logging feature in eSignature settings, not to Connect logs.
optionExplanations.C: Connect logs are deleted automatically after 15 days; they are not kept indefinitely.
optionExplanations.D: The documented count is 100, not 1,000.

concept.title: Connect logs are short-lived
concept.line: Connect keeps only the latest 100 log entries for 15 days, so they help with recent troubleshooting rather than long-term records.

stem: Which Developer Console testing feature needs only a registered extension app, with no API proxy or authorization provider account in place?

options.text: Connection test
Extension tests
Functional tests
App Center preview
Workflow publish check

answerText: App Center preview
explanation: In the test prerequisites table, App Center preview requires only the registration; integration tests also need any API proxy and an account with the authorization provider, and functional tests additionally need passing connection and extension tests.
whyNotOthers: D is right. The trap is A: the connection test is the first test you run, but it needs credentials from the authorization provider. B and C have even more prerequisites, and E is not an extension app test.

optionExplanations.A: Integration tests, including the connection test, need the authorization provider account (and a proxy if required).
optionExplanations.B: Extension tests are integration tests and need authorization and any proxy.
optionExplanations.C: Functional tests also need successful connection and extension tests.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. Registration is the only prerequisite for App Center preview.
optionExplanations.E: Not a Developer Console test type for extension apps.

concept.title: Preview needs only registration
concept.line: App Center preview needs only registration; integration tests need proxy and auth provider access; functional tests need passing integration tests.

topic: Configuration-level OAuth for a second identity provider
stem: Meridian Health's Docusign account has two custom Connect configurations: one sends claims events to a platform protected by Okta, and the other sends HR events to a platform behind Microsoft Entra ID. Account-level OAuth for Connect is currently set up with Okta. The HR security team now requires that the HR listener only accept bearer tokens issued by Entra ID, and the claims team will not give up Okta. The HR configuration subscribes to four events and the claims configuration includes documents. What should the developer do?

options.text: Replace the account-level OAuth settings with the Entra ID values, because an account can only use one identity provider for all of its Connect configurations
Add Basic authentication to the HR configuration alongside the account-level OAuth, so the HR listener receives both a password and the Okta token
Move HR envelopes to envelope-level webhooks and supply the Entra ID credentials in each envelope's eventNotification, keeping Okta at the account level
Enable HMAC on the HR configuration only and have the HR listener ignore the Okta token, since a valid signature already proves the message came from Docusign
Enable configuration-level OAuth on the HR configuration with the Entra ID token URL, client ID and secret, which overrides the account-level Okta settings for it

answerText: Enable configuration-level OAuth on the HR configuration with the Entra ID token URL, client ID and secret, which overrides the account-level Okta settings for it
explanation: Configuration-level OAuth (Include Configuration Level OAuth in the UI, or enableOAuthPerConfiguration in the API) gives one configuration its own credentials, overriding the account-level OAuth, so each configuration can use a different identity provider.
whyNotOthers: E is right because per-configuration OAuth lets the HR configuration use Entra ID while the claims configuration keeps the account-level Okta setup. The trap is A: it reflects how account-level OAuth works on its own, but configuration-level OAuth removes the one-provider limit, and replacing Okta breaks the claims team. C fails because configuration-level OAuth is not available for envelope-level Connect; B fails because Basic authentication cannot be combined with OAuth; D ignores the requirement for Entra ID tokens.

optionExplanations.A: Configuration-level OAuth lets different configurations in one account use different identity providers, and replacing Okta would break the claims integration.
optionExplanations.B: Basic authentication cannot be used together with OAuth for Connect, and it would still not deliver an Entra ID token.
optionExplanations.C: Configuration-level OAuth is available for organization- and account-level configurations but not for envelope-level Connect.
optionExplanations.D: HMAC proves origin and integrity, but the HR team specifically requires Entra ID bearer tokens.
optionExplanations.E: Correct. Credentials set at configuration level override the account-level OAuth settings for that configuration only.

decode.needs: Configuration-level OAuth (enableOAuthPerConfiguration) on the HR configuration
clues: HR listener only accepts Entra ID tokens, claims keeps Okta -> two identity providers in one account
account-level OAuth already set up with Okta -> override it for one configuration only
four events, includes documents -> red herrings

concept.title: Per-configuration OAuth credentials
concept.line: A Connect configuration can carry its own OAuth credentials that override account-level OAuth, so one account can use several identity providers.

stem: Which two workflow start methods are supported for Maestro API integrations that embed workflow instances in their own web application? (Select two)

options.text: From a Link
Manually in Docusign
From an API call
From a CLM workflow
From an envelope event

answerText: From a Link; From an API call
explanation: For integrations that embed workflow instances, the supported start methods are From a Link and From an API call.
whyNotOthers: A and C are right per the embedding restrictions. The trap is B: Manually in Docusign is a real start method, but it is for internal users running Run Workflow inside Docusign. D is also a start inside Docusign, and E is not a documented embedding start method.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. From a Link is supported for embedded instances.
optionExplanations.B: Run Workflow inside Docusign is not an embedding start method.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. From an API call is supported and recommended when trigger_inputs carry starting values.
optionExplanations.D: Starting from a CLM workflow happens inside Docusign, not in your application.
optionExplanations.E: Not one of the documented start methods for embedding.

concept.title: Embedding start methods
concept.line: Embedded workflow instances support only the From a Link and From an API call start methods.

stem: An app creates an envelope with status created and immediately calls EnvelopeViews:createRecipient for the signer, who has a clientUserId. The call fails. What is the fix?

options.text: Add the returnUrl value to the integration key's redirect URIs and retry the call
Call EnvelopeViews:createSender instead, since the signer needs a draft view
Send the envelope first (status sent), then request the recipient view
Remove the clientUserId so the signer can open the draft from email

answerText: Send the envelope first (status sent), then request the recipient view
explanation: The recipient view is only available for envelopes in the sent status, which is why embedded signing requires status sent.
whyNotOthers: C is right. The trap is A: registering the returnUrl is a real requirement but not this failure. B opens the wrong view for a signer, and D abandons embedded signing.

optionExplanations.A: A new returnUrl does need to be registered, but the cause here is the envelope's draft status.
optionExplanations.B: The sender view is for the sender preparing a draft, not for a signer.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. createRecipient is only used with envelopes in sent status.
optionExplanations.D: Without clientUserId the signer is remote, and a draft envelope sends no email anyway.

concept.title: Recipient view needs a sent envelope
concept.line: EnvelopeViews:createRecipient works only for envelopes in sent status; drafts must be sent first.

stem: A single-page app will send eSignature requests directly from the browser using CORS. Which two scopes must it request in the authorization URI? (Select two)

options.text: impersonation
extended
openid
signature
cors

answerText: signature; cors
explanation: For an eSignature integration that uses CORS the authorization URI must include signature and cors.
whyNotOthers: D and E are right. The trap is A: it is usually paired with signature, but only for JWT. B and C are optional scopes with other purposes.

optionExplanations.A: impersonation is for JWT Grant, which is not used in a browser app.
optionExplanations.B: extended gives a reusable refresh token in Authorization Code Grant; it is not needed for CORS.
optionExplanations.C: openid returns an ID token; it is not required for CORS calls.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. signature is the basic scope for most eSignature endpoints.
optionExplanations.E: Correct. cors is required to send CORS requests.

concept.title: CORS scopes
concept.line: CORS integrations request signature plus cors; impersonation is only for JWT.

stem: Before a planning-permit campaign, Hatherleigh Council's administrator selects Update Hourly Limit, but an Improve App Efficiency window appears and lists three of the council's six apps. The campaign starts in three weeks. The biggest offender is the permits app, which makes most of the council's calls; the other two listed apps are small and rarely used. The council's IT team is also migrating email providers this month. What approach gives the best chance of raising the limit in time?

options.text: Fix the two small apps first because they are quickest to change, then retry Update Hourly Limit the next morning, when every score will have been recalculated
Disable the three listed apps for a week so that they stop making calls, which removes them from the window and unlocks Update Hourly Limit
Fix each listed app's API Efficiency issues, permits app first, and check daily, as scores need about 48 hours to start improving and eight days in full
Fix the permits app's recommended issues first, then retry Update Hourly Limit an hour later, because efficiency scores are recalculated at the top of every hour

answerText: Fix each listed app's API Efficiency issues, permits app first, and check daily, as scores need about 48 hours to start improving and eight days in full
explanation: Docusign advises working through each listed app's API Efficiency recommendations, highest call volume first, and checking daily; scores start improving after about 48 hours and fully reflect changes in up to eight days. The clue 'three weeks' fits that timeline.
whyNotOthers: C is right because it follows the documented order and timeline. The trap is D: it prioritises the right app but assumes hourly recalculation, which is wrong. A starts with the low-volume apps, which slows progress, and B is not a documented fix and could leave too little call history for analysis.

optionExplanations.A: Docusign recommends fixing the highest-volume apps first, and scores do not fully update overnight.
optionExplanations.B: Switching apps off is not a documented fix and may leave too little call history for analysis.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. Fix each app's recommendations, highest volume first; allow about 48 hours to start and up to eight days.
optionExplanations.D: Scores are not recalculated hourly; improvement starts after about 48 hours.

decode.needs: Unlock a limit increase by fixing flagged apps' efficiency issues, highest volume first, and allowing days for scores.
clues: Improve App Efficiency window -> efficiency issues block the limit change
permits app makes most calls -> fix highest volume first
three weeks -> enough for scores to update (48 hours to start, up to 8 days)
email migration -> red herring

concept.title: Efficiency before limit increase
concept.line: Flagged apps must be fixed before the limit rises; scores improve after about 48 hours and fully within eight days.

stem: Before calling EnvelopeRecipientTabs:update to change a recipient's existing fields, what must the app obtain?

options.text: The documentId of each document, from EnvelopeDocuments:list
A lock token from EnvelopeLocks:create for every tab update
The anchorString used when the tab was created
The tabId of each tab to change, from EnvelopeRecipientTabs:list

answerText: The tabId of each tab to change, from EnvelopeRecipientTabs:list
explanation: The course steps are: list the recipient's tabs, store the tabId of each tab to update, then PUT the entire tab objects with the changes.
whyNotOthers: D is right. The trap is B: locking is used when editing an in-process envelope, but the update itself is keyed by tabId. A and C identify other things.

optionExplanations.A: documentId identifies documents; tabs are updated by tabId.
optionExplanations.B: Locks are optional while editing; they are not the input the update needs.
optionExplanations.C: Existing tabs are identified by tabId, not anchors.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. List the recipient's tabs, store each tabId, then PUT the full tab objects with changes.

concept.title: Updating tabs needs tabId
concept.line: Call EnvelopeRecipientTabs:list for tabIds, then update with the full tab objects.

topic: Permissions needed to create a Connect configuration
stem: Juniper Clinics' onboarding script uses JWT Grant to impersonate a service user, svc-esign, which has sender permissions only. When the script calls POST /v2.1/accounts/{accountId}/connect to create its account-level configuration in production, the call fails with an authorization error. The same request body worked in the demo environment using the developer's own administrator user, and Connect is enabled on the production account. What should the team change?

options.text: Have the configuration created by an account administrator, for example by granting svc-esign administrator rights, because Connect endpoints require an account administrator
Request the extended scope in the JWT assertion, because creating Connect configurations needs a long-lived refresh token
Set allowEnvelopePublish to true in the body, because a configuration that is not enabled is rejected for non-administrator users
Switch the script from JWT Grant to Authorization Code Grant, because Connect endpoints do not accept tokens obtained by impersonation
Create the configuration through the Organization Admin API instead, because account-level configurations cannot be created through the eSignature REST API

answerText: Have the configuration created by an account administrator, for example by granting svc-esign administrator rights, because Connect endpoints require an account administrator
explanation: The Connect API reference says that to call any Connect endpoint you must be an account administrator, and Connect must be enabled on the account; the stem confirms Connect is enabled, so the missing piece is administrator rights.
whyNotOthers: A is right because Connect configuration calls require an account administrator. The trap is C: without allowEnvelopePublish the configuration is created disabled, but it is still created; that does not cause an authorization error. B misuses the extended scope (Authorization Code Grant only), D is false because JWT tokens work with administrator rights, and E is false because account-level configurations are created with ConnectConfigurations:create.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. Connect endpoints require an account administrator, and Connect must be enabled on the account, which the stem confirms.
optionExplanations.B: The extended scope gives a reusable refresh token in Authorization Code Grant; it has nothing to do with Connect permissions.
optionExplanations.C: Omitting allowEnvelopePublish creates a disabled configuration; it does not cause an authorization failure.
optionExplanations.D: JWT impersonation works if the impersonated user is an administrator; the grant type is not the problem.
optionExplanations.E: Account-level configurations are created with the eSignature REST API (ConnectConfigurations:create).

decode.needs: The impersonated user must be an account administrator
clues: sender permissions only -> not an administrator
worked in demo with the developer's administrator user -> same body, different permissions
Connect is enabled on the production account -> rules out the other prerequisite

concept.title: Connect APIs need an admin
concept.line: Calling Connect endpoints requires an account administrator, and Connect must be enabled on the account.

topic: Identifying the trigger in a JSON SIM message
stem: A team migrating to JSON SIM used to start workflows from "status": "sent". Which JSON SIM element should the listener read instead to know what triggered the message?

options.text: data.envelopeSummary.status
configurationId
event
uri
retryCount

answerText: event
explanation: Every JSON SIM message has an event element (for example envelope-sent) that identifies what generated the message, and Docusign says workflows that checked status should use it instead.
whyNotOthers: C is right because the event element names the trigger. The trap is A: an envelope summary can include status, but it is optional and describes the envelope rather than the triggering event. B identifies the configuration, D is the envelope's REST path, and E counts delivery retries.

optionExplanations.A: The envelope summary is optional and describes the envelope state, not the event that generated the message.
optionExplanations.B: configurationId identifies the Connect configuration that sent the message.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. The event element, such as envelope-sent, identifies the triggering event.
optionExplanations.D: uri is the REST path of the envelope, not the trigger.
optionExplanations.E: retryCount shows how many delivery retries occurred.

concept.title: Read the event element
concept.line: In JSON SIM, the event element names what triggered the message; use it instead of checking envelope status.

topic: Regions in the demo App Center
stem: A public extension app is Live with publicationRegions limited to the European Union. Who can install it from the demo App Center?

options.text: Only demo accounts whose region is the European Union
Only the developer account that registered the app
Nobody, because Live apps appear only in the production App Center
Only demo accounts added to an account allow-list by ID
Users of any demo account, regardless of region

answerText: Users of any demo account, regardless of region
explanation: Globalization guidance: region restrictions apply only in the production App Center. In the demo App Center, published extension apps are available to all users, regardless of region.
whyNotOthers: E is right. The trap is A: it applies the EU restriction everywhere, but the restriction is enforced only in production. B describes a Draft, C is false, and D describes private sharing.

optionExplanations.A: Region restrictions are enforced only on the production App Center.
optionExplanations.B: That is how an unpublished Draft behaves, not a Live public app.
optionExplanations.C: Published apps are also listed in the demo App Center.
optionExplanations.D: Account lists apply to private distribution, not public apps.
optionExplanations.E: Correct. Region restrictions apply only in the production App Center; in demo, published apps are available to all users.

concept.title: Regions enforced only in production
concept.line: publicationRegions limits installs only in the production App Center; the demo App Center shows published apps to all regions.

topic: CORS: endpoints without an account ID
stem: Halvard's internal single-page admin dashboard uses CORS and Public Authorization Code Grant. Its envelope list, template list and envelope status widgets all work from the browser. A new widget that calls the Diagnostics category to show the API request log fails in the browser with a CORS error, although the same call works from Postman with the same token. No back end exists yet. The dashboard uses a dark theme. What explains the failure?

options.text: Diagnostics endpoints have no account ID in the path, and CORS covers only endpoints that do, so this call needs a back-end proxy
GET is not among the integration key's allowed HTTP methods, so the browser blocks the preflight for the new widget
The dashboard's origin must be added again in Apps and Keys for each new API category that it calls
The access token lacks the cors scope, which Postman does not need but the browser widget does

answerText: Diagnostics endpoints have no account ID in the path, and CORS covers only endpoints that do, so this call needs a back-end proxy
explanation: CORS works with all eSignature endpoints that include the account ID in the path; Diagnostics, Notary and BillingPlans do not and therefore do not support CORS. Postman is not a browser, so CORS does not apply there.
whyNotOthers: A is right. The trap is B: allowed methods are a real CORS setting, but the other GET widgets work. C misplaces origin settings, and D is ruled out by the working widgets.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. Docusign lists the Diagnostics category among the resources without an account ID that do not support CORS.
optionExplanations.B: The other widgets also read data and work, so the method list is not the difference.
optionExplanations.C: Allowed origins apply to the app, not per API category.
optionExplanations.D: The token works for other CORS calls from the same browser app, so the scope is present.

decode.needs: Endpoints without accountId (e.g. Diagnostics) do not support CORS
clues: other widgets work from the browser -> app CORS setup is fine
works from Postman -> only a browser CORS restriction
dark theme -> red herring

concept.title: CORS endpoint coverage
concept.line: eSignature CORS covers endpoints with an account ID in the path; Diagnostics, Notary and BillingPlans need a server-side call.

stem: According to the eSignature brand settings, which two items can be set for the signing view but are not listed for the sending view? (Select two)

options.text: A custom logo
A redirect URL for all branded envelopes
The colors of the UI
Footer links
A default language and additional signer languages

answerText: A redirect URL for all branded envelopes; A default language and additional signer languages
explanation: Signing branding adds a redirect URL, header links, languages and a resource file on top of the colors, logo and footer links that sending also has.
whyNotOthers: B and E are right because they appear only in the signing view settings. The trap is D: footer links feel signing-specific, but they can be set for the sending view too. A and C apply to both views.

optionExplanations.A: Logos can be set for both the sending and signing views.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. A redirect URL for branded envelopes is a signing setting.
optionExplanations.C: UI colors can be set for both views.
optionExplanations.D: Footer links can be set for the sending view as well.
optionExplanations.E: Correct. Default and additional languages are signing settings.

concept.title: Signing versus sending branding
concept.line: Both views take colors, logo and footer links; signing adds redirect URL, header links, languages and resource files.

topic: Reading a paused-configuration message in the dashboard
stem: On Monday morning, Osprey Realty's support analyst sees Connect dashboard entries from the weekend that read "This event was skipped due to the configuration being paused". The listener's own monitoring shows it was healthy all weekend. A colleague confirms that she paused the account-level configuration during Friday evening maintenance and forgot to unpause it. The configuration uses JSON SIM and includes the certificate of completion. What does the message mean, and what should the analyst do?

options.text: The listener rejected those deliveries with an error, so the analyst should fix the listener and then republish the events from the failure log
The events were discarded because the configuration was paused, so the analyst must send the envelopes again with the historical publish endpoint
Deliveries due while the configuration was paused were skipped but kept, so unpausing lets them continue at their next scheduled retry
The configuration was disabled after being paused, so the analyst must recreate it with allowEnvelopePublish set to true and republish everything
The events were filtered out because they were not in the configuration's events list, so the analyst should add those events to the configuration

answerText: Deliveries due while the configuration was paused were skipped but kept, so unpausing lets them continue at their next scheduled retry
explanation: The dashboard message marks events skipped because the configuration was paused; skipped events are not lost, and after unpausing they resume at the next scheduled retry. A weekend pause is far from the 15-day window and the 14-day auto-disable.
whyNotOthers: C is right because paused events are skipped but kept, and unpausing resumes them on schedule. The trap is B: the word skipped suggests loss, but skipped events are not discarded. A contradicts the healthy listener, D applies only after 14 consecutive paused days, and E describes a different cause than the one the message states.

optionExplanations.A: The message names the pause as the cause, and the listener was healthy all weekend.
optionExplanations.B: Skipped events are not discarded; they continue at the next scheduled retry after unpausing.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. Pausing skips scheduled deliveries without losing them; once unpaused, processing resumes at the next scheduled retry.
optionExplanations.D: Automatic disabling happens only after 14 consecutive paused days, not after a weekend.
optionExplanations.E: Unsubscribed events are never generated; the message clearly says they were skipped because of the pause.

decode.needs: Unpause the configuration; skipped events resume on their retry schedule
clues: This event was skipped due to the configuration being paused -> paused, not failed
listener healthy all weekend -> not a listener error
weekend only -> well under the 14-day auto-disable and the 15-day window
includes the certificate of completion -> red herring

concept.title: Skipped while paused is not lost
concept.line: Events skipped while a configuration is paused stay in their retry cycle and resume at the next scheduled retry after unpausing.

topic: Data IO property missing from the write step
stem: Kestrel Housing's Data IO app exposes a Tenant concept to Maestro. Workflow designers can pick Tenant and its MoveInDate property in a read step, but MoveInDate never appears in the write step, so the date captured in the move-in web form cannot be sent back to the housing management system. MoveInDate is a DateTime in the Concerto model, and the housing system does allow the field to be changed. The housing system is hosted by a third-party provider in the same region. What should the developer change?

options.text: Add the IsRequiredForVerifyingType decorator to the MoveInDate property so that Maestro treats it as a required input field and offers it in the write step.
Change MoveInDate to a String property, because Data IO cannot send DateTime values and only read steps support dates.
Add an UpdateRecord action for Tenant to the manifest, because Patch Record only changes properties already populated on the record.
Add a term decorator with a display name to MoveInDate, because write steps hide every property that lacks a display name.
Change the Get Type Definitions response so MoveInDate's CRUD annotation marks it as creatable and updateable, since CRUD settings decide which steps show a field.

answerText: Change the Get Type Definitions response so MoveInDate's CRUD annotation marks it as creatable and updateable, since CRUD settings decide which steps show a field.
explanation: The clue is that the property shows in the read step but not in the write step: in the Data IO data model, CRUD operations determine which workflow steps objects and fields appear in (readable in read steps, updateable or creatable in write steps).
whyNotOthers: E is right because write-step visibility follows the creatable/updateable setting. The trap is A: it is a real Concerto decorator, but it belongs to connected fields verification. B is false about dates, C names a non-existent action, and D confuses display names with step visibility. The hosting provider is a red herring.

optionExplanations.A: IsRequiredForVerifyingType is a connected fields decorator for verification, not a Data IO write control.
optionExplanations.B: Data IO supports date-time values; Docusign sends them in ISO 8601 UTC in Create Record, Patch Record and Search Records.
optionExplanations.C: There is no UpdateRecord action; Data IO uses Create Record and Patch Record for writes.
optionExplanations.D: Term decorators set display names; they do not control whether a property appears in write steps.
optionExplanations.E: Correct. For Data IO, CRUD operations on concepts and properties decide where they appear: readable in read steps, creatable or updateable in write steps.

decode.needs: Mark the Data IO property as creatable/updateable in its Concerto definition so it appears in write steps.
clues: 'appears in read step but not write step' -> CRUD settings in the type definition
'housing system allows the field to be changed' -> the model, not the back-end, is the blocker
'hosted by a third-party provider' -> red herring

concept.title: CRUD settings control step visibility
concept.line: In Data IO type definitions, readable properties appear in read steps; creatable or updateable properties appear in write steps.

stem: Fairholm Bank is building a browser-based contract lookup for its relationship managers. Each manager must sign in with their own Docusign credentials so the lookup acts as that person, never through a shared service account. The lookup reads agreements, parties and provisions from Agreement Manager and also shows envelope status from eSignature. The bank's identity team already runs single sign-on for Docusign, and the pilot will use the developer environment. Which two choices are correct? (Select two)

options.text: Use JWT Grant with an impersonated service user, because the Agreement Manager API accepts only JWT access tokens.
Use Authorization Code Grant so each manager signs in and consents, as Agreement Manager accepts eSignature tokens.
Request a separate Agreement Manager API key, because Agreement Manager calls are authorized apart from eSignature OAuth.
Request only the signature scope, because a token with that scope already covers reads from Agreement Manager as well.
Request adm_store_unified_repo_read alongside signature, because reading agreements needs a Navigator scope on the token.

answerText: Use Authorization Code Grant so each manager signs in and consents, as Agreement Manager accepts eSignature tokens.; Request adm_store_unified_repo_read alongside signature, because reading agreements needs a Navigator scope on the token.
explanation: Agreement Manager uses the same OAuth access tokens as eSignature (Authorization Code, Implicit or JWT Grant), but the token must include a Navigator scope such as adm_store_unified_repo_read. 'Sign in with their own credentials' points to Authorization Code Grant.
whyNotOthers: B and E are right: a per-user grant plus the Navigator read scope on one token. The trap is D: the shared token idea is correct, but the signature scope alone does not authorize Agreement Manager. A contradicts both the per-user rule and the docs (all three grant types work), and C invents a separate key scheme.

optionExplanations.A: All three grant types are accepted, and an impersonated service user breaks the 'never a shared service account' rule.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. Authorization Code Grant has each manager sign in, and the resulting token works for Agreement Manager as well as eSignature.
optionExplanations.C: There is no separate API key; Agreement Manager uses the same OAuth access tokens as eSignature.
optionExplanations.D: The signature scope does not include Agreement Manager; a Navigator scope must be requested too.
optionExplanations.E: Correct. GetAgreementsList and GetAgreement require adm_store_unified_repo_read on the access token.

decode.needs: Authorization Code Grant per user, with signature plus adm_store_unified_repo_read scopes.
clues: sign in with their own credentials, never a shared service account -> Authorization Code Grant, not JWT impersonation
reads agreements, parties and provisions -> adm_store_unified_repo_read scope
also shows envelope status -> the same token also carries the signature scope
single sign-on, developer environment -> red herrings

concept.title: Same token, extra Navigator scope
concept.line: Agreement Manager accepts eSignature OAuth tokens from any grant type, but the token must carry a Navigator scope such as adm_store_unified_repo_read.

stem: In Agreement Manager, how does a reviewer recognize a value that AI populated and no user has confirmed yet?

options.text: A yellow warning triangle next to the field name
The value is shown in italics until approved
A Needs review banner across the agreement
A purple star to the left of the value

answerText: A purple star to the left of the value
explanation: Metadata populated by AI and not yet confirmed by a user is marked with a purple star to the left of its value; reviewing or updating the field removes the flag.
whyNotOthers: D is right per the Navigator concepts documentation. The trap is C: a review banner sounds plausible for a review process, but the marker is per value. A and B describe markers that do not exist.

optionExplanations.A: No warning triangle is used for AI-populated values.
optionExplanations.B: Values are not shown in italics to indicate AI origin.
optionExplanations.C: The flag is per value, not a banner across the agreement.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. A purple star marks AI-populated values that no user has confirmed; confirming removes it.

concept.title: Purple star flags AI values
concept.line: AI-populated values not yet confirmed by a user carry a purple star; reviewing or updating the value removes the flag.

stem: A Confidential Authorization Code Grant app builds its /oauth/auth URL with response_type=code and scope. Which two other query parameters are required? (Select two)

options.text: client_id
state
code_challenge
redirect_uri
login_hint

answerText: client_id; redirect_uri
explanation: The authorization request requires response_type, scope, client_id (the integration key) and redirect_uri.
whyNotOthers: A and D are right. The trap is B: state is strongly recommended to prevent CSRF, but it is not one of the required parameters. C is required only for Public Auth Code Grant (optional with Confidential), and E is an optional convenience.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. client_id carries the integration key.
optionExplanations.B: Recommended against CSRF, but optional.
optionExplanations.C: Required for Public Auth Code Grant; optional PKCE for Confidential.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. redirect_uri must match a URI registered on the integration key.
optionExplanations.E: login_hint is optional.

concept.title: Authorization URL parameters
concept.line: /oauth/auth needs response_type, scope, client_id and redirect_uri; state is recommended, code_challenge required only for Public.

stem: An administrator's upload of a 450 KB PNG as a brand's primary logo is rejected. What is the cause?

options.text: PNG is not a supported logo format
The file exceeds the 300 KB logo size limit
Primary logos must first be set as the email logo
Logos larger than 296 x 76 pixels are rejected

answerText: The file exceeds the 300 KB logo size limit
explanation: Brand logos accept JPG, GIF and PNG up to 300 KB. The clue is the 450 KB size.
whyNotOthers: B is right because 450 KB is over the 300 KB maximum. The trap is D: 296 x 76 pixels is only the recommended size, and larger images are resized, not rejected. A is false because PNG is supported, and C invents an ordering rule.

optionExplanations.A: JPG, GIF and PNG are all supported.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. The maximum logo file size is 300 KB.
optionExplanations.C: Primary, secondary and email logos are set independently.
optionExplanations.D: 296 x 76 is recommended; larger images are resized.

concept.title: Brand logo limits
concept.line: Brand logos (primary, secondary, email) accept JPG, GIF or PNG up to 300 KB; larger dimensions are resized.

stem: According to Docusign's webhook listener guidance, how quickly should a listener respond to each Connect request?

options.text: Within 500 milliseconds
Within 2 seconds
Within 30 seconds
Within 5 seconds

answerText: Within 5 seconds
explanation: Docusign's listener guidance says to respond to each request from Docusign within five seconds, which is why the listener should queue the message and return 200 before processing it.
whyNotOthers: D is right because the documented guidance is five seconds. The trap is C: 30 seconds sounds like a generous HTTP timeout, but it is far longer than the guidance. A and B are stricter values that are not in the guidance.

optionExplanations.A: 500 milliseconds is not the documented figure.
optionExplanations.B: Two seconds is not the documented figure.
optionExplanations.C: 30 seconds is much longer than the guidance allows.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. Respond to each request within five seconds, ideally by queueing the message and returning 200 at once.

concept.title: Answer Connect within five seconds
concept.line: A listener should respond to each Connect request within five seconds, so it should queue the message and process it later.

topic: Focused view after web form submission
stem: Granite Peak Credit Union embeds a template-based membership web form in its online banking app with Docusign JS. Product owners want members to sign the generated agreement right after submitting, inside the same page, in a minimal signing interface that shows only the agreement and a navigation bar. During testing, members are instead emailed a link to start signing, and the minimal interface never appears. useFocusedViewForSigning is left at its default. What should be changed?

options.text: Set useFocusedViewForSigning to true explicitly, because its default value of false falls back to the email-initiated signing flow.
Create the instances as remote instances with sendOption now, so that the generated agreement opens in focused view in the banking app.
Call EnvelopeViews:createRecipient for the generated envelope with a returnUrl, which replaces the email with an embedded focused view.
Disable the configuration's Initiate signing session from email setting, because focused view is not available while that setting is on.

answerText: Disable the configuration's Initiate signing session from email setting, because focused view is not available while that setting is on.
explanation: Focused view for the generated envelope is not available when the configuration's Initiate signing session from email setting is enabled. The clue is 'members are instead emailed a link to start signing'.
whyNotOthers: D is right. The trap is A: useFocusedViewForSigning already defaults to true, so setting it changes nothing. B moves delivery to email entirely, and C is the eSignature embedded signing call, not the web form flow.

optionExplanations.A: useFocusedViewForSigning defaults to true; the email setting is what blocks focused view.
optionExplanations.B: Remote instances are delivered by email, the opposite of the goal.
optionExplanations.C: The web form flow presents the envelope through Docusign JS; the email setting is the blocker.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. Turn off Initiate signing session from email to allow focused view.

decode.needs: In-page signing after submission requires the email-initiated signing setting to be off.
clues: 'inside the same page' -> embedded signing of the generated envelope
'only the agreement and a navigation bar' -> focused view
'emailed a link to start signing' -> Initiate signing session from email is on

concept.title: Web form focused view
concept.line: Docusign JS shows the generated envelope in focused view only when Initiate signing session from email is disabled.

stem: In Workflow Builder, which step category contains the Send an Email step and the branching rule steps?

options.text: Docusign steps
Apps steps
Agreement Desk steps
Writeback steps
Utility steps

answerText: Utility steps
explanation: Utility steps cover notification actions such as sending an email and workflow control actions such as branch rules.
whyNotOthers: E is right per the course's step categories. The trap is A: Docusign steps are built-in too, but they are for features such as ID Verification, Web Forms and eSignature. B and D are for third-party extension apps, and C appears only when Agreement Desk is enabled.

optionExplanations.A: Docusign steps cover features such as Web Forms, ID Verification and eSignature.
optionExplanations.B: Apps steps run third-party extension apps.
optionExplanations.C: Only available when Agreement Desk is enabled; not the home of email or branching.
optionExplanations.D: Writeback is a subtype of Apps steps that updates external systems.
optionExplanations.E: Correct. Utility steps include Send an Email, Set Up Invite, Show a Confirmation Screen and branching steps.

concept.title: Three step categories
concept.line: Docusign steps (features), Utility steps (email, invites, confirmation, branching), Apps steps (third-party extensions).

stem: Sennet Telecom's connected fields app verifies business customers against its CRM. The data model's customer object requires account number and postcode for verification and also offers an optional 'preferred contact' field. A sales assistant, wanting a shorter form, built an envelope with only the preferred contact field on the document. When the signer types a value, verification fails every time, even for valid customers. The CRM logs show no errors. What explains this and what is the fix?

options.text: Optional connected fields are verified only after signing completes; mark the field Must verify to sign so that it is checked during signing.
The CRM ignores optional fields; move the preferred contact property into the required fields of the data model and reconnect the app.
An optional connected field without the required fields of its group fails verification; place the account number and postcode fields too.
The field was placed by a sales assistant without admin rights; have an administrator place the field so that verification can run.

answerText: An optional connected field without the required fields of its group fails verification; place the account number and postcode fields too.
explanation: If an optional connected field is added without the required connected fields, verification fails when the optional field is filled. The clue is 'only the preferred contact field on the document'.
whyNotOthers: C is right because verification needs the required fields of the group. The trap is B: changing the data model is unnecessary, since the fields simply need to be placed together. A misdescribes when verification runs, and D invents a permission rule.

optionExplanations.A: Verification runs during signing; Must verify to sign does not fix missing required fields.
optionExplanations.B: The model is fine; the envelope is missing the required fields of the group.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. Required fields of the group must be on the document for verification to succeed.
optionExplanations.D: Verification does not depend on the preparer's admin rights.

decode.needs: Place the whole required field group along with the optional connected field.
clues: 'requires account number and postcode' -> required fields of the group
'only the preferred contact field' -> required fields missing
'CRM logs show no errors' -> the problem is on the envelope side

concept.title: Connected field groups
concept.line: Connected fields are verified as a group; an optional field without the group's required fields fails verification.

stem: Halvorsen Bank's connected fields app verifies a payee's account details while customers sign transfer authorizations. The operations team wants its case management system to record, for every envelope, whether verification succeeded, without polling Docusign and without staff reading certificates. The bank already runs an account-level Connect listener that receives envelope-completed events in the legacy XML format for its archive. What should the developer set up?

options.text: Enable the extension-executed event on the current XML listener configuration so that verification results arrive in the archive's existing messages.
Read each envelope's history with the eSignature API after every completed event and parse the verification entries into the case system.
Have the extension app call the case management system directly after each verification by adding an action to the manifest's connections object.
Create a Connect configuration that uses the JSON SIM event model and subscribes to the extension-executed event, and post results to the case system.

answerText: Create a Connect configuration that uses the JSON SIM event model and subscribes to the extension-executed event, and post results to the case system.
explanation: Verification results are delivered by the Connect extension-executed event, which is supported only with the JSON SIM event model. The clues are 'without polling' and 'legacy XML format'.
whyNotOthers: D is right because only a JSON SIM configuration can receive extension-executed events. The trap is A: the existing listener uses XML, which does not support this event. B is polling-style extra calls, and C misuses the manifest connections object, which holds authentication to the external system.

optionExplanations.A: extension-executed is supported only with JSON SIM, not legacy XML.
optionExplanations.B: Extra API calls per envelope; Connect can push the result directly.
optionExplanations.C: The connections object defines authentication; it is not a notification mechanism.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. A JSON SIM Connect configuration can subscribe to extension-executed.

decode.needs: Push connected fields verification results to a back-office system.
clues: 'without polling Docusign' -> Connect
'legacy XML format' -> cannot carry extension-executed
'whether verification succeeded' -> extension-executed event

concept.title: Connected fields results
concept.line: Verification results arrive through the Connect extension-executed event (JSON SIM only) and appear in envelope history and the certificate.

stem: What does BulkSend:getBulkSendBatchStatus return for a batch?

options.text: Counts of sent, queued and failed envelopes, plus any error messages
The canBeSent flag showing whether the list and envelope are compatible
The listId and the bulk copies stored in the list
The signed documents of every envelope in the batch

answerText: Counts of sent, queued and failed envelopes, plus any error messages
explanation: Checking a bulk send with the batchId returns counts of sent, queued and failed envelopes, as well as error messages.
whyNotOthers: A is right. The trap is B: it is the response of the optional test step, not the status check. C and D belong to other calls.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. The batch status reports sent, queued and failed counts and errors.
optionExplanations.B: canBeSent comes from createBulkSendTestRequest.
optionExplanations.C: These come from the bulk send list endpoints.
optionExplanations.D: Documents are downloaded per envelope.

concept.title: Bulk send return values
concept.line: List returns listId; test returns canBeSent; send returns batchId; batch status returns sent, queued and failed counts.

stem: Harrow Utilities sends service-transfer agreements to new tenants. The legal team wants a second factor beyond the email link, delivered by Docusign itself, and tenants have mobile phones but many are recent arrivals without US credit history. Tenants should be able to pick a voice call or a text message. The tenant platform builds envelopes with eSignature REST API v2.1 in Java. How should the developer configure each tenant?

options.text: Set idCheckConfigurationName to ID Check on the signer, so that the tenant answers questions and then receives a code on the phone number on file.
Add identityVerification to the signer with the Phone Authentication workflowId from IdentityVerifications:list and supply the tenant's phone number.
Generate a random accessCode for the signer and have the tenant platform text it to the tenant's mobile phone before the envelope is sent.
Add identityVerification to the signer with the ID Verification workflowId from IdentityVerifications:list, so the tenant scans a photo ID by phone.

answerText: Add identityVerification to the signer with the Phone Authentication workflowId from IdentityVerifications:list and supply the tenant's phone number.
explanation: Phone authentication sends a code by call or text, and recipients choose which; it is set with identityVerification and the Phone Authentication workflowId. The clues are 'delivered by Docusign itself' and 'pick a voice call or a text message'.
whyNotOthers: B is right because phone authentication matches every requirement. The trap is C: the code would be texted by the tenant platform, not Docusign. A is knowledge-based authentication, which relies on US public records, and D asks for a photo ID, which is more than a phone second factor.

optionExplanations.A: ID Check is KBA, which relies on US public records these tenants may lack.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. Phone authentication with its workflowId lets the tenant choose call or SMS.
optionExplanations.C: The tenant platform, not Docusign, would deliver the code.
optionExplanations.D: ID Verification requires a government ID, not a code by call or text.

decode.needs: A Docusign-delivered code by call or SMS: phone authentication via identityVerification.
clues: 'delivered by Docusign itself' -> not an access code from your own system
'without US credit history' -> KBA is unsuitable
'voice call or a text message' -> phone authentication
'in Java' -> red herring

concept.title: Phone authentication setup
concept.line: Phone authentication uses identityVerification with the Phone Authentication workflowId; recipients choose call or SMS.

stem: Thornbury Group's account administrator collects five automation requests from business units that want something to happen after agreements are signed. IT will build a listener only for requests that a pre-built Connect solution cannot handle. Which two requests need a custom Connect configuration with Thornbury's own listener? (Select two)

options.text: Copy every completed lease into the property team's Box folder so the agents can find it without logging in to Docusign
Start provisioning the customer's broadband line in the in-house order system as soon as the service contract is completed
Keep the Docusign for Salesforce app updated with envelope status so sales reps see progress on their opportunities
Store each signed document in the group's homegrown records management system, which exposes its own REST API
Tell the eOriginal platform that a completed loan transaction is ready to be vaulted as a transferable record

answerText: Start provisioning the customer's broadband line in the in-house order system as soon as the service contract is completed; Store each signed document in the group's homegrown records management system, which exposes its own REST API
explanation: Docusign recommends custom configurations for internal systems, such as triggering provisioning after completion or storing documents in a custom storage system; Box, Salesforce and eOriginal have pre-built Connect solutions.
whyNotOthers: B and D are right because both target in-house systems with no pre-built integration. The trap is E: notifying an external platform after completion sounds like custom integration work, but Connect for eOriginal is a pre-built solution that does exactly this. A uses the pre-built Box integration, and C uses the pre-built Salesforce integration.

optionExplanations.A: Connect for Box is a pre-built solution that pushes completed documents to a Box folder.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. Starting provisioning in an internal system after completion is a typical custom Connect use case.
optionExplanations.C: Connect for Salesforce is pre-built and pushes data updates to the Docusign for Salesforce app.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. Storing signed documents in an organization's own storage system calls for a custom configuration.
optionExplanations.E: Connect for eOriginal is pre-built and informs eOriginal that a transaction to be vaulted is complete.

decode.needs: Custom configurations for in-house targets; pre-built for Box, Salesforce and eOriginal
clues: in-house order system, homegrown records system -> custom listener
Box folder, Docusign for Salesforce, eOriginal vaulting -> pre-built solutions exist
IT builds a listener only when nothing pre-built fits -> separate the two groups

concept.title: Custom versus pre-built Connect
concept.line: Use pre-built Connect for Box, OneDrive, Salesforce and eOriginal; use custom configurations for internal systems and follow-on business actions.

stem: A regulator asks Ashby Lettings to hand over proof of how each tenant's identity was verified for a disputed tenancy. The compliance lead wants a file the regulator can check was produced by Docusign and not altered by the company afterwards; a spreadsheet built from the raw data would not satisfy this. Evidence storage already retains the needed data, and the developer has a working resource token flow. What should the integration request?

options.text: Call Events:list in json format with include_media set to true, then save the response with a SHA-256 hash recorded in the company's database.
Download the envelope's combined PDF with the certificate of completion, which embeds the full ID Evidence event log and the ID images.
Call Events:list in pdf format, because ID Evidence applies a digital signature to the PDF to guarantee the origin and integrity of the data.
Call the media endpoint for each event and convert the images to PDF pages signed with the company's own document-signing certificate.

answerText: Call Events:list in pdf format, because ID Evidence applies a digital signature to the PDF to guarantee the origin and integrity of the data.
explanation: Events:list supports json and pdf formats; with pdf, ID Evidence digitally signs the file to guarantee origin and integrity. The clue is 'produced by Docusign and not altered by the company'.
whyNotOthers: C is right because only the Docusign-signed PDF proves origin and integrity. The trap is A: a hash stored by the company does not prove Docusign produced the data. B overstates the certificate, which does not embed the ID Evidence log and images, and D signs with the company's own certificate.

optionExplanations.A: A company-held hash cannot prove the data came from Docusign unaltered.
optionExplanations.B: The certificate of completion does not contain the ID Evidence event log and images.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. The pdf format is digitally signed by ID Evidence.
optionExplanations.D: A company signature proves only that the company signed it, not Docusign origin.

decode.needs: A Docusign-signed export of ID evidence events.
clues: 'produced by Docusign and not altered' -> digitally signed by Docusign
'spreadsheet ... would not satisfy' -> raw JSON is not enough
'disputed tenancy' -> red herring

concept.title: Signed ID Evidence export
concept.line: Request ID Evidence events in pdf format to get a file digitally signed for origin and integrity.

stem: During a migration, Lindqvist Retail imported contracts from two regional file shares, and some supplier contracts existed on both shares, so they now appear twice in Agreement Manager. The finance ERP shows doubled contract values for those suppliers. Compliance requires that a person confirms each duplicate before anything is removed, and one copy of every contract must stay in the repository. The migration vendor charges per file imported. Which two steps fit? (Select two)

options.text: Delete automatically every record whose party and execution date match another record, because such a match proves it is a duplicate.
Merge each pair with a PUT on the agreement that combines both records into one, then resync the ERP from the merged record.
Find candidate pairs with GetAgreementsList filtered on parties.name_in_agreement and provisions.execution_date for review.
Delete both records of each pair and import the contract once more, so that a single clean record remains in the repository.
After the reviewer confirms a pair, call DeleteAgreement on the duplicate's agreementId only, and drop that record from the ERP.

answerText: Find candidate pairs with GetAgreementsList filtered on parties.name_in_agreement and provisions.execution_date for review.; After the reviewer confirms a pair, call DeleteAgreement on the duplicate's agreementId only, and drop that record from the ERP.
explanation: GetAgreementsList filters on party name and execution date to surface likely pairs, and DeleteAgreement (DELETE .../agreements/{agreementId}) removes the confirmed copy. The clue 'a person confirms each duplicate before anything is removed' requires review between the two steps.
whyNotOthers: C and E are right: detect with filtered list calls, then delete only the confirmed duplicate. The trap is A: matching on party and date is the right detection idea, but deleting without review breaks the compliance rule. B invents an update operation, and D deletes the original and pays for a needless re-import.

optionExplanations.A: Deleting without human confirmation violates the compliance rule, and two genuine contracts can share a party and date.
optionExplanations.B: The API has no update or merge operation; only list, get, delete and create summary exist.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. Party and execution_date filters surface likely duplicate pairs for a reviewer.
optionExplanations.D: This removes the copy that must stay and costs another import fee for no benefit.
optionExplanations.E: Correct. DeleteAgreement removes only the confirmed duplicate, leaving one copy in the repository.

decode.needs: List-based detection, human confirmation, then DeleteAgreement on the confirmed duplicate.
clues: appear twice after import from two shares -> duplicate agreement records
a person confirms before anything is removed -> review step before DeleteAgreement
one copy must stay -> delete only the duplicate's agreementId
vendor charges per file -> red herring that also argues against re-importing

concept.title: Review, then DeleteAgreement duplicates
concept.line: Detect duplicate imports with filtered list calls, have a person confirm, then remove only the duplicate with DeleteAgreement.

stem: In a Workflows:triggerWorkflow request body, what is instance_name?

options.text: A user-defined label for tracking that workflow run
The name of the workflow definition to be started
The participant role that receives the first step
A starting variable declared in the trigger_input_schema
The display name of the returned workflow instance URL

answerText: A user-defined label for tracking that workflow run
explanation: The trigger request requires an instance_name, a user-defined label for tracking the workflow run, plus input data matching the trigger_input_schema.
whyNotOthers: A is right per the TriggerWorkflow reference. The trap is D: instance_name sits next to trigger_inputs in the body, but the starting variables go in trigger_inputs, not instance_name. B is identified by workflowId in the path, C is a participant setting, and E is invented.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. instance_name is a user-defined label for tracking the run.
optionExplanations.B: The workflow is identified by workflowId in the path.
optionExplanations.C: Participant roles are defined in the workflow, not by instance_name.
optionExplanations.D: Starting variable values go in trigger_inputs, which must match the schema.
optionExplanations.E: The response returns an instance ID and URL; instance_name does not name the URL.

concept.title: Trigger request body
concept.line: A trigger request sends instance_name (a tracking label) and trigger_inputs (values matching the trigger_input_schema).

stem: What does the envelope status delivered mean?

options.text: At least one recipient has been sent an email with a link
All recipients have signed and the envelope is being finalised
All recipients have viewed the documents
The envelope has been completed by all recipients

answerText: All recipients have viewed the documents
explanation: Sent means at least one recipient got the link; delivered means all recipients have viewed; signed is temporary; completed ends the lifecycle.
whyNotOthers: C is right. The trap is A: it is the definition of sent. B and D are later statuses.

optionExplanations.A: That is the sent status.
optionExplanations.B: Signed is a temporary processing state before completed.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. Delivered means all recipients have viewed the documents.
optionExplanations.D: That is completed.

concept.title: Envelope lifecycle statuses
concept.line: created (draft) -> sent -> delivered (all viewed) -> signed (temporary) -> completed; voided and declined end it early.

stem: Vireo Group's Docusign organization contains seven accounts. Only the three accounts of its EU subsidiaries must send signing events to a new EU-hosted listener for a GDPR records project; data from the other four accounts must not reach that listener. Central IT wants a single configuration that it manages in one place. The EU accounts send envelopes both from the Docusign web app and from a Workday integration. Which approach fits best?

options.text: Create one organization-level configuration that selects only the three EU accounts and points it at the EU listener
Create one organization-level configuration for all seven accounts and have the EU listener return 200 and discard messages from the other accounts
Create an account-level configuration in each EU account, because organization-level configurations always cover every account in the organization
Add an eventNotification object to the envelopes created by the Workday integration so that they report to the EU listener
Create a Recipient Connect configuration for the EU subsidiaries' domain users so their envelope events reach the EU listener

answerText: Create one organization-level configuration that selects only the three EU accounts and points it at the EU listener
explanation: An organization-level configuration can cover all accounts or selected accounts, so one centrally managed configuration can include just the three EU accounts and capture both web-app and integration sending.
whyNotOthers: A is right because organization-level Connect supports selected accounts in one configuration. The trap is B: returning 200 and discarding is good listener practice, but the stem says other accounts' data must not reach the listener at all. C is based on a false claim (selected accounts are allowed) and creates three configurations; D misses web-app envelopes; E covers envelopes the users receive, not the ones they send.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. Organization-level configurations can listen to all accounts or only selected accounts.
optionExplanations.B: Data from the four non-EU accounts would still be delivered to the EU listener, which the stem forbids.
optionExplanations.C: Organization-level configurations can select accounts, and three account-level configurations break the single-configuration goal.
optionExplanations.D: eventNotification covers only API-created envelopes, so web-app envelopes would be missed.
optionExplanations.E: Recipient Connect reports envelopes the users receive, not envelopes their accounts send.

decode.needs: Organization-level configuration with selected accounts
clues: three of seven accounts, others must not reach the listener -> scope by selected accounts
single configuration managed in one place -> organization level
web app and Workday -> envelope-level is not enough
GDPR records project -> red herring

concept.title: Org Connect can select accounts
concept.line: An organization-level configuration can cover all accounts or only selected accounts, managed centrally in one place.

stem: Corbel Insurance's fraud team wants its case system to pull the date of birth and document number captured when policyholders pass Docusign ID Verification. The integration already gets a resource token and calls the ID Evidence API successfully, but the events contain only the verification status, a transaction number and the name of the third-party verifier. No personal details or images come back for any recipient. What is the cause and fix?

options.text: The include_media parameter was omitted; set it to true so that the personal details and the ID images are included in the events response.
The resource token was requested without the recipient's recipientIdGuid; request it with that GUID so the personal fields are unlocked.
The events were requested in JSON format; request the PDF format, which carries the full personal details as a signed export instead.
ID Evidence storage is not configured to keep those details; an administrator must choose which ID data fields Docusign stores as evidence.

answerText: ID Evidence storage is not configured to keep those details; an administrator must choose which ID data fields Docusign stores as evidence.
explanation: By default IDV stores only the verification status, transaction number and third-party verifier name; personal data is available only if ID Evidence storage is configured. The clue is the exact list of what comes back.
whyNotOthers: D is right because the account never stored the personal data.
