The trap is A: include_media only controls whether stored media is embedded or linked; it cannot return data that was never stored. B fails because a token without the GUID cannot be created at all, and C only changes the format.

optionExplanations.A: include_media controls how stored media is returned, not whether data is stored.
optionExplanations.B: The token endpoint path already requires the recipientIdGuid; the calls are succeeding.
optionExplanations.C: PDF changes the format and adds a signature; it does not add unstored data.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. Without ID Evidence storage, only status, transaction number and verifier are kept.

decode.needs: Retain personal ID data by configuring ID Evidence storage before relying on the API.
clues: 'only the verification status, a transaction number and the ... verifier' -> default storage
'calls the ID Evidence API successfully' -> token flow is fine
'fraud team' -> red herring

concept.title: ID Evidence storage
concept.line: By default IDV keeps only status, transaction number and verifier name; configure ID Evidence storage to retain personal data and images.

stem: Some Docusign API responses arrive without the X-RateLimit headers. How should the app track its remaining hourly allowance?

options.text: Treat the allowance as reset to the full hourly limit
Call a dedicated limits endpoint to fetch the current counters
Assume the limit has been reached and pause until the next hour
Retry the call until a response includes the headers again
Keep using the values from the most recent response that had them

answerText: Keep using the values from the most recent response that had them
explanation: Rate-limit headers are not included with every response; when they are missing, the most recently received values are still valid.
whyNotOthers: E is right. The trap is A: missing headers do not mean the counter reset; the hourly reset happens only at the top of the hour. B invents an endpoint, C pauses needlessly, and D wastes calls.

optionExplanations.A: The allowance resets only at the top of the hour, not when headers are missing.
optionExplanations.B: The documented source is the response headers; no counter endpoint is described for this.
optionExplanations.C: Missing headers do not mean the limit is reached.
optionExplanations.D: Retrying to get headers wastes calls and lowers efficiency.
optionExplanations.E: Correct. If a response lacks the headers, the last values received are still valid.

concept.title: Rate-limit headers not always present
concept.line: Not every response carries X-RateLimit headers; reuse the most recent values received.

stem: Okafor's expense-approval app has failed its Go-Live review twice. The message says some of the app's recent API activity broke the rules, but it does not say which calls. Okafor is an administrator in both the developer and the production accounts and wants to see exactly which of the reviewed transactions caused the failure before he changes any code. He has also noticed that the review page sometimes looks stale after he has been away from his desk. What should he do first?

options.text: Turn on API request logging in My Preferences, rerun the app's test scenario, and download the captured log, which keeps up to 50 requests
Open the API Usage Center in the production account and read the app's efficiency score, because the review is based on production traffic
Select DOWNLOAD LOGS in the Review Results window for the reviewed transactions, refreshing first if the session timed out
Delete the key and create a new one, because a key that has failed review twice stays locked until Docusign Support resets it

answerText: Select DOWNLOAD LOGS in the Review Results window for the reviewed transactions, refreshing first if the session timed out
explanation: Docusign's Go-Live troubleshooting advice is to download the log of the reviewed transactions with DOWNLOAD LOGS in the Review Results window, and to refresh or use a private window if the admin console session has timed out. The clue is 'exactly which of the reviewed transactions'.
whyNotOthers: C is right because it gives the exact transactions the review judged. The trap is A: request logging is a real debugging tool, but it captures new requests, not the ones the review examined. B fails because the app is not live in production yet, and D invents a lock rule.

optionExplanations.A: Request logging records new requests from now on (up to 50), not the transactions the review assessed.
optionExplanations.B: The app has not gone live, so production efficiency data does not describe the failed review.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. DOWNLOAD LOGS in Review Results returns the reviewed transactions; refresh if the session timed out.
optionExplanations.D: No such lock exists; fix the issues found in the log and resubmit.

decode.needs: Find the calls that failed the Go-Live review: DOWNLOAD LOGS in the Review Results window.
clues: exactly which reviewed transactions -> review log, not a new capture
page looks stale after time away -> admin console session timeout, refresh
admin in both accounts -> red herring

concept.title: Review Results logs
concept.line: To see why Go-Live review failed, download the reviewed transactions with DOWNLOAD LOGS in Review Results.

stem: Which request returns the URL for an embedded sending session on a draft envelope?

options.text: POST .../envelopes/{envelopeId}/views/sender
POST .../envelopes/{envelopeId}/views/recipient
POST .../envelopes/{envelopeId}/views/correct
PUT .../envelopes/{envelopeId} with status sent

answerText: POST .../envelopes/{envelopeId}/views/sender
explanation: Embedded sending uses EnvelopeViews:createSender, POST .../envelopes/{envelopeId}/views/sender, on a draft envelope.
whyNotOthers: A is right. The trap is C: the correct view is also a sender-side view, but for envelopes already sent. B is for signers and D sends without UI.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. This is EnvelopeViews:createSender.
optionExplanations.B: This returns a signing URL for a recipient.
optionExplanations.C: This returns the correction view for an envelope already sent.
optionExplanations.D: This sends the draft directly, with no sending UI.

concept.title: Embedded sending endpoint
concept.line: views/sender embeds tagging and sending of a draft; views/recipient embeds signing; views/correct embeds correction.

stem: Which call lists the signature provider names an account can use in recipientSignatureProviders for EU AES or QES signing?

options.text: IdentityVerifications:list
AccountBrands:list
AccountSignatureProviders:list
TabInfo:GetConnectedFieldsTabGroups

answerText: AccountSignatureProviders:list
explanation: AccountSignatureProviders:list (GET /restapi/v2.1/accounts/{accountId}/signatureProviders) returns the providers available for recipientSignatureProviders.
whyNotOthers: C is right. The trap is A: IdentityVerifications:list returns identity verification workflow IDs for identityVerification, not signature providers. B lists brands, and D lists connected fields.

optionExplanations.A: Returns identity verification workflow IDs, not signature providers.
optionExplanations.B: Returns brands.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. It lists the signature providers available to the account.
optionExplanations.D: Returns connected fields tab groups.

concept.title: Signature providers for SBS
concept.line: Use AccountSignatureProviders:list to find names for recipientSignatureProviders; IdentityVerifications:list gives IDV workflow IDs.

stem: Tallis Gym's membership sign-up runs in a mobile web browser and is signed embedded in classic view, because the agreement includes a payment field that charges the joining fee. Members on phones complain that the agreement shown inside an iframe on the sign-up page is cramped and hard to scroll. Desktop users have no complaints. The gym recently changed its pricing tiers. What should the developers do?

options.text: Switch to focused view with Docusign JS and size the container by percentage, so the agreement fits the phone screen
Keep the iframe and set its height to the default 400px so the agreement keeps its designed proportions
Keep classic view and, on mobile browsers, open the signing URL in a new browser tab instead of an iframe
Keep the iframe and generate a new signing URL each time the member scrolls to the bottom of the page

answerText: Keep classic view and, on mobile browsers, open the signing URL in a new browser tab instead of an iframe
explanation: Payment fields require classic view, so the fix is the classic view guidance: let Docusign take full control of the browser window and, on mobile browsers, use a new tab instead of an iframe.
whyNotOthers: C is right. The trap is A: focused view is the usual recommendation, but it does not support payment fields. B keeps the cramped frame, and D does not affect layout.

optionExplanations.A: Focused view would fit better, but payment fields require classic view.
optionExplanations.B: A fixed small frame is the cause of the cramped view; Docusign advises proper sizing, and a new tab on mobile.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. Classic view best practice is to let Docusign control the window and, on mobile browsers, use a new tab rather than an iframe.
optionExplanations.D: Generating more URLs does not change the layout and wastes API calls.

decode.needs: Classic view mobile best practice: new browser tab, not iframe
clues: payment field -> classic view is required
phones, cramped iframe -> open in a new tab on mobile
pricing tiers -> red herring

concept.title: Classic view on mobile
concept.line: In classic view let Docusign take the full window; on mobile browsers open a new tab instead of an iframe.

topic: App Center install blocked by an ad blocker
stem: Wexford Group's private extension app went Live and was shared with two production accounts. Admins of the subsidiary, which sits on its own network, installed it without trouble. At head office, every install attempt ends with 'We encountered an unexpected error. Reload the page and try again.' Head office enforces a strict browser ad-blocking policy across its corporate network, and its account still shows Pending on the developer's sharing list. The help desk has already cleared browser caches twice. What is the most likely fix?

options.text: Add the Docusign endpoint IP addresses for North America to the firewall in front of Wexford's API service so the installation call can complete.
Ask the developer to remove head office from the sharing list and add it again, because a Pending entry expires after 48 hours.
Add the Optimizely addresses that the App Center uses, and ideally the Qualtrics domains, to the allowed list of head office's ad blocker.
Ask the developer to re-run the connection test in the Developer Console, because production installs fail until a recent connection test passes.
Ask Docusign to switch the app to public distribution, because private apps cannot be installed while the account's entry is Pending.

answerText: Add the Optimizely addresses that the App Center uses, and ideally the Qualtrics domains, to the allowed list of head office's ad blocker.
explanation: The clues are the exact message 'We encountered an unexpected error. Reload the page and try again', the strict ad-blocking policy, and the subsidiary on another network succeeding. Docusign documents that ad blockers must allow the Optimizely (and recommended Qualtrics) addresses to install or uninstall apps in the App Center.
whyNotOthers: C is right because the error pattern and network-specific failure match an ad blocker. The trap is A: a firewall allow-list is the other network change in the docs, but it governs Docusign calling Wexford's API and would also have broken the subsidiary. B, D and E misread Pending status or invent prerequisites.

optionExplanations.A: Firewall problems block Docusign's calls to the API (for example 403, 502 or token exchange errors); they would also hit the subsidiary, which installed fine.
optionExplanations.B: Pending simply means the admin has not yet accepted the app; it does not expire.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. The documented symptom of a blocking ad blocker during App Center install or uninstall is exactly this error, and the fix is allow-listing these addresses.
optionExplanations.D: Developer Console tests run in the developer account and do not gate production installs.
optionExplanations.E: Installing is how the admin accepts a Pending private app, and distribution cannot change after Live.

decode.needs: Allow the App Center's Optimizely (and Qualtrics) addresses in the ad blocker so admins can install the app.
clues: 'We encountered an unexpected error. Reload the page' -> ad blocker symptom
'subsidiary on its own network installed fine' -> network-specific, browser-side
'Pending' -> just means not yet accepted

concept.title: Ad blockers can block installs
concept.line: If App Center installs fail with an unexpected error, allow the Optimizely and Qualtrics addresses in the network's ad blocker.

topic: Fresh values in a RAG pipeline
stem: Telmar Energy's contract copilot answers engineers' questions over Agreement Manager data. A vector index of agreement records keyed by agreementId finds the relevant agreements for each question. Contract analysts regularly correct AI-extracted values such as renewal_notice_period in Agreement Manager, and answers have started quoting values that analysts already fixed. Rebuilding the full index takes about four hours, the index runs on the company's own GPU cluster, and the hourly API limit is shared with other integrations. Which change keeps the answers accurate with the fewest extra calls?

options.text: Rebuild the whole index every hour with GetAgreementsList so that the values analysts correct reach the copilot much sooner.
Keep the indexed values as they are, because AI-extracted values are fixed once extraction completes and corrections stay in the UI.
After the index returns candidate agreementIds, fetch their current records with one GetAgreementsList call using the id filter.
After the index returns candidate agreementIds, call CreateAgreementSummary on each of them and answer from the summaries.

answerText: After the index returns candidate agreementIds, fetch their current records with one GetAgreementsList call using the id filter.
explanation: Later GET responses return user-updated values, and GetAgreementsList accepts an id filter with several IDs, so one call per question refreshes exactly the agreements the answer will cite.
whyNotOthers: C is right because it keeps retrieval in the index but takes values from a live, batched read. The trap is A: re-indexing sounds thorough, but a four-hour rebuild cannot run hourly and would drain the shared limit. B is false because UI corrections replace the AI values in API responses, and D returns prose with one call per agreement.

optionExplanations.A: A four-hour rebuild cannot run every hour, and full re-reads waste the shared hourly limit.
optionExplanations.B: User corrections made in Agreement Manager replace the AI values that later GET requests return, so the index goes stale.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. One id-filtered GetAgreementsList call returns the current, user-corrected provisions for the candidates.
optionExplanations.D: Summaries are AI narrative, not the corrected structured values, and need one call per agreement.

decode.needs: Hybrid RAG: index keyed by agreementId for retrieval, then an id-filtered GetAgreementsList for current values.
clues: quoting values analysts already fixed -> user-updated values are not in the index snapshot
fewest extra calls -> batch the candidates with the id filter
rebuild takes four hours -> hourly rebuild is impossible
own GPU cluster -> red herring

concept.title: Retrieve from index, values live
concept.line: In RAG over agreements, keep the index for retrieval but fetch current values by agreementId at answer time, since reviewers can change them.

stem: After acquiring a Sao Paulo distributor, Kerrigan Tools imported 2,500 of the distributor's contracts into Agreement Manager. Its Brazilian legal team, which reads only Portuguese, will review the AI-extracted terms of every contract written in Portuguese. Several Portuguese-language contracts are governed by New York law, and some Brazilian-law contracts were drafted in English. The review queue is fed by a script that runs from a laptop in the Lisbon office. How should the script select the contracts for the Brazilian team?

options.text: Call GetAgreementsList and keep the records whose governing_law provision is Brazil, since a contract's governing law shows its language.
Call GetAgreementsList with the languages filter set to a BCP-47 Portuguese tag such as pt-BR, and page through the results with ctoken.
Call GetAgreementsList with the title filter set to Contrato, since Portuguese-language contracts are expected to carry Portuguese titles.
Call GetAgreementsList with source_name set to the distributor's company name, since imported contracts record the company they came from.

answerText: Call GetAgreementsList with the languages filter set to a BCP-47 Portuguese tag such as pt-BR, and page through the results with ctoken.
explanation: Each agreement lists its languages as BCP-47 codes, and GetAgreementsList filters on languages. The deciding clue is that law and language do not line up ('Portuguese-language contracts governed by New York law').
whyNotOthers: B is right because the languages property records what the document is written in. The trap is A: governing law sounds like a proxy for language, but the stem says the two diverge. C assumes a naming convention nobody guaranteed, and D misreads source_name, which names the originating system, not a company.

optionExplanations.A: Governing law and language diverge in this repository, so this misses Portuguese contracts under New York law and includes English ones.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. The languages filter takes BCP-47 tags and selects contracts by the language they are written in.
optionExplanations.C: Titles are not guaranteed to be in Portuguese, so a title filter is unreliable.
optionExplanations.D: source_name is the originating system (for example eSign or CLM), not the company that held the contract.

decode.needs: Filter imported agreements by the languages property (BCP-47).
clues: reads only Portuguese -> select by document language
Portuguese contracts under New York law, Brazilian-law contracts in English -> governing law is not a proxy
laptop in the Lisbon office -> red herring

concept.title: Filter by languages, not law
concept.line: Agreement records list document languages as BCP-47 codes; filter on languages rather than inferring language from governing law or titles.

topic: When an extension app is part of the solution (multi)
stem: Orrin Telecom's business analyst has listed five requirements for next year's agreement program, and the architect must flag those that are met by building an extension app rather than by Orrin's own systems calling Docusign. Orrin owns a proprietary customer-number database and an in-house contract vault, and already runs Maestro workflows for customer onboarding. The program sponsor wants a single page per requirement for the steering committee, and budget is approved for whichever approach is chosen. Which two requirements call for an extension app? (Select two)

options.text: Send the billing ERP the form data of every completed envelope within seconds of completion, for all envelopes the account sends.
Show the signing session inside Orrin's self-service portal so that the customer never leaves the website.
While a customer signs, check the customer number they type against the proprietary customer database and stop completion if it does not match.
As a step in the Maestro onboarding workflow, store the completed agreement in the in-house contract vault.
Send 3,000 personalised tariff-change letters at once from a spreadsheet of customers.

answerText: While a customer signs, check the customer number they type against the proprietary customer database and stop completion if it does not match.; As a step in the Maestro onboarding workflow, store the completed agreement in the in-house contract vault.
explanation: Extension apps bring an external service into a Docusign process at an extension point: checking typed values against the customer database during signing (connected fields) and saving the agreement to the vault from a Maestro step (file output). The others are Docusign-into-Orrin integrations.
whyNotOthers: C and D are right because Docusign calls Orrin's services at an extension point. The trap is A: it also involves an external system and completed agreements, but Docusign is pushing events out to a listener, which is Connect. B is embedded signing and E is bulk send.

optionExplanations.A: Event-driven push of envelope data to an external system is Docusign Connect with a listener, not an extension app.
optionExplanations.B: This is embedded signing through the eSignature API.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. Verifying signer input against an in-house system during signing is a connected fields extension app.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. Writing workflow documents to a storage system from a Maestro step is the file output cloud storage extension.
optionExplanations.E: This is bulk send through the eSignature API or web app.

decode.needs: Spot requirements where Docusign must call an external service at an extension point (signing, Maestro step).
clues: 'while a customer signs, check against proprietary database' -> connected fields
'step in the Maestro workflow, store in vault' -> file output cloud storage
'within seconds of completion, all envelopes' -> Connect, not an extension app

concept.title: Extension app or API integration
concept.line: Use an extension app when Docusign must call your service inside signing or a workflow step; otherwise use APIs or Connect.

stem: A branch kiosk runs a workflow that ends right after the customer signs. Before stepping away, the customer must see an on-screen message confirming that all of their tasks are finished. Which step should end the workflow?

options.text: A Send an Email step addressed to the customer
A Set Up Invite step for the next customer in the queue
A Branching Rule step on the envelope status
A Show a Confirmation Screen step with an end-of-tasks message
A Collect Data with Web Forms step that shows a thank-you page at the end

answerText: A Show a Confirmation Screen step with an end-of-tasks message
explanation: Show a Confirmation Screen is the utility step that displays a message to the participant, such as the end of the participant's tasks.
whyNotOthers: D is right because the message must appear on screen before the customer leaves. The trap is A: an email also confirms completion, but it is not shown on the kiosk. B starts nothing useful, C only routes, and E would collect more data instead of confirming.

optionExplanations.A: An email is not an on-screen message on the kiosk.
optionExplanations.B: Invites participants to steps; it shows no completion message.
optionExplanations.C: Routes between paths; it displays nothing.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. Show a Confirmation Screen displays an end-of-tasks message to the participant.
optionExplanations.E: A web form collects data; it is not a completion message step.

concept.title: Confirmation screen ends a session
concept.line: Use Show a Confirmation Screen to tell a participant on screen that their tasks are complete.

stem: Riverbend Insurance's claims portal lets a claimant start signing a settlement, leave, and come back days later to finish from the portal. The portal must be able to open a fresh signing session for the same envelope when the claimant returns. Claimants always come back through the portal, never through an email link. The claims database runs on a managed SQL service. Which two values should the portal store for each claimant when it creates the envelope? (Select two)

options.text: The envelopeId returned by Envelopes:create
The signing URL from the first createRecipient call, so the claimant can reopen it
The access token used to create the envelope, so the session can be resumed with it
The returnUrl event received when the claimant left
The clientUserId used for the claimant's recipient

answerText: The envelopeId returned by Envelopes:create; The clientUserId used for the claimant's recipient
explanation: Docusign's best practices say to store the envelope ID for each customer and cache the clientUserId sent for each recipient; the signing URL is requested only when the user is ready.
whyNotOthers: A and E are right. The trap is B: it seems convenient to save the URL, but it expires within minutes and works once. C expires as well, and D is not an input to createRecipient.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. The envelope ID is needed for later calls such as createRecipient.
optionExplanations.B: Signing URLs are short-lived and single-use; request a new one when the claimant returns.
optionExplanations.C: Tokens expire; the app gets a current token when it needs one.
optionExplanations.D: The event is useful for routing the user, but it is not needed to reopen the session.
optionExplanations.E: Correct. createRecipient must repeat the same clientUserId, so cache it per recipient.

decode.needs: Persist envelopeId and clientUserId; request a new recipient view on return
clues: come back days later -> new signing URL needed
fresh session for the same envelope -> envelopeId + matching clientUserId
managed SQL service -> red herring

concept.title: Persist IDs, not URLs
concept.line: Store the envelopeId and each recipient's clientUserId; generate a new signing URL whenever the user is ready to sign.

topic: Partner account and demo key use
stem: Lindqvist Software, an ISV in the Docusign partner program, promoted its HR product's key into the complimentary partner production account last month. The sales team now wants to run live prospect demos and new-hire training from that partner account because 'it is production and looks real'. QA also asks where to run the weekly checks that catch Docusign platform changes before customers do. The company has offices in Stockholm and Austin. What should the integration lead decide?

options.text: Run prospect demos and training from the partner production account, and run QA's weekly checks against a customer's production account with that customer's permission
Run demos, training and weekly regression in the partner production account, because the developer copy of the key stops working once the key has been promoted
Run demos and training in a developer account, but run weekly regression in the partner production account so that the tests reflect the live platform
Keep demos, training and weekly regression testing in the developer environment with the demo copy of the key, and use the partner account only to manage production keys

answerText: Keep demos, training and weekly regression testing in the developer environment with the demo copy of the key, and use the partner account only to manage production keys
explanation: The complimentary partner account exists to manage production keys, not to send envelopes; demos and training belong in a developer account, and the still-working demo copy of the key should be used for weekly regression testing. The clues are 'complimentary partner account' and 'weekly checks'.
whyNotOthers: D is right because it follows each documented rule. The trap is C: it gets demos right but puts regression into the partner account, which is not for sending. A sends from the partner account and tests in a customer's account, and B is wrong because the demo copy of the key keeps working after promotion.

optionExplanations.A: The partner account is not for sending envelopes, and testing in a customer's account is not the documented approach.
optionExplanations.B: The demo copy of the key keeps working after Go-Live; it is duplicated, not moved.
optionExplanations.C: Weekly regression belongs in the developer environment, not in the key-management partner account.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. Developer environment for demos, training and weekly regression; partner account for key management only.

decode.needs: Use the partner production account only to manage keys; demos, training and regression use the developer environment.
clues: complimentary partner production account -> for managing keys, not sending envelopes
weekly checks for platform changes -> regression testing with the demo key
Stockholm and Austin offices -> red herring

concept.title: Partner account manages keys
concept.line: ISV partner production accounts manage keys; demos, training and weekly regression run in the developer environment.

topic: Connected fields missing after template upload
stem: Marwick Group's subsidiary in Ireland built an eSignature template with connected fields from a private extension app installed in its own Docusign account. Head office downloaded the template and uploaded it into the group account, where the same documents will be sent. In the group account the template opens, but the app's fields are missing from the Add Fields view and senders cannot add verified fields. The extension app is published privately to both accounts. What is the most likely cause?

options.text: The extension app is not installed and connected in the group account, so the uploaded template has no connection there to use.
Templates with connected fields cannot be moved between accounts, so the fields must be rebuilt in a new template from scratch.
The template still points to the Irish account's connection, which is shown only to users in that account's sending group.
The group account's senders lack the adm_store_unified_repo_read scope, which the Add Fields view needs to list connected fields.

answerText: The extension app is not installed and connected in the group account, so the uploaded template has no connection there to use.
explanation: Connected fields appear only when the extension app is installed and connected in the account. The clue is 'published privately to both accounts', which makes it available but does not install or connect it.
whyNotOthers: A is right because publication is not installation. The trap is D: that scope is needed for the Connected Fields API, not for senders using the web app. B is false because uploaded templates work once the app is connected, and C invents cross-account group visibility.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. Install and connect the app in the group account.
optionExplanations.B: Uploaded templates work when the app is installed and connected in the target account.
optionExplanations.C: Connections are per account; there is no cross-account group sharing.
optionExplanations.D: That scope applies to API calls, not to the Add Fields view in the web app.

decode.needs: Make the connected fields available in the new account: install and connect the app there.
clues: 'uploaded it into the group account' -> different account
'published privately to both accounts' -> available, not installed
'subsidiary in Ireland' -> red herring

concept.title: Connected fields per account
concept.line: Connected fields need the extension app installed and connected in each account that uses them.

stem: Fairhaven Insurance prefills its claims web form. The backend's Instances:createInstance request sets formValues policy_number to the customer's current policy, and the configuration has a default of 'unknown' for the same field. A front-end developer also added prefillValues to the Docusign JS webFormOptions, copying a cached value from the customer's previous session. Customers with renewed policies now see their old policy number. What explains this?

options.text: The configuration default overrides API prefill values, so the default for policy_number must be removed in the Web Forms builder.
Docusign JS prefillValues override createInstance formValues, which override configuration defaults; remove or refresh the cached value.
formValues in createInstance apply only to remote instances; embedded instances read prefill data only from Docusign JS prefillValues.
createInstance values override Docusign JS prefillValues, so the old number must come from a previous instance reused through refreshToken.

answerText: Docusign JS prefillValues override createInstance formValues, which override configuration defaults; remove or refresh the cached value.
explanation: Values in Docusign JS prefillValues override values from createInstance, and prefill values override configuration defaults. The clue is the cached value copied into prefillValues.
whyNotOthers: B is right because the front-end cached value wins. The trap is D: it reverses the order of precedence. A also reverses precedence, and C is false because formValues prefill embedded instances too.

optionExplanations.A: Prefill values override configuration defaults, not the other way round.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. Docusign JS prefillValues win over createInstance values, which win over defaults.
optionExplanations.C: formValues prefill embedded instances as well.
optionExplanations.D: It is the reverse: Docusign JS prefillValues override createInstance values.

decode.needs: Know which prefill source wins: Docusign JS over createInstance over defaults.
clues: 'prefillValues to the Docusign JS webFormOptions' -> highest precedence
'cached value from the previous session' -> stale data source
'default of unknown' -> lowest precedence, a distraction

concept.title: Web form prefill precedence
concept.line: Docusign JS prefillValues override createInstance formValues, which override configuration defaults.

topic: Fields returned by the Connected Fields API
stem: An optional property in a connected fields data model appears in the Add Fields view but not in the TabInfo:GetConnectedFieldsTabGroups response. Why?

options.text: The API returns only mandatory fields or ones with IsRequiredForVerifyingType
The connection must be refreshed before the API can list optional fields
Optional fields are returned only for public extension apps in the App Center
The API returns optional fields only when the extended scope is requested

answerText: The API returns only mandatory fields or ones with IsRequiredForVerifyingType
explanation: Unlike the Connected Fields UI, the API endpoint returns only fields that are mandatory or carry the IsRequiredForVerifyingType decorator.
whyNotOthers: A is right. The trap is B: refreshing reloads the model, but the field is already in the model since the UI shows it. C and D invent conditions.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. The API returns only mandatory or IsRequiredForVerifyingType fields.
optionExplanations.B: The field already shows in the UI, so the model is current.
optionExplanations.C: Public versus private publication does not change the API response.
optionExplanations.D: Scopes do not change which fields are returned.

concept.title: Connected Fields API response
concept.line: GetConnectedFieldsTabGroups returns only mandatory or IsRequiredForVerifyingType fields, unlike the Add Fields UI.

stem: Which pre-built Connect integration notifies an external platform that a completed transaction is ready to be vaulted?

options.text: Connect for Box
Connect for eOriginal
Connect for OneDrive
Connect for Salesforce

answerText: Connect for eOriginal
explanation: Connect for eOriginal pushes an event telling eOriginal that a transaction that needs to be vaulted is complete.
whyNotOthers: B is right because eOriginal is the vaulting integration. The trap is A: Box, like OneDrive, receives completed documents, which sounds like storage, but it does not vault transactions. D pushes data updates to the Docusign for Salesforce application.

optionExplanations.A: Connect for Box pushes completed documents to a Box folder; it does not signal vaulting.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. Connect for eOriginal informs eOriginal that a transaction that needs to be vaulted is complete.
optionExplanations.C: Connect for OneDrive pushes completed documents to a OneDrive folder.
optionExplanations.D: Connect for Salesforce pushes data updates to the Docusign for Salesforce application.

concept.title: Four pre-built Connect solutions
concept.line: Box and OneDrive receive completed documents, Salesforce receives data updates, and eOriginal is told a transaction is ready for vaulting.

stem: Which property in a Configurations:getForm response tells an app whether the configuration can be used for remote (emailed) web form instances?

options.text: type set to hasEsignTemplate
allowSending set to true
status set to active
sendOption set to now

answerText: allowSending set to true
explanation: allowSending true means the configuration can create remote instances; false or missing means it cannot.
whyNotOthers: B is right. The trap is A: a template-based type is necessary, but attachment fields or an older release can still block remote delivery. C only means the form is activated, and D is a createInstance request property.

optionExplanations.A: Template-based is required but not sufficient for remote delivery.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. allowSending indicates remote instance support.
optionExplanations.C: Active status is needed to create any instance; it does not indicate remote support.
optionExplanations.D: sendOption is sent in createInstance, not returned by getForm.

concept.title: Remote delivery support
concept.line: allowSending in getForm or listForms shows remote support; standalone, attachment fields or old releases block it.

topic: Choosing the composite model for growth
stem: Ampersand HR, a startup, needs only one agreement today: an NDA built from a single server template. Its product roadmap, however, adds offer letters that combine several templates and generated documents next year, and the CTO does not want to rewrite the integration then. Both products will be sold to the same customers through one admin console. The team has a comfortable schedule. Which envelope model should the developers use now?

options.text: The template reference model, because the current requirement is a single template and it needs the least code
The direct documents model, because it is the quickest to build and more documents can simply be added later
The template reference model now, adding a second templateId to the request when the offer letters arrive
The composite templates model, because it covers today's single template and can add templates and documents later

answerText: The composite templates model, because it covers today's single template and can add templates and documents later
explanation: The deciding clue is 'does not want to rewrite the integration' while the roadmap combines several templates; composite templates support both today's need and that growth, and the schedule allows the extra planning.
whyNotOthers: D is right. The trap is A: correct for today's single template, but it cannot grow to multiple templates. B is the least flexible model, and C assumes a capability the template reference model lacks.

optionExplanations.A: Fine for a single template, but it cannot be expanded to multiple templates, so it would need a rewrite next year.
optionExplanations.B: Direct documents uses no templates and is the least flexible to expand.
optionExplanations.C: The template reference model takes a single template; a second templateId is not supported.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. The course recommends composite templates when growth is expected, since it supports every simpler case and scales.

decode.needs: Composite templates model chosen for future flexibility
clues: several templates and generated documents next year -> composite needed eventually
does not want to rewrite -> choose composite now
comfortable schedule -> composite's planning cost is acceptable

concept.title: Composite templates scale
concept.line: Choose composite templates when requirements will grow; template reference handles exactly one template and cannot expand.

stem: An integration key's Go-Live status in Apps and Keys shows Review Passed. What does this status mean?

options.text: The key is enabled in production and appears in the production account
The app's recent API calls are still being checked against the requirements
The app needs a manual review; submit the linked form with more account details
The review lapsed because the key was not promoted within 90 days
It passed and awaits promotion into a production account you administer

answerText: It passed and awaits promotion into a production account you administer
explanation: Review Passed means the app passed and is ready to be duplicated into a production account of your choice, in which you must be an administrator.
whyNotOthers: E is right. The trap is A: 'passed' sounds like done, but that describes Live, which comes after you select the production account. B is Under Review, C is Declined and D is Review Expired.

optionExplanations.A: This describes Live, which comes after promotion.
optionExplanations.B: This describes Under Review.
optionExplanations.C: This describes Declined.
optionExplanations.D: This describes Review Expired.
optionExplanations.E: Correct. Review Passed waits for you to confirm and select a production account where you are an admin.

concept.title: Go-Live status sequence
concept.line: Under Review -> Review Passed (select a production account) -> Live; Declined means manual review, Review Expired after 90 days.

stem: When the ID Evidence API returns the image of the front of a recipient's photo ID, which statement is true?

options.text: It can be resubmitted for a later IDV check
It is a link to the third-party verifier's site
It is returned only for KBA verifications
It has a honeycomb overlay and cannot be reused

answerText: It has a honeycomb overlay and cannot be reused
explanation: The returned ID image has a honeycomb pattern superimposed on it and cannot be used to make additional IDV requests.
whyNotOthers: D is right. The trap is A: the image looks like a usable ID copy but is deliberately marked so it cannot be reused. B and C misdescribe the media endpoint, which serves images captured by Docusign ID Verification.

optionExplanations.A: The overlay prevents reuse for further IDV requests.
optionExplanations.B: The media endpoint returns the stored image itself, not a third-party link.
optionExplanations.C: Media comes from ID Verification image capture, not KBA.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. A honeycomb pattern is superimposed and the image cannot be reused for IDV.

concept.title: ID Evidence media
concept.line: ID images from the ID Evidence media endpoint carry a honeycomb overlay and cannot be reused for new IDV checks.

stem: Ellery Rentals' template-based rental application web form, embedded in its website, includes an attachment field with the API reference name 'payslip', where applicants upload pay slips as JPG or PDF files. The tenancy system must store each uploaded file against the application after submission. The developer reads formValues from Instances:getInstance but finds no file content there. What is the correct retrieval approach?

options.text: Take the envelope ID from the envelopes array, call EnvelopeDocuments:list, and download the documents named __payslip__ plus the file name.
Call Configurations:getForm for the payslip component and download each applicant's uploaded files from that component's attachment URLs.
Call Instances:getInstance with an include_attachments option set to true so each uploaded file is returned Base64-encoded in formValues.
Take the envelope ID from the envelopes array and download the uploaded files as signer attachments in their original JPG or PDF format.

answerText: Take the envelope ID from the envelopes array, call EnvelopeDocuments:list, and download the documents named __payslip__ plus the file name.
explanation: Uploaded files are appended to the generated envelope, converted to PDF, and named with the field's API reference name between double underscores. The clue is 'attachment field with the API reference name payslip'.
whyNotOthers: A is right. The trap is D: it reaches the right envelope but uploads are converted to PDF documents, not kept as original-format signer attachments. B confuses the field definition with user data, and C invents a getInstance option.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. Uploads become PDF envelope documents named __payslip__ followed by the file name.
optionExplanations.B: getForm returns field definitions, not users' uploaded files.
optionExplanations.C: getInstance has no such option; files are not in formValues.
optionExplanations.D: Uploaded files are converted to PDF and appended as envelope documents.

decode.needs: Fetch uploaded files from the generated envelope's documents.
clues: 'template-based' -> an envelope exists
'API reference name payslip' -> document name prefix __payslip__
'JPG or PDF files' -> all uploads are converted to PDF

concept.title: Web form attachment retrieval
concept.line: Attachment uploads become PDF documents in the generated envelope, named __componentName__ plus the file name.

stem: Galloway Freight's developers plan to create the company's six carrier-agreement templates from a deployment script that calls Templates:create and places every signature and date field by code. The contracts team, who are not developers, expects to adjust field positions several times a year as the agreements are revised. The integration itself only needs to send the agreements. The company is moving from demo to production next month. What should the architect recommend?

options.text: Build and maintain the templates in the web app, and reference each by a templateId kept in per-environment configuration
Keep the deployment script, but run Templates:create in each environment so the template IDs are generated automatically at every release
Build the templates in the web app and hard-code their demo templateId values, because template IDs carry over to production at go-live
Drop templates and send each agreement with the direct documents model and fixed x/y tab positions defined in code

answerText: Build and maintain the templates in the web app, and reference each by a templateId kept in per-environment configuration
explanation: The course best practice is to create templates in the web app and reference them by ID, because placing tags by code is cumbersome; template IDs must be updated per environment.
whyNotOthers: A is right because the contracts team can edit templates without code and IDs stay configurable. The trap is C: authoring in the web app is right, but demo IDs do not work in production. B keeps the cumbersome scripted approach, and D hard-codes layouts.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. Docusign recommends setting templates up once in the web app and referencing them by ID; IDs differ between demo and production, so keep them in configuration.
optionExplanations.B: Creating templates by API is possible but cumbersome, and the contracts team could not edit layouts without a release.
optionExplanations.C: Template IDs differ between developer and production accounts; go-live does not copy them.
optionExplanations.D: This removes the contracts team's ability to edit layouts and is the least flexible model.

decode.needs: Templates built in the web app, referenced by templateId from config
clues: not developers, adjust fields several times a year -> author in the web app
moving to production -> template IDs differ per environment
six carrier agreements -> red herring

concept.title: Author templates in the web app
concept.line: Create templates once in the eSignature web app and reference them by templateId, configured per environment.

stem: Oakhurst Lettings wants applicants on its website to complete a tenancy workflow (a web form, a phone-authentication identity check, then signature) without leaving the site. A contractor proposes building a separate embedded view for each step: a Web Forms JS SDK instance for the form, an identity session for the check, and an eSignature recipient view for signing, all stitched together by the site's server. The site's server already triggers the workflow and receives the instance URL. The site is being translated into Polish. What is the recommended integration?

options.text: Build the per-step views as proposed, because a triggered workflow instance only runs the steps that have no user interface of their own
Redirect the applicant's browser to the instance URL, because instance URLs cannot be framed and must always open directly on the Docusign platform
Place the instance URL in an iframe on the site, which loads the first step and gives the applicant the whole browser-based workflow experience
Place the instance URL in an iframe for the form and identity steps, and generate a separate eSignature recipient view for the signing step
Change the start method to From a Link and put the copied workflow link in the iframe, because only link-started instances can be framed

answerText: Place the instance URL in an iframe on the site, which loads the first step and gives the applicant the whole browser-based workflow experience
explanation: The instance URL returned by the trigger call is embedded in an iframe; the iframe loads the first step and provides a complete browser-based workflow experience, including web form, phone-authentication IDV and signing steps.
whyNotOthers: C is right because one embedded instance URL covers all of the applicant's steps. The trap is D: it reflects eSignature habits, but Send Documents for Signature steps run inside the embedded instance (only focused view is unsupported), so no separate recipient view is needed. A and B are false, and E is wrong because From an API call is also supported for embedding.

optionExplanations.A: The instance runs every step, including UI steps such as forms and signing.
optionExplanations.B: Framing the instance URL in an iframe is the documented embedding option.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. One iframe with the instance URL delivers the whole workflow experience.
optionExplanations.D: Signing steps run inside the embedded instance; a separate recipient view is unnecessary.
optionExplanations.E: Both From a Link and From an API call are supported for embedding.

decode.needs: Embed the instance URL in an iframe
clues: without leaving the site -> embedded instance
separate view for each step -> unnecessary; the instance covers all steps
phone-authentication identity check -> supported when embedded
Polish translation -> red herring

concept.title: One iframe, whole workflow
concept.line: Embedding the trigger's instance URL in an iframe gives users the complete workflow, with no separate per-step views.

topic: Where connection authorization values come from
stem: Pellham Insurance protects its policy API with the company's Okta tenant, and every caller must get a token from Okta before calling it. Pellham is registering a private connected fields app that checks policy numbers during signing, and the developer filling in the connection asks where the authorization values should come from. Pellham also has a Docusign integration key, configured for JWT, that its claims portal uses to send envelopes, and the security team insists on least privilege everywhere. Which values belong in the connection?

options.text: Okta's authorization URL, token URL and required scopes, plus a client ID and client secret from a client registered in Okta for Docusign to use.
The claims portal's Docusign integration key and secret key, because Docusign authenticates to the policy API with its own registered credentials.
Okta's URLs together with the RSA private key of the claims portal's integration key, because the connection obtains tokens with a JWT assertion.
Docusign's account server endpoints for authorization and token, with the signature and extended scopes requested during installation.
No authorization values, because a private app may rely on the Docusign IP allow-list alone to protect the policy API.

answerText: Okta's authorization URL, token URL and required scopes, plus a client ID and client secret from a client registered in Okta for Docusign to use.
explanation: The clue is 'every caller must get a token from Okta': the connection's authorization details (authorization URL, token URL, client ID, client secret, scopes) come from the identity provider, here Okta.
whyNotOthers: A is right because the identity provider supplies the connection's authorization details. The trap is B: the integration key is Pellham's Docusign credential, but it authenticates Pellham to Docusign, not Docusign to Pellham. C and D mix in Docusign OAuth artefacts, and E drops authorization altogether. The JWT claims portal is a red herring.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. When an identity provider handles authorization, the connection uses that provider's authorization URL, token URL, client ID, client secret and scopes.
optionExplanations.B: The integration key identifies Pellham's app to Docusign; the connection needs credentials that Pellham's own identity provider issues.
optionExplanations.C: Connections use Authorization Code or Client Credentials grants with a client ID and secret, not Docusign JWT keys.
optionExplanations.D: Those endpoints and scopes are for calling Docusign APIs, not for Docusign calling Pellham's API.
optionExplanations.E: Private apps still need a connection with authorization; IP allow-listing is only a network control.

decode.needs: Obtain the connection's OAuth values (auth URL, token URL, client ID/secret, scopes) from the external service or its identity provider.
clues: 'every caller must get a token from Okta' -> Okta is the authorization provider for the connection
'Docusign integration key configured for JWT' -> red herring, wrong direction
'checks policy numbers during signing' -> connected fields, private

concept.title: Connection credentials come from your IdP
concept.line: The extension app connection uses the external service's or identity provider's auth URL, token URL, client ID, secret and scopes.

stem: Which statement about a recipient access code set through the eSignature API is correct?

options.text: Minimum 8 characters, case-sensitive
Maximum 50 characters, not case-sensitive
Generated and texted by Docusign
Maximum 50 characters, case-sensitive

answerText: Maximum 50 characters, not case-sensitive
explanation: An access code is a string of 50 characters or less that the sender provides, and it is not case-sensitive.
whyNotOthers: B is right on both length and case. The trap is D: the length limit is right, but access codes are not case-sensitive. A invents a minimum, and C describes phone authentication.

optionExplanations.A: There is a 50-character maximum, and codes are not case-sensitive.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. Up to 50 characters and not case-sensitive.
optionExplanations.C: The sender sets the access code and shares it out of band.
optionExplanations.D: Correct length, but access codes are not case-sensitive.

concept.title: Access code rules
concept.line: Access codes are sender-defined, up to 50 characters, not case-sensitive, and exclude the characters <, >, & and #.

stem: What is the maximum number of integration keys that can be created for one eSignature account?
explanation: eSignature account limits allow up to 100 integration keys (and 100 Connect configurations, 50 signing groups) per account.
whyNotOthers: E is right. The trap is C: 50 is the signing-group limit, a nearby account limit. A, B and D are not documented limits.

optionExplanations.A: Not a documented limit; the maximum is 100.
optionExplanations.B: Not a documented limit; the maximum is 100.
optionExplanations.C: 50 is the signing-group limit, not the integration-key limit.
optionExplanations.D: Not a documented limit; the maximum is 100.
optionExplanations.E: Correct. An account can have up to 100 integration keys.

concept.title: Account limits
concept.line: Per account: up to 100 integration keys, 100 Connect configurations and 50 signing groups.

stem: Pendleford Estates' records system keeps a table of every agreement it has ever sent, about 9,000 rows. Each night an unattended job walks the whole table and requests each agreement's status one by one, including agreements that were completed or voided months ago. The job now hits the account's hourly ceiling and squeezes out the daytime lettings app. Connect cannot be used yet because the security review of the listener is still open. The records system runs on an on-premises SQL server. What should the job do instead?

options.text: Spread the 9,000 individual status requests evenly across the night, so that no single hour goes over the account's 3,000-call allowance
Pause about 1.2 seconds between individual status requests, so that the job never comes near the 30-second burst limit while it walks the table
Ask an administrator to raise the hourly limit, so that the nightly job and the daytime app both fit, and leave the job's logic unchanged
Skip agreements already completed, declined or voided, and check the rest with one listStatusChanges call covering the time since the last run

answerText: Skip agreements already completed, declined or voided, and check the rest with one listStatusChanges call covering the time since the last run
explanation: Docusign says not to poll an object once it has reached a terminal state, and to use list methods with a time span instead of per-envelope calls when Connect is unavailable. The clue 'completed or voided months ago' shows the waste.
whyNotOthers: D is right because it removes thousands of pointless calls. The trap is B: pacing is good practice, but the problem is the hourly total, not the burst rate. A still makes 9,000 needless calls, and C raises the limit without fixing an inefficient app, which also blocks the limit increase.

optionExplanations.A: Spreading the same 9,000 calls still wastes the allowance on agreements that can never change.
optionExplanations.B: Pacing avoids burst errors but does not reduce the hourly total, which is the real problem.
optionExplanations.C: An inefficient app is exactly what blocks Update Hourly Limit; fix the calls instead.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. Never poll terminal envelopes; one listStatusChanges call covers the rest.

decode.needs: Stop polling envelopes in a terminal state; use one listStatusChanges call for the rest.
clues: completed or voided months ago -> terminal state, never changes
one by one for 9,000 rows -> per-envelope polling instead of a list call
Connect cannot be used yet -> efficient polling is the fallback
on-premises SQL server -> red herring

concept.title: No polling of terminal envelopes
concept.line: Do not poll envelopes in a terminal state; batch remaining status checks with listStatusChanges.

stem: An account's hourly limit has been raised to 5,000 through API limit management. Which calls count toward those 5,000?

options.text: Only eSignature REST API calls; SOAP calls have their own allowance
Only calls made by the integration key whose owner raised the limit
All eSignature REST and SOAP calls, plus /oauth/userinfo requests
Every Docusign API, including the Admin, Rooms and Click APIs
eSignature REST and SOAP calls combined, from all of the account's apps

answerText: eSignature REST and SOAP calls combined, from all of the account's apps
explanation: Limit updates apply to the eSignature REST API and the eSignature SOAP API together, counting calls from all apps associated with the account.
whyNotOthers: E is right. The trap is C: REST and SOAP is correct, but userinfo requests have their own separate limits per user and per integration key. A leaves out SOAP, B treats the limit as per key, and D extends it beyond eSignature.

optionExplanations.A: Limit updates cover REST and SOAP together; SOAP is not separate.
optionExplanations.B: The hourly limit is per account, shared by all its apps.
optionExplanations.C: Userinfo requests have their own per-user and per-key limits.
optionExplanations.D: Limit management applies to eSignature REST and SOAP calls only.
optionExplanations.E: Correct. A raised limit counts eSignature REST and SOAP calls from all apps on the account.

concept.title: Scope of the hourly limit
concept.line: A raised hourly limit covers eSignature REST and SOAP calls combined, from all apps on the account.

topic: Template reference with an embedded signer
stem: Wexford Dental's check-in kiosk asks each patient to sign a consent form that already exists as a server template with a role named patient. The patient signs immediately on the kiosk's screen and must not get an email from Docusign. The front desk does not want any paper copies. The practice-management system assigns each patient a chart number that is unique to that patient. The kiosk software is supplied by a hardware vendor. How should the integration build the Envelopes:create request?

options.text: templateId plus a templateRoles entry with roleName patient, name and email, and status sent; then pass the chart number as clientUserId in createRecipient
templateId plus a templateRoles entry with roleName patient, the patient's name and email, and a clientUserId such as the chart number, with status sent
templateId plus a templateRoles entry with roleName patient, name, email and clientUserId, with status created so the kiosk can open the draft
templateId plus a recipients.signers entry with roleName patient and clientUserId, with status sent

answerText: templateId plus a templateRoles entry with roleName patient, the patient's name and email, and a clientUserId such as the chart number, with status sent
explanation: In the template reference model each person is assigned through templateRoles, so the clientUserId that makes the patient an embedded signer goes there, with status sent.
whyNotOthers: B is right. The trap is A: createRecipient does take clientUserId, but it must match a value set at envelope creation. C leaves the envelope as a draft, and D uses the direct documents structure.

optionExplanations.A: clientUserId must be set on the recipient when the envelope is created; createRecipient must match it, it cannot add it later.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. In the template reference model the embedded flag goes on the templateRoles entry, and embedded signing needs status sent.
optionExplanations.C: A recipient view needs the envelope in sent status; a draft cannot be signed.
optionExplanations.D: The template reference model assigns people to roles through templateRoles, not a recipients array.

decode.needs: templateRoles entry with clientUserId, status sent
clues: signs immediately on the kiosk, no email -> embedded signer (clientUserId)
consent form exists as a server template -> template reference model, templateRoles
hardware vendor -> red herring

concept.title: Embedded signer from a template
concept.line: With the template reference model, put clientUserId on the templateRoles entry at creation and send with status sent.

stem: Which Agreement Manager operation is documented as a data source for RAG applications and copilots that answer questions across many agreements?

options.text: CreateAgreementSummary
GetAgreementsList
DeleteAgreement
getAgreementSummary

answerText: GetAgreementsList
explanation: The GetAgreementsList reference lists 'providing data for RAG applications or Copilots' as a use case, because it returns agreements with parties, provisions and metadata.
whyNotOthers: B is right because the list operation supplies structured data across agreements. The trap is A: it is an AI feature, but it writes an overview of a single agreement rather than serving as the data source. C removes agreements, and D does not exist.

optionExplanations.A: CreateAgreementSummary creates an AI overview of one agreement; it is not the documented RAG data source.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. GetAgreementsList returns agreements with parties, provisions and metadata and is documented for RAG and copilots.
optionExplanations.C: DeleteAgreement removes an agreement; it supplies no data.
optionExplanations.D: There is no getAgreementSummary operation; summaries come from the POST CreateAgreementSummary.

concept.title: List operation feeds RAG
concept.line: GetAgreementsList is the documented data source for RAG apps and copilots over Agreement Manager data.

stem: When delivery of a Connect message fails, Docusign retries with exponential back-off. Which sequence describes the retries?

options.text: After 1, 2, 4 and 8 minutes, then every hour until the listener responds or 24 hours have passed
After 5, 10, 20 and 40 minutes, then 1 hour, 2 hours and 1 day, then once a day for a 15-day span
Every 15 minutes for the first day, then once a day for a 15-day span
After 5 minutes, then every hour for 15 days until the listener responds with a 2xx

answerText: After 5, 10, 20 and 40 minutes, then 1 hour, 2 hours and 1 day, then once a day for a 15-day span
explanation: The documented retry sequence is 5, 10, 20 and 40 minutes, then one hour, two hours and one day, then once per day for a 15-day span.
whyNotOthers: B is right because it matches the documented back-off. The trap is D: it has the right first step and the right 15-day limit, but not the doubling intervals in between. A doubles but ends far too early, and C mixes up the 15-minute polling rule with retries.

optionExplanations.A: The steps and the 24-hour limit do not match the documented schedule.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. 5, 10, 20, 40 minutes, 1 hour, 2 hours, 1 day, then daily for a 15-day span.
optionExplanations.C: This mixes up the 15-minute polling limit with the retry schedule.
optionExplanations.D: The first step and 15-day span are right, but the retries back off exponentially rather than running hourly.

concept.title: Connect retry back-off
concept.line: Failed deliveries retry at 5, 10, 20, 40 minutes, 1 hour, 2 hours, 1 day, then daily for a 15-day span.

stem: Brindle Insurance points two configurations at the same listener: an account-level configuration for envelopes Brindle sends, and a Recipient Connect configuration for envelopes that partner firms send to Brindle's claims staff. Both deliver JSON SIM messages, and the payloads look the same. The listener must route recipient-side events to a separate queue for the claims team without guessing from the content. Which approach does Docusign suggest?

options.text: Check the event name, because Recipient Connect messages use event names that start with recipient- rather than envelope-
Check the userId element, which identifies the envelope's sender in both kinds of message
Switch the Recipient Connect configuration to XML, so the two kinds of message arrive in different formats
Compare the accountId with Brindle's account, because recipient-side messages carry the sending firm's account ID
Give the Recipient Connect configuration its own listener URL, or add a query parameter such as ?customrecipient to its URL

answerText: Give the Recipient Connect configuration its own listener URL, or add a query parameter such as ?customrecipient to its URL
explanation: Connect and Recipient Connect deliver the same payloads; Docusign suggests a separate listener for Recipient Connect or a query parameter such as ?customrecipient on its URL to identify those messages.
whyNotOthers: E is right because a distinct URL or query parameter identifies the configuration without guessing from the payload. The trap is D: accountId does differ, but for Recipient Connect it identifies the recipient's account, not the sender's, so the stated rule is wrong. A fails because Recipient Connect also sends envelope-completed, B is false because userId identifies the recipient in Recipient Connect, and C fails because Recipient Connect is JSON-only.

optionExplanations.A: Recipient Connect also supports envelope-completed, so the event prefix is not reliable.
optionExplanations.B: In Recipient Connect messages, userId identifies the recipient, not the sender.
optionExplanations.C: Recipient Connect messages are always JSON, so the formats cannot be split this way.
optionExplanations.D: For Recipient Connect, accountId identifies the recipient's account, so this rule misreads the field.
optionExplanations.E: Correct. Docusign suggests a dedicated listener or a query parameter such as ?customrecipient to identify Recipient Connect messages.

decode.needs: Separate listener URL or ?customrecipient query parameter
clues: two configurations, same listener, payloads look the same -> identify by URL
without guessing from the content -> do not infer from event names or IDs
partner firms send to claims staff -> Recipient Connect side

concept.title: Mark Recipient Connect by URL
concept.line: Account and Recipient Connect payloads are the same; use a separate URL or a query parameter to tell them apart.

stem: A compliance report must include only agreements whose status is COMPLETE. Which GetAgreementsList query parameter does this?

options.text: status=COMPLETE
metadata.status=COMPLETE
provisions.status=COMPLETE
state=COMPLETE

answerText: status=COMPLETE
explanation: GetAgreementsList has a top-level status query parameter; agreement status values include PENDING, COMPLETE and INACTIVE.
whyNotOthers: A is right because status is a top-level agreement property and filter. The trap is B: metadata holds record history such as created_at and created_by, not status. C and D name parameters that do not exist.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. status is a top-level filter on GetAgreementsList.
optionExplanations.B: metadata carries record history (created_at, created_by), not the agreement status.
optionExplanations.C: provisions hold contract terms such as dates and values, not the agreement status.
optionExplanations.D: There is no state parameter on GetAgreementsList.

concept.title: Top-level status filter
concept.line: Agreement status (for example PENDING, COMPLETE, INACTIVE) is a top-level property and GetAgreementsList filter.

stem: What does PUT {baseUri}/restapi/v2.1/accounts/{accountId}/envelopes/{envelopeId}/docGenFormFields do?

options.text: Lists the document generation fields available in the envelope
Fills in the document generation field values of a draft envelope
Sends the draft envelope once all fields are filled
Updates the tab values of a standard template's recipients

answerText: Fills in the document generation field values of a draft envelope
explanation: The docGenFormFields path is read with GET and updated with PUT; PUT supplies the values (and applies conditional content).
whyNotOthers: B is right. The trap is A: same path, but listing is GET. C is a different call, and D confuses doc gen fields with tabs.

optionExplanations.A: Listing uses GET on the same path.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. This is DocumentGeneration:updateEnvelopeDocGenFormFields.
optionExplanations.C: Sending is Envelopes:update with status sent.
optionExplanations.D: Tab values are updated through the recipient tabs endpoints.

concept.title: Doc gen field endpoints
concept.line: GET .../docGenFormFields lists fields; PUT .../docGenFormFields sets values before the envelope is sent.

topic: What the OAuth for Connect token is for
stem: Sable Logistics enabled OAuth for Connect with its Okta tenant, so each Connect message arrives with a bearer token in the Authorization header. A developer proposes reusing that token to call the eSignature API and download the signed documents, which would save building a JWT Grant flow. The listener runs on AWS Lambda and handles about 2,000 messages a day. Which statement is correct?

options.text: The token can call the eSignature API, because Docusign obtained it with the Client Credentials grant, which is a server-to-server flow
The token works for the eSignature API only if the Okta client is also registered as an integration key in the Docusign account
The token is issued by Docusign's account server, so the listener can exchange it for an eSignature access token
The token only proves to the listener that the message came from Docusign; the listener validates it, and API calls still need a Docusign token such as JWT Grant
The token is a signature over the message body, so it replaces HMAC and proves that the content was not changed after sending

answerText: The token only proves to the listener that the message came from Docusign; the listener validates it, and API calls still need a Docusign token such as JWT Grant
explanation: OAuth for Connect uses Client Credentials with your own authorization server; unlike other Docusign OAuth grants it is not used to get a token for Docusign API calls, and verifying the token is the listener's responsibility.
whyNotOthers: D is right because the token only authenticates Connect messages to your listener. The trap is A: the grant really is Client Credentials, but the token comes from Sable's own Okta and is not valid for the Docusign API. B and C invent links between Okta and Docusign's account server, and E confuses a bearer token with HMAC's body signature.

optionExplanations.A: The grant is Client Credentials, but the token is issued by Sable's Okta for its own listener, not for Docusign APIs.
optionExplanations.B: Registering the Okta client in Docusign does not make an Okta token valid for the eSignature API.
optionExplanations.C: The token comes from Sable's own authorization server, not from Docusign's account server.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. OAuth for Connect authenticates the messages; the listener must verify the token, and API calls need a normal Docusign access token.
optionExplanations.E: A bearer token does not sign the body, so it gives no integrity check; HMAC does that.

decode.needs: Keep a separate Docusign OAuth flow for API calls; the Connect token only authenticates inbound messages
clues: bearer token in the Authorization header -> OAuth for Connect, issued by the company's own IdP
reuse it to call the eSignature API -> not what the token is for
AWS Lambda, 2,000 messages a day -> red herrings

concept.title: Connect OAuth tokens are inbound-only
concept.line: The OAuth for Connect token authenticates messages to your listener; it cannot call Docusign APIs, and your listener must validate it.

stem: In an Envelopes:create request, which signer property and value require knowledge-based authentication?

options.text: accessCode set to KBA
idCheckConfigurationName: ID Check
requireIdLookup set to ID Check
authenticationMethod set to KBA

answerText: idCheckConfigurationName: ID Check
explanation: The KBA how-to sets idCheckConfigurationName to the string ID Check on the signer.
whyNotOthers: B is right. The trap is D: authenticationMethod only records an authentication your own app performed; it enforces nothing. A would make KBA the literal access code, and C names a different property.

optionExplanations.A: This would make the literal text KBA the access code.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. idCheckConfigurationName with ID Check requests KBA.
optionExplanations.C: idCheckConfigurationName, not requireIdLookup, carries the ID Check value.
optionExplanations.D: authenticationMethod records your own authentication; it does not enforce KBA.

concept.title: KBA in Envelopes:create
concept.line: KBA is requested with idCheckConfigurationName set to ID Check; authenticationMethod only records your own authentication.

stem: Besides calling /oauth/userinfo, where can a developer find the base URI of the production account that hosts the app?

options.text: The developer account's Apps and Keys page, which shows the production URI after promotion
The email Docusign sends when the key's status changes to Live
The API Limit panel of the API Usage Center
The Account Base URI section of the production account's Apps and Keys page

answerText: The Account Base URI section of the production account's Apps and Keys page
explanation: The production data center for API calls can be taken from base_uri in /oauth/userinfo or from the Account Base URI section of the Apps and Keys page in the production account.
whyNotOthers: D is right. The trap is A: Apps and Keys is the right page, but in the developer account it shows the developer base URI. B and C do not show base URIs.

optionExplanations.A: The developer account's Apps and Keys shows the developer environment's base URI, not production's.
optionExplanations.B: The Live notification does not provide the account base URI.
optionExplanations.C: The API Limit panel shows hourly and burst limits only.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. The production account's Apps and Keys page lists the Account Base URI.

concept.title: Production base URI sources
concept.line: Get the production base URI from /oauth/userinfo (cached) or from Account Base URI in production Apps and Keys.

stem: Each HMAC key defined for Connect adds its own X-DocuSign-Signature-N header to messages. Up to how many HMAC keys can be defined?

options.text: Unlimited

explanation: Connect adds one header for each HMAC key you define, up to one hundred, each containing the body hashed with that key using HMAC-SHA256.
whyNotOthers: D is right because the documented limit is one hundred keys. The trap is A: examples usually show two keys during rotation, but two is not the limit. B is too low and C is wrong because there is a limit.

optionExplanations.A: Two keys is the common rotation example, not the limit.
optionExplanations.B: Ten is below the documented limit.
optionExplanations.C: There is a documented maximum, so the number is not unlimited.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. Each message includes one signature header per defined key, up to one hundred.

concept.title: One header per HMAC key
concept.line: Connect adds one X-DocuSign-Signature-N header per defined HMAC key, up to one hundred keys.

topic: Rotating an HMAC secret without rejecting messages
stem: Pelican Pharmacy's security policy requires its Connect HMAC secret to be rotated every 90 days, and no genuine Connect message may be rejected or lost during a rotation. The account currently has one active HMAC key, the listener validates X-DocuSign-Signature-1, and deployments to the listener take about an hour to reach every region. Which rotation sequence meets the policy?

options.text: Delete the current key, create a new one, and deploy the new secret to the listener right afterwards, accepting a short window of rejected messages
Create a new key, then change the listener to validate only X-DocuSign-Signature-1, because Docusign always puts the newest key in the first header
Turn off HMAC during the rotation and rely on Basic authentication until the new key has been deployed to every region
Create a new key and delete the old one at once, because messages already in a retry cycle are re-signed with the new key
Add a second key so messages carry two signature headers, deploy a listener that accepts a match on either, then delete the old key once every region uses the new one

answerText: Add a second key so messages carry two signature headers, deploy a listener that accepts a match on either, then delete the old key once every region uses the new one
explanation: Each HMAC key adds its own X-DocuSign-Signature-N header, and a match on any one verifies the message; adding a second key before removing the first lets the listener switch secrets without rejecting genuine messages.
