whyNotOthers: E is right because overlapping keys keep messages verifiable during the hour-long deployment. The trap is D: it sounds efficient, but deleting the old key at once leaves regions still on the old secret unable to verify messages. A accepts rejected messages, B assumes header order that Docusign does not define that way (headers follow the keys in order), and C drops HMAC protection during rotation.

optionExplanations.A: The policy does not allow any genuine message to be rejected.
optionExplanations.B: Header N carries the hash for key N, so the newest key is not moved to header 1.
optionExplanations.C: Turning off HMAC removes the integrity check during the rotation.
optionExplanations.D: Regions still on the old secret would fail to verify messages until the deployment finishes.
optionExplanations.E: Correct. With two keys each message carries two headers, and matching either verifies it, so the old key can be removed safely afterwards.

decode.needs: Overlapping HMAC keys during rotation
clues: no genuine message may be rejected -> keep both keys active during the change
deployments take about an hour -> listeners need to accept either signature for a while
rotated every 90 days -> red herring about the schedule

concept.title: Overlap HMAC keys to rotate
concept.line: Add a new HMAC key alongside the old one, accept either signature, then remove the old key, so no genuine message is rejected.

stem: Ostrava Shipping's JWT Grant service has sent charter agreements for a year as the user charters-bot, which consented once with scope=signature impersonation. The analytics team now wants the same service to pull AI-extracted agreement data through the Navigator API, so a developer added adm_store_unified_repo_read to the scope claim of the JWT. Token requests now fail with consent_required, although the eSignature calls worked yesterday and the RSA key has not changed. The service runs on a managed container platform. What is the fix?

options.text: Remove impersonation from charters-bot's original consent, because it conflicts with the Navigator scopes
Keep the JWT scope as signature only, because scopes beyond signature are ignored once consent has been granted for a user
Get charters-bot's consent again for signature impersonation adm_store_unified_repo_read and keep the scope in the JWT
Generate a new RSA key pair, because adding a scope invalidates every assertion signed with the old private key
Send adm_store_unified_repo_read as a body parameter of the token request instead of in the JWT scope claim

answerText: Get charters-bot's consent again for signature impersonation adm_store_unified_repo_read and keep the scope in the JWT
explanation: consent_required means the user has not consented to the app or to a scope it now requests. Consent must be granted again with the new scope included before the JWT can ask for it.
whyNotOthers: C is right because the existing consent covered only signature and impersonation. The trap is B: dropping the scope makes tokens issue again, but the Navigator calls would then lack the scope they need. A breaks JWT consent, D is unrelated to scopes, and E puts the scope in the wrong place.

optionExplanations.A: impersonation is required for JWT consent; removing it would break the service.
optionExplanations.B: Tokens would issue, but without adm_store_unified_repo_read the Navigator calls are not permitted.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. Re-consent with the added scope, then the JWT may request it.
optionExplanations.D: Scopes are not tied to the RSA key; the key is still valid.
optionExplanations.E: Scopes for JWT Grant are requested in the JWT's scope claim.

decode.needs: Collect consent again including the Navigator scope
clues: 'consented once with signature impersonation' -> new scope not covered
'added a scope, now consent_required' -> consent missing for the requested scope
'RSA key has not changed' and 'managed container platform' -> red herrings

concept.title: New scope needs new consent
concept.line: A token can only carry scopes the user has consented to; adding an API scope later means collecting consent again.

stem: Fenwick Machinery's equipment contracts are signed in order by the customer's buyer, the customer's CFO (often on a phone) and finally Fenwick's sales director. The warehouse must schedule a shipment only when a contract is fully executed, and logistics will not accept false starts. Sales operations sometimes adds a legal reviewer after the sales director by correcting the envelope. A listener already receives messages from an account-level JSON SIM configuration, and each contract has three documents. Which trigger should start shipment scheduling?

options.text: Subscribe to recipient-completed and schedule shipment when the buyer's event arrives, because the buyer is the party that places the order
Subscribe to envelope-sent and schedule shipment right away, then cancel the shipment if the contract is later declined or voided
Subscribe to recipient-completed and schedule shipment when the sales director's event arrives, because the director is the last signer in the routing order
Poll Envelopes:get for each open contract every 15 minutes and schedule shipment when the returned status is completed
Subscribe to envelope-completed and start shipment scheduling when that event arrives, because it is sent only after every recipient in the final routing has finished

answerText: Subscribe to envelope-completed and start shipment scheduling when that event arrives, because it is sent only after every recipient in the final routing has finished
explanation: "Fully executed" means the envelope is complete, and envelope-completed is pushed only when every recipient has finished, even if the routing changes through a correction.
whyNotOthers: E is right because envelope-completed is the definitive signal that every recipient is done. The trap is C: the director is normally last, but the stem says a legal reviewer is sometimes added after the director, so the director's recipient-completed can arrive before the contract is complete. A and B start too early, and D works but polls when a push event is already available.

optionExplanations.A: The buyer signs first; shipping on that event ignores the CFO and the director.
optionExplanations.B: Starting at envelope-sent creates exactly the false starts logistics rejects.
optionExplanations.C: The director is not always last, because a legal reviewer is sometimes added afterwards by correction.
optionExplanations.D: Polling every 15 minutes is allowed but adds API calls and delay when the listener already receives pushed events.
optionExplanations.E: Correct. envelope-completed fires once every recipient has completed, whatever the final routing.

decode.needs: Subscribe to envelope-completed
clues: only when fully executed, no false starts -> envelope-level completion, not a recipient event
a legal reviewer is sometimes added after the director -> the last signer can change
CFO signs on a phone, three documents -> red herrings

concept.title: Envelope-completed means fully executed
concept.line: Use envelope-completed for actions that need every recipient done; recipient-completed suits steps tied to one signer.

stem: A DevOps team wants its CI pipeline to create and activate new web form configurations from JSON definitions through the Web Forms API. What is true?

options.text: The API can create them, but activation is manual
Configurations can be created only as standalone forms
Configurations cannot be created through the API
Instances:createInstance can create a configuration

answerText: Configurations cannot be created through the API
explanation: Web form configurations cannot be created through the API; they are created and activated in the Web Forms builder, and the API creates instances from them.
whyNotOthers: C is right. The trap is A: activation is indeed required before instances can be created, but creation is not available by API either. B and D invent capabilities.

optionExplanations.A: Neither creation nor activation of configurations is available in the API.
optionExplanations.B: No configuration type can be created through the API.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. Configurations are built and activated in the Web Forms builder.
optionExplanations.D: createInstance creates instances from an existing, activated configuration.

concept.title: Web form configurations by API
concept.line: Configurations are built and activated in the Web Forms builder; the API reads them and creates instances.

stem: AccountBrands requests fail in a newly provisioned account. Which account settings must be enabled for the brands API to be used?

options.text: canSelfBrandSend, canSelfBrandSign, or both
Both canSelfBrandSend and canSelfBrandSign together
canSelfBrandSign only, as brands affect recipients
None; only the brand's group assignment matters

answerText: canSelfBrandSend, canSelfBrandSign, or both
explanation: Branding for sending or signing must be enabled: canSelfBrandSend, canSelfBrandSign, or both must be true.
whyNotOthers: A is right because either setting is enough. The trap is B: both are allowed but not both required. C ignores sending branding, and D confuses who may use a brand with whether branding is enabled.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. Either setting, or both, enables the brands resource.
optionExplanations.B: Either setting alone is sufficient; both are not required.
optionExplanations.C: canSelfBrandSend alone also enables branding.
optionExplanations.D: Group assignment controls use of a brand, not whether branding is enabled.

concept.title: Branding account settings
concept.line: The AccountBrands API needs branding enabled: canSelfBrandSend, canSelfBrandSign, or both.

stem: Kittering Logistics' carrier-onboarding portal uses Confidential Authorization Code Grant and works in its test environment. The team stood up a new staging site and now sends users to /oauth/auth with redirect_uri=https://staging.kittering.com/auth/callback/ but Docusign returns an invalid redirect URI error instead of completing the sign-in. The integration key lists https://staging.kittering.com/auth/callback as a redirect URI. The staging site runs on a new Kubernetes cluster with a freshly issued TLS certificate, and the test environment still works normally. What should the team do?

options.text: Add the staging domain to the CORS allowed origins on the integration key so that Docusign accepts the redirect
Make the redirect_uri match a registered URI exactly, trailing slash included, or register the slash form
URL-encode the redirect_uri a second time, because a single encoding leaves the slashes ambiguous to Docusign
Move the redirect_uri from the /oauth/auth request to the /oauth/token request, where Docusign validates it
Register only https://staging.kittering.com on the key, because Docusign matches redirect URIs by prefix

answerText: Make the redirect_uri match a registered URI exactly, trailing slash included, or register the slash form
explanation: The redirect URI in the request must match one registered on the integration key exactly, including slash characters; the request has a trailing slash that the registered value lacks.
whyNotOthers: B is right because Docusign requires an exact string match. The trap is E: registering only the domain fails because matching is exact, not by prefix. A confuses redirect URIs with CORS origins, C breaks the value, and D is wrong because the redirect URI is used on the /oauth/auth request.

optionExplanations.A: CORS origins control browser API calls; they do not register redirect URIs.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. Redirect URIs must match exactly, including a trailing slash.
optionExplanations.C: Double encoding produces a different string that still will not match.
optionExplanations.D: Docusign needs the redirect URI on the authorization request to know where to send the code.
optionExplanations.E: Matching is exact, not prefix-based, so a bare domain does not cover the callback path.

decode.needs: Fix an exact-match failure of the registered redirect URI
clues: 'callback/' versus registered 'callback' -> trailing slash mismatch
'invalid redirect URI error' -> registration does not match exactly
'new Kubernetes cluster, fresh TLS certificate' -> red herrings

concept.title: Redirect URIs match exactly
concept.line: The redirect_uri sent to /oauth/auth must exactly match a URI registered on the integration key, including slashes.

stem: A developer wants a timeline of one integration's successful and failed requests over the last two months, with a call log she can filter by response code. Which tool provides this?

options.text: API request logging under My Preferences
The API Dashboard under Admin > Apps and Keys
The API Usage Center's API Calls graph
The Connect logs in eSignature Admin

answerText: The API Dashboard under Admin > Apps and Keys
explanation: The API Dashboard shows a timeline of successful and failed requests for an integration for up to the last 90 days, plus a call log filterable by time interval and response code.
whyNotOthers: B is right because of the 90-day range and response-code filter. The trap is C: the API Usage Center also charts calls with a succeeded or failed view, but its date ranges go back only 30 days. A keeps up to 50 requests, and D covers webhook deliveries, not API calls.

optionExplanations.A: Request logging keeps at most 50 requests, not a two-month timeline.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. The API Dashboard covers up to 90 days and filters the call log by response code.
optionExplanations.C: The API Usage Center's date ranges stop at 30 days, so two months is out of reach.
optionExplanations.D: Connect logs describe webhook deliveries, not the app's API requests.

concept.title: API Dashboard scope
concept.line: The API Dashboard shows up to 90 days of successful and failed requests per integration, filterable by response code.

stem: Crestmoor Clinics built a patient-intake process with the Web Forms API in its developer account: staff send each patient a web form, and a consent agreement is generated after submission. The clinic has taken eSignature integrations live before through Apps and Keys. Its production plan was bought two years ago for basic sending. Go-live is due in a month, and the clinic is also opening a new site with its own reception staff. What should the team plan?

options.text: Press Start Go live in Apps and Keys as for its eSignature apps; the web form configurations are copied into production together with the integration key
Recreate each web form by hand in the production account first, then press Start Go live so that the review can see the forms working in production
Confirm the production plan includes the Web Forms API, request go-live through a Support case, and move each form configuration by download and upload
Change nothing in the plan, because the Web Forms API is part of every production plan, and copy the forms with the eSignature template migration tool

answerText: Confirm the production plan includes the Web Forms API, request go-live through a Support case, and move each form configuration by download and upload
explanation: The Web Forms API is available in all developer accounts but only in certain production plans; its go-live is requested through a Docusign Support case, and web form configurations must be downloaded from the developer environment and uploaded to production. The clue 'plan bought for basic sending' makes the plan check essential.
whyNotOthers: C is right because it covers plan, route and migration. The trap is A: Start Go live is the eSignature route, and configurations are never copied with the key. B also relies on Start Go live, and D wrongly assumes every plan includes Web Forms.

optionExplanations.A: Web Forms go-live is requested through Support, and configurations are never copied with the key.
optionExplanations.B: Rebuilding by hand is unnecessary, and Start Go live is not the Web Forms route.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. Check the plan, request go-live through Support, and transfer configuration files.
optionExplanations.D: Web Forms API is only in certain production plans, and configurations move by download and upload.

decode.needs: Plan a Web Forms API go-live: plan includes Web Forms, Support case, move configuration files.
clues: Web Forms API in the developer account -> available in all developer accounts, not all production plans
plan bought for basic sending -> check the plan includes the Web Forms API
went live through Apps and Keys before -> Web Forms uses a Support case instead
new site opening -> red herring

concept.title: Web Forms API go-live
concept.line: Web Forms API go-live needs a plan that includes it, a Support case, and configurations moved by download and upload.

topic: Including envelope custom fields in messages
stem: Quarry Hill Software's sales app sends quotes through the API and stores the CRM opportunity number in an envelope custom field. Finance's listener, fed by an account-level JSON SIM configuration subscribed to envelope-completed, must post each closed deal to the right opportunity without calling the eSignature API back. Today the messages contain only accountId, userId and envelopeId. The configuration must stay JSON SIM because the same listener also handles Maestro workflow events. What change meets the need?

options.text: Add recipients to the configuration's includeData, so the opportunity number appears with each signer's details in the envelope summary
Add custom_fields to the configuration's includeData, so the envelope custom field values arrive in the envelope summary of each message
Add tabs to the configuration's includeData, so the opportunity number arrives together with the field values the signers completed
Switch the configuration to XML aggregate, which always sends the full envelope including its custom fields with every message
Have the listener call Envelopes:get after each message to read the envelope's custom fields and find the opportunity number

answerText: Add custom_fields to the configuration's includeData, so the envelope custom field values arrive in the envelope summary of each message
explanation: JSON SIM messages are small by default; includeData lets you add parts of the envelope summary, and custom_fields carries the envelope custom fields where the opportunity number is stored.
whyNotOthers: B is right because the number is in an envelope custom field, which includeData custom_fields adds. The trap is C: tabs is the right choice for values signers type into document fields, but the opportunity number is an envelope custom field, not a tab. A adds recipient data, D breaks the JSON SIM requirement, and E makes the API call the stem forbids.

optionExplanations.A: Recipient data does not include envelope custom fields.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. includeData custom_fields adds envelope custom field values to the envelope summary in each message.
optionExplanations.C: tabs carries document field values; the opportunity number is an envelope custom field, not a tab.
optionExplanations.D: The configuration must stay JSON SIM because Maestro workflow events require it.
optionExplanations.E: Calling the API back is exactly what the stem rules out.

decode.needs: includeData custom_fields on the JSON SIM configuration
clues: opportunity number stored in an envelope custom field -> custom_fields, not tabs
without calling the eSignature API back -> the data must be in the message
must stay JSON SIM for Maestro events -> no switch to XML

concept.title: Choose includeData items deliberately
concept.line: JSON SIM messages are minimal by default; add only the needed includeData items, such as custom_fields or tabs, to the envelope summary.

stem: Besides the eSignature scopes, which OAuth scope must an app request to call TabInfo:GetConnectedFieldsTabGroups?

options.text: extended
aow_manage
webforms_read
adm_store_unified_repo_read

answerText: adm_store_unified_repo_read
explanation: Calling the Connected Fields API requires adm_store_unified_repo_read in addition to the eSignature scopes.
whyNotOthers: D is right. The trap is B: aow_manage is the Maestro workflow scope, another api-d.docusign.com service. A is for long-lived refresh tokens and C is a Web Forms scope.

optionExplanations.A: extended relates to refresh token lifetime, not connected fields.
optionExplanations.B: aow_manage is the Workflow Builder (Maestro) API scope.
optionExplanations.C: webforms_read is for the Web Forms API.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. adm_store_unified_repo_read is required for the Connected Fields API.

concept.title: Connected Fields API scope
concept.line: Calling TabInfo:GetConnectedFieldsTabGroups needs adm_store_unified_repo_read plus the eSignature scopes.

stem: A developer at Calloway Freight writes a helper that calls Workflows:getWorkflowTriggerRequirements, reads the url property, and then removes everything after the question mark before posting the trigger request, because the company's API gateway logs full URLs. Since then every trigger attempt is rejected, even though the token includes signature and aow_manage, instance_name is set, and trigger_inputs match the schema exactly; the published workflow itself has not changed. The gateway was also upgraded last week. What is the fix?

options.text: Add the workflowId as a query parameter on the shortened URL, because the trigger URL needs the workflow ID in order to know which workflow to start
Request a new token with aow_manage, because the gateway strips the scopes from the bearer token whenever it rewrites the request URL
Move trigger_inputs into query parameters on the shortened URL, because the trigger endpoint reads starting values only from the query
Post to the full url with its mtid and mtsec query parameters, which Maestro generates at publication to authenticate and identify the workflow
Republish the workflow before each call, because the trigger URL's query parameters expire after every successful trigger and must be renewed

answerText: Post to the full url with its mtid and mtsec query parameters, which Maestro generates at publication to authenticate and identify the workflow
explanation: The trigger url includes the query parameters mtid and mtsec, generated when the workflow is published and 'used to authenticate the request and identify a valid workflow'; removing them breaks the trigger.
whyNotOthers: D is right because the only change was stripping the query string. The trap is A: identifying the workflow sounds like the missing piece, but the generated mtid and mtsec do that job and also authenticate the call. B blames scopes that the stem says are present, C moves the body into the query, and E invents expiry.

optionExplanations.A: The workflow is identified by the generated mtid/mtsec values, which were removed.
optionExplanations.B: The token already has the right scopes; a gateway rewrite does not change them.
optionExplanations.C: trigger_inputs belong in the JSON body.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. Keep the full url with mtid and mtsec; they authenticate the request and identify the workflow.
optionExplanations.E: The parameters are generated at publication; nothing says they expire per call.

decode.needs: Use the full trigger URL including mtid and mtsec
clues: removes everything after the question mark -> query parameters lost
scopes, instance_name and inputs are correct -> rules out the usual causes
gateway upgrade -> red herring

concept.title: Keep mtid and mtsec
concept.line: The trigger URL's mtid and mtsec query parameters authenticate the request and identify the workflow; never strip them.

stem: Whitmore Legal's matter-management system refreshes a signing dashboard every 30 minutes. Each refresh calls Envelopes:listStatusChanges to find changed envelopes, then makes a separate recipients call and a separate custom-fields call for every changed envelope. On busy days the app's efficiency score drops because of excessive recipient status requests. The firm's network policy forbids any inbound traffic and any cloud relay, so webhooks are not an option. The dashboard is used by about 60 partners. What change best reduces the calls?

options.text: Use the include parameter on the listStatusChanges call to return recipients and custom fields with the changed envelopes in one response
Keep the extra per-envelope calls but refresh every 15 minutes instead of 30, so that each refresh has fewer changed envelopes to process
Drop listStatusChanges and call EnvelopeRecipients:list for every active envelope at each refresh, so that recipient data is always complete
Add an envelope-level eventNotification to each new envelope for recipient events, which avoids creating an account-wide webhook configuration

answerText: Use the include parameter on the listStatusChanges call to return recipients and custom fields with the changed envelopes in one response
explanation: In eSignature REST API v2.1 the include parameter of Envelopes:listStatusChanges returns subsidiary objects such as recipients and custom fields in the same response. The clue 'separate recipients call for every changed envelope' is the waste to remove.
whyNotOthers: A is right because one call replaces many. The trap is D: envelope-level webhooks avoid polling, but they still need inbound traffic, which the policy forbids. B doubles the refreshes without removing per-envelope calls, and C replaces one list call with many per-envelope calls.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. include returns recipients and custom fields with listStatusChanges, removing per-envelope calls.
optionExplanations.B: More frequent refreshes add calls and keep the per-envelope pattern.
optionExplanations.C: Polling recipients for every active envelope is exactly the excessive recipient status pattern.
optionExplanations.D: eventNotification is still a webhook that needs inbound delivery, which the network policy forbids.

decode.needs: Fetch recipients and custom fields inside listStatusChanges with include instead of per-envelope calls.
clues: separate recipients call per changed envelope -> excessive recipient status requests
no inbound traffic or cloud relay -> no Connect or eventNotification
every 30 minutes -> refresh rate is not the problem

concept.title: Use include on list calls
concept.line: Use the include parameter on listStatusChanges to fetch recipients and other objects in one call.

stem: From where does a developer start the Go-Live request for an eSignature integration key?

options.text: The production account's Apps and Keys: Add App and Integration Key, then paste the developer key
A Docusign Support case asking for the key to be copied into production
The developer account's API Usage Center: Actions > Promote to production
The developer account's Apps and Keys: Actions > Start Go live, then log in to the production account

answerText: The developer account's Apps and Keys: Actions > Start Go live, then log in to the production account
explanation: Go-Live starts in the developer account's Apps and Keys list: Actions > Start Go live, then you log in to and select the production account that will host the key.
whyNotOthers: D is right because promotion starts from the key in the developer account. The trap is A: the key does end up in the production Apps and Keys, but you do not add it there by hand. B is the route for some other APIs such as the Web Forms API, not for eSignature keys, and C names a tool that only reports usage.

optionExplanations.A: You do not paste keys into production; Go-Live duplicates the key into the selected production account.
optionExplanations.B: A Support case is used for some APIs, such as Web Forms, but eSignature keys use Start Go live.
optionExplanations.C: The API Usage Center monitors efficiency and limits; it has no promote action.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. Actions > Start Go live in the developer Apps and Keys, then log in and select the production account.

concept.title: Start Go live in developer account
concept.line: Go-Live is started from the key in the developer account's Apps and Keys via Actions > Start Go live.

stem: Which field of the /oauth/token response tells an integration how long the new access token will remain valid?

options.text: exp, as a Unix epoch timestamp
expires_at, as an ISO 8601 date
token_lifetime, in hours
expires_in, in seconds
expires_in, in minutes

answerText: expires_in, in seconds
explanation: The token response includes expires_in, the number of seconds before the access token expires.
whyNotOthers: D is right: expires_in is given in seconds. The trap is E: the field name is right but the unit is wrong. A is a claim inside the JWT you build, not the token response, and B and C are not fields of the response.

optionExplanations.A: exp is a claim in the JWT assertion, not a token response field.
optionExplanations.B: There is no expires_at field.
optionExplanations.C: There is no token_lifetime field.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. expires_in is the number of seconds until the access token expires.
optionExplanations.E: expires_in is expressed in seconds, not minutes.

concept.title: Reading the token response
concept.line: The /oauth/token response returns access_token, token_type Bearer, expires_in (seconds), scope and, for Auth Code, refresh_token.

stem: Merrow Housing Association stores every signed tenancy agreement in cloud storage through a Store Files step from a file output extension app. During testing the step was given the hard-coded file name 'Tenancy agreement', and the storage system now holds dozens of files with the same name that the records team cannot match to tenants. Each stored file name must now be unique and traceable to the specific signed envelope and tenant, with no change to the app's code. The association is also moving to a new office in spring. What should the process builder do?

options.text: Ask the app's developers to add the List Directory Contents capability, so the step creates a separate folder automatically for every tenant
Change the file naming convention to include workflow variables, such as the envelope ID from the signing step and the participant's name
Add a Writeback step before Store Files that renames the previous file in storage, so the new agreement can reuse the fixed file name
Enable connected fields in the app so the tenant reference is written into the stored file's metadata rather than into its file name
Set the folder option to New Folder with the hard-coded name 'Tenancies', so each stored agreement is placed in its own new folder

answerText: Change the file naming convention to include workflow variables, such as the envelope ID from the signing step and the participant's name
explanation: A Store Files step's file naming convention can combine hard-coded text with workflow variables (step variables such as the envelope ID, participant variables such as name, instance variables), giving a unique name per agreement at run time.
whyNotOthers: B is right because variables make each name unique and traceable 'with no change to the app's code'. The trap is A: List Directory Contents enables folder selection, needs code changes, and does not create per-tenant folders by itself. C invents renaming, D misapplies connected fields (not supported in Maestro), and E uses a hard-coded name, so every new folder gets the same name.

optionExplanations.A: Requires code changes, and the capability only lets the UI list folders; it does not name files.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. Workflow variables such as the envelope ID and participant name make each file name unique at run time.
optionExplanations.C: Writeback updates records in a system of record; it is not a file-renaming tool.
optionExplanations.D: Connected fields are an eSignature extension and are not supported in Maestro workflows.
optionExplanations.E: A hard-coded folder name is identical for every instance, so nothing becomes traceable.

decode.needs: Use workflow variables in the Store Files naming convention
clues: unique and traceable to envelope and tenant -> envelope ID and participant variables
no change to the app's code -> step configuration only
office move -> red herring

concept.title: Variables in file naming
concept.line: File and folder naming in Store Files steps can mix fixed text with step, participant and instance variables for unique names.

stem: Marlow Realty's agent portal already lets agents sign and send specific documents. Agents now want to open their full Docusign workspace inside the portal, to browse their inbox and sent items, check statuses and use templates, without logging in to a separate site. Each agent has a Docusign user in the brokerage account, and the portal authenticates them with Authorization Code Grant. The portal was recently redesigned. Which call should the portal use?

options.text: EnvelopeViews:createSender on a new draft envelope, so the agent sees the Docusign sending screen
EnvelopeViews:createConsole, opening the returned URL for the signed-in agent
EnvelopeViews:createRecipient with the agent's clientUserId
EnvelopeViews:createCorrect for the agent's most recent envelope

answerText: EnvelopeViews:createConsole, opening the returned URL for the signed-in agent
explanation: To embed the whole Docusign web app (inbox, sent items, templates) for a user, use the console view, EnvelopeViews:createConsole.
whyNotOthers: B is right. The trap is A: the sender view is the closest embedded view, but it covers one draft envelope. C and D are also single-envelope views.

optionExplanations.A: The sender view is limited to preparing and sending one draft envelope, not the full workspace.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. The console view embeds the Docusign web app for the authenticated user.
optionExplanations.C: The recipient view is a signing session for one envelope.
optionExplanations.D: The correct view edits one sent envelope.

decode.needs: Embedded console view: EnvelopeViews:createConsole
clues: full Docusign workspace, inbox, sent items, templates -> console view
each agent is a Docusign user -> session for the authenticated user
portal recently redesigned -> red herring

concept.title: Embedded console view
concept.line: createConsole embeds the whole web app for a user; createSender, createRecipient and createCorrect each target one envelope.

stem: A records team imports a batch of legacy contracts into Agreement Manager. What happens to AI extraction for these contracts?

options.text: Nothing until the integration calls CreateAgreementSummary for each contract
Nothing, because AI extraction runs only on completed eSignature envelopes
It runs only after an administrator approves each contract for analysis
It runs automatically, filling in type, parties and provisions

answerText: It runs automatically, filling in type, parties and provisions
explanation: Whenever documents are uploaded to Agreement Manager or an envelope completes, AI analyzes them and populates type, parties and provisions automatically.
whyNotOthers: D is right because extraction is automatic for imported and envelope-sourced agreements. The trap is A: CreateAgreementSummary sounds like the trigger, but it only returns an AI overview. B ignores imported documents, and C invents an approval gate; review happens after extraction, not before.

optionExplanations.A: CreateAgreementSummary produces an AI-written overview; it does not start extraction.
optionExplanations.B: Uploaded documents are analyzed too, not only completed envelopes.
optionExplanations.C: There is no approval gate before analysis; reviewers confirm or correct values after extraction.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. Imported agreements are analyzed automatically and their AI insights are attached to the agreement.

concept.title: Extraction runs automatically
concept.line: Agreement Manager runs AI extraction automatically on imported documents and completed envelopes; no API call starts it.

stem: In JWT Grant, which body parameter of the /oauth/token request carries the signed JWT?

options.text: code
client_assertion
assertion
id_token
jwt

answerText: assertion
explanation: The request body is grant_type=urn:ietf:params:oauth:grant-type:jwt-bearer and assertion=<signed JWT>.
whyNotOthers: C is right: Docusign's token request names the field assertion. The trap is B: client_assertion is used by some other OAuth providers, but Docusign uses assertion. A belongs to Authorization Code Grant, D is the OpenID token returned for admin consent, and E is not a parameter.

optionExplanations.A: code is the authorization code in Authorization Code Grant.
optionExplanations.B: Docusign does not use client_assertion; the field is assertion.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. assertion holds the signed JWT, alongside grant_type jwt-bearer.
optionExplanations.D: id_token is returned when openid is requested; it is never sent to obtain a token.
optionExplanations.E: There is no jwt parameter.

concept.title: JWT token request fields
concept.line: JWT Grant posts grant_type=urn:ietf:params:oauth:grant-type:jwt-bearer and assertion=<signed JWT> to /oauth/token.

topic: Starting points for a new workflow
stem: Besides a blank canvas, a workflow template or an imported workflow, which two other starting points does Workflow Builder offer when creating a workflow? (Select two)

options.text: A sent envelope
An eSignature template
A PowerForm
A CLM document type
A Web Form

answerText: An eSignature template; A Web Form
explanation: You can build workflows from a new canvas, from a workflow template, from an eSignature template, from a Web Form, or by importing a workflow.
whyNotOthers: B and E are right per the course. The trap is C: a PowerForm is a self-service eSignature feature that sounds like a natural source, but it is not a starting point. A and D are not listed.

optionExplanations.A: Not a starting point for a workflow.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. A workflow can be created from an eSignature template.
optionExplanations.C: PowerForms are not a Workflow Builder starting point.
optionExplanations.D: CLM document types are not a starting point.
optionExplanations.E: Correct. A workflow can be created from a Web Form.

concept.title: Ways to create a workflow
concept.line: Create workflows from a blank canvas, workflow template, eSignature template, Web Form, or by importing one.

stem: Which statement about the sequence property in a composite templates request is correct?

options.text: Every server template and inline template needs a sequence, unique across the whole compositeTemplates array
Only inline templates need a sequence, because server templates are always applied first
Each server and inline template needs a sequence that is unique within its composite object, starting at 1
The sequence values decide the order in which documents appear in the envelope

answerText: Each server and inline template needs a sequence that is unique within its composite object, starting at 1
explanation: Every serverTemplate and inlineTemplate needs a sequence; values must be unique within a composite template object, and numbering should start at 1 in each.
whyNotOthers: C is right. The trap is A: it widens the uniqueness rule to the whole array. B drops server template sequences, and D confuses sequence with array order.

optionExplanations.A: Uniqueness applies within each composite template object, not across the array.
optionExplanations.B: Both server and inline templates need a sequence.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. Sequence values are required and must be unique within each composite template object.
optionExplanations.D: Document order follows the order of objects in the compositeTemplates array.

concept.title: Composite sequence rules
concept.line: Each server and inline template needs a sequence unique within its composite object; document order follows array order.

stem: Greywell Group's contract portal went live into the parent company's production account, which now manages the key. Greywell has just set up a separate production account for a newly formed business unit, with its own administrators and billing. Staff in that unit will sign in to the same portal with Authorization Code Grant. The project manager has budgeted two weeks for 'a second Go-Live into the new account' and asks whether it is needed. The portal's hosting contract renews next month. What is the right plan?

options.text: No second Go-Live: the promoted key can call any production account, so the unit's staff sign in, consent, and the portal uses their base URI
Run Start Go live again and select the new account, because a promoted key can call only the production account into which it was originally promoted
Create a new integration key in the new account and take it through Go-Live, because each production account must manage its own key for its own users
Move the business unit's users into the parent account, because one integration key cannot serve users who belong to two different production accounts

answerText: No second Go-Live: the promoted key can call any production account, so the unit's staff sign in, consent, and the portal uses their base URI
explanation: A promoted key is tied to one production account only for management purposes; after promotion it can make API calls against any production account. The clue 'separate production account' tempts a second promotion that is not needed.
whyNotOthers: A is right because management account and calling account are different ideas. The trap is B: the key is linked to the account it was promoted into, but only for management. C and D add work based on the same misunderstanding.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. The key can call any production account; users of the new account simply authenticate and consent.
optionExplanations.B: The promotion account manages the key; it does not restrict which accounts the key can call.
optionExplanations.C: A second key is unnecessary; one key can serve users of many production accounts.
optionExplanations.D: There is no need to merge accounts; one key works across production accounts.

decode.needs: Know that a promoted key is managed by one account but can call any production account.
clues: key managed by the parent's account -> management account only
separate production account for the new unit -> another account the same key can call
Authorization Code Grant -> users sign in and consent; base URI from userinfo
hosting contract renewal -> red herring

concept.title: Management account vs calling account
concept.line: A promoted key belongs to one production account for management but can call any production account.

stem: An app adds a webhook to individual envelopes it creates and wants JSON SIM messages. Where is the JSON SIM format specified?

options.text: In the account's Connect settings in eSignature Admin, which then apply to every envelope's webhook
On the Connect page of Organization Admin, which controls the format for all levels
In a ConnectConfigurations:create call with configurationType set to envelope
Nowhere, because envelope-level webhooks always send the legacy XML format
In the envelope's eventNotification object, alongside its URL and events

answerText: In the envelope's eventNotification object, alongside its URL and events
explanation: For envelope-level Connect, the JSON SIM settings are defined inside the envelope's eventNotification object together with the other envelope-level Connect values.
whyNotOthers: E is right because everything about an envelope-level webhook, including its format, is set in eventNotification. The trap is A: account settings define account-level configurations, but they do not set the format of per-envelope webhooks. B and C name configuration routes that do not apply to envelope-level webhooks, and D is false because JSON SIM is supported at envelope level.

optionExplanations.A: Account-level settings create account-level configurations; per-envelope webhooks carry their own settings.
optionExplanations.B: Organization Admin manages organization-level configurations, not the format of individual envelope webhooks.
optionExplanations.C: ConnectConfigurations:create takes configurationType custom or customrecipient; envelope-level webhooks use eventNotification instead.
optionExplanations.D: JSON SIM is supported for organization-, account- and envelope-level Connect.
optionExplanations.E: Correct. The JSON SIM syntax for envelope-level configurations is defined in the envelope's eventNotification object.

concept.title: Envelope webhook settings live in eventNotification
concept.line: An envelope-level webhook's URL, events and JSON SIM format are all set in the envelope's eventNotification object.

stem: Hollins Pharmacy lets patients update their insurance details through an embedded standalone web form, using the patient number as clientUserId. Some patients submit the form several times in a month. A nightly job must write each patient's most recent submitted details back to the pharmacy system. The job knows the configuration ID and the patient number but does not store instance IDs. How should it find the right instance?

options.text: Call Instances:getInstance with the patient number as the instance ID, because the clientUserId becomes the instance's identifier on creation.
Call Instances:listInstances filtered by client_user_id and take the instance with the earliest createdDateTime as the authoritative submission.
Call Instances:listInstances with the client_user_id query parameter and pick the SUBMITTED instance with the latest lastModifiedDateTime.
Read the envelopes array of the newest instance and call EnvelopeCustomFields:list on that envelope to get the submitted insurance details.

answerText: Call Instances:listInstances with the client_user_id query parameter and pick the SUBMITTED instance with the latest lastModifiedDateTime.
explanation: listInstances accepts a client_user_id query parameter; when several SUBMITTED instances share a clientUserId, instanceMetadata.lastModifiedDateTime identifies the most recent. The clue is 'most recent submitted details'.
whyNotOthers: C is right. The trap is B: it uses the right filter but picks the oldest instance. A fails because the instance ID is a Docusign GUID, and D fails because standalone configurations create no envelope.

optionExplanations.A: Instance IDs are GUIDs returned by createInstance, not the clientUserId.
optionExplanations.B: Right filter, but the earliest instance is not the most recent submission.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. Filter by client_user_id and take the latest SUBMITTED instance.
optionExplanations.D: Standalone configurations create no envelope, so the envelopes array is empty.

decode.needs: Find a user's latest submitted instance without stored instance IDs.
clues: 'patient number as clientUserId' -> client_user_id filter
'most recent submitted details' -> latest SUBMITTED instance
'standalone web form' -> no envelope to read

concept.title: Locating instances by user
concept.line: Filter Instances:listInstances by client_user_id and use instanceMetadata.lastModifiedDateTime to find the latest submission.

stem: A legacy integration calls eSignature REST API v2. The team now needs phone authentication and ID Verification using the identityVerification property with a workflowId. What must change?

options.text: Nothing; v2 supports identityVerification
Create those envelopes with REST API v2.1
Switch the integration to the Web Forms API
Use idCheckConfigurationName for both on v2

answerText: Create those envelopes with REST API v2.1
explanation: Phone authentication and ID Verification with identityVerification are eSignature REST API v2.1 only.
whyNotOthers: B is right because identityVerification requires v2.1. The trap is D: idCheckConfigurationName sets KBA or older named methods, not ID Verification. A is false, and C is unrelated to envelope authentication.

optionExplanations.A: identityVerification is v2.1 only.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. Use REST API v2.1 for identityVerification.
optionExplanations.C: The Web Forms API does not replace envelope recipient authentication.
optionExplanations.D: idCheckConfigurationName cannot request ID Verification.

concept.title: identityVerification needs v2.1
concept.line: Phone authentication and ID Verification through identityVerification and a workflowId are available only in eSignature REST API v2.1.

stem: Orbis Streaming wants new subscribers to accept updated terms of service inside its web app with a single 'I agree' button. Legal wants the acceptance captured in Docusign with a full audit trail, but there is nothing for the subscriber to type, initial or sign. The product team wants the experience to blend into the app's design. The terms are updated twice a year. How should the integration present the terms?

options.text: Create the envelope with the subscriber as an embedded recipient with no fields, and show it with classic view in an iframe so the full signing toolbar is available
Add a single checkbox field labelled I agree for the subscriber and show it with classic view
Send the terms to the subscriber as a carbon copy recipient so they can read them by email
Create the envelope with the subscriber as an embedded recipient with no fields, and show it with focused view, which falls back to a click-to-agree experience

answerText: Create the envelope with the subscriber as an embedded recipient with no fields, and show it with focused view, which falls back to a click-to-agree experience
explanation: With focused view, an envelope that has no fields for the recipient is shown as a click-to-agree experience, and focused view blends into the app.
whyNotOthers: D is right. The trap is A: same envelope, wrong view; click-to-agree fallback is listed as a focused view benefit. B adds a field and the full UI, and C records no acceptance.

optionExplanations.A: Classic view shows the full Docusign signing interface; the automatic click-to-agree fallback is a focused view feature.
optionExplanations.B: This forces a field and the full classic UI, which the product team wanted to avoid.
optionExplanations.C: A carbon copy captures no acceptance.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. Focused view with no tabs for the recipient automatically becomes a clickwrap-style agreement with an agree button.

decode.needs: Focused view + recipient with no tabs = click-to-agree
clues: single I agree button, nothing to type or sign -> no tabs
blend into the app's design -> focused view
updated twice a year -> red herring

concept.title: Focused view click-to-agree
concept.line: In focused view a recipient with no fields gets a clickwrap-style agree button automatically.

stem: Halcyon Travel updates its booking system of record from Connect events. After a three-hour cloud region outage last month, the auditors asked for a nightly safety net that finds any envelope status changes the system missed, and the check must not depend on Connect delivery. The team must not break Docusign's polling rules, and about 6,000 envelopes are open at any time, and the check should use as few API calls as possible. Which approach should the team add?

options.text: A nightly job that calls Envelopes:get for every envelope sent in the last 30 days and updates any record whose status differs
A scheduled job that calls Envelopes:listStatusChanges with time windows that overlap the previous run, and reconciles any envelope whose status differs
Turning off Connect and calling Envelopes:listStatusChanges every 15 minutes instead, because polling cannot miss an event
Relying only on Connect's automatic retries, because the 15-day retry window means every missed event is eventually delivered
A second Connect configuration that posts the same events to the same listener, so that each event is delivered twice

answerText: A scheduled job that calls Envelopes:listStatusChanges with time windows that overlap the previous run, and reconciles any envelope whose status differs
explanation: Docusign's guidance for catch-up is Envelopes:listStatusChanges with overlapping time spans; it is an independent check that does not depend on Connect and avoids per-envelope polling.
whyNotOthers: B is right because overlapping listStatusChanges windows are the recommended catch-up method alongside Connect. The trap is D: retries do recover most outage gaps, but the auditors require a check that does not depend on Connect delivery. A makes thousands of per-envelope calls, C throws away push delivery for frequent polling, and E still depends entirely on Connect.

optionExplanations.A: One Envelopes:get per envelope means thousands of calls a night; the stem asks for as few API calls as possible, and per-envelope status polling is what Docusign's guidance steers away from.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. listStatusChanges over overlapping windows catches anything missed without per-envelope polling and without depending on Connect.
optionExplanations.C: Replacing Connect with frequent polling loses real-time push and adds API load.
optionExplanations.D: Retries help, but the auditors want an independent check that does not depend on Connect.
optionExplanations.E: A second configuration still depends on Connect and only doubles the traffic.

decode.needs: Envelopes:listStatusChanges with overlapping windows as a catch-up job
clues: must not depend on Connect delivery -> retries and extra configurations do not count
must not break polling rules, as few API calls as possible -> no per-envelope GET loop
6,000 open envelopes, three-hour outage -> red herrings about scale

concept.title: Catch up with listStatusChanges
concept.line: Pair Connect with a periodic Envelopes:listStatusChanges job using overlapping time windows as an independent catch-up check.

topic: Troubleshooting: 401 after an hour with JWT
stem: Dunmore Logistics runs an unattended overnight job that uses JWT Grant to impersonate a service user and send customs declarations. The job gets one access token at 1:00 a.m. and reuses it. Every night, calls succeed until shortly after 2:00 a.m., when every eSignature request starts returning 401 Unauthorized, and the remaining declarations wait until morning. The job does not use any interactive login. The job runs on a new container platform. What should the developers change?

options.text: Store the refresh token returned with the JWT token and use it to renew the access token at 2:00 a.m.
Add the extended scope to the JWT request so the access token stays valid for the whole night
Ask the account administrator to grant consent again, because consent expires after an hour of continuous use
Track the token's expiry and request a new JWT access token shortly before the hour is up

answerText: Track the token's expiry and request a new JWT access token shortly before the hour is up
explanation: The failure starts about an hour after the token was issued, which matches the JWT access token lifetime. JWT has no refresh token, so the job requests a new token.
whyNotOthers: D is right. The trap is A: refreshing sounds natural, but JWT Grant does not return refresh tokens. B applies an Authorization Code Grant feature, and C blames consent, which does not expire hourly.

optionExplanations.A: JWT Grant never returns a refresh token; refresh tokens belong to Authorization Code Grant.
optionExplanations.B: The extended scope gives a reusable refresh token in Authorization Code Grant only; it does not lengthen JWT tokens.
optionExplanations.C: Consent does not expire hourly; the 401 comes from the expired access token.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. JWT access tokens last about an hour and JWT never returns a refresh token, so the job must mint a new token.

decode.needs: Request a new JWT access token before the 1-hour expiry
clues: one token at 1:00, failures after 2:00 -> one-hour token lifetime
unattended job, JWT Grant -> no refresh token, mint a new JWT
new container platform -> red herring

concept.title: JWT token renewal
concept.line: JWT access tokens last about one hour and come with no refresh token; request a new token before expiry.

topic: Embedded signing: recording the app's authentication
stem: Penrose Bank's online banking portal logs customers in with a password and a one-time code from the bank's mobile app, and loan agreements are then signed embedded in the portal. The compliance team wants the certificate of completion to show how the bank verified the customer and when, but they do not want customers to face any extra Docusign check, because the bank's login is already strong. The portal runs in three languages. What should the integration do?

options.text: Add an accessCode to the signer and display the code in the portal after login so the customer can type it
Add an identityVerification object with a phone workflow so Docusign confirms the customer's mobile number
In createRecipient, set authenticationMethod to describe the portal login and authenticationInstant to the login time
Put the login method and time in envelope custom fields so that they are stored alongside the envelope record

answerText: In createRecipient, set authenticationMethod to describe the portal login and authenticationInstant to the login time
explanation: In embedded signing the app authenticates the user, and createRecipient's authenticationMethod (with authenticationInstant and related fields) records that on the certificate of completion without enforcing anything.
whyNotOthers: C is right because it records rather than enforces. The trap is A: an access code is the lightest enforced method, but it is enforced, and the stem wants no extra check. B enforces a heavier check, and D stores data outside the certificate.

optionExplanations.A: An access code enforces an extra Docusign step, which compliance did not want, and does not record the bank's login method.
optionExplanations.B: This enforces an additional verification inside Docusign, which the stem rules out.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. These parameters record the app's own authentication on the certificate of completion; they do not add a check for the signer.
optionExplanations.D: Custom fields store metadata but are not the authentication record on the certificate of completion.

decode.needs: createRecipient authenticationMethod / authenticationInstant (record, not enforce)
clues: certificate of completion to show how and when -> authenticationMethod, authenticationInstant
no extra Docusign check -> record only, no accessCode or IDV
three languages -> red herring

concept.title: Record vs enforce authentication
concept.line: createRecipient's authenticationMethod records your app's login on the certificate; accessCode, phone and IDV enforce extra checks.

stem: Besides copying it from the template page in the web app, how can an integration retrieve a template's templateId?

options.text: Call Templates:get with the template's name
Call the Templates:list endpoint
Call Envelopes:listStatusChanges
Read it from the integration key settings in Apps and Keys

answerText: Call the Templates:list endpoint
explanation: The template ID can be copied in the web app or retrieved with the Templates:list endpoint.
whyNotOthers: B is right. The trap is A: Templates:get does return a template, but it takes the templateId in its path, so it cannot be used to discover the ID from a name. C and D hold no template IDs.

optionExplanations.A: Templates:get needs the templateId in the request path; it cannot look a template up by name, so it cannot be how you find the ID.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. Templates:list returns the account's templates with their IDs.
optionExplanations.C: This lists envelope status changes, not templates.
optionExplanations.D: Apps and Keys holds app settings, not template IDs.

concept.title: Getting template IDs
concept.line: Copy templateId in the web app or call Templates:list; IDs differ between demo and production accounts.

stem: Thornbury Housing will move the metadata of 25,000 signed tenancy agreements from Docusign into a new system of record over one weekend, using an unattended script. The same production account also serves a tenant-facing kiosk app and the lettings team's CRM integration all weekend. The architect wants the migration to finish without starving the other apps or getting blocked, and the CFO has asked for the work to be logged for audit. Which two practices should the script follow? (Select two)

options.text: Register the script under its own integration key, so that its calls draw on a fresh 3,000-per-hour allowance that does not affect the kiosk or the CRM
Read X-RateLimit-Remaining and X-RateLimit-Reset on responses and, once the hourly allowance is used up, make no further calls until the reset time
When a call is blocked by the hourly limit, retry it immediately in a tight loop so that the script grabs capacity as soon as it frees up
Fetch each agreement's metadata with separate per-envelope GET calls rather than list calls, since smaller requests count less against the limit
Start at a modest call rate and ramp up gradually, logging usage and alerting when the account nears its hourly limit so that the other apps keep headroom

answerText: Read X-RateLimit-Remaining and X-RateLimit-Reset on responses and, once the hourly allowance is used up, make no further calls until the reset time; Start at a modest call rate and ramp up gradually, logging usage and alerting when the account nears its hourly limit so that the other apps keep headroom
explanation: Docusign recommends reading the limit headers and pausing until the reset once the limit is reached, logging and alerting near the limit, and scaling up gradually. The clue 'same production account also serves the kiosk and CRM' shows the shared allowance.
whyNotOthers: B and E are right. The trap is A: the hourly limit belongs to the account and is shared by all its apps, so a new key adds no allowance. C produces blocked calls that hurt efficiency, and D increases the call count because every request counts the same.

optionExplanations.A: The hourly limit is per account and shared by every app, so a separate key gives no extra allowance.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. Read the headers and stop calling until the reset once the allowance is exhausted.
optionExplanations.C: Tight retries after a block create more blocked calls and lower the efficiency score.
optionExplanations.D: Every request counts as one call; per-envelope GETs multiply the total.
optionExplanations.E: Correct. Ramp up gradually, log usage and alert near the limit.

decode.needs: Run a bulk job inside the shared account limit: read headers, pause at the limit, ramp up and alert.
clues: same account serves kiosk and CRM -> hourly limit shared by all apps
without getting blocked -> read X-RateLimit headers and pause at the limit
logged for audit -> red herring (usage logging is also good practice)

concept.title: Shared limit, gradual scaling
concept.line: The hourly limit is shared by all apps on an account; read headers, pause at the limit and scale up gradually.

topic: Contact Support button in API Limit
stem: Rosa administers Brindle Retail's production account and opens the API Usage Center to raise the hourly limit before the holiday peak. In the API Limit panel she sees a Contact Support button and a limit expiration date where she expected an Update Hourly Limit button. Her plan includes API limit management, her apps score well, and they have made plenty of calls this week. The account has four sending users in two stores. What does the panel tell her?

options.text: Her plan does not include limit management after all, so the panel offers Support as the only route to a higher limit
Docusign Support has set a temporary hourly limit, and she can change the limit herself after the expiration date shown
One or more apps have efficiency issues that must be fixed before the hourly limit can be changed
Her apps have not made enough calls in the last seven days for Docusign to analyse their efficiency

answerText: Docusign Support has set a temporary hourly limit, and she can change the limit herself after the expiration date shown
explanation: A Contact Support button with a limit expiration date means Docusign Support has set a temporary limit; she can change the limit after it expires. The clue is 'expiration date'.
whyNotOthers: B is right. The trap is A: when the plan lacks limit management, the API Limit panel shows no button at all. C would show an Improve App Efficiency window after selecting Update Hourly Limit, and D would show a message about insufficient calls; the stem also rules both out.

optionExplanations.A: Without limit management in the plan, the panel shows no button rather than a Contact Support button.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. A Support-set temporary limit shows Contact Support and an expiration date; she can change it afterwards.
optionExplanations.C: Efficiency issues produce the Improve App Efficiency window, and the stem says the apps score well.
optionExplanations.D: Too little call history produces a message when updating; the stem says the apps made plenty of calls.

decode.needs: Read the API Limit panel: Contact Support plus expiration date means a Support-set temporary limit.
clues: Contact Support button with a limit expiration date -> temporary limit set by Support
plan includes limit management, apps score well, plenty of calls -> other blockers ruled out
four users in two stores -> red herring

concept.title: Support-set temporary limit
concept.line: A Support-set temporary limit blocks self-service changes until it expires; the panel then shows Contact Support.

topic: Replacing a document in an in-process envelope
stem: Ashby Construction sent a subcontract for signature this morning. Before anyone has signed, the project manager notices that the payment schedule attached as document 2 has an outdated rate. Legal wants to keep the same envelope, its recipients and its history, and simply swap in the corrected schedule. The integration already stores the envelope ID. The subcontractor is working on a remote site. Which call should the integration make?

options.text: EnvelopeRecipientTabs:update for the subcontractor with the corrected rate in the payment schedule's text tab
EnvelopeDocuments:update for the envelope with documentId 2 and the corrected file
Envelopes:update with status voided, then create a new envelope with the corrected schedule
EnvelopeDocuments:delete for document 2, leaving the subcontractor to sign without a payment schedule

answerText: EnvelopeDocuments:update for the envelope with documentId 2 and the corrected file
explanation: The in-process envelope can be modified with EnvelopeDocuments:update, specifying the documentId, to replace or add a document while keeping the envelope.
whyNotOthers: B is right. The trap is A: updating tabs is a valid in-process change, but the wrong rate is in the document content. C discards the envelope, and D removes the document entirely.

optionExplanations.A: Tabs are fields placed on documents; the rate is printed in the document itself, which must be replaced.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. EnvelopeDocuments:update adds or replaces a document in an in-process envelope.
optionExplanations.C: Voiding ends this envelope; legal wants to keep it.
optionExplanations.D: Deleting removes the schedule without providing the corrected one.

decode.needs: EnvelopeDocuments:update on the sent envelope
clues: before anyone has signed -> in-process envelope can still be modified
keep the same envelope and history -> no void
swap in the corrected schedule -> replace document 2
remote site -> red herring

concept.title: Modifying in-process documents
concept.line: EnvelopeDocuments:update adds or replaces documents in an in-process envelope; EnvelopeDocuments:delete removes them.

stem: Moreton Logistics' unattended dispatch service uses JWT Grant to send delivery agreements on behalf of whichever of five depot managers owns each shipment. It currently requests a brand-new access token before every single API call, even for the same depot manager seconds apart, and authentication traffic now dwarfs the eSignature calls. The service runs on three load-balanced nodes in the company's own data center and is monitored by a small operations team. What is the recommended pattern?

options.text: Cache an access token for each depot manager and reuse it for every call until it is close to expiry, requesting a new one only then or after a restart
Request one new token per minute for each depot manager, which keeps every token fresh while cutting authentication traffic sharply
Switch to Authorization Code Grant with refresh tokens, so each depot manager signs in once and the service refreshes the token before every call
Use a single token obtained for one depot manager for all shipments, because any token issued to the key can send on behalf of every user

answerText: Cache an access token for each depot manager and reuse it for every call until it is close to expiry, requesting a new one only then or after a restart
explanation: Docusign's guidelines say not to run an OAuth flow unless the previous token has expired or is about to, a different user's token is needed, or the app restarted; apps that switch between impersonated users should cache each user's token. The clue is 'brand-new token before every single call'.
whyNotOthers: A is right because each manager's token is reused until near expiry. The trap is B: it cuts traffic, but it still requests tokens that are not needed. C needs people to sign in to an unattended service and still refreshes per call, and D sends as the wrong user, because a JWT token acts only for the user named in sub.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. Cache one token per impersonated user and request a new one only near expiry or after a restart.
optionExplanations.B: Fixed-interval renewal still requests tokens while valid ones exist.
optionExplanations.C: No one is available to sign in, and refreshing before every call is the same waste.
optionExplanations.D: A token represents the impersonated user only; agreements would go out as the wrong depot manager.

decode.needs: Cache JWT access tokens per impersonated user; request a new one only near expiry or after a restart.
clues: new token before every call -> unnecessary OAuth flows
five depot managers -> several impersonated users, cache a token per user
three load-balanced nodes, own data center -> red herring

concept.title: Cache tokens per user
concept.line: Request a new access token only when the old one is near expiry, a different user is needed, or the app restarts.

topic: Test credentials on the review submission
stem: Ellery Analytics is submitting its first public extension app for Docusign review. The app calls Ellery's risk-scoring API, which requires a user to sign in during authorization. On the submission form, a junior developer proposes entering the company's Docusign admin login so the reviewers can get in, and the team lead offers his own Ellery production login because it has the richest data. Connection, extension and functional tests passed last week in the developer account. What should go in the Test credentials field?

options.text: Credentials for a test-only Ellery account set up for the review, so reviewers can authorize against the risk-scoring service without anyone's personal login.
The company's Docusign admin login, because the reviewers install the app into Ellery's own Docusign account and need its admin rights to test it end to end.
The team lead's Ellery production login, because reviewers must see real customer data to judge the business and functional aspects.
The connection's client ID and client secret, because reviewers authorize with Client Credentials Grant instead of signing in as a user.
Nothing, because the Test credentials field is used only for private apps whose production accounts reviewers cannot access.

answerText: Credentials for a test-only Ellery account set up for the review, so reviewers can authorize against the risk-scoring service without anyone's personal login.
explanation: The submission form's Test credentials are 'typically username and password' for your own service, from a test-only account set up for the review, never personal credentials and not Docusign credentials. The clue is that the API 'requires a user to sign in during authorization'.
whyNotOthers: A is right because reviewers need a dedicated test login for Ellery's service. The trap is B: reviewers do work in Docusign, but the field is for the external service's credentials. C exposes a personal production login, D uses a grant only allowed for private apps, and E skips information the reviewers need.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. Test credentials are for your own service, should belong to a test-only account created for this purpose, and must not be personal credentials or Docusign credentials.
optionExplanations.B: The field is for credentials to your own service, not Docusign credentials.
optionExplanations.C: Docusign says not to give your own private credentials; use a test-only account.
optionExplanations.D: The app uses a sign-in during authorization, and Client Credentials Grant is limited to private apps anyway.
optionExplanations.E: The field applies to the review of any submitted app and helps reviewers test it.

decode.needs: Provide a test-only account for your own service in the review submission's Test credentials field.
clues: 'requires a user to sign in during authorization' -> reviewers need credentials for Ellery's service
'Docusign admin login' -> wrong system
'his own production login' -> personal credentials are not allowed

concept.title: Review needs test-only credentials
concept.line: On review submission, give credentials for a test-only account on your own service, never personal or Docusign credentials.

topic: Bulk send: v2.1 model vs legacy v2
stem: Ironwood College inherited a scholarship-renewal integration written against eSignature REST API v2, which sends one agreement to each of several hundred students by attaching a bulk recipients file to the envelope. The team is moving the integration to v2.1 and wants to follow the current bulk send model. The financial aid office also wants the emails to come from a shared mailbox. Where does the list of students go in v2.1?

options.text: Into a bulk recipients CSV file attached to the envelope's signer, as before, because v2.1 still reads it
Into a bulk send list created with BulkSend:createBulkSendList, whose copies hold each student's recipient details
Into the templateRoles array of one envelope, one entry per student
Into an eventNotification object, so Connect delivers a copy to each student

answerText: Into a bulk send list created with BulkSend:createBulkSendList, whose copies hold each student's recipient details
explanation: Bulk send in v2.1 uses BulkSend resources: create a bulk send list with copies, then send it against a draft envelope or template. The v2 BulkEnvelopes model is legacy.
whyNotOthers: B is right. The trap is A: it describes the v2 approach the team is leaving. C creates one shared envelope and D misuses Connect.

optionExplanations.A: That is the legacy v2 BulkEnvelopes approach; v2.1 changed the construction model to bulk send lists.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. In v2.1 the recipients for each copy are stored in a bulk send list, then sent with createBulkSendRequest.
optionExplanations.C: That would put every student on one envelope.
optionExplanations.D: eventNotification configures webhooks, not recipients.

decode.needs: v2.1 bulk send list (BulkSend:createBulkSendList)
clues: written against v2 with a bulk recipients file -> legacy BulkEnvelopes
moving to v2.1 current model -> bulk send lists
shared mailbox -> red herring

concept.title: Bulk send in v2.1
concept.line: v2.1 bulk send stores recipients in bulk send lists; the v2 BulkEnvelopes resource is the legacy model.

stem: Calloway Legal's matter system stores engagement terms as Word (.docx) files. A developer proposes building a conversion service that turns each file into a PDF before sending it for signature with the direct documents model, which will take two sprints. The partners want the agreements sent next week, the matter system already exports each file as bytes, and the files contain anchor text for the signature lines. What should the lead developer recommend?

options.text: Build the conversion service first, because the eSignature API accepts only PDF documents
Upload each .docx file as a server template by hand and then send it with the template reference model
Send the .docx files as base64, but replace the anchor tabs with fixed x/y positions, because anchors only work in PDFs
Send the .docx files as base64 documents with fileExtension docx, since Docusign accepts DOCX, and keep the anchor tabs

answerText: Send the .docx files as base64 documents with fileExtension docx, since Docusign accepts DOCX, and keep the anchor tabs
explanation: Docusign accepts a wide variety of document types including PDF, DOCX, RTF and PNG, so the files can be sent as they are with the correct fileExtension.
whyNotOthers: D is right. The trap is A: PDF is common, but not the only accepted type. B adds manual template work, and C drops robust anchor placement for no reason.

optionExplanations.A: Docusign accepts PDF, DOCX, RTF, PNG and more; conversion is unnecessary.
optionExplanations.B: This turns each one-off document into a template and adds manual work.
optionExplanations.C: Anchor tabs locate text in the document; there is no PDF-only rule, and fixed positions are less robust.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. Docusign accepts many file types, including DOCX, so no conversion service is needed.

decode.needs: Direct documents with DOCX, fileExtension docx
clues: Word files, conversion service -> unnecessary, DOCX is accepted
send next week -> simplest working approach
anchor text for signature lines -> keep anchor tabs

concept.title: Accepted document types
concept.line: Docusign accepts PDF, DOCX, RTF, PNG and others; set fileExtension so the file is converted on upload.

stem: Which brand resource file type customizes the text of the embedded (captive) signing experience?

options.text: sending
signing
email
signing_captive

answerText: signing_captive
explanation: Brand resource files are sending, signing, email and signing_captive; signing_captive controls the captive (embedded) signing experience.
whyNotOthers: D is right because captive means embedded signing. The trap is B: signing covers the remote signing experience. A covers sending and C covers email messages.

optionExplanations.A: Controls the sending experience.
optionExplanations.B: Controls remote signing, not the captive experience.
optionExplanations.C: Controls email messages.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. signing_captive is for embedded (captive) signing.

concept.title: Brand resource files
concept.line: Brands use four resource files: sending, signing, email and signing_captive (embedded signing).

stem: A support agent at Dunmore Utilities takes a call from a customer who says her service-transfer request 'seems stuck'. Support staff have the workflow Create and Use permissions but no developer access. The team lead wants them to see, for that one customer's run, which steps are completed, which step is currently active and which are still to do, plus who completed each step and when.
