The customer is calling from abroad, and her request was started from the website link two weeks ago. What should the support agent use?

options.text: Workflows:getWorkflowInstance with the customer's instance ID, which returns each step's completion status and participant for the whole run
View Instances for the workflow in Workflow Builder, then View details on that instance, and View Details on a step for participant and time
The workflow's Activity Log, which lists the edits, publishes and pauses made to the workflow and the people who carried out each of those actions
Cancel the instance and restart it with Run Workflow, because cancelled instances show a full step-by-step history in the instance list
The eSignature envelope history of the signing step, which records every workflow step that ran before the envelope was sent

answerText: View Instances for the workflow in Workflow Builder, then View details on that instance, and View Details on a step for participant and time
explanation: Users with Create and Use permissions can open View Instances, then View details for an instance, which shows completed, active and incomplete steps; View Details on a step shows the participant name, completion date and time, and step ID.
whyNotOthers: B is right because staff have no developer access and need per-step detail. The trap is A: getWorkflowInstance is the API route for status, start and end times and started_by, but it needs code, and its documented fields are instance-level, not per-step. C covers actions taken on workflows, D destroys the run, and E sees only the envelope.

optionExplanations.A: Requires API code, and its documented fields are instance-level (status, times, started_by).
optionExplanations.B: Correct. Instance details show completed, active and incomplete steps; step details show participant and completion time.
optionExplanations.C: The Activity Log records actions taken across workflows, not one run's step progress.
optionExplanations.D: Cancelling stops all further steps; it is not a way to inspect progress.
optionExplanations.E: Envelope history covers only the signing envelope, not the other workflow steps.

decode.needs: Use the instance details view in Workflow Builder
clues: no developer access -> UI, not API
which steps are completed, active, still to do -> instance details view
who completed each step and when -> step View Details
calling from abroad -> red herring

concept.title: Instance details in Workflow Builder
concept.line: View Instances > View details shows each step's state for one instance; step details add participant, time and step ID.

stem: An eligible administrator raises the account's hourly API limit in the API Usage Center. Which statement is accurate?

options.text: The limit changes in steps of 500 and takes effect within about 10 minutes
The limit changes in steps of 1,000 and takes effect at the start of the next day
The limit changes in steps of 500, and the 30-second burst limit rises in proportion
The limit can be set to any value up to 10,000 once Support approves the request

answerText: The limit changes in steps of 500 and takes effect within about 10 minutes
explanation: Limit management lets an eligible admin drag a slider in increments of 500, up to the plan's maximum, and the change takes effect within 10 minutes without Docusign intervention.
whyNotOthers: A is right. The trap is C: the step size is correct, but the burst limit cannot be changed. B has the wrong step and timing, and D wrongly adds Support approval, which limit management avoids.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. Increments of 500, effective within about 10 minutes.
optionExplanations.B: The step is 500 and changes apply within minutes, not the next day.
optionExplanations.C: The burst limit is fixed and does not follow the hourly limit.
optionExplanations.D: No Support approval is needed within the plan's maximum; going above it requires Support.

concept.title: Hourly limit changes
concept.line: Eligible admins change the hourly limit in 500-call steps, up to the plan maximum, effective within about 10 minutes.

topic: Recipient types: certified delivery and carbon copy
stem: Fernhill Energy must send customers a rate-change disclosure. Regulators require proof that each customer actually opened the disclosure, but the customer does not sign anything. The customer's account manager should also receive the disclosure for reference without having to do anything. Nobody else is involved in the process. The disclosure is produced by the billing platform each month and sent from an unattended job. Which two recipient settings meet these needs? (Select two)

options.text: Add the customer as a certifiedDeliveries recipient
Add the customer as a carbonCopies recipient
Add the account manager as a carbonCopies recipient
Add the account manager as a signer with no tabs
Add the account manager as an agents recipient

answerText: Add the customer as a certifiedDeliveries recipient; Add the account manager as a carbonCopies recipient
explanation: Certified delivery is the 'needs to view' recipient type, so it proves the customer opened the document; carbon copy is for someone who only gets a copy.
whyNotOthers: A and C are right. The trap is B: the customer would receive the document, but a carbon copy records no required viewing. D and E give the manager an action.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. A certified delivery recipient must open the documents, which records that they viewed them, without signing.
optionExplanations.B: A carbon copy needs no action, so it gives no proof that the customer opened the disclosure.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. A carbon copy recipient receives a copy and takes no action.
optionExplanations.D: A signer must act to complete the envelope; the manager should not have to do anything.
optionExplanations.E: An agent must act by naming the next recipient; it is not a reference copy.

decode.needs: certifiedDeliveries for the customer, carbonCopies for the manager
clues: proof that each customer opened it, no signature -> certified delivery
for reference without having to do anything -> carbon copy
produced by the billing platform each month -> red herring

concept.title: Non-signing recipient types
concept.line: Certified delivery must view the documents (proof of receipt); carbon copy just receives a copy; agents and signers must act.

stem: What does a successful Envelopes:create response return?

options.text: The envelopeId and a signing URL for the first recipient in routing order
The envelopeId, the bulk batchId and the number of queued envelopes
The envelopeId and the base64 bytes of the combined document
The envelopeId, a URI for the envelope, the envelope status and a timestamp

answerText: The envelopeId, a URI for the envelope, the envelope status and a timestamp
explanation: The create response supplies the new envelopeId, a URI snippet for the envelope, its status and a timestamp.
whyNotOthers: D is right. The trap is A: embedded flows need a URL, but it is requested separately with createRecipient. B is a bulk send response and C a document download.

optionExplanations.A: A signing URL comes only from EnvelopeViews:createRecipient.
optionExplanations.B: batchId comes from createBulkSendRequest.
optionExplanations.C: Documents are downloaded with EnvelopeDocuments:get.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. The response returns envelopeId, uri, status and statusDateTime.

concept.title: Envelope create response
concept.line: Envelopes:create returns envelopeId, uri, status and statusDateTime; views and documents need separate calls.

stem: Marlow Mutual's call-center CRM, hosted in the company's private cloud, lets 600 agents trigger policy-cancellation notices. Compliance requires every notice to be sent from one approved Docusign user, Notices Desk, and the agents have no Docusign licences. The owner of the Notices Desk mailbox will sign in once during setup and never again, and some lines of business go a full quarter without a single cancellation. The CRM is written in .NET and logs every agent action to a SIEM. Which approach fits?

options.text: JWT Grant impersonating Notices Desk after its one-time consent, signing a new JWT whenever a fresh token is needed
Confidential Authorization Code Grant with extended, with Notices Desk signing in once and the CRM refreshing before each send
Confidential Authorization Code Grant, with each agent signing in using Notices Desk's credentials kept in the CRM vault
Public Authorization Code Grant with PKCE, with Notices Desk signing in once from a browser on the CRM server
JWT Grant impersonating each of the 600 agents after admin consent, so every notice shows the agent as sender

answerText: JWT Grant impersonating Notices Desk after its one-time consent, signing a new JWT whenever a fresh token is needed
explanation: A single system user acting for everyone, with no one signing in after setup, is the JWT Grant pattern; after one consent the CRM can sign a new JWT at any time, however long the gap between sends.
whyNotOthers: A is right because a quarter-long gap rules out any refresh-token chain. The trap is B: extended makes the refresh token last 30 days from the last refresh, so a 90-day gap lets it expire and forces a new sign-in. C shares one user's credentials among 600 people, D has a 24-hour refresh token and needs a browser, and E impersonates agents who have no Docusign accounts.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. One consent, then a new signed JWT whenever a one-hour token is needed.
optionExplanations.B: With extended the refresh token still expires 30 days after the last refresh, and a quarter passes with no sends.
optionExplanations.C: Sharing one user's credentials across agents is not an OAuth design and still needs interactive sign-in.
optionExplanations.D: Public refresh tokens last up to 24 hours, so this fails after a day without sends.
optionExplanations.E: The agents have no Docusign licences, so they cannot be impersonated, and compliance wants one sender.

decode.needs: JWT Grant impersonating the single approved sender
clues: 'every notice from one approved user' -> single system account: JWT
'sign in once and never again' and 'a full quarter without a cancellation' -> no refresh-token chain can survive
'agents have no Docusign licences' -> cannot impersonate agents
'.NET, SIEM' -> red herrings

concept.title: Single system user means JWT
concept.line: When all sends come from one system user and no one signs in after setup, use JWT Grant; refresh chains break after long idle gaps.

topic: Admin rights on the production account
stem: Imogen, a developer at Calloway Foods, created the developer account with her personal developer email. She starts Go-Live for the procurement app, logs in with her work email to Calloway's paid production account, where she is an ordinary sender, and cannot complete the promotion. The account administrator works in the finance department. Imogen wonders whether she must rebuild everything under a developer account that uses her work email, which would delay the launch by a week. What should she do?

options.text: Recreate the developer account and the key under her work email, because the developer and production logins must share the same email address for the promotion to work
Ask the production account's administrator to give her administrator rights there, then select the account again; her developer login may keep a different email
Ask the administrator to add API access to her sender permission set, since API access is the only permission that the promotion checks on the production account
Change the key's classification to Third-party integration key, because only that classification can be promoted by a user who is not an administrator

answerText: Ask the production account's administrator to give her administrator rights there, then select the account again; her developer login may keep a different email
explanation: The person selecting the production account must be an administrator of it, and the production account may use a different email from the developer account. The clue 'ordinary sender' is the blocker.
whyNotOthers: B is right because admin rights are the missing requirement. The trap is C: API access sounds relevant, but the rule is administrator access to the production account. A fails because different emails are explicitly allowed, and D misuses classification, which describes the business model, not permissions.

optionExplanations.A: Docusign allows the production account to use a different email from the developer account.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. Administrator access to the selected production account is required; the emails may differ.
optionExplanations.C: The requirement is administrator access, not an API-access permission.
optionExplanations.D: Classification reflects the business model and never removes the admin requirement.

decode.needs: The submitter must be an admin of the chosen production account; emails may differ from the developer account.
clues: ordinary sender in the production account -> not an administrator
personal email in the developer account, work email in production -> allowed
administrator in finance -> the person who can grant admin rights

concept.title: Admin of production account
concept.line: Only an administrator of a paid or partner production account can select it during Go-Live; emails may differ.

stem: At Bellweather Pharmacy, a two-person team is building an internal web tool, hosted on company servers, that lets regional managers send store-lease renewals. Each manager signs in to the tool personally, nothing runs on a schedule, and the tool never needs to act for a manager who is away. One developer proposes JWT Grant because it 'avoids login screens and refresh tokens', citing a sample found online. The security architect pushes back and asks the team to follow the published guidance for choosing a flow. Which response reflects Docusign's guidance?

options.text: Accept JWT, because it is the most secure flow and is recommended whenever a server can protect a private key
Accept JWT, but request the extended scope in the JWT so that its access tokens last longer than one hour
Reject JWT and use Public Authorization Code Grant, because a server-hosted tool should not hold any secret
Reject JWT and use Implicit Grant, which also avoids refresh tokens but keeps the managers' login screen
Reject JWT and use Confidential Authorization Code Grant, as JWT's power to impersonate users is not needed

answerText: Reject JWT and use Confidential Authorization Code Grant, as JWT's power to impersonate users is not needed
explanation: Docusign notes that JWT impersonation involves a high degree of granted trust and says that if an integration does not need impersonation or automated operations, it should use an Authorization Code Grant; a server-hosted tool with signed-in users fits Confidential.
whyNotOthers: E is right because users are present and nothing is automated. The trap is A: JWT's RSA key is secure, but the documentation names the Authorization Code flows as the most secure options and warns about JWT's high trust. B misuses extended, C is wrong because a server can and should keep the secret, and D picks the legacy Implicit Grant.

optionExplanations.A: Docusign calls the Auth Code flows the most secure; JWT is for service integrations that need impersonation.
optionExplanations.B: extended applies only to Authorization Code refresh tokens, not JWT.
optionExplanations.C: Public Auth Code is for apps that cannot store a secret; this server can.
optionExplanations.D: Implicit Grant is legacy and not recommended.
optionExplanations.E: Correct. No impersonation or automation is needed, so Confidential Auth Code avoids granting JWT-level trust.

decode.needs: Confidential Authorization Code Grant, because no impersonation is needed
clues: 'each manager signs in personally, nothing on a schedule' -> user-present flow
'never acts for a manager who is away' -> no impersonation
'hosted on company servers' -> can keep a secret: Confidential
'sample found online' -> red herring

concept.title: JWT is high trust
concept.line: Use JWT only when impersonation or automation is needed; for signed-in users on a server, use Confidential Auth Code.

stem: Which two statements about integration key classifications are accurate? (Select two)

options.text: A private custom integration may be used only by your own employees, never by your customers' employees
A third-party integration key is what an ISV chooses when it ships its own key inside its product
A public integration requires joining the Docusign Partner Program
With a public integration, customers use the features through your Docusign account
An embedded integration requires an ISV Embed partner licence

answerText: A public integration requires joining the Docusign Partner Program; An embedded integration requires an ISV Embed partner licence
explanation: Public integrations require the Docusign Partner Program, and embedded integrations (customers use your account) require ISV Embed partnership with a special licence.
whyNotOthers: C and E are right. The trap is A: private custom does cover your own employees, but also your customers' employees. B reverses the third-party case, where a customer supplies its own key to a partner's app, and D describes the embedded model, not the public one.

optionExplanations.A: Private custom integrations cover your employees or your customers' employees.
optionExplanations.B: A third-party key is supplied by a customer to someone else's partner integration, not shipped by the ISV.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. Launching a public integration requires the Docusign Partner Program.
optionExplanations.D: Using the features through your account is the embedded model; public customers use their own accounts.
optionExplanations.E: Correct. The embedded model requires an ISV Embed partner licence.

concept.title: Classification requirements
concept.line: Public needs the Partner Program; Embedded needs an ISV Embed licence; Private custom covers your or customers' employees.

stem: Ashgrove Partners, a law firm, uses Recipient Connect for its partners so the matter system logs when engagement letters sent by clients are completed. A client recently sent one letter with two Ashgrove partners as signers, and the matter system logged envelope-completed twice for the same envelope within a second. The listener answered both calls with 200 in about 40 milliseconds, and only one configuration exists. A clerk suspects a Docusign fault. What explains this and what should the team do?

options.text: Connect retried the message because the first response was too slow, so the team should add capacity so the listener answers faster
A second Connect configuration must be posting to the same URL, so the team should list the configurations and delete the duplicate
Recipient Connect generates a message for each subscribed recipient for each event, so the listener should deduplicate on envelope ID and event
envelope-completed is sent once per document in the envelope, so the team should subscribe to recipient-completed instead
The client's own account-level configuration also posts to the firm's listener, so the client should be asked to remove it

answerText: Recipient Connect generates a message for each subscribed recipient for each event, so the listener should deduplicate on envelope ID and event
explanation: When several subscribed recipients are on the same envelope, Recipient Connect generates one message per recipient per event, so two subscribed partners produce two envelope-completed messages.
whyNotOthers: C is right because the duplicate comes from two subscribed recipients, which the listener should handle by deduplicating. The trap is A: retries are a common cause of duplicates, but the stem says both calls got a 200 in about 40 milliseconds, so nothing failed. B contradicts "only one configuration exists", D is false because events are per envelope, not per document, and E has no basis since a client's configuration would send to the client's own URL.

optionExplanations.A: Retries happen only after a failure or timeout; a 200 in 40 milliseconds is a success.
optionExplanations.B: The stem states that only one configuration exists.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. With multiple subscribed recipients, Recipient Connect sends a message for each recipient for each event.
optionExplanations.D: envelope-completed is one event per envelope, not per document.
optionExplanations.E: A sender's configuration sends to the sender's own listener, not to the firm's.

decode.needs: Expect one message per subscribed recipient; deduplicate in the listener
clues: two Ashgrove partners as signers -> two subscribed recipients on one envelope
answered with 200 in about 40 ms -> not a retry
only one configuration exists -> not a duplicate configuration

concept.title: Recipient Connect sends per recipient
concept.line: Recipient Connect generates one message per subscribed recipient per event, so listeners should deduplicate by envelope and event.

topic: Routing order: parallel and sequential recipients
stem: Quillon Ventures closes seed investments with a single subscription agreement. The two co-founders of the startup must both sign, in either order, before the lead investor countersigns. After the investor signs, the fund's legal team needs a copy but takes no action. The fund administrator, who prepares the documents in the fund's deal-tracking system, also wants the envelope to finish as quickly as possible. Which recipient setup should the integration send?

options.text: Co-founders as signers with routingOrder 1 and 1, the investor as a signer with routingOrder 2, and legal as a carbon copy with routingOrder 3
Co-founders as signers with routingOrder 1 and 2, the investor as a signer with routingOrder 3, and legal as a carbon copy with routingOrder 4
Co-founders and the investor as signers with routingOrder 1, and legal as a carbon copy with routingOrder 2
Co-founders as signers with routingOrder 1 and 1, the investor as a signer with routingOrder 2, and legal as a certified delivery recipient with routingOrder 3

answerText: Co-founders as signers with routingOrder 1 and 1, the investor as a signer with routingOrder 2, and legal as a carbon copy with routingOrder 3
explanation: Same routingOrder means parallel; increasing routingOrder means sequential. The co-founders sign 'in either order' (same number), the investor 'countersigns' after (next number), and legal 'takes no action' (carbon copy).
whyNotOthers: A is right because it allows parallel founders, then the investor, then a copy. The trap is B: the sequence is valid, but it makes the founders sign one after the other. C lets the investor sign too early, and D gives legal a required viewing step.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. Recipients with the same routing order act in parallel; higher numbers wait until the lower step is finished.
optionExplanations.B: This works but forces the second co-founder to wait for the first, which the stem says is not needed and slows completion.
optionExplanations.C: The investor would be able to sign before the co-founders, breaking the required countersignature order.
optionExplanations.D: A certified delivery recipient must open the documents to complete the envelope, which adds an action; legal only needs a copy.

decode.needs: routingOrder 1,1 for founders, 2 for investor, carbon copy at 3
clues: both sign in either order -> same routingOrder (parallel)
before the lead investor countersigns -> higher routingOrder
needs a copy but takes no action -> carbonCopies
deal-tracking system -> red herring

concept.title: Parallel and sequential routing
concept.line: Recipients sharing a routingOrder act in parallel; a higher routingOrder waits until all lower ones finish.

stem: Which two statements about mutual TLS for Docusign Connect are correct? (Select two)

options.text: Docusign starts mutual TLS by sending a certificate request to the listener during the TLS handshake
Mutual TLS proves message integrity end to end, even after a proxy has terminated the TLS session
The listener's server requests Docusign's certificate during the TLS handshake and then validates it
Mutual TLS cannot be combined with OAuth for Connect on the same configuration
The listener's trust settings must be kept up to date when Docusign renews its certificate, roughly yearly

answerText: The listener's server requests Docusign's certificate during the TLS handshake and then validates it; The listener's trust settings must be kept up to date when Docusign renews its certificate, roughly yearly
explanation: Mutual TLS is initiated and controlled by the listener, which requests and validates Docusign's certificate in the handshake, and it must be updated when the Docusign certificate is renewed about every year.
whyNotOthers: C and E are right because the server side requests the client certificate and must track Docusign's certificate renewals. The trap is A: it describes the same certificate request, but the roles are reversed; Docusign is the client and the listener sends the request. B describes HMAC, not mutual TLS, and D is false because OAuth for Connect can be combined with mutual TLS.

optionExplanations.A: Docusign is the client in a Connect delivery; the listener's server sends the certificate request.
optionExplanations.B: Mutual TLS only protects the hop where TLS ends; end-to-end integrity is what HMAC provides.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. The server sends a Certificate Request in the handshake, and Docusign responds with its certificate for the server to validate.
optionExplanations.D: Docusign documents combining OAuth for Connect with mutual TLS.
optionExplanations.E: Correct. Mutual TLS must be updated when the Docusign certificate is renewed, about every year.

concept.title: Listener drives mutual TLS
concept.line: In Connect mutual TLS the listener requests and validates Docusign's certificate during the handshake and must track yearly certificate renewals.

topic: Request URL: what changes at go-live
stem: Mirela's integration logs this call from the developer environment: POST https://demo.docusign.net/restapi/v2.1/accounts/4b1c...9e/envelopes. Her company's production account is hosted on the na4 site, and the app will keep using eSignature REST API v2.1 after go-live. Nothing else about the request will change. The QA lead asks which parts of this URL must come from production values rather than the demo configuration. Which two parts? (Select two)

options.text: The host, which becomes the production authentication server https://account.docusign.com
The host, which becomes the production base URI such as https://na4.docusign.net
The /v2.1 segment, which becomes /v2 for production accounts
The account ID segment, which becomes the production account's ID
The /restapi segment, which becomes /api in production

answerText: The host, which becomes the production base URI such as https://na4.docusign.net; The account ID segment, which becomes the production account's ID
explanation: The URL is {baseUri}/v2.1/accounts/{accountId}/envelopes. The base URI and the account ID both differ between demo and production; the path and version stay the same.
whyNotOthers: B and D are right. The trap is A: account.docusign.com does replace account-d.docusign.com at go-live, but it is the OAuth server, not the host of eSignature REST calls; API calls go to the base URI such as https://na4.docusign.net. C and E invent path changes.

optionExplanations.A: account.docusign.com is the production OAuth (authentication) server used to get tokens and call userinfo; eSignature API calls go to the account's base URI on its site, not to the auth server.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. Production uses https://{site}.docusign.net/restapi, read from base_uri.
optionExplanations.C: The version stays v2.1 in production.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. accountId differs between developer and production accounts; read it from userinfo.
optionExplanations.E: Both environments use /restapi.

decode.needs: Base URI and accountId change between demo and production
clues: demo.docusign.net vs na4 site -> base URI changes
accounts/4b1c...9e -> account ID differs per environment
keeps using v2.1 -> version segment unchanged

concept.title: Environment-specific URL parts
concept.line: Base URI and accountId change between demo and production; /restapi/v2.1 and resource paths stay the same.

stem: A relationship manager at Kestrel Wealth sent a trust amendment to a client who had to pass knowledge-based authentication. The client failed the questions twice, and the envelope now shows a delivery failure. The client says the questions referred to addresses she never lived at. She lives in the United States, wants to finish today, and ID Verification is enabled for the account. What should the sender do?

options.text: Use Correct to switch the client to ID Verification, because KBA failures usually mean the service could not validate her identity.
Use Resend on the envelope now so she gets a new KBA question set, because a fresh attempt is always available straight after a failure.
Void the envelope and send a new one with KBA, because a recipient who fails KBA cannot be given another method on the same envelope.
Ask an administrator to look up the KBA answers in the envelope details and give them to the client by phone so that she can pass.

answerText: Use Correct to switch the client to ID Verification, because KBA failures usually mean the service could not validate her identity.
explanation: KBA failures are most often due to the service being unable to validate the signer, and the sender can use Correct to change the authentication method. The clues are 'failed twice' and 'wants to finish today'.
whyNotOthers: A is right because a different method avoids the public-records problem. The trap is B: Resend is a valid action, but accounts commonly lock signers out for 24 hours after two failures within 24 hours, and the records issue would remain. C is false because Correct can change the method, and D is not possible.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. Correct lets the sender change the method, and IDV avoids the public-records issue.
optionExplanations.B: A common configuration locks the signer out for 24 hours after two failures, and the bad records remain.
optionExplanations.C: The authentication method can be changed with Correct; voiding is unnecessary.
optionExplanations.D: Senders and administrators do not get KBA answers to share.

decode.needs: Recover the failed KBA envelope quickly with a different method.
clues: 'failed the questions twice' -> possible lockout
'addresses she never lived at' -> public-record data problem
'ID Verification is enabled' -> an alternative method exists

concept.title: KBA failure handling
concept.line: After authentication failure, Resend gives another attempt or Correct changes the method; KBA failures usually mean identity could not be validated.

topic: Verification extensions available in Web Forms
stem: Which data verification extension can be invoked from a Docusign Web Form as well as from eSignature?

options.text: Postal address verification
Email address verification
Business FEIN verification
SSN verification
Bank account verification

answerText: Email address verification
explanation: Per the supported extensions table, email address verification and phone verification are the data verification extensions whose extension points include Web Forms; the others are eSignature only.
whyNotOthers: B is right. The trap is A: address checks seem natural on a web form, but postal address verification is listed only for eSignature. C, D and E are also eSignature only.

optionExplanations.A: Postal address verification is listed only for the eSignature Add Fields view and signing.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. Email and phone verification support both the eSignature Add Fields view and signing and Web Forms.
optionExplanations.C: FEIN verification is eSignature only.
optionExplanations.D: SSN verification is eSignature only.
optionExplanations.E: Bank account verification is eSignature only.

concept.title: Web Forms verify email and phone
concept.line: Only email and phone verification extensions run in Web Forms; other data verification extensions are eSignature only.

stem: Instances:getInstance returns an overall status of INPROGRESS. What does this mean?

options.text: The user opened the form but has not typed anything
The user submitted it and the envelope is being signed
The user selected Finish Later and the values were saved
The instance passed its expiration without a submission

answerText: The user selected Finish Later and the values were saved
explanation: For the overall instance status, INPROGRESS means the user selected Finish Later after partly filling the form, and the values were saved.
whyNotOthers: C is right. The trap is A: that describes instanceRecipientStatus INPROGRESS (opened, not submitted), not the overall status. B would be SUBMITTED and D would be EXPIRED.

optionExplanations.A: That matches instanceRecipientStatus, not the overall status.
optionExplanations.B: A submitted instance has status SUBMITTED.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. Overall INPROGRESS means Finish Later was used.
optionExplanations.D: An expired instance has status EXPIRED.

concept.title: Web form instance statuses
concept.line: Overall status: INITIATED, INPROGRESS (Finish Later), SUBMITTED, EXPIRED, FAILED; instanceRecipientStatus tracks each user's view.

stem: A Recipient Connect configuration is being set up for the claims staff. Which of these events can it subscribe to?

options.text: envelope-sent
envelope-voided
envelope-corrected
recipient-delivered
envelope-created

answerText: recipient-delivered
explanation: Recipient Connect supports envelope-completed and the recipient events authenticationfailed, completed, declined, delivered, deliveryfailed and sent; recipient-delivered is on that list.
whyNotOthers: D is right because recipient-delivered is one of the supported Recipient Connect events. The trap is A: envelope-sent is a common account-level event, but the recipient side uses recipient-sent instead. B, C and E are sender-side envelope events that Recipient Connect does not offer.

optionExplanations.A: envelope-sent is not on the Recipient Connect list; the receiving side uses recipient-sent.
optionExplanations.B: envelope-voided is not among the events Recipient Connect can subscribe to.
optionExplanations.C: envelope-corrected is a sender-side envelope event that Recipient Connect does not offer.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. recipient-delivered is one of the supported Recipient Connect events.
optionExplanations.E: envelope-created describes a draft in the sender's account, which Recipient Connect does not report.

concept.title: Recipient Connect event list
concept.line: Recipient Connect supports envelope-completed plus recipient events such as sent, delivered, completed, declined, authenticationfailed and deliveryfailed.

stem: What is the maximum length of an extension app's name, which must also be unique?

options.text: 50 characters
64 characters
100 characters
30 characters
255 characters

answerText: 30 characters
explanation: The registration form and best practices state the app name must be unique and is limited to 30 characters; it appears in the App Center listing, Maestro step selection and the Add Fields view.
whyNotOthers: D is right. The trap is A, a common limit in other systems; B, C and E are also above the 30-character limit.

optionExplanations.A: Too long; the documented limit is 30.
optionExplanations.B: Too long; the documented limit is 30.
optionExplanations.C: Too long; the documented limit is 30.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. The app name must be unique and is limited to 30 characters.
optionExplanations.E: Too long; the documented limit is 30.

concept.title: App name: unique, 30 characters
concept.line: An extension app name must be unique and at most 30 characters; it shows in App Center, Maestro steps and Add Fields.

stem: Cobalt Credit Union's three-person IT team runs its Connect listener on a single on-premises server that is patched every Sunday night for about two hours. The compliance officer requires that every signing event be accepted at the moment Docusign sends it, including during patching, and will not accept a design that depends on Docusign retrying later. Members sign loan documents at all hours, and the configuration includes documents. What should the team do?

options.text: Put a small serverless function in front that writes each message to a cloud queue and returns 200, and let the on-premises app drain the queue after patching
Rely on Connect's retry schedule to redeliver messages missed during the patch window, since retries continue for up to 15 days
Pause the Connect configuration every Sunday during patching, so that no events are generated while the server is offline
Switch to calling Envelopes:listStatusChanges after each patch window to collect the status changes missed while the server was down
Switch the configuration to aggregate mode, so that fewer messages are generated while the listener is unavailable

answerText: Put a small serverless function in front that writes each message to a cloud queue and returns 200, and let the on-premises app drain the queue after patching
explanation: Docusign advises 99% or better listener availability and, where that is hard, a cloud queuing system that receives and buffers messages; this accepts every event "at the moment Docusign sends it" even while the server is patched.
whyNotOthers: A is right because a cloud queue accepts every message on time while the back end is offline. The trap is B: retries would eventually deliver the events, but the officer will not accept a design that depends on retries. C relies on skipped retries too (pausing does not stop events, it skips deliveries), D replaces push with polling, and E only changes message grouping.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. A cloud listener and queue buffer messages so the on-premises app can process them when it is back, without missed deliveries.
optionExplanations.B: Retries do resend failed messages, but the stem explicitly rejects relying on them.
optionExplanations.C: Pausing skips deliveries and retries during the pause, so events are still not accepted when sent.
optionExplanations.D: Polling after the fact is a catch-up method, not a way to accept events at the time they are sent.
optionExplanations.E: Aggregate mode only combines similar events; it does nothing for availability.

decode.needs: Cloud listener plus queue in front of the on-premises system
clues: accepted at the moment Docusign sends it, including during patching -> needs an always-on receiver
will not accept a design that depends on retrying -> retries and pause are ruled out
configuration includes documents, three-person team -> red herrings

concept.title: Buffer Connect with a cloud queue
concept.line: When a listener cannot stay highly available, a cloud function and queue accept messages on time and let the back end process them later.

topic: Individual consent in Auth Code Grant
stem: Pemberton Schools is launching a contracts portal, hosted on its own servers, for 40 head teachers, using Confidential Authorization Code Grant with the signature scope. The project manager has scheduled a separate sprint to build a consent page that each head teacher must visit before first using the portal, and asks the developer to confirm the plan. The schools' Docusign organization does not have Access Management, and the portal was styled with Bootstrap. What should the developer tell the project manager?

options.text: No separate page is needed: the first sign-in through /oauth/auth shows each teacher the consent screen for the scopes requested
The sprint is needed, because individual consent must be collected through a URL with the impersonation scope before Auth Code works
The sprint can be dropped, because an organization administrator can grant consent for all teachers in Docusign Admin
The sprint is needed, because each teacher's consent must be requested by email through the Docusign account administrator
The sprint can be dropped, because Confidential Authorization Code Grant never needs user consent when a secret key is used

answerText: No separate page is needed: the first sign-in through /oauth/auth shows each teacher the consent screen for the scopes requested
explanation: In Authorization Code Grant, the user signs in at /oauth/auth and is shown a consent screen for the requested scopes if they have not consented before; allowing access is the individual consent.
whyNotOthers: A is right because consent is built into the Auth Code sign-in. The trap is B: a separate consent URL with impersonation is the JWT Grant pattern. C is wrong because admin consent needs Access Management, which the schools lack; D invents an email process; and E is wrong because consent is still needed, it is simply collected during sign-in.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. Docusign shows the consent screen during sign-in if the user has not yet consented to the app and its scopes.
optionExplanations.B: Separate consent with impersonation is for JWT Grant, not Authorization Code Grant.
optionExplanations.C: Admin consent requires Access Management, which this organization does not have.
optionExplanations.D: There is no email-based consent process through the account administrator.
optionExplanations.E: Consent is still required; it is collected as part of the sign-in.

decode.needs: Individual consent happens during the Authorization Code sign-in
clues: 'Confidential Authorization Code Grant' -> users sign in at /oauth/auth and see the consent screen there
'no Access Management' -> admin consent is not available
'Bootstrap' -> red herring

concept.title: Consent inside Auth Code sign-in
concept.line: Auth Code Grant collects individual consent at sign-in; a separate consent URL with impersonation is needed only for JWT.
